records.title: Continuous positive airway pressure for early pulmonary atelectasis in infants with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: B. Fabrizzi1, A. Peruzzi1, L. Luciani1, M. Bordicchia1, N. Caporelli1
records.affiliations_text: 1CF Centre- AOU delle Marche, Ancona, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Background: Pulmonary atelectasis may represent an early radiological manifestation of lung disease in infants with cystic fibrosis (CF). In early life, therapeutic options are limited, and supportive respiratory strategies may play a role in preventing progression of lung abnormalities.

Methods: Since 2024 in our CF Centre, infants underwent to low-dose chest CT at 3-6 months of age. Infants with CT evidence of pulmonary atelectasis were admitted to our hospital for bronchoalveolar lavage followed by empirical intravenous antibiotic therapy adjusted by microbiological data. Prophylactic continuous positive airway pressure therapy (CPAP) was initiated in hospital setting in infants with body weight ≥5 kg. CPAP was delivered via nasal mask at 4–6 cmH₂O and continued at home. Clinical and adherence follow-up was conducted at least every 3 months.

Results: Between 2023 and 2024, six infants with CF were diagnosed at our CF Centre and underwent early chest CT; all showed pulmonary atelectatis lesions at 3 months of age. CPAP therapy was initiated in four infants with severe atelectasis. Two infants did not require ventilatory support due to mild severity of atelectasis. Long-term CPAP was well tolerated, with no discontinuations. During follow-up, treated infants showed reduction of existing atelectasis and no development of new pulmonary lesions. None received CFTR modulator therapy during the study period.

Conclusions: In the absence of approved CFTR modulator therapy for CF infants, early CF management still requires a multidisciplinary approach, including supportive respiratory interventions. Our preliminary experience suggests that nocturnal CPAP is feasible, well tolerated, and may be effective in reducing and preventing pulmonary atelectasis in infants with CF.

records.title: Evolving physiotherapy challenges through a lung cancer journey in a woman with cystic fibrosis

person.title: Ms.
person.institution: University Hospitals of Leicester NHS Trust

records.authors_text: N. Mills1
records.affiliations_text: 1University Hospitals of Leicester, Adult Cystic Fibrosis Service, Leicester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
66 year old woman with Cystic Fibrosis (CF) diagnosed 2002 aged 44 via cascade screening. She had a 40 pack year smoking history, stopped March 2023. History of emphysema, osteopenia, depression, anxiety, agoraphobia, breathing pattern disorder (BPD) and chronic pain. Started Elexacaftor/Tezacaftor/Ivacaftor October 2021; FEV1 improved from 1.43L (67%) to 1.59L (74%), FVC 2.24 L (83%) to 2.53 (97%).

October 2024 she presented with haemoptysis, shortness of breath, increased cough and sputum. Chest x-ray showed slight left lower lobe collapse, resolved with intravenous antibiotics, physiotherapy and tranexamic acid, but then recurred 6 weeks later. High resolution CT scan showed left lower lobe collapse suspicion of pulmonary mass. Subsequent PET CT scan and endobronchial ultrasound biopsy diagnosed lung cancer T3N1M0.

She commenced 3 chemotherapy cycles 3 weeks apart, in preparation for lung resection. Physiotherapy pre-operatively comprised optimisation of airway clearance with autogenic drainage (AD), and nebulised Dornase alpha and 3% saline. Her airway clearance and inhaled medications needed regular modification due to the significant and fluctuating side effects of chemotherapy, particularly nausea and vomiting. We continued to work on breathing pattern correction and anxiety management, as this was significantly contributing to her breathlessness, and breathing control during exertion. We visited regularly at home to support with pre-operative rehabilitation; using a new treadmill she gradually increased her exercise tolerance and breathing control, within the limits of chemotherapy side effects, until she was managing 20-30 minutes walking twice daily. A 6 minute walk test was completed for anaesthetic assessment. Her fitness for surgery was questioned; the go ahead from anaesthetics was positively influenced by the progress made with the intensive physiotherapy and prehabilitation.

April 2025 she underwent left lower lobectomy and lymphadenectomy via open, extended thoracotomy. Post-operative physiotherapy consisted of AD through the PEP, twice daily nebulised Dornase Alpha and 3% saline, regular supported mobility and anxiety management. Pain was a significant limiting factor and she developed left lung volume loss 3 days post-operatively. Her CRP increased to 450, and other infective markers raised. A debate about whether the cause was post-surgical complications and pleural collection, or her CF occurred between the CF and surgical teams. A CT scan showed it to be predominantly CF airway related. Her intravenous antibiotics were changed, airway clearance frequency and exercise intensity increased, working closely with the pain team. She gradually improved and was discharged after 4 weeks. All physiotherapy interventions were delivered collaboratively with the thoracic surgery physiotherapy team.

The CF physiotherapy team continued to support her at home following discharge, ensuring optimal airway clearance and increasing exercise tolerance. This led to supported walks in her local park, with anxiety management and she then started to walk her dog in the park independently for the 1st time in over 10 years. Her breathing pattern is the best it has been in 20 years.

Could we have been more proactive with suspecting a cancer diagnosis at 1st presentation? Could we have prevented post-operative complications with more intensive physiotherapy early? Collaborative working with the surgical physiotherapy team was very effective.

person.title: Ms.
person.institution: University Hospitals of Leicester NHS Trust
person.biography: Nicky Mills is an advanced practitioner physiotherapist working in the Leicester Adult Cystic Fibrosis (CF) service, University Hospitals of Leicester, UK. She has led the adult CF physiotherapy service in Leicester for 23 years and has a particular interest in airway clearance, inhalation therapy and breathing pattern management in CF and bronchiectasis. She is also an independent prescriber. She has embedded the assessment and management of breathing pattern disorders in to routine CF care and presented conference abstracts reporting the incidence and presentation of breathing pattern disorders in CF, and is currently completing a service evaluation looking at clinical outcomes following management of breathing pattern disorders in patients attending the Leicester service. Nicky is the current chair of the Association of Chartered Physiotherapists in Cystic Fibrosis (ACPCF).

records.title: ExACT comparison in cystic fibrosis: endurance training VS HIIT Circuit. Single case
records.authors_text: A. Scorretti1, A. Peruzzi1, L. Luciani1, M. Bordicchia1, N. Caporelli1, V. Zamponi1, B. Fabrizzi1
records.affiliations_text: 1AOU delle Marche, CF Centre, Ancona, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Background: Exercise as an Airway Clearance Technique (ExACT) is an exercise-based airway clearance program that includes at least 20 minutes of aerobic exercise at an intensity sufficient to induce deep breathing, combined with breath-control techniques, huffing, and coughing.

Objective: To compare two aerobic exercise modalities used as substitutes for traditional airway clearance techniques (ACT), assessing their ability to maintain clinical stability and to determine whether one provides superior clinical benefit.

Methods: A 23-year-old man with CF, undergoing elexacaftor–tezacaftor–ivacaftor (ETI) treatment for 3 years, stable clinical condition for at least 3 months prior to starting the study, poor expectoration, and with FEV1 ≥ 80% of predicted value, was enrolled.

During the study, the second daily traditional ACT session was replaced for 4 months with two alternating ExACT modalities: a running session (endurance training) during the 1st and 3rd months, and a high-intensity interval training circuit (HIIT) during the 2nd and 4th months. Both modalities were performed once daily on at least 5 days per week, for a total of 20 sessions per month, with exercise intensity reaching at least 70% of the theoretical maximum heart rate and a Borg scale rating ≥ 7/10 for 30 minutes.

ExACT is structured according to the FITT principle (Frequency, Intensity, Time, and Type) to ensure a standardized yet individualized exercise prescription.

FEV1, 6-minute walking distance (6MWD), Borg, overnight oximetric monitoring, Numeric Rating Scale on perceived sleep quality (NRS), Bioelectrical Impedance Analysis (BIA), hand-grip strength test, Visual Analogic Scale (VAS), Cystic Fibrosis Questionnaire-revised (CFQ-R) and training adherence (through the use of a monitoring platform) were administered at T0, T1 (after 4 weeks), T2 (after 8 weeks), T3 (after 12 weeks) and T4 (after 16 weeks).

Results: The practice of ExACT, in both modalities, improved and ensured clinical stability, as evidenced by a 10% improvement in FEV₁ maintained throughout the entire study period, a progressive increase in 6MWD (T0: 720 m; T4: 811 m), improved mean nocturnal oxygen saturation and perceived sleep quality, as well as favorable changes in body composition and muscle mass, with improvements in physical energy and emotional well-being as assessed by the CFQ-R.

Conclusion: The case report shows that both ExACT modalities are effective in maintaining clinical stability and are well appreciated by the patient, who in this case demonstrated high adherence to the prescribed program (70 out of 80 days), monitored via a telemonitoring system.

records.title: Functional and respiratory improvement through physiotherapy: optimizing exercise response, airway clearance, and quality of life

person.title: MM
person.institution: Hospital Infantil de México Federico Gómez

records.authors_text: A. Mena-Córdova1, M. Reyes-Apodaca2, J. Belmont-Sánchez1, J.L. Lezana-Fernández3
records.affiliations_text: 1Hospital Infantil de México Federico Gómez, Rehabilitation Department, Mexico City, Mexico, 2Hospital Infantil de México Federico Gómez, Research and Diagnosis Unit in Nephrology and Bone Mineral Metabolism, Mexico City, Mexico, 3Hospital Infantil de México Federico Gómez, Cystic Fibrosis Clinic, Mexico City, Mexico
records.abstract_text:
Background: People with Cystic Fibrosis (PwCF) struggle with exercise intolerance and dyspnea, which can gradually limit participation in daily activities. Beyond the physiological burden, repeated episodes of breathlessness may also generate fear or avoidance of physiotherapy, particularly airway clearance techniques. In this context, supervised and individualized physiotherapy may play a role not only in improving physical performance but also in rebuilding confidence and treatment adherence.

Case Description: We report the case of a 9-year-old boy with CF who presented with exercise-related dyspnea, increased oxygen requirements during physical activity, and marked discomfort during airway clearance. These difficulties appeared to interfere with school attendance, recreational play, and independent mobility. At the time of intervention, no acute radiological changes were identified, and the patient was clinically stable.

Physiotherapy Problems Identified: The main issues identified were an inefficient breathing pattern, early onset of dyspnea during exertion, slow recovery after exercise, and reliance on higher supplemental oxygen flow. In addition, fear associated with coughing and airway clearance seemed to affect technique execution and overall adherence to physiotherapy.

Physiotherapy Intervention: A supervised physiotherapy program was implemented over a three-month period. Sessions combined breathing retraining with airway clearance techniques, including diaphragmatic breathing, autogenic drainage, total slow expiration with open glottis in lateral decubitus (ETGOL), cough training, and the use of an Aerobika® device. These were followed by aerobic and strength training.

Aerobic exercise consisted of 20 minutes of treadmill walking at approximately 65% of the speed achieved during the six-minute walk test (6MWT). Strength exercises focused on pectoral muscles, anterior and middle deltoids, and the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles, using a yellow TheraBand®, with 10 repetitions per exercise. Airway clearance and strengthening exercises were also prescribed for home practice. For cardiopulmonary safety, all supervised sessions were performed with supplemental oxygen at 4 L/min.

Outcome Measures and Discussion: Changes were assessed using the 6MWT, oxygen requirements during exercise, post-exercise recovery to baseline cardiopulmonary parameters, and perceived exertion and dyspnea measured by the Borg scale. While the distance walked did not change substantially, oxygen requirements during exercise decreased by 3 L/min, and recovery after exertion was noticeably faster. The Borg score also declined, suggesting less perceived fatigue and dyspnea. (Table 1)

These changes appeared to extend beyond exercise performance, translating into better tolerance of school activities, play, and daily mobility. Interestingly, the patient also reported less fear when performing airway clearance, which may reflect improved symptom control and greater confidence developed through supervision. From a broader perspective, this case highlights how physiotherapy-related benefits may not be fully captured by distance-based outcomes alone, particularly when gains in recovery, perceived exertion, emotional comfort, and overall participation in everyday life point toward a meaningful improvement in quality of life.

Background: People with Cystic Fibrosis (PwCF) struggle with exercise intolerance and dyspnea, which can gradually limit participation in daily activities. Beyond the physiological burden, repeated episodes of breathlessness may also generate fear or avoidance of physiotherapy, particularly airway clearance techniques. In this context, supervised and individualized physiotherapy may play a role not only in improving physical performance but also in rebuilding confidence and treatment adherence.
Case Description: We report the case of a 9-year-old boy with CF who presented with exercise-related dyspnea, increased oxygen requirements during physical activity, and marked discomfort during airway clearance. These difficulties appeared to interfere with school attendance, recreational play, and independent mobility. At the time of intervention, no acute radiological changes were identified, and the patient was clinically stable.
Physiotherapy Problems Identified: The main issues identified were an inefficient breathing pattern, early onset of dyspnea during exertion, slow recovery after exercise, and reliance on higher supplemental oxygen flow. In addition, fear associated with coughing and airway clearance seemed to affect technique execution and overall adherence to physiotherapy.
Physiotherapy Intervention: A supervised physiotherapy program was implemented over a three-month period. Sessions combined breathing retraining with airway clearance techniques, including diaphragmatic breathing, autogenic drainage, total slow expiration with open glottis in lateral decubitus (ETGOL), cough training, and the use of an Aerobika® device. These were followed by aerobic and strength training.
Aerobic exercise consisted of 20 minutes of treadmill walking at approximately 65% of the speed achieved during the six-minute walk test (6MWT). Strength exercises focused on pectoral muscles, anterior and middle deltoids, and the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles, using a yellow TheraBand®, with 10 repetitions per exercise. Airway clearance and strengthening exercises were also prescribed for home practice. For cardiopulmonary safety, all supervised sessions were performed with supplemental oxygen at 4 L/min.

records.title: Physiotherapy as a key driver of adherence in an adolescent with cystic fibrosis: a case presentation
records.authors_text: A.A. Lukács1, É. Gács1, A. Párniczky1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Heim Pál National Pediatric Institute, Budapest, Hungary, 2University of Pécs, Institute for Translational Medicine, Medical School, Pécs, Hungary
records.abstract_text:
Adolescence is a well-known risk period for reduced adherence to cystic fibrosis (CF) therapies. Despite CFTR modulator therapy, effective airway clearance and inhaled antibiotics remain essential to prevent pulmonary exacerbations and preserve lung function. Physiotherapists support adolescents and their families in maintaining adherence during this complex period.

We present a 14-year-old female with CF (ΔF508 heterozygous), diagnosed at the age of 2 years, with intermittent disease severity (Leeds criteria). Triple combination CFTR modulator therapy was initiated in January 2024. She lives with foster parents and a foster sibling, with limited socioeconomic and educational resources, living in a home with suboptimal hygiene and exposure to caregiver smoking. Despite regular outpatient physiotherapy visits and repeated education, adherence to airway clearance and inhalation therapy remained poor, with inconsistent family involvement. The patient denied sputum production and questioned the necessity of physiotherapy, while members of the CF team consistently observed productive cough and mucus retention. She was admitted in May 2025 for a two-week inpatient treatment period combining intravenous antibiotics, physiotherapy and education.

Key challenges included poor adherence to inhalation and airway clearance therapy, ineffective mucus clearance and limited engagement in treatment.

An individualised physiotherapy program was implemented, focusing on age-appropriate airway clearance, stepwise goal setting, device selection, and supervised daily sessions (40-90 minutes). Therapy emphasised proper inhalation technique, airway clearance (ACBT, PEP/RMT mask, OPEP device), and equipment hygiene. Patient-centred engagement strategies and positive reinforcement were applied. The patient was encouraged to participate in treatment decisions, fostering self-management and awareness of her therapeutic options. Psychological support addressed adherence barriers, and multidisciplinary collaboration supported the continuity of daily care.

By discharge, successful sputum expectoration was achieved for the first time, allowing sample collection. Lung function clinically improved (FVC from 83% to 97%, FEV1 from 67% to 80%, FEF25-75 from 36% to 50% predicted). Although adherence remained fragile, engagement with therapy improved. Subsequent outpatient follow-up confirmed that sputum samples could be obtained with ongoing physiotherapy support.

How can physiotherapists support adherence when motivation remains fragile in adolescence? How to define meaningful progress when full adherence is not achievable? How to provide autonomy with sufficient supervision in adolescent CF care?

records.title: Physiotherapy management of prolonged admission required for Mycobacterium abscessus eradication
records.authors_text: A. Leeney1
records.affiliations_text: 1St. Vincents University Hospital, Physiotherapy, Dublin, Ireland
records.abstract_text:
We present two cases of prolonged admission in patients with Cystic Fibrosis colonised with Mycobacterium Abscessus.

Patient A presented with multiple episodes of haemoptysis, one large volume requiring embolisation. He previously failed NTM eradication, required multiple courses of intravenous (IV) antibiotics, more recently commencing IV bacteriophage therapy. Admission lasted 18 months.

Patient B presented unwell with a background history of NTM, on a maintenance oral regime. NTM pneumonias were discovered on CT, requiring eradication therapy. Admission lasted 17 weeks.

Physiotherapy management involved increased treatment time, airway clearance modification to maximise secretion clearance, minimising airway trauma to limit further haemoptysis, airway humidification, ongoing oxygen assessment, rehabilitation of strength and aerobic training, and new habit formation.

Our main role in these patients’ care was functional preservation, achieved by maintaining adequate airway clearance. Given the risk of serious haemoptysis, this was a delicate balance between achieving sufficient flow/shearing forces within the airways to mobilise secretions, and exceeding these forces, risking haemoptysis. Positive pressure was useful in providing airway stability and cough control. Mucolytics in Patient A were contra-indicated given his predisposition to haemoptysis but this was not problematic with Patient B. Airway humidification in both patients became a cornerstone of secretion management.

Both patients had increased metabolic demand. A close working relationship with dietetics allowed the patients to meet their caloric requirements and allow cardiovascular and strength training. Nausea and fatigue were limiting factors to participation in all aspects of physiotherapy. Exercise prescription included walking/cycling 3 to 4 times a week, and strength work 2 to 3 times, focusing on closed chain work.

records.title: A one-year follow-up of a patient with cystic fibrosis receiving home non-invasive ventilation in Kazakhstan
records.authors_text: A. Serikova1, I. Mukatova1, S. Kim1, E. Amelina1
records.affiliations_text: 1Astana Medical University, Department of Internal Medicine №3, Astana, Kazakhstan
records.abstract_text:
Background: Progressive decline in pulmonary function in CF is accompanied by the development of chronic respiratory failure. Long-term non-invasive ventilation (NIV) helps correct hypercapnia, improve oxygenation, and can be used as a component of comprehensive respiratory support.

Objective: To present the first one-year follow-up of a CF patient and hypercapnic respiratory failure receiving long-term home NIV.

Materials and Methods: A 19-year-old male CF patient was observed. He received low-flow oxygen therapy for 6 months without clinical benefit. Due to the progression of respiratory failure, long-term home NIV was initiated. Assessments were performed at baseline and after 6 and 12 months and included gas exchange analysis, weight changes, and quality of life using the EQ-5D-3L.

Results: Baseline arterial blood parameters: PaCO₂ - 58.6 mmHg, PaO₂ - 59.1 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ - 30.2 mmol/l. NIVL was well tolerated. After 6 months, a decrease in dyspnea (mMRC from 4 to 3), a decrease in hypercapnia (PaCO₂ - 49.7 mmHg), an improvement in oxygenation (PaO₂ - 68.7 mmHg) and a weight gain of 2 kg were noted. After 12 months, gas exchange parameters remained stable: PaCO₂ - 48.3 mmHg, PaO₂ - 68.2 mmHg; the total weight gain was 5 kg.

According to the EQ-5D-3L data, an improvement in mobility, daily activity and a decrease in anxiety and depressive manifestations were recorded after one year; Subjective health assessment increased from 40 to 60 points.

Conclusions: Long-term home NIV in a CF patient and hypercapnic respiratory failure resulted in sustained correction of gas exchange disorders, improved nutritional status, and enhanced quality of life over a one-year follow-up period. This case is the first reported experience of long-term management of a CF patient on NIV in Kazakhstan.

person.biography:
Prof Davies works between the National Heart & Lung Institute, Imperial College London and the Royal Brompton Hospital, London, UK. Jane trained in paediatric respiratory medicine, with additional posts in infectious diseases and immunology, before settling on cystic fibrosis as a speciality. The Brompton clinic is one of the largest in Europe, caring for almost 900 people from infancy to late stage disease.
Her main areas of research interest are chronic lung infection and clinical trial design. She leads a UK CF Trust funded Strategic Research Centre for Pseudomonas, a multidisciplinary group seeking to improve detection, understanding and therapy of this prevalent organism. She advises many of the pharma companies developing CF drugs on trial design, co-leads the site’s trials team and established a pan-London network of CF trial sites under the umbrella of the UK’s Clinical Trials Accelerator Platform. The team has participated in many CF drug trials ranging from gene therapy, CFTR modulators to mucolytics and antimicrobials. She directs the ECFS Core Facility for Lung Clearance Index, which is supporting standardised procedures across sites, providing trials in younger, healthier children with a sensitive outcome measure, and is also closely involved in the ECFS Strategic Planning Task Force to speed up access to new therapies.
She is current President of the ECFS.

person.biography: <u>Carlos M Farinha</u> is currently Associate Professor with Habilitation at Faculty of Sciences, University of Lisboa and PI at the BioISI research centre. His research focuses on the molecular mechanisms of cystic fibrosis (CF), in particular the endoplasmic reticulum retention and early degradation of CFTR’s most common mutant as well as its rescue strategies, through modified folding or circumvention of quality control mechanism. He is particularly interested in the identification of novel CFTR interactors regulating CFTR trafficking, that may constitute novel therapeutic targets to tackle CF and also in characterizing the effect of rare CF-causing mutations. He has supervised 8 successfully completed PhD students. He is author of over 75 refereed international papers and one book on “CFTR and Cystic Fibrosis”. He received the 2012 ERS Romain Pauwels Research Award from the European Respiratory Society for “research into the different aspects of CFTR biology”. Since 2022, he is an elected member of the ECFS Board.

I help patients with optimal management of their CF drugs, support their adherence to therapy, deal with side effects and interactions and optimise their dose in close collaboration with the pulmonologists and pediatricians. Many patients face difficulties with taking their CF drugs correctly and on time and therefore in my PhD I am investigating new ways to support CF patients with adherence, ultimately maximizing patient benefits from treatment at minimum side effects.

content.biography:
Professor Milan Macek Jr. MD, DSc is the chairman of the largest academic medical / molecular genetics institution in the Czech Republic – Department of Biology and Medical Genetics of Charles University Prague-2nd School of Medicine and Motol University Hospital, and of the National Coordination Centre for Rare Diseases (www.nkcvo.cz; NKCVO) responsible for implementation of the ten year national strategy on rare diseases and resulting three national action plans. In addition, he is chairing the national Rare Disease Taskforce at the Ministry of Health. In this capacity his institute has been serving as a "clearing centre" for the dissemination of knowledge gathered within various international projects on rare disease-related research and diagnostics (e.g. EuroGentest.org, RD-Connect.eu, Solve-RD.eu, Norway Grants) to partners in Eastern Europe, Transcaucasia and the Middle East. In this capacity Prof. Macek is also the Czech National coordinator of Orpha.net. In his capacity as chairman of NKCVO he assured that since 2017 Czechia is ranking first within EU13 in terms of participation in European Reference Networks (ERN) for rare diseases.
 
Prof. Macek is also the past President of the European Society of Human Genetics (www.eshg,org; 2010-2011 ESHG), currently serves at the ESHG liaison for European National Human Genetics Societies (https://www.eshg.org/76.0.html). Under his leadership medical genetics was recognized as an official EU specialty in the Professional Qualifications Directive in 2011. He also closely collaborated with the Council of Europe on the ratification of the Additional protocol on genetic testing for health purposes to the Oviedo convention (2019). He had also been the past-board member of the European Cystic Fibrosis Society (ECFS.eu; 2007-2014) and is the current member of the European Cystic Fibrosis Registry board (https://www.ecfs.eu/ecfspr), whereby he published seminal papers on the disparities in  cystic fibrosis care between the “New” and “old” EU Member States. Moreover, he had also been the board member of the European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology (www.eshre.eu; ESHRE) where he was responsible for three joint position statements of ESHG and ESHRE in the field of reproductive genetics as their senior author. Prof. Macek served at the European Commission Expert Group on Rare Diseases (formerly www.eucerd.eu) and is currently involved in the European Board of Member States for European Reference Networks for Rare Diseases (https://ec.europa.eu/health/ern_en), including the newly formed EU Advisory Board on ERN sustainability. He had also been member of the Diagnostic Committee of the International Rare Disease Consortium (www.irdirc.org). Prof. Macek is currently the president of the Czech Society of Medical Genetics and Genomics (www.slg.cz). Finally, he was the chief government advisor of the CZ EU Council presidency under which the EU Council recommendation on a field of action in rare diseases was been adopted in 2009.
 
Prof. Macek did his postdoctoral studies at the Department of Medical and Human Genetics at Humboldt University Berlin (1989-1992) followed by McKusick-Nathans Centre for Genetic Medicine, Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore (1992-1996). In 1992 he was also a fellow at Harvard School of Medicine in the field of non-invasive prenatal diagnosis of rare diseases.
 
His main research and clinical interests are in the field of molecular genomics of rare diseases, including their deep phenotyping, and in ways on how to bring genomics knowledge to the bedside via targeted therapies with orphan medicinal products. He has also been involved in health economics “cost of illness” studies in this regard. His citation index is over 11,000x with H –index of 33.

person.biography: Dr. Valerie Waters is a Senior Associate Scientist and Professor in the Division of Infectious Diseases, Department of Pediatrics. She is the infectious diseases consultant for the Cystic Fibrosis Clinic at SickKids and St Michael’s Hospital, as well as a CF researcher. Dr Waters' research program is focused on the investigation of the epidemiology and treatment of multi-drug resistant bacterial pathogens causing lung infections in patients with cystic fibrosis (CF). She is particularly interested in the way these organisms grow as communities of bacteria known as biofilms, which are associated with increased antimicrobial resistance. The Waters Lab has developed novel biofilms models to test the efficacy of compounds against Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilms, in the context of host factors and other microbes. They are currently studying the interaction between Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa grown within biofilms in the context of failure of early eradication treatment of P. aeruginosa in children with CF and in pulmonary exacerbations. In addition, the team has also recently conducted a clinical trial of oral prednisone as an adjuvant therapy in CF patients with pulmonary exacerbations.

person.biography:
Dr. Verkleij, clinical psychologist and Cognitive Behavioral Therapist (CBT) supervisor is a senior researcher at Amsterdam University Medical Center, the Netherlands. She co-chaired the ECFS Mental Health Working Group from 2019 to 2022, served on the recent ECFS Standards of Care Committee, is a Board Member of the Expert Panel Quality of Care for CF in the Netherlands and a member of the US Mental Health Advisory Committee—Research Subcommittee, focusing on implementation of mental health screening and interventions and the psychological effects of CFTR modulators for CF. In 2018, she co-founded the European Respiratory Society (ERS) Scientific Working Group 09.04, "Psychologists and behavioural scientists”.
She has won several awards, including the Dutch CF Innovation Award for her pilot study of an adherence intervention for adolescents with CF. As an international collaboration, Drs. Verkleij, Friedman and Georgiopoulos (USA) have developed a blended care program that integrates therapist-guided online self-management modules with in-person/synchronous telehealth sessions, “eHealth CF-CBT” in English and Dutch (Vertex Circle of Care award, 2018, Corno Grant 2019 & 2023). EHealth CF-CBT is the first therapist-guided internet-delivered CBT-based intervention for adults with CF to prevent and treat anxiety and depression, and has been implemented into regular CF care in the Netherlands. EHealth CF-CBT will be adaptable for use in countries with a wide range of resource availability and health care systems and will be disseminated in Europe. This unique international collaboration is therefore at the cutting edge of innovations to address depression and anxiety in people with CF worldwide.

​Dr. Nicola J. Rowbotham is a Paediatric Respiratory Medicine Consultant at Leeds Children’s Hospital and research associate at the University of Nottingham. 
Prior to studying medicine, she completed a BSc in Microbiology and PhD in Immunology at Imperial College London. Her primary clinical research focus has been in Cystic Fibrosis. She has led systematic reviews on Infection Prevention and Control in CF, Evidence Gaps in CF treatments, plus contributed to several Cochrane reviews. She is currently involved in the CF Foundation and CF Trust Infection Prevention and Control International Guideline. A particularly rewarding aspect of her research work has been her involvement with the James Lind Alliance Priority Setting Partnership in CF and its refresh. In this role, she collaborated closely with patients, families, and healthcare providers to help identify and explore the top ten global research priorities for CF in 2018 and then again in 2023 to see if priorities changed in the post-modulator era. She is deeply committed to keeping the patient voice at the heart of her work, striving to ensure that future research continues to address the everyday realities and needs of the CF community.

Sarah Carroll is Principal Specialist Clinical Psychologist in Children’s Health Ireland (CHI) where she has worked on the Cystic Fibrosis team for 14 years. Currently, she is a Mental Health Expert on the ENHANCE study, a 5 year international study recording the natural history of children taking novel CF modulator therapies, and on RECOVER, a multi-centre, real world non-interventional study examining the impact of the new triple combination CFTR modulator compound, Kaftrio®. Sarah is also currently Co-Investigator and Key Knowledge User on Pathways, a HRB funded study focused on improving transition to adult services and enhancing self-management in adolescents with CF.
Sarah recently received a CHI Research and Innovation Award to develop a network of professionals and resources to support a unified approach to supporting children with needle procedures across CHI, and a HSE Spark award to develop a parent support programme, Parenting a Child with a Chronic Illness, the first psychosocial support programme to be extended across all CHI sites, and medical teams.
Sarah is a committee member of the European Cystic Fibrosis Society Mental Health Working Group. She is also a founding member, and Chair since 2020, of the Psychological Society of Ireland’s Special Interest Group in Paediatric Psychology (SIGPeP), which aims to join researchers and clinicians with an interest in Paediatric Psychology.
As well as working clinically, Sarah also lectures on the Doctorate in Clinical Psychology in University College Dublin.

Professor Nicholas Simmonds is Associate Director and Consultant Physician of the Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre at the Royal Brompton Hospital, and Professor of Practice (Respiratory Medicine) at the National Heart and Lung Institute, Imperial College London. He graduated in medicine from the University of Nottingham, United Kingdom in 1999, and subsequently gained a doctorate from Imperial College. His research interests include CF survival variability, particularly variable CFTR gene/protein function, and the investigation of novel CF therapies – he is a Principal Investigator on numerous global multicentre trials and is Deputy Director of the European Cystic Fibrosis Society (ECFS) Clinical Trials Network and is Chair of the Protocol Review Committee. He is a specialist in the diagnosis of CF in equivocal or unusual cases. He has extensive experience of novel diagnostic techniques and was Vice Coordinator of the European CF Society Diagnostic Network Working Group, 2019-2025. Prof Julian Forton (MA MB BChir MRCPCH PhD) is Consultant and Clinical Lead for Paediatric Respiratory Medicine at The Children's Hospital for Wales in Cardiff, UK. He trained at the Universities of Cambridge and then Oxford and worked at Duke University Medical Center, North Carolina through the Duke-Oxford Exchange residency program. He is co-author of the Oxford Handbook of Paediatric Respiratory Medicine.
Prof Forton runs the CF-SpIT research group, a group of research-active clinicians ad scientists who are interested in how best to describe airway infection in children with CF. He is chief investigator and senior author of the CF Sputum Induction Trial (CF-SpIT) which showed that sputum induction in young children with CF is superior to oropharyngeal sampling and comparable to Gold-standard 2-lobe bronchoalveolar lavage for pathogen detection (Ronchetti et al. 2018. Lancet Respiratory Medicine). His team have used matched samples from multiple respiratory niches to analyse early compartmentalised infection in young children, to interrogate how pathogen-dominance is established with time, and work to identify a clinical role for respiratory microbiota analysis in cystic fibrosis. The more recent CF-HomeSpIT trials in both children and adults aim to identify a clincial role for home sampling in patients with CF.

person.title: Dr.
person.biography: I am interested in the correction of nonsense mutations by Nonsense-Mediated mRNA decay inhibition and/or readthrough activation. For that, we screen small molecule libraries and characterize hits before evaluating their therapeutic potential on various genetic disease models (cell lines, patient cells, organoids dzrived from patient cell, mouse models). We identified and characterized several molecules including 2,6-diaminopurine (DAP) as an efficient UGA readthrough compound. DAP has been shown to rescue the expression and the function of CFTR in patient cells, organoids and mouse carrying a UGA nonsense mutation. I then founded Genvade Therapeutics to develop molecules with nonsense mutation correction activity in 2021.

person.biography: Dr. Daniel Stevens is a professor at Dalhousie University in Halifax, Canada. He holds a faculty position in the School of Health and Human Performance in the Division of Kinesiology, and is cross appointed with the Department of Paediatrics in the Faculty of Medicine. Daniel also has a local affiliation with the IWK Health Centre (Women and Children's Hospital) as a research scientist. Daniel is also an associate editor for the Journal of Cardiopulmonary Rehabilitation and Prevention. Daniel has been working in the research field of exercise and cystic fibrosis for 20 years in both the UK and Canada. These include the Royal Devon and Exeter Hospital while a PhD student at the Children's Health and Exercise Research Centre (University of Exeter); St. Michael's Hospital in Toronto (affiliated with the University of Toronto); and the IWK Health Centre. Daniel's work looks at the role of exercise and physical activity in people living with cystic fibrosis and its value in standard healthcare practice. His work also investigates the use of exercise testing for prognosis and assessment of exercise induced symptoms. Daniel's most recent work looks at breathing patterns during exercise in individuals living with cystic fibrosis, and methods used to assess and treat dysfunctional breathing in this patient group.

records.title: Initiation of CFTR modulator therapy in the first 2 years of life: real-world outcomes with elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor
records.authors_text: A. Le1, N.H. Truong2, M. Baravalle3, S.N. Benaboud2, H. Corvol4, L. Couderc5, F. Foissac2, A. Gabsi6, G. Labe7, C. Ohlmann8, T. Perrin8, E. Peulier-Maitre4, M. Ribault9, N. Stremler3, C. Tillard10, M. Mittaine11, I. Sermet-Gaudelus1, MODUL-CF Study Group
records.affiliations_text: 1Necker Enfants Malades Hospital, Paris, France, 2Cochin Hospital, Paris, France, 3Timone Hospital, Marseille, France, 4Trousseau Hospital, Paris, France, 5Rouen Hospital, Rouen, France, 6Versailles Hospital, Le Chesnay-Rocquencourt, France, 7Clermont Ferrand Hospital, Clermont Ferrand, France, 8Hospices Civils de Lyon, Lyon, France, 9Fougères Hospital, Fougères, France, 10Hôpital Alexandra Lepève, Dunkerque, France, 11Toulouse Hospital, Toulouse, France
records.abstract_text:
Background: Advances in newborn screening and supportive care have significantly improved early cystic fibrosis (CF) outcomes. Early use of highly effective CFTR modulators is an emerging strategy, but data on elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) in children under 2 years remain scarce. We report early outcomes of ETI in infants included in the MODUL-CF study (NCT04301856).

Methods: The initiation of ETI was decided after a multidisciplinary discussion in patients with severe cystic fibrosis. Follow-up included clinical assessment, sweat testing, microbiology, laboratory tests, CFTR modulator plasma levels, and chest CT. Age- and weight-based ETI dosing were extrapolated from ivacaftor monotherapy recommendations.

Results: Eleven infants carrying at least one F508del allele were treated for severe respiratory disease, including lung atelectasis (n=9) and/or bronchiectasis (n=4) on CT, despite maximal therapy. ETI was initiated at a mean age of 7.2 months (range 3–14). Rapid improvement in respiratory symptoms was observed and resolution of CT abnormalities in the 2 children who underwent chest CT at 3 months ETI at 01/01/2026. Mean sweat chloride decreased from 114 mmol/L (85-114) to 31.7 mmol/L at 1 month (21-47). Fecal elastase improved from 48.8 (0-251) to 314 µg/g (0-591). Treatment was generally well tolerated. Two infants experienced mild, transient sleep disturbances, and one had a transient elevation of liver enzymes not attributed to ETI. Plasma ETI levels were within adult reference ranges.

Conclusion: ETI in children under 2 years with severe respiratory disease is associated with clinical improvement and good tolerance consistent with that observed in older age group. These findings support further investigation of early ETI initiation to modify CF lung disease progression.

records.title: Organoid testing to implement theratyping for CFTR modulator therapy
records.authors_text: A. Müller1, E. Romanowska2,3, S. Reusch1, G. Kliem1, C. Klotz1, C. Schwarz2,3,4
records.affiliations_text: 1Robert Koch Institute, Department of Infectious Diseases, Unit for Mycotic and Parasitic Agents and Mycobacteria, Berlin, Germany, 2HMU University Potsdam, Internal Medicine, Potsdam, Germany, 3Klinikum Westbrandenburg, Potsdam, Germany, 4Clinic Ernst von Bergmann, CF Center, Potsdam, Germany
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The successful history of CFTR modulator therapy in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) began in 2012 with the corrector ivacaftor. Thirteen years later, two highly effective CFTR modulator therapies are already available in Europe for the treatment of non-class I mutations. The extent to which the CFTR modulator therapy response using patient-derived intestinal organoids (PDIOs) correlates with the clinical response is of great importance, as theratyping could provide a basis for deciding between one CFTR modulator or another.

Methods: Human intestinal organoids were established from biopsy specimens by standard methods. Human colonic and duodenal biopsy specimens were obtained from CF-patients and one healthy individual at Charité Virchow Clinic, Berlin and at CF Center Potsdam (with ethics approval: #2022-40-BO). For the forskolin-induced swelling (FIS)-assay multiple rounds were performed, in which 6-8 organoid cultures from different 66 donors were tested in parallel. For comparison, 1 healthy control and 1 homozygous F508del/F508del control culture were included in each round. The image analysis for quantification of the organoid surface area increase over time was performed using the ImageJ-software with Bio-Formats plugin. Human intestinal organoids were treated with CFTR modulator therapy (elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor and vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor). In this prospective study, organoid responses were compared with clinical biomarker response.

Results: In total, 32 pwCF were enrolled into the study. The triple CFTR modulator therapy with elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor was inferior compared to vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor in the PDIOs swelling assay.

Conclusions: The new, once daily triple CFTR modulator therapy with vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor shows a higher response in the forskolin-induced swelling-assay in intestinal organoids compared to elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor.

records.title: Real-world experience of switching from elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor to vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor in a UK adult cystic fibrosis centre
records.authors_text: W.T. Cheong1, C. Bradshaw1, J. Cunningham1, A. Higton1, C. Orchard1, A. Ewence1, A. Lillis1
records.affiliations_text: 1Frimley Health NHS Foundation Trust, Frimley, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To evaluate decision-making, clinical outcomes and tolerability of switching from elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) to vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor (VTD) in a UK adult cystic fibrosis centre.

Methods: Eligible patients were offered to switch to VTD following discussion of benefits and risks. Demographics, decisions, clinical parameters (weight, FEV₁, FVC, liver function) and side effects were recorded. Baseline and three-month data were compared using paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.

Results: Of 159 patients on ETI, 78 chose to switch, 69 declined and 12 were undecided. No significant difference in age (p=0.27) or baseline FEV₁ %predicted (p=0.69) existed between those who chose to switch and those who declined. Reasons for switching were patient preference (52%), non-adherence to twice daily ETI (31%) and ETI side effects (17%), while patients declined mainly due to stability with good adherence (65%), monitoring burden (14%) and family planning (10%). At three months, no significant changes were observed in weight (p=0.15), FEV₁ (p=0.51), FVC (p=0.79), bilirubin, ALP, ALT, GGT and AST (p>0.05) among those on VTD. Of 38 respondents, 27 reported no side effects. Itching (n=3) and headache (n=2) resolved spontaneously. Six patients developed new or worsening diarrhoea: three resolved spontaneously within three months, with one aided by increased Pancreatic Enzyme Replacement Therapy (PERT) dosage and probiotics; one reverted to ETI due to tripled PERT requirement; two remain ongoing. Two patients had transient creatine kinase elevation (2,114 U/L and 813 U/L) which normalised within two weeks without intervention.

Conclusions: VTD switching showed comparable three-month clinical outcomes with good tolerability. Patient preference and adherence concerns drove switching decisions, whilst stability on ETI therapy was the primary reason for declining. Gastrointestinal side effects, particularly diarrhoea, warrant close monitoring.

Demographics, decisions, clinical parameters (weight, FEV₁, FVC, liver function) and side effects were recorded. Baseline and three-month data were compared using paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.
Results: Of 159 patients on ETI, 78 chose to switch, 69 declined and 12 were undecided. No significant difference in age (p=0.27) or baseline FEV₁ %predicted (p=0.69) existed between those who chose to switch and those who declined. Reasons for switching were patient preference (52%), non-adherence to twice daily ETI (31%) and ETI side effects (17%), while patients declined mainly due to stability with good adherence (65%), monitoring burden (14%) and family planning (10%). At three months, no significant changes were observed in weight (p=0.15), FEV₁ (p=0.51), FVC (p=0.79), bilirubin, ALP, ALT, GGT and AST (p>0.05) among those on VTD. Of 38 respondents, 27 reported no side effects. Itching (n=3) and headache (n=2) resolved spontaneously. Six patients developed new or worsening diarrhoea: three resolved spontaneously within three months, with one aided by increased Pancreatic Enzyme Replacement Therapy (PERT) dosage and probiotics; one reverted to ETI due to tripled PERT requirement; two remain ongoing. Two patients had transient creatine kinase elevation (2,114 U/L and 813 U/L) which normalised within two weeks without intervention.
Conclusions: VTD switching showed comparable three-month clinical outcomes with good tolerability. Patient preference and adherence concerns drove switching decisions, whilst stability on ETI therapy was the primary reason for declining. Gastrointestinal side effects, particularly diarrhoea, warrant close monitoring.

records.abstract_text:
Objective: Elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor (ETI) has transformed outcomes for people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF), but adverse events (AEs) may require dose modifications. Limited evidence exists to guide dose reduction strategies in paediatric patients.

To evaluate the clinical outcomes and AE resolution following ETI dose reduction in children and adolescents with CF.

Methods: This multicentre, retrospective observational study included pwCF aged 6-18 years from seven Italian CF centres who underwent ETI dose reduction due to drug-related AEs between August 1, 2021 and December 31, 2024. Clinical parameters including lung function, sweat chloride, body mass index z-score (BMI), and laboratory data were assessed at baseline (T0), AE onset (T1), and 3 (T2), 6 (T3) and 12 (T4) months post-dose reduction.

Results: Among 593 paediatric pwCF on ETI therapy, 50 (8.5%) showed AE related to ETI and 31 (5%) required dose reduction (median age 11.7 years, IQR 9.1-15.8). The most common AEs were elevated liver transaminases (19/31, 61%), gastrointestinal symptoms (4/31, 13%), and neuropsychiatric symptoms (4/31, 13%). Median time from ETI initiation to AE onset was 131 days (IQR 41-364). Dose reduction strategies varied significantly among centres. AE resolution occurred in 22/31 subjects (70%), with highest success rates for hepatic (13/19, 68%) and gastrointestinal events (4/4, 100%). Clinical efficacy parameters remained stable following dose reduction, with no significant deterioration in lung function, BMI.

Conclusion: In this exploratory multicentre study, individualized dose reduction strategies resolved AEs in 70% of cases without short-term clinical deterioration, though the heterogeneity of approaches limits definitive recommendations. Prospective trials with standardized protocols are urgently needed.

records.abstract_text:
Background: CFTR-modulator therapy improved the clinical outcome of people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) remarkably. So far, little is known on pancreatic function recovery especially in children. Individual case descriptions indicate a recovery of the pancreatic function in young children with early initiation of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) therapy. We therefore aimed to systematically evaluate the pancreatic function in preschool children with ETI treatment.

Methods: In a multicenter manner four large CF centers in Germany collected stool samples from newly ETI eligible children aged 2-5 years prior and after 3 and 12 months of ETI therapy. Fecal-elastase (< 200µ/g defines pancreatic insuffenciency) was determined prospectively in each center.

Results: 68 children were included. Median age was 3.5 years at ETI start (range 2.0-6.1). 59 were pancreatic insufficient prior ETI therapy. Thereof 3 (4,4%) became pancreatic sufficient after a median of six months (range 3-9) on ETI. On average, the level of fecal elastase increased 50µg/g(p=0.002).

Conclusions: In preschool children fecal elastase should be monitored after ETI start as the pancreas resumes functioning in some children. Further and longer studies are needed to assess this effect, especially if pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy is reduced.

records.title: Impact of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor dose reduction in a paediatric population on sweat chloride
records.authors_text: T. Moore1, J. Parr1, L. Walker2, T. Lee1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Leeds, Leeds, United Kingdom, 2Leeds Children's Hospital, Children's Respiratory and Cystic Fibrosis, Leeds, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a multisystem genetic disease leading to defective chloride transport. Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ELX/TEZ/IVA)) has demonstrated significant clinical benefit but adherence may be limited by side effects. Dose reduction is a potential strategy to improve tolerability while maintaining efficacy; however, there is limited data for paediatric populations. This study aims to investigate when children have significant side effects on full dose ELX/TEZ/IVA, whether a reduced dose is still associated with a clinically relevant improvement in sweat chloride whilst lowering the burden of side effects in children.

Methods: A retrospective cohort study using data obtained from the Leeds Children’s Hospital Paediatric Cystic Fibrosis Centre. Data on sweat chloride concentrations were used as a biomarker for drug efficacy. The study analysed 119 children (aged 2–17 years) with at least one F508del mutation treated with ELX/TEZ/IVA.

Results: Of 119 patients, 100 had complete results at either full dose or half dose ELX/TEZ/IVA. 88 were on full dose and 12 on half dose with a mean age of 10.65 years. Mean sweat chloride decrease from diagnosis in those on full dose was 62.33 ± 21.94 mmol/L, and mean sweat chloride decrease on half dose was 55.42 ± 14.83 mmol/L. Both decreases were significant (p<0.001). Mean sweat chloride at a half dose was 36.67 mmol/L. The difference in mean sweat chloride between full dose and half dose (6.91 mmol/L) was not statistically significant (p>0.05). Patients on half dose with only one copy of F508del variant had a larger mean decrease than those with two copies (62 and 53 mmol/L respectively) but this was a small sample size and not statistically significant (p=0.3758).

Conclusion: In this population, a half dose of ELX/TEZ/IVA still showed a significant reduction of sweat chloride from baseline. Dose reduction may be effective in improving tolerability in children with side effects whilst maintaining a clinically relevant improvement in sweat chloride from pre-treatment baseline.

records.title: Real-life experience with elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor in children with cystic fibrosis: dose reduction for adverse events
records.authors_text: M. Van de Walle1, J. Houben1, F. Vermeulen1, M. Boon1, C. Ruelens1, M. Proesmans1
records.affiliations_text: 1Univeristy Hospital Leuven Belgium, Pediatrics, Leuven, Belgium
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a multisystem, genetic disease caused by mutations in the CFTR gene. The CFTR modulator combination elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) has significantly improved clinical outcomes in people with CF, including pediatric patients. However, real-world data on adverse events and dose management, particularly in younger children, remain limited. The aim of this study is to evaluate the frequency of adverse events in children with CF treated with ETI, to assess dose adjustments in response to these events, to explore the effect of dose reduction on CFTR function and lung function and to document the recurrence of adverse events after dose modification.

Methods: This observational real-world study included 80 children with CF aged 2–18 years (median age 10 years, IQR 6–12.5) treated with ETI at UZ Leuven. Clinical data were collected during routine outpatient visits. Outcomes included adverse events, dose reductions, sweat chloride concentration (SCC), forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) and frequency of pulmonary exacerbations.

Results: Adverse events were reported in 28% of patients, with neuropsychiatric symptoms, such as irritability, mood changes, behavioral alterations and sleep disturbances, being the most frequent. Dose reduction was implemented in affected patients and proved effective in alleviating symptoms. Importantly, dose reduction had only a limited impact on CFTR function as assessed by SCC, while clinical benefits were preserved. The recurrence of adverse events after dose modification is still being investigated.

Conclusion: Individualized dose reduction appears to be an effective strategy to manage adverse effects without substantially compromising therapeutic efficacy. These findings support careful monitoring and personalized dosing strategies in younger children receiving ETI.

Objectives: CFTR modulator therapy with elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) is a cornerstone of cystic fibrosis (CF) treatment. Whether the manufacturer’s three fixed dosage levels adequately account for changes in body weight and composition in growing children remains unclear. In addition, drug–drug interactions and dose reductions due to adverse effects highlight the need for therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM).

records.abstract_text:
The aim to evaluate the efficacy of the generic drug ivacaftor+tezacaftor+elexacaftor, ivacaftor TN Trilexa® in a group of patients who have not received this type of therapy previously.

Objectives and Methods: An analysis was performed in 2 groups of patients: Group 1 - 28 pediatric patients (12 boys/16 girls) who started receiving therapy with the drug TN Trilexa, Group 2 - the comparison group - included 34 pediatric patients (14 boys/20 girls) who received the drug TN Trikafta. The groups were comparable in age, gender, age at the start of targeted therapy, and the main indicators of the disease course. Observation continued for 3 months.

Results: An increase in BMI was noted in both groups of patients: in group 1 Me (Q1-Q3) BMI kg/m2 at the start was 17.0 (15.5; 19.8), after 3 months 17.8 (16.2; 20.3) p<0.001, in group 2 Me (Q1-Q3) BMI kg/m2 at the start was 16.7 (15.2; 18.6), after 3 months 17.9 (16.6; 19.8) p<0.001. The sweat test values (conductivity, mmol/l) differed both at the start of therapy and after a month in each group: group 1 at the start Me (Q1;Q3) 108.0 (96;115), after 1 month - 43.5.0 (35;49) p=0.028. Group 2 at the start 123.0 (102;133), after 1 month - 75.0 (62;93), p=0.036. The comparing of the sweat test Me (Q1; Q3) (mmol/l) between the groups revealed significant difference at the start of therapy, p=0.011, and after 30 days of therapy, p=0.009. The difference between the average change of the sweat test in both groups was comparable - group 1 - 43 (35.5; 55), group 2 - 42 (32; 50.3) mmol/l, p=0.86. FEV1 and FVC showed a tendency to improve with two drugs. The groups did not differ in the number of adverse events (AE), which were not severe and did not lead to drug discontinuation.

Conclusion: The generic drug TN Trilexa® is effective and safe for use in patients with CF. The spectrum of reported AE with Trilexa® is comparable to that with the original drug Trikafta. The study was carried out as part of the research RCMG (122032300396-1).

records.affiliations_text: 1Faculty of Medicine in Pilsen, Charles University and University Hospital Pilsen, Department of Paediatrics, Pilsen, Czech Republic, 2Second Faculty of Medicine, Charles University - Motol and Homolka University Hospital, Department of Pneumology, Prague, Czech Republic, 3Second Faculty of Medicine, Charles University - Motol and Homolka University Hospital, Department of Biology and Medical Genetics, Prague, Czech Republic, 4Second Faculty of Medicine, Charles University - Motol and Homolka University Hospital, Department of Paediatrics, Prague, Czech Republic, 5Second Faculty of Medicine, Charles University - Motol and Homolka University Hospital, Department of Medical Microbiology, Prague, Czech Republic
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Clinical response to ETI among eligible people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) is heterogeneous. A lower-than-expected response compared with clinical trial outcomes may reflect primary non-responsiveness or secondary, potentially modifiable factors. The aim of this registry-based project is to identify low responders in real time and develop an algorithm for their subsequent management.

Methods: Annual SwCl and FEV1 data were analyzed for all Czech pwCF who had been treated with ETI for ≥ 6 months. They were identified as primary low responders if their first SwCl measurement (usually within 4-6 months of ETI initiation) showed values ≥60 mmol/L with <20% reduction from baseline, together with <5% absolute ppFEV₁ improvement. Secondary low responders were defined as those who met these SwCl criteria in any subsequent (not the first) year and showed a ≥10% persistent decline in ppFEV₁ from the best on-treatment value over the preceding 6 months. A stepwise evaluation was performed on all low responders, including CFTR genotype reanalysis, assessment of adherence and drug–drug interactions, and screening for complications or comorbidities. Follow-up comprised clinical reassessment and repeat SwCl measurement. Persistent cases were referred for inpatient monitored ETI therapy, multidisciplinary review, and ex vivo CFTR function testing.

Results: Of 535 pwCF receiving ETI, 21 met entry criteria of the SwCl-based algorithm. Data collection is ongoing to further clarify causes of low response. Preliminary validation indicates that confirmed low responders are rare, with five pwCF classified as primary low responders.

Conclusions: This registry-based national strategy supports individualized management of rare low responders to ETI and identifies missing or incomplete data. Regular annual registry-based reviews are essential for timely identification of secondary low responders. SwCl and ppFEV₁ should be interpreted within a long-term and broader clinical context.

records.title: Real-life experience with a generic formulation of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor in patients with cystic fibrosis with responding variants
records.authors_text: A. Teper1, V. Rodriguez1, S. Lubovich1, S. Zaragoza1, E. Rodriguez1, F. García Bournissen2
records.affiliations_text: 1Hospital de Niños R Gutierrez, Respiratory Center, Buenos Aires, Argentina, 2Schulich School of Medicine and Dentistry Western University, Department of Paediatrics, London, Canada
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: CFTR modulators (mCFTR) have led to vast improvements in clinical outcomes for patients with CF (pwCF) with responding variants; however, high cost prohibits access for many. Generic formulations of ETI (ETIgf) are more affordable and can help improve access.

Objective: We assessed the real-world outcomes of treatment with ETIgf in pwCF with responding variants, with and without prior treatment with an mCFTR.

Patients and methods: Our single center, prospective study included pwCF >6 years, indicated for treatment with ETIgf (Trixacar, Gador Argentina) for 12 months or more. We assessed pulmonary function (percent predicted forced expiratory volume in 1 second [ppFEV1]; Lung Clearance Index [LCI]), BMI z-score, quality of life (Cystic Fibrosis Questionnaire Revised [CFQ-R], respiratory domain), sweat chloride, fecal elastase, and respiratory exacerbations prior to initiation and after 6–12 months of treatment.

Results: A total of 71 pwCF were included in this study. 43 pwCF (60%; 24 females, median age 10.6 years) were treatment-naïve and included in group 1; and 28 pwCF (40%; 7 females, median age 10.9 years) had received previous treatment with an mCFTR and were included in group 2. Treatment with ETIgf demonstrated significant improvements in pulmonary function (ppFEV1: +21 and 19%; LCI (−13 and 11%), and quality of life (CTF-R respiratory domain: +66 and 30%), and decreases in sweat chloride measurements (−53 and 58%) and severe respiratory exacerbations (−95%), for groups 1 and 2, respectively. Median (IQR) BMI z-score at baseline and after 12 months treatment was −0.2 (-0.9 to 0.3) and 0.3 (-0.3 to 1.1) (p<0.001), and -0.1 (-0.8 to 0.6) and -0.1 (-0.8 to 0.8) (p=0.3) for groups 1 and 2, respectively

Conclusions: In pwCF and responding variants in the real-world, treatment with ETIgf demonstrates significant clinical efficacy and is well tolerated.

records.authors_text: L. Ibarra1, G. Manonolles2, V. Rodriguez3, E. Rodriguez3, S. Lubovich3, S. Zaragoza3, A. Teper3
records.affiliations_text: 1Hospital de Niños Ricardo Gutierrez, Microbiology, Buenos Aires, Argentina, 2Hospital de Niños Ricardo Gutierrez, Infectius Disease, Buenos Aires, Argentina, 3Hospital de Niños Ricardo Gutierrez, Respiratory Center, Buenos Aires, Argentina
records.abstract_text:
Objective: To evaluate the long-term effect of a generic triple modulator therapy formulation (ETIg) on airway infection in paediatric patients with Cystic Fibrosis (pwCF).

Patients and Methods: Prospective cohort study included pwCF aged 6 to 18 years with responsive variants, who initiated ETIg (Trixacar, Gador Argentina) treatment between Nov. 2021 and Nov. 2023. Bacterial isolates identified in quarterly cultures of spontaneous sputum (ss) or cough swab (cs), according to patient capability, were analysed. Bacteriological results obtained over a period of two years of follow-up were compared with those from the year prior to ETIg initiation. Variables were analysed using Fisher’s exact test.

Results: Sixty-nine pwCF were included in this study (39 male). Median (IQR) age was 10.9 (8.6-14.1) years.

Previous yr (A): 69 patients, 272 cultures, 209 ss (77%)/ 63 cs (23%)

1st yr (B): 69 patients, 274 cultures, 142 ss (52%)/ 132 cs (48%) (p<0.001)

2nd yr (C): 68 patients, 241 cultures, 119 ss (49%)/ 122 cs (51%) (p<0.001)

Positive cultures in A, B and C, respectively, were:

P. aeruginosa (Pa): 73/272 (27%), 40/274 (15%) and 33/241 (14%) (p<0.001)

MSSA: 166/272 (61%), 132/274 (48%) and 125/241 (52%), (p<0.03)

MRSA: 66/272 (24%), 48/274 (17%) and 42/241 (17%) (p=0.036)

records.abstract_text:
Background&Objectives: Limited evidence exists to guide Elexacaftor-Tezacaftor-Ivacaftor (ETI) use in adults with cystic fibrosis (awCF) and preserved lung function (ppFEV1 >90%). To address the resulting variability in prescribing practices, we conducted a European survey among a group of adult CF centres aiming at identifying factors influencing ETI initiation decisions in adults with preserved lung function.

Methods: Between April and June 2024, we invited 25 ECFS prescribers from 25 adult CF centres to participate in a web-based survey to explore factors influencing ETI initiation in adults with CF and ppFEV₁ >90%. The survey questionnaire collected data on centre characteristics, prescribing ETI attitudes, and the impact of specific clinical variables on ETI prescription decision in this subgroup.

Results: Twenty-three CF specialists (92%) responded. Most specialists (69.6%) favoured early treatment initiation in all eligible patients. Key factors influencing ETI initiation decisions were the presence of respiratory symptoms. In adults with preserved lung function, however, microbiological and imaging features emerged as the most influential factors driving treatment decision. While patient willingness and symptoms strongly encouraged ETI use, factors like age over 50, a history of mental health issues, and pregnancy desire resulted in conflicting prescribing attitudes among centers.

Conclusions: Although several disease markers more consistently support the decision to initiate ETI in individuals with preserved lung function, the absence of clear clinical guidance contributes to heterogeneous prescribing practices across centres. This highlights the need for longitudinal studies to clarify the long-term outcomes of ETI in this population.

person.biography:
I am associate professor at Milan University and consultant in pulmonology at the IRCCS Ca’ Granda Ospedale Maggiore Policlinico in Milano.
My clinical activity is mainly focused on cystic fibrosis and bronchiectasis. In our academic hospital, we have the largest adult CF Centre in Italy. Since 2022 I am part of the executive committee of the ECFS Standards-of-Care Group; I participated in the development of the latest standards of care documents. In 2023 I've been elected Chair of the Adult CF Group at the European Respiratory Society.
I am the author of more than 120 publications on peer-reviewed journals (H-index 24) and a current member of both the ECFS and ERS.

content.biography:
I am assistant professor at Milan University (Università degli Studi di Milano) and consultant in pulmonology at the IRCCS Ca’ Granda Ospedale Maggiore Policlinico in Milano.
My clinical activity is mainly focused on cystic fibrosis and bronchiectasis. In our academic hospital, we have the largest adult CF Centre in Italy under the care of pulmonologist. In this facility, I take care of transition programme and the start of new CFTR modulators. Before COVID-19 disrupted our organization, I had started a clinic dedicated to CFTR-RD. In 2019 I was elected to the board of the CF patient association as scientific advisor.
I am the author of more than 60 publications on peer-reviewed journals (H-index 17) and a current member of the ECFS and the ERS.

records.title: Pancreatic elastase dynamics in patients 2-5 years old treated with elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor

records.authors_text: E. Zhekayte1,2, A. Voronkova1,2, E. Kondratyeva1,2, G. Tsurkin1,2, V. Shadrina1,2, V. Kovalev2
records.affiliations_text: 1Research Centre for Medical Genetics, Scientific Clinical Department of Cystic Fibrosis, Moscow, Russian Federation, 2Scientific Research Clinical Institute for Childhood, Mytishchi, Russian Federation
records.abstract_text:
Studies of the effects of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) on pancreatic function in patients with cystic fibrosis (PwCF) have yielded conflicting data regarding increases in fecal elastase-1 (FE-1). This may be due to the inclusion of older patients in the studies.

Objective: To evaluate exocrine pancreatic function using FE-1 levels in PwCF aged 2-5 years receiving ETI therapy.

Materials: Data from the Russian Federation CF Patient Registry, therapy with CFTR modulators section, were used. The study included 54 patients (48.1% boys, 51.9% girls) with CF who had elastase-1 data recorded before and during the year of ETI therapy. The median age was 3.5 (2.7; 4.5), min 0.3, max 6.1 years. All patients had a severe genotype (homozygotes F508del 48.1%, compound heterozygotes F508del/non F508del 46.3%, non F508del/non F508del 5.6%). Children received ETI granules in doses corresponding to their weight. Pancreatic function was assessed by the concentration of FE-1 at the start of therapy and during the year of observation. The best result of elastase-1 achieved during the year of observation after the start of therapy was assessed.

Results: In 54 children at the start of therapy the median FE-1 was 15(15;40)μg/g. During the year of observation, the median was 19.5(15;136), p<0.001. An increase in FE-1 levels during the year of observation was noted in 21 patients (38.8%). 14 of 21 patients (66.6%) showed an increase in FE-1 More than 100mcg/g at the start of therapy, Me (Q1;Q3) 15 (15;15)mcg/g, over the course of a year — 369 (155;500) mcg/g (p<0.001). 10 of the 14 patients normalized FE-1 levels (more than 200mcg/g).

Conclusion: When using ETI in a group of young children, pancreatic function improved in 38.8% of cases, and FE-1 levels normalized in 18.5%. It is necessary to strive to prescribe CFTR modulators as early as possible. Further observations are needed to determine the duration and sustainability of the improvement and normalization of FE-1 levels.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: CFTR modulators have improved clinical outcomes in people with Cystic Fibrosis (pwCF), yet many still require complex supportive therapy regimens. Adherence to supportive therapies remains variable, and the role of structured medication reviews in optimising treatment is not well established. This study aimed to assess medication adherence across CF therapies using pharmacy refill and self-reported data, to compare adherence within individuals, and to identify Drug Related Problems (DRPs) and related interventions through structured pharmacist-led medication reviews.

Methods: A single-centre cross-sectional study was conducted at the CF centre of Maastricht University Medical Centre+ (February-April 2025), including adults and children. Adherence to CFTR modulators and supportive therapies was assessed using pharmacy refill data (Medication Possession Ratio, MPR) and self-reported adherence (Medication Adherence Report Scale-5, MARS-5). Structured pharmacist-led medication reviews were performed to identify DRPs and interventions were proposed to physicians. Data were analysed descriptively.

Results: Forty-three pwCF (mean age 23.3 years, SD 14.4, range 6 months - 50 years) were included. Adherence to CFTR modulators was high (MPR 94.4%; MARS-5 91.2%), whereas adherence to supportive therapies was lower and more variable (MPR 45.5-69%; MARS-5 46.7-86.7%). Within-patient adherence was significantly higher for CFTR modulators than for supportive therapies (p<0.001). Medication reviews were completed in 41 participants and identified 51 DRPs, most commonly overtreatment (33.3%) and medication use or adherence problems (31.4%), resulting in 51 interventions.

Conclusion: Adherence to CFTR modulators is high, while adherence to supportive therapies was suboptimal. Structured medication reviews revealed important opportunities to optimise treatment and improve adherence, highlighting a key role for pharmacists in routine CF care.

records.title: Long-term dynamics of sweat chloride concentration during elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor Therapy
records.authors_text: K. Zybert1,2, M. Postek1,2, L. Wozniacki1,2, K. Walicka-Serzysko1,2, J. Milczewska1,2, U. Borawska-Kowalczyk1,2, A. Wolkowicz1,2, D. Sands1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Institute of Mother and Child, Cystic Fibrosis, Warsaw, Poland, 2Paediatric Hospital, Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Dziekanow Lesny, Poland
records.abstract_text:
Background: Sweat testing, based on sweat chloride concentration (SCC), is a widely used tool for assessing CFTR channel function. SCC directly reflects CFTR activity in sweat glands; therefore, it serves as a sensitive biomarker of treatment response in cystic fibrosis and is useful for monitoring the effects of CFTR modulators over time.

Objective: To evaluate sweat chloride concentration (mmol/L) longitudinally in patients with cystic fibrosis treated with elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) and to assess the dynamics and durability of treatment response.

Materials and Methods: Among 57 patients who initiated ETI therapy in 2022, 32 remained under follow-up for >12 months and were included in the long-term analysis. Changes in SCC (mmol/L) were evaluated between consecutive time points (0–6, 6–12, 12–18, and 18–36 months) and as the overall change from baseline to 36 months. Sex-stratified analyses were performed.

Results: SCC decreased significantly in the early period (Δ0–6 mean −42.18 mmol/L; p < 0.001) and subsequently stabilized, with no significant changes thereafter. At 36 months, SCC remained significantly lower than baseline (Δ0–36 mean −35.88 mmol/L; p < 0.001). Sex-stratified analyses indicated a difference between women and men during the 18–36 month period (p = 0.035), with women showing an increasing trend in sweat chloride concentration.

Conclusions: An early decrease in sweat chloride concentration following ETI therapy was observed, with values remaining relatively stable over time. Exploratory analyses at later follow-up suggested a possible sex-related divergence, with higher sweat chloride concentrations observed in women.

records.title: Awareness and perceptions of a novel once-daily CFTR modulator (deutivacaftor/tezacaftor/vanzacaftor) in people with cystic fibrosis

person.institution: Northern Ireland Regional Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre

records.authors_text: J. Hanna1, S. Armstrong1, S. Bansal2, J. Faughey1, V. Mills1, E. Wright1, S. Caskey1, D. Downey1,3
records.affiliations_text: 1Northern Ireland Regional Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, BHSCT, Belfast, United Kingdom, 2Queen’s University Belfast, School of Medicine, Belfast, United Kingdom, 3Centre for Experimental Medicine, Queen's University Belfast, Belfast, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: Advances in CFTR modulation continues to change outcomes for people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). Deutivacaftor/tezacaftor/vanzacaftor (DTV) is a next-generation once-daily CFTR modulator demonstrating non-inferiority to existing triple therapy; therefore, understanding pwCF awareness of novel therapies and factors influencing decisions to switch is crucial. Exploring patient motivations, perceived benefits, and concerns is critical for successful integration of DTV into clinical practice.

Methods: A structured questionnaire was developed by the CF team in Belfast. Eligible, consenting adult pwCF attending routine clinic appointments were offered the questionnaire over a 3-month period. Anonymised responses were transcribed into Microsoft Excel and coded for descriptive statistical analysis.

Results: Eighty-eight pwCF participated in the survey. Familiarity with DTV was low (2% “very familiar”), with most learning of DTV from the CF team (60%) or social media (22%). Most frequent reasons for considering switching were “once-daily dosing” (70%), “trial to improve lung function” (61%), and “to improve quality of life” (60%). Concerns that current modulator treatment was ineffective was rare (8%). Fears around switching centred most frequently on “potential side effects” (42%), “may not be as effective” (41%), “risk of destabilising current health” (31%), and “feeling well on current treatment” (31%). Concerns relating to “peer influences” (1%) or for “additional monitoring” (8%) were minimal.

Conclusion: Awareness of DTV among pwCF was limited. Key motivators to switch included once-daily dosing and hope for further clinical benefit. Hesitancy around switching centred on the potential side effects and perceived efficacy, rather than peer influence or monitoring. These findings highlight the need for patient education and shared decision-making when introducing novel CFTR modulators. Further research in warranted to understand perceptions in greater detail.
