records.title: Factors associated with response to CFTR modulator therapy in cystic fibrosis

person.department: Department of Pediatrics and Cystic Fibrosis

records.authors_text: P. Famulska1, I. Wojsyk-Banaszak2, E. Sapiejka1, A. Steinert-Dymecki1, M. Osińska1, B. Więckowska3, B. Narożna2, A. Musiał4, A. Szczepankiewicz2, K. Tąpolska – Jóźwiak2, A. Wiesner2, M. Jóźwiak1
records.affiliations_text: 1Polanki Children’s Hospital, Department of Pediatrics and Cystic Fibrosis, Gdańsk, Poland, 2Poznan University of Medical Sciences, Department of Paediatric Pulmonology, Allergy and Clinical Immunology, Poznań, Poland, 3Poznan University of Medical Sciences, Department of Computer Science and Statistics, Poznań, Poland, 4Poznan University of Medical Sciences, Department of Diabetology, Auxology and Pediatric Obesity, Poznań, Poland
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator modulators (CFTRm) improve nutritional status, lung function and quality of life (QoL) in people with cystic fibrosis (PwCF); however, the magnitude of response varies considerably. Identification of baseline factors associated with treatment response may support individualised clinical assessment and follow-up.

Methods: In this prospective observational cohort study, 146 PwCF aged 2–56 years treated with CFTRm were evaluated at two specialised cystic fibrosis (CF) centres in Poland. Assessments were performed immediately before treatment initiation and after 12 months. Primary outcomes included 12-month changes (Δ) in body mass index (BMI), forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV₁), forced vital capacity (FVC), reactance at 10 Hz (X₁₀), sweat chloride concentration (SwCl) and the respiratory domain of the Cystic Fibrosis Questionnaire–Revised (RD-CFQ-R). For each outcome, patients were classified as super-responders (>90th percentile) or non-responders (<10th percentile). Greater SwCl reduction indicated stronger response. Ridge regression models were applied to identify baseline predictors while accounting for multicollinearity.

Results: Response to CFTRm therapy varied markedly across clinical domains. Greater improvements were associated with lower baseline lung function, poorer nutritional status and higher inflammatory markers. Chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonisation was linked to more pronounced responses in several outcomes. Treatment with elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) was associated with a higher likelihood of super-responder status compared with tezacaftor/ivacaftor (TI) or lumacaftor/ivacaftor (LI).

Conclusion: Baseline clinical, microbiological and inflammatory characteristics influence the magnitude of response to CFTRm therapy. These findings support phenotype-informed prognostication and personalised monitoring strategies in contemporary CF care.

records.authors_text: E. Kondratyeva1,2, A. Voronkova1,2, N. Odinaeva2, E. Zhekayte1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Research Centre for Medical Genetics, Scientific Clinical Department of Cystic Fibrosis, Moscow, Russian Federation, 2Scientific Research Clinical Institute for Childhood, Mytishchi, Russian Federation
records.abstract_text:
Triple therapy with elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) has demonstrated the greatest efficacy. Two ETI-containing drugs are registered in the Russian Federation: the original drug Trikafta® and the generic drug Trilexa®.

Objective: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of ETI therapy in children with cystic fibrosis (CF) in two age groups after switching drugs within the same INN.

Materials and methods: Data from the Russian CF Patient Registry for the period from 01 Jan 2025 to 01 Aug 2025 were analyzed. Efficacy and safety parameters were assessed at baseline (last day of original therapy) and after 30 and 90 days of generic therapy. A total of 151 patients were included and divided into two groups: 55 children aged 6–11 years (group 1) and 96 adolescents aged 12–18 years (group 2).

Results: Both groups showed further increases in weight and height after 3 months of therapy (p<0.05); BMI also improved in group 1 (p<0.05). Spirometry parameters achieved with the original drug remained stable during 90 days of generic therapy. Sweat conductivity remained within borderline values after 1 month; it decreased in group 1 without statistical significance (p=0.451) and increased in group 2 (p=0.048). In group 2, median AST decreased from 22.5 (16.8;29.0) to 21.0 (16.0;26.0) U/L (p=0.005). Median total bilirubin decreased to 12.25 (9.4;17.4) μmol/L after 3 months (p=0.017). All parameters remained within reference ranges. The incidence of adverse events (AE) was low and did not require dose adjustment or drug discontinuation.

Conclusion: Switching between ETI drugs within the same INN in children with CF maintained the therapeutic effect achieved with the original drug. The incidence of AE with the generic did not exceed that observed with the original therapy. Further studies of Trilexa® efficacy and safety are ongoing.

Spirometry parameters achieved with the original drug remained stable during 90 days of generic therapy. Sweat conductivity remained within borderline values after 1 month; it decreased in group 1 without statistical significance (p=0.451) and increased in group 2 (p=0.048). In group 2, median AST decreased from 22.5 (16.8;29.0) to 21.0 (16.0;26.0) U/L (p=0.005). Median total bilirubin decreased to 12.25 (9.4;17.4) μmol/L after 3 months (p=0.017). All parameters remained within reference ranges. The incidence of adverse events (AE) was low and did not require dose adjustment or drug discontinuation.
Conclusion: Switching between ETI drugs within the same INN in children with CF maintained the therapeutic effect achieved with the original drug. The incidence of AE with the generic did not exceed that observed with the original therapy. Further studies of Trilexa® efficacy and safety are ongoing.

records.title: Prenatal modulator treatment to prevent cross infection in an infant with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: C. Hansen1
records.affiliations_text: 1Skåne University Hospital, Pediatrics, Lund, Sweden
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Several cases of prenatal treatment of meconium ileus in infants with cystic fibrosis (CF) through treating their healthy mother have been described. We present a case of prenatal treatment to avoid cross infection from an older sibling with CF.

Methods: An older sibling with CF (homozygous with F508) has chronic, pulmonary infection caused by Burkholderia cepacia complex since the first visit in a Swedish CF centre. This child suffered from recurrent exacerbations with fever and purulent mucus and required intravenous antibiotics every two months prior to modulator treatment with Elexacaftor/Tezacaftor/Ivacaftor (ETI) at the age of 5 years. After initiation of ETI, cultures remained positive for Burkholderia but exacerbations were fewer and the need for intravenous treatment decreased to every 6 months. Cultures showed resistance to almost all antibiotics. When the mother became pregnant with another CF child, the discussion of prenatal treatment was initiated with the mother, within the team and with paediatric colleagues working in CF centres. The goal of the treatment was to prevent cross infection from the older sibling.

Results: Treatment of the mother was initiated during gestational week 23 in December 2024. Treatment continued until the baby started treatment at 6 weeks of age. We did liver enzyme testing on the mother before treatment and after 3 months of treatment. The baby was breastfed and thus received some dose of ETI in the breastmilk. First faecal elastase (FE) was 35 μg/g, second FE at 3 months was 207 μg/g. Pancreatic enzymes were started after the first FE but discontinued after ETI was initiated and the stool became normal. Liver enzymes are normal, and the baby thrives.

Conclusion: The possibility of prenatal treatment of CF foetuses may change the newborn clinical status of these children and even their future.

records.abstract_text:
CFTR modulators are combinations of CFTR potentiators and correctors that improve chloride channel function. The most effective combination is elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI). Data on long-term efficacy and safety of ETI in real-world practice in the Russian Federation (RF) are limited.

Aim – To analyze the efficacy and safety of therapy with ETI over 36 months.

Methods: A retrospective study using the Russian Cystic Fibrosis Patient Registry, Targeted Therapy section, for 2021–2024. A total of 1,025 pwCF (529/51.6%female, 496/48.4%male) over 6 years of age who received ETI were included. Efficacy was assessed in pairs of patients using sweat testing, anthropometric data, and pulmonary function tests (FVC, FEV1; % predicted) at therapy initiation and during 3 years. Safety was evaluated using ALT, AST, total bilirubin, and adverse events (AE).

Results: Median sweat chloride at baseline was 112 (96;121) mmol/L and decreased to 63.0 (49;78) mmol/L after one year (p<0.0001), with sustained results at years 2 and 3. Pulmonary function improved during the first year and remained stable thereafter. Median FVC increased from 82.15 (69.17;94.25)% to 95.5 (82.25;103.52)% after 3 years (p<0.0001). Median FEV1 increased from 75 (59.55;93.77)% to 90.5 (77.25;104)% (p<0.0001). Median BMI increased from 16.0 (14.6;18.2) to 18.58 (16.6;21.0) (p<0.0001). Liver function parameters remained within reference ranges. AE were reported in 9.4% of patients at therapy initiation and were rare after 3 years, mainly related to mental health.

Conclusion: Pw CF who received three-component ETI therapy showed significant positive dynamics in basic health indicators compared to the initial ones they had while receiving only basic therapy. The long-term efficacy and safety of the ETI has been demonstrated for three years.

records.title: Early clinical and inflammatory response to elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor in children with cystic fibrosis: first paediatric single-center experience from Lithuania
records.authors_text: V. Mejeryte1, N. Jotautaite1, G. Oboleviciene1, V. Miseviciene1
records.affiliations_text: 1Lithuanian University of Health Sciences, Medical Academy, Pediatric Department, Kaunas, Lithuania
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Highly effective CFTR modulator therapy has transformed cystic fibrosis (CF) care worldwide. However, in Lithuania CFTR modulators became available only in October 2024 with the introduction of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI). This study aimed to assess early clinical, inflammatory, and respiratory changes over one year in children initiating ETI for the first time.

Methods: This prospective observational single-center study included children aged 2–17 years with at least one F508del mutation. Clinical assessment, sweat chloride, fecal elastase, inflammatory blood markers, spirometry (FEV₁), and Lung Clearance Index (LCI2.5) were evaluated at baseline and after 1, 3, 6, and 12 months. Paired comparisons were performed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

Results: Fifteen patients (median age 7 years) were analyzed. All reported clinical improvement. Cumulative inpatient days decreased from 134 to 84. BMI increased modestly but significantly (15.21 to 15.86, p=0.023), while fecal elastase remained unchanged. Sweat chloride decreased significantly from month 1 onward (p<0.05), with greater reductions in F508del homozygous patients. Inflammatory changes were delayed: neutrophils and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio decreased at 6 and 12 months, while total leukocytes decreased only at 12 months; CRP and platelets remained stable. Mean baseline FEV₁ was normal (99.8% predicted) and increased significantly within the first three months, remaining higher than baseline at 12 months. LCI2.5 showed a non-significant decrease (10.68 to 9.12).

Conclusion: ETI induced rapid clinical and FEV₁ improvement in previously modulator-naive children, while inflammatory markers, growth, and pancreatic function showed limited early response. Minimal LCI change suggests persistent small airway disease. These findings highlight that spirometry alone may overestimate early treatment success, supporting multidimensional monitoring.

records.title: The efficacy of vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor in modulator naïve patients with non-class I CFTR mutations
records.authors_text: R. O'Reilly1, C. Benn1, S. Brown1,2, C. Pao1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Royal London Children's Hospital, London, United Kingdom, 2Queen Mary University of London, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: In 2025 vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor (Alyftrek®) was licensed and commissioned by the National Health Service (NHS) for treatment of people with cystic fibrosis over 6 years of age in the United Kingdom. The development of this new modulator has broadened eligibility criteria. From our cohort, we have been able to prescribe Alyftrek® to three patients with non-class I mutations that were previously modulator naïve, including ‘off label’ prescriptions. The aim of this study is to follow our three modulator naïve patients and their response to Alyftrek®.

Methods: Our primary end point was to assess a change in sweat chloride and lung function. Patients had baseline sweat chloride, FEV1 and Lung Clearance Index (LCI) prior to starting modulator therapy. Response to treatment was assessed with repeat lung function and sweat chloride 6-8 weeks after commencing therapy and again at 4-6 months. Our secondary end point was to assess a change in reported clinical symptoms at these intervals.

Results: The three patients were female, between the ages of 9 and 16 with rare CFTR mutations. At present two of our three patients have commenced Alyftrek®. At 6 weeks after commencing modulator therapy, patient 1 (homozygous 3199del6) demonstrated a 20 mmol/L reduction in sweat chloride (119 to 99 mmol/L) as well as an improvement in ppFEV1 of 11.8% (110.6 to 122.4%). Further, patient 1 describes an improvement in appetite with a weight gain of 3 kg as well as resolution of nocturnal cough. Patient 2 (homozygous Y569D) is yet to have a repeat sweat test and has been on modulator therapy for 3 weeks. Her lung function remains unchanged at this stage (FEV1 93%). Patient 3 (G542X/ deletion of exon 2) will start modulator therapy in January 2026.

Conclusion: Patient 1’s improvement in sweat chloride, lung function and reported clinical symptoms is promising. Data collection is in progress and will be complete by the end of May.

records.title: Follow-up of people with cystic fibrosis receiving elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor at a reference center in Northeastern Brazil: overcoming inequalities
records.authors_text: F.R. Silva1, M.P.R. de Oliveira1, V.H.V. Bomfim1, J.C.B. Costa2, F.M. Fontenelle2, V.M. Guedes2, R. Terse-Ramos1,2, E.L.D. Souza1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Faculdade de Medicina da Bahia da Universidade Federal da Bahia, Medicine, Salvador, Brazil, 2Hospital Universitário Professor Edgard Santos, Salvador, Brazil
records.abstract_text:
Objective: To evaluate clinical outcomes after 6 months of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) treatment in a low-income population.

Methods: It was a prospective, longitudinal, observational study. Follow-up was assessed at two time points: T0 (initiation of therapy) and T1 (6 months after initiation). Outcomes included nutritional status (weight [kg], height [cm], body mass index [BMI]), pulmonary function (percent predicted forced vital capacity [FVC] and forced expiratory volume in 1 second [FEV1]), sweat chloride levels (mmol/L), and adverse events. Paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used to compare baseline and follow-up outcomes, depending on data distribution.

Results: Twenty-eight individuals were included; 60.7% were male, mean age (SD) was 15.6 (5.1) years. After 6 months, the percent predicted FVC increased from 95.9 (18.3)% to 100.4 (9.4)%, but the difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.32). Percent predicted FEV1 increased from 86.4 (20.6)% to 96.6 (13.4)%, without a statistically significant difference (p = 0.05). There was a statistically significant reduction in mean sweat chloride levels (p < 0.005), from 97.2 (14.2) mmol/L to 40.3 (24.8) mmol/L. Anthropometric parameters showed significant improvement during follow-up, with an increase in weight (p < 0.005) from 40.7 (19.2) kg to 44.4 (18.6) kg and in height (p < 0.005) from 145.5 (18.5) cm to 148.4 (17.2) cm. BMI (kg/m²) also increased significantly (p < 0.005), from 18.1 (4.7) to 19.4 (4.6). Twelve individuals reported adverse events, most of them mild. Four children required temporary discontinuation of the medication due to adverse reactions, with no recurrence after ETI reintroduction.

Conclusion: During follow-up, all clinical parameters improved. Approximately 50% of individuals experienced adverse events, none of which were severe. Despite the low-income setting, ETI therapy was highly effective.

records.affiliations_text: 1University Clinic for Respiratory Diseases in Children, CF, Skopje, North Macedonia, The Republic of, 2Ss Cyril and Methodius University, Faculty of Medicine, Skopje, North Macedonia, The Republic of
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The CFTR modulator therapies (mCFTR), especially elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI), has improved CFTR function and clinical efficacy in patients with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). The aim of this study was to determinate the effect of mCFTR on nutritional status, pulmonary function and sputum isolates, 18 months after initiation of therapy in pwCF.

Methods: We have included 28 adolescent and adult pwCF, from the CF Center in University Clinic for Respiratory Diseases in Children “Kozle”- Skopje, Republic of North Macedonia. Body mass index (BMI), Forced expiatory volume in 1 s (FEV1) expressed % of predictive value and microbiological data were assessed before the first dose of mCFTR and after 18 months.

Results: Median age was 29.03 years (range 16-45), 16 male (57%) and 12 female (43%). The mean values of BMI at baseline and 18 months after starting mCFTR were 23.03 (±3.80) and 24.15 (±4.73), respectively. FEV1, baseline mean values 67.01% (±25.79) and after 18 months 71.05% (±24.00). We have observed there was no statistically significant change in the BMI and FEV1, p=0.494, p=0.246, respectively. Before starting ETI almost all participants had positive culture, 39.28% (11 patients) Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA), 28.57% (8 patients) Staphylococcus aureus (SA) and methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) 14.2% (4 patients). After 18 months positive were 17.8% (5 patients) for PA, 7.14% (2 patients) for SA and 3.57% (1 patients) for MRSA.

Conclusion: Our study provides evidence of the beneficial effect of ETI treatment in pwCF 18 months after initiation in microbiological isolates, there was increase in the number of negative cultures, but there is no significant impact on nutritional status and FEV1.

records.abstract_text:
Objective: Lumacaftor–ivacaftor (LUM-IVA) is a CFTR modulator approved for children aged >1 year who are homozygous for the F508del variant, targeting the underlying molecular defect. Despite evidence from clinical trials, real-world data in preschool-aged children remain limited. This study evaluated the effectiveness, safety, and tolerability of LUM-IVA in this population over 12 months of follow-up.

Methods: We conducted a multicenter, prospective study in Italy including 69 children with CF aged 1–6 years treated with LUM-IVA. Anthropometric, laboratory, microbiological, and functional parameters were collected at baseline, and after 3, 6 and 12 months.

Results: The median age was 3.82 years. LUM-IVA treatment was associated with significant reductions in sweat chloride concentration and pulmonary exacerbation frequency between baseline and 3/6 months. Weight improved significantly between T0 and T3 and between T1 and T2. Lung Clearance Index (LCI) also showed significant improvement between baseline and 6-12 months. Adverse events were mild and manageable; temporary treatment interruptions occurred, with no permanent discontinuations.

Conclusion: In this real-world cohort of preschool children with CF homozygous for F508del, LUM-IVA therapy was associated with improvements in sweat chloride, pulmonary exacerbation frequency and weight over 12 months, with an acceptable safety profile. These observational findings support the feasibility of early CFTR modulator therapy.

records.title: Clinical evaluation of CFTR modulator therapy in patients with cystic fibrosis in Latvia
records.authors_text: E. Aleksejeva1,2, A. Kleina3
records.affiliations_text: 1Children's Clinical University Hospital, Pediatric Pulmonology and Allergology, Riga, Latvia, 2Rigas Stradiņš University, Pediatric, Riga, Latvia, 3Rigas Stradiņš University, Postgraduate Medical Education, Riga, Latvia
records.abstract_text:
Background: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a rare autosomal recessive disease caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, leading to impaired chloride transport, viscous secretions and progressive multi-organ involvement. The introduction of CFTR modulator therapy has substantially changed CF management; however, real-world data from smaller national cohorts remain limited.

Aim: To evaluate the clinical effectiveness and safety of CFTR modulator therapy during the first year after initiation in patients with CF in Latvia.

Methods: A prospective cohort study was conducted between August 2023 and February 2025. Patients with confirmed CF and at least one F508del mutation were included. Clinical, functional and laboratory parameters were assessed at therapy initiation and after 6 and 12 months. Outcomes included anthropometric measurements, lung function (forced expiratory volume in one second, FEV1), sweat chloride concentration, liver function tests, fat-soluble vitamins, trace elements and adverse events classified by severity.

Results: Fifteen patients were included (mean age 22.7 ± 8.8 years). Mean body weight increased by 4.4 kg and body mass index by 1.3 kg/m². Sweat chloride concentration decreased by 37.7%. Mean FEV1 increased by 0.5 L, and FEV1 per cent predicted improved by 7%. No respiratory exacerbations were observed in the male subgroup. Liver function parameters remained stable and exceeded the upper limit of normal only once. Mild to moderate adverse events were reported, including tinnitus and skin rash; one severe psychiatric adverse event was recorded.

Conclusions: CFTR modulator therapy was associated with clinically meaningful improvements in nutritional status, lung function and sweat chloride concentration without significant hepatic toxicity. These findings are consistent with previously published real-world studies. Larger studies are needed to evaluate long-term effectiveness and safety.

records.title: First experience with the generic elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor targeted therapy in pediatric CF patients in Kazakhstan

person.title: MD, PhD
person.institution: Federal Pulmonology Research Institute, Federal Medical and Biological Agency

records.authors_text: T. Marshalkina1, E. Amelina2, N. Zhanuzakova1, A. Zaitova1
records.affiliations_text: 1Scientific Center of Pediatrics and Pediatric Surgery, Pediatric Pulmonology, Almaty, Kazakhstan, 2Astana Medical University, Department of Internal Medicine with a Course of Nephrology, Hematology, Allergology, Immunology, Astana, Kazakhstan
records.abstract_text:
Background: The triple combination elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) is one of the most effective CF therapies. Information on the efficacy and safety of its generic forms remains scarce. In Kazakhstan, triple therapy has been used in pediatric practice.

Objective: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of the generic ETI drug Trilexa® (Tutor S.A.C.I.F.I.A., Buenos Aires, Argentina) in children with CF after 12 months of treatment in real-life clinical practice.

Methods: 21 patients aged 6 to 18 years receiving a generic ETI were observed. Efficacy and safety indicators were assessed every 3 months during one year.

Results: Sweat conductivity before ETI therapy was equivalent to 116.7±24.3 (83-157) mmol/l NaCl, and after 12 months of therapy – 74.67±28.2 (38.0-101) mmol/l NaCl, p<0.001.

Body mass index (BMI) at the start of therapy was 15.54±3.09 (10.65-22.2) kg/m2, after one year of treatment it was 17.208±3.29 (13.58-23.95) kg/m2. Improvement of respiratory function (FEV1): baseline values 78.6±31.3%, after 6 months – 84.9±21.7%, after one year 89.7±23.6%. Clinical improvement was noted, including the disappearance or reduction of cough, sputum volume, and increased exercise tolerance. Adverse events were hypertension (1), anxiety (1), increased cough (1), increased sputum production (1), elevated transaminases levels, and rash. These adverse events did not require discontinuation of the therapy.

Conclusion: The efficacy and safety of generic ETI therapy were demonstrated in a pediatric clinical practice.

Results: Sweat conductivity before ETI therapy was equivalent to 116.7±24.3 (83-157) mmol/l NaCl, and after 12 months of therapy – 74.67±28.2 (38.0-101) mmol/l NaCl, p<0.001.
Body mass index (BMI) at the start of therapy was 15.54±3.09 (10.65-22.2) kg/m2, after one year of treatment it was 17.208±3.29 (13.58-23.95) kg/m2. Improvement of respiratory function (FEV1): baseline values 78.6±31.3%, after 6 months – 84.9±21.7%, after one year 89.7±23.6%. Clinical improvement was noted, including the disappearance or reduction of cough, sputum volume, and increased exercise tolerance. Adverse events were hypertension (1), anxiety (1), increased cough (1), increased sputum production (1), elevated transaminases levels, and rash. These adverse events did not require discontinuation of the therapy.
Conclusion: The efficacy and safety of generic ETI therapy were demonstrated in a pediatric clinical practice.

records.title: Inpatient management of adult CF patients in Kazakhstan and changes under the effect of targeted therapy with CFTR modulators
records.authors_text: Y. Kenzhebayeva1, I. Mukatova2, S. Kim2, E. Amelina2
records.affiliations_text: 1Multidisciplinary Hospital No1, Department of Pulmonology, Astana, Kazakhstan, 2Astana Medical University, Department of Internal Diseases No3, Astana, Kazakhstan
records.abstract_text:
Objective: To present the real-life clinical practice of inpatient CF treatment in Kazakhstan and the impact of CFTR modulators on it.

Materials and methods: A retrospective analysis of the medical records of pwCF hospitalized in 2020–2025. 10 pwCF (5 men), aged 18–36 years, were hospitalized due to severe respiratory exacerbation and/or progression of respiratory failure (RF). 9 were infected with Pseudomonas aeruginosa, 9 had malnutrition, 8 were on long-term oxygen. Hospitalizations before and after initiation of therapy with generic CFTR modulators elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (Trilexa®, Tuteur S.A.C.I.F.I.A., Argentina) were analyzed.

Results: Before the initiation of targeted therapy, severe respiratory exacerbations were the cause of hospitalization in 10 patients, 1 with hemoptysis. All patients had RF, their BMI was 16.72 kg/m². Patients received intravenous antibiotics, inhaled Dornase, bronchodilators, hypertonic saline, physiotherapy; PERT, all required oxygen therapy, 2 had NIV in BiPAP mode. At discharge, 6 patients required home oxygen therapy and continued oral antibiotic therapy. The average in-hospital stay in this group was 14.5 days. After initiation of CFTR modulator therapy in 2023, only five patients in this group required hospitalization. Only 2 patients still have RF, and the BMI in the group increased to 19.2 kg/m². The duration of intravenous antibacterial therapy and hospitalization was reduced to 8.5 hospital days.

Conclusion: The use of CFTR modulators reduces the number and severity of CF exacerbations and decreases the need for inpatient management and its duration.

records.title: Targeted therapy with elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor in adults with cystic fibrosis: a real-world clinical practice experience
records.authors_text: S. Kim1, I. Mukatova1, E. Amelina2, A. Serikova1, Y. Kenzhebaeva3
records.affiliations_text: 1Astana Medical University, Department of Internal Medicine No. 3, Astana, Kazakhstan, 2Federal State Budgetary Institution “Research Institute of Pulmonology” of the Federal Medical and Biological Agency of Russia, Moscow, Russian Federation, 3Municipal State Enterprise on the Right of Economic Management “Multidisciplinary City Hospital No. 1” of the Akimat of Astana, Astana, Kazakhstan
records.abstract_text:
Background: Elexacaftor/Tezacaftor/Ivacaftor (ETI) is one of the most effective treatments for cystic fibrosis (CF). However, drug availability remains limited in many countries, leading to interruptions in therapy. Data on the clinical outcomes of these interventions remain limited.

Objective. To evaluate the efficacy of ETI triple therapy in adult patients with CF in Kazakhstan in a real-world clinical practice setting.

Methods: The study included 19 adult patients (7 men), with a mean age of 26 years. Patients received a generic ETI (Trilexa®, Tuteur S.A.C.I.F.I.A., Argentina). The dynamics of clinical parameters were assessed during the full dose and after therapy discontinuation.

Results: Nineteen patients received the ETI at the full dose for 10–22 months. Forced therapy discontinuation due to lack of drug availability occurred in 7 of 19 patients (36.8%) within 2–4 months.

After receiving the full dose, all patients experienced a regression of respiratory symptoms and an increase in exercise tolerance. BMI was 19.7 kg/m² (baseline 17.6 kg/m²), the frequency of pulmonary exacerbations decreased from 5.5±2.7 to 2.1±1.3; FEV1 from 43.5% to 61.1%; FVC — from 56.1% to 72.8%. Sweat chlorides decreased from 101.3±8.9 to 64.1±5.7 mmol/L.

After complete discontinuation of therapy, all patients developed a pulmonary exacerbation within 1–2 weeks, requiring antibacterial therapy. Clinical characteristics worsened: BMI—17.9 kg/m², FEV1—49.3%, FVC—61.5%, sweat chlorides 81.8 mmol/L.

Conclusion: Triple therapy with a generic ETI demonstrated high efficacy. Forced discontinuation of therapy is associated with clinical deterioration and a high risk of exacerbations. Continuity of treatment is a key factor in targeted therapy.

records.title: Increased risk of chalazion and hordeolum in people with cystic fibrosis treated by elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor: insights from a national case control survey
records.authors_text: E. Weinzaepfel1, M. Savadogo2, B. Bertin3, L. Kodjikian4, I. Durieu5, Q. Reynaud6, T. Lopinnet7, P. Reix8
records.affiliations_text: 1Hopices Civils de Lyon, Hôpital de la Croix-ROUSSE, Lyon, France, 2Resource and Competence Center for Cystic Fibrosis, Hôpital Femme Mère Enfant Hospices Civils de Lyon, Bron, France, 3Regional Pharmacovigilance Center, Hospices Civils de Lyon, Lyon, France, 4Croix-Rousse Hospital, Hospices Civils de Lyon, Lyon, France, 5Cystic Fibrosis Reference Center, Lyon Sud Hospital, Hospices Civils de Lyon, Oullins-Pierre-Bénite, France, 6Cystic Fibrosis Reference Center, Lyon Sud Hospital, Oullins-Pierre-Bénite, France, 7Clinical Investigation Center, Hospices Civils de Lyon, Lyon, France, 8Hôpital Femme Mère Enfant, Bron, France
records.abstract_text:
Background: There have been reports of children with cystic fibrosis (CF) presenting with chalazions or hordeola (C/H) while receiving elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor (ETI). To gain a broader perspective and better assess the implications of ETI, we conducted a national case-control survey through the network of 47 French CF centers.

Objectives: Our primary objective was to report the prevalence of C/H in people with CF (pwCF) who were treated or not with ETI. Our secondary objectives were to evaluate the association between ETI initiation timing, eye dryness, and other known C/H risk factors.

Material and methods: Physicians and pwCF constructed the questionnaires. Photographs were included to help pwCF recognize eyelid lesions. Dry eye was evaluated using the Ocular Surface Disease Index (OSDI) score. Treatment, progression, and impact on quality of life were also evaluated. QR codes were sent through French CF centers and the patient organization's social media.

Results: A total of 975 questionnaires concerning pwCF treated with ETI and 119 questionnaires concerning pwCF without ETI were received from 46 centers. Seventy-five percent of the responses were from adults. C/H has occurred at least once since the initiation of ETI in 330 (34%) of the ETI group. It occurred in 14 (12%) in the control group. C/H were unilateral (50.4%) or bilateral (14%). The treated group reported a mean of 2.9 (2.3) episodes. The time to onset was longer than 6 months in two-third of cases (median 1.5 years IQR 0.4-2.6). Three pwCF stopped taking ETI, 2 suspended it, and 2 needed an ETI dosage adjustment. Main ETI-related C/H risk factors were adult female sex, eye dryness (high OSDI), rosacea, and blepharitis.

Conclusion: Our large-scale study suggests the role of ETI and other risk factors in the development of C/H in pwCF. Both CF professionals and ophthalmologists must be aware of this potential adverse eyelid event in order to provide appropriate counsel.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To assess long-term safety and efficacy of vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor (VTD) in people with CF aged ≥12yrs, with ≥1 F508del or an elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI)-responsive allele without F508del, and who completed the pivotal studies SKYLINE 102 or 103.

Methods: Study VX20-121-104 is an ongoing phase 3, open-label extension study of VTD consisting of Parts A (96 wks) and B (48 wks); Part A is reported here. Primary endpoint is safety/tolerability; efficacy endpoints include absolute change from baseline on ETI in the parent study in ppFEV1 and sweat chloride (SwCl), proportion with SwCl <30 and <60mmol/L, and number of pulmonary exacerbations (PEx).

Results: 822 participants (pts) were enrolled and dosed. 96.8% of pts had an adverse event (AE); most were mild (23.6%) or moderate (60.7%) in severity and were consistent with manifestations of CF. Rates of serious AEs and AEs leading to treatment discontinuation were low (18.21 and 2.46 events/100 patient-yrs). Event rates of rash, transaminase and creatine kinase elevations, and cataracts were consistent with the established VTD safety profile. Neuropsychiatric events/rates were consistent with those observed with background neuropsychiatric events in the CF population and those in the parent studies. Efficacy was similar regardless of treatment arm in the parent study (Table 1).

Conclusion: VTD was generally safe and well tolerated, consistent with the established safety profile. VTD demonstrated sustained improvements in clinical outcomes and further restoration of CFTR function, with more pts achieving SwCl <60 and <30mmol/L compared to ETI. Stable lung function and low PEx rates through 96 wks demonstrate the sustained, clinical impact of CFTR restoration, which is important because greater CFTR function (lower SwCl levels) is associated with better clinical outcomes.

Objectives: To assess long-term safety and efficacy of vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor (VTD) in people with CF aged ≥12yrs, with ≥1 F508del or an elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI)-responsive allele without F508del, and who completed the pivotal studies SKYLINE 102 or 103.
Methods: Study VX20-121-104 is an ongoing phase 3, open-label extension study of VTD consisting of Parts A (96 wks) and B (48 wks); Part A is reported here. Primary endpoint is safety/tolerability; efficacy endpoints include absolute change from baseline on ETI in the parent study in ppFEV1 and sweat chloride (SwCl), proportion with SwCl <30 and <60mmol/L, and number of pulmonary exacerbations (PEx).
Results: 822 participants (pts) were enrolled and dosed. 96.8% of pts had an adverse event (AE); most were mild (23.6%) or moderate (60.7%) in severity and were consistent with manifestations of CF. Rates of serious AEs and AEs leading to treatment discontinuation were low (18.21 and 2.46 events/100 patient-yrs). Event rates of rash, transaminase and creatine kinase elevations, and cataracts were consistent with the established VTD safety profile. Neuropsychiatric events/rates were consistent with those observed with background neuropsychiatric events in the CF population and those in the parent studies. Efficacy was similar regardless of treatment arm in the parent study (Table 1).
Conclusion: VTD was generally safe and well tolerated, consistent with the established safety profile. VTD demonstrated sustained improvements in clinical outcomes and further restoration of CFTR function, with more pts achieving SwCl <60 and <30mmol/L compared to ETI. Stable lung function and low PEx rates through 96 wks demonstrate the sustained, clinical impact of CFTR restoration, which is important because greater CFTR function (lower SwCl levels) is associated with better clinical outcomes.

records.title: Pregnancy and neonatal outcomes in women with cystic fibrosis receiving elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor

person.institution: University Hospital Essen, University Duisburg-Essen, Germany

records.authors_text: N.-K. Vagt1, S. Dietz-Terjung2, M. Picker1, C. Thoms1, S. Straßburg1, C. Taube1, G. Weinreich1, J. Judickiene1, M. Panagi1, S. Sutharsan1, M. Welsner1
records.affiliations_text: 1University Hospital Essen, University Duisburg-Essen, Germany, Department of Pulmonary Medicine, Ruhrlandklinik, Essen, Germany, 2University of Duisburg-Essen, University Hospital Essen-Ruhrlandklinik, Department of Sleep and Telemedicine, University Hospital Essen-Ruhrlandklinik, Essen, Germany
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The increasing number of pregnancies in women with cystic fibrosis (wwCF) receiving elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor(ETI) therapy highlights the need for data on maternal safety and pregnancy outcomes. The aim of this study was to assess maternal health during ETI therapy and to evaluate neonatal outcomes.

Methods: Clinical data on lung function, body mass index (BMI), gestational weight gain and antibiotic use before, during and after pregnancy were retrospectively collected from medical records of wwCF receiving ETI therapy. Neonatal outcomes were assessed using maternity records from 12 pregnancies, including gestational age, birth weight, Apgar score and mode of delivery.

Results: The study included 18 wwCF with a mean age of 31 years (SD=5) at the start of pregnancy. Three wwCF (17%) required intravenous antibiotics, nine (50%) received oral antibiotics during pregnancy.

Median percent predicted FEV₁ before pregnancy (n=15) was 70% (range 32–113), with a median change of -1% (range -9–4) from pre-pregnancy to pregnancy. In 16 women with available weight data, median pre-pregnancy BMI was 22kg/m² (range 18–33). The weight gain goals according to pre-pregnancy BMI were met by 5 women (31%), 9 (56%) gained less and 2 (13%) more than recommended.

Neonatal outcome data were available for 12 pregnancies. The caesarean section rate was 58% (n=12). Median Apgar score at 5 minutes was 10 (range 8–10, n=12). Two (18%) of 11 births were born preterm, while nine (82%) were delivered at term with median gestational age of 38.1 weeks (range 36.4–41.1). Median birthweight percentile was 55 (range 12–100, n=11), two infants (17%) were macrosomic and none were small for gestational age.

Conclusion: ETI therapy appears to be compatible with stable maternal health during pregnancy and generally favourable neonatal outcomes. Most infants were delivered at term with appropriate growth. Inter-individual differences highlight the importance of continued monitoring.

records.title: Switching children and young people with cystic fibrosis from elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor to vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor

person.title: Dr.
person.institution: University Hospitals of North Midlands NHS Trust

records.authors_text: K. Bakewell1, C. Jolley1, S.-A. Ho1, W. Carroll1,2, J. Chapman1, F. Gilchrist1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1University Hospitals of North Midlands NHS Trust, North West Midlands CF Centre, Stoke on Trent, United Kingdom, 2Keele University, Faculty of Medicine and Health Sciences, Keele, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor (VTD) was approved for use in individuals with cystic fibrosis aged ≥6 years by the UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) in March 2025 and recommended for NHS use by the National Institute for Clinical excellence (NICE) in July 2025. Whilst VTD has similar clinical benefits to elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI), it has the advantage of being given once rather than twice a day.

Methods: The possibility of switching from ETI to VTD was discussed with all eligible children and young people (CYP) at our centre. The CYP/parent made the final decision but were advised more strongly to switch if they had a suboptimal response to ETI. We report the number who chose to switch and the factors affecting their decision.

Results: Fifty-three CYP with a mean (SD) age of 13.5 (3.7) years were eligible to switch from ETI to VTD (30 homozygous and 23 heterozygous for Phe508del). Their mean (SD) FEV1 percentile (n=52) was 94 (18) and their mean (SD) drop in sweat chloride after starting ETI (n=50) was 52 (24) mmol/L. Thirty-four (64%) have agreed to start VTD, 14 (26%) declined and 5 (9%) are as yet undecided. The commonest reasons for declining to switch were not wanting additional blood tests and being happy with their response to ETI. Of the 50 children with a sweat chloride result whilst on ETI, 5/6 (83%) whose sweat chloride was ≥60mmol/L switched to VTD, compared to 29/44 (66%) with a chloride <60mmol/L.

Conclusion: The convenience of VTDs once daily administration was the major reason the majority of CYP at our centre chose to switch from ETI to VTD. Despite this, a number decided to remain on ETI due to the inconvenience or fear of additional blood tests and being happy with their response to ETI. We plan compare quality of life scores and sweat chloride results before and after switching to VTD.

records.title: Model-informed dose reduction of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor therapy in adult people with cystic fibrosis: a simulation study
records.authors_text: T. Zwart1, S. Baromeo2, I. Bronsveld3, H. Heijerman3, E. Wilms4, R. van der Meer5
records.affiliations_text: 1Haga teaching Hospital, The Hague, Netherlands, 2Haga teaching Hospital, Pharmacy, The Hague, Netherlands, 3University Medical Center Utrecht, Pulmonology, Utrecht, Netherlands, 4Apotheek Haagse Ziekenhuizen, Pharmacy, The Hague, Netherlands, 5Haga teaching Hospital, Pulmonology, The Hague, Netherlands
records.abstract_text:
Background: Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) therapy is used by most people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). While generally efficacious, some patients experience adverse events. This is typically managed by empirical dose reduction, but the optimal regimen remains unknown. We evaluated the pharmacokinetic (PK) and pharmacodynamic (PD) impact of ETI dose reduction using model-based simulations.

Methods: Available ETI population PK models were used to simulate ETI PK under five dose reduction strategies. First, standard dose ETI PK was simulated, after which individuals were selected for dose reduction based on elexacaftor trough levels (Cmin). Subsequently, ETI exposure was translated to predicted efficacy using pharmacodynamic models constructed from available exposure-response data.

Results: Demographic data of 885 pwCF were available from the Dutch CF registry. Dose reduction for pwCF showing elexacaftor Cmin >75th percentile (9075 µg/L) yielded limited PK and PD impact compared to the standard dose. Reduction to a 100/50/75 mg ETI morning dose with a 150 mg (regimen A) or 75 mg (regimen B) ivacaftor evening dose resulted in limited shifts in relative effect medians of 94.0% to 92.9% and 89.9% to 88.6% for elexacaftor and tezacaftor, and 96.2% to 95.8% and 96.2% to 95.5% for ivacaftor. records.title: Rationale and design of a Phase 2b study in people with cystic fibrosis carrying the 3849 +10 Kb C->T mutation to evaluate the combined effect of SPL84 and CFTR modulators
records.authors_text: L. Friedman1, E. Kerem1,2, G. Hart1
records.affiliations_text: 1SpliSense Ltd., Jerusalem, Israel, 2CF Center, Department of Pediatrics, Hadassah Medical Center and Faculty of Medicine, Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Jerusalem, Israel
records.abstract_text:
Background: SPL84 is an inhaled antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) for the treatment of pwCF carrying the 3849 +10kb C->T (3849) mutation. SPL84 was shown to fully restore CFTR function in HNEs and HBEs from pwCF. In addition, SPL84 and ETI had a comparable and additive effect on HBEs from 3849/F508del pwCF.

SPL84-002 is a global Phase 2a study in 3849 pwCF to evaluate the safety and preliminary efficacy of SPL84 as mono therapy. Twelve participants received 9 weekly doses of 25 or 50 mg SPL84 (n=6 each). SPL84 lead to a clinically meaningful improvement in ppFEV1 in up to ~70% of participants per cohort, with an average absolute change from baseline in ppFEV1 of 5 for both cohorts.

Real-world data shows that ETI provides only moderate and variable benefit for 3849 pwCF, due to limited residual WT CFTR. Meanwhile, SPL84 corrects the underlying splicing defect and may complement ETI by restoring CFTR through a distinct MoA. Evidence of a ceiling effect for ETI further supports the need for alternative approaches. There, an additional cohort in study SPL8-002 is planned to examine the combined effect of SPL84 and CFTR modulators.

Methods: Forty 3849 pwCF will participate in the SPL84-modulator combo cohort (3:1 active:placebo). Participants must be stable on ETI or VTD for at least 3 months and have ppFEV1 40-80. The study will consist of a 28-day screening period, a 28-day run-in period to confirm ppFEV1 is stable on modulators, a 9-week treatment period where participants will received 50 mg SPL84 once-weekly, and a 28-day follow up.

Results: The primary objective of the study is safety. The secondary objective is preliminary efficacy, which will be evaluated by spirometry and CFQ-R RSS.

Conclusions: Clinical and preclinical data demonstrates that SPL84 has the potential to provide substantial additive improvement over available CFTR modulator therapy (ETI/VTI) when given in combination to 3849 pwCF.

records.title: Standard Aggressive Chemotharapy versus capecitabine in pancreatic adenocarcinoma with lung metastasis in cystic fibrosis patients
records.authors_text: O. Ali1, M. Ibrahim2, E. Sabry3
records.affiliations_text: 1Faculty of Medicine Mansoura University, Pulmonary, Mansoura, Egypt, 2Oncology Center, Medical\Pulmonology, Mansoura, Egypt, 3Faculty of Medicine, Lab Departennt, Mansoura, Egypt
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: This study investigated the impact of standard combination chemotherapy versus single-agent therapy in metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma in cystic fibrosis patients. The aim was to compare objective response rate, toxicity, progression-free survival, and overall survival.

Methods: Involved 35 CF patients with newly diagnosed metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma, maintained on CFTR modulators, bronchodilators, dornase alfa, and chest physiotherapy. 18 patients received standard chemotherapy (combination of Folinic acid, Fluorouracil, Irinotecan, Oxaliplatin), and 17 received single-agent chemotherapy (Capecitabine). TNF-α levels were measured before and after six cycles to monitor CF activity.

Results: Among group A, 72% achieved disease control and 28% had progressive disease while, in group B, 43% achieved disease control and 57% had progressive disease with significant differences (P=0.04). Group A observed better PFS (median, 7 months vs. 5 months; P=0.043). Also, group A demonestrated longer OS (median, 11 months vs. 9 months; P=0.033). A significant drop in basal CA 19.9 (Carbohydrate Antigen 19-9) after sex cycles of treatment in group A (mean ±SD; 235 ±124 U/mL drop to 65±32 U/mL) versus group B (P=0.001). No significant increase in TNF-α after finishing sex cycles of chemotherapy in both treatment groups. In group A basal TNF-α was 132 ± 40 pg/mL while, after sex cycles of chemotherapy it was 140 ± 31 pg/mL with P=0.12. No significant difference observed between both groups regarding chemotherapy toxicity; neutropenia (P=0.1), chest infection (P=1.0), GI upset (P=0.3) and hepatotoxicity (P=0.2).

Conclusion: This study suggests that standard combination chemotherapy, possibly mFOLFIRINOX, is a more effective treatment option for this specific patient population, offering higher disease control, improved survival, and reduced CA 19.9, with tolerable toxicity and without significantly affecting CF disease activity.

records.title: Tolerability and efficacy of rheumatoid arthritis medications in cystic fibrosis patients with concurrent rheumatoid arthritis
records.authors_text: Y. Hussein1, A. Shabana2, Y. Sadeq3
records.affiliations_text: 1Dakahlia INsurance Hospital, DK, Egypt, 2Mansoura University Hospital, Immunology and Rheumatology, Mansoura, Egypt, 3Mansoura University Hospital, Clinical Pathology, Mansoura, Egypt
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Tolerability and toxicity of RA medications on pulmonary CF patients. Monitor the levels of CRP and serum Calprotectin for RA treatment response. Evaluate serum IL-17 levels (as a biomarker for both CF and RA).

Methods: 28 CF patients with recent-onset RA. All CF patients were managed either with CFTR modulators (for those with at least one F508del mutation) or standard treatments such as Dornase alfa, bronchodilators, and chest physiotherapy. Patients received treatment with Hydroxychloroquine, either alone or in combination with Sulfasalazine.

Results: 24 patients completed the six-month study; four discontinued due to non-pulmonary adverse events (gastrointestinal upset, skin rash). Importantly, no patients experienced worsening lung function attributable to the study medications. Manageable recurrent chest infection was observed in 12.5% of patients, hemoptysis in 4.1%, and pneumothorax in 8.3%; no respiratory failure was documented.

Significant reductions were observed after sex months of treatment in key inflammatory markers. Mean CRP levels decreased from mean ±SD of 18.2 ± 7.3 mg/L to 8.9 ± 5.6 mg/L (over 50% reduction), correlating with improved DAS28-CRP criteria. Serum Calprotectin levels dropped from a mean ±SD of 3,630 ± 1,250 ng/mL to 1,550 ± 640 ng/mL, correlating with DAS28-CRP and ultrasound synovitis. Serum IL-17 levels significantly decreased mean ±SD; 58.6 ± 12.2 pg/mL to 24.4 ± 8.1 pg/mL, correlating with clinical improvement. A concordance of drop in these biomarkers was observed in 70.8% of evaluated patients.

Conclusion: Hydroxychloroquine and Sulfasalazine are well-tolerated and demonstrate a favorable pulmonary safety profile in CF patients with co-existing RA. The observed reductions in CRP, Calprotectin, and IL-17, coupled with improvements in clinical assessments, suggest these medications are effective in managing RA activity in this complex patient population.

records.title: Beyond CFTR modulators: a randomized controlled trial of intensified vitamin D supplementation to improve bone health in paediatric cystic fibrosis

person.title: PhD Msc, Research Pediatric Metabolic Dietitian
person.institution: Hospital Infantil de México Federico Gómez
person.department: Research and Diagnosis Unit in Nephrology and Bone Mineral Metabolism

records.authors_text: M. Reyes-Apodaca1, R. Vázquez-Frias2, J.L. Lezana-Fernández3, M. Medeiros4
records.affiliations_text: 1Hospital Infantil de México Federico Gómez, Research and Diagnosis Unit in Nephrology and Bone Mineral Metabolism, Mexico City, Mexico, 2Hospital Infantil de México Federico Gómez, Deputy Director of Research Management Gastroenterologist and Pediatric Nutritionist, Mexico City, Mexico, 3Hospital Infantil de México Federico Gómez, Cystic Fibrosis Clinic, Mexico City, Mexico, 4Hospital Infantil de México Federico Gómez, Research Direction, Mexico City, Mexico
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To evaluate the efficacy of an intensified vitamin D supplementation strategy to achieve and sustain serum vitamin D (vitD) levels >30 ng/mL in pediatric patients with cystic fibrosis (CF). Secondary objectives included assessment of bone health and evaluation of safety and tolerability in the context of optimized standard CF care beyond CFTR modulator therapies.

Methods: Double-blind, randomized controlled trial including children and adolescents aged 5–18 years with CF followed at a tertiary multidisciplinary CF center. Participants with baseline serum vitD levels between 10 and 30 ng/mL were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive either an intensified supplementation regimen with a fixed initial dose of 4000 IU/day of cholecalciferol or supplementation according to Cystic Fibrosis Foundation (CFF) guidelines. Vitamin D doses were adjusted during follow-up based on serial vitD measurements across seven visits over 12 months. All other aspects of CF management followed standard multidisciplinary practice.

Results: Seventeen participants completed follow-up. The intensified supplementation group achieved and sustained vitD levels >30 ng/mL more consistently than the CFF-guided group (p=0.021). A significant improvement in total body less head (TBLH) z-score from baseline to final visit was observed in the intervention group (p = 0.03). In contrast, no significant change occurred in the control group (p = 0.89). Overall, bone outcomes showed upward trends, with greater gains in the intensified group. No bone density decline or supplementation-related adverse events were observed.

Conclusion: Intensified vitamin D supplementation was safe and more effective than CFF-guided dosing for achieving and sustaining adequate vitD levels and was associated with improved bone health. These findings support optimized vitamin D strategies as a feasible component of pediatric CF care beyond CFTR modulator therapies.

Objectives: To evaluate the efficacy of an intensified vitamin D supplementation strategy to achieve and sustain serum vitamin D (vitD) levels >30 ng/mL in pediatric patients with cystic fibrosis (CF). Secondary objectives included assessment of bone health and evaluation of safety and tolerability in the context of optimized standard CF care beyond CFTR modulator therapies.
Methods: Double-blind, randomized controlled trial including children and adolescents aged 5–18 years with CF followed at a tertiary multidisciplinary CF center. Participants with baseline serum vitD levels between 10 and 30 ng/mL were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive either an intensified supplementation regimen with a fixed initial dose of 4000 IU/day of cholecalciferol or supplementation according to Cystic Fibrosis Foundation (CFF) guidelines. Vitamin D doses were adjusted during follow-up based on serial vitD measurements across seven visits over 12 months. All other aspects of CF management followed standard multidisciplinary practice.
Results: Seventeen participants completed follow-up. The intensified supplementation group achieved and sustained vitD levels >30 ng/mL more consistently than the CFF-guided group (p=0.021). A significant improvement in total body less head (TBLH) z-score from baseline to final visit was observed in the intervention group (p = 0.03). In contrast, no significant change occurred in the control group (p = 0.89). Overall, bone outcomes showed upward trends, with greater gains in the intensified group. No bone density decline or supplementation-related adverse events were observed.

Conclusion: Intensified vitamin D supplementation was safe and more effective than CFF-guided dosing for achieving and sustaining adequate vitD levels and was associated with improved bone health. These findings support optimized vitamin D strategies as a feasible component of pediatric CF care beyond CFTR modulator therapies.

records.title: Plasma lipidome after double-blind randomized lipid supplementation for 1 year in patients with cystic fibrosis

person.department: Dept of Laboratory Medicine, Clinical Chemistry

records.authors_text: B. Strandvik1, V. Tillander2, J. Walkowiak3, S. Dryzymala-Czyz4, E. Bakkeheim5, M. Kolsgaard5, C. Colombo6, A. Bulfamante6, A.R. Qureshi1
records.affiliations_text: 1Karolinska Institutet, CLINTEC, Stockholm, Sweden, 2Karolinska Institutet, Dept of Laboratory Medicine, Clinical Chemistry, Stockholm, Sweden, 3Poznan University of Medical Sciences, Dept of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Metabolic Diseases, Poznan, Poland, 4Poznan University of Medical Sciences, National Resource Bromatology, Poznan, Poland, 5Oslo University Hospital, Centre for Cystic Fibrosis, Oslo, Norway, 6University of Milan, Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Fondatione IRCCS Ca Granda, Ospedele Maggiore Polioclinica, Milan, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Background: Cystic fibrosis (CF) patients with pancreatic insufficiency, pathological sweat tests, and pulmonary symptoms have long been known to develop linoleic acid (LA) deficiency, documented for over 60 years. Abnormal profiles of other fatty acids, such as palmitoleic acid, Mead acid, and often docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), are also common.

Objectives: This randomized, double-blind study investigated the effects of LA supplementation in children with CF. Patients aged 5–15 years, carrying class I–II mutations and classical CF symptoms, were assigned to receive either LA or oleic acid (10 g/day) for one year. All participants also received DHA (400 mg/day). Forty patients completed the study. Standard CF treatment remained unchanged, except for antibiotic therapy during infectious exacerbations. Anthropometry, biochemical analyses, pulmonary function, and exacerbation frequency were monitored. The study was approved by the local ethic committees.

Methods: Clinical and biochemical assessments, along with plasma lipidomic, were performed at baseline and after 12 months. Lipidomic was conducted on total lipid extracts from 40 µL plasma using LC-MS/MS, covering >350 lipid species across six lipid classes. Each species was normalized to the total concentration of its respective class.

Results: Of LA-containing lipid species, 24% increased significantly in the LA+DHA group and 4% in the DHA group. Of DHA-containing species, 54% were elevated in the control group and 22% in the LA group. In the control group significant increases (p < 0.01) were observed, most of them containing DHA. In contrast, the DHA+LA group showed both increases and decreases in various lipids ; PE species and the total amount of PE decreased.

Conclusion: Supplementation of LA or LA and DHA showed unforeseen changes in the lipidomic.

records.title: The CARMUCI study design: a double-blind, cross-over sham-controlled trial of indoor air purification in people with cystic fibrosis and primary ciliary dyskinesia
records.authors_text: P. Anagnostopoulou1, M. Kakkoura1, P. Kouis1, A. Michanikou1, P. Bargiotas1, T. Adamides2, P. Ioannou3, S.F. Louka4, M. Neophytou5, G.K. Nikolopoulos1, C. Skevaki6,7,8, P. Koutrakis8, P. Yiallouros1

records.abstract_text:
Background: People with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) and primary ciliary dyskinesia (pwPCD) are particularly vulnerable to the harmful effects of air pollution due to the impairment of mucociliary clearance (MCC). Despite growing evidence supporting the use of indoor air purification in common lung conditions, its role in CF and PCD remains unexplored.

Methods: The Clean Air for Rare MUcociliary Clearance dIsorders (CARMUCI) study is a randomized, double-blind, cross-over, sham-controlled trial aiming to evaluate the impact of indoor air purification on respiratory health of pwCF and pwPCD (children and adults) in Cyprus. Sixty-two participants will receive two 3-month intervention periods using identical-looking air purifiers: one 3-month period with active filtration via high efficiency filters and one 3-month period with a sham unit. Primary outcome will be a mean difference of at least 10% change in lung clearance index (LCI), and secondary outcomes will include spirometry, pulmonary exacerbations, inflammatory biomarkers, and health-related quality of life. Exposure to indoor particulate matter (PM) will be continuously monitored using device operation logs and wearable activity trackers.

Results: By August 2025, 24 pwCF and 26 pwPCD (20 females, age: 31 [16.1] years) have been enrolled. CARMUCI continues enrolment and started data collection in September 2025. Results are expected to provide novel evidence on the efficacy of air purification in reducing indoor PM exposure and improving respiratory outcomes in people with chronic MCC disorders.

Conclusion: CARMUCI trial first results will be released in late-2027. The conclusions of this study are expected to inform future clinical guidelines and environmental health strategies for managing rare MCC disorders.

records.title: CF-Pain study: pain in patients with cystic fibrosis is a relevant and often underestimated issue regardless of age

person.institution: University Children`s Hospital of Ruhr University Bochum at St. Josef-Hospital

records.authors_text: S. Dillenhöfer1, A. Schlegtendal1, L. Eitner1, C. Maier1, S. Sutharsan2, F. Stehling3, A. Hoffmann1
records.affiliations_text: 1University Children`s Hospital of Ruhr University Bochum at St. Josef-Hospital, Pediatric Pulmonology, Cystic Fibrosis Center, Bochum, Germany, 2University Hospital Essen - Ruhrlandklinik, Department of Pulmonary Medicine, Adult Cystic Fibrosis Center, Essen, Germany, 3University Hospital Essen, Pediatric Pulmonology, Pediatric Cystic Fibrosis Center, Essen, Germany
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Pain is a common and often underestimated problem. Self-medication has a risk of adverse drug reaction and interactions. Most studies to date have been conducted without validated questionnaires. There is few information about pain in children and adolescents. The aim of the ongoing CF Pain study is to develop and review a standardized pain questionnaire for people with CF (pwCF) and started in 2022.

Methods: We use a pain questionnaire and interview children and adolescents aged 6 years and older and caregiver at the same time or adults with CF by phone. PwCF were treated in three locations of the Christiane-Herzog-Centre Ruhr. Additionally the first 10 patients of each age group were asked for feedback regarding the questionnaire. We supplement our data with clinical data of CF.

Results: Until now we included 23 adults, 16 adolescents and their caregiver and 40 children and their caregiver. It is noteworthy here that adolescents often reject the study. In children 55% were female with a median FEV1 of 91%. In adolescents 62,5% were female with a median FEV1 of 91,5%. In adults 26% were female with a median FEV1 of 90%. Asked for any pain in the last 3 months 32,5% of the children affirmed, 56% adolescents affirmed and 78% adults affirmed. The most common location of pain in children was initially abdominal pain, followed by headaches, while in adolescents and adults it was headaches, followed by abdominal pain. 50% of all pwCF took pain medication in the last 3 months; ibuprofen was the most common in 80%. 60% of pain medication was freely available for purchase. When asked about everyday limitations caused by pain, most people in all age groups reported limitations in meeting friends and participating in sports.

Conclusion: Pain is important in pwCF at any age with little attention given by treatment team. A validated questionnaire is needed. Therefore, we would like to increase our numbers and also use the questionnaire on healthy subjects.

records.title: Body composition as a determinant of exercise capacity in people with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: C. Falkenberg1,1, 1Christian Falkenberg, 1Paula Ontyd, 1Olaf Schnabel, 1Christian Werner, 1 Bianca Minke, 1Christian Falkenberg1,2Wolfgang Gruber
records.affiliations_text: 1Fachklinik Satteldüne, Nebel, Germany
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To investigate the relationship between body composition parameters, VO₂peak, and peak workload (Wpeak) in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF).

Methods: Forty-seven pwCF (28 female/19 male; mean age 17.7 ± 10.7 years, range 10–49 years; mean ppFEV₁ 85.0 ± 17.9, range 40–114%) participated. Cycle ergometry was performed to determine VO₂peak and Wpeak. Body composition was assessed using bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA), including fat mass (FM), fat mass index (FMI), fat-free mass (FFM), and fat-free mass index (FFMI). Data were collected during a four-week inpatient rehabilitation program.

Results: Exercise capacity was VO₂peak at 78.6 ± 17.1% predicted and Wpeak at 82.7 ± 16.6% predicted. After controlling for age and lung function (FEV₁%predicted), partial correlation analyses revealed significant correlations between FFM derived parameters and exercise capacity parameters. FFM was positively correlated with absolute Wpeak (W; r = 0.420, p = 0.005) and VO₂peak (L·min⁻¹; r = 0.443, p = 0.003), while FFMI was correlated with VO₂peak (L·min⁻¹; r = 0.306, p = 0.046). No significant partial correlations were observed between FM or FMI and VO₂peak or Wpeak (all p > 0.10). VO₂peak (% predicted) and Wpeak (% predicted) were not associated with any body composition parameter after adjustment for age and FEV₁.

Conclusion: Across a broad age range from childhood to adulthood, exercise capacity in pwCF was associated with fat-free mass–derived body composition parameters, whereas fat mass showed no association with VO₂peak or peak workload after adjustment for age and lung function. These findings highlight the relevance of fat-free mass alongside established pulmonary markers when interpreting exercise capacity.

records.title: Supporting world class innovative research – how the UK Clinical Trials Accelerator Platform (CTAP) business development strategy is advancing new treatments for cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: D. Haworth1, R. Brendell1, C. Walter1, O. Castellucci1, H. Barr2, L. Allen1
records.affiliations_text: 1Cystic Fibrosis Trust, Research and HealthCare Data Directorate, London, United Kingdom, 2University of Nottingham, Faculty of Medicine and Health Sciences, Nottingham, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
The aim of business development activity at Cystic Fibrosis Trust is to attract global sponsors and increase the number of commercial clinical trials aimed at improving the health of people with CF. It is guided by the Trust’s four research goals and forms part of a global collaboration of accelerating CF research alongside the European Cystic Fibrosis Society and the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation.

The Trust’s business development activity includes horizon scanning and monitoring the global CF pipeline. The objective is to work with global sponsors to maintain a broad and dynamic portfolio of CF research which covers a range of therapeutic areas and different trial phases. The aim is to initiate conversations with commercial sponsors early in their trial development process, working closely with them through their planning stages and offering ongoing support throughout the life of the clinical trial. The Trust has recently launched a cohesive Industry support package, CF Accelerate, to bring together our commercial services to assist Industry sponsors. records.title: Exploring perspectives of patients receiving outpatient palliative care alongside usual CF treatment: A qualitative study within a Randomized Controlled Trial

person.department: Department of Family and Preventive Medicine

records.authors_text: M. Uehling1, J. Emery2, J. Lowers2, D. Kavalieratos2
records.affiliations_text: 1Emory University, Department of Sociology, Atlanta, United States, 2Emory University, Department of Family and Preventive Medicine, Atlanta, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Many people with cystic fibrosis have significant unmet physical, emotional, and care planning needs. Prior work has indicated that palliative care may improve a range of outcomes for people with CF. The present RCT compared the addition of specialty palliative care to outpatient CF clinic care vs usual care at five North American sites. Participants received four outpatient telehealth palliative care visits over 12 months, with visits focusing on needs assessment, symptom management, and advanced care planning.

Methods: We conducted semi-structured interviews with 48 participants. Interview questions centered on general experiences in the study, perceptions of the role of palliative care, and their relationships with the palliative care clinician compared to usual CF treatment.

Results: Participants generally reported experiencing significant benefit from outpatient palliative care, specifically in the domains of care coordination, emotional and psychological stress, advanced care planning, and physical symptom burden. Participants varied significantly in which domains they experienced the greatest benefit. Many participants noted that a strong relationship with their clinician had a positive impact on their overall experience with palliative care, regardless of symptom burden. Some participants furthermore noted that the palliative care clinician was able to address long-standing or previously unaddressed symptoms or challenges of their illness, due to the open-ended nature of the visits, the less time-constrained structure of the conversations, and the close relationships with the clinicians. Finally, the vast majority of participants indicated they would recommend palliative care to other CF patients after their experiences in the study.

Conclusions: People with CF found adjunctive specialist palliative care helpful for addressing ongoing symptoms and other challenges of CF not addressed in usual care.

records.title: Exploring the experiences of healthcare professionals recruiting infants with cystic fibrosis into research: a survey based study

person.title: Research Service Lead
person.institution: Royal Brompton & Harefield Hospitals, Part of Guys and St Thomas’ Trust

records.authors_text: C. Saunders1,2, R. Dobra2,1, M. Abkir1,2, J. Davies2,1
records.affiliations_text: 1Royal Brompton & Harefield Hospitals, Part of Guys and St Thomas’ Trust, Cystic Fibrosis, London, United Kingdom, 2National Heart and Lung Institute, Imperial College London, Cf&CLI, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Research in infants with CF (iwCF) is imperative to understand pathophysiology in the early months and to ensure safe, effective treatments can be started early. There are several observational and interventional studies active in iwCF, however infant research poses practical and ethical challenges. We aimed to understand the experiences of research active healthcare professionals (HCPs) to support recruitment of iwCF to studies.

Methods: An anonymous survey was distributed via Qualtrics to UK-based HCPs with experience recruiting iwCF to research Apr-May ‘25. Closed & open-ended questions were organised around five themes.

Results: Respondents (n=23) highlighted the importance of navigating recruitment of iwCF appropriately but flagged that training rarely focusses on skills needed to recruit infants/families. Respondents shared facilitators/barriers to recruiting iwCF. Research participation can provide families with hope following a CF diagnosis. Comprehensive knowledge and strong communication between clinical/care teams, allowing adequate time to consider participation, approaching families at a suitable time, accommodating families’ needs & an environment in which research is valued were highlighted as key to successful recruitment of iwCF. Respondents reported that these can be supported by staff training & effective collaboration between research/care teams. Complex studies, language barriers & poor principal investigator engagement were identified as hindering recruitment, representing key, measurable targets for improvement.

Conclusions: Studies in iwCF are critical to optimise care. Ways to support recruitment may include developing training specific to recruiting/consenting iwCF and their families. Increasing awareness of barriers to participation may reveal tangible strategies to overcome such challenges. Characterising the team dynamics associated with successful recruitment of iwCF to research may guide others to optimise interactions.

records.title: Eliciting clinical trial estimands for cystic fibrosis: a Bayesian framework

person.institution: Université Paris Cité, Inserm, Inria, UMRS1346, HeKA

records.authors_text: W. Shin1,2, M. Ursino1, D. Muilwijk3, C.K. van der Ent3, I. Huys2, S. Zohar1
records.affiliations_text: 1Université Paris Cité, Inserm, Inria, UMRS1346, HeKA, Paris, France, 2KU Leuven, Department of Pharmaceutical and Pharmacological Sciences, Leuven, Belgium, 3University Medical Center Utrecht, Wilhelmina Children's Hospital, Department of Pediatric Pulmonology, Utrecht, Netherlands
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Since its introduction in the ICH E9 (R1) guideline, estimands have been considered an important element in designing clinical trials. While the use of classical and well-known estimands is straightforward, the building of new ones lacks detailed methodological guidance, and this may be attributable to the limited usage of the estimand framework in more complex clinical trials. In our study, we propose a framework for constructing estimands using expert elicitation and Bayesian statistical models.

Methods: We designed a two-stage elicitation process to obtain expert opinions on organoids and on estimand attributes under prespecified scenarios. Using the data, we applied a series of hierarchical joint Bayesian statistical models to identify appropriate estimand attributes that showed the highest relative rankings.

Results: Ten individuals from the ORGESTRA consortium provided opinions, primarily regarding organoids, for designing four clinical trial scenarios during the first-stage elicitation. Next, 39 participants, recruited mainly from the European cystic fibrosis networks, contributed expert input on estimand attributes. Across the four scenarios, FEV1, LCI (lung clearance index), and pulmonary exacerbations were selected, either individually or in combinations of two, based on their rankings. Discontinuation of treatment due to lack of improvement was identified as the most likely, and death as the least likely, intercurrent event in all the four scenarios. Full estimand attributes were constructed based on the selected endpoints and intercurrent events.

Conclusion: This study demonstrates a framework for establishing clinical trial estimands using Bayesian expert elicitation. With this framework, we intend to support future clinical studies involving novel cystic fibrosis treatments and innovative biological platforms, such as organoids.

records.title: Reduce and reform: reducing bureaucracy in clinical trials: European guidance
records.authors_text: K. Hill1,2, R. Doeswijk3
records.affiliations_text: 1Queen's University, Belfast, United Kingdom, 2European Cystic Fibrosis Society, Karup, Denmark, 3European Hematology Association, The Hague, Netherlands
records.abstract_text: Excessive bureaucracy in clinical trials burdens investigators and limits patient access to innovative treatments. The ECFS is part of the cross-disciplinary Coalition for Reducing Bureaucracy in Clinical Trials which was founded in 2020 by medical societies and patient advocates. The coalition developed new EU-level recommendations to streamline regulatory processes, improve safety reporting and make informed consent more patient-centred. These include: A: Regulatory: 1. harmonising clinical trial processes across the EU: streamlining the EU clinical trial assessment framework (coordinating the Reporting Member State training); aligning informed consent form requirements; establishing a European fast-track mechanism for public health emergencies; harmonising contract writing and negotiation; facilitating direct upload of hospital records into a European database. 2. Improving proportionality in regulatory requirements and the application process: extending the definition of non-interventional clinical studies; case-by-case assessment of low-intervention clinical trials; reducing regulatory barriers to paediatric and critical care research; flexible deadlines for academic sponsors during the clinical application process; streamlining patient consent with digital signatures. 3. Reducing CTR ambiguity and enhancing comprehension: clarifying reporting roles for serious breaches & facilitating access to guidance and targeted advice on regulatory requirements. B: Safety reporting: 1. Harmonising and simplifying adverse event reporting; 2. making use of the protocol to reduce excessive reporting from investigators to sponsors/CROs; 3. following the CTR and guidelines to reduce excessive reporting from sponsors/CROs to investigators. C: Informed Consent: 1. Use of appendices for supplementary information; 2. Focusing on the most frequent side-effects; 3. Use of visual aids. These recommendations can shape a more efficient and patient-centred future for clinical research.
