records.title: Access for all – how CTAP is ensuring everyone with CF in the UK has opportunities to take part in research
records.authors_text: O.V. Castellucci1, R. Brendell1, D. Haworth1, G. Wilson1, S. Sketchley1, M. Kisanga1, L. Cameron1, C. Walter1
records.affiliations_text: 1Cystic Fibrosis Trust, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
With support from the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation Cystic Fibrosis Trust launched the Clinical Trials Accelerator Platform (CTAP) in 2017. In collaboration with the European Cystic Fibrosis Society’s Clinical Trials Network CTAP has built a nationwide network consisting of 25 Cystic Fibrosis (CF) centres with 26 trial coordinators, providing a robust infrastructure and resourcing to increase capacity for CF clinical research across the UK.

CTAP has developed an efficient and collaborative national recruitment model that advocates collaboration between all UK CF centres to broaden access of CF clinical research to the UK CF community. Several projects have been facilitated by CTAP to support this model:

Championship Scheme – encourages CTAP trial coordinators to collaborate with regional CF centres and clinics to establish referral pathways and share study opportunities

Regional Networks – four networks spanning geographically significant areas (TransPennine, London, Southwest England, Scotland and Northen England) bring together CF centres to discuss study opportunities and referral of patients between centres for research participation on a regular basis.

Other CTAP initiatives to ensure fair and equitable access to CF clinical research for the community, include the creation of the Trials Tracker, an online database listing CF studies in set-up and open to recruitment. In addition, the CTAP Diversity in Clinical Trials project is exploring ways under-represented groups of the UK CF community can learn about research opportunities, producing information resources on taking part in research which have been translated into four languages.

Since launching 9 years ago the CTAP centre network now covers approximately 90% of the UK CF population and has supported over 6,200 study enrolments across nine therapeutic areas. CTAP is confident that the above initiatives will continue to ensure fair and equitable access to clinical research to the UK CF population.

records.title: Discontinuing therapy in children with cystic fibrosis on CFTR modulators

person.institution: Hospital de Santa Maria, Unidade Local de Saúde de Santa Maria

records.authors_text: M. Ferreira Duarte1, M. Lima1, C. Constant2, L. Pereira2
records.affiliations_text: 1Hospital de Santa Maria, Unidade Local de Saúde de Santa Maria, Serviço Pediatria Médica, Departamento Pediatria, Lisboa, Portugal, 2Hospital de Santa Maria, Unidade Local de Saúde de Santa Maria, Unidade de Pneumologia Pediátrica, Serviço Pediatria Médica, Departamento Pediatria, Lisboa, Portugal
records.abstract_text:
Background: The introduction of highly effective cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) modulators has shifted the treatment paradigm of cystic fibrosis (CF). Reducing treatment burden is now a priority for patients/caregivers and healthcare professionals.However, guidance for CF therapy stepdown is not standardized. We aimed to evaluate the impact of dornase alfa (DA) discontinuation on pulmonary function, quality of life (QoL), and the frequency of respiratory exacerbations in clinically stable paediatric CF patients receiving CFTR modulators.

Methods: Longitudinal observational study conducted at a CF reference centre. Fifty-four children with CF were included; 29 clinically stable patients discontinued DA. Spirometry was assessed before and after discontinuation, with a minimum follow-up of six months. QoL was evaluated using the CF Questionnaire-Revised (CFQ-R). Respiratory exacerbations requiring antibiotic therapy were analysed before and after DA discontinuation using intra-individual analysis. Descriptive analysis was done.

Results: DA discontinuation was not associated with clinically significant pulmonary function decline. Mean ppFEV₁, ppFVC, and FEV₁/FVC values were similar before and after discontinuation (change in ppFEV1 −0.34 %; in ppFVC −2.14% and FEV₁/FVC +0.006). QoL scores remained stable, with no significant pre- and post-discontinuation differences. In the three years prior to discontinuation, patients experienced a mean of three respiratory exacerbations per year. After discontinuation, five patients experienced a single exacerbation requiring antibiotic therapy, with no hospitalizations recorded.

Conclusions: In clinically stable CF children receiving highly effective CFTR modulators, DA discontinuation appears to be a safe short- to mid-term strategy, with no relevant negative impact on pulmonary function or QoL . This encourages a more personalized approach to disease management and treatment burden reduction.

person.title: MD
person.institution: Adult Cystic Fibrosis Unit, National Reference Centre for Congenital Disorders (CRENADECER), BPS

records.authors_text: M.A. Rey1, A. Arriola1, A. Licio1, D. Murillo1, C. Mosteiro1, S. Guillen1, M. Silva1, L. Ferro1, M.C. Pinchak1
records.affiliations_text: 1Adult Cystic Fibrosis Unit, National Reference Centre for Congenital Disorders (CRENADECER), BPS, Montevideo, Uruguay
records.abstract_text:
Background: Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) leads to rapid improvements in lung function in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). However, real-world data on the long-term trajectory and durability of lung function response beyond the first year remain limited.

Objectives: To evaluate the longitudinal trajectory of percent predicted forced expiratory volume in one second (ppFEV1) up to 36 months after ETI initiation in routine clinical practice.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective observational study including pwCF who initiated ETI at a single CF center and completed at least 12 months of treatment. Lung function was assessed at baseline and at 12, 18, 24, and 36 months. Changes in ppFEV1 were analyzed using paired comparisons with an available-case approach, reporting the number of patients contributing data at each timepoint. Secondary outcomes included changes in sweat chloride concentration, hospitalizations, oxygen therapy use, and lung transplant listing at 12 months.

Results: Thirty-nine pwCF initiated ETI (mean age 31.4 ± 11.7 years; baseline ppFEV1 51.5 ± 22.7%). At 12 months (n=37), mean ppFEV1 increased by 11.4 percentage points (p<0.001). Among patients with available follow-up, ppFEV1 remained higher than baseline at 18 months (mean change +12.8; n=22; p<0.001), 24 months (+13.2; n=19; p<0.001), and 36 months (+12.5; n=11; p<0.001). The improvement observed at 12 months was maintained over time among patients with continued follow-up. At 12 months, significant reductions were observed in hospitalizations, oxygen therapy use, and active lung transplant listing (all p<0.05). Sweat chloride concentration also decreased significantly.

Conclusions: In this real-world cohort, ETI was associated with sustained improvement in lung function for up to 36 months. These findings support the long-term durability of ETI benefits beyond the first year of treatment in routine clinical practice.

records.title: Changes in Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 Second in patients with cystic fibrosis on elexacaftor /tezacaftor/ivacaftor since 2020. Data from a UK Cystic Fibrosis centre

person.title: Ms.
person.institution: University Hospitals of Leicester NHS Trust

records.authors_text: N. Mills1, P. Tinley2
records.affiliations_text: 1University Hospitals of Leicester NHS Trust, Cystic Fibrosis, Leicester, United Kingdom, 2University Hospitals of Leicester, Adult Cystic Fibrosis Service, Leicester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: Elexacaftor/Tezacaftor /Ivacaftor (ETI), a Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator modulator therapy for Cystic Fibrosis (CF), gained European authorisation in August 2020 and was available on the National Health Service in England shortly after. At the Leicester Adult CF Unit our first patients commenced ETI in March 2020 on a managed access scheme. Here we present data from our centre on Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 Second (FEV₁) for patients who commenced ETI in 2020.

Inclusion: 72 modulator naïve patients commenced ETI in 2020. All values are presented as change in FEV₁ % predicted and peak is defined as the highest FEV₁ % predicted.

Results: Mean change from baseline to peak FEV₁ % predicted was +20.36% (range +58 to -5). 1 patient had decreased lung function, 3 no change (defined as range +1 to -1 %) and 68 increased. Mean change in FEV₁ % predicted from peak to latest was -7.34 (range +1 to -29), 61 lost lung function and 11 remained stable. Mean change in FEV₁ % predicted from starting ETI to latest was +13.29% (range +51 to -9). 63 patients remained higher than baseline FEV₁, 2 were stable and 7 were lower than baseline.

Discussion: In our experience, most patients treated with ETI gained an initial significant increase in lung function however the majority (84.7%) also experienced a drop from their peak. Some patients were back to baseline and 9.7% of patients had a lower FEV₁ than their baseline. The cause for this loss of FEV₁ is likely to be multifactorial and individual. The natural disease course for patients with lower lung function and decreased CF treatment adherence, including with ETI, are possible contributing factors.

Limitations: This is data from one centre. Spirometry was obtained in clinic, not in a controlled research environment. The patient numbers are small, but represent our whole modulator naïve cohort who started ETI in 2020. The cause for the loss of FEV₁ needs further investigation.

person.biography: Nicky Mills is an advanced practitioner physiotherapist working in the Leicester Adult Cystic Fibrosis (CF) service, University Hospitals of Leicester, UK. She has led the adult CF physiotherapy service in Leicester for 23 years and has a particular interest in airway clearance, inhalation therapy and breathing pattern management in CF and bronchiectasis. She is also an independent prescriber. She has embedded the assessment and management of breathing pattern disorders in to routine CF care and presented conference abstracts reporting the incidence and presentation of breathing pattern disorders in CF, and is currently completing a service evaluation looking at clinical outcomes following management of breathing pattern disorders in patients attending the Leicester service. Nicky is the current chair of the Association of Chartered Physiotherapists in Cystic Fibrosis (ACPCF).

records.title: Beyond spirometry: forced oscillation technique for monitoring lung disease in cystic fibrosis on highly effective CFTR modulator therapy

person.department: Centre for Cystic Fibrosis Children and Adults, Clinic for Respiratory Diseases

records.authors_text: A. Vukić Dugac1, M. Đuzel2, M. Banić2, I. Bambir3, T. Odobašić Palković1, I. Barišić1, D. Tješić Drinković3
records.affiliations_text: 1University Hospital Centre Zagreb, Centre for Cystic Fibrosis Children and Adults, Clinic for Respiratory Diseases, Zagreb, Croatia, 2University Hospital Centre Zagreb, Clinic for Respiratory Diseases, Zagreb, Croatia, 3University Hospital Centre Zagreb, Centre for Cystic Fibrosis Children and Adults, Zagreb, Croatia
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Lung disease monitoring in cystic fibrosis (CF) relies on spirometry and body plethysmography. In the era of highly effective CFTR modulator therapy (HEMT), lung function is often preserved, increasing the need for sensitive non-invasive methods to detect subtle airway abnormalities. The forced oscillation technique (FOT) enables assessment of respiratory mechanics during tidal breathing. The aim of this study was to evaluate correlations between FOT parameters and conventional spirometric and plethysmographic indices in adults with CF.

Methods: Fifty-five adult CF patients receiving HEMT were included. All participants underwent spirometry, body plethysmography and FOT. FOT parameters included respiratory resistance (Rrs), reactance (Xrs), resonant frequency (Fres) and area of reactance (AX). Statistical analysis was performed using Spearman rank correlation (JASP, version 0.95.2.0); p < 0.05 was considered significant.

Results: The median age was 26.0 years; 56.4% were female, 76.3% were homozygous for F508del, and 62% had normal spirometric lung function. FOT parameters showed significant correlations with airflow obstruction and air trapping. Rinsp and Rexp at 5 Hz, X5insp and AX correlated negatively with FEV₁/FVC (r = −0.57, −0.51, −0.44 and −0.51, respectively; all p < 0.001). Reactance-based parameters (AX and Fres) correlated positively with RV/TLC (r up to 0.57, p < 0.001). Correlations with MMEF were less consistent, while correlations with PEF were weak or absent. Significant correlations with FEV₁ were also observed (r up to −0.59, p < 0.001), although associations were stronger with FEV₁/FVC and RV/TLC.

Conclusion: In adults with CF receiving HEMT, FOT provides a rapid, non-invasive assessment of airway mechanics and may serve as a useful complementary tool for routine lung disease monitoring when conventional spirometric measures are preserved.

records.title: The real-life efficacy of ETI therapy in young children with cystic fibrosis and at least one F508del allele
records.authors_text: K. Walicka-Serzysko1,2, M. Postek1,2, J. Milczewska1,2, K. Zybert1,2, A. Wołkowicz1,2, U. Borawska-Kowalczyk1,2, Ł. Woźniacki1,2, D. Sands1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Institute of Mother and Child, Cystic Fibrosis Department, Warsaw, Poland, 2Paediatric Hospital, Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Dziekanow Lesny, Poland
records.abstract_text:
Background: Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) has proven efficacy in clinical trials in individuals with cystic fibrosis (CF), including the paediatric population. However, real-world data in young children is limited, and the consistency of outcomes with older age groups remains to be established.

Objective: This post-approval, retrospective, single-centre study aimed to assess the effects of ETI on CFTR biomarkers and lung function over 6 months of clinical use in Polish paediatric patients.

Methods: In CF children aged 2–12 years with at least one F508del allele who initiated ETI therapy between May and November 2025, demographic and clinical characteristics were analysed, including changes from baseline in sweat chloride (SwCl) concentration and lung clearance index 2.5 (LCI2.5) through 6 months.

Results: Among 128 patients receiving ETI therapy (mean age 7.3 ± 2.8 years), 61 patients (mean age 8.75 ± 2.4 years; 32 females; F508del homozygous/heterozygous: 28/33 ) with diagnostic-quality multiple-breath nitrogen washout and SwCl measurements were included. Mean LCI₂.₅ decreased significantly from baseline (7.98 ± 1.80) to 3 months (6.94 ± 1.20) and remained significantly lower at 6 months (7.04 ± 1.32; p < 0.001 vs baseline for both time points), with no significant difference between 3 and 6 months (p = 0.054). The mean change in LCI₂.₅ was −1.20 at 3 months and −0.89 at 6 months. SwCl concentration decreased significantly after 6 months of therapy (−33.3 mmol/L). No correlation was found between LCI₂.₅ and SwCl changes, and treatment response did not differ by genotype or sex.

Conclusions: In a real-world setting, ETI therapy in young children led to clinically meaningful reductions in SwCl concentration and LCI2.5 within 3 months, which were sustained at 6 months, indicating rapid improvements in lung function and CFTR biomarker response. These findings are consistent with clinical trial data and observations in the older population.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To evaluate the clinical response to elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor(ETI)in pediatric cystic fibrosis(CF)patients and to identify factors associated with limited or no treatment response in a real-world setting.

Methods: This retrospective study analyzed 90pediatric CFpatients treated with ETI for ≥3months. Genotype,sweat chloride(SwCl),pulmonary function(FEV₁),and anthropometric parameters were evaluated. Patients were classified as “responsive/responsive”(R/R) or “responsive/unresponsive”(R/U) based on ETI eligibility.Treatment response was evaluated according to the Canadian Clinical Consensus Guideline for CFTR Modulator Therapies.

records.title: Respiratory outcomes after one year of triple combination modulator therapy elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor in people with cystic fibrosis aged 2 to 5 years
records.authors_text: C. Rico Pérez1, A. Morales Tirado2, J. Quaresma Vázquez2, E. Blitz Castro2, A. Tabares González2, C. Gascón Galindo2, D. San Miguel2, A. Merino2, C.M. López Cárdenes2
records.affiliations_text: 1Hospital Ramón y Cajal, Paediatric Cystic Fibrosis Unit, Madrid, Spain, 2Hospital Ramón y Cajal, Madrid, Spain
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To evaluate the respiratory impact of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) treatment in people with Cystic Fibrosis (pwCF) aged 2 to 5 years. To describe baseline demographic and clinical characteristics.

Methods: single-center, prospective observational study including pwCF initiating ETI, with a year follow-up. Demographic, clinical, and microbiological data were collected. Respiratory cultures, pulmonary exacerbations (PEx), and antibiotic courses during the first year of ETI therapy were compared to the previous year. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS software.

Results: Data were obtained from 18 pwCF, with a median age of 3 years (IQR 2–4), 66.7% male. All were diagnosed via newborn screening; 27.8% were F508del homozygous. Pancreatic insufficiency was present in 88.9%; none had CF-related diabetes or liver disease. Previously, 22% had received a CFTR modulator. Lung function data were available for only 7 patients (median FEV1 0.93; IQR - 0.90–2.38).

Oxygen saturation remained normal during the follow-up period. Regarding PEx, a median of 2­ exacerbations per year (IQR 1–1.25) was recorded, with no significant differences before ETI (p>0.05). No significant modifications were observed in hospital admissions or oral antibiotic cycles (1, IQR 0-2), p>0.05. Sweat test (chloride concentration) showed a median of 31.5 (IQR: 15.5–38) with statistically significant results (p<0.05). Respiratory cultures showed microbiological changes, with increased Haemophilus influenzae and reduced Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

Conclusions: In this cohort, ETI did not significantly alter the number of pulmonary exacerbations, antibiotic requirements, or admissions compared to the previous year. A microbiological shift was observed, notably a reduction in P. aeruginosa. Larger studies with longer follow-up are necessary to confirm these results.

records.title: Two-year real-world effectiveness and safety of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor in a Colombian cystic fibrosis cohort.
records.authors_text: C. Vasquez Sagra1,2, M. Higuera Carrillo3,4, J. De la Hoz-Valle5,6, L. Varon Portela2, B. Rios1, M. Gantivar1, F. Bermejo1
records.affiliations_text: 1Hospital Infantil Universitario San José, Bogota, Colombia, 2Fundacion Universitaria Ciencias de la Salud, Bogota, Colombia, 3Universidad Nacional de Colombia, Pediatrics, Bogotá, Colombia, 4Universidad El Bosque, Bogota, Colombia, 5Fundacion Santa Fe de Bogota, Bogota, Colombia, 6Universidad de Los Andes, Bogotá, Colombia
records.abstract_text:
Objective: To describe long-term clinical outcomes and safety of ETI in a Colombian cohort of patients with CF.

Methods: We conducted a descriptive longitudinal study including patients with CF followed at a CF center (Hospital Infantil Universitario de San José in Bogotá) who completed 24 months of ETI treatment. Anthropometric measures and lung function were assessed quarterly, and liver function tests semiannually. Clinical data were collected during each visit of the cystic fibrosis clinic. Longitudinal changes were analyzed using mixed-effects models.

Results: Thirty-one patients were included; 70% were female, mean age at ETI initiation was 16.6 (±7.5) years, and 51.6% were <18 years. Pancreatic insufficiency was present in 93% of patients, cystic fibrosis–related diabetes in 25%, and chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection in 35%. Median ppFEV₁ improved from 51% (IQR 37–76) at baseline to 70% (IQR 54–93) at 24 months. A significant improvement in FEV₁ was observed from 3 months onward and remained sustained through 24 months (+15.7 percentage points; 95% CI 11.8–19.5; p<0.001). Improvements were greater in patients <18 years (+17.9% at 3 months and +18.6% at 24 months) compared with adults, who also showed significant improvement. Body mass index increased from 16.10 (IQR 14.60–17.75) to 18.85 (IQR 16.45–21.25) at 24 months, with an adjusted mean change of +2.28 (95% CI 1.79–2.77; p<0.001). Handgrip strength improved from 15.6 (IQR 12.03–21.8) to 18.45 (IQR 13.75–29.3), with an adjusted increase of +3.83 (95% CI 2.20–5.46; p<0.001). Liver enzymes remained stable; mild increases in bilirubin were observed without clinical relevance.

Conclusions: In this real-world Colombian cohort, ETI was associated with sustained improvements in pulmonary function, nutritional status, and muscle strength over two years, with an acceptable safety profile, despite challenges in treatment access and continuity.

records.title: Real-world outcomes of CFTR modulation in advanced cystic fibrosis lung disease - in a Portuguese cystic fibrosis reference centre

person.title: 5th year Pulmonology Resident
person.institution: North Lisbon University Hospital Centre, ULS Santa Maria, Lisbon, Portugal

records.authors_text: R. Silva1, E. Fragoso1,2, P. Azevedo1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1North Lisbon University Hospital Centre, ULS Santa Maria, Lisbon, Portugal, Pulmonology, Lisbon, Portugal, 2Faculdade de Medicina da Universidade de Lisboa, Lisbon, Portugal
records.abstract_text:
Background: Advanced cystic fibrosis lung disease (ACFLD) remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality among young people with cystic fibrosis (CF), despite highly effective CFTR modulators.

Objective: To study the eficacy and safety of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) in ACFLD.

Methods: Retrospective observational study including patients with ACFLD followed at the CF Reference Centre of Hospital de Santa Maria between March 2021 and December 2025 on treatment with ETI for at least 36 months.

Results: Of 78 adult patients followed at the centre, 11 were enrolled in the study. 54.5% were female; 72.7% were aged 18–39 years. Median age at initiation of ETI was 31 years. All patients carried at least one F508del mutation; two patients had prior exposure to Lumacaftor/Ivacaftor.

At baseline median FEV₁ was 0.95 L/35% of predicted. Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) was required in 36.4% of patients and non-invasive ventilation (NIV) in 9.1%. Prior to ETI initiation, hemoptysis was present in 36.4% of patients and recurrent pneumothorax in 18.2%.

After ETI initiation, lung function improved early. Median absolute FEV₁ change from baseline was +0.16 L at 3 months, +0.27 L at 6 months, peaking at +0.85 L at 9 months, +0.32 L at 12 months and maintained at 36 months (+0.32 L). Median sweat chloride decreased from 78 mmol/L pre-ETI to 32.5 mmol/L at 6 months. Nutritional status improved, with median BMI increasing from 21.1 kg/m² pre-ETI to 23.0 kg/m² at 12 months.

Clinical improvement allowed discontinuation of inhaled antibiotic therapy in 36.4% of patients.

Hemoptysis persisted in only one patient and no new pneumothoraces were recorded. One patient stopped LTOT, one patient underwent lung transplantation and one death occurred.

Conclusions: ETI was associated with early functional, biological and nutritional improvements followed by sustained stabilisation, supporting its use in ACFLD and potentially preventing the need for lung transplantation.

records.title: SNOT-22 scores for sino-nasal symptoms improved following elexecaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) introduction
records.authors_text: M. Thomas1, D.D Derry1, D.J Waine1
records.affiliations_text: 1University Hospitals Plymouth NHS Trust, Plymouth Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Plymouth, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
The SNOT- 22 (sino-nasal outcome test) questionnaire is a validated tool used to measure symptom severity in chronic rhinosinusitis, and the impact on quality of life.

Objectives: We tested the hypothesis that SNOT-22 score would improve after the introduction of elexecaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI). This has previously been documented in a retrospective review in Germany, but not with prospectively collected data.

Methods: SNOT-22 scores were recorded prospectively during annual reviews of adult patients with cystic fibrosis. We analysed these retrospectively, comparing the mean scores from 2018-2019 (pre ETI) and 2021-2025 (post ETI), using paired t-test for normally distributed paired data, Wilcoxon signed rank test for non-parametric paired data, and Mann-Whitney U test for non-paired non-parametric data.

Results: Of 72 patients in our centre with SNOT-22 scores, 31 patients had scores before and after the introduction of Kaftrio (mean age 39.3, SD 11.7, 74% male). Median score was 13.0 before ETI and 5.0 after (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.019). During the study period, 12 had at least one elevated total IgE (mean SNOT-22 score 16.5) and 19 had never had an elevated total IgE (mean SNOT-22 score 12.7), Mann-Whitney U-test p=0.027. No statistically significant improvement in score was seen when comparing pre-ETI and post-ETI within each of those groups.

Conclusions: SNOT-22 scores improved after the introduction of ETI therapy, though not to the degree expected. Scores were higher in atopic than non-atopic individuals.

The SNOT- 22 (sino-nasal outcome test) questionnaire is a validated tool used to measure symptom severity in chronic rhinosinusitis, and the impact on quality of life.
Objectives: We tested the hypothesis that SNOT-22 score would improve after the introduction of elexecaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI). This has previously been documented in a retrospective review in Germany, but not with prospectively collected data.
Methods: SNOT-22 scores were recorded prospectively during annual reviews of adult patients with cystic fibrosis. We analysed these retrospectively, comparing the mean scores from 2018-2019 (pre ETI) and 2021-2025 (post ETI), using paired t-test for normally distributed paired data, Wilcoxon signed rank test for non-parametric paired data, and Mann-Whitney U test for non-paired non-parametric data.

Median score was 13.0 before ETI and 5.0 after (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.019). During the study period, 12 had at least one elevated total IgE (mean SNOT-22 score 16.5) and 19 had never had an elevated total IgE (mean SNOT-22 score 12.7), Mann-Whitney U-test p=0.027. No statistically significant improvement in score was seen when comparing pre-ETI and post-ETI within each of those groups.
Conclusions: SNOT-22 scores improved after the introduction of ETI therapy, though not to the degree expected. Scores were higher in atopic than non-atopic individuals.

records.title: One-year effects of highly effective modulator therapy on lung function, anthropometric parameters, and lipid profile in children with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: A. Ünlü1, I. Bilgiç1, M. Kürtül Çakar1, G. Akca Dinç1, H. Yetişgin1, Ç. Yıldırım1, G.D. Tuğcu1, D. Ademhan Tural2, S. Eryılmaz Polat1, G. Cinel2
records.affiliations_text: 1Ankara Bilkent City Hospital, Pediatric Pulmonology, Ankara - Çankaya, Turkey, 2Ankara Yıldırım Beyazıt University Facuty of Medicine, Pediatric Pulmonology, Ankara - Çankaya, Turkey
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The aim of this study was to evaluate the effects of the highly effective modulator treatment (HEMT) on lipid profiles in children with cystic fibrosis (CF).

Methods: This retrospective cohort study includes 29 children with CF who have received HEMT for at least 1 year. Clinical, anthropometric, spirometric, and lipid parameters were compared at baseline and after one year of treatment.

Results: Descriptive characteristics of the patients are given in Table 1. After one year, BMI increased significantly from 15.7 to 16.2 kg/m² (p = 0.043), whereas the BMI Z-score remained stable (p = 0.259). Pulmonary function improved significantly: forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) lt, FEV1%, and FEV1 Z-score all increased (p < 0.05 for all), as did forced vital capacity (FVC) (L) and FVC Z-score (p < 0.001), while FVC % showed no significant difference (Table 2). Among lipid parameters, only high-density lipoprotein (HDL) increased significantly, from 42 to 46 mg/dL (p = 0.044); low-density lipoprotein (LDL), very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL), total cholesterol, and triglycerides did not change significantly. Changes in lipid parameters did not differ between children with and without BMI increase.

Conclusions: CFTR modulator therapy in children leads to significant improvements in lung function and nutritional status without inducing an atherogenic lipid profile. The selective rise in HDL, together with stable LDL and triglycerides, suggests a metabolically favorable effect of CFTR modulation that is independent of BMI gain.

records.title: Development and validation of a human scalp hair analysis for determining long-term exposure to CFTR modulators

person.title: PharmD
person.institution: University of Groningen, University Medical Center Groningen

records.authors_text: C.M. Hansen1,2, A.M.A Wessels1, P.M. van den Bemt1, J.F. van Boven1,2, D.J. Touw1,2,3
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Groningen, University Medical Center Groningen, Clinical Pharmacy and Pharmacology, Groningen, Netherlands, 2Medication Adherence Expertise Center of the northern Netherlands (MAECON), Groningen, Netherlands, 3University of Groningen, Department of Pharmaceutical Analysis, Groningen Research Institute of Pharmacy (GRIP), Groningen, Netherlands
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance regulator (CFTR) modulators (elexacaftor (ELX), tezacaftor (TEZ), ivacaftor (IVA), lumacaftor (LUM) are the cornerstone of CF’s pharmacologic treatment. While adherence to CFTR modulators is critical for effectiveness, a reliable noninvasive method for determining long-term medication adherence is lacking. Direct measurements such as plasma only reflect a snapshot of last day’s adherence and are invasive to perform. Therefore, we aimed to develop and validate a method for quantification of CFTR modulators in human scalp hair.

Methods: LC-MSMS was used for quantification. For method development scalp hair from people with CF (pwCF) using CFTR modulators was used. Blanc hair for quality control (QC) and calibration samples was donated by healthy volunteers. Solvents to remove external contamination, extraction and extraction times were tested. After method optimization, validation was carried out following guidelines from FDA, EMA and Society of Hair testing (SoHT).

Results: Isopropanol showed to be the best washing solvent, with methanol being the most optimal extraction solvent. Optimization of the extraction time resulted in a 90-minute extraction time using ball mill. Selectivity of the developed method was confirmed for IVA, its metabolite IVA-M1, ELX, LUM and TEZ. For linearity, all calibration curves met the acceptance criteria of bias less than 15%. Accuracies of the QC samples for IVA, IVA-M1 and LUM did not comply with FDA/EMA criteria of being between 85% and 115%. ELX and TEZA accuracies were between 86.2% and 98.5% and complied. Precision for ELX and TEZ (LLOQ, LOW, MEDIUM and HIGH) ranged between 1.0-7.0% and 0.0-2.7% (intra cv’s), and 3.4-6.6% and 2.7-7.4% (inter cv’s).

Conclusion: A hair analysis method for CFTR modulators was developed and validated, demonstrating that elexacaftor and tezacaftor can be reliably quantified in human hair.

person.biography:
In 2019, I obtained my PharmD at the University in Groningen (The Netherlands). Currently, besides my research work as a PhD student, I am working as a clinical and outpatient pharmacist as part of the multidisciplinary CF teams of the University Medical Center Groningen for adults and children.
I help patients with optimal management of their CF drugs, support their adherence to therapy, deal with side effects and interactions and optimise their dose in close collaboration with the pulmonologists and pediatricians. Many patients face difficulties with taking their CF drugs correctly and on time and therefore in my PhD I am investigating new ways to support CF patients with adherence, ultimately maximizing patient benefits from treatment at minimum side effects.

records.title: The “last families” in cystic fibrosis: equity, non-responders, and the translational imperative
records.authors_text: C. Landon1, P. Lyanage2, J. Lee2, K. Arora2, A. Naren2
records.affiliations_text: 1Ventura County Medical Center, Pedistrics, Ventura, United States, 2Cedars Sinai, Los Angeles, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Highly effective CFTR modulators have transformed outcomes for approximately 90% of patients in the United States. Individuals with Class I mutations, disproportionately Hispanic and Black, derive no benefit from these therapies and continue to experience the full burden of disease. These “last families,” identified from birth as non-responders, represent a growing equity and translational gap.

Methods: Through a CFF Research Development Program, our rural CF center partnered with Cedars-Sinai to implement a patient-derived nasal epithelial “nose-on-a-chip” platform for individualized drug testing. We conducted a longitudinal clinical and social evaluation of a 19-year-old Hispanic male with a Class I R75X/R75X genotype. Multidisciplinary interventions included digital adherence monitoring, pharmacy surveillance, home visits, and intensive social work engagement. Social vulnerability was assessed using the Childhood Opportunity Index and Area Deprivation Index.

Results: Engagement with conventional care was delayed due to prior sibling mortality, reliance on traditional healing practices, and immigration-related concerns. Social vulnerability indices demonstrated high structural disadvantage. With culturally concordant support, the family consented to nasal epithelial sampling. In vitro testing of a five-drug combination demonstrated restoration of CFTR protein production not achievable with approved modulator therapies.

Conclusions: This case highlights the emerging population of CF non-responders who remain excluded from therapeutic advances and are disproportionately affected by structural inequities. Equity-centered translational platforms and culturally responsive engagement strategies are essential.

Registry Implications: CF registries should stratify patients by therapeutic responsiveness, incorporate social vulnerability indices, and track participation in individualized translational platforms to prevent systematic underrepresentation of unmet needs.

Results: Engagement with conventional care was delayed due to prior sibling mortality, reliance on traditional healing practices, and immigration-related concerns. Social vulnerability indices demonstrated high structural disadvantage. With culturally concordant support, the family consented to nasal epithelial sampling. In vitro testing of a five-drug combination demonstrated restoration of CFTR protein production not achievable with approved modulator therapies.
Conclusions: This case highlights the emerging population of CF non-responders who remain excluded from therapeutic advances and are disproportionately affected by structural inequities. Equity-centered translational platforms and culturally responsive engagement strategies are essential.
Registry Implications: CF registries should stratify patients by therapeutic responsiveness, incorporate social vulnerability indices, and track participation in individualized translational platforms to prevent systematic underrepresentation of unmet needs.

records.abstract_text:
Aim: To assess the dynamics of infection and survival of adult patients with cystic fibrosis (CF) in groups of patients with chronic respiratory tract infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa(Pa) and Burkholderia cepacia complex(Bcc); to compare the group of Pa and Bcc by age, age of diagnosis, genotype, anthropometric parameters, spirometry, frequency of major complications of CF, volume of the received therapy.

Methods: To analyse survival, we compared groups of adult patients with chronic Рa/Bсс infection (852 patients in total, 188 of them with Bсс) observed from November 1992 to December 2025. Survival was assessed using the Kaplan-Meier curve. A one-time analysis of Рa/Всс groups was conducted in December 2025 (a total of 862 patients, 89 of them with Всс).

Results: Тhe median survival for the Pa/Bcc was 28,1 [95%CI: 25,21-30,98] and 12,6 years [95%CI: 10,95-14,32](the differences are significant: LogRank Test: χ2 = 97,7, p<0,001). The proportion of patients who survived the period of 3,5,7,10, and 15 years for the Ра/Bсс groups: 98,5% and 89,1%, 95,2% and 82,3%, 92,4% and 77,2%, 82,1% and 59,0%, and 72,8% and 24,6%, respectively. A one-time analysis show no significant differences between the Pa/Bcc groups. In the Всс group, the age of diagnosis was significantly lower: 1,2 years against 4,3 years in the Pa group (p=0,001). The Bcc group is also characterized by a lower prevalence of gastroesophageal reflux disease (p=0,053) and a significantly higher percentage of patients taking ursodeoxycholic acid(UDCA)(p=0,004).

Conclusion: Bcc infection significantly reduces the life expectancy of patients with CF. When comparing groups of patients with Pa/Bcc infection, no significant differences were found in the main parameters of the severity of the disease, however, the Bcc group is characterized by an earlier diagnosis and a high percentage of patients taking UDCA.

records.title: Impact of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor on neutrophil homeostasis: evidence from 12-month therapy in cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: V. Cvejoska Cholakovska1,2, E. Krsteska1, A. Andreevska Stepanovska1, L. Spirevska1, A. Jovanovska3,2, S. Fushtikj Naceva1,2

Cyril and Methodius University in Skopje, Skopje, North Macedonia, The Republic of, 3University Children's Clinic, Department of Haematology and Oncology, Skopje, North Macedonia, The Republic of
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is characterized by persistent neutrophil-driven inflammation, which plays a central role in progressive lung disease and systemic inflammatory burden. While the triple cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) modulator therapy elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) has significantly improved lung function and clinical outcomes, its effects on circulating inflammatory markers, particularly peripheral blood neutrophil counts, remain insufficiently characterized.

Methods: We conducted a prospective, observational study including 56 people with CF (pwCF), aged 8–41 years. Peripheral blood neutrophil counts were measured at baseline and after 12 months of ETI therapy. As data were non-normally distributed, paired comparisons were performed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Effect size was estimated using rank-biserial correlation. A responder analysis was conducted based on relative neutrophil reduction, and associations between baseline neutrophil counts and treatment-related changes were assessed using Spearman rank correlation.

Results: The median absolute neutrophil count decreased from approximately 5.6 ×10⁹/L at baseline to 3.4 ×10⁹/L after 12 months of therapy, representing a 40–45% reduction. The median absolute change was −2.2 ×10⁹/L, with a large effect size (r ≈ 0.6). The reduction was statistically significant (p < 0.001) and observed in more than 90% of patients; approximately 80% achieved a clinically relevant reduction (≥20%). Comparable reductions were observed across genotypes and in both sexes. Baseline neutrophil counts were moderately correlated with the magnitude of reduction (ρ ≈ 0.5, p < 0.01). Neutrophil counts remained within normal reference ranges.

Conclusion: ETI therapy is associated with significant and sustained reductions in circulating neutrophils, a marker of systemic inflammation, supporting its systemic anti-inflammatory effect.

records.abstract_text:
Aim: To evaluate the microbiological characteristics of adult patients with chronic Bсс infection, including those taking CFTR modulators.

Methods: The analysis included 188 adult patients with Bcc, who were observed at the CF center from November 1992 to December 2025. The onset of infection was considered the time when Bcc appeared in a sputum culture, followed by chronic infection. Survival was assessed using the Kaplan-Meier curve. A one-time analysis was performed in 89 patients with Bcc infection as of December 2025.

Results: As a result of intraspecific typing by molecular genetic methods, it was shown that the main type of Bcc in the Moscow CF Center is B.cenocepacia- 84%, followed by B.multivorans- 7%, B.gladioli- 3%, B.contaminans- 3% and B.stabilis- 2%. At the same time, B.cenocepacia is represented by hospital genotypes ST709- 85% and ST208-14%(ST-sequence type). The median survival from the moment of infection with genotypes ST709 + ST208/other ST was 11,9 years [95% CI: 10,6-13,2] and 15,8 years [95% CI: 14,8-16,8] (p=0,5). A one-time analysis showed that 72% of patients with Bcc receive CFTR-modulators, of which 86% are on the three-component modulator. Analysis of sputum in patients on CFTR-modulator therapy showed that Bcc is not detected by standard microbiological culture methods in 8% of patients,in 92% there is a decrease in the degree of Bcc colonization in sputum and an increase in microbial species diversity.

Conclusion: The main type of Bcc in Russia is B.cenocepacia, which is represented by hospital genotypes ST709 and ST208, with a predminance of ST709. Infection with hospital genotypes ST709 and ST208 significantly limits the life expectancy of patients infected with them. During CFTR-modulator therapy, a decrease in the sputum contamination with B. cenocepacia and an increase in microbial species diversity were observed in most patients, as well as several cases of absence of Bcc seeding in sputum culture.

records.title: The effect of Staphylococcus aureus in the lung epithelial barrier in cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: A. Montes Gomez1, N. Robinson1, R. Carvajal Quisalema1, R. Gray1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Glasgow, School of Infection and Immunity, Glasgow, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: The bronchial epithelium acts as first defence against a wide range of exogenous substances and pathogens by forming a barrier that prevents them from penetrating the tissue. The epithelial barrier function is maintained by apical junctional proteins (AJP) that form between neighbouring cells and consist of apical tight junctions (TJ) such as claudins, occludin and JAM-A and adherent junctions (AJ) such as E-cadherin. People with cystic fibrosis (CF) have a weakened lung epithelial barrier; at the same time, CF patients are also more susceptible to infections such as Staphylococcus aureus(Sa), in part due to this same weakened barrier. It has been proposed that CFTR interacts with some AJPs to help form the barrier in the lung epithelium and they miss-localise in the absence of CFTR, contributing to the weakened barrier, however, the effect of the Sa at the barrier level and AJPs in CF has not been investigated.

Aim: 1. To determine the effect of Staphylococcus aureus infection in TJ and AJ proteins in CF cells at the protein level and their cellular localisation.

Methods: CF and non-CF cells are infected with Staphylococcus aureus strain USA300 and TJ and AJ proteins are evaluated at the mRNA and protein level. Cells are also infected and the cellular localisation of TJ and AJ proteins are evaluated by immunofluorescence.

Results: No differences in the expression of the TJ proteins or AJ at the mRNA or protein level were observed. However, we found that upon Sa infection, in the absence of CFTR, some cells express more E-cadherin and JAM-A, possibly as a compensatory mechanism to tighten the barrier. On the contrary, occludin is observed at high levels at the membrane of non-CF cells and decreases drastically upon infection. This protein is observed already in low levels in CF cells and seems to almost completely disappear upon infection.

Conclusion: Staphylococcus aureus causes miss-localisation of AJPs with a more severe effect in CF cells.

records.authors_text: M. Conte1,2, F. Nicola1,2, M. Contarini3, G. Saldarini4, C. Ferrari2, C. Britto-Leon5, F. Blasi3, D.M. Cirillo2, S. De Pretis4, A. Gramegna3, N.I. Lorè2
records.affiliations_text: 1Università Vita - Salute San Raffaele, Emerging Bacterial Pathogens Unit, Milan, Italy, 2IRCCS San Raffaele Scientific Institute, Emerging Bacterial Pathogens Unit, Milan, Italy, 3Fondazione IRCCS Ca' Granda Ospedale Maggiore Policlinico, Department of Pathophysiology and Transplantation - Internal Medicine Department, Respiratory Unit and Cystic Fibrosis Adult Center, Milan, Italy, 4IRCCS San Raffaele Institute, Center for Omics Sciences, Milan, Italy, 5Yale University School of Medicine, Department of Internal Medicine, Division of Pulmonary, Critical Care, and Sleep Medicine, New Haven, United States
records.abstract_text:
People with cystic fibrosis (PwCF) are at high risk of Mycobacterium abscessus complex (MABSC) infection and show heterogeneous clinical outcomes, ranging from asymptomatic colonization to non-tuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease (NTM-PD), a chronic condition associated with progressive lung damage. While systemic immune signatures have improved disease characterization, local airway immune responses remain limited, highlighting the need for reliable biomarkers reflecting lung disease severity. Sputum represents an accessible surrogate of the airway microenvironment, although its application for high-resolution profiling is limited by viscosity and fixation-related constraints. Here, we applied an optimized single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) workflow to formalin-fixed sputum samples to resolve airway immune complexity in pwCF with NTM lung infection.

To do so, we collected 30 sputum samples from pwCF and stratified into three clinical groups (uninfected, MABSC-colonized, and MABSC pulmonary disease (MABSC-PD). Twenty-four samples were successfully profiled using the 10x Genomics Chromium platform and analyzed with Seurat. Sputum supernatants’ analysis for pro-inflammatory markers by Luminex technology is ongoing.

We identified fourteen transcriptionally distinct airway cell populations. Integration with publicly available CF airway datasets supported clustering robustness and cell-type annotation. Comparative analyses revealed enhanced immune activation signatures in neutrophils and inflammatory monocyte/macrophage subsets across disease groups. Recruited monocytes/macrophages displayed the highest number of differentially expressed genes in MABSC-PD compared with uninfected and colonized individuals.

Overall, scRNA-seq profiling of formalin-fixed sputum enables high-resolution characterization of airway immune responses in pwCF with NTM lung infection and supports the identification of tissues biomarkers associated with NTM-PD.

records.title: Tenascin-C in children with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: E.M. Karakuş1, D. Ademhan Tural2,3, Ç. Yıldırım3, I. Bilgiç3, G. Akça Dinç3, S. Eryılmaz Polat3, G.D. Tuğcu3, S. Erdoğan4, G. Cinel2,3
records.affiliations_text: 1Ankara Yildirim Beyazit University, Medical School, Ankara, Turkey, 2Ankara Yildirim Beyazit University, Pediatric Pulmonology, Ankara, Turkey, 3Ankara Bilkent City Hospital, Pediatric Pulmonology, Ankara, Turkey, 4Ankara Bilkent City Hospital, Biochemistry, Ankara, Turkey
records.abstract_text:
Objective-aim: Tenascin-C is an extracellular matrix protein involved with immunomodulatory properties that plays a role in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, tissue regeneration, and lung development. We aimed to investigate the role of tenascin-C in cystic fibrosis (CF).

Method: This is a cross-sectional, observational study that included 44 children with CF and 44 healthy subjects. Serum of Tenascin-C, interleukin (IL)-8, and neutrophil elastase (NE) were determined by the enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) method. Relationships between tenascin-C concentrations and clinical parameters in patients with CF were also evaluated. The study was granted by TUBİTAK 2209-A.

Results: There were no significant differences between patients and controls in age and gender (p=0.857 and p=0.829, respectively) (Table 1). NE concentrations were higher in the patient group than in healthy controls, and tenascin-C was higher in healthy controls (p=0.001 and p=0.016, resp.) (Table 2). However, there were no significant differences between groups according to IL-8 concentrations. There was a negative correlation between Tenascin-C and NE (rho=-0.457, p=0.002). However, tenascin-C levels did not correlate with age, gender, BMI, or laboratory parameters. Serum tenascin-C, NE, and IL-8 did not significantly differ between patients using modulators and those not using modulators.

Conclusion: This is the first study investigating tenascin-C levels in CF. Tenascin-C levels in CF patients were lower than in healthy controls. Serum tenascin-C levels play a limited role in CF inflammation. Further studies are necessary to determine this role.

records.title: High-dimensional spectral flow cytometry profiling reveals systemic immune dysregulation in pediatric cystic fibrosis

person.institution: Instituto de Investigación del Hospital Universitario La Paz
person.department: The Innate Immune Response Group - Immunomodulation Laboratory

records.authors_text: L. Bravo Robles1, P. Mata-Martínez1, G. Bıçakcıoğlu1, L. Hurtado-Navarro2, O. Fernández-Medina3, P. Almellones-Araiz3, L. Minute1, V. Terrón2, J. Fernández1, E. López-Collazo2,4,5, C. de Manuel-Gómez6, M. Ruiz de Valbuena-Maiz6, C. Calvo7, C. del Fresno8
records.affiliations_text: 1Instituto de Investigación del Hospital Universitario La Paz, The Innate Immune Response Group - Immunomodulation Laboratory, Madrid, Spain, 2Instituto de Investigación del Hospital Universitario La Paz, The Innate Immune Response Group - Tumor Immunology Laboratory, Madrid, Spain, 3Hospital Universitario La Paz, Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Endometriosis Unit, Madrid, Spain, 4Instituto de Salud Carlos III, CIBERES, CIBERINFEC, Madrid, Spain, 5UNIE University, Madrid, Spain, 6Hospital Universitario La Paz, Pediatric Pulmonology, Madrid, Spain, 7Hospital Universitario La Paz, Department of Pediatrics, Madrid, Spain, 8Instituto de Investigación del Hospital Universitario La Paz, The Innate Immune Response Group, Madrid, Spain
records.abstract_text:
Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a rare, life-limiting genetic disorder affecting 1 in 5000 newborns in Spain. CF arises from mutations that disrupt or abolish Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator (CFTR) protein function. The lungs are most severely affected due to thick mucus that impairs mucociliary clearance, leading to a self-perpetuating cycle of infection and inflammation. CFTR modulators have improved protein function and quality of life, but airway inflammation often persists, and their effect on immune-mediated inflammation remains unclear. Children with CF also exhibit intrinsic innate immune abnormalities; innate cells may be developmentally immature or functionally impaired, reducing bacterial clearance and promoting chronic inflammation from early life. Understanding these early immune alterations is crucial for novel therapies. Thus, we wanted to evaluate the immunological profile of circulating immune cells in pediatric patients with CF.

Using 1mL of peripheral blood from pediatric patients followed at La Paz University Hospital, we performed a comprehensive immunophenotyping with a 37-color full-spectrum flow cytometry panel designed for this study, rendering 371 immunological variables per patient. This panel assesses lineage, activation, and immune checkpoints (ICs) across T and B lymphocytes, NK and NKT cells, monocytes, dendritic cells, neutrophils, and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs).

Comparison with healthy donors identified over 50 immune parameters that differed significantly in pediatric CF patients, including a generalized downregulation of the PD-1/PD-L1 axis and other ICs, while population frequencies were unchanged.

Therefore, these spectral cytometry analyses distinguish pediatric CF patients from healthy children at the systemic level, revealing immune features that reflect clinically relevant aspects of disease. This work provides the foundation for future translational and therapeutic studies.

records.title: The IκB-kinase-β (IKKβ) inhibitor PS-1145 modulates inflammatory response and oxidative stress in F508del-CFTR airway epithelial cells
records.authors_text: C. Allegretta1, G. Cabrini2, O. Laselva1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Foggia, Clinical and Experimental Medicine, Foggia, Italy, 2University of Ferrara, Life Sciences and Biotechnologies, Ferrara, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Prolonged P. aeruginosa infections have been linked to chronic inflammation in Cystic Fibrosis (CF) lung, worsening the damage to lung tissue by neutrophil-derived reactive oxygen species (ROS) and proteases. Current anti-inflammatories are poorly effective and have dramatic side effects in people with CF (pwCF). Therefore, identifying innovative, effective, and safe drugs to restore redox balance and mitigate inflammation remains a critical unmet need.

Methods: We performed a dose-response of an IkB-kinase-b (IKKb) inhibitor, PS-1145, in F508del-CFTR CFBE cells and primary nasal epithelial (HNE) cells from pwCF bearing F508del mutation. Inflammatory and oxidative status were evaluated by detecting specific markers. We investigated pro-inflammatory cytokine gene expression and protein release (via RT-qPCR and ELISA) and assessed the antioxidant activity of the compound by measuring intracellular ROS levels (using a ROS-sensitive fluorescent probe) in both F508del-CFTR CFBE and HNE cells under inflammatory conditions.

Results: PS-1145 significantly reduced IL-6 and IL-8 levels (both mRNA and protein) in a dose-dependent manner in both CFBE and HNE cells. To further investigate the antioxidant activity of these compounds, we developed a high-throughput fluorometric assay to measure ROS levels using a ROS-sensitive fluorescent probe. We performed a dose-response of PS-1145 to investigate its antioxidant activity. Interestingly, PS-1145, exhibited antioxidant activity, in a dose-dependent manner, in F508del-CFTR CFBE cells treated with H₂O₂.

Conclusion: These findings provide strong evidence that PS-1145 can prevent redox imbalance and attenuate inflammation in CF airway epithelial cells, potentially limiting the drivers of chronic lung damage.

records.authors_text: R.E. Maher1, S. Weinberg2,3, Z.G. Şahin4, G. Einarsson5, F. Frost4, P. Barry3,2, J. Duckers6, S. Doe7, D. Peckham8, E. Caamaño Gutiérrez4, A. Jones3,2, M. Tunney5, A. Horsley3,2, E. Emmott1, R. Lord3,2
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Liverpool, Biochemistry, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 2University of Manchester, Manchester, United Kingdom, 3Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust, Manchester, United Kingdom, 4University of Liverpool, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 5Queen's University Belfast, Belfast, United Kingdom, 6All Wales Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Penarth, United Kingdom, 7Newcastle upon Tyne Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, Newcastle, United Kingdom, 8Leeds Institute of Medical Research, Leeds, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: Pulmonary exacerbations are a major cause of morbidity in cystic fibrosis and are commonly triggered by viral infection and dysregulated airway immune responses. The upper airway plays a key role in shaping responses to viral exposure and downstream lower airway inflammation. The nasal mucosa provides an accessible site in which upper airway immune processes may offer insight into mechanisms underlying pulmonary exacerbations.

Methods: Nasal mucosal lining fluid was collected from people with cystic fibrosis (PwCF; n=12) and age-matched healthy controls (n=8). These samples represent the initial participants from the CF-Tracker study; an ongoing study investigating pulmonary exacerbations, with longitudinal clinical data and viral exposures. Samples were analysed using liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry–based DIA proteomics. Multivariate, differential abundance and functional enrichment analyses were performed.

Results: Proteomic profiling demonstrated clear differences between PwCF and healthy controls. Principal component analysis showed group separation, most evident along the PC2 axis. Differential abundance analysis identified widespread alterations in protein expression in PwCF, with enrichment of pathways related to immune activation, metabolic reprogramming, and cellular stress responses. Proteins involved in intracellular protein transport and localisation were downregulated.

Conclusion: The nasal proteome captures disease-associated immune and metabolic alterations in cystic fibrosis, supporting the upper airway as a biologically informative compartment. These initial data provide a foundation for future analyses integrating nasal proteomics with longitudinal clinical data to define relationships between upper airway immune responses, viral exposures, and pulmonary exacerbation risk.

Funding: LifeArc / Cystic Fibrosis Trust Innovation Hub Network.

records.title: Phase 2 population pharmacokinetics (popPK) of verducatib (BI 1291583) in people with cystic fibrosis and non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis (CFBE and NCFBE)
records.authors_text: A. Henrich1, F. Gallais1, W. Sauter2, G. Benitez3, J. Korell3,4
records.affiliations_text: 1Pharmetheus AB, Uppsala, Sweden, 2Boehringer Ingelheim International GmbH, Ingelheim am Rhein, Germany, 3Boehringer Ingelheim Pharmaceuticals, Inc., Ridgefield, United States, 4Metrum Research Group, Boston, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Bronchiectasis, a chronic lung disease, is driven by dipeptidyl peptidase 1 (DPP1)-activated neutrophil serine proteases. Verducatib, a DPP1 inhibitor, reduced pulmonary exacerbation risk in people with NCFBE and had similar safety, PK and pharmacodynamic profiles in adults with CFBE and NCFBE in Phase (Ph) 2 studies (CLAIRAFLY® and AIRLEAF®). To support the verducatib dose in the Ph 3 AIRTIVITY™ study, a popPK model was developed to characterise and simulate exposure, and evaluate steady-state exposure, in adults with CFBE vs. NCFBE.

Methods: PopPK analysis, including covariates, was performed using NONMEM®. Individual parameter estimates of primary and secondary PK parameters for the Ph 2 population were derived from the final model. Exposure simulations evaluated the Ph 3 dose (verducatib 2.5 mg once daily).

Results: Overall, 288 people (63 healthy, 210 with NCFBE, 15 with CFBE) were included in the analysis (median age, 54.5 years; median weight, 65.1 kg; 55% male; 75% White). Visual predictive checks and exposure simulations showed no meaningful differences in CFBE and NCFBE steady-state exposure. The final two-compartment model included dose-dependent bioavailability, categorical clearance (CL higher at Day 1 and lower thereafter) and linear distribution.

Conclusion: The final PK model provided an adequate fit to the Ph 2 data. These results support the use of verducatib 2.5 mg in both those with CFBE and NCFBE in AIRTIVITY™; recruitment began in June 2025.

records.title: Asthma biologic therapy in patients with cystic fibrosis in an adult cystic fibrosis centre in the United Kingdom

person.institution: Royal Devon University Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust

records.authors_text: D. Crowle1, P. Mitchelmore1,2, N. Withers1, L. Dobson1
records.affiliations_text: 1Royal Devon University Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust, Exeter, United Kingdom, 2University of Exeter, Exeter, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Asthma is present in 8.9% of adult patients with cystic fibrosis (pwCF)1. Biological therapies have been used safely in the management of severe asthma in non-CF patients for a number of years. Use of these drugs in the CF population is limited thus far and there have been some anecdotal reports of CF patients deteriorating after starting them in other centres.

Methods: Patients in our adult CF centre who had been prescribed asthma biologics were retrospectively identified and data collected before and after biologic started. Data collected included demographics, oral corticosteroid (OCS) burden, infective exacerbation rate and lung function. This was done for each biologic if patients had taken multiple biologics.

Results: Demographical data is demonstrated in Table 1.

Benralizumab was taken by 3 patients, with all experiencing reduced number of OCS courses or maintenance steroid doses. Tezepelumab was taken by 3 patients, with reduced OCS courses reported in two of these patients. Median (IQR) months on benralizumab was 8 (6.0-31.5) and was 4 (3.5-5.5) on tezepelumab. There was no change in infective exacerbation rate. There was no significant change in median forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) after at least three months. There were no reported biologic-associated adverse reactions in any patient.

Conclusion: While our dataset is limited, there is no evidence of harm in the use of asthma biologics in these patients and most have reduced steroid burden. Further research is required to fully understand the use of these medicines in pwCF.

References: 1. UK Cystic Fibrosis Registry 2024 Annual Data Report (2025), Cystic Fibrosis Trust. London

records.title: Reducing multiple-breath washout test burden: agreement between the first acceptable trial and mean lung clearance index

person.department: Division of Respiratory Medicine, Department of Pediatrics

records.authors_text: N. Escobar1, E. Ben Meir2, R. Jensen3, M. Shaw3, F. Ratjen1,3,4
records.affiliations_text: 1The Hospital for Sick Children, Division of Respiratory Medicine, Department of Pediatrics, Toronto, Canada, 2Hadassah Medical Center and Faculty of Medicine, Pediatric Pulmonology Unit and Cystic Fibrosis Center, Jerusalem, Israel, 3The Hospital for Sick Children, Translational Medicine, Research Institute, Toronto, Canada, 4University of Toronto, Department of Paediatrics, Toronto, Canada
records.abstract_text:
Background: The lung clearance index (LCI) derived from multiple-breath washout (MBW) testing is a sensitive marker of early lung disease in cystic fibrosis (CF). However, widespread clinical implementation remains limited, partly due to long test duration. Current ATS/ERS technical standards recommend reporting LCI as the mean of at least three technically acceptable trials. Previous studies have shown minimal differences in group mean LCI when reducing repetitions from three to two; however, agreement between the first technically acceptable trial and the mean LCI has not been evaluated.

Methods: We performed a retrospective analysis of MBW test occasions from three large studies (TRACK, SIMPLIFY and PROSPECT)1-3, including children and adults with CF and healthy controls. Visits with at least three technically acceptable trials, defined using a predefined quality control framework, were included and the mean LCI was calculated according to ATS/ERS criteria. The first technically acceptable LCI trial was compared with the mean LCI using Bland–Altman analysis, intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), and Pearson correlation.

Results: A total of 1,394 MBW test occasions from 530 unique participants (age range 5–56 years), including 46 healthy controls, were analyzed. Across studies, agreement between the first acceptable run and mean LCI was excellent (ICC = 0.99; r = 0.99). Mean (SD) LCI was 7.76 (2.54), 7.83 (2.63) for the first acceptable trial. Mean bias (0.06 LCI units), limits of agreement (−0.72 to 0.84). Results were unchanged when the mean LCI was calculated using two instead of three technically acceptable trials.

Conclusion: In three independent cohorts, the first technically acceptable MBW trial demonstrated excellent agreement with the mean LCI. Under strict quality criteria, reliance on the first acceptable run may represent a pragmatic approach to reduce test burden and duration while maintaining measurement reliability.

records.title: People with cystic fibrosis not treated with CFTR modulators in Sweden differ in lung clearance index but not in forced expiratory volume in 1 second: A registry based study

person.institution: Stockholm CF Center, Karolinska University Hospital Huddinge

records.authors_text: M. Uzel1,2, S. Wilhelmsson1,2, P. Mendoza Del Aguila3, L. Pedersen1,2, C. Krantz4, A. Lindblad5, U. Lindberg6, M. Macek Jr7, T. Pincikova1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Stockholm CF Center, Karolinska University Hospital Huddinge, Stockholm, Sweden, 2Department of Paediatrics, CLINTEC, Karolinska Institutet, Stockholm, Sweden, 3Clinical Genetics and Genomics Department, Karolinska University Hospital Solna, Stockholm, Sweden, 4Department of Women´s and Children´s Health, Uppsala University, Uppsala, Sweden, 5Department of Gothenburg CF Centre, Queen Silvia Children’s Hospital, Gothenburg, Sweden, 6Department of Pulmonology and Allergology, Skåne University Hospital, Lund, Sweden, 7Department of Biology and Medical Genetics, 2nd Faculty of Medicine, Charles University and Motol University Hospital, Prague, Czech Republic
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Description of people with CF (pwCF) not treated with CFTR modulators (CFTRm) is needed to improve health of this population. We aimed to describe pwCF not treated with CFTRm in Sweden.

Methods: Data entered in the National Swedish CF Registry were used. PwCF not receiving CFTRm treatment at the annual visit during 2024 (+/- 6 months) were classified as not treated with CFTRm. Lung-transplanted pwCF were excluded (n=75). Chi-square and Mann-Whitney U test were used. A multiple linear regression (MLR) model was created with FEV1 (% predicted) as dependent variable and CFTRm treatment, bronchodilator use, P. aeruginosa colonization, age, body mass index, immunoglobulin G (IgG), and leukocyte count as independent variables.

Results: Out of 737 pwCF identified in the registry, 152 were not treated with CFTRm. There was no difference in sex between the groups (p=0.627), but the group not treated with CFTRm was younger (14 vs. 24 years, p<0.001) and had lower prevalence of pancreatic insufficiency (65 vs. 89%, p<0.001). Despite that, pwCF not treated with CFTRm had higher leukocyte count (7.2 vs. 6.1 x109/L, p<0.001) and sedimentation rate (8.0 vs. 6.0 mm, p=0.003) and higher Lung Clearance Index (LCI, 7.8 versus 6.9, p<0.001). FEV1 did not differ between the groups (87.2% vs 88.7%, p=0.692). CFTRm treatment was not a significant determinant of FEV1 in the MLR model (B=-0.066 (95 CI -0.150 – 0.017); p=0.12; adj. R2=0.33). Within the group not treated with CFTRm, pwCF carrying two non-responsive class I CFTR variants (n=45) had higher prevalence of P. aeruginosa colonization (51.1% vs. 13.5%, p<0.001), higher treatment burden, and higher serum IgG (11.6 vs. 9.6 g/L, p<0.001) but they did not differ in FEV1 (p=0.201) or in LCI (p=0.467).

Conclusion: PwCF not treated with CFTRm in Sweden differed from pwCF treated with CFTRm in LCI but not in FEV1. Within this group, pwCF carrying two non-responsive class I CFTR variants had higher infection and treatment burden.

Objectives: Description of people with CF (pwCF) not treated with CFTR modulators (CFTRm) is needed to improve health of this population. We aimed to describe pwCF not treated with CFTRm in Sweden.
Methods: Data entered in the National Swedish CF Registry were used. PwCF not receiving CFTRm treatment at the annual visit during 2024 (+/- 6 months) were classified as not treated with CFTRm. Lung-transplanted pwCF were excluded (n=75). Chi-square and Mann-Whitney U test were used. A multiple linear regression (MLR) model was created with FEV1 (% predicted) as dependent variable and CFTRm treatment, bronchodilator use, P. aeruginosa colonization, age, body mass index, immunoglobulin G (IgG), and leukocyte count as independent variables.
Results: Out of 737 pwCF identified in the registry, 152 were not treated with CFTRm. There was no difference in sex between the groups (p=0.627), but the group not treated with CFTRm was younger (14 vs. 24 years, p<0.001) and had lower prevalence of pancreatic insufficiency (65 vs. 89%, p<0.001). Despite that, pwCF not treated with CFTRm had higher leukocyte count (7.2 vs. 6.1 x109/L, p<0.001) and sedimentation rate (8.0 vs. 6.0 mm, p=0.003) and higher Lung Clearance Index (LCI, 7.8 versus 6.9, p<0.001). FEV1 did not differ between the groups (87.2% vs 88.7%, p=0.692). CFTRm treatment was not a significant determinant of FEV1 in the MLR model (B=-0.066 (95 CI -0.150 – 0.017); p=0.12; adj. R2=0.33). Within the group not treated with CFTRm, pwCF carrying two non-responsive class I CFTR variants (n=45) had higher prevalence of P. aeruginosa colonization (51.1% vs. 13.5%, p<0.001), higher treatment burden, and higher serum IgG (11.6 vs. 9.6 g/L, p<0.001) but they did not differ in FEV1 (p=0.201) or in LCI (p=0.467).
Conclusion: PwCF not treated with CFTRm in Sweden differed from pwCF treated with CFTRm in LCI but not in FEV1. Within this group, pwCF carrying two non-responsive class I CFTR variants had higher infection and treatment burden.

records.title: Correlation between Lung Clearance Index, spirometry and Bhalla Score in paediatric patients with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: G.E. Rodriguez Novoa1, V. Rodriguez1, S. Zaragoza1, S. Lubovich1, C. Demeco2, D. Ursino3, A. Teper1
records.affiliations_text: 1Hospital de Niños Ricardo Gutierrez, Respiratory Center, Buenos Aires, Argentina, 2Hospital de Niños Ricardo Gutierrez, Image Center, Buenos Aires, Argentina, 3Universidad de Buenos Aires, Statistics Department, Buenos Aires, Argentina
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To correlate LCI and spirometry with structural damage measured by the Bhalla Score.

Methods: Spirometry, LCI and computed tomography (the latter two within the last two years) were measured in patients with Cystic Fibrosis attending the Respiratory Centre of Hospital Gutiérrez.

A descriptive analysis of demographic variables, infection by pathogens, presence of the p.F508del variant, LCI, spirometric values (FEV1 and FEF) and Bhalla Score was performed.

All patients with FEV1 above the lower limit of normal were included.

LCI, FEV1 (z-score), FEF and Bhalla Score were correlated using bivariate analysis with Spearman’s ρ coefficients. For group variables (LCI–Bhalla), the Mann–Whitney test was used.

Results: A total of 33 pCF patients (23 male and 10 female), aged between 6 and 18 years (mean 11.8, SD 3.68), were included. All had FEV1 values above the lower limit of normal on spirometry. Of these, 60.6% were homozygous for p.F508del and 33.1% were heterozygous for this allele. Regarding infection by pathogens, normal flora was found in 81.8%, Pseudomonas aeruginosa in 9.1%, Burkholderia cepacia in 6.1%, and Mycobacterium abscessus in 3%.

The mean (SD) values were: FEV1 96 (12.97), FEV1 z-score 0.27 (1.33), FEF 97.7 (26.5), LCI 9.07 (2.81), Bhalla Score 20.42 (3.98).

When comparing spirometric variables FEV1 and FEF with the Bhalla Score, correlations of 0.38 and 0.37 (p < 0.05), respectively, were obtained, while LCI correlated with FEV1 z-score at -0.49 (p < 0.01).

Patients with abnormal LCI (>7.8) had a mean (SD) Bhalla Score of 20 (3.89), whereas those with normal LCI had a mean score of 25 (2.96). This difference was statistically significant (p = 0.032).

Conclusions: The correlation between LCI and Bhalla Score was adequate and superior to that of spirometry.

In this group of patients with normal spirometry, 75.8% had abnormal LCI. This group showed a higher median Bhalla Score compared with those who had normal values. It is noteworthy that only one patient presented abnormal FEF.

records.affiliations_text: 1ULS Santa Maria, Paediatric Lung Function Laboratory, Department of Paediatrics, Lisbon, Portugal, 2ULS Santa Maria, Paediatric Pulmonology Unit, Department of Paediatrics, Lisbon, Portugal, 3University of Lisbon, Faculty of Medicine, Lisbon, Portugal, 4ULS Santa Maria, Cystic Fibrosis Reference Centre, Lisbon, Portugal
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: The Lung Clearance Index (LCI) determined Nitrogen Multiple breath washout(N₂-MBW) allows detection of early peripheral airways disease. However, the relation between LCI, spirometry and lung volumes remains poorly characterized in clinical practice.

Objective: Our aim was to determine the agreement between LCI in absolute value and z-score(zsc), evaluate the correlation of LCI with FEV1 and MMEF75–25 and compare FRC measured by N₂-MBW with TGV obtained by plethysmography.

Methods: Cross-sectional observational study included children with cystic fibrosis (CF) who underwent N₂-MBW, spirometry and whole-body plethysmography on the same day in 2025. Lung function parameters were analyzed according to ERS/ATS and GLI guidelines and expressed in absolute values and zsc. Correlations between LCI and spirometric indices and between FRC (MBW) and volumes (plethysmography), were evaluated using Spearman coefficients and multiple linear regression (p<0.05).

Results: Thirty-one children were included, 16(21%) female, mean age 11.5±3.3 years. The absolute LCI was 7.5±1.4 and in zsc 2.08±2.02, FRC absolute was 1.6±0.6L and in zsc −0.02 ±0.84. Spirometry showed globally preserved ventilatory function(FEV₁zsc 0.46±1.06; FEV₁/FVCzsc 0.02±0.87; MMEF75-25zsc 0.19±1.08). Plethysmography revealed TGV absolute 1.9±0.6L and zsc 0.32±0.65. There was strong agreement between LCI absolute values and zsc. In multiple linear regression, neither FEV1 nor MMEF75-25 proved to be independent predictors of LCI (FEV1: B=-0.227; β=-0.120; p=0.612; MMEF75-25: B=-0.700; β=-0.376; p=0.118). The N₂-MBW FRC correlated strongly with TGV in absolute values (ρ=0.93; p<0.05) and zsc(ρ=0.60; p<0.05).

Conclusion: Despite a preserved ventilatory function, LCI revealed impairment in some patients, as previously described. Concerning lung volumes there was high volumetric reliability between the N2-MBW and plethysmography, reinforcing the use of N2-MBW in integrated functional assessment of CF patients.

records.title: Can CF caregivers reliably predict home spirometry usage in pwCF?
records.authors_text: A. Azam1,2, A.M. Jones1,2, R.J. Bright-Thomas1,2, A. Horsley1,2, P.J. Barry1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Manchester Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Manchester, United Kingdom, 2The University of Manchester, Manchester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Home spirometry has been widely adopted in the delivery of cystic fibrosis (CF) care. While existing literature largely supports its feasibility and positive outcomes, behaviour around home disease monitoring remains poorly understood. This study aimed to evaluate healthcare professionals’ (HCPs') ability to estimate home spirometry usage pwCF and compare these with actual recorded data.

Methods: Home spirometry data, from a single large adult CF centre, for the year 2024, was obtained from NuvoAir. HCPs (doctors, nurses, and physiotherapists) rated their level of familiarity with each pwCF and categorised them as infrequent, expected, or highly frequent spirometry users. They were also asked to estimate spirometry usage as an open-ended numerical response. CF experience was defined by the number of years the HCP had worked at the centre. Estimation accuracy was assessed using mean bias and mean absolute error (MAE).

Results: 10 doctors (35.7%), 6 nurses (21.4%), and 12 physiotherapists (42.9%) responded to the survey, with an overall response rate of 96.6%. There were 790 completed categorical estimates and 794 numerical estimates. The mean (±SD) CF experience was 15.7 (±8.2) years. Across all roles, HCPs systematically underestimated home spirometry usage. Additionally, HCPs were better at identifying pwCF who underuse home spirometry than those who overuse it i.e; the more frequently an individual performed spirometry, the more likely HCPs were to underestimate it. No significant differences in estimation accuracy (mean bias and MAE) were observed based on professional role, HCP's reported familiarity level with pwCF or years of CF experience.

Conclusion: This study found that CF caregivers tend to underestimate home spirometry usage, in contrast to other studies showing they often overestimate treatment adherence. This highlights gaps in understanding behaviour in pwCF and the need for CF teams to adapt to evolving models of remote monitoring.

person.biography: Dr Azam is currently a respiratory registrar/ pulmonary fellow in the North West of England. He is currently taking time out of training to do a fellowship in cystic fibrosis at the Manchester Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre and undertaking an MD/PhD with the University of Manchester. He is currently investigating the role of home spirometry in adults with cystic fibrosis, focusing on the longitudinal use and it's clinical applicability in the CF cohort, from the point of view of the patients and healthcare providers. He also has interests in pulmonary infection, pleural medicine and medical training, with various conference abstracts and publications around this area.
