records.abstract_text:
Objective: CFTR modulator therapies can suppress chronic inflammation in patients with cystic fibrosis (CF), potentially leading to improvement in upper airway obstruction. This study aimed to compare sleep parameters before and during CFTR modulator therapy in patients with CF.

Methods: Patients with CF, aged 2–19 years, followed in the Pediatric Pulmonology Clinic between 2023-2026 and treated with CFTR modulators for at least 3 months were included. Pediatric Sleep Questionnaire (PSQ) scores, home sleep study data, growth parameters, and spirometry results were retrospectively evaluated.

Results: Fifteen patients (60% male), aged 6-19 years, were included. The mean age was 13.6±4.3 years. The median body weight Z-score was −0.96, height Z-score was −0.77, and body mass index Z-score was −1.23. Ten patients received elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor and five patients received ivacaftor.

The median apnea–hypopnea index (AHI) decreased from 2.1 to 0.6 during treatment; however, this reduction did not statistically significant(p = 0.147). Obstructive apnea index (OAI), hypopnea index (HI), oxygen desaturation index (ODI) and mean oxygen saturation remained unchanged.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Sleep disorders among people with cystic fibrosis (PwCF) appear to be an important comorbidity that is frequently underdiagnosed. The aim of this study is to evaluate sleep disorders in adult, stable PwCF and to correlate these disorders with their lung function, as well as other clinical parameters.

Methods: Stable adult PwCF who are systematically examined in the Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre of the Respiratory Department of AUTH were included. The participants underwent pulmonary lung function testing, evaluation of their vital signs and 6 minute walking test. Also, they were asked to answer the following sleep related questionnaires: Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) and Athens Insomnia Scale (AIS). They also answered the mMRC questionnaire, in order to evaluate their dyspnea. The Kerem questionnaire was also completed evaluating the quantity of cough during the day and the night.

Results: 18 adult PwCF (13 men and 5 women) in a stable condition were included in this study. Their mean age was 30.17±7.21 years and their mean value of BMI was 21.36±2.95 kg/m2. As far as their respiratory function is concerned, the mean value of % predicted FEV1 and FVC was 58.93± 25.07 and 75.37± 26.14 respectively. The average score of ESS was 6.61±3.05, of PSQI 5.06±4.15 and of AIS 4.39±4.67. However, 38,8% of the perticipants reported an abnormal score at leat in one questionnaire. A statistically important negative correlation between SpO2% and PSQI score (p=0.03) was found. Furthermore, there was a statistically important positive correlation between nocturnal cough and AIS (p=0.008) and PSQI score (p=0.001). Finally, the score in the Kerem nighttime questionnaire differed importantly, depending on chronic infection with P.aeruginosa.

Conclusion: Sleep disorders are common among PwCF and therefore, quality of sleep should be systematically evaluated. Lung function and nocturnal cough seem to correlate with sleep quality of PwCF.

person.institution: Division of Pulmonology, Department of Paediatrics, Hacettepe University Faculty of Medicine, Ankara, Turkey

records.authors_text: Ö.F. İpek1, N. Emiralioğlu Ordukaya1, R. Atan1, H.İ. Demir1, E. Yalçın1, D. Doğru Ersöz1, U. Özçelik1
records.affiliations_text: 1Division of Pulmonology, Department of Paediatrics, Hacettepe University Faculty of Medicine, Ankara, Turkey, Altındağ, Turkey
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a chronic multisystemic disease characterised by malnutrition and progressive lung disease. Sleep-related breathing disorders (SRBD) can negatively affect quality of life and disease progression. Data regarding SRBD prevalence in the paediatric population remain limited. This study retrospectively evaluates nocturnal oxygen requirements and the relationship between SRBD and pulmonary function test (PFT) parameters in children with CF.

Methods: We reviewed the medical records of children with CF who underwent polysomnography (PSG) at the Hacettepe University Paediatric Pulmonology Sleep Laboratory between 01/01/2017 and 25/03/2025 due to snoring or hypoxia. Data included demographic characteristics, pulmonary function test (PFT) parameters (FEV1 z-score), genotypes, and PSG parameters.Correlation between the apnea-hypopnea index(AHI) and PFT results was examined.

Results: Fifteen children with CF were included (median age 13.5 years; range 3–17.5 years). The median AHI was 0.7 (0-3.5). While 53.3% of patients had no sleep apnea, 46.7% exhibited mild obstructive sleep apnea.Median nocturnal oxygen saturation was 89% (83%–95%), and 73.3% of patients required nocturnal oxygen supplementation.Hypoventilation was not observed.Median FEV1 z-score was -6.87 (-8.75;2.78).No significant difference was found between children with and without sleep apnea regarding PFT parameters (p=1.000) or oxygen needs (p=0.87).Children with mild sleep apnea underwent PSG at a significantly younger age (median 10vs14.5 years;p=0.042).No significant correlation was found between AHI and PFT parameters (r=0.077; p=0.786).

Conclusions: Mild sleep apnea was detected in nearly half of the children. High nocturnal oxygen requirements (73.3%) likely reflect the selection of patients with suspected respiratory failure. In this cohort, PFT results were not significantly associated with sleep apnea. Larger studies are needed to further elucidate these relationships.

records.affiliations_text: 1University of Manchester, Manchester, United Kingdom, 2Manchester Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Wythenshawe, Manchester, United Kingdom, 3Cardiff and Vale University Health Board, Cardiff, United Kingdom, 4The Newcastle upon Tyne Hospitals NHS FT, Newcastle upon Tyne, United Kingdom, 5Leeds Institute of Medical Research, University of Leeds, Leeds, United Kingdom, 6Adult CF Centre, Liverpool Heart and Chest Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 7University of Liverpool, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 8Queen's University Belfast, School of Pharmacy, Belfast, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: Sleep disturbance is common in adults with cystic fibrosis (CF) and is likely multi-factorial. Both subjective and objective assessments demonstrate impaired sleep quality, but data is limited on which individuals with CF are more affected and how sleep relates to clinical parameters.

Methods: Clinically stable adults with CF were recruited as part of the CF-Tracker study, an ongoing longitudinal observational study investigating and profiling pulmonary exacerbations. Subjective sleep quality was assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI; good is ≤5). Objective sleep was measured at home over one month using wrist actigraphy.

Results: Data are available from the first 44 study participants; 25 (57%) were female, median age of 39 years (range 20-77). Median FEV1 (FEV1pp) was 59.7% predicted (range 25.2-103.7). Subjective sleep quality was impaired, with a median global PSQI score of 6 (range 1-14); 23 (52%) reported PSQI > 6. The median PSQI sleep efficiency component score was 1 (75-84% sleep efficiency). No statistically significant associations were observed between PSQI score and sex (Mann–Whitney U test), age, BMI, FEV1pp, or reported breathlessness (Spearman’s rank correlation). To date 11 participants have completed actigraphy monitoring for mean duration of 30 days (IQR range 14-43). Mean sleep duration was 6.9 hours per night, and median actigraphy-derived sleep efficiency was 85.3% (IQR range 74.9-90.4%).

Conclusion: Adults with CF report impaired subjective sleep quality, with objective measures indicating reduced sleep duration and efficiency. Ongoing recruitment and longitudinal follow-up within CF-Tracker will enable evaluation of relationships between sleep, disease severity, and pulmonary exacerbations.

Funding: LifeArc/Cystic Fibrosis Trust Innovation Hub Network.

person.biography:
Dr. Sharon Weinberg is a senior registrar in respiratory and general internal medicine based in Manchester, UK, and a clinical research fellow within the Pulse CF Hub at the University of Manchester, supervised by Professor Alex Horsley.
She graduated from New York University with a BA, followed by an MBBS from St George’s, University of London. She has trained internationally, including in Cyprus and Israel, before moving to the UK, where she is completing her specialist training in respiratory and general internal medicine in the North West of England. She has also completed a specialist fellowship at the National Aspergillosis Centre in Manchester.
Her work centres on cystic fibrosis, with a particular emphasis on pulmonary exacerbations and their role in disease progression. Dr. Weinberg is actively involved in the design and coordination of major clinical research studies at the Manchester Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, including the CF-Tracker and Unified-CF projects.
She is currently undertaking a PhD investigating the impact of environmental pollution, viral infections, and treatment adherence on pulmonary exacerbations in cystic fibrosis. Her research aims to identify modifiable risk factors and inform preventative strategies to improve long-term outcomes for people living with the condition.

Objectives: 2789+5G>A variant is reported most frequently in Türkiye among European countries in ECFSPR 2023 annual data report.This study aimed to evaluate the demographic and clinical characteristics of patients carrying the 2789+5G>A variant registered in the CF Registry of Türkiye (CFRT) .

Methods: 2024 annual data of patients carrying 2789+5G>A variant were retrospectively analyzed within this cohort. Findings were compared with 282 patients homozygous for the F508del variant registered in the same database.

Results: 96 patients carrying 2789+5G>A variant (median age:10.37 years) were included.Compared with F508del homozygotes,patients with 2789+5G>A were diagnosed at a later age (median 0.33 vs 0.25 years;p<0.0001).Nutritional status was significantly better in the 2789+5G>A group,with higher BMI z-scores in patients under 18years (median 0.14vs−0.70; p<0.0001). Lung function was also superior (median FEV1:94.5%vs90.0%;p=0.044),and sweat chloride levels were significantly lower (84.76±23.37 vs 92.44±22.49 mmol/L; p=0.005). F508del homozygotes experienced more pulmonary exacerbations(19.1%vs9.4%;p=0.026) and had higher rates of Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonization (29.1%vs18.7%; p=0.044). Pancreatic sufficiency was significantly more common in 2789+5G>A patients (p<0.0001); also, acute pancreatitis occurred more frequently in this group as expected (2.1%vs0%; p=0.012). CF-related diabetes (11% vs 1%) and liver disease (34.7% vs 9.4% )were significantly more prevalent in F508del homozygotes (p<0.0001).

Conclusions: The 2789+5G>A variant is associated with a milder CF phenotype, including later diagnosis, better nutritional status, and preserved lung function. Despite lower therapeutic burden and higher pancreatic sufficiency,these patients have an increased risk of acute pancreatitis, highlighting the need for variant-specific clinical follow-up.

records.title: Successful transition to adult cystic fibrosis care after initiation of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor in the paediatric setting: a Slovenian single- centre experience
records.authors_text: J. Rodman Berlot1,2, Z. Jagodic1, B. Salobir3, S. Škrgat3,2, U. Krivec1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1University Children's Hospital Ljubljana, Department of Paediatric Pulmonology, Ljubljana, Slovenia, 2Faculty of Medicine, University of Ljubljana, Ljubljana, Slovenia, 3University Medical Centre Ljubljana, Department of Pulmonary Diseases and Allergy, Ljubljana, Slovenia
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The transition from paediatric to adult cystic fibrosis (CF) care is a vulnerable period associated with decreased adherence and clinical deterioration. During the initial rollout of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) in Slovenia, a temporary strategy was implemented whereby adolescents approaching transition received ETI initiation within their established paediatric team to preserve therapeutic relationships.

Methods: A retrospective analysis was conducted on adolescents who received ETI initiation in paediatric care prior to transition between 2021 and 2024. We analysed ppFEV₁ and BMI one year before transition, during the transition year, and one year post- transition. The Friedman test was employed for three-group comparisons, and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test for two-group comparisons. Adherence to therapy and pregnancy outcomes were documented.

Results: Thirteen young adults with CF (62% female) were included in the study. Mean age at transition was 22.8±1.7 years. No significant changes were observed in the median ppFEV₁ (98 before vs 90 during vs 87 % after transition; p=0.679) or median BMI (21.7 vs 21.7 vs 22.0 kg/m2; p=0.739). The change in ppFEV₁ before and after transition was not significant (2 vs 0 %; p=0.814). ETI adherence remained excellent, consistent with real- world adolescent data. Three of eight females (38%) became pregnant during the transition year (one planned, two unplanned).

Conclusions: Initiating ETI in adolescents whilst under paediatric care facilitated a smooth transition without clinical deterioration. High adherence likely reflected the preservation of therapeutic relationships. The 38% pregnancy rate highlights the urgent need for earlier reproductive health counselling in adolescents receiving ETI, as pregnancy rates have increased substantially in the ETI era. Family planning discussions should become routine in adolescent CF care and transition preparation, ideally beginning well before the transition occurs.

records.title: Children with Cystic Fibrosis Screen Positive, inconclusive Diagnosis (CFSPID) followed at a cystic fibrosis center
records.authors_text: T. Unlu1, T. Sismanlar Eyuboglu1, A.T. Aslan1
records.affiliations_text: 1Gazi University Medicine Faculty, Pediatric Pulmonology, Yenimahalle, Turkey
records.abstract_text:
Introduction and Aim: CFSPID describes infants with a positive newborn screening result for cystic fibrosis (CF) who do not meet diagnostic criteria and therefore require clinical follow-up. We aimed to evaluate the clinical and genetic features of CFSPID in patients followed at our center under the IRT/IRT protocol.

Methods: CFSPID patients followed between 2017 and 2025 were retrospectively reviewed. Age, sex, clinical findings, sweat chloride, CFTR genetics, and pancreatic status were recorded.

Results: Nineteen patients were included, of whom 12 (63.2%) were female. The mean age was 12±11.2 (1–56) months and the mean sweat chloride was 38.1±7 mmol/L (20.6–58.2). No patient had pseudo-Bartter syndrome, pancreatic insufficiency, or additional clinical findings. The mean follow-up time was 12.4±11.8 (2–48) months. The mean daily weight gain at presentation was 29.8±5.6 (21–39) g/day, and growth percentiles remained normal. Six patients had no CFTR variant. Nine had one variant (3 CF-causing, 1 CFTR-related disorder–causing, 2 VUS, 2 non–disease-causing, 1 not in databases) and four had two variants (2 VUS/non–disease-causing, 1 non–disease-causing/non–disease-causing, 1 CFTR-related disorder–causing/not in databases). The mean follow-up duration was 16.41±18.13 (1–60) months. During follow-up, 2 patients (10.5%) could not be classified because their variants were not found in the database, whereas 17 patients (89.4%) continued to be followed with a diagnosis of KFKOT.

Conclusion: Most CFSPID patients remain asymptomatic; therefore, longitudinal follow-up is crucial to allow timely identification of clinically significant manifestations while minimizing unnecessary medical interventions.

records.title: Working to improve out-of-hours care for cystic fibrosis patients presenting in a district general hospital
records.authors_text: M. Tavabie1, C. Barrett2, D. Lacey3, L. Edwards3, K. Redmond3
records.affiliations_text: 1Wirral University Teaching Trust, Paediatrics, Wirral, United Kingdom, 2Wirral University Teaching Hospital, Paediatrics, Wirral, United Kingdom, 3Wirral University Trust Hospital, Wirral, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: Local paediatric DGH hospital in the North west caring for 34 children with cystic fibrosis. Most of the care for these children is done by the specific CF team, however out of hours the on-call general paediatric team are responsible for them. Incidents occurred where out of hours prescribers did not alter the dosing for antibiotics when the patient was on modulator therapy. This project aims to improve the prescribing in out-of-hour care for patients with CF.

Method: A survey of non-CF specialist resident doctors, nurse practitioners and consultants was carrier out to assess confidence in prescribing for patients with CF. A survey was also sent out to assess the confidence patients and families of those with CF had in the prescribers out-of-hours.

Results: 13 prescribers responded with 76% being aware of modulator therapy. Confidence in prescribing for children on modulator therapy was low with a median result of 3.5/10 and 38% of prescribers reporting 0 or 1/10 for confidence. No prescribers felt confident in altering doses of modulator therapy.

17 patients responded with 23% being unaware of modulator therapy interacting with commonly used medications. All reported were happy to carry alert cards to improve awareness of modulator therapy and the impact this can have on other medications.

Outcome: A teaching program has been implemented in department to update the non-CF doctors and prescribers. A repeat survey following this is expected to show improved confidence in prescribing. A medication alert card has been issued to all children on modulator therapy with cystic fibrosis to emphasize the need for consideration in prescribing additional medication.

Conclusion: Care for CF patients remains largely managed by specialist CF teams however in emergency and out-of -hours situations non-specialist prescribers need to be aware of the impact of their prescribing. Education and alert cards can improve the confidence of both prescribers and families.

1Wirral University Teaching Trust, Paediatrics, Wirral, United Kingdom, 2Wirral University Teaching Hospital, Paediatrics, Wirral, United Kingdom, 3Wirral University Trust Hospital, Wirral, United Kingdom

Background: Local paediatric DGH hospital in the North west caring for 34 children with cystic fibrosis. Most of the care for these children is done by the specific CF team, however out of hours the on-call general paediatric team are responsible for them. Incidents occurred where out of hours prescribers did not alter the dosing for antibiotics when the patient was on modulator therapy. This project aims to improve the prescribing in out-of-hour care for patients with CF.
Method: A survey of non-CF specialist resident doctors, nurse practitioners and consultants was carrier out to assess confidence in prescribing for patients with CF. A survey was also sent out to assess the confidence patients and families of those with CF had in the prescribers out-of-hours.
Results: 13 prescribers responded with 76% being aware of modulator therapy. Confidence in prescribing for children on modulator therapy was low with a median result of 3.5/10 and 38% of prescribers reporting 0 or 1/10 for confidence. No prescribers felt confident in altering doses of modulator therapy.
17 patients responded with 23% being unaware of modulator therapy interacting with commonly used medications. All reported were happy to carry alert cards to improve awareness of modulator therapy and the impact this can have on other medications.
Outcome: A teaching program has been implemented in department to update the non-CF doctors and prescribers. A repeat survey following this is expected to show improved confidence in prescribing. A medication alert card has been issued to all children on modulator therapy with cystic fibrosis to emphasize the need for consideration in prescribing additional medication.
Conclusion: Care for CF patients remains largely managed by specialist CF teams however in emergency and out-of -hours situations non-specialist prescribers need to be aware of the impact of their prescribing. Education and alert cards can improve the confidence of both prescribers and families.

records.title: Regional experience in monitoring children with cystic fibrosis on targeted therapy in the Republic of Tatarstan

person.institution: The State Autonomous Healthcare Institution «Children's Republican Clinical Hospital of the Ministry of Health of the Republic of Tatarstan»

records.authors_text: O. Pyaterkina1, O. Karpova1, I. Zakirov1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1The State Autonomous Healthcare Institution «Children's Republican Clinical Hospital of the Ministry of Health of the Republic of Tatarstan», Kazan, Russian Federation, 2Kazan (Volga Region) Federal University, Kazan University, Kazan, Russian Federation
records.abstract_text:
Objective: To present the regional experience of the Republic of Tatarstan in the use of ivacaftor+tezacaftor+elexacaftor in children with cystic fibrosis (CF) with a change in the brand name of the drug.

Methods: Safety and efficacy of the therapy in 52 CF patients were monitored 14 days after the start of therapy, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months and 12 months.

Results: A comprehensive assessment of the child's functional capacity was conducted before initiating and when changing triple therapy. During the triple targeted therapy, patients showed improvement in respiratory function parameters (FEV1 and FVC), as well as positive weight and height dynamics. When changing drugs within the same international nonproprietary name (INN), respiratory function parameters did not decrease. Three patients lost weight during the first 14 days, but after 3 months of treatment, all children gained weight. During the 6-month follow-up period, there were no CF exacerbations requiring hospitalization. During the assessment at 6 months. When changing therapy within the same INN, a local decrease in lens transparency was detected in 1 patient.

Conclusion: Observation of children receiving triple therapy ivacaftor+tezacaftor+elexacaftor showed a good safety profile. Changing the drug within the same INN does not reduce the clinical efficacy of triple therapy; there was no significant increase in the incidence of adverse reactions in patients.

person.title: Dr
person.institution: Hacettepe University İhsan Doğramacı Children Hospital

records.authors_text: M. Yıldız Kayaoğlu1, E. Güneş Yalçın1, U. Kavgacı1, T. Kantemir1, N. Emiralioğlu1, D. Doğru1, U. Özçelik1
records.affiliations_text: 1Hacettepe İhsan Doğramacı Children Hospital, Pediatric Pulmonology Department, Ankara, Turkey
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Regulator Protein-Related Disorder (CFTR-RD) is a clinical entity that results from dysfunction of the Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Regulator (CFTR) protein but does not fully meet the diagnostic criteria for Cystic Fibrosis (CF).

Methods: In this study, we retrospectively reviewed the data of 21 pediatric patients diagnosed with CFTR-RD who were followed up at Hacettepe İhsan Doğramacı Children's Hospital.

Results: Regarding the presentation characteristics of the patients: 4 (19%) presented with elevated immunoreactive trypsinogen (IRT) levels on newborn screening, 4 (19%) presented with recurrent pancreatitis, 9 presented with pseudobartter syndrome (PBS) (42.9%), 4 presented with respiratory complaints such as chronic cough and pneumonia (19%), and 1 patient presented because their sibling had been diagnosed with CFTR-RD (4.8%). The mean sweat test result in the diagnosis was 38.81 ± 14.1 mmol/L. Aquagenic palmoplantar keratoderma (APK) testing was performed in 12 patients (57.1%), and the test was positive in 5 of these patients (41.6%).

Conclusion: Re-evaluation of patients, particularly those with intermediate sweat test results, based on clinical diagnostic criteria and databases is crucial for confirming this diagnosis. This is important because CFTR modulators are not indicated for treatment in CFTR-RD group. Pseudo-Bartter syndrome (PBS) was observed in 42.9% of our cohort; although PBS is not currently included among the universally accepted clinical diagnostic criteria for CFTR-RD, recent studies have demonstrated that variant analyses in such patients are consistent with CFTR-RD, moreover, physiological evidence supports that this subgroup should also be considered within the CFTR-RD spectrum.

records.title: Early vascular dysfunction in adults with cystic fibrosis: a controlled observational study
records.authors_text: B. Pessoa1, M. de Fuccio2, I. Carvalho-Ribeiro1, A. Guedes1, I. Vasconcelos1, R. Borges1, M. Velloso3, M.d.G. Rodrigues-Machado1
records.affiliations_text: 1Faculdade Ciências Médicas, Belo Horizonte, Brazil, 2Júlia Kubitschek Hospital, Belo Horizonte, Brazil, 3Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais, Belo Horizonte, Brazil
records.abstract_text:
Objective: To compare arterial stiffness, arterial compliance and vascular resistance indices between adults with cystic fibrosis (CF) and age and sex matched healthy controls.

Methods: This was a controlled, cross-sectional observational study involving clinically stable adults with a confirmed diagnosis of CF and no known history of cardiopathy. Patients using systemic corticosteroids and smokers were excluded. Cardiovascular parameters were assessed using the Mobil-O-Graph®, which non-invasively estimates central vascular and hemodynamic parameters. The augmentation index adjusted to a heart rate of 75 bpm (AIx@75) was calculated as the pressure difference between the peak of the reflected wave (P2) and the peak of the incident wave (P1), expressed as a percentage of central pulse pressure (PP) [(AIx@75 = [P2–P1]/cPP × 100)]. Arterial compliance (stroke volume index/PP) and vascular resistance (PP/stroke volume index) were derived from hemodynamic parameters.

Results: A total of 82 adults with CF and 82 controls were evaluated, with mean ages of 31.09±11.74 and 31.21±11.59 years, respectively. AIx@75 (29.11±10.22 vs. 18.48±7.93%, p<0.0001), reflection coefficient (62.44±6.54 vs. 57.71±6.24, p<0.0001), and augmentation pressure (6.52±2.89 vs. 5.30±2.39 mmHg, p=0.0045) were significantly higher in the CF group compared with controls. Central and peripheral vascular compliance were significantly lower in the CF group (1.16±0.29 and 0.84±0.21 mL/m²/mmHg) compared with controls (1.29±0.30 and 0.92±0.23 mL/m²/mmHg). Central and peripheral vascular resistance were significantly higher in the CF group (0.91±0.22 and 1.25±0.31 mmHg/ml/m2) compared with controls (0.82±0.24 and 1.14±0.28 mmHg/ml/m2).

Conclusion: CF in adults is associated with central and peripheral vascular alterations consistent with accelerated vascular aging. These findings indicate an increased cardiovascular risk and reinforce the need for early cardiovascular screening in this population.

records.title: A-STEP performance test and its correlation with muscle strength and clinical parameters in patients diagnosed with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: T. Sözer1, O. Kenis Coskun1, B. Yıldız1, C. Bilekyiğit Kurt1, E. Karadağ Saygı1, P. Ergenekon2, E. Erdem Eralp2, Y. Gökdemir2, B. Karadağ2
records.affiliations_text: 1Marmara University, Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation Department, Istanbul, Turkey, 2Marmara University, Pediatric Pulmonology, Istanbul, Turkey
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: A-STEP is a novel exercise test used to monitor the performance of patients diagnosed with cystic fibrosis (CF). It is done by climbing up and down a step board in an gradually increasing velocity to detect cardiopulmonary performance It has previously been shown to be applicable in a pediatric population in our clinic, however the previous work has not been applied within the required standards, and did not investigate its correlation with muscle strength, other field tests and quality of life(QoL). This study has applied A-STEP as intended and aims to investigate its correlation with these parameters.

Methods: Children and adults above the age of 10 diagnosed with stable CF who were followed up in our center were tested with the help of a metronome, step board and appropriate tracking devices. Reaching level 9 on the Borg scale was considered to be the achievement of at least one maximum effort criterion. Spearman correlation analyzes were used to ensure compatibility of A-step test results with clinical parameters such as FEV1, quality of life measured with AWESCORE test, performance parameters such as 6 minute walk test (6MWT) and biceps curl and gluteus and quadriceps strength as measured by hand-held dynamometer.

Results: A total of 40 patients were included in this study. The average age of the patients was 17.20 (SD: 5.21) (minimum 11 - maximum 33) and their average FEV1 level was 80.90 (SD: 20.43) (minimum 30 - maximum 122). Median A-STEP level of the patients was 7 (IQR: 4.25-8). Only 2 patients have reached the maximum level. The A-STEP levels of the patients showed a significant correlation with 6MWT (rho=0.49, p=0.001), biceps curl (rho=0.53 p=0.001), FEV1 levels (rho=0.41 p=0.008) and AWESCORE (rho=0.39 p=0.13). No correlations were found with muscle strength.

Conclusion: A-STEP test is applicable in pwCF above the age of 10 and shows medium correlation with other performance parameters, clinical parameters and quality of life.

records.title: Standardized exercise testing in the cystic fibrosis (CF) clinic – feasibility and relevance
records.authors_text: A. Hebestreit1, C. König1, M. Popp1, D. d´Alquen1, H. Hebestreit1
records.affiliations_text: 1Pediatric University Hospital, Christiane Herzog Zentrum für Mukoviszidose, Würzburg, Germany
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Routine assessment of physical fitness is recommended for people with cystic fibrosis (PwCF). The objective of this retrospective single center study was to describe feasibility and impact of a simple incremental cycle ergometry test in outpatient care.

Methods: Between 01.01.2025 and 31.12.2025 77 PwCF (36 female, 41 male, age 21±11 [7-55] years, FEV1 92±21 [40-129] %predicted) completed a standardized incremental cycle ergometry test (ErgoSelelct 900, Ergoline) following the protocol of the ERS (Radtke et al. ERR 2019) and using work rate increments proposed by Godfrey et al. (Clin Sci 1971). All tests were performed during routine outpatient visits in the clinic room. In 67 PwCF corresponding measures of body composition analyses (InBody 770) were available.

Results: Exercise testing was feasible during routine outpatient visits in all PwCF and required only 15 min of extra time per test. FEV1 %predicted (FEV1%), peak heart rate, minimal oxygen saturation (SpO2) and peak work rate expressed as %predicted (Wpeak%, Hebestreit et al. Respiration 2015) did not differ between male and female PwCF. Average Wmax% of the 77 PwCF was 98.1±18.4% and did not correlate with age, sex, peak heart rate or minimal SpO2. Seven PwCF (five female) had a Wpeak% ≤73%. These seven PwCF did not differ – as a group – from the more fit PwCF in FEV1%, peak heart rate and minimal SpO2, but had a higher percentage of body fat (%BF). However, three PwCF with poor fitness were among those with lowest FEV1% and one male had the highest %BF of all male PwCF.

Conclusions: A cycle ergometry test is easily implemented in the CF clinic routine and confirmed that most PwCF at our center have a good to excellent aerobic fitness. However, seven PwCF had a Wpeak% ≤73% associated with a decreased 10-year survival (Hebestreit et al., AJRCCM 2019), some of whom unexpectedly. Thus, the test is informative indicating additional work-up and targeted care for these seven PwCF.

1Pediatric University Hospital, Christiane Herzog Zentrum für Mukoviszidose, Würzburg, Germany

Objectives: Routine assessment of physical fitness is recommended for people with cystic fibrosis (PwCF). The objective of this retrospective single center study was to describe feasibility and impact of a simple incremental cycle ergometry test in outpatient care.
Methods: Between 01.01.2025 and 31.12.2025 77 PwCF (36 female, 41 male, age 21±11 [7-55] years, FEV1 92±21 [40-129] %predicted) completed a standardized incremental cycle ergometry test (ErgoSelelct 900, Ergoline) following the protocol of the ERS (Radtke et al. ERR 2019) and using work rate increments proposed by Godfrey et al. (Clin Sci 1971). All tests were performed during routine outpatient visits in the clinic room. In 67 PwCF corresponding measures of body composition analyses (InBody 770) were available.
Results: Exercise testing was feasible during routine outpatient visits in all PwCF and required only 15 min of extra time per test. FEV1 %predicted (FEV1%), peak heart rate, minimal oxygen saturation (SpO2) and peak work rate expressed as %predicted (Wpeak%, Hebestreit et al. Respiration 2015) did not differ between male and female PwCF. Average Wmax% of the 77 PwCF was 98.1±18.4% and did not correlate with age, sex, peak heart rate or minimal SpO2. Seven PwCF (five female) had a Wpeak% ≤73%. These seven PwCF did not differ – as a group – from the more fit PwCF in FEV1%, peak heart rate and minimal SpO2, but had a higher percentage of body fat (%BF). However, three PwCF with poor fitness were among those with lowest FEV1% and one male had the highest %BF of all male PwCF.
Conclusions: A cycle ergometry test is easily implemented in the CF clinic routine and confirmed that most PwCF at our center have a good to excellent aerobic fitness. However, seven PwCF had a Wpeak% ≤73% associated with a decreased 10-year survival (Hebestreit et al., AJRCCM 2019), some of whom unexpectedly. Thus, the test is informative indicating additional work-up and targeted care for these seven PwCF.

person.biography: Alexandra Hebestreit is a Consultant and Paediatrc Pulmonologist at the Children‘s Hospital, University of Würzburg, Germany. Her main clinical work focusses on out- and inpatient care for people with cystic fibrosis of all ages. As a researcher she has published on the effects and risks of exercise in cystic fibrosis and contributed to respective guidelines for 25 years. She was and is investigator in several clinical trials on the effects of physical training and on CFTR-modulators. Alexandra Hebestreit is acting as co-lead of the German Working Group on Exercise and Sports in the Mukoviszidose e.V. since 2000 and in the ECFS Exercise Working Group since 2025.

records.title: Physical activity and exercise capacity in school-aged children and adolescents living with cystic fibrosis in South Africa

person.department: Department of Paediatrics and Child Health

records.authors_text: R. Fortune1, B. Morrow1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Cape Town, Department of Paediatrics and Child Health, Cape Town, South Africa
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Physical activity (PA) is an essential component of cystic fibrosis (CF) management, yet PA levels and exercise capacity in African paediatric CF populations are largely unexplored. This study aimed to describe PA levels, muscle strength, and exercise tolerance in South African children and adolescents with CF.

Methods: A cross-sectional study involved clinically stable children and adolescents with CF aged 7-18 years. All participants completed modified Physical Activity Questionnaires for children and adolescents (PAQ-CA), handgrip dynamometry, and the 10-meter 25-level modified shuttle test (MST-25). Clinical data including lung function (FEV₁% predicted), genotype, BMI, and Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator (CFTR) modulator use were extracted from participant’s medical records. Descriptive statistics and correlation analyses were performed.

Results: Thirty participants (age 12.4±3.1 years; 53.3% male; FEV₁% 83.6±20.2%) were enrolled. Mean PAQ-CA score was 2.92±0.76, indicating low to moderate PA levels. Mean handgrip strength was 16.35 ± 5.73 kg, below age-predicted norms for healthy children. Mean MST-25 distance was 400±117.6 metres (range 150 -560), substantially lower than reported MST values in other CF paediatric cohorts. Self-reported PA levels (r=0.52; p=0.003), FEV₁ (r=0.44; p=0.02), and combined handgrip strength were significantly associated with MST-25 distance (r=0.55, p=0.002). Participants receiving CFTR modulator therapy (40%) demonstrated better exercise tolerance (432.50±108.40 vs 381.10±123.40 metres on MST-25).

Conclusion: South African children and adolescents with CF demonstrate low to moderate PA levels, reduced muscle strength, and impaired exercise tolerance compared to published data and healthy norms. These findings highlight the importance of structured exercise assessments and individualized exercise prescription to improve outcomes in resource-limited CF care settings.

records.title: Implementation of lung clearance index testing in adult cystic fibrosis clinics and in CFTR related disorder assessment
records.authors_text: I. Waller1, C. Fordyce1, R. Bright-Thomas1, J. Mitchell1, P. Barry1, A. Horsley1
records.affiliations_text: 1Manchester Foundation Trust, Cystic Fibrosis, Manchester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: Lung Clearance Index (LCI) is now a routine test in many CF paediatric clinics, but use in adults to monitor early disease progression is more limited. It has added potential to detect and follow lung disease in those with CFTR-related disorders. Implementation requires MBW equipment, trained staff, clinical buy-in, and effective clinic integration.

Objective: To summarise clinical data and practical experience since implementing LCI testing in a routine clinic at a large adult CF centre.

Results: 31 Adults with CF (mean age 35yrs, M:F 18:13) have completed at least one LCI assessment. Mean FEV1 was 94% predicted (range 76-131%). In 2 cases (6%), reliable LCI measurement could not be obtained. Median session time was 25mins (IQR 20-29 mins, n=20). Mean LCI was 8.0 (range 5.7-14.1), mean LCI z score was 2.5 (range -1.9 to 10.6). 17 adults (55%) had elevated LCI (z score >2), compared to 39% with FEV1 <90% predicted.CFTR-RD patients (n=8) had a mean LCI 7.1 (mean z score 1.5, n=7). Mean FEV1 was 97% predicted. All CFTR-RD had normal LCI except for a single patient (LCI z score 3.8) with a known diagnosis of asthma.

Conclusions: LCI testing is feasible in routine clinics with the right infrastructure and training. Allowance must be made by staff and patients for an additional 30mins for test completion. Challenges include equipment, clinic structure, and the availability of trained testing staff. CFTR-RD patients have predominantly normal LCI. Data collection is ongoing to define this population further, but LCI could provide a sensitive and practical method of tracking longer term changes.

records.title: The role of physical activity in bone health among people with cystic fibrosis: a scoping review

person.institution: Children's Health and Exercise Research Centre , University of Exeter
person.department: Faculty of Health and Life Sciences

records.authors_text: Z. A. Alharbi1,2, D. Vlachopoulos1, M. Bianchim3, C. A. Williams1
records.affiliations_text: 1Children's Health and Exercise Research Centre , University of Exeter, Faculty of Health and Life Sciences, Exeter, United Kingdom, 2Jouf University, Faculty of Applied Medical Sciences, Al Qurayyat, Saudi Arabia, 3Bangor University, School of Health Sciences, Bangor, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: With modulator therapy, People With Cystic Fibrosis (pwCF) live longer but face increasing age-related comorbidities. Osteoporosis is multifactorial and increasingly prevalent in pwCF, with risk factors including reduced physical activity (PA). PA is part of routine care; yet remains inconsistent and poorly characterised. Previous reviews show PA's favourable effect on health outcomes, but evidence examining PA's role in bone health (BH) among pwCF is scarce. We aimed to map existing literature on PA's role in BH, assess measurement methods, and identify knowledge gaps.

Methods: Following PRISMA scoping review methodology, we included studies assessing BH and PA or providing PA interventions in pwCF (children and adults), excluding reviews, and animal studies. We systematically searched ten databases using a set of keywords. Two independent reviewers checked eligibility and extracted data.

Results: From 3,662 references, 29 studies were included (24 cross-sectional, four longitudinal and one interventional). PA assessment was heterogeneous and included: questionnaires (n=18), interviews (n=2), diary (n=1), combined methods (n=4), and device-based measures (n=4). Studies assessed BH using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, accompanied by computed tomography–based imaging (n=5), quantitative ultrasound, single X-ray absorptiometry (n=1 each), and bone biomarkers (n=13). PA–BH associations were reported in 23 studies: no significant associations were found in children (n=7); six of 12 studies reported positive associations in young adults/adults; and two of four studies reported positive associations in mixed-age samples.

Conclusion: Evidence shows potential benefits of PA for BH in adults with CF, but conclusions are constrained by an over-reliance on self-reported PA, especially in children. Evidence for PA's role in CF bone health is limited and equivocal in adults. More robust studies with comprehensive PA and BH assessments are needed.

records.title: Socioeconomic factors of physical activity enjoyment in adults with cystic fibrosis - results from a single center study
records.authors_text: L. Lechtenberg1, W. Gruber2, F. Stehling2, J.-S. Schermaul1, J.G. Ortiz1, C. Taube1, M. Welsner1
records.affiliations_text: 1University Hospital Essen - Ruhrlandklinik, Department of Pneumology, Essen, Germany, 2University of Duisburg-Essen, Pediatric Pulmonology and Sleep Medicine, Essen, Germany
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To asses enjoyment of physical activity and motivation in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) along with socioeconomic variables.

Methods: The study was investigator initiated and conducted in a cross-sectional design at the Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre at the Ruhrlandklinik Hospital in Essen, Germany. During routine out-patient visits, we recruited pwCF aged ≥ 18 years with a genetically confirmed diagnosis of Cystic Fibrosis. Informed written consent was obtained. We assessed forms of motivation and enjoyment using the Physical Activity Enjoyment Scale (PACES). The participants were also asked to provide information on marital status, level of education, job qualification and employment situation. Data was assessed for normality and non parametric tests were performed.

Results: Group wise comparisons showed significant differences between pwCF of differing levels of education and job qualification (total n=173). PwCF with university qualification scored lower in amotivation (p=0.03) and higher in identified (p=0.5) and intrinsic (p=0.02) regulation as well as relative autonomy index (p=0.41). With regards to job qualifcation, PwCF with university degrees scored lower in amotivation (p=0.48) with a higher relative autonomy index (p=0.41) compared to pwCF with finished job training. There were no significant differences between pwCF grouped by marital status or employment situation.

Conclusion: There were significant differences in enjoyment of physical activity between pwCF grouped by socioeconomic factors. In our sample, higher levels of education and higher job qualification were significantly associated with enjoyment of physical activity and forms of motivation associated with sustained physical activity. Further studies are required to assess the effects of socioeconomic factors on health outcomes in pwCF, specifically as mediated by physical activity.

records.title: Impact of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor on Six-Minute Walking Test performance in cystic fibrosis children and adolescents

person.institution: Meyer Children's Hospital IRCCS, Cystic Fibrosis Regional Reference Centre, Department of Paediatric Medicine

records.authors_text: C. Cimbalo1, E. Masi2, C. Fevola1, S. Del Vespa1, B. Ferrari2, D. Innocenti2, C. Castellani2, C. Degl'innocenti2, M. Masolini2, A. Benucci2, D. Salvatore3, G. Carreras1, V. Terlizzi1
records.affiliations_text: 1Meyer Children's Hospital IRCCS, Cystic Fibrosis Regional Reference Centre, Department of Paediatric Medicine, Florence, Italy, 2Rehabilitation Unit, Meyer Children's Hospital, IRCCS, Florence, Italy, Florence, Italy, 3CF Centre, Hospital San Carlo, Potenza, Italy
records.abstract_text:
To evaluate the longitudinal impact of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) therapy on functional exercise capacity assessed by the 6-Minute Walk Test (6MWT) in children and adolescents with cystic fibrosis (CF)

We conducted a retrospective, observational, single-center study. Children aged 6–18 years eligible for ETI therapy were enrolled between 2021 and 2025. Clinical, anthropometric, respiratory, and functional data were collected at baseline and after 3–6, 12 and 24 months of treatment. Outcomes included 6MWT distance and percentage of predicted distance, ppFEV1, lung clearance index (LCI), BMI z-score, sweat chloride concentration. Longitudinal changes were analyzed using mixed-effects models, with stratified analyses by age group.

Seventy-one patients (median age 11.9 years were enrolled. ETI was associated with a significant increase in absolute 6MWT distance over 24 months (p<0.001) and a modest but significant improvement in percentage of predicted distance (p=0.0076). Functional response differed by age: adolescents (12–18 years) showed progressive and sustained gains, peaking at 12 months, whereas younger children demonstrated earlier improvement followed by stabilization or slight decline. BMI z-score, ppFEV1 and LCI improved significantly after ETI initiation, alongside a sustained reduction in sweat chloride levels. In multivariable analyses, lower LCI values were independently associated with higher percentages of predicted 6MWT distance, particularly in adolescents. In younger children, higher BMI z-scores were inversely associated with functional performance.

ETI therapy confers sustained clinical benefits in pediatric CF patients. The 6MWT appears to be a more robust marker of cardio-respiratory improvement in adolescents, closely linked to ventilation homogeneity, while functional performance in younger children may be influenced by non-respiratory factors. LCI emerges as a key functional biomarker for monitoring ETI efficacy.

In multivariable analyses, lower LCI values were independently associated with higher percentages of predicted 6MWT distance, particularly in adolescents. In younger children, higher BMI z-scores were inversely associated with functional performance.
ETI therapy confers sustained clinical benefits in pediatric CF patients. The 6MWT appears to be a more robust marker of cardio-respiratory improvement in adolescents, closely linked to ventilation homogeneity, while functional performance in younger children may be influenced by non-respiratory factors. LCI emerges as a key functional biomarker for monitoring ETI efficacy.

records.title: Correlation between 1-minute sit-to-stand test performance and FEV1 in adults with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: E. Baran1, E. Zattera1, S. Gastal1
records.affiliations_text: 1Hospital Rossi, La Plata, Argentina
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To evaluate the correlation between functional capacity (assessed via the 1-minute Sit-to-Stand Test (STST)) and lung function parameters (absolute FEV1 and FEV1%) in a cohort of patients with Cystic Fibrosis (CF), determining if this field test serves as a reliable predictor.

Methods: A cross-sectional descriptive study was conducted analyzing data from 40 adults patients. The following variables were recorded: lung function (absolute FEV1 (L) and FEV1 percentage (FEV1%) predicted; functional capacity (total number of repetitions achieved in the STST. Statical analysis: Pearson correlation coefficient (r) was used to determine the strength of the association between variables.

Results: A moderate positive correlation (r=0.55) was found between VEF1% vs STST. Patients with higher FEV1% values generally demonstrated better performance in the STST. It was observed that patients with severe FEV1% (< 30%) did not exceed 20 repetitions, whereas those with normal lung function frequently performed above 25 repetitions. STST repetitions ranged from 16 to 41. We identified that muscular strength (STST) does not always follow a strictly linear relationship with FEV1, suggesting that other factors—such as nutritional status or peripheral muscle conditioning—significantly influence functional capacity.

Conclusion: There is a significant correlation between FEV1% and performance in the STST.

These results suggest that the STST is a valuable, low-cost, and easy-to-implement clinical tool for monitoring functional capacity in CF patients. However, the observed variability indicates that functional assessment should complement spirometry, as some patients maintain relatively high muscle strength despite moderate declines in lung function.

records.title: Body composition and muscular strength in adults with cystic fibrosis in the post-modulator era
records.authors_text: B. Griffiths1, I. Clifton2, R. Watson2, G. Sploletini2, C. Webster2, H. Saumtally2, D. Peckham2,3, O. Price1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Leeds, School of Biomedical Sciences, Faculty of Biological Sciences, Leeds, United Kingdom, 2St James's University Hospital, Leeds Adult Cystic Fibrosis Unit, Leeds, United Kingdom, 3University of Leeds, Leeds Institute of Medical Research, Leeds, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Highly effective CFTR modulator therapy has improved lung function and body mass in adults with cystic fibrosis (awCF). However, whether these improvements translate into preserved skeletal muscle mass, strength and functional capacity remains unclear. We compared absolute measures of muscle function and body composition in awCF receiving modulator therapy with age-, sex- and BMI-matched healthy controls (HC).

Methods: Fifteen male awCF and nine HC were assessed. Maximal hand grip strength and isometric knee extensor strength were measured using dynamometry. Whole-body fat mass (FM) and fat-free mass (FFM) were quantified by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry. Functional capacity was assessed using 6-min walk distance (6MWD). Data are presented as median (IQR) and compared using Mann–Whitney U tests.

Results: Despite similar age (awCF: 38 [34–44] vs. HC: 34 [31–37] years, P=0.074) and BMI (25.5 [23.8–27.6] vs. 24.8 [23.2–26.0] kg·m-2, P=0.420), awCF had lower FEV₁ (%predicted) than HC (70 [57–80] vs. 109 [101–119], P<0.001). Hand grip strength was reduced in awCF (43.0 [35.5–47.5] vs. 51.0 [44.0–58.5] kg, P=0.014), with numerically lower knee extensor strength that did not reach statistical significance (117 [85–142] vs. 132 [115–177] Nm, P=0.057). awCF exhibited lower FFM (53.6 [48.3–61.8] vs. 61.6 [60.9–65.9] kg, P=0.025), with trends toward higher FM. Functional capacity was reduced in awCF, evidenced by lower 6MWD (657 [627–687] vs. 775 [693–834] m, P=0.004), despite comparable free-living physical activity between groups.

Conclusion: In the post-modulator era, awCF demonstrate reduced absolute muscle mass, strength and functional capacity compared with BMI-matched HC. Preserved BMI may therefore mask clinically relevant deficits in muscle quantity and force-generating capacity, supporting the rationale for targeted non-pharmacological interventions to optimise musculoskeletal health as the CF population ages.

person.biography: Daniel Peckham is Professor of Respiratory Medicine and Deputy Director of the Leeds Institute of Medical Research at the University of Leeds. He is the clinical lead for the Regional Leeds Adult Cystic Fibrosis, Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia and Bronchiectasis Services. He pioneered the design and implementation of chronic disease electronic patient records and established a strong base for clinical and basic research in Cystic Fibrosis. Active research programs focus on CF-related inflammation, CFTR modulators, gut dysbiosis, cancer, drug allergy, big data, electronic patient records and clinical trials. He is passionate about education and was the founding Director of Education for the European Cystic Fibrosis Society.

records.title: The relationship between handgrip strength, and pulmonary function, body mass index, and peak power in adults with cystic fibrosis.

person.title: Dr
person.institution: Royal Devon University Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust Hospital

records.authors_text: T. Kent1, G. Walker1, C. Williams1,2, L. Dobson1, P. Mitchelmore1,2, O. Tomlinson1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Royal Devon University Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust Hospital, Cystic Fibrosis, Exeter, United Kingdom, 2University of Exeter Medical School, Faculty of Health and life Science, Faculty of Health and life Science, Exeter, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Handgrip Strength (HGS) is an assessment of forearm grip strength and is often used alongside a nutritional assessment, with lower results often linking to negative health outcomes, whilst also acting as a proxy for exercise function and musculoskeletal health. As part of a Cystic Fibrosis (CF) patients annual review, HGS was introduced alongside other regular exercise tests. This study sought to assess whether there is a relationship between HGS, Pulmonary Function Tests (PFT), Body Mass Index (BMI) and Peak Power Output (PPO).

Methods: Forty-nine adult patients with CF (PwCF) (19 females, 30 males) with a mean (SD) age of 36.4 ± 13.1 years, and FEV1 of 3.09 ± 1.15 L (82 ± 22%) performed a HGS test on a Jamar Plus handheld dynamometer, completing a total of six tests (three on left hand, three on right hand). The best result from each patient was then correlated against PFT, BMI and PPO using Pearson's correlation coefficients.

Results: Mean maximal HGS was 42.4 ± 14.2 kg (99.6 ± 22.2 %) ranging from 19.0 – 79.6 kg (52 – 145%). Correlations between absolute HGS and PFT were significant (r = 0.45, p < 0.01) as were HGS and PPO (r = 0.59, p < 0.01). When correlating HGS against BMI data, there was not a significant association (r = -0.00, p = 0.98) however, HGS was correlated against body weight (BW) (r = 0.30, p < 0.05).

Conclusion: The significant correlation between HGS, FEV1 and PPO, indicate its use as a proxy for disease status and exercise function. It also, however, calls into question the validity of HGS for use as a nutritional assessment tool in PwCF given varied associations between HGS, BMI and BW.

records.title: Substrate oxidation during submaximal exercise in children with cystic fibrosis on elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor therapy

person.department: Child Health & Exercise Medicine Program, Pediatrics

records.authors_text: S.M da Silva1, L. Pedder2, B.W Timmons1,3, J. Obeid1,3
records.affiliations_text: 1McMaster University, Child Health & Exercise Medicine Program, Pediatrics, Hamilton, Canada, 2McMaster University, Division of Respirology, Pediatrics, Hamilton, Canada, 3McMaster University, Kinesiology, Hamilton, Canada
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Exercise is a well-established therapy for children with cystic fibrosis (CF). As CF health continues to evolve with elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor (ETI) therapy, understanding fuel metabolism during exercise is increasingly important to support a healthy, active lifestyle. This study aims to compare substrate oxidation during exercise in children with CF who were short-term and long-term users of ETI.

Methods: Children aged 8 to 17 y, were divided into short-term (G1) or long-term (G2) ETI therapy groups using a median split of ETI duration. Basic anthropometric measurements were collected. Aerobic fitness, defined as the highest 20-sec oxygen uptake (VO2peak), was measured on a treadmill using a Bruce protocol. Participants completed a 20-minute steady-state treadmill test at an intensity equivalent to 45% of VO2peak. Conclusion: Children with longer ETI therapy oxidized higher amounts of CHO, but no differences were found in the rate or contribution to EE between groups. Future research with a larger, longitudinal sample is needed to monitor changes over time as children with CF continue ETI therapy.

records.title: Skeletal muscle mass and physical activity after CFTR modulator therapy in adults with cystic fibrosis in Croatia

person.title: MSc Physiotherapy
person.department: Cystic Fibrosis Centre for Children and Adults

records.authors_text: H. Krstanović1, M. Ćubić1, N. Perak1, A. Vukić Dugac1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1University Hospital Centre Zagreb, Cystic Fibrosis Centre for Children and Adults, Zagreb, Croatia, 2School of Medicine, University of Zagreb, Zagreb, Croatia
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The objective of this study was to evaluate longitudinal changes in skeletal muscle mass and physical activity levels in adults with cystic fibrosis before and after initiation of CFTR modulator therapy, and to explore the association between physical activity and changes in body composition.

Methods: A retrospective longitudinal study was conducted in adult patients with cystic fibrosis treated at the Cystic Fibrosis Center at University Hospital Centre Zagreb, Croatia. Skeletal muscle mass and body fat percentage were assessed using bioelectrical impedance analysis at the last visit before CFTR modulator initiation and at annual follow-up visits thereafter. Physical activity was recorded from clinical interviews and classified according to the type of activity and categorized by intensity. Changes over time were analyzed in relation to time since treatment initiation.

Results: An increase in skeletal muscle mass was observed during the first year of CFTR modulator therapy, with further stabilization or gradual improvement during subsequent follow-up. Patients reporting moderate to high levels of physical activity demonstrated greater increases in muscle mass and a more favorable body composition profile compared with less active individuals, who showed a higher proportion of fat mass gain. Physical activity level was positively associated with longitudinal changes in skeletal muscle mass.

Conclusion: CFTR modulator therapy is associated with beneficial changes in skeletal muscle mass in adults with cystic fibrosis, particularly in those who remain physically active. These findings support the importance of promoting regular physical activity and structured physiotherapy as an integral part of care in the era of CFTR modulator treatment.

records.title: Playphysio: gamification of airway clearance physiotherapy for children with cystic fibrosis - A feasibility randomised clinical trial.
records.authors_text: A. Walsh1, S. Davies1,2, W. Jackson3, R. Jackson4, R. Thursfield5,6
records.affiliations_text: 1Alder Hey Children’s Hospital, Physiotherapy Department, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 2University of Liverpool, School of Allied Health Professionals, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 3Playphysio C.I.C, Cambridge, United Kingdom, 4University of Liverpool, Department of Health Data Science, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 5Alder Hey Children’s Hospital, Respiratory Department, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 6University of Liverpool, School of Medicine, Liverpool, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Airway clearance techniques (ACT) contribute to a high burden of care for young people with Cystic Fibrosis (CF). Treatment compliance is important to help maintain health and combat respiratory infections. Technology now makes gamification and monitoring of ACT possible. Playphysio® was developed as a social venture with the goal of supporting ACT and making a positive impact on the lives of children and their families. This pilot study aimed to assess feasibility of the technology within clinical practice. Secondary outcomes around treatment quality, compliance and quality of life (CFQ-R) were also captured.

Method: Single site, investigator single blinded randomised controlled feasibility trial. Participants were provided with a physioPal™ (sensor), that detected oscillations from the users ACT adjunct and a paired smart device, preloaded with the Playphysio® games app. Children were randomised (1:1) to ‘gamification’ or ‘blank’ mode group for their daily ACT. Baseline compliance was captured over 28 days, gamification was then activated for the intervention & the control was presented with a blank display. Both assignments remained this way throughout the trial (112 days). An open label extension with gamification for all was then unlocked.

Results: 59 patients (aged 5-11) were recruited. Both compliance [mean (sd): 40 (7) Vs 10 (2); p-value = 0.001)] and treatment quality [mean(sd): 37.6 (5.42), 12.6 (3.15); p<0.001] demonstrate improved performance with gamification which was statically significant during the intervention phase vs the control. No significant changes were observed in CFQ-R.

Conclusion: The intervention was well tolerated and feasible for implementation within clinical practice. While CFQ-R scores showed no significant changes during the study period, gamification resulted in significant improvements in both treatment compliance and quality - key factors for maintaining long-term respiratory health in children with CF.

records.title: Benchmarking sputum induction (SI) practice across UK cystic fibrosis (CF) centres

person.institution: Royal Brompton Hospital, Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust

records.authors_text: A. Ahmad1, N.J. Simmonds1,2, G. Stanford1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Royal Brompton Hospital, Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust, Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, London, United Kingdom, 2Imperial College London, National Heart and Lung Institute, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: Sputum induction (SI) is used in CF when patients cannot provide a spontaneous sample; however, SI practice varies widely across UK CF centres in terms of protocols and devices used. Although the European Cystic Fibrosis Society Clinical Trials Network (ECFS-CTN) has published a standard operating procedure (SOP) for SI, recommending jet or ultrasonic (US) nebulisers for use in clinical trials, the extent to which this informs routine clinical practice remains unclear.

Methods: A national benchmarking survey was distributed September-December 2025 to all UK CF centres. The questionnaire was circulated to physiotherapists via the Association of Chartered Physiotherapists in CF (ACPCF), and direct email contact. Responses were analysed descriptively to benchmark current practice and identify variation across centres.

Results: 30 centres responded, 60% adult (table). The primary indication for SI was clinical need (93%). Most centres performed more than one SI per month. 97% of centres used 7% hypertonic saline. eFlow®rapid were most used (55%), followed by jet (48%), US (21%), and Aerogen® (10%) devices, with several centres using more than one device. SI typically lasted 16–30 minutes. Only 17% of centres used a protocol with repeated cycles of nebulisation, airway clearance and spirometry per procedure. SI was undertaken predominantly by specialist physiotherapists (97%). While most centres reported having a local SOP, only 23% had formal competencies in place and 47% were aware of the ECFS-CTN SOP.

Respondents were able to select more than one option.

Conclusion: This benchmarking survey demonstrates substantial variation in SI practice across the UK, with wide differences in nebuliser devices and protocols. It highlights gaps in standardised competencies and shows that the ECFS-CTN SOP is not inclusive of devices currently used, supporting the need for further research to inform SOPs aligned with contemporary practice.

records.title: Sustained feasibility and success of induced sputum sampling in the era of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor: a real-world single-centre study

person.department: Department of Child and Adolescent Health, Paediatrics III

records.authors_text: D. Appelt1, J. Eder2, K. Niedermayr2, I. Geißler2, A. Nöstlinger2, T. Grinschgl-Leis2, O. Eberharter2, H. Ellemunter3, T. Fuchs1
records.affiliations_text: 1Medical University of Innsbruck, Department of Child and Adolescent Health, Paediatrics III, Innsbruck, Austria, 2Tirol Kliniken, Department of Child and Adolescent Health, Paediatrics III, Innsbruck, Austria, 3Cystic Fibrosis Centre Innsbruck, Medical Research Affiliate, Innsbruck, Austria
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The introduction of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) therapy has been associated with a substantial reduction in sputum production. Nevertheless, routine surveillance of bronchopulmonary pathogens via sputum samples remains central to the clinical management of cystic fibrosis (CF). This study aimed to compare the success rates of induced sputum (IS) collection before and after the initiation of ETI in a real-world cohort.

Methods: Clinical data and IS success rate were retrospectively analysed over a 3-year period. Sputum frequency and estimated volume were recorded on the day of IS collection using a standardized scale. All IS procedures were performed by trained physiotherapists in accordance with local protocols.

Results: 581 IS samples one year prior and 966 samples obtained during the subsequent two years from 103 people with CF (62% adults, 52% female, mean age 22 years [range 6–48]) were analysed. Both adult and paediatric cohorts exhibited sustained and significant reductions in patient-reported sputum frequency and volume following ETI initiation (p<0.001 and p<0.05, respectively). Despite this, IS collection remained highly successful, with an overall success rate of 97–100% across all age groups, even though 18% of adults and 43% of paediatric patients reported no spontaneous sputum production on the day of sampling. Following ETI initiation, clinically relevant pathogens were identified in 32% of IS samples, prompting the initiation of antibiotic therapy.

Conclusion: This real-world study demonstrates that routine sputum induction is safe and feasible. Despite substantially reduced sputum production, IS samples were successfully obtained in nearly all cases and enabled the detection of clinically relevant pathogens that might otherwise have remained undetected. Routine implementation of sputum induction two to four times per year should therefore be considered, particularly in patients without chronic bronchopulmonary colonisation.

Methods: Clinical data and IS success rate were retrospectively analysed over a 3-year period. Sputum frequency and estimated volume were recorded on the day of IS collection using a standardized scale. All IS procedures were performed by trained physiotherapists in accordance with local protocols.
Results: 581 IS samples one year prior and 966 samples obtained during the subsequent two years from 103 people with CF (62% adults, 52% female, mean age 22 years [range 6–48]) were analysed. Both adult and paediatric cohorts exhibited sustained and significant reductions in patient-reported sputum frequency and volume following ETI initiation (p<0.001 and p<0.05, respectively). Despite this, IS collection remained highly successful, with an overall success rate of 97–100% across all age groups, even though 18% of adults and 43% of paediatric patients reported no spontaneous sputum production on the day of sampling. Following ETI initiation, clinically relevant pathogens were identified in 32% of IS samples, prompting the initiation of antibiotic therapy.
Conclusion: This real-world study demonstrates that routine sputum induction is safe and feasible. Despite substantially reduced sputum production, IS samples were successfully obtained in nearly all cases and enabled the detection of clinically relevant pathogens that might otherwise have remained undetected. Routine implementation of sputum induction two to four times per year should therefore be considered, particularly in patients without chronic bronchopulmonary colonisation.

records.title: The role of induced sputum, oropharyngeal swabs and cough swabs in non-expectorating children with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: A. Delaney1, M. Doumit1, B. Prentice2, B. McMullan3
records.affiliations_text: 1Sydney Children's Hospital Randwick, Physiotherapy, Randwick, Australia, 2Sydney Children's Hospital Randwick, Respiratory Medicine, Randwick, Australia, 3Sydney Children's Hospital Randwick, Infectious Diseases, Randwick, Australia
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Children with cystic fibrosis (CF) often have difficulty spontaneously expectorating sputum. Induced sputum (IS), oropharyngeal swabs (OPS) and cough swabs (CS) are commonly used. Evidence for diagnostic accuracy of samples in the post modulator setting is limited and no study has compared OPS to CS. It is also unknown if clinical features (cough quality and sample appearance) are useful in determining best sampling approach.

Methods: In this prospective study, children undergoing clinically indicated IS provided paired IS, OPS and CS. Diagnostic accuracy of OPS and CS was calculated with IS treated as the reference standard. Feasibility was assessed using collection time and distress ratings. Associations between cough quality (wet/dry), sample appearance (sputum/saliva) and pathogen detection were examined.

Results: Seventy-four participants (mean age 12, range 4-18yrs) provided 102 complete sample sets. IS, OPS and CS were pathogen positive in 39%, 40% and 9% of samples respectively. OPS had superior diagnostic accuracy compared to CS. Sensitivity for Pa detection was 100% (95%CI 51-100) for OPS and 0% (95%CI 0-49%) for CS. For Sa, sensitivity for OPS was 57% (95%CI 39-73) and CS 18% (95%CI 8-36). Samples from children with dry cough versus wet cough on presentation were pathogen positive in 53% and 54% of cases respectively. Samples which appeared to contain sputum and samples that were salivary in appearance were pathogen positive in 42% and 67% cases respectively. All three sampling methods were acceptable with low levels of distress, however induced sputum was most time/resource consuming.

Conclusions: Among swab-based methods, OPS showed the closest agreement with IS and CS showed low pathogen detection. Neither cough quality nor sample appearance reliably identified samples likely to yield pathogens, indicating a dry cough on presentation or a sample of salivary appearance should preclude induced sputum being collected and analysed.

records.title: Feasibility of sputum collection in adults with cystic fibrosis in the CFTR modulator era
records.authors_text: A. Orr1, C. Fordyce1, S.E Weinberg2,1, G.G Einarsson3, P. Barry2,1, J. Duckers4, S. Doe5, D. Peckham6, F. Frost7, E. Caamaño Gutiérrez8, R. Lord2,1, R.E Maher8, A.M Jones2,1, M.M Tunney3, A. Horsley2,1
records.affiliations_text: 1Manchester Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Wythenshawe, Manchester, United Kingdom, 2University of Manchester, Manchester, United Kingdom, 3Queen's University Belfast, School of Pharmacy, Belfast, United Kingdom, 4Cardiff and Vale University Health Board, Cardiff, United Kingdom, 5The Newcastle upon Tyne Hospitals NHS FT, Newcastle upon Tyne, United Kingdom, 6Leeds Institute of Medical Research, University of Leeds, Leeds, United Kingdom, 7Adult CF Centre, Liverpool Heart and Chest Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 8University of Liverpool, Liverpool, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: Sputum is a key biofluid in cystic fibrosis (CF) clinical studies. However, sputum volume is often markedly reduced following initiation of CFTR modulator therapies. Many people with CF (pwCF) experience decreased cough and sputum production, and some report being unable to expectorate at all following treatment. These changes have raised concerns about the feasibility of sputum-based endpoints in clinical studies.

Methods: Sputum was collected from pwCF as part of the CF-Tracker study (www.pulse-cf.com/tracker-study). Eligible participants must have experienced a pulmonary exacerbation within the past 12 months; those a priori known to be unable to produce sputum, even with saline induction, are excluded. Sputum samples were collected at each face-to-face visit and weighed prior to processing. A minimum sputum weight of 500 mg at baseline is required for study participation; participants who were unable to spontaneously expectorate this volume underwent enhanced physiotherapy manoeuvres and/or sputum induction with 7% hypertonic saline.

Results: Forty-eight pwCF were recruited across the United Kingdom, of whom 46 (95.8%) are prescribed CFTR modulator therapy. Mean FEV1 was 1.87 litres (52.9% predicted). Across all study visits (n=96), 70 sputum samples were obtained. Eight participants (17%) required induced sputum during the study period. The mean sputum weight was 2,140 mg, with a median of 1,651 mg (range 466–8,783 mg). Two participants (4.16%) were unable to provide a baseline sputum specimen and were excluded.

Discussion: These findings demonstrate that sputum-based clinical studies remain feasible in the era of CFTR modulator therapy. Careful population selection and engagement of respiratory physiotherapists are important to optimise sputum collection using airway clearance techniques and sputum induction when required.

Funding: LifeArc / Cystic Fibrosis Trust Innovation Hub Network.

records.title: Detection of dysfunctional breathing patterns in children and young people with cystic fibrosis during cardiopulmonary exercise testing
records.authors_text: N. Dayman1,2, E. Gaillard1,2, J. Madge1, B. Potter1, M.I. Ahmed1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1University Hospitals of Leicester, Paediatric Respiratory, Leicester, United Kingdom, 2University of Leicester, Respiratory Sciences, Leicester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Breathing patterns may reflect physiological responses to respiratory disease; however, in the absence of organic pathology they may represent dysfunctional breathing. Dysfunctional breathing can occur in children and young people (CYP) with cystic fibrosis (CF), where symptoms may overlap with disease-related limitation and be difficult to distinguish clinically. This study aimed to evaluate the incidence and characteristics of dysfunctional breathing patterns identified on cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) in this population.

Methods: We retrospectively analysed CPETs performed between January 2022 and December 2025 in children and young people with CF attending a tertiary centre. Inclusion criteria were age 8–17 years, height ≥130 cm, and completion of a maximal CPET as part of routine annual assessment; tests with incomplete data or premature termination were excluded. CPET reports were reviewed following combined clinical and physiological assessment.

Results: Ninety five CPETs from 36 CYP with CF were analysed. 2 patients had submaximal CPET data. Dysfunctional breathing was identified in 28 CPETs (29.47%), representing 20 CYP (55.5%). Of these CPET, 13 (46.4%) demonstrated exercise-induced hyperventilation. Within the dysfunctional breathing cohort, VO₂ peak was normal in 13 CYP (72.2%) and reduced in 5 CYP (27.7%). Abnormal breathing patterns occurred at variable stages of exercise testing. All affected CYP were referred for physiotherapy.

Conclusion: Dysfunctional breathing was identified in a substantial proportion of CYP with cystic fibrosis undergoing routine cardiopulmonary exercise testing, with exercise-induced hyperventilation present in nearly half of affected tests. These findings suggest that dysfunctional breathing may coexist with CF-related respiratory limitation. CPET may be a useful objective tool to identify dysfunctional breathing and support targeted physiotherapy intervention.

records.title: International practice in the assessment and management of dysfunctional breathing in cystic fibrosis: a cross-sectional survey
records.authors_text: I. Ahmed1, D. Stevens2, D. Urquhart3, T. Radtke4, H. Hebestreit5
records.affiliations_text: 1University Hospitals of Leicester, Leicester, United Kingdom, 2Dalhousie University, Halifax, Canada, 3Royal Hospital for Children and Young People, Edinburgh, United Kingdom, 4University of Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland, 5University Children's Hospital, Wuerzburg, Germany
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Dysfunctional breathing (DB) is increasingly recognised in cystic fibrosis (CF), yet no internationally standardised definition, diagnostic pathway, or treatment framework exists. The objective was to describe international clinical practice in DB assessment, diagnosis, and management in CF, and to identify priorities for standardisation.

Methods: An international, cross-sectional, anonymous online survey of healthcare professionals working in CF centres was conducted. Developed by the European Cystic Fibrosis Society (ECFS) Exercise Working Group, the survey explored terminology, diagnostic and management approaches, and perceived challenges. Data were analysed descriptively.

Results: 64 responses were received from centres, mainly in Europe. DB assessment or management was reported by 59% of centres, with marked variation in terminology, classification and diagnostic approaches. DB was most commonly assessed at rest and during exercise (85%). Diagnostic methods included observation (97%), spirometry (74%), questionnaires (62%), and cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) (50%). Questionnaires were widely viewed as poorly validated and focused on hyperventilation. CPET use varied considerably, with key challenges including reliance on clinician experience (89%) and lack of diagnostic criteria (72%). Management was predominantly physiotherapist-led and individualised, with few centres using formal protocols. Barriers included limited specialist expertise, resource constraints, and low service prioritisation. Over 90% supported the need for international standardised definitions, assessment frameworks, CPET criteria and treatment pathways.

Conclusions: DB practice in CF is highly variable, with limited specialist expertise and inconsistent diagnostic approaches, particularly for CPET. These findings will inform ongoing work by the ECFS Exercise Working Group to develop international consensus standards to support equitable, evidence-based DB care.
