records.title: Respiratory morbidity and chronic respiratory infections in cystic fibrosis patients from the Republic of Moldova

person.institution: Nicolae Testemitanu State University of Medicine and Pharmacy

records.authors_text: S. Sciuca1,2, C. Tomacinschii1,2, D. Efros1, N. Buga1, L. Rusu3, C. Conica1,2, A. Cotoman2, R. Selvestru1, E. Gudumac4
records.affiliations_text: 1Nicolae Testemitanu State University of Medicine and Pharmacy, Pediatrics, Chișinău, Moldova, Republic of, 2Institute of Mother and Child, Chișinău, Moldova, Republic of, 3Emergency Clinical Hospital for Children, Cluj Napoca, Romania, 4Nicolae Testemitanu State University of Medicine and Pharmacy, Pediatric Surgery, Orthopaedics and Anaesthesiology, Chișinău, Moldova, Republic of
records.abstract_text:
Chronic respiratory infections and pulmonary exacerbations remain a major driver of morbidity and mortality in cystic fibrosis (CF).

Aim: To describe the prevalence of chronic respiratory infections, treatment burden and lung function in a national cohort of CF patients from the Republic of Moldova (RM).

Methods: This retrospective study analyzed microbiological, clinical and lung function data from CF patients followed at the national outpatient CF center during 2024.

Results: A total of 60 patients were included, of whom 52 were actively followed (36 patients <18 years, 16 patients ≥18 years); chronic respiratory infection was highly prevalent. At least one pulmonary exacerbation treated with IVAs occurred in 77.8% of children and 56.3% of adults. Among those treated, multiple exacerbations were common: ≥2 IV-treated exacerbations in 39.3% of children and 55.6% of adults. Mean total days on IV antibiotics ranged from 14 to 17 days in children and 12 days in adults, with a substantial proportion requiring hospitalization.

Airway microbiology revealed a high prevalence of chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection (52.8% of children and 87.5% of adults); Staphylococcus aureus (children 83.3%; adults 93.8%). Stenotrophomonas maltophilia was infrequently isolated and limited to paediatric patients and Aspergilus fumigatus was found in 18 patients. Despite intensive standard therapy, including inhaled antibiotics in 69.2%, rhDNase in 65.3%, and hypertonic saline in 78.8% of patients, infection burden remained substantial. Mean lung function values reflected moderate pulmonary impairment with a mean FEV₁ of 73.1% predicted and mean FVC of 84.9% predicted. Two deaths due to respiratory causes were recorded during the study period.

Conclusions: CF patients in the RM experience a very high respiratory diseases burden. These findings highlight the urgent need for strengthened access to comprehensive CF care and advanced therapies in underrepresented Eastern European settings.

records.title: Five years of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor therapy improve lung function, exercise capacity, nutrition status and quality of life in people with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: M. Picker1, C. Thoms1, S. Straßburg1, C. Taube1, G. Weinreich1, J. Judickiene1, M. Panagi1, S. Sutharsan1, M. Welsner1
records.affiliations_text: 1Ruhrlandklinik-University Hospital Essen, Department of Pulmonary Medicine, Essen, Germany
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) has transformed cystic fibrosis (CF) care, representing a major therapeutic milestone.

While short-term benefits are well documented, long-term outcomes beyond one year remain limited.

Five-year follow-up (5y-FU) data are scarce, and no studies have compared baseline parameters with those obtained after five years of continuous therapy.

Methods: In the Ruhrlandklinik we included 87 people with CF (pwCF) who initiated ETI in 2020 and completed 5y-FU in 2025.

Analysed parameters were demographics such as gender, age, genotype, Body Mass Index (BMI), percent predicted forced expiratory volume in one second (ppFEV₁), six-minute walk test (6MWT), sweat chloride levels, and the respiratory domain of the Cystic Fibrosis Questionnaire-Revised (CFQ-R).

The results are presented as mean with standard deviation (SD).

Results: In our cohort, 56.3% of pwCF were male and the age at therapy initiation was 32.4±10.4 years. With regard to genotype, 52 pwCF (59.8%) were homozygous for F508del, while 35 (40.2%) were F508 del heterozygous.

Over 5y-FU, BMI increased from 20.7±2.92 to 22.5±3.03 kg/m² (p<0.001), and ppFEV₁ improved from 45.5±18.9 to 63.2±22.4 (p<0.001). The 6MWT distance was higher at 5y-FU (512.3±115.6 m vs. 577.3±95.2 m, p=0.003).

Sweat chloride decreased from 104.3±16 mmol/L to 50.9±15.9 mmol/L (p<0.001). CFQ-R respiratory scores rosed from 54.5±21.6 to 81.2±18.5 (p<0.001).

Conclusion: Five years of ETI therapy led to sustained improvements in nutrition, lung function, exercise capacity, and quality of life.

These real-world results show that ETI is a highly effective long-term treatment for adult pwCF.

records.abstract_text:
Objective: To describe the characteristics of patients (pts) with cystic fibrosis and the scope of therapy.

Methods: The 2024 Registry included data on 4,355 pts: 3,550 alive and 23 deceased observed in the current year.

Results: The average age of pts was 13.6 (8.3-20.5) years, with 32.5% being over 18 years of age. The age at diagnosis was 0.3 (0.1-2.4) years. The diagnosis was made by neonatal screening in 56.7% of pts. The proportion of pts with 2 identified genetic variants was 95.7%. Respiratory function according to FEV1 was 85.7±27.6%, FVC was 91.5±22.2%. BMI Me (25th–75th pctl) was 37.4 (14.8-66.6) among children; 20.2 (18.4-22.5) among adults. Sa was detected in the respiratory tract of 66.5% of pts, MRSA– in 6%, Pa -38%, Bcc-4.3%. Chronic sinusitis with nasal polyps was diagnosed in 36%, without polyps in 31.6%, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis-2.9%, pneumothorax requiring drainage-0.2%, liver cirrhosis with portal hypertension and hypersplenism-3.7%, without portal hypertension /hypersplenism-2.4%, diabetes mellitus with insulin use-5.6%, osteoporosis (low bone mass)-3.5%, pulmonary hemorrhage-0.7%, electrolyte disorders-1.8%, cancer-0.3%, amyloidosis-0.4%, depression-4.4%, pancreatitis-2.7%, distal intestinal obstruction syndrome-1.3%, arthritis-1.7%, gastroesophageal reflux disease -12.3%, bronchial asthma-4.4%. Dornase alfa therapy was received by 92.1%, hypertonic saline-69.8%, mannitol- 12.3%, physiotherapy-72%, inhalation antibacterial drugs-39%, intravenous-39.1%, oral-60.4%, azithromycin in a subinhibitory dose-16.9%, UDCA-84.1%, pancreatic enzymes-89.2%, fat-soluble vitamins-89%, oxygen therapy-3.3%. CFTR modulator therapy was used in 2262 pts (60.5%), including 684 adult (55.1%) and 1614 children (63%).

Conclusion: 90% of Russian pts are included in the registry, an increase in lung function to normal levels and a high percentage of gram-negative infections are noted, while the number of pts receiving CFTR modulators increases to 60.5%.

Methods: We analyzed clinical data before initiation, at one year and 2,5years after receiving ETI for 7 adult pwCF with at least one F508del allele and severe lung disease at CF center Kozle, University clinic for respiratory diseases in children, Skopje, R.N. Macedonia. Assessments included FEV1%, weight, BMI, sweat chloride, use of pancreatic enzymes and insulin, and incidence of DIOS over 1 and 2.5 years after ETI initiation. Sweat chloride concentration decreased from 105.6 mmol/L (CI 130-75) before to 51.1 mmol/L (CI 90-30) after first year, and 58 mmol/l (100-30 CL) at 2, 5 years (p<0.01). BMI z-scores increased slightly but with no statistical significance (baseline 23.6, first year 24.7 and after 2,5y BMI was 24).Pancreatic enzyme use remained with no decrease in use. Insulin utilization was equally unchanged, and DIOS incidence remained low (around 2.5%). This cohort experienced significant improvements in FEV1% (p<0.01) from baseline of 32.6% (20-40FEV1%), at first year was 49.6 %( 22-65%) and 46.9 % ( 23-65%) at 2.5 years. 5 pw CF discontinued inhalator therapy on their own, one had no effect of ETI due to double complex alleles L467F-508F, 2 had depression and one patient died because of cardiorespiratory failure. records.title: Mortality in cystic fibrosis: analysis of causes and predictors of death in patients from the Republic of Moldova

person.institution: Nicolae Testemitanu State University of Medicine and Pharmacy

records.authors_text: C. Conica1,2, C. Tomacinschii1,2, D. Efros1,2, L. Rusu3, N. Buga2, A. Cotoman1, R. Selevestru2, S. Sciuca2
records.affiliations_text: 1Mother and Child Institute, Pediatrics, Chișinau, Moldova, Republic of, 2State University of Medicine and Pharmacy „Nicolae Testemitanu”,, Chișinau, Moldova, Republic of, 3Children Emergency Hospital, Cluj Napoca, Romania
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Cystic fibrosis(CF) is a multisystem genetic disease associated with significant morbidity and mortality, mainly due to progressive lung damage and infectious complications. Despite therapeutic advances and the introduction of CFTR modulator therapies, death still occurs at young ages. Mortality analysis provides valuable insight into the natural course of the disease and its clinical and imaging prognostic factors. The aim is to evaluate mortality characteristics among patients with cystic fibrosis in the Republic of Moldova.

Methods: A retrospective descriptive study was conducted, including deceased CF patients followed at the National Cystic Fibrosis Centre of the Republic of Moldova between 2022 and 2025. Data regarding causes of death, pulmonary imaging findings, comorbidities, and paraclinical parameters were analysed, acknowledging limitations related to irregular medical follow-up.

Results: Seven patients were included, with a mean age at death of 14.29 ± 9.5 years (range 1–26 years); 71.4% were female. The mean age at diagnosis was 2 years, with 57% diagnosed during the first year of life. Death was predominantly associated with advanced lung disease and severe infectious complications. Sepsis was the leading cause of death in 57% of cases. CT findings suggestive of advanced lung disease were identified in 85,71% of patients, and bronchiectasis in 71,43%. P. aeruginosa and S. aureus were detected in 100% of sputum cultures. The delF508 genotype and severe pancreatic insufficiency were present in all patients; related diabetes in 28,57% and pulmonary aspergillosis in 57,14%, including 1 case of invasive bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.

Conclusions: Mortality in cystic fibrosis in the Republic of Moldova occurs predominantly at young ages and is strongly associated with advanced structural lung disease, as evidenced by thoracic CT abnormalities in 85,71% of cases. Severe infectious complications, particularly sepsis, were the main causes of death.

records.title: Baseline nutritional and pulmonary status in Ukrainian individuals with cystic fibrosis prior to CFTR modulator introduction: registry-based analysis

person.institution: Ivan Franko National University of Lviv

records.authors_text: Y. Poliakova1, L. Bober2, O. Lyga2, T. Okul3, N. Hlliadielova4, K. Petrychko5, O. Vashchuk6, N. Matiytsiv1, H. Makukh7,8
records.affiliations_text: 1Ivan Franko National University of Lviv, Lviv, Ukraine, 2West Ukrainian Specialised Children Hospital, Lviv, Ukraine, 3Regional Clinical Children's Hospital, Department of Pulmonology, Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, 4Shupyk National Healthcare University of Ukraine, Kyiv, Ukraine, 5Regional Children's Clinical Hospital, CF Center, Mukachevo, Ukraine, 6Lviv Regional Hospital of Veterans of Wars and Repressed Named after Yu.Lypa, Lviv, Ukraine, 7Scientific Medical Genetic Center LeoGENE, Lviv, Ukraine, 8Lviv Regional Clinical Perinatal Center, Regional Center of Neonatal Screening, Lviv, Ukraine
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Nutritional status and lung function (LF) are key prognostic factors in cystic fibrosis (CF). The global shift towards highly effective CFTR modulators has transformed CF care, with rapid weight gain reported as early treatment effects. This study aimed to establish a pre‑modulator baseline of nutritional and pulmonary status in Ukrainian patients with CF and to examine how BMI and CFTR genotype relate to LF prior to widespread ETI therapy.

Methods: We conducted a cross‑sectional analysis of 512 Ukrainian patients with CF recorded in the 2023 European Cystic Fibrosis Society Patient Registry (ECFSPR). Patients were grouped into three CFTR genotype categories: F508del homozygous, F508del heterozygous and other genotypes. Associations between BMI and LF were assessed using Spearman’s rank correlation and multivariable linear regression adjusting for age and sex. Genotype differences were evaluated using the Kruskal–Wallis test with Bonferroni‑adjusted Dunn post hoc comparisons.

Results: Among 512 patients (51.2% male), the median age was 12.5 y. and the median BMI z-score was −0.8 (Q1 −1.7, Q3 −0.03). Analyses were performed in 278 patients with complete anthropometric and LF data. BMI z-score was positively correlated with FEV₁% (ρ=0.21, p<0.001) and FVC% (ρ=0.21, p<0.001). Higher BMI z-score was associated with higher FEV₁% (β=5.97, 95% CI 3.02–8.92, p<2.7×10⁻⁹) and FVC% (β=5.63, 95% CI 2.78–8.48, p<3.1×10⁻⁸), while age showed a strong negative effect. BMI z-score did not differ between genotype groups. In contrast, FEV₁% and FVC% were higher in F508del homozygous and heterozygous patients compared with other genotypes (p<0.002; p<0.001), partly reflecting differences in age distribution (median age 10.4 vs 12.0 years).

Conclusions: Better nutritional status, reflected by higher BMI z-scores, was consistently associated with better LF, as is well established. Further analysis will assess nutritional and pulmonary association following ETI introduction.

records.title: Effects of air pollution on pulmonary exacerbations: longitudinal analysis of the CF registry
records.authors_text: M. Leemans1,2, R. Epaud2,3, T. Benoussaid4, A. Bessou5, A. Coman6, I. Coll6, S. Lanone2, E. Audureau1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Assistance Publique – Hôpitaux de Paris (APHP), Hôpital Henri-Mondor, Service Santé Publique & Unité de Recherche Clinique (URC Mondor), Créteil, France, 2Université Paris-Est Créteil, Inserm, IMRB U955, Créteil, France, 3Centre Hospitalier Intercommunal de Créteil, Deptartment of Pneumology, Créteil, France, 4Université Paris Cité and Univ Paris Est Creteil, CNRS, LISA, Paris, France, 5Vaincre la Mucoviscidose, Paris, France, 6Univ Paris Est Creteil and Université Paris Cité, CNRS, LISA, Créteil, France
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Cystic fibrosis (CF) exhibits heterogeneous lung disease progression, which may be worsened by environmental exposures such as air pollution. We aimed to evaluate the non-linear and age-specific effects of PM₁₀, PM₂.₅, and NO₂ on pulmonary exacerbations in children with CF using data from the French CF Registry.

Methods: Data from 909 children (ages 6–12) were analyzed. Pulmonary exacerbations were modeled with a negative binomial generalized linear mixed model accounting for nested clustering. Non-linear pollutant effects and age interactions were assessed using departmental air quality data.

Results: Predicted exacerbation counts increased non-linearly with PM₁₀, PM₂.₅, and NO₂, showing clear age-specific patterns. Six- and 8-year-olds exhibited substantial increases with PM₁₀ and NO₂ (p<0.001), whereas 10- and 12-year-olds were less affected. PM₂.₅ effects were pronounced in 12-year-olds (p<0.001) but minimal in younger children. These findings highlight strong age-dependent vulnerability to air pollution.

Conclusion: Air pollution is associated with higher pulmonary exacerbations in CF, especially among younger children. Considering non-linear and age-specific effects is critical for risk assessment and supports targeted interventions to reduce exposure in vulnerable populations.

Acknowledgements: We thank Vaincre la Mucoviscidose, CF centres, and all patients for participation. This work is part of the REMEDIA project, funded by EU Horizon 2020 (Grant No. 874753).

records.title: Regional differences in waitlist and lung transplant outcomes for adults with cystic fibrosis: the United States experience
records.authors_text: A. Oak1, L. Fan1, A. Feng1, A. Bermudez1, A. Casillan1, S. Agbor-Enoh1, E. Bush1, C. Merlo1
records.affiliations_text: 1Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, Baltimore, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a key indication for lung transplantation (LT). Despite medical advances, many adults develop end-stage lung disease and require LT. The geographical impact on access to LT is unclear. We aimed to quantify differences in waitlist outcomes by geographical region, as defined by the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS).

Methods: We utilized the UNOS database, including adults listed for single-organ LT from January 2005 to November 2023. We analyzed baseline characteristics with Chi-square and Kruskal-Wallis tests. Waitlist outcomes (transplant, death/deterioration) were modeled using Fine-Gray competing risks; subdistribution hazard ratios (sHRs) were reported as 95% confidence intervals. Models adjusted for age, BMI, lung allocation score (LAS), diabetes history and sex. Summary data was reported as overall median [IQR] and the median [IQR] of the medians of each region.

Results:

records.title: Your Life and CF: a longitudinal summary
records.authors_text: K. Earlam1, A. Billin1
records.affiliations_text: 1Cystic Fibrosis Trust, Policy and Public Affairs, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: For four years, Cystic Fibrosis Trust (CFT) has run Your Life and CF, an annual survey capturing the lived experiences of people with cystic fibrosis (CF) across the UK. While triple-therapy CFTR modulators have improved clinical outcomes for many, CF remains a lifelong, multisystem condition requiring intensive specialist care. Significant financial pressures, treatment burden, and psychosocial challenges persist. Your Life and CF builds on the 2022 Cost of CF baseline to track these experiences over time.

Objectives: To describe the scale of need, year-on-year trends, and changes in lived experience reported by people affected by CF between 2022 and 2025.

Methods: Between 2022 and 2025, CFT conducted annual surveys with around 40 mixed-method questions covering physical and mental health, cost of living, treatment burden, neurodiversity, and access to care. Core measures were repeated annually to monitor trends.

Results: Across four years, findings show persistent financial and treatment burden despite clinical progress. In 2022, 87% worried about money, three in ten had run out of food, and one in three missed essential appointments due to cost. Subsequent surveys show continued cost-of-living pressures affecting food, travel, energy, and household essentials. In 2025, respondents spent almost four hours per day on treatments. Mental health concerns remained high: 70% felt lonely at least some of the time and 90% worried about the future. Nearly 29% identified as neurodiverse in 2025, with most reporting an impact on their CF care.

Conclusions: The longitudinal data demonstrate that, despite the advent of transformative therapies, people with CF continue to face substantial financial, mental health, and treatment burdens that shape daily life and future prospects. These insights underline the importance of holistic policy responses that extend beyond clinical benchmarks to include social, economic, and psychological dimensions of living with CF.

records.title: Impact of parenthood on pulmonary exacerbation frequency among people with cystic fibrosis: findings from the HOPeCF retrospective cohort study

person.title: Dr.
person.institution: University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine

records.authors_text: T. Kazmerski1, O. Stransky1, M. Lee2, R. Jain3, A. Georgiopoulos4, J. Billings5, E. Dellon6, K. Ramos7, N. West8, J. Taylor9
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, Pediatrics, Pittsburgh, United States, 2University of Texas Houston, Houston, United States, 3University of Texas Southwestern, Dallas, United States, 4Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, United States, 5University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, United States, 6University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, United States, 7University of Washington, Seattle, United States, 8Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, United States, 9National Jewish Health, Denver, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Using Health Outcomes of Parents with CF (HOPeCF) retrospective data, we examined pulmonary exacerbation (PEx) rates among parents and nonparents with CF (PwCF; NPwCF).

Methods: We surveyed PwCF who became new parents between 2012-2022 and NPwCF and linked results to their 2010-2023 patient registry data. We assessed PEx for two cohorts (2012-2018; 2019-2022). We designated time points as year -1 and -2 (pre-parenthood), year 0 (parenthood onset; assigned as 2015 and 2021 for NPwCF), and year 1-5 (post-parenthood). We evaluated longitudinal change in PEx rate using multivariable longitudinal negative binomial regression models adjusted for age, race, lung function, ever ivacaftor or elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor (ETI) use, insurance status, number of children, and years of parenthood.

Results: We recruited 970 participants (253 PwCF/717 NPwCF). PwCF were 59% female, 91% White, 17% Medicaid-insured, and 90% ever used ivacaftor/ETI. In the 2012-2018 cohort, longitudinal change in PEx rate differed significantly between PwCF and NPwCF(p=0.02). PwCF had a significant increase in PEx rate year -1-0 (adjusted rate ratio =1.38[1.09,1.76]; p<0.01). In year 1-2, PwCF had a decrease in PEx rate (0.81[0.64,1.02]; p=0.07) and NPwCF a significant increase (1.21[1.08,1.35]; p<0.01). Both groups experienced a significant decrease in PEx year 4-5 (likely due to widespread ETI use). In the 2019-2022 cohort, longitudinal change in PEx rate did not significantly differ between PwCF and NPwCF(p=0.11). Both experienced a significant decrease in PEx from year -2 to -1 while only PwCF had a significant decrease in PEx from year -1-0 (likely due to ETI). Comparing mothers vs. fathers, we found no significant differences in PEx rates over time.

Conclusions: Parenthood largely does not impact longitudinal PEx rates among people with CF especially in the ETI era. Furthermore, we found no differences in PEx rates by parental sex.

records.title: Pregnancy care and outcomes in patients with cystic fibrosis at a UK specialist centre

person.institution: Oxford Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Oxford University Hospitals

records.authors_text: A. Yue1, H. Caterson1, A. Gates1, N. Hough1
records.affiliations_text: 1Oxford Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Oxford University Hospitals, Oxford, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Advances in cystic fibrosis (CF) therapies, including highly effective modulator therapy, have resulted in increased pregnancies among people with CF (pwCF). Currently there are no clear guidelines on the management of pregnancy in pwCF. The Oxford Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre (OACFC) provides regional specialist care for pwCF. We aimed to evaluate pregnancy management, and maternal and infant outcomes in pwCF under our care.

Methods: Pregnancies between 2005 and 2025 were identified using the UK Cystic Fibrosis Registry and cross-referenced with electronic patient records. Data were collected on maternal characteristics, pregnancy complications, delivery outcomes, infant outcomes, and clinician management practices.

Results: Data were available for 15 pwCF, comprising 24 pregnancies. 15 pregnancies resulted in live births (11 vaginal deliveries and four caesarean sections), 4 miscarriages and 5 terminations. Twelve pregnancies occurred in individuals receiving CFTR modulator therapy. Mean baseline lung function (FEV1) was 74.7% (range 18-118%). 5 pregnancies were identified as high risk by lung function and BMI; 3 resulted in a live birth at term, 2 required pre-term Caesarean section. Pulmonary exacerbations occurred in 11 pregnancies. Obstetric complications included pre-eclampsia (n=2) and gestational diabetes (n=4), with 5 pregnancies in patients with pre-existing diabetes. Low birth weight was documented in 3 infants (1115-2410kg). Most pregnancies were managed jointly with maternal medicine specialists. Gaps in data were identified, particularly lung function, maternal weight change, and infant health outcomes.

Conclusion: Pregnancy in pwCF is increasingly common and often complicated by CF-related and obstetric comorbidities. Despite this, outcomes are generally favourable highlighting the need for specialist multidisciplinary care. Further work is required to establish standards of care, formalise clinical pathways, and improve data collection.

records.title: Pregnancy under elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor: frequency, outcomes and impact on clinical practice in a single adult cystic fibrosis centre

person.title: MD
person.institution: Adult Cystic Fibrosis Unit, National Reference Centre for Congenital Disorders (CRENADECER), BPS

records.authors_text: M.A. Rey1, A. Arriola1, A. Licio1, D. Murillo1, C. Mosteiro1, S. Guillen1, M. Palazuelo1, M. Silva1, L. Ferro1, M.C. Pinchak1
records.affiliations_text: 1Adult Cystic Fibrosis Unit, National Reference Centre for Congenital Disorders (CRENADECER), BPS, Montevideo, Uruguay
records.abstract_text:
Background: The introduction of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) has improved health and fertility in women with cystic fibrosis (CF). However, real-world data on pregnancy frequency and outcomes remain limited, particularly outside large registries.

Objectives: To describe pregnancy frequency, maternal characteristics and pregnancy outcomes in women with CF receiving ETI, and to assess the impact of these findings on clinical practice.

Methods: We performed a retrospective review of adult women with CF treated with ETI at a single centre from June 2021 to January 2026. Women of reproductive age (<40 years) were identified. Maternal nutritional and pulmonary status was described using the closest available post-ETI measurements prior to pregnancy. Pregnancy outcomes were recorded.

Results: Among 15 women receiving ETI, 11 were of reproductive age. Five women (range 45.5%) experienced at least one pregnancy. Median time from ETI initiation to conception was 8.4 months (2.3–40.1). Only one pregnancy was planned.Maternal status prior to pregnancy was heterogeneous (BMI 19.1–27.0 kg/m²; ppFEV1 27–90%), including advanced lung disease, with two women requiring oxygen therapy and one listed for transplantation.ETI was continued throughout gestation.At analysis, five pregnancies had reached an outcome: one live birth at 36 weeks, one extremely preterm birth at 27 weeks with neonatal death, one fetal demise at 36 weeks due to hydrops, one early miscarriage, and one elective termination at 11 weeks. Two additional pregnancies were ongoing.

Conclusions: In this experience, nearly half of women of reproductive age receiving ETI conceived, most without prior planning. Outcomes were heterogeneous, precluding causal inference. These findings prompted changes in clinical practice, including systematic reproductive counselling, proactive contraceptive guidance at ETI initiation, and multidisciplinary management of pregnancies within high-risk obstetric care pathways.

These findings prompted changes in clinical practice, including systematic reproductive counselling, proactive contraceptive guidance at ETI initiation, and multidisciplinary management of pregnancies within high-risk obstetric care pathways.

records.title: Effects of discontinuing inhaled corticosteroids: a target trial emulation using the UK Cystic Fibrosis Registry

person.institution: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

records.authors_text: E. McClenaghan1, J. Rouette2, E. Granger1, G. Davies3, R. Keogh1, J. Tazare1
records.affiliations_text: 1London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, Department of Medical Statistics, London, United Kingdom, 2GSK, Global Epidemiology, Montreal, Canada, 3UCL Great Ormond Street Institute of Child Health, Population, Policy & Practice Dept, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) remain commonly prescribed in cystic fibrosis (CF) despite limited evidence of benefit and substantial treatment burden. A randomised controlled trial (CF-WISE, PMID:1655669) concluded discontinuation of ICS appears safe. We aimed to estimate the causal effect of discontinuing ICS on clinical outcomes using real-world data, applying a target trial emulation framework.

Methods: We conducted a population-based cohort study using UK CF Registry data (2016-2018), emulating a target trial based on CF-WISE. Eligible individuals were aged ≥6 years, had FEV1 ≥40% predicted, and received ≥3 months ICS therapy. Two innovative causal study designs were implemented: (i) prevalent new-user design, and (ii) sequential trials design. ICS discontinuation was compared with continued use, defined using exact prescription start and stop dates in the Registry.

Primary outcome was time to first pulmonary exacerbation, defined as intravenous antibiotic treatment. Secondary outcome was change in percent predicted FEV1 over six months. Analyses adjusted for measured confounding using propensity-score based weighting and regression adjustment for methods (i) and (ii) respectively.

Results: Among 3516 people meeting eligibility criteria for the emulated trial, 423 (12%) discontinued inhaled corticosteroids during the study period, while 3093 (88%) continued treatment. Median (IQR) length of ICS use prior to eligibility was 55 months (27-145), and 67% experienced at least one pulmonary exacerbation during the study period. Effect estimates for pulmonary exacerbation and lung function will be presented and compared across study designs, with benchmarking against the CF-WISE trial.

Conclusion: This study applies and compares robust causal inference methods to address a clinically important question in CF. Findings will inform safety of ICS discontinuation and demonstrate the utility of target trial emulation for evaluating treatment strategies in CF.

records.title: Investigating CFTR modulator effectiveness with target trial emulation: lessons from the Dutch CF Registry
records.authors_text: D.D. Zomer-van Ommen1, J. Stoelinga2, D.L. Weir2, C. Leopold2, R.W. Hofland3, H.M. Janssens4, J.J. Noordhoek-van der Staay1, R. Okhuijsen-Kos1, K.M. de Winter-de Groot5, W.G. Goettsch2,6, Dutch CF Registry Steering Committee
records.affiliations_text: 1Dutch CF Foundation, Soest, Netherlands, 2Utrecht University, Pharmaceutical Sciences, Utrecht, Netherlands, 3University Medical Center Utrecht, Pulmonary Medicine, Utrecht, Netherlands, 4Erasmus University Medical Center, Sophia Children's Hospital, Pediatrics, Rotterdam, Netherlands, 5Wilhelmina Children's Hospital, University Medical Center, Utrecht University, Pediatric Pulmonology, Utrecht, Netherlands, 6National Healthcare Institute, Diemen, Netherlands
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: CFTR modulator therapy, such as elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI), has greatly improved treatment of people with Cystic Fibrosis (pwCF). While their efficacy has been established in randomized controlled trials, Real-World Evidence (RWE) is key to understanding long-term effectiveness in clinical practice. Real-world data collected through disease registries can help inform the optimal use of ETI in clinical practice, if effectiveness is assessed using robust methods like Target Trial Emulation (TTE). We aimed to assess whether the Dutch CF Registry is suitable for estimating ETI effectiveness via TTE.

Methods: We compared two strategies: switching from dual modulator therapy to ETI versus staying on dual therapy. Outcomes included lung function, sweat chloride concentration, and quality of life (CFQ-R). Data were obtained from the Dutch CF registry, which extracts data from electronic patient records. Data quality was evaluated using the European Medicines Agency data quality framework.

Results: The Dutch CF Registry contains longitudinal data (2010-2024) of 1,735 pwCF (~95% coverage). Of these, 1,312 initiated ETI, of whom 831 previously received dual modulator therapy. Among the 932 dual therapy users, the number eligible to serve as a comparator group was limited (approximately 101 individuals at specific time points). We noticed changing measurement guidelines and evolving clinical practice over the years, which can impact the consistency of some outcome variables measured.

Conclusion: Despite high coverage, estimating real-world effectiveness from a national CF registry remains challenging. Limitations of the current dataset may impact the use of TTE to guarantee methodological rigor. Our findings suggest future adaptations to the Dutch CF Registry to enable more reliable RWE using TTE on CFTR modulator effectiveness.

records.title: Incidence, prevalence and patterns of Stenotrophomonas maltophilia infection in people with cystic fibrosis across Europe

person.title: Dr
person.institution: Pediatric Pulmonology Institute, Schneider Children’s Medical Center

records.affiliations_text: 1Pediatric Pulmonology Institute, Schneider Children’s Medical Center, Petah Tiqwa, Israel, 2Faculty of Medical and Health Sciences, Tel Aviv University, Tel Aviv, Israel, 3Laboratory of Medical Statistics, Biometry and Epidemiology “G. records.abstract_text:
Introduction: Stenotrophomonas maltophilia (SM) is increasingly detected in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF), but its clinical significance remains uncertain. This study aimed to track SM prevalence over time, describe infection patterns and assess its clinical implications.

Methods: In this longitudinal study based on the European Cystic Fibrosis Society Patient Registry (ECFSPR), we analyzed the prevalence and incidence of SM airway infection and its association with demographic and clinical characteristics. Logistic regression models were used to assess temporal trends.

Results: In 2023, the prevalence of SM (chronic and intermittent) ranged from 0.26% in Romania to 19.3% in Serbia. Overall, 2556/51566 pwCF across 42 European countries were infected (5.0%; 95% CI: 4.8 to 5.2). SM was associated with older age, increased treatment burden, and more complications (including ABPA and CFRD); chronic SM was also associated with higher steroids and antibiotics use. The prevalence of SM rose markedly between 2018 and 2023, with an inflection point around 2019—showing an upward trend beforehand and a gradual decline thereafter. Among 32,724 pwCF, the most common infection patterns were as follows: 75.2% (24,594) had no infections, 24.8% (8,130) had SM infection in at least one year, and 11.1% (3,640) had SM infection for at least two years.

Conclusion: This large analysis offers a detailed view of SM infection in the European CF population, revealing that while most individuals remained uninfected, nearly one-quarter experienced infection between 2018 and 2023. Chronic infection was increased with age and was consistently linked to greater co infection burden. Temporal patterns—rising until 2019 and gradually declining in the CFTR modulator and post COVID era—indicate that medical advancements and shifts in healthcare practice influence SM epidemiology. These findings highlight the need for continued surveillance to guide care and research.

Prof Prais, specialist in Pediatrics and Pediatric Pulmonology, graduated from Hadassah Medical School in Jerusalem and is currently the Director of the Pediatric Pulmonology Institute at Schneider Children's Medical Center. Is actively involved in teaching medical students and resident training.
Prof. Prais holds the position of Associate professor at the School of Medicine, Faculty of Medical and Health Sciences, Tel Aviv University, and has published tens of peer-reviewed articles in medical journals.
He is the Director of the Graub Cystic Fibrosis Center and a former member of the Clinical Trials Network executive committee at the European Cystic Fibrosis Society.
His primary focuses of clinical and research interest are, among others, cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, bronchiolitis, chronic lung disease of t premature, and bronchopulmonary dysplasia.

records.title: UNC bug bank and the NTM cohort experience: automated integration of clinical data of NTM isolates in CF and non-CF cohorts
records.authors_text: S.M. Caceres1,2, C.E. Wate3, T.A. Miner4, B.C. Ramachandran3, R.L. Bradford5, K. Ndura5, R. Patel5, K. Sternat5, K. Alby6, T.M. Andermann7, K.N. Olivier8, Q. Liu4, J.E. Gross1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of North Carolina, Pediatrics-Pulmonology, Chapel Hill, United States, 2National Jewish Health, Medicine- Pulmonary, Denver, United States, 3University of North Carolina, Global Health and Infectious Disease, Chapel Hill, United States, 4University of North Carolina, Genetics, Chapel Hill, United States, 5University of North Carolina, TraCS Institute, Chapel Hill, United States, 6University of North Carolina, Division of Pathology, Chapel Hill, United States, 7University of North Carolina, Med-ID Trnsplt Compromised Hst, Chapel Hill, United States, 8University of North Carolina, Medicine- Pulmonary, Chapel Hill, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Access to bacterial isolates and clinical data is essential for advancing research, yet researchers often face challenges. The University of North Carolina (UNC) developed a Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap®)-based Automated Microbial Pipeline (RAMP) that identifies clinical bacterial isolates and combines clinical and bacterial data. Here, we describe the use of RAMP for identifying nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) positive cultures at UNC in people with and without Cystic Fibrosis (CF).

Methods: The IRB-approved, consent-waived RAMP protocol automatically screens microbiology data uploaded to the electronic health record (EPIC) and extracts relevant isolate and clinical data. Clinical data from defined cohorts, including NTM cohort, are retrieved from the Carolina Data Warehouse for Health (CDWH) using computable phenotypes, transformed into REDCap format, and uploaded into the RAMP project via REDCap API. Within the NTM cohort, RAMP provides demographics, AFB smear and culture results, chronic NTM infection status and antimicrobial susceptibility disclosing minimal protected health information. Isolates are collected, sequenced and banked in a de-identified manner while preserving linkages to identified data.

Results: NTM cohort data extraction began in mid-December 2025. Within the first month, RAMP identified 108 NTM isolates from 89 unique subjects. Most specimens were sputum (84.2%) followed by bronchial lavages (15%). NTM species distribution included Mycobacterium abscessus (41%), M. intracellulare (36.7%) and M. avium complex (17.3%). Specimen and data collection are ongoing.

Conclusions: RAMP is an efficient tool for researchers, facilitating rapid access to isolates and data without disrupting clinical workflows. Early implementation revealed minor limitations requiring manual extraction. These findings demonstrate RAMP’s potential to enhance CF-related NTM research and expand collaboration without major infrastructural changes.

records.title: Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor treatment and odds of Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus in a cohort of children and adolescents with cystic fibrosis: analysis of Canadian registry data

person.institution: London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine

records.authors_text: K. Ebbert1,2, M. Njoroge3
records.affiliations_text: 1London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, Epidemiology, London, United Kingdom, 2University of Calgary, Pediatrics, Calgary, Canada, 3London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, Medical Statistics, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To assess whether elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) is associated with decreased odds of respiratory pathogens P. aeruginosa and methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) in 6-17-year-old persons with cystic fibrosis (pwCF).

Methods: This observational cohort study used previously collected secondary anonymised Canadian Cystic Fibrosis (CF) Registry data. 6-17-year-old pwCF with ≥1 F508del, available Registry data June 1, 2020-December 31, 2023, initiating ETI June 2021-December 2022, and ≥1 CF respiratory culture in the 12 months pre- and post-ETI initiation were included. P. aeruginosa or MSSA outcomes were defined positive if present in any density on ≥1 culture. Individual data for discordant pairs comparing the 12 months pre- and post-ETI initiation were assessed using McNemar's Χ2 test, estimating an odds ratio (OR) for the association between ETI initiation and P. aeruginosa and MSSA.

records.title: Antimicrobial coatings on adhesive copper tapes as a method for preventing hospital-acquired infections and cross-contamination of patients

person.institution: Federal State Budgetary Institution «National Research Center for Epidemiology and Microbiology named after the Honorary Academician N.F. Gamaleya

records.authors_text: M. Chernukha1,2, L. Avetisyan1, E. Domblides1, A. Emelyanenko2, L. Boinovich2
records.affiliations_text: 1Federal State Budgetary Institution «National Research Center for Epidemiology and Microbiology named after the Honorary Academician N.F. Gamaleya, Moscow, Russian Federation, 2Frumkin Institute of Physical Chemistry and Electrochemistry, Russian Academy of Sciences, Moscow, Russian Federation
records.abstract_text:
Nosocomial infections (NIs) remain a major healthcare challenge and pose a major threat to cystic fibrosis patients. The spread of pathogens occurs not only from patients but also via contaminated surfaces. This leads to cross-infection. Innovative approaches, such as the use of antimicrobial coatings on high-touch surfaces, are being developed to reduce the infection risk.

Objective: To evaluate the effectiveness of antimicrobial coatings on adhesive copper tapes, developed at the A.N. Frumkin Institute of Physical Chemistry and Electrochemistry (Moscow), in preventing NIs.

Materials and Methods: A 5-month clinical study was conducted in a hospital setting. 1,440 swabs were taken from 24 touch surfaces (elevator buttons, switches, door handles). 4 surface types were compared: K (control) – stainless steel, A – copper oxide/titanium oxide composite on laser-textured copper foil, T – laser-textured copper foil, M – smooth copper foil. Bacteriological methods and MALDI-TOF were used, with positive cultures from surfaces recorded (grant 23-73-30004 Russian Science Foundation).

Results: Control surfaces showed 64.63% positive samples, whereas laser-textured copper had only 22.67%. Smooth copper and the composite demonstrated 28–29% positive results. A total of 40 bacterial species were isolated from all surfaces, with Staphylococcus epidermidis, Micrococcus luteus, and Staphylococcus aureus being dominant. Notably, copper and composite surfaces exhibited lower microbial diversity and significantly reduced pathogen detection rates, especially for S. aureus (cell count ratio for surfaces K/M/T/A = 43/2/1/1.4). The overall microbial load on textured copper was 26.8 times lower than on stainless steel (p<0.05). Composite coatings also displayed strong antimicrobial properties.

Conclusion: Antimicrobial coatings, particularly textured copper and its composite derivatives, demonstrate high efficacy in reducing bacterial contamination and can be recommended for preventing NIs.

records.title: Where do we stand in immunisation? Vaccination status and attitudes in cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: E.E. Baysal1, G. Taştan2, Ş. Karabulut1, C.A. Yıldız1, N.M. Çakar1, M.M. Akkitap Yiğit1, F. Özdemircioğlu1, B. Özgünay1, E. Uğurlu1, G. Alışbeyli1, F. Gafarova1, B. Uzunoğlu2, C. Yılmaz Yeğit1, A.P. Ergenekon1, Y. Gökdemir1, E.E. Eralp1, F. Karakoç1, B. Karadağ1
records.affiliations_text: 1Marmara University School of Medicine, Division of Paediatric Pulmonology, Istanbul, Turkey, 2Marmara University School of Medicine, Selim Çöremen Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Istanbul, Turkey
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a lifelong genetic disease in which respiratory infections substantially contribute to morbidity and mortality. Immunisation is a key preventive strategy in CF care. This study evaluated vaccination status and attitudes among patients with CF and presents baseline data from an ongoing quality improvement initiative.

Methods: A retrospective review was conducted among 465 patients with CF followed at a tertiary cystic fibrosis centre. Completeness of the national mandatory immunisation schedule was assessed in patients with available national digital immunisation records (n=317), whereas uptake of influenza and polysaccharide pneumococcal vaccines was evaluated in the entire cohort (n=465) using digital records, supplemented by patient/caregiver reports. Vaccination attitudes were assessed using the Vaccine Attitudes Examination (VAX) scale. Clinical and demographic data were obtained from the centre database.

Results: Of the cohort (n=465), 53.5% were male, with a median age of 12.7 years (7.6–19.7). Median FEV1% was 87.4 (67.9–100.4), and mean BMI z-score was −0.17± 0.05. Among patients with available digital records (n=317), 53.6% had a fully completed mandatory immunisation schedule. Uptake of influenza vaccine during the last season and polysaccharide pneumococcal vaccine was low (12.7% and 4.9%, respectively). Parents/caregivers demonstrated higher preference for natural immunity scores on the VAX scale compared with adult patients (p=0.002). During follow-up, influenza vaccination coverage increased to approximately 45%.

Conclusion: Mandatory immunisation was completed in a proportion of patients; however, important gaps remained, especially in influenza and polysaccharide pneumococcal vaccination. On the basis of these findings, a reminder- and education-based quality improvement initiative was initiated and is ongoing.

records.title: Positive airway pressure initiation is associated with improved lung function in persons with cystic fibrosis

person.title: Dr.
person.institution: St. Michael's Hospital, University of Toronto

records.authors_text: N. Vozoris1, I. Sharpe2, J. Sykes1, C. Ryan3, E. Tullis1, A. Stephenson1
records.affiliations_text: 1St. Michael's Hospital, University of Toronto, Respirology, Toronto, Canada, 2Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences, Toronto, Canada, 3University Health Network, University of Toronto, Respirology, Toronto, Canada
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: It is uncertain if treating sleep breathing disorders in the setting of cystic fibrosis (CF) improves pulmonary outcomes. Among persons with CF, our purpose was to evaluate the relationship between incident positive airway pressure (PAP) receipt and respiratory-related hospitalizations and lung function trajectory.

Methods: This retrospective, data-linkage, population-based, self-controlled interval risk study linked data from the Canadian CF Registry and Ontario health administrative databases. All persons with CF newly receiving PAP between January 1, 2009-December 31, 2020, who remained alive and did not receive lung transplantation during follow-up, were included. Rate of respiratory-related hospitalizations and the rate of change in %predicted forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) were evaluated in the 6-months before vs. 6-months after PAP receipt. We separately evaluated our outcomes amongst incident continuous PAP (CPAP) recipients and incident bi-level PAP (BPAP) recipients. Because each participant served as his/her own control, we only adjusted for changes in receipt of CF-specific treatments in the pre- vs. post-PAP periods.

Results: We identified 28 incident CPAP recipients and 44 incident BPAP recipients. In adjusted analyses, non-significant reduced rates of respiratory-related hospitalizations were observed post- vs. pre-PAP for both PAP groups (CPAP: rate ratio [RR] 0.97, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.56-1.69; BPAP: RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.53-1.08). In adjusted analyses, rate of change in %predicted FEV1 was significantly improved post- vs. pre-PAP for BPAP recipients (+3.2 vs. -12.9 %predicted/year, p<0.0001), but not for CPAP recipients (+2.4 vs. +0.2 %predicted/year, p=0.45).

Conclusions: Amongst persons with CF newly receiving BPAP (but not CPAP), a significant improvement in lung function trajectory post-PAP receipt was observed, accompanied by non-significant trends towards lower rates of respiratory-related hospitalizations.

person.biography: Dr. Stephenson completed her internal medicine training at the University of Toronto, Respiratory Medicine at the University of British Columbia and her PhD in Clinical Epidemiology at U of T in 2010. Dr. Stephenson is an Associate Professor and Clinician Scientist at St. Michael’s Hospital in Toronto. She has been caring for adults living with CF at the Adult CF Clinic at St. Michael's Hospital since 2001 and is the Medical Director of the Canadian Cystic Fibrosis Registry. In addition to her clinical work caring for adults living with CF at the Adult CF Clinic at St. Michael's Hospital, she conducts population-based research using national CF Registry data as well as health administrative databases. More recently, she has expanded her work to compare health outcomes in CF internationally.

records.title: Investigation of the correlation between changes in sweat chloride concentration and clinical improvement following initiation of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor
records.authors_text: T. Bryrup1,2, H.K. Råket1,3,4, M. Jeppesen1,5, I.H.M. Mathiesen1,2, T. Qvist1,2, H.V. Olesen1,6, M.F. Olsen1,2,7, J. Petersen1,3,8

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: It is well-established that higher Sweat Chloride (SwCl) concentrations are associated with more severe cystic fibrosis (CF) phenotypes, and SwCl has been used as a surrogate marker of CFTR function restoration in clinical trials. After the introduction of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI), clinical outcomes have improved dramatically. In this study we aimed to examine the association between SwCl concentrations and improvements in clinical outcomes during ETI treatment.

Methods: We conducted a nationwide observational study using the Danish CF Cohort, including individuals aged ≥6 years with at least one F508del mutation who have initiated ETI. Pre-ETI baseline was defined as the 12 months prior to initiation; follow-up was 2 years for individuals aged ≥12 years and 1 year for those aged 6–11 years. Associations between SwCl and key outcomes (ppFEV1, BMI/BMI-z, LCI2.5, and CFQ-R scores) were assessed with ANCOVA models adjusted for age, sex, CF center, and baseline values of outcome measure and SwCl.

Results: A total of 58 individuals aged 6–11 years and 269 aged ≥12 years old were included. Mean ages were 9 and 29 years, respectively. Both groups had approximately 80% F508del homozygous individuals. In the ≥12-year group, delta ppFEV1 (95% CI) were 10.6 (8.6–12.6) for SwCl<30 mmol/l, 12.7 (11.5–13.9) for 30≤SwCl<60, and 9.6 (7.6–11.5) for SwCl≥60 between treatment and baseline period. In the 6–11-year group, delta estimates were 7.7 (5.2–10.2) for <30 mmol/L and 7.5 (5.5–9.5) for ≥30 mmol/L. All other outcomes showed similar patterns, with no differences between SwCl categories.

Conclusion: In this cohort, the prespecified SwCl categories during ETI treatment were not associated with changes in clinical outcomes following ETI initiation. Clinical benefits of ETI appear independent of changes in SwCl concentrations. Further research is needed to elucidate the mechanisms underlying this discordance.

records.abstract_text:
Background: Proton pump inhibitors (PPI) are widely used in people with CF (pwCF); while improving airway surface liquid (ASL) pH, they may increase susceptibility to bacterial infections. We assessed factors associated with their use, as well as association with FEV1 and infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PsA).

Methods: European Cystic Fibrosis Society Patient Registry (ECFSPR) data (2019-2024) were used. PwCF were grouped by longitudinal PPI exposure: never used (reference), use from 2020 with 3–5 consecutive years of treatment (cohort 1), and persistent use across all years (cohort 2). Annual ppFEV1 and PsA over time were analyzed with mixed-effect regression models. Multiple logistic regression assessed factors associated with starting PPI.

Results: A total of 39,767 pwCF were included (reference n=17367; cohort 1 n=957; cohort 2 n=6471); annual PPI use was 31–35%. Adjusted ppFEV1 was consistently higher in never-users (reference) than persistent users (cohort 2): 2019: 76.8 vs 71.9; 2024: 83.8 vs 77.9; overall p<0.001. Adjusted chronic PsA infection was lower in never-users than persistent users at baseline (2019: 34.9% vs 40.1%, p<0.001) and declined over follow-up, with narrowing between-cohort differences (2024: 25.2% vs 23.9%, p=0.029).

In the logistic model (n=15,774), odds of starting PPI were higher with pancreatic enzyme use (OR 2.21, 95%CI 1.80–2.70), oral steroids (2.38, 1.69–3.34), chronic PsA (1.27, 1.17–1.38), insulin-treated diabetes (1.37, 1.13–1.66) and female sex (1.20, 1.06–1.36); higher ppFEV1 reduced odds (OR 0.87, 0.78–0.98); age/BMI effects were non-linear, with higher odds around age 20 years, and at both low and high BMI z-scores.

Conclusions: In ECFSPR, PPI use is common and identifies pwCF with more severe disease. Initiation is strongly linked to pancreatic enzyme treatment and markers of advanced disease, including chronic PsA. Ongoing work will evaluate disease trajectories by PPI use and by duration of PPI exposure.

records.title: Comparative evaluation of cardiometabolic risk-factors in cystic fibrosis compared to other disease: a retrospective cohort study
records.authors_text: S. Humfress1, D. Nazareth2,3, G. Lip1, F. Frost1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Liverpool, Cardiovascular and Metabolic Medicine, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 2Liverpool Heart and Chest Hospital, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 3LCCS, Liverpool, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background and Objectives: An aging cystic fibrosis (CF) population means that diseases of aging, including cardiovascular disease (CVD), are emerging as new concerns and may become more prevalent in people with CF (PwCF). PwCF are at an increased risk of adverse cardiovascular (CV) events, such as heart attack, stroke, and diabetes. However, CVD risk profiles remain poorly described in this group.

Methods: A retrospective observation cohort study was performed utilising TriNetX global health network to determine CV risk profiles in adults with CF and observe 1-year CV outcomes (myocardial infarction, atrial fibrillation, heart failure, and a composite endpoint). Cardiometabolic disease codes were explored and compared in adults with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), and migraine. Analyses were conducted before and after propensity score matching.

Results: In total, 3,558 PwCF aged ≥ 16 years who had a recorded outpatient appointment between 1 and 4 years ago. The CF cohort had a mean age of 29.3 (SD = 13.4) and were 49.5% female. The CF cohort was less likely to be female compared to the RA cohort (49.5% vs 73.7%, p<0.001), the SLE cohort (49.5% vs. 88.0%, p<0.001), and the migraine cohort (49.5% vs. 81.8%, p<0.001). PwCF had higher prevalence of diabetes (39.1%) than RA (20.2%, p<0.001), SLE (11.0%, p<0.001), and migraine (11.3%, p<0.001), but lower prevalence of hypertension was seen in CF (14.1%, p<0.001) compared to RA (52.4%, p<0.001), SLE (39.3%, p<0.001), and migraine (28.5%, p<0.001).

Conclusions: PwCF have markedly different CVD risk profiles compared to people living with other inflammatory diseases considered high-risk for CVD. This highlights the importance of specific CV risk prediction models.

records.title: Understanding cystic fibrosis-associated colorectal polyp and cancer development: bridging clinical insights and molecular mechanisms.

person.department: Department of Pediatrics, Regenerative Medicine Center Utrecht

records.authors_text: V.J.A. Niessen1, M.I. van der Wijst1, D. Muilwijk2, I. Bronsveld3, E.C. van der Hout3, J.M. Beekman1, S. Spelier1, R.W. Hofland3
records.affiliations_text: 1UMC Utrecht, Department of Pediatrics, Regenerative Medicine Center Utrecht, Utrecht, Netherlands, 2Wilhelmina Children's Hospital, Department of Pediatric Respiratory Medicine, Utrecht, Netherlands, 3UMC Utrecht, Department of Pulmonary Medicine, Utrecht, Netherlands
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: People with Cystic Fibrosis (pwCF) are living longer, primarily due to the introduction and optimization of CFTR modulator therapy. However, ageing in pwCF is associated with long-term complications, such as colorectal cancer (CRC) and polyps. PwCF aged 40-49 show a CRC prevalence of ~23%, compared to 2-5% in age-matched non-CF individuals. Thus, pwCF undergo surveillance colonoscopies for early detection of colorectal polyps and cancer.

This study aims to improve understanding of CF-related CRC by combining epidemiological data with molecular analysis of corresponding patient-derived polyp tissue.

Methods: Clinical data from pwCF who underwent surveillance colonoscopies was extracted from patient files at the University Medical Centre Utrecht (the Netherlands) and was expanded with national data acquired by the Dutch Cystic Fibrosis Foundation (NCFS). The dataset includes demographic variables, CF-specific information (e.g., mutation type, CFTR modulator use) and polyp pathology reports. An appropriate control group is currently being established.

Furthermore, a biorepository of polyps from pwCF and people without CF was set up for spatial transcriptomics.

Results: Colorectal polyp incidence among 213 screened pwCF is 38%. Subgroup analysis will be performed stratified by demographic factors, lung transplantation status and modulator use, among others. The subgroup, polyp characteristics and spatial analyses are expected to be finalized in the spring of 2026.

Conclusion: This study will provide insights into colorectal polyp incidence and risk and protective factors for CRC in pwCF. Spatial analysis will explore molecular pathways leading to polyp formation and CRC progression, which may reveal new therapeutic targets.

records.title: Audiological profiling in an era of CFTR modulation, including extended high frequency hearing assessment in a cohort of adult people with Cystic Fibrosis (pwCF). Preliminary results of 104 screened

records.authors_text: E. Sweeney1, B. Mirza2, K.F Deasy2,3, P. O'Regan4, T. Vagg2, C. Fleming2, M. McCarthy2, J. Dorgan2, H. Ibrahim2,3, A. El Refaie1, L. Kirwan4, B.J Plant2,3, P. O'Sullivan5,6

records.abstract_text:
Introduction: pwCF are at increased risk of sensorineural hearing loss due to cumulative exposure to ototoxic therapies and CF-related comorbidities.

Methods: A total of 104 adult pwCF were recruited. Baseline demographic data were collected, followed by comprehensive audiological assessment, including extended high-frequency pure-tone audiometry (250 Hz–20 kHz). Associations between covariates and hearing severity across all frequencies were analysed using multinomial ordinal regression with a repeated-measures random effect.

Results: Age was significantly associated with hearing loss severity; for each additional year of age, participants were 19% more likely to be classified in a worse hearing threshold category (OR = 1.19, p < 0.001). Lung function was significantly associated with hearing level. A 10% absolute decline in ppFEV1 corresponding to a 64% increased likelihood of being in a worse hearing threshold category (OR = 1.64, p = 0.006), across all tested frequencies. Participants identified pre-test as having hearing loss, demonstrated a higher probability of more severe hearing loss at frequencies ≤10 kHz. Cystic fibrosis related diabetes (CFRD) was associated with hearing loss at 2 and 4 kHz. Genotype, CFTR modulation, maintenance macrolide and aminoglycoside exposure (in previous 4 years) showed no significant association with hear loss severity.

Conclusion: Hearing loss in pwCF is significantly associated with increasing age and declining lung function, with effects observed across both standard and extended high frequencies. These findings suggest that hearing impairment in this population reflects cumulative disease burden and aging rather than ototoxic exposure alone. Frequency-specific associations with pre-existing hearing loss and CFRD further highlight the need for individualized risk assessment. Routine comprehensive audiological monitoring, may support earlier identification of hearing loss in pwCF.

Frequency-specific associations with pre-existing hearing loss and CFRD further highlight the need for individualized risk assessment. Routine comprehensive audiological monitoring, may support earlier identification of hearing loss in pwCF.

records.affiliations_text: 1University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, Pediatrics, Pittsburgh, United States, 2University of Texas Houston, Houston, United States, 3University of Texas Southwestern, Dallas, United States, 4Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, United States, 5University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, United States, 6University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, United States, 7University of Washington, Seattle, United States, 8Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, United States, 9National Jewish Health, Denver, United States

Objective: We examined body mass index (BMI) between parents and nonparents with CF (PwCF; NPwCF) using retrospective data from the Health Outcomes of Parents with CF (HOPeCF) study.

Methods: We surveyed PwCF who became new parents between 2012-2022 and NPwCF and linked results to 2010-2023 patient registry data. We created 2012-2018 and 2019-2022 cohorts and designated time points as year -1 and -2 (pre-parenthood), year 0 (parenthood onset or 2015 and 2021 for NPwCF), and year 1-5 (post-parenthood). We evaluated longitudinal BMI change using multivariable longitudinal linear regression models adjusted for age, race, lung function, ever ivacaftor or elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor(ETI) use, insurance status, number of children, and parenthood years.

Results: We recruited 970 participants (253 PwCF/717 NPwCF). PwCF were 59% female, 91% White, 17% Medicaid-insured, and 90% ever ivacaftor/ETI use. In the 2012-2018 cohort, longitudinal BMI change differed significantly between PwCF and NPwCF(p<0.01). PwCF had a significant BMI increase from year -2 to -1 (adj mean change=0.36[0.12,0.59];p<0.01); NPwCF had no significant change. From year -1-0, NPwCF had a significant BMI increase (0.15[0.01,0.29];p=0.04); PwCF had no significant change. From year 0-1, PwCF had a significant BMI decrease (-0.26[-0.49,-0.03];p=0.03) and NPwCF had a significant BMI increase (0.27[0.13,0.41];p<0.01). Both groups experienced significant BMI increases years 3-4, 4-5, and 5-6 (likely due to widespread ETI use). In the 2019-2022 cohort, longitudinal BMI change also differed significantly between groups(p<0.01). Both had significantly increased BMI from year -2 to -1 and only NPwCF had a significant increase year -1-0 (likely due to ETI).

Conclusions: Before widespread ETI use, PwCF experienced a decrease in BMI in the first year of parenthood; however, in the modern era, parenthood largely does not impact BMI over time. Analyses are ongoing to investigating pregnancy and parental sex impacts.

records.title: Newborn screening and early outcomes in cystic fibrosis: ECFS Patient Registry Data
records.authors_text: L. Kirwan1, N. Adhikari2, R. Bhatnagar2, R. Doherty1, G. Fletcher1, B. Linnane3, S. Gambazza4,5, P. Gkolia5, A. Zolin4,5, P. Fitzpatrick2
records.affiliations_text: 1Cystic Fibrosis Registry of Ireland, Dublin, Ireland, 2University College Dublin, UCD School of Public Health, Physiotherapy and Sport Science, Dublin, Ireland, 3University Hospital Limerick, Limerick, Ireland, 4University of Milan, Milan, Italy, 5European Cystic Fibrosis Society Patient Registry, Karup, Denmark
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Newborn screening (NBS) for cystic fibrosis (CF) enables early diagnosis and prompt initiation of treatment. This study compares clinical outcomes in children with CF diagnosed through NBS with those diagnosed clinically.

Methods: Data were obtained from the European Cystic Fibrosis Society Patient Registry (ECFSPR), which in 2023 included over 56,000 people with CF from 42 countries. To account for temporal changes in care and outcomes, screen-detected (SD) and clinically diagnosed (CD) patients were compared across three five-year birth cohorts: 2008–2012 (SD n=4,118; CD n=3,755), 2013–2017 (SD n=5,292; CD n=2,803), and 2018–2022 (SD n=5,282; CD n=1,181). Outcomes included lung function (ppFEV1), weight-for-age z-scores, and chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa) infection. Generalised linear mixed models were fitted adjusting for age, cohort, cohort-by-age interaction, sex, genotype, country income status, and use of CFTR modulators, long-term antibiotics, azithromycin, and pancreatic enzymes, with random effects for repeated measures.

Results: A total of 22,431 children with CF were included. Preliminary analysis shows that SD patients generally demonstrated superior outcomes. In the 2008–2012 cohort, lung function remained stable in the SD group, whereas the CD group declined by 0.43 ppFEV1 per year (p<0.001). In the 2013–2017 cohort, lung function improved in both groups, with greater improvement in SD patients (difference 0.32 ppFEV1; p=0.040). Weight trajectories similarly favoured SD patients, with sustained advantages in the earlier cohort and lower weight z-scores in CD patients at early age in the most recent cohort. CD patients were approximately 2.5 times more likely to have chronic Pa infection at ≤2 years (p<0.001), although higher acquisition rates over time in SD patients led to convergence with age.

Conclusion: Across three European birth cohorts, diagnosis through NBS was associated with improved early clinical outcomes in children with CF.

person.biography: Laura Kirwan is the Head of Research at the Cystic Fibrosis Registry of Ireland (CFRI). She holds a PhD in Statistics and has built a broad career as a statistician, working across environmental science, health, and nutrition before joining the CFRI in 2016. Laura serves on the executive committee of the European Cystic Fibrosis Society Patient Registry (ECFSPR) and is a member of the core working group for the Global CF Registry collaboration. She also lectures in Statistical Programming and Research Methods at University College Dublin. Her research centres on strengthening the quality, sustainability, and impact of patient registries, and on advancing their role in generating real-world evidence to inform care, research, and policy—ultimately contributing to improved outcomes for people with cystic fibrosis.

records.title: An evaluation of Cystic Fibrosis Screen Positive Inconclusive Diagnosis (CFSPID) patients across the Alder Hey Children's Hospital shared-care network since the implementation of new-born screening
records.authors_text: L. Healy1, C. Lawrence1, L. Thomas1, C. Jeffkins2, R. Thursfield1
records.affiliations_text: 1Alder Hey Children's Hospital, Paediatric Respiratory, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 2University of Liverpool, Liverpool, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: Alder Hey Children’s Hospital (AHCH), UK, receives several notifications from the new-born screening team every year. Most of the children identified are diagnosed with cystic fibrosis (CF) and follow clear care pathways. Fewer children are diagnosed with cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator-related metabolic syndrome/cystic fibrosis screen positive, inconclusive diagnosis (CRMS/CFSPID). In 2021 Barben, Jürg et al published ‘Updated guidance on the management of children CRMS/CFSPID’ in the Journal of Cystic Fibrosis, to help standardise care in this smaller population.

Objectives: To identify all children diagnosed with CFSPID across the network since the introduction of new-born screening in 2007 and evaluate how the care they received compared to the standards described by Barben et al.

Methods: The population was selected from new-born screening notifications. After identifying the children diagnosed with CFSPID, medical notes were reviewed to highlight if key care standards were obtained. Key standards were taking from the published guidance by Barben et al in 2021. If care differed from the guidance, then a comment was made as to why.

Results: In total 297 children were identified to AHCH via new-born screening since 2007. From those identified, 19 were diagnosed with CFSPID. Other diagnosis includes CF (n=242), CF gene carrier (n=14), false positive test results (n=11), other (n=11). The median age of CFSPID children at the time of the audit was 11 years (IQR 6-15). The children’s care was managed across 9 different centres, with a median number of 2 patients (IQR 1-3) with CFSPID per centre.

Conclusion: Children with CFSPID make up 6% of all new-born screening referrals. Many of the network hospitals look after only one child with CFSPID. Having a small population in network hospitals makes consistency of care difficult to obtain. However, they are an important group to monitor, so regular review of the population is required.

records.title: Temporal and spatial trends in cystic fibrosis incidence over 35 years of newborn screening in Brittany (western France)
records.authors_text: J. Derrien1, C. L'Hostis1, M.-P. Audrézet1,2, S. Ramel1,3, C. Belleguic4, E. Deneuville5, B. Arnoaut6, V. Storni6, C. Férec1, V. Scotet1
records.affiliations_text: 1Inserm UMR 1078, Brest, France, 2Laboratory of Molecular Genetics, University Hospital, Brest, France, 3CF Centre, Ildys Foundation, Roscoff, France, 4CF Centre, University Hospital, Rennes, France, 5CF Centre, South Hospital, Rennes, France, 6CF Centre, Chubert Hospital, Vannes, France
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Brittany (western France) is known to have one of the highest incidences of cystic fibrosis (CF) worldwide. The very early implementation of newborn screening (NBS) for CF in this region - 35 years ago - offers the opportunity to accurately monitor long-term trends in incidence and detection of initial potential changes due to the advent of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI). The aim of this study was to explore temporal and spatial trends in the incidence of CF in Brittany since NBS for CF was set up.

Methods: This study included all newborns with CF detected in Brittany since the implementation of NBS in 1989 (n=358). Temporal and spatial changes in incidence rates were modelled using Poisson regression and summarised as the percentage of change between periods or departments. Spatial disparities were mapped using Philcarto software.

Results: Since the introduction of NBS for CF in Brittany, the incidence rate has declined significantly by 1.4% per year (p=0.013). The rate decreased significantly from 1/3,102 to 1/4,361 between the 1990-99 and the 2015-24 decades (p=0.024). Beyond this overall decrease, the west-to-east gradient in incidence persists nowadays and even appears to have strengthened. In the 1990s, the incidence rate was 60.9% higher in western Brittany (1/2,339 in Finistère vs. 1/3,763 in Ille-et-Vilaine; p=0.046). Currently, it is 84.9% higher (1/3,120 vs. 1/5,769; p=0.035). No significant variation in incidence has been noted since the advent of ETI.

Conclusion: This study reports a significant decline in the incidence of CF in Brittany over the past 35 years and highlights the persistence of spatial disparities. Due to its peninsular geography and more limited population mixing, western Brittany continues to exhibit one of the highest incidences worldwide, whereas eastern Brittany shows an incidence similar to the French average. Ongoing monitoring of incidence remains essential to assess the potential effect of the advent of ETI.

person.biography:
Virginie SCOTET
Associate researcher in Epidemiology
Inserm UMR 1078 “Genetic, functional Genomics and Biotechnologies”, Brest, France.

Virginie Scotet is an associate researcher in epidemiology at the French Institute for Health and Medical Research (Inserm). After training at the Institute of Public Health and Epidemiology of the University of Bordeaux, in 1998 she joined the team of Prof. Claude Férec in Brest. 
Her research is devoted to the study of genetics diseases common in Brittany (western France) and she has over 20-y. experience in the field of epidemiology of CF. She coordinates epidemiological studies to better understand the molecular epidemiology of this disease in Brittany, where a newborn screening program for CF was launched early (1989). To carry out her research, she set up a registry of the CF patients born in Brittany since the 1970s. These data allow her to study the dynamics of CF, to precisely analyze the distribution of CF and its mutations, to measure the incidence and its temporal trends, and to study the phenotypic variability and survival in CF. She also assesses the impact of public health policies implemented on CF such as newborn screening, prenatal diagnosis or family testing. 
Her research program provides precise data on the molecular epidemiology of CF and helps to improve diagnostic strategies and refine genetic counseling.

She coordinates epidemiological studies to better understand the molecular epidemiology of this disease in Brittany, where a newborn screening program for CF was launched early (1989). To carry out her research, she set up a registry of the CF patients born in Brittany since the 1970s. These data allow her to study the dynamics of CF, to precisely analyze the distribution of CF and its mutations, to measure the incidence and its temporal trends, and to study the phenotypic variability and survival in CF. She also assesses the impact of public health policies implemented on CF such as newborn screening, prenatal diagnosis or family testing. 
Her research program provides precise data on the molecular epidemiology of CF and helps to improve diagnostic strategies and refine genetic counseling.

records.title: Benchmarking Dutch cystic fibrosis care: integrating centre metrics with patient‑reported experience measures to inform national guidelines
records.authors_text: R. Kos1, H.M. Janssens2, R. Van der Meer3, J.J. Noordhoek1, D.D. Zomer-van Ommen1, On Behalf of the CF Working Groups from NVALT and NVK-SKL
records.affiliations_text: 1Dutch Cystic Fibrosis Foundation, Soest, Netherlands, 2Sophia Children's Hospital, Pediatric Pulmonology and Allergology, Rotterdam, Netherlands, 3Haga Teaching Hospital, Department of Pulmonology, The Hague, Netherlands
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Variation in the organization and delivery of cystic fibrosis (CF) care may affect patient experience and clinical outcomes. Previously, we demonstrated that patient-driven quality of care improvement is possible (Noordhoek, JCF, 2023). We aimed to benchmark Dutch CF centres in the CFTR-modulator era, using patient‑reported experience measures (PREMs), and inform revision of the Dutch CF standard‑of‑care guidelines.

Methods: All Dutch CF centres (7 adult, 7 paediatric) completed a survey in 2025 on team composition, diagnostics, treatments, and organization. Parallel online questionnaires collected PREMs and overall care ratings from people with CF (pwCF) and parents of children with CF. Analyses were descriptive.

Results: All centres reported multidisciplinary teams, online consultations and supported home spirometry. In concordance with the standards of care: annual comprehensive assessments in ≥80% of pwCF were reported by 92% of centres; quarterly cultures by 25%; annual NTM/fungal cultures by 58%; and annual P. aeruginosa susceptibility testing by 83%.

Questionnaires were completed by 303 adults with CF and 166 parents, representing 27% and 30% of the Dutch CF population. Mean overall care ratings were high (children 8.9/10; adults 8.4/10). Satisfaction with pulmonologist expertise was 97% (children) and 96% (adults). Information clarity was rated positively by 89% (children) and 84% (adults). Annual access to psychological care differed substantially (children 33% vs adults 6%). Satisfaction with paediatric‑to‑adult transition preparation was 28%. Satisfaction with shared decision‑making was 78% (children) and 90% (adults).

Conclusion: Dutch CF care is characterized by strong multidisciplinary organization and high patient‑reported satisfaction, with inter‑centre variation in access to psychological care and transition to adult care. Integrating centre‑level metrics with PREMs provides a patient‑centred evidence base for national CF care standards.
