records.title: A low-cost, standardized cystic fibrosis registry architecture for low- and middle-income countries: the International Cystic Fibrosis Training Network (ICFTN) experience
records.authors_text: H. Gutierrez1, B. Joy2, M. Cestari3, C. Mims4, D. Panjwani2
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Alabama at Birmingham, Pediatrics, Birmingham, United States, 2University of Alabama at Birmingham, Information Technology, Department of Medicine, Birmingham, United States, 3Hospital Pediatrico Humberto Notti, Mendoza, Argentina, 4The Children Hospital of Alabama, Birmingham, United States
records.abstract_text:
Background: Patient registries are key to improving cystic fibrosis (CF) care and enabling outcomes research. Many low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) lack access to national CF registries due to financial, infrastructure, and technical constraints, resulting in underrepresentation of these populations in global CF data.

Methods: We aimed to develop a CF registry on the REDCap platform, designed for low-cost deployment and rapid implementation. The registry was activated in June 2022 and currently includes 11 participating centers from two countries, with 554 unique patients and 72 active clinical users. To ensure international standardization, the registry integrated Global Lung Function Initiative (GLI) reference equations via an application programming interface (API) for spirometry interpretation. We incorporated automated Z-score and percentile calculations for height-for-age, weight-for-age, weight-for-length (0-2 years), and BMI-for-age, with the option to select WHO or CDC standards based on point-of-care anthropometric values. Custom reporting tools were also created to extend beyond standard REDCap functionalities.

Results: The architecture enabled real-time, standardized interpretation of lung function and nutritional status without relying on local reference tables, proprietary software, or advanced statistical expertise. Automated calculations reduced data-entry errors and ensured methodological consistency at the point of capture. Custom reporting supported longitudinal follow-up, QI, and benchmarking.

Conclusions: A REDCap-based CF registry with automated GLI and WHO/CDC standardization and custom reporting is a scalable, equitable solution for CF data capture in LMICs. It complements existing national registries, addresses a gap in global CF data infrastructure, and enables broader participation in CF research and QI efforts. Funded by the CF Foundation.

records.title: Evaluation of professional quality of life and prevalence of burnout: A national survey of healthcare providers on cystic fibrosis (CF) care teams

person.title: Senior Scientist
person.institution: Joe DiMaggio Cystic Fibrosis, Pulmonary and Sleep Center

records.authors_text: A. Quittner1, E. Seng2, B. Smith3, R. Wei4, S. Graziano5, P. Lomas6, E. Muther7, M. Schechter8, L. Tillman9, M. Verkleij10, N. Chaudhary11, C. Toth12, A. Georgiopoulos4
records.affiliations_text: 1Joe DiMaggio Cystic Fibrosis, Pulmonary and Sleep Center, Pulmonary Department, Hollywood, United States, 2Yeshiva University, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, New York, United States, 3Jacobs School of Medicine and Biomedical Sciences, Buffalo, United States, 4Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, United States, 5Bambino Gesu Children's Hospital, Psychology Unit, Child & Adolescent Psychiatry Unit, Rome, Italy, 6Cystic Fibrosis Foundation, Bethesda, United States, 7University of Colorado, Denver, United States, 8Virginia Commonwealth University, Richmond, United States, 9Community Partner, Northville, United States, 10Amsterdam University Medical Center, Child & Adolescent Psychiatry & Psychosocial Care, Amsterdam, Netherlands, 11Massachusetts General Hospital, Psychiatry, Boston, United States, 12Cedar Chest College, Allentown, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: CF team-based care may reduce burnout. We examined moderators of the relationship between Burnout and Professional Satisfaction.

Methods: CF clinicians completed Maslach Burnout Inventory (MBI), Professional Quality of Life Scale (ProQOL). Principal Factoring Analysis (PFA) with promax rotation identified which subscales formed composite factors. PFA and general linear models evaluated moderation.

Results: N=569: 24.9% physicians, 21.9% nurses/advanced practitioners, 29.4% allied health, 23.8% mental health providers (MH); 48.3% pediatric, 47.8% in CF >10 years. PFA yielded 2 factors: 1)“Burnout:” MBI Depersonalization (0.72), MBI Emotional Exhaustion (0.94), ProQOL Burnout (0.90), ProQOL Secondary Traumatic Stress (0.65); and 2) “Professional Satisfaction:” MBI Personal Accomplishment (0.77), ProQOL Compassion Satisfaction (0.89). Higher Burnout was associated with lower Professional Satisfaction (r =-0.55, p<.001).

Professional Role was associated with “Burnout” [F(3, 558)=4.27, p=0.005] but not “Professional Satisfaction” [F(3, 558)=2.16, p=0.092]. Physicians had higher Burnout vs. MH (M Difference=0.35, 95% CI = 0.08, 0.62). Years in CF was associated with “Burnout” [F(2, 564)=3.65, p=0.027] and “Professional Satisfaction” [F(2, 564)=6.84, p=0.001]. Those in CF 10-14 years reported higher “Burnout” vs. <10 years (M Difference=0.24, 95% CI=0.01, 0.47), and lower “Professional Satisfaction” vs. <10 (M Difference=-0.28, 95% CI =-0.54, -0.03) or 15+ years (M Difference=-0.41, 95% CI=-0.68, -0.14). Neither Professional Role nor Years Working in CF moderated the direct effects between Burnout and Professional Satisfaction (p’s 0.48-0.62).

Conclusions: CF clinicians reported high burnout, low-moderate Professional Satisfaction. Professional Role and Years Working in CF did not moderate this relationship. Next steps: replicate in Europe and test potential mediators.

person.biography: Dr. Quittner is a Senior Scientist at Joe DiMaggio CF Center and has been a Professor for over 30 years. She has been continuously funded by NIH and other foundations and has published over 230 articles and book chapters. She received an award from the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation for her development of the first health-related quality of life measures for cystic fibrosis (CFQ-R) and a second award for her international study of depression and anxiety, and development of guidelines for mental health care in CF. She is leading a national dissemination, implementation effort to integrate mental health into CF Care, is Co-PI on development of the General Mental Health Screener for CF, and is Co-leading the new TIDES 2.0 study screening mental health in young children.

records.title: PESQI: Peer-led Evaluation for Shared learning and Quality Improvement in cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: J. Witt1, J. Nightingale2, S. Lewis1, S. Basford3, D. O'Neill4, H. Douglas5, J. Lowdon6, K.-L. Watson7, M. Puckey8, C. Oliver2, P. Wilson9,10, J. Osmond1, I. Ahmed11, J. Duckers12, J. Legg13,14, K. Brownlee15, K.W Southern16

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Clinical peer review is a formal process whereby health professionals evaluate a service or colleague’s practice to improve care and facilitate shared learning. In a resource restricted health system, we sought to develop a pragmatic, cost-neutral approach to peer-led review of multidisciplinary cystic fibrosis (CF) care in the United Kingdom (UK).

Methods: An initial online consultation was carried out with CF professionals to gather views on value and preferred format of peer review. A dedicated Executive of CF professionals and community representatives was set up to co-create an initial model, which was then refined with input from the CF Medical Association and Cystic Fibrosis Trust Clinical Advisory Group.

Results: The online consultation received 108 responses, showing a clear appetite among CF professionals for peer review. They suggested an approach focused on service improvement and shared learning that leverages existing data and reduces burden on those involved.

The proposed Peer-led Evaluation for Shared learning and Quality Improvement (PESQI) model is entirely virtual, to minimise costs and burden. It is led by a panel of clinicians and community members, consisting of three phases:

Baseline Assessment: Existing insights on outcomes, patient experiences and staffing are collated. Service completes a self-reflection, and additional patient feedback is gathered. These insights are shared with the panel.

Review Day: Virtual conversations between panel members and staff at the service under review, followed by an end-of-day debrief.

Reporting and Feedback: Panel outline existing best practices and actionable improvement ideas in a report that is shared with the service.

Conclusion: Based on stakeholder feedback, we developed a new model for CF peer review. The programme will be piloted to test feasibility of a virtual-only approach and to explore capacity needed, as well as value gained, to ensure this is a worthwhile and ethical enterprise.

records.title: The Canadian cystic fibrosis consensus guidelines: integrating the role of the multi-disciplinary team
records.authors_text: M. Richmond1, J. Kocourek2, E. Tullis3, P. Eckford2, M. Chilvers1, Canadian Consensus Guidelines Steering Committee
records.affiliations_text: 1BC Children's Hospital, Vancouver, Canada, 2Cystic Fibrosis Canada, Toronto, Canada, 3St. Michael's Hospital, Toronto, Canada
records.abstract_text:
Objective: To describe the integration of the multi-disciplinary team roles into the Canadian cystic fibrosis (CF) consensus guidelines

Methods: In 2022, CF Canada began developing the Canadian CF consensus guidelines. Informed by updated standards from the European CF Society and CF Foundation, CF Canada sought to develop a holistic set of guidelines that integrated the role of the multi-disciplinary team, encompassed care across the lifespan for people with CF (pwCF) and reflected changes in practice since the introduction of modulator therapies; all from a uniquely Canadian perspective. A steering committee was formed that had representation from across Canada and all roles. Each member was responsible for liaising with their profession group for feedback. Discipline-based groups met to discuss the guidelines and ensure that their role was represented across all clinical contexts.

Results: The completed guidelines were circulated to Canadian CF teams for initial implementation in late 2025. The work highlights each team member’s role and responsibilities across the lifespan of pwCF and different co-morbidities/scenarios (Table 1). Given the vast Canadian landscape and different practice settings (e.g. urban vs. rural, large vs. small clinics), it is recognized that not all CF teams have the full complement of team members. By identifying overlapping responsibilities smaller teams can be strengthened with flexibility in their roles while still providing thorough care. The tool can also be used to advocate for funding/clinical needs in under-resourced clinics.

Table 1

Canadian consensus guidelines: outline of the multi-disciplinary roles & clinical scenarios

Multi-disciplinary roles

physician, nurse practitioner, nurse coordinator/registered nurse, registered dietitian, pharmacist, physiotherapist, psychologist, respiratory therapist, social worker

Clinical scenarios

Age based (infant, preschool, child, adolescent, young adult, adult – minimal/mild/moderate lung disease)

Transition to adult care

Advanced lung disease

Rapidly declining lung function

Pregnancy

CF related diabetes

CF hepatobiliary involvement

Emotional wellness/mental health

Post-lung transplant

Conclusion: The integration of the multi-disciplinary team into the Canadian guidelines represents the collaboration of Canadian CF teams. This is the first time roles have been thoroughly reviewed to identify opportunities for cross scope to improve clinic efficiencies. Ongoing projects include the development of a web-based tool that allows filtering by profession for a role-tailored document.

records.title: A mixed-methods evaluation of the International Cystic Fibrosis Training Network program, a multidisciplinary training model to improve cystic fibrosis care in low- and middle-income countries
records.authors_text: H. Gutierrez1, N. Charles2, L. Hearld2, C. Mims3, S. Self1, K. Hearld2
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Alabama at Birmingham, Pediatrics, Birmingham, United States, 2University of Alabama at Birmingham, Department of Health Services Administration, Birmingham, United States, 3The Children Hospital of Alabama, Birmingham, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objective: To evaluate the potential influence of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) therapy on the progression of pancreatic imaging abnormalities in patients with Cystic Fibrosis.

Methods: A total of 196 patients with Cystic Fibrosis treated with ETI and who underwent High-Resolution Computed Tomography (HRCT) were included (93 males, 103 females; mean age at first CT 15 years; mean age at start of therapy 24 years). A longitudinal evaluation of the pancreatic parenchyma included in the caudal portions of chest HRCT scans was performed using available pre- and post-therapy examinations (mean follow-up 88 months; 774 CT scans analyzed). Pancreatic parenchyma was independently segmented by two readers, and Hounsfield Unit (HU) density histograms were computed using dedicated research image analysis software (Mango, Research Imaging Institute, UTHSCSA). A multivariate analysis using a generalized linear mixed model was conducted to assess the effect of ETI therapy on changes in the distribution of acinar (18–70 HU) and adipose (–34 to –190 HU) pancreatic components before and after treatment.

Results: A statistically significant time-related increase in the adipose component (β = 9.04; p = 0.0036) and a reduction in the acinar component (β = –12.85; p = 0.0031) were observed. Although pancreatic involution continued over time, a significant difference in the temporal response slope (β) was found post-treatment compared to pre-treatment for both the adipose (β = –0.40; p = 0.0022) and acinar components (β = 0.63; p = 0.0011) (p < 0.001). These findings indicate that ETI therapy induces significant changes in both intercept and slope for pancreatic adipose and acinar components.

Conclusion: Despite the ongoing loss of acinar tissue and increase in adipose tissue, ETI therapy appears to significantly influence the progression of pancreatic structural changes in patients with Cystic Fibrosis.

records.title: Advancing cystic fibrosis care in Canada: developing a national quality improvement model
records.authors_text: J. Kocourek1, P. Eckford2,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Cystic Fibrosis Canada, Mission- Healthcare program, Toronto, Canada, 2Cystic Fibrosis Canada, Toronto, Canada
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Rapid advances in cystic fibrosis (CF) therapy have reshaped clinical needs in Canada. In response, Cystic Fibrosis Canada collaborated with clinicians and community members (2023–25) to develop new Canadian Consensus Guidelines for CF Care. Evidence shows that guideline implementation declines without structured planning and monitoring. To address this, Cystic Fibrosis Canada is developing a national quality improvement (QI) program to support uptake, adherence, and identification of care gaps.

Methods: An environmental scan and literature review were conducted to identify comparable QI models, indicators, and outcomes. Interviews will be conducted with clinicians to explore the role of QI and implementation science, processes needed to support QI in CF care, links to the new guidelines, and proposed implementation and outcome indicators. We also aim to determine how Cystic Fibrosis Canada can best facilitate QI efforts nationally.

Results: The environmental scan identified adaptable QI frameworks such as audit and feedback cycles, outcome dashboards, and multidisciplinary learning collaboratives. Common indicators included guideline adherence, care process reliability, patient reported outcomes, and clinic level variation. Anticipated interview findings include strong support for embedding QI and implementation science into routine CF care, and the need for clear, measurable indicators aligned with the new guidelines. Clinicians are expected to highlight the value of practical tools, site visits, and national learning networks. These insights will inform a draft QI program integrating guideline aligned indicators, structured improvement cycles, and continuous evaluation.

Conclusion: A national QI program aligned with the new guidelines offers an opportunity to strengthen consistency, equity, and evidence based CF care in Canada. Early findings highlight both the need and readiness for a structured approach to guideline implementation and evaluation.

records.title: The role of the paediatrician in managing patients with cystic fibrosis in the absence of specialised centers
records.authors_text: M. Sharipova1, L. Jumaeva1,2, S. Davlatova1, N. Kashirskaya3, M. Khusenova1, B. Shamsov2
records.affiliations_text: 1SEI «Avicenna Tajik State Medical University», Department of Children’s Diseases № 2, Dushanbe, Tajikistan, 2SEI «Republican Scientific Clinical Center - Paediatrics and Children's Surgery», Dushanbe, Tajikistan, 3Research Centre for Medical Genetics, Moscow, Russian Federation
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: In recent decades, advances in the diagnosis and treatment of cystic fibrosis (CF) have significantly increased the life expectancy and quality of life of people with CF (pwCF) in developed countries. However, in countries without specialised CF centers, there are a number of acute problems that make our study very important.

Aim: To study the clinical features of of children with CF (cwCF) in our hospital and determine the role of the paediatrician in managing cwCF in the absence of a specialised center.

Methods: Eight cwCF, from 1 to 6 years old (all diagnosed in the Russian Federation (RF)), were monitored by a paediatrician, of whom 6 were repeatedly hospitalized in the National Medical Center of the Republic of Tajikistan's paediatric pulmonology department. Two cwCF were observed on an outpatient basis by a local paediatrician in conjunction with video consultations with CF specialists from the RF. The following data were analysed: clinical manifestation of CF, numbers of lungs’ exacerbations and hospitalizations, nutritional status, the paediatrician's management tactics at the outpatient level.

Results: Seven cwCF suffered from chronic cough with viscous sputum, including 6 with frequent bronchial obstruction and 3 with sinusitis and nasal polyposis. Five cwCF (62.5%) had steatorrhea, 4 (50%) had severe malnutrition (-3 and -4 on the Z-score scale). Three cwCF had bronchiectasis, and one had liver fibrosis, salt loss syndrome and diabetes mellitus. One of the cwCF died at 6.3 years old.

Conclusion: In regions without specialised CF centers, paediatricians become mentors to families, combining medical, psychological and social assistance. Limited access to modern drugs for treating CF complicates the prognosis, but proper organization of patient care can significantly improve the course of the disease. Educational programs and international cooperation are needed to improve the quality of care for cwCF in countries with limited resources.

records.title: Building and implementing a data core team to support a cystic fibrosis learning network.
records.authors_text: B. Horton1, R. List2, D. Brighton1, S. Shen1, D. Albon2
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Virginia, Department of Public Health Sciences, Charlottesville, United States, 2University of Virginia, Department of Medicine, Charlottesville, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The United States Cystic Fibrosis Learning Network (CFLN) is a maturing, collaborative, multisite, multi-stakeholder, data-driven network that aims to improve outcomes for all people with CF (PwCF) and their families. The structure of CFLN relies on timely and reliable data summaries that are transparently distributed to the network to enhance their quality improvement aims. The University of Virginia Data Core (UVADC) is a collaborative group of professionals with diverse backgrounds aiming to support quality improvement initiatives for the CFLN. Our goal is to build, implement, and adapt tools to support quality improvement projects through rigorous data capture systems and enhanced communication for the learning network, with high-quality and transparent reports for all CF clinical care programmes and their patient and family partners in the learning network.

Methods: The data core was initiated as a multidisciplinary team with expertise in CF clinical care, quality improvement science, database development and management, and data analysis and visualisation. UVADC members meet weekly as a team and with CFLN leaders and quality improvement support group and project leaders.

Results: From August 2023 to January 2026, the UVADC has supported CFLN activities and collaborative projects bridging quality improvement initiatives with data from the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation Patient Registry. The UVADC employs innovative, transformative, and agile tools to create outcome reports, a web application to identify missing data and data errors in real-time, and provides manuscript support for all activities.

Conclusion: Curating a diverse team of UVADC members is essential to ensure rigorous data collection, analysis, reporting, and interpretation to support multicentre learning and improvement. The approach used to develop UVADC to support the CFLN can be translated to support other learning networks, both in cystic fibrosis as well as other clinical areas.

Objectives: There is a need for greater consensus on the outcomes used in cystic fibrosis (CF) clinical trials to enable results to be compared and synthesised across trials. The development of a universal Core Outcome Set for CF (COS-CF) aims to address this need by defining outcomes that should be measured in all late-phase interventional trials in CF, regardless of their specific focus.

Methods: Our protocol is registered on Figshare (DOI: 10.6084/m9.figshare.28044917) and the COMET initiative database. Three rounds of eDelphi survey are being conducted to gain consensus among stakeholders about the most important outcomes to measure in CF trials. In rounds 1 and 2, participants rate the importance of outcomes on a 9-point Likert scale. Outcomes are deemed ‘consensus out’ and dropped after rounds 1 and 2 if ≤50% of participants in each stakeholder group score them 7-9. Outcomes scored 7-9 by ≥70% of participants and 1-3 by ≤15%, among all stakeholder groups, are considered ‘consensus in’. The third round, translated into multiple languages, will ask participants to rank their top 5 outcomes from those remaining.

Results: The eDelphi process is ongoing; the first round has concluded, with 187 people rating 49 outcomes. Participants were people with CF or families (n=105), healthcare professionals (n=62) or researchers (n=20). After round 1, 7 outcomes were voted ‘consensus out’ and excluded from round 2. Seven outcomes were voted ‘consensus in’, with the remaining 35 classified as ‘no consensus’.

Conclusion: The large number of outcomes deemed ‘no consensus’ indicates substantial variation in the views of individuals and between stakeholder groups. In the second round, participants will review their own scores alongside the average scores of each stakeholder group to promote greater consensus. Following completion of the eDelphi process, remaining outcomes will be reviewed and ratified during an online multi-stakeholder workshop in Summer 2026.

records.title: Measuring what matters: physiotherapy outcomes in cystic fibrosis care

person.title: Mrs.
person.department: West of Scotland Adult CF Unit

records.authors_text: L. Morrison1, J. Hauser2,3, E. Coulter4, S. Pollock4, Global Data Harmony Working Group, REACH for CF, International Virtual Network
records.affiliations_text: 1Queen Elizabeth University Hospital, West of Scotland Adult CF Unit, Glasgow, United Kingdom, 2Royal Hobart Hospital, Tasmanian Adult Cystic Fibrosis Unit, Tasmania, Australia, 3CFphysio.com Inc, Hobart, Australia, 4Glasgow Caledonian University, Department of Allied Health Professions, Glasgow, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: Cystic fibrosis (CF) registries underpin population surveillance, service planning and evaluation of therapeutic outcomes. Registry datasets infrequently capture functional or physiotherapy-related outcomes central to contemporary care. This study considered the heterogeneity of physiotherapy outcome-measures (OMs) and the value of clinically relevant OMs for possible inclusion in expanding registry datasets.

Methods: An online survey was distributed to physiotherapists working in CF across UK, Europe, Australia, New Zealand, USA and Canada. Quantitative data summarised the frequency and consistency of OM use, while qualitative data explored the contextual and organisational factors shaping OM decisions, either for research or clinical practice.

Results: Responses from 167 experienced physiotherapists were collated. Results demonstrated clear convergence in OMs routinely assessed. Respiratory monitoring was almost universal where 97% of respondents routinely recorded spirometry, with 98% rating it as clinically valuable. Auscultation (79%), cough assessment (81%), and sputum assessment (92%) were widely embedded and considered clinically relevant.

Exercise testing, showed variation across regions with a large majority of respondents in Australia and New Zealand (86%) but a smaller proportion in some European centres (69%).Similarly, physical-activity participation ranged from 90% to 76%.

Conclusion: Clinically relevant physiotherapy OMs are standardised, widely used and routinely collected. Their variable inclusion in CF registries can limit the ability to benchmark practice, evaluate service models and demonstrate long term clinical impact. A construct-based physiotherapy dataset, supported by feasible documentation workflows, would allow registries to capture functional and behavioural OMs increasingly relevant in the modulator era. Registry evolution is necessary to maintain relevance, sensitivity and completeness of population-level CF surveillance.

person.biography: I have worked in Cystic Fibrosis care for 30+ years encompassing both paediatric and adult care. I am now responsible for the team of 5 CF physiotherapists providing holistic care for the 380 patients attending a Regional Adult CF unit. I have developed a research forum within the CF physiotherapy department and participated in successful teaching of junior members of staff. I have participated in the development of local, national and international guidelines into various aspects of CF care. I have direct responsibility for the physiotherapeutic management of all patients attending the regional CF unit, from transition through to terminal care. I am the physiotherapy lead for the CF unit and manage and supervise the highly complex respiratory patients, i.e. those frequently requiring ventilation or other complex therapies. I am currently undertaking a part time PhD “Exploring the role of digital health technologies to support the future care of people with cystic fibrosis”.

records.title: Comparison of hospitalisation rates in screen detected & clinically diagnosed children with cystic fibrosis in first five years:Findings from Irish Comparative Outcomes Study of Cystic Fibrosis(ICOS)

person.department: School of Public Health, Physiotherapy and Sports Science

records.authors_text: R. Bhatnagar1, R. Segurado1, N. Bhardwaj1, G. Masukume1, B. Linnane2, M. Herzig3, M. Ni Chroinin4, D. Mullane4, D. Cox5, P. McNally5, S. Javadpour5, R. O'Reilly5, B. Elnazir6, P. Greally6, F. Healy7, M. Williamson7, D. Slattery7, L. Kirwan8, P. Fitzpatrick1
records.affiliations_text: 1University College Dublin, School of Public Health, Physiotherapy and Sports Science, Dublin, Ireland, 2University Hospital Limerick, Limerick, Ireland, 3University Hospital Galway, Galway, Ireland, 4Cork University Hospital, Cork, Ireland, 5Children’s Health Ireland at Crumlin, Dublin, Ireland, 6Children’s Health Ireland at Tallaght, Dublin, Ireland, 7Children’s Health Ireland at Temple Street, Dublin, Ireland, 8Cystic Fibrosis Registry of Ireland, Dublin, Ireland
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Newborn screening for cystic fibrosis (CF) was introduced in Ireland in 2011. The ICOS national cohort study compares children with CF (CWCF) diagnosed through newborn screening with those diagnosed clinically. We examined risk factors for hospitalisation due to pulmonary exacerbations and other CF-related conditions in first five years.

Methods: Study includes CWCF born between July 2008 - June 2023. Hospitalisation data were collected on both screen-detected and clinically diagnosed cohorts from birth to 60 months from CF Registry, Ireland and hospital charts. Logistic regression was used to identify demographic and clinical factors associated with hospitalisation in first 60 months of life in CWCF ≥ 60 months.

Results: Of 300 (≥ 60 months) CWCF recruited, 225 were screen-detected (born 2011 - 2018) and 75 clinically diagnosed (born 2008 - 2011). Being diagnosed clinically (adjusted OR: 3.80, 95% CI: 1.07-13.43, p=0.038) and ΔF508 homozygous mutation (adjusted OR: 14.34, 95% CI: 1.74-118.33, p=0.013) were significantly associated with hospitalisation for pulmonary CF exacerbations when adjusted for gender, sibling with CF and modulator type. Use of CF modulators was highly protective, reducing risk of hospitalisation for both any CF-related issues (Orkambi/Symkevi adjusted OR: 0.21, 95% CI: 0.07-0.67, p=0.008; Kaftrio/Ivacaftor adjusted OR: 0.10, 95% CI: 0.04-0.24, p<0.001) and also pulmonary exacerbations (Orkambi/Symkevi adjusted OR: 0.07, 95% CI: 0.007-0.58, p=0.015; Ivacaftor/Kaftrio adjusted OR: 0.001, 95% CI: 0.00-0.011, p<0.001).

Conclusion: Clinical diagnosis and ΔF508 homozygous mutation are associated with increased early childhood hospitalisations, while modulator therapy reduces this risk, highlighting benefits both screening combined with targeted treatment in CF care.

records.title: Updating the Cystic Fibrosis Questionnaire-Revised (CFQ-R) in the era of highly effective modulators: A qualitative and crosswalk study to develop the CFQ-M

person.title: Senior Scientist
person.institution: Joe DiMaggio Cystic Fibrosis, Pulmonary and Sleep Center

records.authors_text: A. Quittner1, A. Foster2, K. Kelly2, F. Sowell2, S. Taneja2, E. van Roil2, M. Kosinski2
records.affiliations_text: 1Joe DiMaggio Cystic Fibrosis, Pulmonary and Sleep Center, Pulmonary Department, Hollywood, United States, 2IQVIA Patient Centered Solutions, Durham, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Developed in 2000, the Cystic Fibrosis Questionnaire-Revised (CFQ-R) has been used extensively in clinical and behavioral studies and considered the “gold standard” health-related quality of life (HRQoL) measure for people with cystic fibrosis (PWCF) ages 2+ years. With the advent of highly effective modulators (ETI, VTD), substantial improvements in lung function, body mass index, and HRQoL have been documented. Thus, the lived experience of PWCF has changed dramatically, requiring an expansion of items and scales on the CFQ-R to reflect this clinical progress. This study aims to conduct qualitative research with PWCF to elicit concepts for a modulator-specific version of the CFQ-R (CFQ-M) and evaluate the comprehensibility and relevance of new items. After finalizing the CFQ-M, a crosswalk study is planned to calibrate items from both CFQ-R and CFQ-M on a common latent variable using item-response theory (IRT).

Methods: The study team will use a 4-phase approach: (1) qualitative interviews with up to 75 PWCF to elicit new and relevant concepts (e.g., symptoms and impacts) to be included in the age-appropriate CFQ-M; (2) development of the CFQ-M informed by a concept mapping exercise of the phase 1 findings; (3) cognitive debriefing interviews with up to 62 PWCF to assess the appropriateness of the CFQ-M; and (4) application of IRT to calibrate the new CFQ-M item content with the CFQ-R.

Results: Phase 1 interviews will aim to expand the range of functioning measured by CFQ-R scales with new item content and define key concepts reflecting patient experience with modulators. Findings from this phase will guide the implementation of subsequent phases.

Conclusions: In line with regulatory guidance, qualitative and psychometric research will be conducted to capture and measure concepts that are relevant and meaningful for PWCF on new modulators, producing a reliable and valid CFQ-M while maintaining comparability of scores with previous studies using CFQ-R.

person.biography: Dr. Quittner is a Senior Scientist at Joe DiMaggio CF Center and has been a Professor for over 30 years. She has been continuously funded by NIH and other foundations and has published over 230 articles and book chapters. She received an award from the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation for her development of the first health-related quality of life measures for cystic fibrosis (CFQ-R) and a second award for her international study of depression and anxiety, and development of guidelines for mental health care in CF. She is leading a national dissemination, implementation effort to integrate mental health into CF Care, is Co-PI on development of the General Mental Health Screener for CF, and is Co-leading the new TIDES 2.0 study screening mental health in young children.

records.title: Mapping current practice & preferences in the use of PROMs in the clinical setting in Ireland and an international review of the inclusion of PROMs in Cystic Fibrosis patient registries
records.authors_text: R. Doherty1, L. Kirwan1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Cystic Fibrosis Registry of Ireland, Dublin, Ireland, 2UCD School of Public Health, Physiotherapy and Sport Science, Dublin, Ireland
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The use of patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), including symptom scores, wellbeing measures, and Health-Related Quality of Life measures, are of increasing interest to help measure the burden of CF. While there has been recent interest in the use of PROMs as outcome measures in clinical trials, there is limited long-term real-world data published by registries. Longitudinal PROMs data can track change, help inform clinical practice and empower patients to better understand and manage their condition. Patient registries play an important role to support these goals given their longitudinal nature and rich clinical outcome datasets.

To explore the feasibility of the inclusion of PROMs within a registry context, the objectives of this study are to:

Define current practice with respect to the use of PROMs in clinical CF practice in Ireland

Define current practice with respect to the inclusion of PROMs in international CF registries

Methods: This study adopts a multi-method approach to gather data including the following:

A pseudo-anonymous online survey of clinical staff at any CF-specialist centre in Ireland to map the use of and attitudes towards PROMs in clinical CF practice in Ireland

A desk-based international review of Cystic Fibrosis Registry practice in the use of PROMs utilising publicly available/shared documents (e.g., variable lists and annual reports).

Results: Results of the survey and desk-based review are descriptively analysed and presented to understand current practices and preferences in the use of PROMs in clinical practice in Ireland and in international registries.

Conclusions: Findings from this study will inform the feasibility for the inclusion of PROMs in the Irish CF registry in terms of existing data availability and accessibility. This study will make recommendations on current practice, the potential for future work on the implementation of PROMs in CF registries, and inform discussions for international harmonisation.

records.affiliations_text: 1Health Institutes of Turkiye, Institute of Public Health and Chronic Diseases, Ankara, Turkey, 2Istanbul University-Cerrahpasa, Cerrahpasa Faculty of Medicine, Department of Pediatric Pulmonology, Istanbul, Turkey, 3Bakırköy Dr. Sadi Konuk Training and Research Hospital, Department of Pediatric Pulmonology, Istanbul, Turkey, 4Bezmialem Vakif University Hospital, Department of Pediatric Pulmonology, Istanbul, Turkey, 5Amsterdam University of Applied Sciences, Faculty of Health, Sport and Physical Activity, Department of Nutrition and Dietetics, Amsterdam, Netherlands, 6King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: The Twinning Expansion Project aims to develop a long-term centre-to-centre partnership in which an established cystic fibrosis (CF) centre guides and supports another site to optimise care for people with CF. Istanbul-Cerrahpasa and King’s College London were matched as mentii and mentor in 2024 spring.

Objective: To assess the early phase of this partnership using SWOT analysis.

Methods: Some team members first met in person during the ECFS Conference in Glasgow. An online meeting followed in July 2024 to introduce both teams and plan the process. Cerrahpasa presented the organisation of the centre and patient characteristics. To date, four cross-site clinical and teaching meetings have taken place. In November 2024, the mentee centre visited the mentor centre in London, observed both paediatric and adult CF teams in inpatient and outpatient settings, and engaged MDT meetings. The process was evaluated using a SWOT framework.

Results: The main Strength was the open sharing of treatment approaches and clinical experiences. Staff issues limited the planned sub-groups and were identified as a Weakness. Opportunities included ongoing collaboration, discussion of complex cases, and future education. High workloads at both centres created scheduling difficulties and were considered a Threat. Other strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats were presented in Table 1.

Conclusion: The early phase of the project created a useful link between the two CF centres and supported communication, shared learning, and reviewing practice. This shows that twinning can help both clinical and organisational development. Continued collaboration may increase the long-term impact of this partnership.

records.title: Experience of the ECFS-Twinning project between Cluj-Napoca and Brussels

person.title: Teaching assistant
person.institution: "Iuliu Hațieganu" University of Medicine and Pharmacy

records.authors_text: C.E. Szabo1,2, O. Voivod3, M.P. Chira2, G. Feron4, S. Braun4, F. Heyvaert4, S. Teerlinck4, E. De Wachter4
records.affiliations_text: 1"Iuliu Hațieganu" University of Medicine and Pharmacy, Mother and child, Cluj-Napoca, Romania, 2Children's Emergency Clinical Hospital, Romania, Cluj-Napoca, Romania, 3Patient's representative, CF Europe, Cluj-Napoca, Romania, 4UZ Brussels, CF Clinic, Pediatric Pulmonology, Brussels, Belgium
records.abstract_text:
Background: The goal of ECFS-Twinning project is to set up a site-to-site partnership, aiming to fill the gap between European countries regarding care and clinical outcomes in people with CF. Twinning combines mentorship-led knowledge transfer with practical implementation to the selected mentee site. In 2020, collaboration between the CF centre of the Pediatrics Clinic 1 Cluj, Romania, (mentee) and UZ Brussel, Belgium, (mentor) started as part of this project.

Methods: First online meetings were exploring and showed an important language barrier, complicating real conversations. Consequently, Dr Szabo followed English course. It took a year before regular virtual meetings could take place. The first on-site visit (15 - 16 May 2023) was in Cluj-Napoca, by the CF doctor, physiotherapist and CF-nurse from UZ Brussel. Presentations were given, CF patients were seen, mainly focusing on physiotherapy sessions. Barriers for optimal CF-care were identified and discussed. Since then, genuine and committed cooperation has been possible. Virtual meetings were interspersed with personal contacts during ECFS activities. Recently, the Cluj team (CF doctor, physiotherapist, patient representative) visited the centre of Brussels (14 -16 Oct 2025).

Results: Improved multidisciplinary competencies at the mentee site, adoption of harmonized CF protocols and infection control practices. Due to emerging changes in the organization of CF-care at the Pediatrics Clinic 1 Cluj, from 1st January 2026, the CF centre is facing challenging times, in both personnel and infrastructure. The Brussels' mentor site and ECFS supported the actions undertaken by the local staff of the CF clinic in Cluj and follow-up further developments closely.

Conclusion: Providing courses in English for mentee sites prior to active involvement could be helpful. Twinning has been a phantastic journey so far, allowing both sites to learn a lot, highlighting the slogan “together stronger”.

records.title: How to deliver digital health literacy training to PwCF, families, and caregivers: results of an Irish survey

person.title: Research Fellow
person.institution: Cork University Hospital, University College Cork

records.authors_text: T. Vagg1,2,3, M.J. O’Sullivan4, A.-M. Shier4, C. Byrne4, C.-A. O’Rielly4, C. Fleming1, M. McCarthy1, J. Dorgan1, K. Cronin1, F. Holmes1, E. Madden1, S. Twohig1, V. Matthews1, C. Quigney1, H.I. Ibrahim1,2,3, B.J. Plant1,2,3
records.affiliations_text: 1Cork University Hospital, University College Cork, Cork Centre for Cystic Fibrosis (3CF), Cork, Ireland, 2University College Cork, The HRB Funded Clinical Research Facility, Cork, Ireland, 3University College Cork, Department of Medicine, Cork, Ireland, 4Cork University Hospital, University College Cork, Digital Health Literacy (DHL) Public Patient Involvement (PPI) Team, 3CF, Cork, Ireland
records.abstract_text:
Background: Digital Health Literacy (DHL) combines health literacy and digital skills to safely and confidently use digital health tools. CF Digital Health Tools (DHT) such as telehealth, AI searches, remote monitoring, and online forums are increasingly common in CF care, creating a need to build DHL knowledge.

Aim & objective: To identify effective modes for delivering DHL training and resources to PwCF and their caregivers in Ireland.

Methods: A Public Patient Involvement (PPI) team of 8 members (5 PwCF, 3 parents of PwCF) developed a survey for the Irish CF community to explore their understanding of DHL and how best to deliver this training and resources. This survey was digitised and made available online using Qualitrics. Ethical approval was granted from the Clinical Research Ethics Committee at Cork. The survey was advertised via social media through the national patient association, Cystic Fibrosis Ireland. The survey was made available for 8 months.

Results: 37 participants responded to the survey. 21 were PwCF, 16 were family/carers of a pwCF (Age range 16-60, mean age-range 36-40, 25 Female). 8 had knowledge of health literacy, 10 of digital skills, and 6 of DHL. 37 actively sought out CF health information through known CF medical websites. 21 used social media to locate information (mainly Instagram). Preferred training resources included the development of an online multimodal platform (website/app) using text, video, and images for each topic. Topics should be grouped for easier understanding and social media sharing. Additionally, paper-based and email resources are recommended to support users with lower digital skills.

Conclusion: Within Ireland, DHL does not appear to be well known and needs to be an area for future educational focus. When delivering resources to PwCF and family/carers, online multimedia with accompanying paper resources is preferrable.

Funding: Supported by a Vertex CF-RIA award.

Tamara is a multidisciplinary Research Fellow with the Cork Centre for Cystic Fibrosis (3CF) at the Cork University Hospital and University College Cork. As of 2022, she co-ordinates data collection at the Cork adult service for the Cystic Fibrosis Registry of Ireland. Tamara’s previous research (PhD & Postdocs) has focused on Virtual Reality, Gamification/Serious Games, Interactive 3D, Educational Animations, Mobile Multimedia, mHealth, and eHealth for Cystic Fibrosis and other areas in medicine and healthcare.

records.title: Cloud-based remote care for cystic fibrosis: feasibility and patient outcomes

person.title: Pulmonary specialist nurse
person.department: Norwegian Centre for Rare Diseases, Unit for Pulmonology and Cystic Fibrosis

records.authors_text: B.A. Groeterud1, P.L. Finstad1, M. Kolsgaard1, E. Bakkeheim1
records.affiliations_text: 1Oslo University Hospital, Norwegian Centre for Rare Diseases, Unit for Pulmonology and Cystic Fibrosis, Oslo, Norway
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Digital Home Hospital (DHH) solutions can transform cystic fibrosis (CF) care by enabling remote monitoring, reducing clinic visits, and providing personalised support. At Oslo University Hospital (OUH), the Dignio platform, a cloud-based mobile system, was introduced to track patient-reported data and clinical metrics. This study evaluated treatment adherence, patient satisfaction, the accuracy of home spirometry (HS) versus stationary spirometry (SS), and whether lung function remained stable during DHH.

Methods: Of 61 adults with CF (≥17 years) in the Norwegian CF Registry with forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV₁%) >40 and receiving full care at OUH, 14 participants were randomly selected for one year of DHH follow-up (10 male; 13 with ≥1 F508del variant; 11 pancreatic insufficient; mean age 30.3 years, range 19.2–58.1). Adherence was calculated as completed sessions out of 12 scheduled. Satisfaction was assessed via forms. Agreement between HS and SS was analysed using paired measurements within ≤3 days. Registry data from the study year and the next were compared using paired tests to assess lung function stability.

Results: One participant did not engage. Among the remaining 13, HS adherence ranged 42–100% (mean 76%). One relied exclusively on Dignio; others combined digital monitoring with limited consultations. Most had 1–2 consultations; only one attended both two hospital visits and two phone consultations. Satisfaction was high: 10 of 11 respondents were largely or very satisfied, and all would choose digital follow-up again. HS and SS showed strong agreement (mean difference 0.01 L; range −0.6 to 0.5 L; p=0.90), confirming HS reliability. Lung function remained stable (mean FEV₁ 3.6 L both years; p=0.25), indicating DHH did not negatively impact outcomes.

Conclusion: DHH follow-up for people with CF demonstrated good adherence, high satisfaction, accurate HS, and stable lung function, supporting its feasibility in routine care.

Objective: Digital Home Hospital (DHH) solutions can transform cystic fibrosis (CF) care by enabling remote monitoring, reducing clinic visits, and providing personalised support. At Oslo University Hospital (OUH), the Dignio platform, a cloud-based mobile system, was introduced to track patient-reported data and clinical metrics. This study evaluated treatment adherence, patient satisfaction, the accuracy of home spirometry (HS) versus stationary spirometry (SS), and whether lung function remained stable during DHH.
Methods: Of 61 adults with CF (≥17 years) in the Norwegian CF Registry with forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV₁%) >40 and receiving full care at OUH, 14 participants were randomly selected for one year of DHH follow-up (10 male; 13 with ≥1 F508del variant; 11 pancreatic insufficient; mean age 30.3 years, range 19.2–58.1). Adherence was calculated as completed sessions out of 12 scheduled. Satisfaction was assessed via forms. Agreement between HS and SS was analysed using paired measurements within ≤3 days. Registry data from the study year and the next were compared using paired tests to assess lung function stability.
Results: One participant did not engage. Among the remaining 13, HS adherence ranged 42–100% (mean 76%). One relied exclusively on Dignio; others combined digital monitoring with limited consultations. Most had 1–2 consultations; only one attended both two hospital visits and two phone consultations. Satisfaction was high: 10 of 11 respondents were largely or very satisfied, and all would choose digital follow-up again. HS and SS showed strong agreement (mean difference 0.01 L; range −0.6 to 0.5 L; p=0.90), confirming HS reliability. Lung function remained stable (mean FEV₁ 3.6 L both years; p=0.25), indicating DHH did not negatively impact outcomes.
Conclusion: DHH follow-up for people with CF demonstrated good adherence, high satisfaction, accurate HS, and stable lung function, supporting its feasibility in routine care.

records.title: Mapping current practices of digital health in respiratory disease management: national survey
records.authors_text: H. Alshuwaikhat1, C. Williams1, S. van Beurden1
records.affiliations_text: 1The University of Exeter, Exeter, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: Chronic respiratory diseases are long-term, irreversible disorders associated with substantial treatment burden and ongoing care needs. Digital health technologies are increasingly promoted to support self-management, monitoring, and care delivery in long-term conditions. However, evidence on their actual use, implementation, and perceived impact within respiratory care remains limited.

Objectives: This study aimed to (1) describe current use (or non-use) of digital health technologies in the management of respiratory diseases among patients and healthcare professionals, (2) identify reported barriers, enablers, and potential inequalities influencing its use and implementation within NHS settings, and (3) explore perceived impacts on day-to-day care, self-management, quality of care.

Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted with patients with respiratory diseases and healthcare professionals involved in respiratory care. The surveys captured digital health use, reasons for use or non-use, and perceived impacts on care delivery and experience. Surveys were distributed via six NHS Trusts, professional and charitable organisations, social media, and community channels. To support accessibility and inclusion, participants could, if preferred, complete the survey via a paper-based format.

Results: At the time of abstract submission, the survey was ongoing and scheduled to conclude in February 2026. To date, the survey had been initiated online by 354 patients with respiratory diseases and 41 healthcare professionals. Preliminary data indicates substantial variation in digital health use across patient and healthcare professional groups. Full analyses will examine patterns of use, perceived impacts on care and service provision, and reported barriers and inequalities following completion of data collection.

records.title: Feasibility and acceptability of a digital, cognitive behavioural therapy-based group intervention for adolescents with chronic physical illness and their parents: a Swedish adaptation of On Track
records.authors_text: E. Bergenmar Ivarsson1, J. Strand1, S. Weineland1, E.-L. Bratt2, L. Scholten3, S. Buratti1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Gothenburg, Psychology, Gothenburg, Sweden, 2University of Gothenburg, Institute of Health and Care Sciences, Gothenburg, Sweden, 3Amsterdam University, Medical Center for Research, Amsterdam, Netherlands
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: digital treatment formats are essential to improve equitable access to healthcare and reduce treatment burden. Around 20% of children in western countries live with chronic physical illness (CPI), such as cystic fibrosis. CPI limits daily functioning and entails psychosocial challenges, across different CPI, including anxiety and depression. Parents play a key role in adolescents’ well-being and coping with illness-related stress, underscoring the need for interventions involving both adolescents and parents. To address this, the psychosocial support program On Track (OT), a digital, transdiagnostic group intervention based on Cognitive Behavioural Therapy, was developed in the Netherlands, to provide targeted support.

This study examines feasibility and acceptability of a Swedish adaptation of OT in a clinical setting, focusing on implementation and participant experiences.

Methods: semi-structured interviews were conducted with two adolescents and six parents who completed OT. Recruitment challenges limited the sample size. Inductive thematic analysis identified four themes: mutual exchange and understanding; digital format as an enabler; improved ability to regulate emotions; and enhanced family communication.

Results: sharing experiences within the group was highly valued. The digital format was seen as accessible and flexible. The transdiagnostic approach was well received, although careful group composition appears important for engagement. The CBT framework combined with group interaction supported the adoption of new coping strategies, particularly for emotional regulation. Parents reported improved illness-related communication. Recruitment was slower than anticipated and required substantial effort.

Conclusion: findings indicate that OT is a feasible and acceptable intervention for addressing psychosocial difficulties. Future research should focus on optimizing recruitment strategies and evaluating OT’s effectiveness in the Swedish context.

records.title: Virtual clinical reviews in paediatric CF care - development of a service based on patient experience and clinical parameters

person.title: Ms.
person.institution: Great Ormond Street Hospital NHS Trust

records.authors_text: C. Dawson1, C. Edmondson2, A. Turnbull2
records.affiliations_text: 1Great Ormond Street Hospital NHS Trust, Cystic Fibrosis Unit, London, United Kingdom, 2Great Ormond Street Hospital NHS Trust, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: Advances in CF care have resulted in lower morbidity in children with CF (CwCF). Telehealth has the potential to allow clinical monitoring of CwCF with less disruption to daily life. Adoption of telehealth in CwCF has been slow, due to factors such as unreliability of equipment in younger children, reliance on parents to recognise subtle changes in their child’s health, safeguarding concerns & parental wishes. Within our centre we aimed to ascertain parental views on the development of a virtual clinic (VC) and develop a clinical checklist to stratify patient suitability for a VC appointment based on their annual assessment (AA) results.

Methods: A PREM was sent to all families within the CF centre to explore views on the development of a virtual clinic.

All members of the CF MDT were asked to identify AA triggers or results that would constitute a cause for concern, forming the basis of the checklist.

Results: PREM results: 109/180 (61%) of families responded, with a higher proportion of responses from families with CwCF between 13 & 14yrs (14%) and lowest response from families of CwCF aged below 1 year (1%). 68% were in favour of VC,19% ambivalent, & only 10% disagreed. 98% used public transport as part of their journey to hospital. Respondents’ concerns included: no physical examination (80%) & no spirometry (68%). Benefits included less travel expense (80%), less disruption to education/employment (88%/80%), & reduced clinic wait (95%).

The developed checklist comprises 14 domains including respiratory health, anthropomorphic data & social concerns.

Conclusions: Most families were in favour of VCs as an option, but a significant number raised concerns regarding the lack of examination or investigations. These concerns may be addressed in the future with the growth of remote technology. Our checklist is currently being utilised within our service to stratify patients, with PREMs being sent after the VC to assess feedback from families.

person.biography:
Charlotte has been the Clinical Nurse Specialist with the CF team at Great Ormond Street Hospital since 2004 following 10yrs clinical nursing on the specialist respiratory unit, Badger Ward. Her current role includes coordinating the care and support for approx 200 CF patients between the ages of 0-18yrs at Great Ormond Street Hospital (specialist centre), local hospitals and within the community, as well as being the lead CF CNS and co-lead for the CF Service at GOSH.
 
Charlotte received her RSCN qualification in 1994 after successful completion of her training at both Great Ormond Street and Queen Elizabeth Hospital, London and has an honours degree – BSc (Hons) Children’s Nursing and Social Care.
She regularly attends and participates in national and international conferences and in the past has been the chair of the UK National CF Nurses Association (CFNA) and currently is a member of the ECFS scientific committee.
Miss Dawson has presented oral, poster and symposium presentations at the North American and European CF Conferences and organised regional workshops and national study days for the UK CF Nurses association.
She has actively contributes to the coordination and management of research within the CF unit at GOSH and the London Collaborative Clinical Trials Network and is currently a PI for clinical research study.

records.title: Clinical utility of point-of-care sweat chloride testing across contemporary cystic fibrosis care scenarios: a provider survey

person.title: Professor of Medicine and Pediatrics
person.institution: Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine

records.authors_text: M. Jain1, R. Nelson1, S. McColley2, T. Cybulski3, M. Sala3, M. Prickett3, J. Rogers4, R. Ghaffari5, A. Aranyosi5, N. Mayer-Hamblett6, C. Goss6
records.affiliations_text: 1Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, Medicine, Pulmonary Critical Care, Chicago, United States, 2Ann & Robert H. Lurie Children's Hospital of Chicago, Chicago, United States, 3Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, Chicago, United States, 4Northwestern, University Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Evanston, United States, 5Epicore Biosystems, Inc, Cambridge, United States, 6Seattle Children's Research Institute, Seattle, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Sweat chloride is a validated biomarker of CFTR function and response to CFTR modulators, yet its use beyond diagnosis is limited by logistical barriers. Emerging point-of-care (POC) technologies may enable rapid assessment of CFTR modulation in routine care. We evaluated clinician perceptions of the realism and clinical utility of POC sweat chloride testing across contemporary cystic fibrosis (CF) care scenarios.

Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional survey of CF clinicians evaluating seven scenarios in which rapid (10–15 minute) POC sweat chloride results could inform care, including CFTR modulator adherence, drug–drug interactions, atypical modulator response, exercise-related hydration management, modulator dose reduction due to hepatic impairment or mental health adverse effects, and monitoring during pregnancy. Respondents rated each scenario for realism and clinical utility.

Results: A total of 105 CF clinicians responded, representing pediatric, adult, and mixed practices, with most having over five years of CF experience. Assessment of adherence and drug–drug interactions were considered realistic by 59% and 69% of respondents, respectively. Modulator dose reduction due to hepatic impairment or mental health adverse effects was viewed as realistic by ~71%. Pregnancy-related monitoring and exercise-related hydration management were considered realistic by 46% and 31%. POC sweat chloride testing was perceived as clinically useful across all scenarios, with highest utility for modulator dose modification due to hepatic impairment (87%) and mental health adverse effects (88%). Adherence assessment and drug–drug interactions were also frequently identified as useful (82–84%).

Conclusion: CF clinicians perceive POC sweat chloride testing as a clinically useful biomarker across diverse real-world care scenarios, supporting prospective evaluation of its role in individualized CFTR modulator management and physiologic monitoring.

records.title: Maintaining skills, evolving roles, enhancing knowledge: physiotherapy in cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: J. Hauser1, J. Bishop2, R. Cobb3, N. Ward4, B. Button
records.affiliations_text: 1CFPhysio.com Inc, Hobart, Australia, 2Adult CF Unit, Westmead Hospital, Sydney, Australia, 3Adult CF Centre, The Prince Charles Hospital, Brisbane, Australia, 4Heart and Lung Program Central Adelaide Local Health Network, Adelaide, Australia
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: With highly effective modulators and specialised multidisciplinary care reshaping cystic fibrosis (CF) management, physiotherapy roles continue to evolve. While many individuals experience reduced symptom burden, others face complex exacerbations, or limited access to modulators, and increased complexity with ageing. To ensure ongoing access to evidence-based resources, Australian physiotherapists (with ongoing input from global clinicians) established CFPhysio.com Inc (CFP Inc), a not-for-profit organisation supporting professional development (PD) through digital technology.

Method: Specialist physiotherapists translated evidence-based guidelines into an online learning platform offering free, self-paced modules in written, video, and illustrated formats. Initiatives such as REACH for CF (Research, education and collaboration for CF) and the Chronic Suppurative Lung Disease Education series extend the site into a collaborative hub for connection and learning.

Outcomes: Analytics of the website, since launch in 2019, report site is accessed by over 2700 clinicians. Registration surveys (n= 846) highlight only 18% of users have completed CF specific PD 12 months prior to visiting the website. Across 9 domains of physiotherapy skills in CF care, self-rating of knowledge and confidence was between low and average, with 50% of respondents rating their knowledge in airway pathogens, inhalation therapy, and autogenic drainage as low or very low. All respondents in a snapshot review of the airway clearance modules (n=113) rated content helpful and improved their knowledge and confidence.

Conclusion: CFP Inc provides sustainable, responsive physiotherapy education for clinicians. By leveraging technology, the organisation continues to overcome barriers in maintaining knowledge, fostering empowerment and supporting the CF community.

Acknowledgements: CFPhysio.com Inc executive committee and clinicians contributing to content and education resource delivery.

Conclusion: CFP Inc provides sustainable, responsive physiotherapy education for clinicians. By leveraging technology, the organisation continues to overcome barriers in maintaining knowledge, fostering empowerment and supporting the CF community.

person.biography:
Dr Brenda Button has been privileged to work in Cystic Fibrosis from newborn screening through childhood, adolescence and adulthood over the past three decades. She is an accredited instructor of modern airway clearance with the International Physiotherapy Group for CF (learning from the originators of modern airway clearance therapy). Her research contribution includes airway clearance therapy, effects on gastroesophageal function, exercise and exercise testing, continence in women and men with lung disease, adherence, use of mucolytic agents and quality of life. She has published more than 60 peer reviewed studies.  She is frequently invited to speak and teach internationally and is a Winston Churchill Fellow investigating managing patients with suppurative lung disease on ECMO bridging to lung transplant. She teaches undergraduate and post graduate physiotherapists and supervises PhD and Masters students at Monash University, Melbourne Australia.

records.title: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based computational modelling of particle deposition in the lungs of people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF)

person.department: Division of Immunology, Immunity to Infection and Respiratory Medicine

records.authors_text: J. Brady1, Y. Brown2, A. Biancardi2, D.-J. Jakymelen2, L. Smith2, J. Wild2, A. Horsley1, C. Whitfield3, Magnify Strategic Research Centre
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Manchester, Division of Immunology, Immunity to Infection and Respiratory Medicine, Manchester, United Kingdom, 2University of Sheffield, POLARIS, University MRI, Division of Clinical Medicine, Sheffield, United Kingdom, 3University of Manchester, Department of Mathematics, Manchester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Optimising the delivery of inhaled therapies for CF requires an understanding of the impact of structural and functional effects of CF lung disease on particle deposition. These are not adequately represented in current computational deposition models. Our aim is to develop a personalised lung deposition model for pwCF based on 1H and 129Xe-MRI.

Methods: In one volunteer with CF (M, age = 44.8 yrs, ppFEV1 = 64.9), ultrashort echo time (UTE) 1H-MRI was used to segment visible airways and then further generate an idealised model of airway structure. From their 129Xe ventilation MRI, ventilation defects were linked to the corresponding airways in the model. These airways were then constricted to achieve optimal agreement between the 129Xe MR image and the ventilation distribution in the model lung after a simulated inspiration.

We then simulated inspiration of a 100ml bolus of 3µm diameter particles at the centre of a 1L tidal breath, in both the unconstricted and constricted models, to mimic aerosol bolus dispersion (ABD) experiments.

Results: The simulated 129Xe MR manoeuvre in the constricted model reproduces the low ventilation percentage (LVP) (37.2% vs. 41.2% in the 129Xe MR image), but overestimates ventilation defect percentage (VDP) (31.8% vs. 22.4%). Deposition increased with airway constriction from 50% of particles inhaled, to 57%, with the greatest increase occurring in airway generation 5 (from 5.7% to 9.0%). The mean percentage change in dose delivered to each airway generation with constrictions introduced was 41%.

Conclusion: The predicted small increase in airway deposition due to constrictions is consistent with previous clinical reports. However, this model also captures the resulting spatial heterogeneity in delivered dose which is significant for drug delivery applications. The ability to generate patient-specific testable predictions, such as ABD experiments, will be used to validate and further improve the model in future studies.

records.title: Evolution of exercise capacity in adults with cystic fibrosis receiving ETI
records.authors_text: I. Waller1, R. McVean1, S. Kiernan1, N. Hodgson1, J. Mitchell1, P. Barry1
records.affiliations_text: 1Manchester Foundation Trust, Cystic Fibrosis, Manchester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background:Prior to the introduction of CFTR modulation CF lung disease was characterised by progressive decline in lung functionCardio-pulmonary exercise testing (CPET) has been reported to provide additional prognostic information beyond lung function measurements. The utilisation of Elexacaftor/Tezacaftor/Ivacaftor (ETI) has resulted in improvements in lung function measurements in adults with CF but less is known on its sustained impact on exercise capacity.Aim:Cystic fibrosis (CF) is associated with progressive decline in lung function and reduced exercise tolerance. However, long-term, real-world changes in exercise capacity after treatment remain limited particularly during and after Kaftrio and a global pandemic. MethodsA retrospective review of CPET data was collected during routine clinical monitoring in adults with CF. Data from a CPET prior to ETI were compared to data from two tests conducted post ETI Results Data from 78 CPETs in 26 adults (median age 27.0 [23.5-34.5] years) were analysed. Baseline tests were conducted a mean of 543±275 days prior to ETI with the first post ETI test being conducted a mean of 694±320 days post ETI and the third test conducted a mean of 735±366 days following this. Mean FEV1 percent predicted increased significantly between post ETI test 1 and baseline (59.4±18.9 vs 69.9±18.6, p<0.001) and was sustained at post test 2 (70.6±20.8, p=0.623). Median pO2 was significantly higher at the both post ETI tests compared to baseline (p<0.001). VO2peak was not significantly different between baseline and any of the post ETI tests but a significant increase was seen between baseline and post test 2 when corrected to percent predicted (75.6±13.7 vs 82.9±15.8, p=0.013). VO2 percent predicted at anaerobic threshold was not significantly different post ETI

Conclusions:VO2peak is maintained over time in adults with CF treated with ETI. Maintaining aerobic capacity may be important in preserving long term health for adults with CF

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa) airway colonization in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) requires close monitoring due to its association with increased pulmonary exacerbations, progressive lung damage and accelerated decline in pulmonary function. Prior studies from our group identified pwCF who produced highly neutralizing antibodies against the type III secretion system (T3SS) of Pa. The aim of this work is to investigate the clinical relevance of these antibodies and immunological mechanisms driving chronic Pa infection.

Methods: We quantified serum T3SS-neutralizing activity in 99 pwCF and 12 healthy individuals. Neutralization capacity was integrated with immunophenotyping, including FACS-based characterization and bulk RNA sequencing of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), as well as clinical parameters. In the CF group, blood samples were collected twice with a time interval of two years.

Results: As expected, high neutralization capacity (Pa-Abhigh) was associated with chronic Pa infection. Immunophenotyping of pwCF with high and low neutralization revealed distinct cellular profiles including specific differences in monocyte and lymphocyte subpopulations, with more non-classical monocytes and fewer naïve CD8+ T-cells in Pa-Abhigh. These cellular alterations were reflected in transcriptomic differences, particularly within cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction and adaptive immunity pathways. Spirometry data showed that Pa-Abhigh individuals had reduced forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1). Moreover, an increase of Pa neutralization over time was linked to a progressive decline in FEV1.

Conclusion: Our findings offer a mechanistic insight into the development of potent neutralizing anti-T3SS antibodies and reveal a unique immunological profile linked to chronic Pa infection and reduced lung function. Incorporating this immune signature into clinical practice may enable early detection of patients at risk of disease progression.

records.abstract_text:
Background: Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) improves F508del-CFTR function and leads to substantial clinical benefits. However, people with CF and the F508del mutation and the complex allele L467F showed limited clinical response to ETI. Recently, vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor (VTD) was approved as an alternative modulator therapy for people with CF and at least one non-class I mutation. However, the effects of VTD in patients carrying the complex allele L467F have not been investigated. Within an ECFS Twinning project in collaboration with the CF center in Skopje, North Macedonia, we therefore assessed the pharmacological rescue of CFTR activity by ETI and VTD in primary nasal epithelial cells (pHNEC) of people with at least one F508del-L467F allele.

Methods: Highly differentiated pHNEC were established from 4 F508del-L467F-homozygous people with CF, 3 people with CF compound heterozygous for F508del-L467F and a minimal function mutation and 3 healthy controls. CFTR activity was assessed by transepithelial short-circuit currents in Ussing chamber after VTD/ETI/DMSO incubation and expressed as % of healthy CFTR function.

Results: Treatment with ETI did not improve CFTR-mediated chloride currents, determined by forskolin peak response (P = 0.16) and CFTRinhb172-inhibited currents (P = 0.53), compared to vehicle-treated control in pHNECs of the 7 patients with at least one F508del-L467F allele. Interestingly, VTD treatment increased CFTR-mediated chloride currents following forskolin/IBMX stimulation compared to vehicle control (P < 0.001) and ETI (P < 0.05). Moreover, CFTR activity was inhibited by CFTRinhb172 in comparison to vehicle control (P < 0.01) and ETI (P < 0.05). PHNEC’s of the whole cohort showed a response to VTD with a mean correction of CFTR activity of about 7% of the healthy controls.

Conclusion: VTD but not ETI treatment improves CFTR function in vitro in people with CF carrying at least one F508del-L467F allele.

Recently, vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor (VTD) was approved as an alternative modulator therapy for people with CF and at least one non-class I mutation. However, the effects of VTD in patients carrying the complex allele L467F have not been investigated. Within an ECFS Twinning project in collaboration with the CF center in Skopje, North Macedonia, we therefore assessed the pharmacological rescue of CFTR activity by ETI and VTD in primary nasal epithelial cells (pHNEC) of people with at least one F508del-L467F allele.
Methods: Highly differentiated pHNEC were established from 4 F508del-L467F-homozygous people with CF, 3 people with CF compound heterozygous for F508del-L467F and a minimal function mutation and 3 healthy controls. CFTR activity was assessed by transepithelial short-circuit currents in Ussing chamber after VTD/ETI/DMSO incubation and expressed as % of healthy CFTR function.
Results: Treatment with ETI did not improve CFTR-mediated chloride currents, determined by forskolin peak response (P = 0.16) and CFTRinhb172-inhibited currents (P = 0.53), compared to vehicle-treated control in pHNECs of the 7 patients with at least one F508del-L467F allele. Interestingly, VTD treatment increased CFTR-mediated chloride currents following forskolin/IBMX stimulation compared to vehicle control (P < 0.001) and ETI (P < 0.05). Moreover, CFTR activity was inhibited by CFTRinhb172 in comparison to vehicle control (P < 0.01) and ETI (P < 0.05). PHNEC’s of the whole cohort showed a response to VTD with a mean correction of CFTR activity of about 7% of the healthy controls.
Conclusion: VTD but not ETI treatment improves CFTR function in vitro in people with CF carrying at least one F508del-L467F allele.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The past decade has seen growth in the number of young people with CF (YPwCF) in the All Wales Adult CF Centre, as well as the introduction of CFTR modulators earlier in life. Given these changes, we compared YPwCF’s involvement in education, employment and training in 2025 with 2015.

Method: Employment and education data collected at annual review in 2015 (n=71, 44 M, 27 F, mean age 21, mean FEV1 76.7%) were compared to 2025 data (n=91, 48 M, 39 F, 4 TG, mean age 20, mean FEV1 93.4%) for patients in the adult service aged 16-24. We also compared the data to the Welsh national statistics for young people (16-24) not in education, employment or training (NEET) in 2015 and 2025.

Results: Data is summarised in the table below.

Alongside the rise in YPwCF in education, the proportion studying at a higher level e.g. degree increased. No YPwCF were parents/carers in 2015, but in 2025, a small number (6/91) were parents/carers, of whom 3/6 were classed as NEET (or economically unavailable), 2/6 worked part-time and 1/6 combined study and PTW.

Conclusion: The proportion of YPwCF who are NEET has declined between 2015 and 2025, showing more engagement in work and study. A rise in FEV1 and drop in health-related benefits indicate improvement in health. Whilst unable to draw firm conclusions it is likely that CFTR modulators contributed to improving health, ability and expectations of YPwCF to pursue study and work. Given likely continued improvements in health, we should consider the support needed for YPwCF to manage health alongside work and study.

records.authors_text: I.P. Michou1,2, S. Spelier2,3, M. Stancampiano4, D. Arosio4, J.M. Beekman2,3, M.D. Amaral1, H.M. Botelho1
records.affiliations_text: 1BioISI-Biosystems and Integrative Sciences Institute, Faculty of Sciences, University of Lisboa, Lisboa, Portugal, 2Regenerative Medicine Utrecht, University Medical Centre, Utrecht University, Utrecht, Netherlands, 3Department of Paediatric Respiratory Medicine, Wilhelmina Children's Hospital, University Medical Centre, Utrecht University, Utrecht, Netherlands, 4Istituto di Biofisica, Consiglio Nazionale delle Ricerche, Trento, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: CFTR modulators have transformed cystic fibrosis (CF) care; however, variability in patient responses highlights the need for more predictive and physiologically relevant functional assays. Patient-derived intestinal organoids (PDIOs) enable high-throughput, yet indirect assessment of CFTR activity through the forskolin-induced swelling (FIS) assay.1 Here, we aim to establish fluorescence-based assays for direct, quantitative, real-time readouts of CFTR activity in PDIO-derived systems using genetically encoded ion-sensitive fluorescent sensors, such as HS-YFP-mKate2 for iodide flux and ClopHensor3 for chloride and pH measurements.

Methods: HS-YFP-mKate and Clop3 constructs were cloned into lentiviral backbones via Gibson Assembly, and lentiviral particles were produced in HEK293T cells to transduce wild-type and F508del/F508del CFTR PDIOs. Fluorescent organoids were fluorescence-activated cell sorted (FACS) to generate homogeneous reporter populations.

Results: Both three-dimensional organoid cultures and two-dimensional monolayer assays are under development to support automated high-throughput microscopy of CFTR-dependent halide and bicarbonate fluxes. Stable fluorescent PDIO populations expressing HS-YFP-mKate or Clop3 were successfully generated, and preliminary data demonstrate CFTR-dependent HS-YFP quenching upon pharmacological activation. Protocol optimisation for combined chloride and pH measurements using ClopHensor is ongoing.

Conclusion: Together, these fluorescent intestinal cell models provide a robust platform for real-time CFTR functional testing and drug screening, with potential to improve the accuracy of patient-specific response assessment to CFTR modulators.

References:

Dekkers JF et al (2013) Nat Med 19: 939-45.

Vijftigschild LA et al (2013) Cytometry A 83:576-84.

Arosio D et al (2010) Nat Methods 7: 516–518
