records.abstract_text:
Objectives: People with cystic fibrosis (CF) have historically been advised to eat an unrestricted high-calorie, high-fat “legacy CF diet”, which is associated with poor diet quality, and may exacerbate gastrointestinal symptoms (GiS). This study examined associations between diet, dietary patterns and GiS.

Method: Adults from three UK CF centres completed GiS questionnaires to derive clusters using Latent Class Analysis. This provided four distinct phenotypes mild, moderate-diarrhoea, moderate-constipation and severe. Participants completed at least one 24-hour dietary recall using Intake24. Following quality checks, mean intake across two days was calculated. Diet quality and inflammatory potential were assessed using the Diet Quality Index-International (DQI-I) and Dietary Inflammatory Index (DII). Symptom phenotypes and diet were analysed using multinomial logistic regression.

Results: 221 adults were included (50.2% male; median age 30 years, range 16-67 years). Median energy intake was lowest in the severe phenotype (1608 kcal/day), although intake was broadly comparable across phenotypes. Fibre intake was also the lowest in the severe phenotype (14 g/day) compared with mild and both moderate groups 16 g/day). Fat intake contributions were broadly similar across phenotypes (median 32–35% energy). The moderate-diarrhoea phenotype exhibited the lowest mean DII score (1.1, SD 1.9), whereas the severe phenotype had the highest (1.9, SD 1.9). Regression analyses showed no significant associations between fat intake, fibre intake, DQI-I score or DII score and symptom phenotypes.

Conclusion: Dietary intake, diet quality and inflammatory potential were not significantly associated with GiS phenotypes. Lower fibre intake and high DII score was observed among participants in the severe phenotype, but associations were not statistically significant. The high DII score in the severe phenotype may suggest a more pro-inflammatory dietary profile.

person.title: Mr.
person.biography: Darren has been a clinical specialist Dietitian working with adults with cystic fibrosis for 15 years. Darren is based at the Wolfson CF Centre for adults in Nottingham, UK. He has a background in sports science with a focus on health and links with exercise and good nutrition. Darren is interested in body composition and its impact of changing nutritional status on body image and the impact of gastrointestinal symptoms in people with cystic fibrosis. Darren has been involved in the GRAMPUS-CF study and investigated the impact of diet on gut symptoms. Darren is active in research and has completed several pieces of work and actively supports recruitment of participants for external studies.

records.affiliations_text: 1Paediatric Academic Health Science Centre, Childrens Health Ireland, Research and Innovation, Dublin 12, Ireland, 2University College Dublin, Dublin, Ireland, 3Childrens Health Ireland, Department of Gastroenterology and Hepatology, Dublin, Ireland
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) modulators have beneficial effects on the respiratory and nutritional status of people with Cystic Fibrosis (CF) but the impact on liver involvement is not clear. The objective was to use a prospective study of children with CF to compare liver status over time in those taking modulators versus those who were not.

Methods: A national longitudinal study collects data on children with CF every five years, with a focus on liver parameters. Children treated with any CFTR modulator who had liver status recorded at T0 (pre-modulator) and T1 (post-modulator) were designated cases and compared to controls not treated with modulator.

Results: 88 cases (M 44) with median age (T0) 9.6years (IQR 7,12.7) and (T1) 14.1years (11.4,17.3) were analysed. 66 controls (M 40) with median age (T0) 9.4years (7.3, 11.7) and (T1) 13.8years (10.6,15.9) were included.

At T0, 61(69.3%) cases had no liver disease, 26(29.5%) had CF Hepatobiliary involvement (CFHBI) and 1(1.1%) advanced CF Liver Disease (aCFLD) versus 35(53%), 27(40.9%) and 4(6.1%) in control group respectively.

At T1, 52(59.1%) cases had no liver disease, 33(37.5%) had CFHBI and 3(3.4%) aCFLD versus 28(42.4%), 32(48.5%) and 6(9.1%) in control population.

From T0 to T1, median weight increased by 11.6kg in control group versus 19.9kg in cases and median FEV1 declined by 7.9% in controls with no decline in cases. AST, ALT and GGT did not change significantly in either group.

Cases n=88Controls n=66P ValueImproved to normal11 (12.5%)9 (13.6%)0.84Progressed to HBI20 (22.7%)15 (22.7%)1.0Progressed to aCFLD2 (2.3%)2 (3%) *1 from normal0.77No change55 (62.5%)40 (60.6%)0.81

*Chi squared test

Table1. Change in liver status over median 4.1year follow-up in cases and control group

Conclusion: Progression/improvement of liver status did not differ with modulator use over the study period. Longer-term multicentre collaboration is needed to determine the true effects of modulators on liver involvement in CF.

Objectives: Cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) modulators have beneficial effects on the respiratory and nutritional status of people with Cystic Fibrosis (CF) but the impact on liver involvement is not clear. The objective was to use a prospective study of children with CF to compare liver status over time in those taking modulators versus those who were not.
Methods: A national longitudinal study collects data on children with CF every five years, with a focus on liver parameters. Children treated with any CFTR modulator who had liver status recorded at T0 (pre-modulator) and T1 (post-modulator) were designated cases and compared to controls not treated with modulator.
Results: 88 cases (M 44) with median age (T0) 9.6years (IQR 7,12.7) and (T1) 14.1years (11.4,17.3) were analysed. 66 controls (M 40) with median age (T0) 9.4years (7.3, 11.7) and (T1) 13.8years (10.6,15.9) were included.
At T0, 61(69.3%) cases had no liver disease, 26(29.5%) had CF Hepatobiliary involvement (CFHBI) and 1(1.1%) advanced CF Liver Disease (aCFLD) versus 35(53%), 27(40.9%) and 4(6.1%) in control group respectively.

session.title: ePoster Session 01 -Targeting pseudomonas in cystic fibrosis: from mechanisms to new therapies

Lyngby, Denmark, 4University of Copenhagen, Department of Clinical Medicine, Faculty of Health and Medical Sciences, Copenhagen, Denmark
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Antibiotic-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa poses a major challenge in chronic airway disease, particularly in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). Carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa is considered a highest-priority bacterial threat, with resistance frequently driven by loss-of-function mutations in the carbapenem uptake porin OprD. However, the broader consequences of these mutations for bacterial physiology and infection dynamics remain poorly understood.

Methods: Clinical P. aeruginosa strains isolated longitudinally from pwCF were analyzed to assess the emergence of oprD mutations. The effects of OprD loss were evaluated using an air–liquid interface airway epithelial model, measuring early bacterial attachment and translocation across epithelial barriers. Biophysical analyses were performed to assess changes in outer membrane properties and mucus interactions due to OprD loss across diverse clinical genomic backgrounds.

Results: Here we show that oprD mutations can arise in clinical strains isolated from pwCF in the absence of carbapenem treatment, suggesting selective pressures beyond direct antibiotic exposure. In the airway epithelial model, oprD mutants displayed enhanced early attachment to epithelial surfaces and increased translocation across the epithelial barrier, a phenotype conserved across diverse clinical genomic backgrounds. Biophysical analyses indicated that loss of OprD alters outer membrane charge and reduces mucus entrapment, thereby facilitating epithelial colonization independently of antimicrobial pressure.

Conclusion: These findings demonstrate that antibiotic resistance mutations can directly modulate host–pathogen interactions during airway infection, reshaping colonization dynamics beyond their impact on antibiotic susceptibility. This highlights the need to consider the wider biological effects of resistance-associated mutations when evaluating infection dynamics and clinical outcomes.

person.title: Dr.
person.biography:
Antimicrobial resistance is one of the most significant global health challenges, threatening the treatment of infectious diseases and many clinical practices that rely on effective antibiotics. Understanding how antibiotic pressure shapes bacterial physiology and adaptation within the infection environment is essential to addressing this crisis.
Pablo Laborda is a postdoctoral researcher supported by an ERS/EU RESPIRE4 Marie Skłodowska-Curie Postdoctoral Research Fellowship at the Infection Microbiology group, Department of Clinical Microbiology, Rigshospitalet (Copenhagen). His research focuses on dissecting the interplay between antimicrobial resistance, metabolic adaptation, and host–microbe interactions during airway infections. He combines classical microbiology with genomics, transcriptomics, and laboratory model systems that mimic human infections in vitro. His work aims to deepen our understanding of bacterial adaptation in the host and to inform strategies to mitigate the impact of antimicrobial resistance.

content.biography: Pablo Laborda is a postdoctoral researcher with an ERS/EU RESPIRE4 Marie Skłodowska-Curie Postdoctoral Research Fellowship in the Infection Microbiology group of the Department of Clinical Microbiology of Rigshospitalet. He obtained a PhD in 2022 after developing his doctoral thesis in the Spanish National Centre for Biotechnology, CNB-CSIC. His thesis emphasized on the study of the evolution of antibiotic resistance in order to identify potential evolution-based approaches to tackle antibiotic-resistant pathogens, with a particular focus on Pseudomonas aeruginosa. From 2023, he has been studying the dynamics of host-microbe interactions that govern bacterial colonization of the lungs. His research is enclosed in more than 20 peer-reviewed publications, including in high impact journals such as PNAS, Molecular Biology and Evolution, Nature Communications or Nature Reviews in Microbiology.

records.title: Personalized medicine for cystic fibrosis (CF) rare genotypes: uncovering a misclassified class I mutation and guiding successful treatment in a person with CF carrying the G542X/622-2A>C genotype

session.title: ePoster Session 02 - Rare genotypes & challenging phenotypes

records.authors_text: Y. Soeffers1, N. Rodrigues Mier2,1, M. Boon1,2, Y. Vande Weygaerde3,4, M. Proesmans1,2, F. Vermeulen1,2, A. S. Ramalho1, on behalf of the Belgian Organoid Project
records.affiliations_text: 1KUleuven, Department of Development and Regeneration, Leuven, Belgium, 2UZLeuven, Department of Pediatrics, Leuven, Belgium, 3Ghent University Hospital, Department of Respiratory Medicine, Ghent, Belgium, 4Ghent University, Department of Internal Medicine and Paediatrics, Ghent, Belgium
records.abstract_text:
Background: People with Cystic fibrosis carrying two class I CFTR mutations are generally considered non-responsive to CFTR modulators. According to recent literature [1], the genotype G542X/622-2A>C is predicted as Class I/I, that would result in no protein production, precluding benefit from CFTR modulators. However, 622-2A>C is a very rare CFTR undercharacterized variant.

Methods: Patient-derived rectal organoids (PDROs) from a woman with with CF carrying the G542X/622-2A>C genotype were analyzed via RT-PCR/sequencing of complete CFTR cDNA, immunoblot, and forskolin-induced swelling (FIS) assays with ivacaftor(I), tezacaftor/I (TI), and elexacaftor/TI (ETI). An off-label treatment was also conducted.

Results: RNA analysis showed 622-2A>C caused alternative splicing, skipping of the first 9-nucleotides of exon 5 leading to the deletion of 3 amino acids in the first intracellular loop (ICL1). Protein analysis showed core-glycosylated CFTR (band B) partially rescued to full-glycosylated (band C) after ET treatment. PDRO theratyping showed significant CFTR function restoration with ETI (0.8µM FIS AUC 2779.44; SD 67.29), supporting ETI sensitivity. Off-label initiation of ETI led to substantial clinical improvement over 6 months: FEV₁ rose from 2.24L (75%) to 2.50L (84%), BMI from 21.9 to 22.7 kg/m², and exacerbations/hospitalizations fell to zero. Sweat chloride improved from 103 to 69 mmol/L. Sweat chloride concentration improved from 103 to 69 mmol/L.

Conclusion: PDRO-based precision medicine identified a misclassified class I mutation, 622-2A>C, and demonstrated in vitro and in vivo responsiveness to ETI. This case shows personalized in vitro CFTR functional testing can uncover unexpected modulator sensitivity in supposed Class I genotypes and reinforces the role of precision-medicine approaches in extending modulator access for patients with very rare CFTR variants.

[1] eClinicalMedicine. 2025 Aug 30;88:103476.

Study funded by KUL C2 grant (C24M/21/041)

records.abstract_text:
There is a relative paucity of research examining the impact of informal caregiving on parents of young children with cystic fibrosis (CF). The aim of this study was to examine caregiver burden and identify risk factors associated with high caregiver burden in parents of young children with CF using the CarerQol questionnaire.

This was a cross-sectional study. The CarerQoL questionnaire is a validated tool composed of two parts: (i) the CarerQol-7D which describes the care situation in terms of the negative and positive impact of caregiving and (ii) the visual analogue scale (VAS) which measures happiness on a scale from 0 (unhappy) -10 (happy). The utility score (US) is a weighted average of the subjective burden (0-100); higher US indicates reduced burden. Univariable and multivariable linear regression models were employed to examine the association between caregiver quality of life (US and VAS scores) and child-related variables including age, gender, genotype, modulator use, and presence of siblings.

258 parents of children with CF participated (response rate 72.3%). The mean age of child with CF at time of questionnaire completion was 7.79 years (SD 4.04 years); 50.4% were male. Most respondents (57.4%) reported experiencing a lot of fulfilment from care tasks, while only 3.9% reported none. 42.6% receiving a lot of support with care tasks, 43.4% receiving some, and 14% reporting none. Problems with mental health were common, with 52.9% experiencing some problems, and 9.3% reporting a lot. Higher scores were found in parents of children aged > 6 years. Parents of male children reporting significantly lower VAS scores compared with those of female children (adj coefficient -0.43; 95%CI -0.85 – - 0.01; p=0.041). No other significant findings were found.

Mental health is a concern in parents of children with CF. Parents of male children were found to have lower quality of life; this finding warrants further exploration.

records.title: Are people with cystic fibrosis, treated with modulator medicines ingesting too much salt, putting them at increased risk of hypertension? A retrospective population cohort study

session.title: ePoster Session 05 - Fuel, frame and function in cystic fibrosis nutrition

records.authors_text: H. Gledhill1, D.D Derry1, D.J Waine1
records.affiliations_text: 1University Hospital Plymouth NHS Trust, Plymouth, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: Historically, people with cystic fibrosis (CF) have been advised to consume a high-sodium diet to compensate for excessive sweat sodium losses caused by CFTR dysfunction. Highly effective CFTR modulator therapy improves CFTR function and reduces sweat sodium losses, potentially altering sodium balance. Persistently high sodium intake increases risk of hypertension, an emerging concern as the CF population ages.

Objective: To investigate whether adults with CF receiving CFTR modulator therapy exhibit high urinary sodium concentrations [uNa] as a proxy for high dietary sodium intake.

Method: Retrospective cohort study using routinely collected spot urinary sodium and sodium/creatinine concentrations. Analysed for patients receiving CFTR modulators and a contemporaneous control group not receiving modulators. Independent t-tests and Mann–Whitney U tests were used, with p<0.05 considered statistically significant.

Results: Sixty-one patients provided urinary samples; 53 were receiving CFTR modulator therapy and 8 formed the control group. Mean urinary sodium concentration was higher in the modulator group (81.2 mmol/L) than controls (67.6 mmol/L), though this difference was not statistically significant. Marked intra- and inter-individual variability was observed. The use of urinary sodium/creatinine ratios (to reduce impact of renal water reabsorption) did not significantly reduce variability; there was still no difference between groups. Patients in receipt of sodium supplementation did not have significantly higher urinary sodium concentrations. Nearly 70% of patients receiving modulators had mean urinary sodium concentrations >50 mmol/L.

Conclusions: Although no statistically significant difference in urinary sodium excretion was demonstrated between groups, many adults with CF receiving CFTR modulator therapy exhibit relatively high [uNa]. These findings raise questions regarding the appropriateness of longstanding high-sodium dietary recommendations in the CFTR modulator era. More robust prospective studies incorporating 24-hour urine collections, dietary assessment, and blood pressure monitoring are required to inform individualised sodium guidance and long-term cardiovascular risk management in CF.

records.affiliations_text: 1Hospital for Sick Children, Toronto, Canada, 2University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada
records.abstract_text:
Background: Pancreas disease is one of the first disease complication in Cystic Fibrosis (CF) reflected by high immunoreactive trypsin (IRT) at birth used as CF screening test. Although a postnatal decline in serum trypsin has previously been described, longitudinal trypsin trajectories across childhood have not been well characterized. We leveraged the longitudinal clinical data and serum trypsin measurements in the Toronto CF Database (TCF) to estimate trypsin trajectories and their association with clinical outcomes.

Method: Retrospective analysis with data from 1984 to 2017. Longitudinal trajectories of trypsin measured in serum as trypsinogen using a radioimmunoassay (RIA) were modeled using repeated-measures linear regression.

Results: Trypsin trajectories were estimated in 265 individuals with at least one measurement <1y and at least one >1y (15 CFSPID, 19 CFPS, and 227 CFPI). Estimated trypsin level at birth was significantly higher in CFPI than CFPS and CFSPID (p < 0.0001 for both comparisons), and higher in CFPS than CFSPID (p = 0.0003). Individuals with CFPI exhibited a steep decline in trypsin levels, crossing the threshold for pancreatic insufficiency by 4.2y. In contrast, CFPS and CFSPID demonstrated more gradual declines, with levels remaining within the pancreatic-sufficient range. The presence of meconium ileus was not associated with trypsin decline (p = 0.6), whereas the MIP score, a measure of CFTR variant severity, was associated with steeper declines (p = 0.011). Analyses assessing the predictive value of trypsin trajectories for clinical outcomes are ongoing.

Conclusions: Longitudinal trypsin decline differs markedly between mild and severe CF phenotypes and genotypes. With recent validation of IRT as a reliable surrogate for serum trypsin (Gummadi et al, 2025), this biomarker is widely accessible, but longitudinal reference ranges for IRT beyond the newborn period need to be established.

person.biography: Tanja Gonska started her academic career at the Hospital for Paediatics and Adolescent Medicine, University of Freiburg, Germany and continued by joining the Fellowship program at the Division of Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition at the Hospital for Sick Children. Appointed as SickKids staff in November 2010 she is now an Associate Professor in the Division of Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition and a Senior Associate to the SickKids Research institute. She is cross appointed at the Institute for Medical science, Department of Physiology, University of Toronto as well as St. Michael’s Hospital. Tanja is an enthusiastic paediatric clinician and teacher with a passion that lies within Cystic Fibrosis. As a translational researcher she is interested in understanding the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms that explain the clinical presentation of a very heterogeneous disease. One is to delineate the threshold of CFTR dysfunction leading to disease manifestation and the other is to evaluate the role of modifier genes function in CF pathogenesis. With her experience in the pulmonary and gastrointestinal aspects of CF disease as well as in functional studies of the CFTR protein, Tanja is ideally poised to conduct bench-bed bridging research to clinic and vice versa. As per her medical expertise, Dr. Gonska provides GI consultation to pediatric and adult patients with CF and runs a Pediatric Pancreas centre at the Hospital for Sick Children.

records.title: Formation and characterization of three-dimensional nasal epithelial cell cultures and in vitro growth kinetics assessed by live imaging

session.title: ePoster Session 04 - Models and mechanisms in CFTR biology

records.authors_text: B. Capraz Yavuz1, H. Yanık2, E. Yalçın1, G. Esendağlı2, U. Kavgaci1, N. Emiralioğlu1, D. Doğru1, U. Özçelik1
records.affiliations_text: 1Hacettepe University, Pediatric Pulmonology, Ankara, Turkey, 2Hacettepe University, Basic Oncology, Cancer Institute, Ankara, Turkey
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: Patient-specific three-dimensional (3D) nasal epithelial cell cultures have strong potential to improve diagnostic accuracy and support biomarker development and functional assays in translational research. These models bridge bench and bedside and enable functional investigation of respiratory diseases such as cystic fibrosis and primary ciliary dyskinesia through assessment of CFTR activity and ciliary function.

Methods: Human nasal epithelial cells obtained via the nasal brushing technique were used to generate three-dimensional spheroid cultures. The primary aim was to assess the feasibility of establishing 3D cultures, while the secondary aim was to investigate in vitro growth kinetics during spheroid formation using live imaging. Cells were embedded in 3D Matrigel to establish spheroid cultures1. Time-lapse images were acquired using an inverted microscope to analyze growth kinetics.

Results: The study population consisted of 7 children with cystic fibrosis (cwCF), 8 children with a preliminary diagnosis of primary ciliary dyskinesia (cwpdPCD), and 1 child with cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator–related disorder (cwCFTR-RD). After 7 and 14 days of culture, spheroid number and size were evaluated using microscopic imaging and morphological analysis. Spheroid formation was successfully achieved in all samples. Spheroids derived from cwpdPCD patients were generated in significantly higher numbers compared with those obtained from cwCF/cwCFTR-RD patients. Moreover, spheroids from cwpdPCD patients exhibited significantly larger diameters at both time points.

Conclusion: This study reports the first successful generation of three-dimensional airway epithelial models from pediatric nasal epithelial cells in Türkiye. These findings provide foundational evidence and represent a major step forward in advancing translational and personalized research in pulmonology nationwide.

records.title: Impact of modulators on colonising PA in patients with cystic fibrosis: phenotypic and genomic changes during adaptation

session.title: ePoster Session 01 -Targeting pseudomonas in cystic fibrosis: from mechanisms to new therapies

records.authors_text: S. Raimondi1, M. Rossitto2, G. Vrenna1, V. Fox2, V. Tuccio Guarna Assanti1, M. Cristiano1, N. Essa1, M.S. Lepanto1, E. Montemitro3, F. Alghisi3, F. Majo3, L. Cristiani3, A. Boni3, R. Cutrera3, I. Paris4, M. Trecca4, R. Papa4, M. Artini4, C.F. Perno1, P. Bernaschi1
records.affiliations_text: 1Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital, Microbiology and Diagnostic Immunology Unit, Rome, Italy, 2Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital, Multimodal Laboratory Medicine, Rome, Italy, 3Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital, Pneumology and Cystic Fibrosis Unit, Rome, Italy, 4Sapienza University of Rome, Department of Public Health and Infectious Diseases, Rome, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA) causes chronic lung infections in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). Small molecules known as modulators partially restore the defective protein causing CF. Despite several patients experience sputum load decreases and apparently resolve chronic bacterial infection, PA may persist through adaptation.

We investigated how PA adapts to the changed environment in pwCF during modulators therapy by integrating phenotypic and genomic data.

Methods: We investigated 563 PA strains isolated from 35 chronically colonised pwCF collected from a maximum of 15 years pre-treatment and up to 3 years post-treatment with elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor (ETI) or previous modulators. Phenotypic resistance and biofilm production under conditions mimicking the CF lung environment were confronted with Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS) data to elucidate changes under modulators' selective pressure.

Results: 31 out of 35 pwCF retained the same Sequence Type (ST) pre-ETI, despite 1 case of prolonged negativity; 9 acquired new STs (even High-Risk Clones) without loss and 4 had clone replacement. Changes observed under modulators involved loss of non-mucoid morphotype, biofilm hyperproduction (up to 18-fold), and changes in antibiotic resistance. Hypermutability appeared under 3 different modulators (8 cases, ETI included) but decreased only under ETI (4 cases). Evolution of colonising PA into novel STs was also observed under ETI. Indeed, in 3 pwCF, ST274 evolved in novel STs, with convergent evolution giving rise to the same novel ST in 2 of them.

Conclusions: Our data indicate variability in the response to modulators, which drive adaptation through phenotypic and genomic changes with ambivalent effects, requiring attention in terms of their clinical implications. Some STs demonstrate reduced persistence in the face of pressure exerted by modulators. This suggests that modulator therapy could have a greater impact on lung colonisation in certain pwCF.

session.title: ePoster Session 02 - Rare genotypes & challenging phenotypes

person.department: College of Medicine and Health, Department of Physiology

records.authors_text: L. Lonetti1, J.B. Murray1, J. Alves2,1,3, C. Black3, H. Morgan3, J. Brewington3, C.M. Lee4, P.T. Harrison3,1
records.affiliations_text: 1University College Cork, College of Medicine and Health, Department of Physiology, Cork, Ireland, 2BioISI-Biosystems and Integrative Sciences Institute, Faculty of Sciences, Universidade de Lisboa, Lisbon, Portugal, 3Cincinnati Children’s Hospital, Division of Pulmonary Medicine, Cincinnati, United States, 4University College Cork, School of Biochemistry and Cell Biology, Cork, Ireland
records.abstract_text:
With over 650 identified disease-causing CFTR variants, approximately 51% of people with Cystic Fibrosis carry a compound heterozygous (CH) genotype; among these, 82% harbour at least one F508del allele – representing around 68,000 people. Hence, it is central to therapeutic advancement to develop strategies that target compound heterozygotes, as correcting or functionally rescuing even one of their pathogenic alleles could shift an individual towards an improved phenotype.

As complex genotypes may necessitate distinct combinations of modulators or gene-editing approaches, a broader strategy that can be tailored to address the specific variants would expand therapeutic possibilities. Building on our previous plasmid-based studies, here we describe the application of an RNA-based delivery approach to correct exon 11 variants in patient-derived cells. Our strategy exploits a Cas9 nickase and two sgRNAs to trigger allele conversion at the mutation site availing of the respective wild type (WT) exon 11 sequence in the homologous chromosome as donor template. The correction is driven by an allele-specific sgRNA creating a nick only on the allele with the target mutation, and an allele-agnostic sgRNA creating a nick on both.

In our preliminary studies in CH patient-derived samples we observed a WT exon 11 increase of 0.92% for F508del CH cells and a 1.22% increase for I507del CH cells relative to the transfection control. This result is in line with what was achieved using the same F508-specific sgRNA combination in 16HBEge F508del/WT (+5.99% WT exon 11) and with a less efficient sgRNA combo in IB3-1/S9 F508del/W1282X cell lines (+0.47% WT exon 11).

Future studies will focus on improving efficiency, carrying out functional assays, and further exploring patient-derived CH samples.

With most variants being clustered in key regions of the CFTR gene, it is also imperative to investigate how nicking two mutations in close proximity affects the editing outcome.

records.title: Physical, mental health, and neurocognitive side-effects in adolescents and adults with cystic fibrosis taking elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor: A 24-month multidimensional assessment

session.title: ePoster Session 03 - From breakthrough to burdens: mental health in modern cystic fibrosis care

person.title: Dr.
person.department: Psychology Unit, Child & Adolescent Psychiatry Unit

records.authors_text: S. Graziano1, C. Di Savino1, A.L Quittner2, F. Alghisi3, L. Cristiani3, F. Majo3, S. Vicari1, R. Cutrera3, D. Menghini1
records.affiliations_text: 1Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital, IRCCS, Psychology Unit, Child & Adolescent Psychiatry Unit, Rome, Italy, 2Joe DiMaggio Hospital, Cystic Fibrosis, Pulmonary & Sleep Center, Hollywood, United States, 3Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital, IRCCS, Cystic Fibrosis and Pulmonology Unit, Rome, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Although clinical studies have reported positive effects of ETI in people with cystic fibrosis (PWCF), longitudinal data are limited. These results are part of an ongoing longitudinal study on the global effects of ETI in adolescents and adults.

Methods: PWCF aged ≥12 years eligible for ETI completed longitudinal assessments at baseline (T0), 1-mos (T1), 3-mos (T2), 6-mos (T3), 12-mos (T4), 18-mos (T5), 24-mos (T6) after ETI. Measures: a) physical parameters (FEV₁, BMI, GI Symptom Tracker); b) HRQoL (CFQ-R); c) depression (PHQ-9) & anxiety (GAD-7); d) cognitive processing (SDMT); e) ad hoc neurocognitive side-effects questionnaire.

Results: A total of 128 PWCF were recruited (F/M=67/61; M age=26.8 yr). FEV₁ increased at T1 and remained stable (T0<T1–T6; p<.001). BMI increased at 18-mos (p<.05). Improvements for GI symptoms: Abdominal (T0>T5; p<.05), Stools (T0>T4=T5; p<.005), Eating (T0>T1–T6; p<.001), Adherence (T0>T4–T6; p<.001). Improvements in HRQoL: Physical, Health, Respiratory and Role (T0<T1–T6; p<.001); Vitality (T0<T1–T4; p<.001); Emotional (T0<T4–T6; p<.05), Eating and Social (T0<T3–T6; p<.001); Treatment Burden (T0<T2=T4=T5=T6; p<.005), Body Image (T0<T4–T6; p<.001), Weight (T0<T1–T6; p<.001); Digestive (T0<T4=T6; p<.001). Treatment Burden remained low (range 54–66). Depression improved (T0>T2–T5; p<.05), anxiety was higher in females (p<.05). Cognitive processing improved at T1 and T2 (p<.001) and was positively correlated with FEV₁ (p<.05). Neurocognitive effects: insomnia (13–34%), headaches (32–39%), memory problems (18–34%), concentration problems (15–38%), brain fog (7–14%). Worsening trends were observed for insomnia (T1<T5=T6; p<.001; F>M, p<.05), memory and concentration problems (T1<T5=T6; p<.005 - T1<T2–T6; p<.001; M>F, p<.001).

Conclusions: Overall, ETI was associated with significant improvements across multiple physical and mental health domains, while neurocognitive side effects persisted, particularly in females. An improvement in GI symptoms was observed after 12 months.

Objectives: Although clinical studies have reported positive effects of ETI in people with cystic fibrosis (PWCF), longitudinal data are limited. These results are part of an ongoing longitudinal study on the global effects of ETI in adolescents and adults.
Methods: PWCF aged ≥12 years eligible for ETI completed longitudinal assessments at baseline (T0), 1-mos (T1), 3-mos (T2), 6-mos (T3), 12-mos (T4), 18-mos (T5), 24-mos (T6) after ETI. Measures: a) physical parameters (FEV₁, BMI, GI Symptom Tracker); b) HRQoL (CFQ-R); c) depression (PHQ-9) & anxiety (GAD-7); d) cognitive processing (SDMT); e) ad hoc neurocognitive side-effects questionnaire.
Results: A total of 128 PWCF were recruited (F/M=67/61; M age=26.8 yr). FEV₁ increased at T1 and remained stable (T0<T1–T6; p<.001). BMI increased at 18-mos (p<.05). Improvements for GI symptoms: Abdominal (T0>T5; p<.05), Stools (T0>T4=T5; p<.005), Eating (T0>T1–T6; p<.001), Adherence (T0>T4–T6; p<.001). Improvements in HRQoL: Physical, Health, Respiratory and Role (T0<T1–T6; p<.001); Vitality (T0<T1–T4; p<.001); Emotional (T0<T4–T6; p<.05), Eating and Social (T0<T3–T6; p<.001); Treatment Burden (T0<T2=T4=T5=T6; p<.005), Body Image (T0<T4–T6; p<.001), Weight (T0<T1–T6; p<.001); Digestive (T0<T4=T6; p<.001). Treatment Burden remained low (range 54–66). Depression improved (T0>T2–T5; p<.05), anxiety was higher in females (p<.05). Cognitive processing improved at T1 and T2 (p<.001) and was positively correlated with FEV₁ (p<.05). Neurocognitive effects: insomnia (13–34%), headaches (32–39%), memory problems (18–34%), concentration problems (15–38%), brain fog (7–14%). Worsening trends were observed for insomnia (T1<T5=T6; p<.001; F>M, p<.05), memory and concentration problems (T1<T5=T6; p<.005 - T1<T2–T6; p<.001; M>F, p<.001).

records.title: Salt intake in cystic fibrosis under highly effective modulator therapy (HEMT): toward an individualized approach

session.title: ePoster Session 05 - Fuel, frame and function in cystic fibrosis nutrition

records.authors_text: H. Attew1, A. Coudrat1, R. Theiler1, M. Argenson1, D. Trioleyre1, J. Genuardi1, J. Tenenbaum2, S. Ramirez1, E. Lamour1, F. Socchi1, R. Chiron1,3
records.affiliations_text: 1CHU de Montpellier, CRCM/Hopital Arnaud de Villeneuve, Montpellier, France, 2CHU de Montpellier, Pédiatrie Spécialisée / Hopital Arnaud de Villeneuve, Montpellier, France, 3Université de Montpellier, HydroSciences Montpellier, CNRS, IRD, Montpellier, France
records.abstract_text:
Optimizing sodium intake in patients with CF (pwCF) under high effective modulator therapy (HEMT) remains challenging. While some suggest requirements match those of the general population. We explored an individualized approach to salt management.

Methods: We performed a retrospective, single-center analysis at the adult and pediatric Montpellier CF Center. Salt requirements were assessed under standardized conditions by comparing patients’ salt intake with French High Authority for Health recommendations and urinary Na/K ratio (A urinary Na/K ratio < 1 may indicate insufficient sodium intake, particularly under high salt loss conditions such as heat or exercise). Analyses were conducted in winter and repeated in summer, incorporating ambient temperature and physical activity data.

Results: In winter, only 0.9% of 112 adults required additional salt at breakfast beyond recommended intakes. Breakfasts were generally low in sodium, with 67% below recommendations, and 6.2% showed a urinary Na/K ratio <1. Among 61 pediatric patients, 21.3% needed salt supplementation despite sodium intakes exceeding age-specific recommendations.

In summer (ambient temperature >30 °C), 47 usable urinary analyses (22 children, 3 adults) revealed that 87% consumed more than 150% of the recommended salt intake. Nevertheless, 21% had a urinary Na/K ratio <1, mainly associated with intense physical activity.

Conclusion: Despite HEMT, certain pwCF continue to require sodium supplementation beyond standard population guidelines. Routine ionogram monitoring can help prevent both hypernatremia and hyponatremia. Sodium management should remain. individualized, with heightened vigilance in pediatric patients—even during winter—and should incorporate age, environmental conditions, physical activity level, urinary Na/K ratio, and baseline dietary intake.

records.title: Cystic fibrosis related diabetes has a distinct gut microbiome dysbiosis

session.title: ePoster Session 06 - Gastrointestinal and hepatic trajectories in cystic fibrosis from early life to adulthood

records.authors_text: R. Marsh1, D. Sills2, H.A Saumtally3,4, J.M Tricker1, W. Cheung1, D. Arends1, A. Párniczky5,6,7, K. Ocskay5,6, D. Peckham3,4, R.C Spiller2,8, L. Marciani2, D.G Downey9, I.D Stewart10, T.M Monaghan2,8, A.R Smyth9,8, D.W Rivett11, C. van der Gast1
records.affiliations_text: 1Northumbria University, Newcastle, United Kingdom, 2University of Nottingham, Nottingham, United Kingdom, 3University of Leeds, Leeds, United Kingdom, 4Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust, Leeds, United Kingdom, 5Heim Pál Children's Hospital, Budapest, Hungary, 6Semmelweis University, Budapest, Hungary, 7University of Pécs, Pécs, Hungary, 8NIHR Nottingham Biomedical Research Centre, Nottingham, United Kingdom, 9Queen’s University Belfast, Belfast, United Kingdom, 10Imperial College London, London, United Kingdom, 11Manchester Metropolitan University, Manchester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Gut microbiome dysbiosis is common across people with CF (pwCF) and may be further exacerbated with additional GI co-abnormalities. CF-related diabetes (CFRD) is a prominent comorbidity in pwCF, yet its impact upon the gut microbiome is not known. We investigated the gut microbiota, metabolome, and lipidome across pwCF with/without CFRD and control participants.

Methods: Stool samples from pwCF with (n=33) and without (n=33) CFRD, alongside controls (n=19), were subjected to full-length 16S rRNA microbiota sequencing. LC/MS analyses (n=57) were conducted on CF stool samples to investigate differences in metabolite and lipid composition. Multivariate approaches and generalised linear models were used to investigate relationships with clinical data.

Results: Microbiota diversity and composition significantly differed between controls and pwCF, including across CF groups (q<0.05). A higher prevalence of gut pathobionts, alongside reduced prevalence of beneficial taxa was observed in CFRD. Strikingly, an increased prevalence of lung pathogens (including Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus) was also observed in CFRD. Additional clinical factors significantly explained microbiota variation. Modulator therapy was not significant. Importantly, after adjusting for such confounders, CFRD remained a significant driver of microbiota composition across pwCF (q=0.024). Lipidomic profiles also significantly clustered based on the presence of CFRD following covariate adjustment (q=0.030). Immunomodulatory lipid species, including increased hexosylceramides (q=0.030) and oxidised phosphatidylcholines (q=0.073), alongside decreased sulphonolipids (q=0.054), were observed across the CFRD group.

Conclusions: We demonstrate for the first time a distinct and worse microbiome dysbiosis in CFRD. The causative nature and clinical consequences of such host-microbe alterations warrant additional research of the CF gut utilising multiomics approaches.

session.title: ePoster Session 04 - Models and mechanisms in CFTR biology

person.department: Département de Médecine, Université de Montréal (UdeM)

records.authors_text: E. Brochiero1, S. Moustadraf1, N. Labonté1, T. Voisin1, C. Landry1, D. Adam1
records.affiliations_text: 1Centre hospitalier de l’Université de Montréal (CRCHUM), Département de Médecine, Université de Montréal (UdeM), Montréal, Canada
records.abstract_text:
Background and objectives: Widely used cystic fibrosis (CF) in vitro models, including cell lines, primary airway epithelial cultures and organoids are essential for testing CFTR modulators (CFTRm), but fail to capture the complexity of native lung tissue. Precision-cut lung slices (PCLS) from healthy or explanted CF lungs retain three-dimensional architecture and cellular diversity, providing a highly relevant ex vivo translational system. Our aim was to develop and validate an optimized human PCLS protocol supporting prolonged tissue viability, preservation of key structural and functional features, and reproducible response to infectious, inflammatory and pharmacological stimuli.

Methods and results: Tissue handling, agarose infusion, Compresstome slicing and cultures conditions were optimized to minimize tissue injury and maximize serial slice yield. Model performance was assessed in fresh and cryopreserved PCLS through viability, cellular composition and functional readouts following exposure to bacterial virulence factors, bronchoalveolar lavages from infected patients and clinically relevant CFTRm.

The optimized workflow generates hundreds of serial slices within 1-2 working days and supports both fresh use or cryostorage. PCLS sustained native multicellular organization and ciliary activity, and remained viable for up to 35 days, enabling longitudinal studies. The model allows standardized infectious/inflammatory challenges and CFTRm treatments, with multimodal readouts including tissue integrity, cytokine production and CFTR rescue.

Conclusion: This human PCLS model preserves the native lung microenvironment for extended ex vivo studies and represents a versatile preclinical tool to examine host-pathogen interaction, inflammatory mechanisms, and inter-individual variability in responses to CFTRm.

Funding: CIHR, AIRS Network

person.biography:
Emmanuelle Brochiero is a Professor in the department of Medicine of the Université de Montréal and researcher at the Centre de Recherche du CHUM (CRCHUM).
Her research focuses on the pathophysiology of lung diseases, especially cystic fibrosis, acute respiratory distress syndrome and primary graft dysfunction after lung transplantation. Her lab has pioneered ion channel-based therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring functional epithelial integrity in damaged lungs, using complementary state-of-the-art approaches, rare human samples, animal models and innovative preclinical models. The main goal of her projects in cystic fibrosis is to develop innovative therapeutic strategies for improvement of CFTR-targeted treatments and restoration of airway epithelial integrity in infected lungs from patients carrying various types of mutations.
Over the past years, Dr. Brochiero has been supported by research grants including from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR), the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC), the Respiratory Health Network of Québec, the Canadian National Transplant Research Program, and the Association Vaincre le Mucoviscidose.
She is the Director of the Respiratory Tissue and Cell Biobank of CRCHUM. Based on her expertise, she has also been invited to chair the Advisory and Scientific Committee of the Respiratory Health Research Network (RHN) of Québec as well as the CF Strategic Group, and then the research axis on pulmonary infections and pathogens of RHN. She also led the Immunopathology research theme of the CRCHUM over the past five years.

records.title: Discriminating old from new: application of Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR) to the reappearance of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in patients with cystic fibrosis

session.title: ePoster Session 01 -Targeting pseudomonas in cystic fibrosis: from mechanisms to new therapies

records.authors_text: M. Cristiano1, S. Raimondi1, M. Rossitto2, G. Vrenna1, V. Fox2, V. Tuccio Guarna Assanti1, N. Essa1, M.S. Lepanto1, E. Montemitro3, F. Alghisi3, F. Majo3, L. Cristiani3, A. Boni3, R. Cutrera3, C.F. Perno1, P. Bernaschi1
records.affiliations_text: 1Bambino Gesù Children's Hospital, Microbiology and Diagnostic Immunology Unit, Rome, Italy, 2Bambino Gesù Children's Hospital, Multimodal Laboratory Medicine, Rome, Italy, 3Bambino Gesù Children's Hospital, Pneumology and Cystic Fibrosis Unit, Rome, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA) is a key pathogen in cystic fibrosis (CF), linked to high morbidity and mortality. Early antibiotic therapy may eradicate new PA, but if it reappears, eradication may not have happened. Distinguishing between strain persistence and new acquisition is crucial for guiding treatment strategies to prevent chronicity. This is also important for CF patients on elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI), re-presenting PA after negativity.

Using Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR), we aimed to assess the clonality of PA strains, focusing on isolates responsible for 1st and 2nd infections, intermittent colonisation and re-emergence on ETI.

Methods: A total of 103 PA isolates causing infection in 36 people with CF (pwCF) were compared by FTIR with post-treatment isolates. Two were chronically colonized and 2 intermittently colonised; 12 had a history of chronic colonization followed by PA negativity after starting modulator treatment; and 20 had received eradication therapy for a first PA infection, in 10 cases either before or after initiating modulators. Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS) was used to validate FTIR results.

Results: FTIR and WGS revealed same-strain persistence in 24 patients, confirming a 100% predictive value for FTIR. Persistence occurred in intermittently and chronically colonised pwCF: 9 on modulators and 11 underwent eradication therapy (6 on modulators). WGS identified 3 FTIR misclassifications (3 pairs of isolates deemed as different), due to phenotypic differences and spectral variability among PA isolates. Significant temporal overlap between new infections and failed eradications demonstrates timing’s unreliability as sole differentiator.

Conclusions: FTIR is an easily implementable diagnostic tool that can define the success of eradicating therapy and optimise therapy. Our study proves its ability to inform appropriate therapeutic decisions for pwCF with recurrent PA infections.

records.title: Closing the screening gap: development of a novel pathway to identify and monitor infants exposed to elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor in British Columbia, Canada

session.title: ePoster Session 02 - Rare genotypes & challenging phenotypes

records.authors_text: C. Blanchette1, A. De Leon1, K. Bunyan2, M.A. Chilvers3
records.affiliations_text: 1BC Children's Hospital, Cystic Fibrosis Newborn Screening Program, Vancouver, Canada, 2Cystic Fibrosis Care BC, Vancouver, Canada, 3BC Children's Hospital, Cystic Fibrosis Clinic, Vancouver, Canada
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: People with Cystic Fibrosis (CF) are achieving successful pregnancies with CF transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) modulator therapy; predominantly elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI). Evidence suggests that exposure to ETI in utero or by breastmilk may partially restore CFTR function in the CF fetus, which can lead to falsely low immunoreactive trypsinogen (IRT) levels. Infants exposed to ETI may be at risk for falsely negative screens with British Columbia's (BC) IRT-DNA-IRT CF newborn screening (NBS) model. As part of a quality improvement initiative, a pathway to identify infants at risk and to monitor those with ETI exposure was developed.

Methods: A working group of registered nurses (RNs), physicians and geneticists developed a process to identify ETI-exposed pregnancies and ensure CF Canada monitoring guidelines were met. An automated alert was integrated into the BC CF registry in October 2025. At any BC CF clinic, new pregnancies recorded in the electronic medical record trigger an email to notify the RNs, linking to a secure dashboard with patient information. RNs then request CFTR genotyping on the infants, regardless of IRT level. RNs coordinate counseling with the families and set up monitoring of liver function tests and an eye exam.

Results: In BC, 26 ETI-exposed infants were born from 2016-2025. Prior to pathway implementation, 50% of these infants had no CFTR genotyping on NBS; 46% had no monitoring. Since implementation, three pregnancies triggered the pathway and 100% of infants have had CFTR genotyping on NBS and completed monitoring. Families reported appreciation for proactive communication and clear guidance.

Conclusion: An automated pregnancy alert is critical to reduce missed ETI-exposed infants. This initiative strengthened communication within the NBS program and leveraged the provincial registry to reduce operational burden. Collaboration with other Canadian CF clinics to create a national pathway is underway.

records.title: Coping and post-traumatic growth of fathers of children and adolescents with cystic fibrosis

session.title: ePoster Session 03 - From breakthrough to burdens: mental health in modern cystic fibrosis care

records.authors_text: R. Zubrzycka1, P. Wójtowicz2
records.affiliations_text: 1The Maria Curie-Sklodowska University, Institute of Pedagogy, Lublin, Poland, 2MATIO Fundacja Pomocy Rodzinom i Chorym na Mukowiscydozę, Kraków, Poland
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The aim of the study was to examine the relationship between stress coping and post-traumatic growth (PTG) in fathers of children with cystic fibrosis (CF).

Methods: The sample consisted of 67 fathers of children and adolescents with cystic fibrosis (average age 37.25 years, SD = 6.50) recruited from the CF Foundation MATIO in Poland. The COPE inventory for Measuring Coping with Stress by Ch. S. Carver, in the Polish adaptation by Juczyński and Ogińska-Bulik (2009) and The Post-traumatic Growth Inventory (PTGI) by Tedeschi and Calhoun, adapted into Polish by Ogińska-Bulik and Juczyński (2010) were used.

Results: The most frequent coping strategies used by fathers of children and adolescents with CF were: Planning, Active coping, and Positive Reinterpretation and Growth. More than 55 % of the examined fathers demonstrated average or high levels of PTG. Coping strategies were found to be correlated with the PTGI total score and all its dimensions. The strategies significantly associated with PTG included: Restrained coping, Focus on and Venting of Emotions, Behavioral Disengagement, Alcohol/substance use, Humour, Seeking Emotional Social Support, Religion, and Acceptance - most of which are classified as emotion-focused ones. Positive correlations were observed for strategies such as: Seeking Instrumental Social Support, Seeking Emotional Social Support, and Religion.

Conclusion: The results of the study may constitute a basis for defining the scope of psychosocial support addressed to fathers of children and adolescents with CF and may inspire further research into correlates of the post-traumatic growth and other positively oriented variables in the studied population.

records.title: Does bone mineral density influence bone health perceptions in adults with cystic fibrosis? Identifying knowledge gaps to inform education

session.title: ePoster Session 05 - Fuel, frame and function in cystic fibrosis nutrition

person.institution: University Hospital Llandough, Cardiff and Vale NHS University Hospital Board
person.department: All Wales Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre

records.authors_text: L. Jones1, C. Knorz1, H. Carter1, J. Duckers1, L. Speight1, D. Proud1
records.affiliations_text: 1University Hospital Llandough, Cardiff and Vale NHS Trust, All Wales Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Cardiff, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: People with Cystic Fibrosis(pwCF) are at risk of low Bone Mineral Density(BMD) and monitoring by Dual Energy Xray Absorptiometry(DXA) is recommended. However DXA attendance is suboptimal at our adult centre. Nutrition and bone health related insight in pwCF is unclear, therefore our aim was to assess knowledge enabling bespoke educational resources development promoting bone health.

Methods: A questionnaire was distributed in clinic from June 2024 to February 2025, consisting of 9 multiple choice or likert scale questions on bone health monitoring and related nutrition topics. ‘Importance’ and ‘personal concern’ rankings were scored 1 to 10(1 being not important, 10 most important). PwCF were divided into BMD group based on most recent DXA reports.

Results: 113 pwCF, 58 men(51%), mean age 33.5yrs, 93(82%) pancreatic insufficient, 52(46%) DF508 homozygous completed the questionnaire.

87(77%) correctly identified that DXA assesses BMD. Table 1 shows the breakdown by BMD group.

Table 1:PwCF perceived importance and concern

BMD Group Total Identified DXA assesses BMD Mean importance score for DXA (out of 10) Mean personal concern score for bone health (out of 10)Normal BMD68 (60%)50 (74%)6.864.1Osteopenia34 (30%)29 (85%)6.974.76Osteoporotic11 (10%)8 (73%)7.26.36

Bone important nutrients identified included vitamin D(n=84) and protein(n=39) whilst 36 identified vitamin K. Dairy foods were identified most as calcium rich foods(milk n=106, yoghurt n=98, cheese n=96), whilst 27 chose fortified milk alternatives.

59 responders declined additional resources, whilst 24 requested more information on ‘lifestyle and bone health’ and ‘what DXA looks at’. Email was preferred to receive resources(n=71).

Conclusion: Results identified positive correlations between importance of monitoring, personal concern and pwCF with worsening BMD. Gaps in bone health knowledge appear to exist and addressing these are crucial with an ageing CF population. Therefore, bespoke resources have been developed and are available for our patients.

records.title: Reduction of abdominal symptom burden in preschool children with cystic fibrosis receiving elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor: real-world results using the CFAbd-Score.kid©

session.title: ePoster Session 06 - Gastrointestinal and hepatic trajectories in cystic fibrosis from early life to adulthood

records.authors_text: P. Sadrieh1,2, V. Greiner1,2, L. Naehrlich3, O. Eickmeier4, S. van Dullemen4, U. Graepler-Mainka5, F. Duckstein1,2, M. vom Hove6, F. Prenzel6, C. Zagoya1,2, J.G Mainz1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Brandenburg University Hospital, CF-Center Westbrandenburg, Brandenburg an der Havel, Germany, 2Brandenburg Medical School (MHB), Brandenburg an der Havel, Germany, 3Justus-Liebig-University, Department of Pediatrics, Giessen, Germany, 4Goethe University, Division of Allergy, Pulmonology and Cystic Fibrosis, Department for Children and Adolescents, Frankfurt am Main, Germany, 5Eberhard-Karls-University, Children's Hospital, Tuebingen, Germany, 6Leipzig University Medical Center, Hospital for Children and Adolescents, Leipzig, Germany
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) has been shown to significantly and clinically relevantly reduce abdominal symptoms (AS) in people with Cystic Fibrosis (CF) aged ≥6 years using the CFAbd-Score© and CFAbd-Score.kid©, respectively. In November 2023, ETI was approved for pre-school children with CF (cwCF), aged 2 to 5 years. This study aimed to capture changes in the burden of AS in cwCF aged 2–5 years during therapy with ETI.

Methods: In this multicentric study, proxies of cwCF aged 2–5 years who received a new ETI-therapy completed the CFAbd-Score.kid© before and during therapy, on behalf and with active involvement of cwCF.

The CFAbd-Score.kid© is a patient-reported outcome measure specifically designed for cwCF aged <12 years. It includes CF-specific gastrointestinal (GI) items, such as the Bristol stool scale and a stool colour chart. Pictograms, plain language, and child-friendly response strategies are implemented. The scoring algorithm, developed according to FDA guidelines, weights items and domains differently, reaching a maximum of 100 points.

Results: A total of n=53 cwCF (n=27 female), with a median age of three years, were recruited in five German CF centres. They completed a total of n=191 questionnaires, according to a median of three questionnaires per participant over the entire observation period. The mean total CFAbd-Score.kid© declined significantly (-15.51%/p<0.05) during ETI therapy, as well as the "disorders of bowel movement" domain (-23.64%, p≤0.01). The other domains revealed positive trends without reaching significance, which we attribute to limitations in by-proxy rating of some AS.

Conclusion: As one of the first real-world studies to examine the effects of ETI on GI symptoms of pre-school children, this study also reveals the effectiveness of ETI for preschool-children. As with schoolchildren and adults, ETI significantly reduces the burden of AS in children aged 2 to 5 years, when the CFAbd-Score© is applied by-proxy.

The other domains revealed positive trends without reaching significance, which we attribute to limitations in by-proxy rating of some AS.
Conclusion: As one of the first real-world studies to examine the effects of ETI on GI symptoms of pre-school children, this study also reveals the effectiveness of ETI for preschool-children. As with schoolchildren and adults, ETI significantly reduces the burden of AS in children aged 2 to 5 years, when the CFAbd-Score© is applied by-proxy.

records.title: A new in vivo model to assess bacterial persistence and host inflammation upon mono- or co-infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates from cystic fibrosis patients

records.authors_text: F. Costes1, F. Nilly1, K. Moreau2, A.-B. Blanc-Potard1
records.affiliations_text: 1Laboratory of Pathogens and Host Immunity (LPHI), Montpellier, France, 2Centre International de Recherche en Infectiologie (CIRI), Lyon, France
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: P. aeruginosa is a major pathogen in cystic fibrosis (CF) patients, causing chronic lung infections associated with strong inflammation. In chronically infected patients, persistent P. aeruginosa form biofilm, which confers protection against host immunity and antibiotics, making infections refractory to treatments. In addition, co-infections with S. aureus are commonly observed in CF patients. To better control chronic infections, we developed a model in zebrafish embryo to study in vivo the bacterial persistence of clinical CF isolates in the context of mono or co-infections.

This work aims to characterize the host inflammatory response associated with persistent bacteria in the context of mono- or co-infections and to determine the localization of persistent bacteria in vivo, assessing whether they adopt a biofilm-like state.

Methods: Zebrafish embryos were infected using a wound infection method with CF isolates. Various fluorescent tools were used: il1b:GFP fish line to assess the inflammatory response, mfap4:mCherry fish line to assess the intra-macrophagic localization of bacteria by confocal microscopy, and a fluorescent biofilm reporter to assess a biofilm-like state of bacteria.

Results: We observed a strong il-1b response during persistent infection by P. aeruginosa CF isolates, which can be modulated in the context of co-infection with S. aureus (Costes et al., 2025). Persistent bacteria were visualized as intra-macrophagic clusters. Preliminary results showed the activation of a biofilm reporter for persistent P. aeruginosa.

Conclusion: The zebrafish embryo is a relevant and powerful in vivo model to study P. aeruginosa persistence in mono- and co-infection. Notably, we have translated main parts of our findings in mammalian models. The visualization of intracellular, biofilm-like bacterial aggregates, associated with a pro-inflammatory response paves the way to identify and test therapeutic strategies efficient against chronic infections.

records.affiliations_text: 1Northwestern University McCormick School of Engineering, Querrey Simpson Institute for Bioelectronics, Evanston, United States, 2Epicore Biosystems, Inc, Cambridge, United States, 3Stanley Manne Children's Research Institute, Ann & Robert H. Lurie Children's Hospital of Chicago, Interdisciplinary Partnerships, Pediatric Pulmonary and Sleep Medicine, Chicago, United States, 4Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, Medicine, Chicago, United States, 5Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, Pediatrics, Chicago, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Quantitative pilocarpine iontophoresis sweat testing is essential for diagnosis of cystic fibrosis (CF), but requires specialised equipment and technical proficiency, limiting widespread availability and contributing to diagnostic delays, especially in less resourced areas or countries.

Methods: We developed and tested a system of two sticker-like flexible, silicone-encased patches, measuring 6.0 × 2.8 × 0.75 cm. The stimulator patch uses a button battery and a pilocarpine hydrogel to induce sweat. The analyser patch uses microfluidic channels, reservoirs, and chemical reagents to enable colourimetric measurement of sweat chloride concentration. Colourimetric analysis is performed via an application on an iOS device. We compared sweat chloride concentrations between this system and the standard of care Macroduct™ system in children and young adults with CF or who were CF Screen Positive, Inconclusive Diagnosis (CFSPID), and in healthy adults.

Results: Of 55 participants, 42 had CF (20 on modulators), 10 CFSPID, and 3 were healthy controls. Demographics were representative of the CF population seen at our Centre's pediatric program (Table 1). There were no quantity not sufficient tests. Sweat chloride ranges were consistent with clinical categorisation. Macroduct™ and colourimetric mean differences were small (Table 2). There was strong correlation between system sweat chloride values (Pearson's r = 0.98, R2 = 0.96). Comparisons between systems were similar to those from previously published comparing right vs. left arm Macroduct values¹ (data not shown). Participant/guardian acceptability was high (data not shown).

Conclusion: Our flexible microfluidic sweat chloride system shows high correlation with the standard of care system and strong potential for use in diagnosis of and pharmacodynamic studies in CF. Inclusion of more infants in future studies is essential for further development.

Reference:

records.title: Gender inequality in caregiver attendance for children with cystic fibrosis: exploring contributing factors

session.title: ePoster Session 03 - From breakthrough to burdens: mental health in modern cystic fibrosis care

records.authors_text: V. Mellqvist1, J. Michelsen2, H. Imberg2, M. Svedberg3
records.affiliations_text: 1Queen Silvia´s childrens´hospital, Cystic fibrosis, Gothenburg, Sweden, 2Institution of Molecular and clinical Medicine, Gothenburg, Sweden, 3Department of Paediatrics, Queen Silvia´s childrens´hospital, Gothenburg, Sweden
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: In pediatric cystic fibrosis (CF) care, Swedish registry data show that mothers attend medical visits more frequently than fathers, with no indication of a narrowing gap. This study quantified gender differences in caregiver attendance and explored factors influencing parental participation.

Methods: We performed a study combining survey and registry data from parents of children with CF with scheduled medical visits in 2023 at the pediatric CF centers in Gothenburg and Lund. Both mothers and fathers were invited. A Theory of Planned Behavior–based questionnaire assessed attitude, subjective norm, and perceived control related to attendance (1–10 scale). Attendance at inpatient, physical outpatient, and digital visits was analyzed using factor analysis and multilevel modelling.

Results: Of 140 eligible parents, 123 completed the survey; 65 (53%) were mothers. In 2023, mothers attended in-person visits in 76% (95% CI 71 to 81%) of cases compared with 56% (95% CI 51 to 61%) for fathers (difference 20%-points; 95% CI 13 to 27; p<0.0001). For digital visits, attendance was 80% (95% CI 72 to 89%) for mothers and 51% (95% CI 41 to 61%) for fathers (difference 29 %-points; p=0.0002). A one-unit increase in attitude score was associated with 13% higher attendance among fathers (95% CI 7 to 20%; p<0.001) but not among mothers (−2%; 95% CI −12 to 9%; p=0.77). Higher subjective norm scores were associated with lower attendance among fathers (−7%; 95% CI −7 to −7%; p<0.001) and mothers (−8%; 95% CI −12 to −4%; p<0.001). Higher perceived control was associated with increased attendance among fathers (16%; 95% CI −1–32%; p=0.058) and mothers (8%; 95% CI 1–14%; p=0.019).

Conclusion: Marked gender inequality persists in caregiver attendance for children with CF. Fathers’ attendance seems more strongly influenced by attitudinal and perceived control factors, indicating that targeted interventions addressing these factors may promote more equitable parental participation.

records.title: CFTR dysfunction and epithelial plasticity in patient-derived intestinal organoids

session.title: ePoster Session 04 - Models and mechanisms in CFTR biology

person.title: PhD Student
person.institution: BioISI—Biosystems & Integrative Sciences Institute, Faculty of Sciences, University of Lisboa

records.authors_text: C.S. Rodrigues1, I. Pankonien1, M.S. Fragoso1, M.D. Amaral1
records.affiliations_text: 1BioISI—Biosystems & Integrative Sciences Institute, Faculty of Sciences, University of Lisboa, Lisboa, Portugal
records.abstract_text:
Background: Emerging studies indicate that people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) have a substantially increased risk (~5-fold) of colorectal cancer (CRC) compared with the general population. Additionally, loss of CFTR function has been shown to promote partial epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), a cellular program that may contribute to cancer progression.

Objective: To elucidate how loss of CFTR impacts epithelial differentiation and promotes EMT and cancer-associated processes.

Methods: Intestinal organoids (IOs) generated from healthy and CF donors were analysed for epithelial and mesenchymal markers and cell-type composition by immunofluorescence and Western blot. CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing is used to introduce p.Phe508del and p.Gly551Asp in homozygosity in non-CF IOs to generate two novel isogenic IO lines.

Results: Both CF and non-CF IOs differentiated into specific cell types, such as, goblet and enteroendocrine cells. Interestingly, the expression of the epithelial marker CK-18 was found to be reduced in CF vs non-CF, whereas expression of the stemness marker LGR5 was increased in CF IOs. Gene edited IOs are currently under clonal selection and will be used to investigate the direct effect of these CFTR variants on intestinal epithelial differentiation and EMT.

Conclusion: Results indicate that defective CFTR alters epithelial differentiation, reflected by reduced CK-18 expression in CF IOs. The novel isogenic IO lines provide a unique platform to study the direct role of CFTR on cancer-related processes.

session.title: ePoster Session 05 - Fuel, frame and function in cystic fibrosis nutrition

records.authors_text: I. Gönczi1, K. Bocskai2, J. Csepiova1, M. Imrei1, K. Ocskay1, A. Párniczky1
records.affiliations_text: 1Heim Pál National Pediatric Institute, Budapest, Hungary, 2Institute of Laboratory Medicine, Semmelweis University, Budapest, Hungary
records.abstract_text:
Background: People with cystic fibrosis (CF) often require supplementation of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E) due to malabsorption. CFTR modulators (CFTRm), particularly elaxacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI), may alter vitamin absorption and metabolism by correcting the underlying CFTR defect.

Aim: To evaluate changes in vitamin D, A and E levels among children with CF treated with CFTRm.

Methods: Single-centre prospective registry data were analysed. Vitamin concentrations were measured at the start of CFTRm therapy (Vitamin D only) and annually thereafter. Pancreas exocrine status was assed using faecal elastase levels.

Results: Vitamin D levels were measured in 76 children with a median follow-up of 3 years (IQR: 2–3.9). Levels declined slightly during follow-up, from 30.4 ng/mL (IQR: 25.8–38.3) to 29.2 ng/mL (IQR: 22.5–35.5) (p=0.030), and the proportion of children with insufficient vitamin D levels increased from 9% to 18%. Participants who showed improvement in pancreatic exocrine function (n=9) had sufficient or elevated vitamin D levels at baseline (8 vs 1) and maintained normal levels during therapy.

Vitamin A and E levels were measured in 42 children after 12–48 months of CFTR modulator therapy. The median vitamin E and A levels were 1.6 mmol/L (IQR: 1.1-1.9) and 18 mmol/L (IQR: 13-24.9), respectively. Most patients had levels within the normal range (vitamin E: 21 [50%], vitamin A: 22 [52%]). Both insufficient (vitamin E: 7 [17%], vitamin A: 6 [14%]) and elevated levels (vitamin E: 14 [33%], vitamin A: 14 [33%]) were observed, but no symptomatic hypervitaminosis occurred.

Conclusion: Regular assessment of fat-soluble vitamin levels is necessary during CFTR modulator therapy to ensure adequate vitamin status while avoiding hypervitaminosis.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: People with cystic fibrosis have an increased risk and earlier onset of colorectal cancer (CRC). Despite CF-specific screening guidelines published in 2018, real-world outcomes are poorly characterised. We aimed to describe colonoscopy completion, pathology detection, repeat colonoscopy and bowel preparation quality.

Methods: A multi-centre retrospective cohort study was conducted across three CF centers (2014–2024). Outcomes included referral-to-procedure completion, pathology (adenoma(s) or ileocolonic malignancy) and bowel preparation quality. Yield was assessed at the patient level (first colonoscopy) and procedure level (all colonoscopies). Guideline yield was assessed on current criteria: aged ≥40 years or ≥30 years and post-solid organ transplant at procedure.

Results: Among 284 referred, 242 (85.2%) completed at least one colonoscopy, 42 (14.8%) did not proceed. At first colonoscopy (n=242), median age 39.9 years [IQR 33.2-46.5], 124 (51.2%) male, 46 (19.0%) post-transplant, adenomas were detected in 30.6% (74/242), and colorectal malignancy in 1.7% (4/242).

Across all 353 colonoscopies, pathology was detected in 32.9% (116/353), 5 malignancies (4 colorectal, one terminal ileal). Second colonoscopy occurred in 34.7% (84/242), and ≥3 in 11.2% (27/242), for symptoms, routine re-screening, or inadequate preparation, with sustained yield; 35.7% (30/84) second; 34.8% (8/23), third. 125 procedures occurred outside guidelines (ages 25-39 years), with pathology identified in 25 (20%), including one malignancy. Bowel preparation was adequate, good/excellent in 71.4% (252/353) while 13.6% (48/353) were poor or unsatisfactory.

Conclusion: In real-world practice, colonoscopy demonstrated high adenoma burden, clinically important malignancy rate and persistent pathology detection. Suboptimal referral-to-procedure completion rate was observed. Findings support robust surveillance and consideration of earlier CF-specific screening thresholds.

records.title: Resistance to colistin in Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilms is modulated by the arn operon and pH

session.title: ePoster Session 01 -Targeting pseudomonas in cystic fibrosis: from mechanisms to new therapies

person.title: PhD student
person.department: Department of Biology and Biotechnology "Charles Darwin"

records.authors_text: M. Cristoferi1, V. Pastore1, G. Sangiorgi1, L. Cavinato1, G. Cimino2, P. Del Porto1, E.G. Di Domenico3, F. Ascenzioni1
records.affiliations_text: 1Sapienza University of Rome, Department of Biology and Biotechnology "Charles Darwin", Rome, Italy, 2Sapienza University of Rome, Department of Pediatrics and Infant Neuropsychiatry, Rome, Italy, 3San Gallicano Dermatological Institute IRCSS, Microbiology and Virology Unit, Rome, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Colistin, a last-resort antibiotic against multidrug resistant Gram-negative bacteria (doi:10.1189/fcimb.2022.851784), targets the bacterial outer membrane (OM) by electrostatic interactions. Bacteria may counteract this mechanism by OM remodeling which in P. aeruginosa is mainly due to lipid A aminoarabinosylation mediated by the arn operon. Based on previous observations showing that P. aeruginosa biofilms are tolerant to colistin (doi: 10.1371/journal.ppat.1000213), we asked whether the arn operon is involved in this phenomenon. For this, colistin MBIC (Minimal Biofilm Inhibition Concentration) and arn genes expression was analyzed in biofilms from colistin sensitive reference strains and cystic fibrosis clinical isolates, both wt and Darn mutants. Additionally, as P. aeruginosa experience a mild acidic environment in CF airways, in which it grows as a biofilm within the mucus, we tested whether pH changes the susceptibility to colistin in biofilms.

Our results showed higher arnT expression in biofilms as compared to planktonic cells, in agreement with higher biofilm resistance to colistin respect to the planktonic counterpart. In agreement with this finding, deletion of arn genes makes P. aeruginosa biofilms more susceptible to colistin. Similarly, blocking the arn operon activity with the ArnT inhibitors FDO and FDO-H (doi:10.1093/jac/dkaa200; 10.1021/acs.joc.0c01459) caused an MBIC reduction ranging from 128- to 8-fold in clinical isolates.

As expected, P. aeruginosa biofilms appeared more resistant to colistin at pH 6 respect to pH 7, with an increase of the colistin of MBIC ranging from 2- to 4-fold, depending on the strains.

Collectively, having confirmed the upregulation of the arn operon and the increased resistance to colistin of P. aeruginosa biofilms, our results support the use of ArnT inhibitors to potentiate colistin activity in the clinical settings in which biofilm-grown cells are prevalent, such as chronic lung infections.

person.department: Department of Biology and Medical Genetics

records.authors_text: A. Holubová1, M. Libik1, L. Dvořáková1, J. Bartošová2, T. Doušová2, M. Macek Jr.1
records.affiliations_text: 1Charles University - 2nd Faculty of Medicine and University Hospital Motol and Homolka, Department of Biology and Medical Genetics, Prague, Czech Republic, 2Charles University - 2nd Faculty of Medicine and University Hospital Motol and Homolka, Department of Paediatrics, Prague, Czech Republic
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Complex CFTR alleles, defined as two or more variants in cis (i.e., on the same CF allele), complicate diagnostic evaluation and genotype–phenotype correlations and may negatively affect the response to CFTR modulator therapy. In Czech pwCF, several complex alleles have been identified, with [L467F;F508del] most frequent, followed by [E292X;R709Q]. Novel complex alleles harbouring two CF-causing variants, including E831X, have recently been detected. This study aimed to describe these clinical cases.

Methods: Data were obtained from the Prague CF Newborn Screening Centre and the Prague CF Centre.

Results: We identified two cases in which the E831X variant occurred within a complex allele harbouring two additional CF-causing variants. The first patient had a positive newborn screening (NBS) and was heterozygous for two CF-causing variants, E831X and R851X. Parental DNA analysis showed that both variants were inherited from the father, whereas no CFTR variants were detected in the mother, indicating that E831X and R851X are in cis. The infant had a negative sweat chloride test. The second case involved an eight-year-old boy with a clinical diagnosis of CF and an initial finding of a single CF-causing variant, N1303K. Subsequent massively parallel sequencing (Devyser CFTR NGS assay; Sweden) identified two additional CF-causing variants: 711+5G>A and E831X. The N1303K variant was detected in the father, while maternal DNA was unavailable. The patient is thus likely a compound heterozygote with the genotype N1303K/[711+5G>A;E831X].

Conclusion: Finding of two CF-causing variants within a complex allele, either during NBS or through postnatal genetic analysis of clinical CF cases, is very rare. Despite their detection by NBS, parental segregation analysis and sweat testing remain essential to establish the final screening/diagnostic outcome.

records.title: A qualitative study of mental health experiences post elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI)

session.title: ePoster Session 03 - From breakthrough to burdens: mental health in modern cystic fibrosis care

person.title: Dr.
person.department: Leeds Regional Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre

records.authors_text: H. Chadwick1,2, L. Haigh1, I.J Clifton1, A. Sawant1, G. Spoletini1, D.G Peckham1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Leeds Teaching Hospital NHS Trust, Leeds Regional Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Leeds, United Kingdom, 2University of Leeds, Respiratory Medicine, Leeds Institute of Medical Research at St James's, Leeds, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: This study aimed to evaluate 1) the impact of ETI on psychological wellbeing and quality of life and 2) how post-ETI changes in health and social circumstances influence psychological wellbeing in people with CF (pwCF).

Methods: Semi-structured one-to-one interviews were conducted face-to-face or via Microsoft Teams. Four questions explored physical and mental health, quality of life, contact with the CF service, family life and relationships, education/work, social activities, and the impact of COVID-19. Transcripts were analysed using Grounded Theory.

Results: Twenty-one pwCF on ETI were interviewed between March 2023 and September 2024; 8 males, mean age 36.5 (SD 8.25) years, mean interview length 32 minutes. Four themes emerged: 1) positive effect on mental health post-ETI dose adjustment, 2) adjusting to changes in health, 3) conflicted emotions, 4) impact on relationships, education, career and finances. Dose adjustment of ETI, which occurred in 8 pwCF, improved negative mental health side effects. The CF team were praised for listening to patients and prioritising both physical and mental health. PwCF express gratitude and relief as they adapt to a new normal marked by stable health and accomplishing tasks once thought impossible. Managing ETI health expectations has been vital, and many had forgotten how much treatment previously dominated their lives. Reduced hospital contact led some to grieve the loss of their CF “extended family”. Whilst ETI has fostered hope for the future, it has also caused survivor guilt, uncertainty regarding long-term prognosis, as well as concerns about career trajectories and financial security, leaving some pwCF feeling “stuck”.

Conclusion: While ETI has had a positive impact on psychological wellbeing, it also associated with survivor guilt, uncertainty regarding long-term prognosis, career trajectories, and financial security. Sustained, targeted support is essential to optimise both physical and mental health.
