records.affiliations_text: 1Cochin Hospital, APHP and Université Paris-Cité, French National Reference CF center, Paris Cedex 14, France, 2Vaincre la Mucoviscidose, Paris, France
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Without CFTR modulators, cystic fibrosis (CF) is associated with an accelerated decline in percent predicted forced expiratory volume in one second (ppFEV1), at a rate of approximately -1.5% per year. Although treatment with elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor (ETI) initially increases ppFEV1, little is known about its impact on subsequent FEV1 decline. Recent analyses of the extension phases of the Phase 3 ETI pivotal studies (Daines et al., AJRCCM, 2025) found no evidence of ppFEV1 decline over four years in patients aged 12 and older who were treated with ETI. Our objectives was to examine the decline in ppFEV1 in a large real-world cohort of adults with CF.

Methods: Data from adults (≥18 years) with CF included in the French prospective national observational ETI study were analyzed over 3 years. Eligible participants were those with at least 3 measures of ppFEV1 between 3 months and 3 years following ETI initiation. The reference ppFEV1 was the best ppFEV1 during the first 3 months of ETI treatment and subsequent decline in ppFEV1 was analyzed using a linear mixed-model effect.

Results: The analysis was based on data from 2321 adults with CF (male, 54.4%; median [IQR] age, 29.2 [23.1;36.7]) ; ppFEV1 prior to ETI initiation 59.7 [39.8;79.1]) treated with ETI for three years. Following ETI initiation, ppFEV1 increased by a median [IQR] + 14.5 [7.9;22.7]% within the first 3 months. The subsequent mean (95% confidence interest) decline in ppFEV1 was -0.70 (-0.83 ;-0.57) per year. No significant difference in ppFEV1 decline was found by age quartiles or sex at birth; ppFEV1 decline appeared greater in participants with higher ppFEV1.

Conclusion: Our results suggest a persistent yet reduced ppFEV1 decline in adults with CF who are treated with ETI. Subgroup analyses will clarify the impact of these findings, particularly for individuals with advanced lung disease.

person.biography:
Pierre-Régis Burgel is currently Professor of Respiratory Medicine at Paris Descartes University in Paris, France, where he is also a senior researcher and co-Principal Investigator in the Acute and Chronic Airway Infection Laboratory (Cochin Institute, INSERM, Paris France). Professor Burgel is a senior consultant at the Respiratory Medicine Department of Cochin Hospital in Paris. He is national coordinator of the French Cystic Fibrosis Reference Centre Network (47 CF centres)
Professor Burgel completed his medical training at the University of Paris, School of Medicine in 1999. After a post-doctoral fellowship at the University of California in San Francisco (USA) (1999-2001), he obtained a PhD in respiratory cell biology at the University of Paris.
His main research interests include cystic fibrosis in adults, bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and host-pathogen interaction during chronic airway bacterial infection. He has published over 370 articles in peer reviewed journals in these areas of lung disease.
Professor Burgel is president of the French Cystic Fibrosis Society and associate editor of The Journal of Cystic Fibrosis. He currently serves as Chair of the Scientific Committee of the ECFS Patient Registry.
He received the 2022 European Respiratory Society mid-career GOLD medal for Cystic Fibrosis and the ECFS award in 2025.

session.title: Workshop 06 - Integrating mental health and neurocognitive care in contemporary cystic fibrosis practice

person.title: Dr.
person.department: Dept. of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

records.authors_text: A.M. Georgiopoulos1, R. Wei1, T.M. Mullen1, N. Chaudhary1, B.A. Smith2, Y. Sher3, A.S. Bruce4, A.L. Quittner5, M.E. Dvorak3, A. O'Leary Amato6, A.R. Thomas-Diceman7, K. Papia8, J. He4, D. Friedman1
records.affiliations_text: 1Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, United States, 2Jacobs School of Medicine and Biomedical Sciences, Buffalo, United States, 3Stanford University School of Medicine, Stanford, United States, 4University of Kansas Medical Center, Kansas City, United States, 5Joe DiMaggio Cystic Fibrosis, Pulmonary & Sleep Center, Hollywood, United States, 6UPMC Presbyterian/Shadyside Hospital, Pittsburgh, United States, 7St. Michael’s Hospital, Unity Health, Toronto, Canada, 8Northwell Health, New Hyde Park, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: CF-CBT is an 8-session intervention to address depression and anxiety in adults with CF (AWCF). Between 2022-25, >200 US and Canadian CF clinicians completed an 8-hour CF-CBT training. We conducted a focus group examining clinician experiences of CF-CBT implementation as part of a mixed-methods randomized implementation trial.

Methods: Nine CF-CBT trained clinicians participated in a focus group in July 2025: 8 (89%) women, 7 (78%) white, 8 (89%) heterosexual; 7 (78%) social workers, 1 psychologist, 1 nurse practitioner; working in CF 0-17 years. The focus group was audio recorded, transcribed, and analyzed in NVivo 14 with a codebook based on the RE-AIM (Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, Maintenance) framework (Table 1).

Results: Clinicians endorsed positive outcomes for AWCF and families, institutional support, group and individual consultation provided by the CF-CBT team, and professional satisfaction (Table 1). Clinicians suggested additional resources such as skills handouts to augment the patient workbook. Several clinicians voiced support for making an asynchronous online CF-CBT training available for new clinicians and to help trained clinicians refresh their CF-CBT delivery skills.

Conclusions: CF-CBT implementation has positively impacted AWCF, clinicians, and institutions. Clinician feedback guided development of the online CF-CBT training and will inform the creation of additional resources to support teams implementing CF-CBT.

Funding: This work was supported by the CF Foundation [FRIEDM22K0]

Table 1. Key themes and exemplar quotes from CF-CBT clinician focus group

RE-AIM ThemeSubthemeExemplar QuoteReach:

How do I reach those who need this intervention?

Process of identifying and approaching AWCF for CF-CBT“I do the mental health screening and if they have mild or moderate scores, I offer the CBT to them…But even if they have [lower scores]…but they talk about feeling anxious or feeling frustrated at work or just not coping very well, I’m starting to offer it to more patients, not just relying on the number.”Challenges in engagement“The main place I’ve been having push back is patients that are wanting in person visits. We don’t offer that because of the infection controls.”Effectiveness: How do I know my intervention is working?

Positives for AWCF“A patient…verbalized to me that the CF-CBT was really helpful in getting her through this past hospitalization…the new perspective of looking at hospitalizations, how to be prepared, how to look at her automatic negative thinking.”Positives for families and caregivers“My patient had mentioned that his grandmother…noticed that he had become much more social. That was a big driving force for him to choose to continue to participate after the initial sessions.” Adoption:

How do I develop organizational support to deliver my intervention?

Perceptions of CF-CBT implementation from institutions“Our clinic director and team are all extremely supportive and see CF CBT as a welcome and needed part of our mental health care of patients.”Center / institutional barriers for CF-CBT implementation"Unfortunately, there is not the institutional support around extra time or protected time for this work...Also, private space is always an issue.”Implementation: How do I ensure the intervention is delivered properly?

Effect of CF-CBT implementation on clinicians“The training had really lifted me out a feeling of being burnt out...I find this to be very rewarding...It's really helped me to feel definitely more eager to show up to work and be more involved in [patients’] emotional well-being in a more meaningful way.”Experience with CF-CBT consultation

“I feel something ongoing is really great. It's all in the group setting. It's always great to connect with colleagues, having different experiences, and cross pollinate, and then have the facilitator there with their expertise.”Sessions requiring more training or information“For session 7...I never quite found like the right way to get through it cohesively, though that was something that we talked about a fair amount in my consultation group as well.”Maintenance: How do I incorporate the intervention, so it is delivered over the long term?Enduring CF-CBT training materials“I would appreciate [the online CF-CBT training] too. Being able to go back and hear a little bit, be reminded of the trainings, or seeing actual role plays of what it looks like could be useful and helpful.”Additional CF-CBT resources“It would be nice to have things like cheat sheets…that summarizes some of the ideas that you can send home with [patients]. Like some of the automatic negative thinking ideas, thinking traps, things like that.”

records.title: Beyond exercise testing: linking exercise capacity, enjoyment and participation among people with cystic fibrosis

session.title: Workshop 07 - Physiotherapy in the CFTR modulator era: integrating exercise capacity, strength, sleep and daily participation

person.title: MSc PhD
person.department: Institute of Human Nutrition and Food Science

records.authors_text: W. Gruber1,2, P. Ontyd1, O. Schabel1, C. Werner1, B. Minke1, C. Falkenberg1
records.affiliations_text: 1Fachklinik Satteldüne, Nebel, Germany, 2University of Duisburg-Essen, Pediatric Pulmonology and Sleep Medicine, Cystic Fibrosis Center, Children’s Hospital, Essen, Germany
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To investigate the relationship between peak exercise capacity and enjoyment of, and motivation for, physical activity (PA) and exercise participation (EP) in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF).

Methods: 56 pwCF (31f/26m, age 18.3±10.5yrs, ppFEV1 84.8±16.9,) participated. A cycle-ergometry was performed to determine VO2peak and Wpeak. German versions of the Physical Activity Enjoyment Scale (PACES-D) was used to assess PA and EP enjoyment, and the Behavioural Regulation in Exercise Questionnaire Version 2 (BREQ-2-D) assessed motivational aspects. Data were collected during an inpatient rehabilitation course.

Results: While participants showed normal exercise capacity (VO₂peak; 80.1±16.2%pred., Wpeak 85.5±17.5% pred.), they reported high enjoyment of PA and EP (67.0±10.2). Their motivation was characterised by high intrinsic (4.10±1.0) and identified regulation (3.6±0.8) versus low introjected (2.1±0.9), low external regulation (1.7±0.8), and amotivation (1.5±0.7). The Relative Autonomy Index (RAI: 9.58 ± 6.11), a weighted composite of all BREQ-2-D subscales, where higher values indicate stronger autonomous motivation, was notably positive. Regression analysis revealed that adding motivational variables to demographic/clinical factors increased explained variance in PA/EP enjoyment from 18% to 62% (ΔR²=.437, p<.001). Intrinsic motivation (β=.824, p<.001), lung function (β=.722, p=.019) and age (β=.766, p=.015) were found to be significant predictors of enjoyment, while exercise VO₂peak/Wpeak showed no association (ΔR²=.002, p=.931).

Conclusion: PA/EP enjoyment was predicted by intrinsic motivation (strongest predictor), lung function and age but not by exercise capacity. The discrepancy between physical capability and of PA/EP enjoyment highlights psychological factors. Promoting an active lifestyle could be achieved by shifting from exercise testing alone to a more holistic physical literacy assessment which incorporates motivational profiling.

records.title: Effects of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor initiation in advance cystic fibrosis-related liver disease in the Netherlands

session.title: Workshop 08 - The hidden burden of cystic fibrosis: liver diseases and the gastrointestinal ecosystem

records.authors_text: S. Kayalibay1, M.I. can der Spek1, F.A. Bodewes1, H.J. Verkade1
records.affiliations_text: 1University Medical Center Groningen, Paediatric Gastroentrology, Groningen, Netherlands
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Elexacaftor–tezacaftor–ivacaftor (ETI) was recently introduced in the Netherlands, including for persons with advanced cystic fibrosis-related liver disease (aCFLD). This retrospective study examined the potential therapeutic and hepatotoxic effects of ETI in persons with aCFLD.

Methods: We compared persons with aCFLD and those without CF-related hepatic involvement (noCFHBI) upon ETI initiation and up to 12 months thereafter, adjusting for prior CFTR modulator use. Using the Dutch Cystic Fibrosis Foundation registry, we analysed between the two groups the liver enzyme levels and fibrosis indices (APRI and GPR) during the 12 months study period.

Results: We included 85 subjects with aCFLD and 613 noCFHBI controls. A significant transient increase in median aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alanine transaminase (ALT), and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) levels was observed in both groups after ETI initiation. Median AST, ALT, and GGT levels were consistently higher in the aCFLD group than in controls at all time points, most pronounced in the first month. Unexpectedly, significant increases in fibrosis indices were observed in the aCFLD group between baseline and 12 months (APRI 0.681 vs. 0.931; GPR 0.807 vs. 1.385; both p<0.05).

Conclusion: Based on fibrosis indices, no hepatic therapeutic improvement of aCFLD was observed 12 months after ETI initiation. Patients with aCFLD demonstrated higher post-ETI elevations in liver enzymes, suggesting a distinct hepatic response to ETI in this group. While longer treatment duration or earlier initiation may still mitigate disease progression, these findings underscore the need for cautious and closely monitored ETI use in patients with aCFLD.

records.title: Shared MSD2 binding site but distinct potency of elexacaftor and vanzacaftor in correcting F508del-CFTR

session.title: Workshop 09 - Deciphering the mechanism(s) of action of modulators

person.institution: Research Institute, The Hospital for Sick Children

records.authors_text: G. Langeveld1, S. Kay1, L.J. Huan1, K. Auw-Yang1, C. Bear1
records.affiliations_text: 1The Hospital for Sick Children, Molecular Medicine, Toronto, Canada
records.abstract_text:
Many individuals with cystic fibrosis (CF) benefit from Trikafta™, a triple CFTR modulator composed of the correctors: elexacaftor (VX-445) and tezacaftor (VX-661), and the potentiator: ivacaftor (VX-770), a.k.a. ETI). In cryo-EM studies, the two correctors have been shown to bind to two different regions on the F508del-CFTR to act in an additive or synergistic manner to induce near-Wt assembly via allostery. ETI treatment has been found to improve lung function in patients with at least one F508del-CFTR mutation. However, a subset shows limited benefit or adverse effects. Whether the FDA-approved Alyftrek™ (vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor; VTD) improves outcomes for this group remains unclear.

We compared the mechanisms of action of elexacaftor (VX-445) and vanzacaftor (VX-121) in HEK-293 cells stably expressing F508del-CFTR. Firstly, when combined with VX-661, the potency of VX-121 is much greater as a corrector than VX-445, i.e, EC50= 0.001uM vs 0.16uM respectively. We found that both small molecules mediate acute potentiation of VX-661 corrected, cyclic-AMP activated F508del-CFTR channel activity. Further, our mutagenesis studies support the hypothesis both small molecules mediate correction by interacting with the same site on the mutant protein. Disruption of the site for elexacaftor binding identified by cryo-EM (Fiedorczuk and Chen) with the mutation: R1102A, abolished correction by both small molecules.

Interestingly, VX-121 (3uM) alone induced near Wt maturation of F508del-CFTR yielding a C/C+B ratio of 0.87 vs 0.92 (p= 0.18). Whereas VX-445 alone didn’t achieve Wt maturation (p= 0.0003) unless co-treated with VX-661 (p = 0.10).

These findings support the hypothesis that allosteric modulation of F508del-CFTR to near wild-type levels can be achieved via high-affinity interaction of a single molecule with MSD2. Future studies include examination of the next generation of corrector molecules (e.g VX-828) to determine if this property is conserved.

records.title: Proof of in vivo Sphingolipid Delta-4 desaturase (DEGS) reversible inhibition in mice pups following administration of ETI to dams during pregnancy and breastfeeding

session.title: Workshop 09 - Deciphering the mechanism(s) of action of modulators

records.authors_text: A. Squarzoni1, G. Boschetti1, S. Mandrup Bertozzi1, M. Summa2, A. Serani3, E. Milandri4, L. Mercolini4, R. Mandrioli4, M. Protti4, C. Montani5, T. Bandiera6, G. Cangemi7, N. Pedemonte7, F. Benfenati8, L. Nobbio5, R. Bertorelli2, A. Armirotti1
records.affiliations_text: 1Fondazione Istituto Italiano di Tecnologia, Analytical Chemistry Facility, Genova, Italy, 2Fondazione Istituto Italiano di Tecnologia, Tranlational Pharmacology Facility, Genova, Italy, 3Fondazione Istituto Italiano di Tecnologia, Genetics and Epigenetics of Behavior, Genova, Italy, 4Università di Bologna, Bologna, Italy, 5IRCCS Ospedale Policlinico San Martino, Genova, Italy, 6Fondazione Istituto Italiano di Tecnologia, D3 Pharmachemistry, Genova, Italy, 7IRCCS Istituto Giannina Gaslini, Genova, Italy, 8Fondazione Istituto Italiano di Tecnologia, Center for Synaptic Neuroscience and Technology, Genova, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Background & Objectives: We demonstrated (Liessi JCF 2023, Ciobanu JCF 2024) that Tezacaftor inhibits the enzyme (DEGS) which converts dihydroceramides (dHCer) into ceramides (Fabrias Prog.Lip.Res. 2012), thus producing increase of dHCer in cells. Since DEGS malfunctioning is often associated with severe neurological impairments linked with aberrant myelin composition and structure (Karsai JCI 2019, Pant JCI 2019), we conducted an in vivo drug safety study, by administering ETI to CD-1 mice during pregnancy and breastfeeding. The aim is to evaluate the potential impact of DEGS inhibition on the formation of the peripheral and central nervous systems (Doretto Plos 2011).

Methods: ETI was incorporated as powder into food, in a high-fat diet regimen. Besides recording weight and size, we also investigated pups' behavior by means of dedicated tests. ETI and dHCer levels as well as changes in the global lipidome were measured by tandem mass spectrometry coupled to liquid chromatography.

Results: Ten days after birth (P10), a significant accumulation of dHCer in the brains of pups born from ETI-fed dams compared to controls occurs. No accumulation was observed in the sciatic nerve of these animals. We also conducted a global lipidomics survey, which revealed other alterations associated with exposure to ETI. During breastfeeding, when exposure to the drug decreases, these alterations revert and virtually disappear at P28, together with other differences in the phenotype and behaviour of the pups observed earlier (Squarzoni JCF 2025).

Conclusions: We have now demonstrated that exposure of dams to ETI induces an increase in dHCer in the pups brain. Despite a few experimental difficulties, which we are overcoming using also a bit of creativity, we are progressing toward a better understanding of the practical implications of these findings.

Fundings: Cystic Fibrosis Foundation (grant ARMIRO24G0 to AA), Fondazione per la Ricerca sulla Fibrosi Cistica (grant FFC#2-2024 to LN).

person.biography: I hold a Master Degree in Chemistry and a Ph,D. in Biochemistry (University of Genova). In 2003 I also earned my Professional certificate in Chemistry. I spent the following 10 years doing PostDoc research activity in the bioanalytical field at the Department of Experimental Medicine of the same University and at the Center for Advanced Biotechnology. I spent 9 months at the Istituto Italiano Tumori (Genova) as Senior Scientist before joining IIT (Italian Institute of Technology), where I hold a Technologist position and I lead the Analytical Chemistry Lab. My research activity mainly focuses on the proteomics and metabolomics characterization of the changes occurring to biological systems following the most various challenges, from drugs to gene silencing. I am also particularly involved in the biomarker discovery field, with a growing focus on neurodegeneration. I am currently PI in WP4, Core 3 of the EU Graphene Flagship Project Horizon 2020 (Grant agreement no. 696656), dedicated to the metabolomics and proteomics of graphene interactions with biological systems. I am also PI in project FFC#1-2019 from the Italian Cystic Fibrosis society, dedicated to the use of proteomics to identify new potential pharmacological targets. I am also the Coordinator of the Italian COVID-19 Mass Spec Coalition. I co-authored  107 papers in international, peer-reviewed journals (9 as First, 12 as Last Author, Total citations (Scopus): 25554 H-index (Scopus): 30 and I am co-inventor of two patents.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Several countries reported a reduction in lung transplants for people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) after elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor (ETI) was introduced. We sought to evaluate how lung transplant indications evolved in relation to CFTR genotypes and the use of ETI.

Methods: All lung transplants performed on pwCF in France between 2015 and 2024 were identified using data from the French Agence de la Biomédecine. Individual-level patient data, including CFTR genotypes and use of ETI at the time of transplant, were obtained from the French CF reference network centers.

Results: Between 2015 and 2024, a total of 538 lung transplants were performed, including 461 first-time transplants and 77 re-transplants. The rate of first-time lung transplant was 13.4 per 1,000 non-transplanted patients/year versus 1.8 per 1,000 non-transplanted patients/year for 2015-2019 (prior to ETI) and 2020-2024 (with ETI), respectively (P<0.0001); the rate of lung re-transplant was 10.2 per 1,000 transplanted patients/year versus 7.7 per 1,000 transplanted patients/year (P=0.70). Treatment with ETI was prescribed prior to transplant in all F508del pwCF who received a first-time transplant since 2021 and in all those with non-F508del responsive variants since 2022. Eleven patients treated with ETI required lung transplant due to adverse effects leading to ETI discontinuation, concomitant severe liver disease or insufficient improvement of respiratory failure.

Conclusion: ETI has reduced, but not eliminated, the need for a first-time lung transplant in pwCF. Indications for a first-time lung transplant persist in a subset of pwCF who respond to ETI and in those with nonresponsive CFTR genotypes. Re-transplant remains an option for selected transplant recipients with chronic lung allograft dysfunction.

person.biography:
Pierre-Régis Burgel is currently Professor of Respiratory Medicine at Paris Descartes University in Paris, France, where he is also a senior researcher and co-Principal Investigator in the Acute and Chronic Airway Infection Laboratory (Cochin Institute, INSERM, Paris France). Professor Burgel is a senior consultant at the Respiratory Medicine Department of Cochin Hospital in Paris. He is national coordinator of the French Cystic Fibrosis Reference Centre Network (47 CF centres)
Professor Burgel completed his medical training at the University of Paris, School of Medicine in 1999. After a post-doctoral fellowship at the University of California in San Francisco (USA) (1999-2001), he obtained a PhD in respiratory cell biology at the University of Paris.
His main research interests include cystic fibrosis in adults, bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and host-pathogen interaction during chronic airway bacterial infection. He has published over 370 articles in peer reviewed journals in these areas of lung disease.
Professor Burgel is president of the French Cystic Fibrosis Society and associate editor of The Journal of Cystic Fibrosis. He currently serves as Chair of the Scientific Committee of the ECFS Patient Registry.
He received the 2022 European Respiratory Society mid-career GOLD medal for Cystic Fibrosis and the ECFS award in 2025.

session.title: Workshop 06 - Integrating mental health and neurocognitive care in contemporary cystic fibrosis practice

person.title: Professor
person.institution: Children's Hospital of Richmond at Virginia Commonwealth University

records.authors_text: J. Kim1, J. He1, A.L. Quittner2, A.M. Georgiopoulos3, B.A. Smith4, M.S. Schechter5
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Kansas Medical Center, Kansas City, United States, 2Joe DiMaggio Children's Hospital, Hollywood, United States, 3Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, United States, 4University of Buffalo, Buffalo, United States, 5Children's Hospital of Richmond at Virginia Commonwealth University, Richmond, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: A 5 year follow-up of US participants in The International Depression Epidemiological Study (TIDES) found a significant increase in mortality among people with CF (PWCF) who screened positive for depression, especially those with severe symptoms. We investigated intermediary outcomes that may contribute to this finding.

Methods: We included untransplanted TIDES participants ages 12+ years followed at 45 collaborating US CF care centers who completed depression screening at a stable visit in 2006-2010 and linked clinical characteristics from the CF Foundation Patient Registry. We compared the association of a positive screen with incidence/duration of IV antibiotic treated pulmonary exacerbations (PEx), decline in FEV1, and regular clinic attendance (≥1x/quarter) at 1, 3 and 5 years for PWCF who screened negative vs. positive (HADS≥8 and/or CES-D≥16) and severely positive (HADS≥11 and/or CES-D≥26) for depression. We adjusted for gender, age, FEV1, CF-related diabetes and insurance status.

Results: Of 999 PWCF, 156 screened in the mild-moderate and 95 in the severe range. Those with severe symptoms had an increased risk of PEx at 3 (IRR 1.3, 95%CI 1.1, 1.6) and at 5 years (IRR 1.3, 95%CI 1.1, 1.6); those with mild-moderate symptoms did not evidence a statistically increased risk. PWCF with severe symptoms had an increased number of IV antibiotic days at 1 (7.33, 95%CI 0.1, 14.6), 3 (19.2, 95%CI 2.1, 36.3), and 5 years (28.7, 95%CI 1.8, 55.5). Overall FEV1 decline was greater by 0.53% predicted/year (95%CI .07, .99) in PWCF with severe depressive symptoms. No difference was seen in quarterly outpatient clinic attendance.

Conclusion: PWCF who screen positive for severe but not mild-moderate depression have an increased risk of PEx and IV antibiotic days and an increased rate of FEV1 decline. Previous research suggests an association between depression and poor adherence, but this is not reflected in outpatient clinic attendance.

records.title: The impact of two-year treatment with elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) on functional exercise capacity and quadriceps muscle strength in patients with cystic fibrosis

session.title: Workshop 07 - Physiotherapy in the CFTR modulator era: integrating exercise capacity, strength, sleep and daily participation

records.authors_text: A.-S. Aubriot1, T. Coppens1, M. Penelle2, C. Song1, C. Goubau1, C. Gonçalvès1, S. Berardis1, L. Santelé1, S. Gohy1
records.affiliations_text: 1Cliniques Universitaires Saint-Luc, Cystic Fibrosis Unit, Brussels, Belgium, 2Cliniques Universitaires Saint-Luc, Brussels, Belgium
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: As reduced exercise capacity and muscle weakness are common in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF), and associated with worse life prognosis and quality of life, we aimed to determine the impact of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) on exercise capacity and peripherical muscle strength in pwCF.

Methods: The 6-Minute Walk Test (6MWT), 1-Minute Sit-to-Stand Test (1STST) and measurement of Maximal isometric Voluntary Contraction of the Quadriceps (MVCQ) with a dynamometer were performed before initiating ETI and after one and two years of ETI.

Results: 82 pwCF (≥12y) were recruited. The 6MWT distance increased significantly after one and two years of ETI compared with baseline (605±73m at baseline; 638±75m after one year of ETI, p<0.0001; 641±72m after two years of ETI, p<0.0001). The number of repetitions of 1STST showed a significant enhancement after one and two years of ETI compared with baseline (52 [39-66] at baseline; 55 [45-66] after one year of ETI, p=0.0242; 57 [46-66] after two years of ETI, p=0.0012). MVCQ also showed a significant improvement after one and two years of ETI compared with baseline (64 [44-79Nm] at baseline; 73 [59-90Nm] after one year of ETI, p=0.0037; 79 [65-95Nm] after two years of ETI, p<0.0001). In contrast, no significant change was noticed while comparing results of 6MWT, 1STST and MVCQ between one and two years of ETI.

Conclusion: 6MWT, 1STST and MVCQ improved after one year of ETI and those improvements persisted at two years, suggesting that restoring CFTR function could enhance exercise capacity and quadriceps strength.

records.title: Evaluation and updating of a prediction model for advanced cystic fibrosis liver disease in children: a 10-year analysis from the Irish longitudinal cohort

session.title: Workshop 08 - The hidden burden of cystic fibrosis: liver diseases and the gastrointestinal ecosystem

person.institution: Paediatric Academic Health Science Centre Children’s Health Ireland

records.authors_text: E. Hokey1, D. Chen2, M. Rowland2, F. Dolan1, D. Fahy1, E. O'Brien1, A. Lester-Grant1, M. Galligan2, E. Fitzpatrick1,2,3
records.affiliations_text: 1Paediatric Academic Health Science Centre Children’s Health Ireland, Research and Innovation, Dublin 12, Ireland, 2University College Dublin, Dublin, Ireland, 3Children's Health Ireland, Department of Gastroenterology and Hepatology, Dublin, Ireland
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Advanced cystic fibrosis liver disease (aCFLD) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in people with cystic fibrosis (CF). Identification of those at risk of aCFLD may facilitate earlier management and potentially avoid complications. The objective was to validate a previously published predictor model for aCFLD in a prospective dataset.

Methods: This study is a prospective cohort of children with CF, with follow-up conducted every 5 years. Liver-focused data are collected at each visit. Primary outcome is the development of aCFLD. The prediction algorithm from the PUSH study (Siegel et al. 2023) was applied to this cohort. Model performance was assessed using measures of discrimination (AUC) and calibration plots, followed by model updating and internal validation using bootstrapping.

Results: The analysis cohort comprised 517 patients: 56% M, median age 7yrs(IQR 3,12). 29 developed aCFLD over the 10-year period. Patients who developed aCFLD had higher baseline levels of AST, ALT, GGT, GGT to Platelet Ratio (GPR), and AST to Platelet Ratio Index (APRI) versus those who did not develop aCFLD. External validation of the model yielded an AUC of 0.712(95% CI:0.66-0.764). Calibration assessment demonstrated poor calibration, with an intercept of -4.926(95% CI:-5.371-4.481) and a slope of 0.423(95% CI:0.21-0.636). The updated model showed improved performance, with an apparent AUC of 0.745(95% CI:0.717-0.773) and an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.729(95% CI:0.63-0.828). Calibration was substantially improved, with an intercept of -0.002(95% CI:-0.393-0.389) and a slope of 1(95% CI:0.565-1.435), both of which showed minimal change following internal validation.

Conclusion: This study externally validated and updated a previously published prediction model for aCFLD. The updated model demonstrated moderate discrimination and excellent calibration, supporting utility for early risk stratification and targeted monitoring of children at risk for aCFLD.

records.title: Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor corrects hippocampal deficits in humanized mice models of cystic fibrosis

session.title: Workshop 09 - Deciphering the mechanism(s) of action of modulators

person.title: MSc.
person.department: Department of Anatomy, Physiology and Pharmacology

records.authors_text: M.T. Vu-Lu1, A.M. Trofimova1, O.O. Morales1, J.J. Botterill1, J.S. Tam1,2, J.P. Ianowski1, V.A. Campanucci1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Saskatchewan, Department of Anatomy, Physiology and Pharmacology, Saskatoon, Canada, 2University of Saskatchewan, Department of Medicine, Division of Respirology, Critical Care, and Sleep Medicine, Saskatoon, Canada
records.abstract_text:
Objective: To investigate whether elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) improves hippocampal function in humanized cystic fibrosis (CF) mice, by modulating chloride homeostasis and synaptic activity. Our study provides a potential insight for the neuropsychiatric symptoms reported in people with CF.

Methods: Hippocampal tissue was obtained from humanized CFTR mice (male, 13-18 weeks) expressing either wild-type CFTR (hWT) or homozygous F508del CFTR (hCF). ETI exposure was either in vitro (48 hours) or in vivo (4 days). We performed patch-clamp electrophysiology on cultured neurons and hippocampal slices to assess synaptic function, plasticity, chloride homeostasis, and neurotransmission in response to excitatory (AMPA, NMDA) and inhibitory (GABA) stimulation. Relevant protein quantification (GluA1, NKCC1, KCC2) and hippocampal slice histology was also performed.

Results: In the hippocampus of hCF mice we found impaired synaptic strength and excitation, accompanied by elevated intracellular chloride concentration. The ETI treatment restored normal hippocampal functions. Protein analysis suggested postsynaptic weakness was mediated by reduced phosphorylation of the GluA1 AMPA subunit and decreased activity of the KCC2 cotransporter.

Conclusions: Our findings uncovered a CNS phenotype in hCF mice, which was highlighted by impaired hippocampal synaptic function and altered chloride homeostasis. The observed phenotype may potentially be the direct result of CFTR dysfunction, as ETI treatment was able to restore synaptic and chloride homeostasis disruption in hCF mice toward hWT levels. Therefore, these results provide the comprehension of CNS involvement in CF and the need for more investigation into the neurological effects of ETI therapy.

Objective: To investigate whether elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) improves hippocampal function in humanized cystic fibrosis (CF) mice, by modulating chloride homeostasis and synaptic activity. Our study provides a potential insight for the neuropsychiatric symptoms reported in people with CF.
Methods: Hippocampal tissue was obtained from humanized CFTR mice (male, 13-18 weeks) expressing either wild-type CFTR (hWT) or homozygous F508del CFTR (hCF). ETI exposure was either in vitro (48 hours) or in vivo (4 days). We performed patch-clamp electrophysiology on cultured neurons and hippocampal slices to assess synaptic function, plasticity, chloride homeostasis, and neurotransmission in response to excitatory (AMPA, NMDA) and inhibitory (GABA) stimulation. Relevant protein quantification (GluA1, NKCC1, KCC2) and hippocampal slice histology was also performed.
Results: In the hippocampus of hCF mice we found impaired synaptic strength and excitation, accompanied by elevated intracellular chloride concentration. The ETI treatment restored normal hippocampal functions. Protein analysis suggested postsynaptic weakness was mediated by reduced phosphorylation of the GluA1 AMPA subunit and decreased activity of the KCC2 cotransporter.
Conclusions: Our findings uncovered a CNS phenotype in hCF mice, which was highlighted by impaired hippocampal synaptic function and altered chloride homeostasis. The observed phenotype may potentially be the direct result of CFTR dysfunction, as ETI treatment was able to restore synaptic and chloride homeostasis disruption in hCF mice toward hWT levels. Therefore, these results provide the comprehension of CNS involvement in CF and the need for more investigation into the neurological effects of ETI therapy.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The aim of this study was to evaluate the effects of highly effective modulator therapy (HEMT) on retinal microvasculature, corneal and ocular surface parameters, and electrophysiological findings.

Methods: This cross-sectional study was conducted between August 2025 and December 2025. Demographic, clinical data, and comprehensive ophthalmologic examinations—including corneal, retinal, and electrophysiological evaluations—were recorded. Patients were categorized according to use of HEMT, and analyses were performed using right eye data.

Results: Patients charecteristics are given in Table 1. Best-corrected visual acuity was logMAR 0 in all patients. Based on non-invasive tear breakup time (NIBUT) measurements, 76.2% of patients had normal tear film stability (≥10s), 11.9% had borderline values (5–9s), and 11.9% exhibited tear film instability (NIBUT<5 s), with no significant differences between the groups. Meibography score, endothelial cell density, and central corneal thickness were not different between the groups. Optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) analysis showed significantly higher superficial foveal vessel density in patients receiving HEMT (p=0.014), whereas parafoveal and deep capillary plexus parameters did not. Increased retinal vascular tortuosity was identified on color fundus photographs in 5 patients (16.7%). Foveal avascular zone (FAZ) area and perimeter (PERIM) values were similar between groups. Electrophysiological assessments revealed trends toward increased Dark-Adapted 0.01 blue electroretinography (ERG) b-wave amplitudes and reduced N95/P50 ratios in the modulator group; however, these changes did not reach statistical significance.

Conclusion: HEMT have no adverse effects on ocular structures or function. They even increased superficial foveal vessel density on OCTA, may indicate a potential favorable microvascular effect.

session.title: Workshop 06 - Integrating mental health and neurocognitive care in contemporary cystic fibrosis practice

person.institution: All Wales Adult CF Service, University Hospital Llandough

records.authors_text: A. Stimpson1, M. Mwelwa1, J. Duckers1, C. O'Leary1
records.affiliations_text: 1All Wales Adult CF Service, University Hospital Llandough, Cardiff, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Neurodiversity refers to differences in brain function and behavioural traits, including conditions such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism. Emerging studies suggest higher rates in pwCF than in the general population and extra burden/ barriers to healthcare. We developed a care pathway to help navigate support for neurodivergent patients who may experience additional challenges to daily life, function and CF management.

Methods: Since January 2025, 248 patients were seen at annual review clinic and alongside routine assessment, were asked Do you have a diagnosis/ difficulty linked to neurodiversity e.g. ADHD, autism? Patients who responded positively were asked to complete a survey and measures of depression (PHQ9) and anxiety (GAD7), offered screening and dependent on outcome, referred to local diagnostic services and offered psychological support.

Results: Forty (16%; 18 M, 18 F, 3 TG and 1 NB) patients reported neurodiversity. Of these 4 had a diagnosis of ADHD and 2 a diagnosis of autism. Sixteen were screened using the ASRSv1.1 or AQ50 and 13 referred on for diagnostic assessment. A further 7 opted in for psychological support.

Thirty (75%) patients reported low mood and anxiety within clinical range (Table 1) compared to just 47% (N=192) of patients not reporting neurodiversity. Notably, mean scores on the PHQ9 (4.9) and GAD7 (4.3) were in the non-clinical range for non-reporters.

Survey feedback indicated that neurodiversity has an important bearing on CF healthcare, but it is ‘overshadowed’ and given little or no consideration by CF professionals.

Conclusion: Around a sixth of patients reported neurodivergence, associated impact on CF care, and poorer mental health. Whilst fewer have a formal diagnosis, screening indicates the likelihood of more receiving a diagnosis in the future. Further work is needed to improve and adapt care for this patient group.

records.title: Exercise capacity vs. sleep time in pwCF vs. healthy controls

session.title: Workshop 07 - Physiotherapy in the CFTR modulator era: integrating exercise capacity, strength, sleep and daily participation

person.institution: Ruth Rappaport Children’s Hospital, Rambam Medical Center
person.department: Pediatric Pulmonary Institute and CF Center

records.authors_text: M. Hanna1,2, R. Bar-Yoseph1,2,3, M. Zucker-Toledano2, L. Bentur1,3, M. Gur1,3
records.affiliations_text: 1Ruth Rappaport Children's Hospital, Pediatric Pulmonary Institute and CF Center, Haifa, Israel, 2Ruth Rappaport Children's Hospital, Physical Activity and Exercise Clinic, Haifa, Israel, 3Technion–Israel Institute of Technology, The Bruce Rappaport Faculty of Medicine, Haifa, Israel
records.abstract_text:
Background: Low exercise capacity is associated with increased morbidity and mortality in the general population and people with Cystic fibrosis (pwCF). In previous studies, reduced sleep led to decreased lung functions in pwCF, while sleep disorders were associated with exercise intolerance and pulmonary exacerbations. Our aim was to assess effects of sleep time and disturbed sleep (nocturnal cough and snoring) on exercise capacity using cardio-pulmonary exercise testing (CPET) in young pwCF compared to healthy controls.

Methods: Prospective study assessing sleep time, disturbed sleep (questionnaire) and CPET in a group of young pwCF (pediatric & young adults) compared to healthy controls.

Results: Thirty-two CF patients (mean age 15.9± 4.9 y/o, 18 males, BMI%tile 47.0±26.9) and ninety-nine healthy controls were evaluated. FEV1, peak oxygen uptake (peak VO2) and anaerobic threshold (AT) were lower in pwCF vs. controls (FEV1 75.2±22.4 vs. 96.9±13.2%, p=0.001; 83.2±20.9 vs. 98.1± 19.2%, p=0.001; 40.6±11.8 vs. 47.4±11.8%, p=0.007, respectively). Sleeping hours were similar between the groups (CF: 7.95±1.6, controls: 8.1±1.4, p=0.7), and a higher proportion of pwCF reported nocturnal cough (18.8% CF vs. 5.1% controls, p=0.015). In the control group, sleep time was correlated with peak VO2 (specific (ml/kg/min) and % pred: r=0.248, p=0.016 and r=0.212., p=0.035, respectively). In CF, sleep time was correlated with AT (r=0.44, p=0.013). PwCF with nocturnal cough had lower FEV1 compared to those without cough (56.8±24.2 vs. 79.4±20.1% pred, respectively).

Conclusions: PwCF demonstrated lower exercise capacity compared to controls, with a positive correlation between sleep time and submaximal exercise (AT); patients with nocturnal cough exhibited lower pulmonary function. Our findings highlight the important effect of sleep time and quality on lung health in PwCF. Further long-term studies will elucidate the effect of improving sleep hygiene on long term outcomes in pwCF.

1Ruth Rappaport Children's Hospital, Pediatric Pulmonary Institute and CF Center, Haifa, Israel, 2Ruth Rappaport Children's Hospital, Physical Activity and Exercise Clinic, Haifa, Israel, 3Technion–Israel Institute of Technology, The Bruce Rappaport Faculty of Medicine, Haifa, Israel

Background: Low exercise capacity is associated with increased morbidity and mortality in the general population and people with Cystic fibrosis (pwCF). In previous studies, reduced sleep led to decreased lung functions in pwCF, while sleep disorders were associated with exercise intolerance and pulmonary exacerbations. Our aim was to assess effects of sleep time and disturbed sleep (nocturnal cough and snoring) on exercise capacity using cardio-pulmonary exercise testing (CPET) in young pwCF compared to healthy controls.
Methods: Prospective study assessing sleep time, disturbed sleep (questionnaire) and CPET in a group of young pwCF (pediatric & young adults) compared to healthy controls.
Results: Thirty-two CF patients (mean age 15.9± 4.9 y/o, 18 males, BMI%tile 47.0±26.9) and ninety-nine healthy controls were evaluated. FEV1, peak oxygen uptake (peak VO2) and anaerobic threshold (AT) were lower in pwCF vs. controls (FEV1 75.2±22.4 vs. 96.9±13.2%, p=0.001; 83.2±20.9 vs. 98.1± 19.2%, p=0.001; 40.6±11.8 vs. 47.4±11.8%, p=0.007, respectively). Sleeping hours were similar between the groups (CF: 7.95±1.6, controls: 8.1±1.4, p=0.7), and a higher proportion of pwCF reported nocturnal cough (18.8% CF vs. 5.1% controls, p=0.015). In the control group, sleep time was correlated with peak VO2 (specific (ml/kg/min) and % pred: r=0.248, p=0.016 and r=0.212., p=0.035, respectively). In CF, sleep time was correlated with AT (r=0.44, p=0.013). PwCF with nocturnal cough had lower FEV1 compared to those without cough (56.8±24.2 vs. 79.4±20.1% pred, respectively).
Conclusions: PwCF demonstrated lower exercise capacity compared to controls, with a positive correlation between sleep time and submaximal exercise (AT); patients with nocturnal cough exhibited lower pulmonary function. Our findings highlight the important effect of sleep time and quality on lung health in PwCF. Further long-term studies will elucidate the effect of improving sleep hygiene on long term outcomes in pwCF.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Gut microbial dysbiosis is common in cystic fibrosis but is typically assessed using non-specific diversity metrics or study‑specific taxonomic signatures, limiting comparability across studies and interventions. We developed a metagenomic, species-level Cystic Fibrosis Microbial Dysbiosis Index (CF-MDI) to enable quantitative assessment of gut microbial imbalance in children with CF (CwCF).

Methods: Stool metagenomic data from the PEARL-CF study (ACTRN12616000797471), including CwCF and age- and gender-matched healthy controls (HC), were analysed using MaAsLin2 to identify taxa enriched or depleted in CF (q<0.05, |coefficient| ≥ 4). CF-MDI was defined as the log10 ratio of summed relative abundances of CF-enriched taxa to those enriched in HC. Reproducibility was evaluated in the independent EARTH cohort (PMID:32295774). Responsiveness to therapeutic modulation was assessed using publicly available metagenomic data from an Elexacaftor/Tezacaftor/Ivacaftor (ETI) study (PMID: 38275294).

Results: PEARL-CF data (70 CwCF, 67 HC; 0-6 years) was used to derive CF-MDI. CF-MDI scores were significantly higher in CF than HC (p<0.001), inversely correlated with species richness (ρ= -0.74, p<0.001), and higher in pancreatic insufficient vs sufficient CwCF (p=0.01). In the EARTH cohort (57 CwCF, 56 HC; 0-18 years) key ecological and clinical associations were replicated, confirming robustness. In the ETI study (39 CwCF; 6-18 years), CF-MDI decreased significantly at 6 and 12 months post-ETI, while alpha-diversity metrics, previously reported as unchanged, remained non-significant.

Conclusions: CF-MDI is a robust, CF-specific metric that captures pathophysiologically relevant microbial restructuring not detected by standard diversity measures. CF-MDI differentiates disease and pancreatic status and sensitively tracks therapeutic modulation of the CF gut microbiome, supporting its use as a novel gut microbiome endpoint for monitoring intervention effects in CF trials.

records.title: Multi-omics analysis of airway epithelial cells following elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) therapy

session.title: Workshop 09 - Deciphering the mechanism(s) of action of modulators

records.authors_text: M. Ma1, M. Badaoui1, M. Chanson1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Geneva, Cell Physiology and Metabolism, Geneve, Switzerland
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: ETI restores anion transport in the most common F508del CFTR mutant; however, some cystic fibrosis (CF) patients continue to experience lung infection and inflammation after 3.5 years of treatment. The variability in phenotype-genotype correlations in patient lung suggests that additional genetic or environmental factors influence clinical outcomes. Here, we aim to identify genome and epigenome changes in airway epithelial cells following CFTR rescue.

Methods: Primary Human Bronchial Epithelial Cell (HBEC) cultures were generated from 6 CF patients and 5 non-CF (NCF) donors. 1 CF patient (referred to as CF1) carried the “2184ΔA/W128A” mutation, while 5 patients were homozygous for F508del (referred to as CF2). CFTR channel function was assessed by Ussing chamber assay after 72 h of ETI treatment. Single nuclei (sn) multi-omics sequencing was performed to profile the epigenome and transcriptome changes of cells before and after ETI treatment.

Results: ETI restored CFTR channel transport function in CF2 cells to 46.3% of wide-type CFTR activity, whereas no restoration was observed in CF1. snRNA-seq analysis revealed significant transcriptional alterations in CF2 cells compared with NCF cells: dysfunction in the “extracellular matrix organization” and “cell cycle and senescence” pathways in basal cells; alteration in the “RNA, protein, and lipid metabolism” pathways in goblet cells; and disruption in the “membrane trafficking” and “cholesterol biosynthesis” pathways in ciliated cells. ETI tended to normalize abnormal pathways in CF2 cells, suggesting metabolic reprogramming. Nevertheless, across all cell types, only a minimal proportion (8.4%) of CF2 abnormally regulated genes was significantly restored following ETI treatment.

Conclusion: We started to uncover the effects of ETI to the different cell types in CF airway epithelium that will be deepened with snATAC-seq data to map the epigenetic landscape underlying ETI-responsive and uncorrected genes.

records.title: Immune-modulatory effects of CFTR triple therapy in cystic fibrosis

session.title: Workshop 05 - Further evolving our understanding of ETI impacts

records.authors_text: V. Meyboom1, S. Sutharsan2, M. Welsner2, D. Westhölter3, S. Straßburg2, C. Taube3, M. Schedel4
records.affiliations_text: 1Translational Pulmonology, Department of Pulmonary Medicine, Rurlandklinik, Essen, Germany, 2Adult Cystic Fibrosis Center, Department of Pulmonary Medicine, Rurlandklinik, Essen, Germany, 3Department of Pulmonary Medicine, Ruhrlandklinik, Essen, Germany, 4Translational Pulmonology, Department of Pulmonary Medicine, Rurlandklinik, University Medical Center Essen, Essen, Germany
records.abstract_text:
Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a life-limiting genetic disease associated with altered immune regulation. CFTR triple modulator therapy (elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor, ETI) improves clinical outcomes in people with CF (pwCF). However, its impact on adaptive immunity remains unclear.

We analyzed peripheral blood CD4⁺ T cells from healthy controls (n=22) and pwCF (n=21) at baseline and 3, 6, and 9 months after ETI initiation. CD4⁺ T cells were immunophenotyped by flow cytometry directly after isolation and after 48 hours in vitro culture with or without activation (αCD3/CD28). Plasma levels of 12 cytokines were quantified at each timepoint by multiplex-ELISA.

At baseline, pwCF showed increased CD69⁺CD4⁺ T cells (p<0.05), along with more resting regulatory T cells (rTreg, CD25+CD127-CD45RA+) and fewer effector regulatory T cells (eTreg, CD25+CD127-CD45RO+, p<0.01), suggesting chronic T-cell activation and impaired immune regulation compared to controls. ETI treatment gradually reduced CD69⁺ T cells to levels similar to those of controls, while the activation capacity in response to αCD3/CD28 activation remained unchanged. ETI progressively lowered rTreg numbers, while giving rise to eTregs, particularly after activation, reaching values comparable to controls. Plasma cytokines mirrored some of the cellular changes. IL-10, a cytokine also released by eTregs, was initially significantly lower in pwCF than in controls but increased post-ETI. This may reflect partial recovery of Treg-associated immunoregulatory function. Despite ETI treatment, IL-22 levels in pwCF remained below those measured in controls (p<0.05), suggesting persistent deficits in epithelial barrier-associated pathways.

Overall, ETI not only improved clinical outcomes in pwCF but also rebalanced CD4⁺ T cell subsets and cytokine profiles. These findings support the concept that CFTR modulators may recover the functional properties of the adaptive immune system, contributing to therapeutic benefits in pwCF.

records.title: 'Knowing I am different makes me strong': a UK survey of children and young people with cystic fibrosis

session.title: Workshop 06 - Integrating mental health and neurocognitive care in contemporary cystic fibrosis practice

records.authors_text: E. Lee Mindel1
records.affiliations_text: 1Cystic Fibrosis Trust, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
We aimed to find out what was important to children and young people with CF in the UK. We wanted to hear their feelings and thoughts about CF, as well as the positive things in their lives.

We ran one survey for children aged 6-11 and another for those aged 12-17. We worked with our Youth Advisory Group to write the questions, based on topics they felt strongly about. 166 children responded.

Respondents gave us an insight into the richness and positivity of their lives. Their hobbies and sources of pride are exciting and diverse. “The best thing about life is knowing that I am different to others. That makes me feel strong.”

We asked children aged 6-11 how CF makes them feel. The most common emotions were feeling ‘unique’ (57%) and ‘special’ (40%). 23% said that CF makes them feel worried and 20% said it makes them feel sad. The most common worry was that they are different from their friends and can’t do all the same things that they can.

We asked those aged 12-17 if they worried about CF and what they worried about. 71% said that they worry about CF ‘a bit’ and 25% said that they worry about CF ‘a lot’ or ‘all the time’. The most frequently mentioned worry was worsening physical health and death.

We asked young people whether they predict that CF will affect what they do in the future and the choices they make. 75% of respondents said that they feel it will have an effect. Some said that their lives would be limited due to deteriorating health and avoiding careers and activities that would be dangerous. Some said that having CF will affect their choices for the better, pushing them to achieve, experience the world and help others. “The knowledge that life is more precious should hopefully inspire me to try everything.”

These surveys reveal a resilient community, proud of their unique strengths and diverse interests despite the challenges they face. Young people acknowledge the impact of CF on their future but are determined to live fulfilling lives.

records.title: Sleep quality and quantity: relationship with overall wellness, energy, exercise and mood in adults with cystic fibrosis before / after elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor at baseline using the AWESCORE

session.title: Workshop 07 - Physiotherapy in the CFTR modulator era: integrating exercise capacity, strength, sleep and daily participation

records.authors_text: B. Button1,2, A. Talbot1,2, M. Dharmakumara1,2, M. Poulsen1,2, C. Rang1, D. Keating1,2, T. Kotsimbos1,2, A. Young3, P. Wark1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Alfred Hospital, Bayside Health, Respiratory Medicine, Melbourne, Australia, 2Monash University, Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences, Melbourne, Australia, 3Box Hill Hospital, Eastern Health, Respiratory Medicine, Melbourne, Australia
records.abstract_text:
Some people with Cystic Fibrosis (pwCF) report insomnia, poor quality and disrupted sleep.

Objective: measure the quality and quantity of sleep before and after starting elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) and its relationship to exercise, energy, mood and general health at baseline function.

Methods: before and after starting ETI measure the 5 domains of wellness using the Alfred Wellness Score (AWESCORE), a recently developed patient reported outcome measure. This comprises 10 wellness items each valued 0-10 and Total Wellness Score 0-100. Higher scores denote greater wellness. We analysed changes in the AWESCORE on ETI. then the relationship between sleep and cough, sputum, energy, exercise participation, appetite, weight, mood and general health.

Results: at study baseline the characteristics of 123 well adults with CF were (mean and std. deviation): age 36.9 (10.7) years; FEV1 63.5 (23.1)% pred.; BMI 24.0 (6.5); AWESCORE Total Score 67.3 (12.6); sleep 6.4 (2.0); cough 6.2 (1.9); sputum 6.2 (1.9); energy 6.2 (1.9); exercise participation 5.9 (2.3); appetite 7.8 (2.1); weight 7.9 (2.1); mood 6.9 (2.3); anxiety 6.9 (2.3); general health 6.8 (2.0). There was an increase in total AWESCORE following treatment with ETI, mean difference 18 (95%CI 15-20, p<0.0001; and a significant increase in sleep score, mean difference 1.3 (95% CI 0.9-1.8), p<0.0001. Table 1: Correlation of change seen between sleep and selected individual scores. These values were analysed using Pearson's correlation.

Change correlated with sleepChange in coughChange in sputumChange in energyChange in exerciseChange in appetiteChange in weightChange in moodChange in general healthR value0.2-0.070.50.30.2-0.060.50.4p value (two-tailed)0.020.4<0.0001=0.00010.020.5<0.0001<0.0001

Conclusions: Treatment with ETI resulted in significant increases in all items of the AWESCORE including sleep. There were highly significant correlations between sleep and scores on energy, exercise participation, mood and sense of general health.

Reference: The AWESCORE, a patient-reported outcome measure: development, feasibility, reliability, validity and responsiveness for adults with CF. ERJ Open Research July 2021, 7 (3) 00120-2021; DOI: 10.1183/23120541.00120-2021.

person.biography:
Dr Brenda Button has been privileged to work in Cystic Fibrosis from newborn screening through childhood, adolescence and adulthood over the past three decades. She is an accredited instructor of modern airway clearance with the International Physiotherapy Group for CF (learning from the originators of modern airway clearance therapy). Her research contribution includes airway clearance therapy, effects on gastroesophageal function, exercise and exercise testing, continence in women and men with lung disease, adherence, use of mucolytic agents and quality of life. She has published more than 60 peer reviewed studies.  She is frequently invited to speak and teach internationally and is a Winston Churchill Fellow investigating managing patients with suppurative lung disease on ECMO bridging to lung transplant. She teaches undergraduate and post graduate physiotherapists and supervises PhD and Masters students at Monash University, Melbourne Australia.

records.title: Variability in gut microbiome responses to elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor therapy in people with cystic fibrosis is associated with distinct intestinal inflammation profiles

session.title: Workshop 08 - The hidden burden of cystic fibrosis: liver diseases and the gastrointestinal ecosystem

records.authors_text: J. Hudson1, L. Birimberg-Schwartz2, J. van Dorst1, B.U. Pushpakumara1, J. Halim1, F. Khan3, T. Gonska3, M. Wilschanski2, C.Y Ooi1
records.affiliations_text: 1UNSW, School of Clinical Medicine, Sydney, Australia, 2Hadassah Medical Center, Department of Pediatric Gastroenterology, Jerusalem, Israel, 3The Hospital for Sick Children, Sickkids Research Institute, Toronto, Canada
records.abstract_text:
Gastrointestinal responses to elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) therapy in individuals with cystic fibrosis (CF) have shown variability across studies. Here, we evaluated longitudinal changes in gut microbiome composition in relation to patient-specific inflammation trajectories.

Thirty-five CF patients were assessed at baseline, 6-and 12-mo after ETI. Stool samples underwent metagenomics and quantification of M2-pyruvate kinase (M2PK) and calprotectin inflammatory markers. Based on changes to intestinal inflammation participants were classified as IMPROVED, NON-IMPROVED, or persistently NORMAL and assessed for ETI-associated changes in the gut microbiome.

Thirteen individuals (41%) showed IMPROVED M2PK following ETI (>50% relative and >2µg decrease from baseline), yet this did not correspond to changes in ⍺ (p>0.05) or β-diversity (p=0.26), or species composition. NON-IMPROVERS (>50% relative and >2µg increase from baseline, or persistent inflammation >4µg, (31%), exhibited shifts in β-diversity over time (p=0.03), and increased E. coli (q=0.21), Bifidobacterium bifidum (q=0.21), and Streptococcus salivarius (q=0.03). Those with NORMAL M2PK [<4µg ( 28%)], showed increased ⍺-diversity (p=0.03) and richness (p=0.04) with ETI. Grouping individuals based on their calprotectin trajectory, showed a moderate consensus between the two markers (k=0.6), but no alterations to microbiome structure or composition were detected.

Changes to GI inflammation (M2PK) in response to ETI appears individualistic and is accompanied by different patterns in microbiome profiles. Only individuals with normal baseline M2PK markers showed improvements in their microbiome structure with ETI, whilst the microbiome pattern of those with reduced inflammation was indicative of ongoing microbial imbalances. In contrast, patients with ongoing inflammation did exhibit changes, suggestive of microbiome instability. Next steps include correlation studies with video capsule endoscopy and symptoms.

person.title: Mr.
person.biography:
Dan is a PhD student at the University of Nottingham, England, and part of the MAGNIFY Strategic Research Centre, which is exploring the use of lung magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in CF. His work is specifically focused on the development of a toolkit of resources to support the communication and understanding of lung MRI results.
Dan has a particular interest in the use of qualitative research methods and public involvement in health research. He has experience of using both in the development of the MRI toolkit, as well as interventions in type 1 diabetes and motor neuron disease.
In 2024, he established the CF Qualitative Research Network, an international group of researchers with an interest in the use of qualitative methods in CF research. The network provides a space for peer support, shared learning & collaboration.

person.title: Ms.
person.biography: Karen Raraigh, MGC, is an Assistant Professor of Genetic Medicine at Johns Hopkins University. She earned her Master’s in Genetic Counseling from the University of Maryland in 2008 and completed a Fulbright fellowship in Dublin, Ireland from 2008-2009. Her work has focused on genotype-phenotype correlations, patient and provider education, and engagement of genetic counselors with CF clinics. Ms. Raraigh co-leads the CFTR2 project and national efforts to advance CF-specific genetic counseling and professional collaboration in the field. She has contributed to development of guidelines related to CF carrier screening, newborn screening, genetic counseling, and genetic testing and is committed to the improvement of CF screening and care through research and education.

content.biography: Karen Raraigh received her Masters in Genetic Counseling from the University of Maryland School of Medicine in 2008.  Immediately after, she completed a Fulbright-funded research project within the adult CF clinic at St. Vincent’s University Hospital in Dublin, Ireland and then joined the Genetics Department at Nationwide Children’s Hospital in Columbus, OH as a pediatric genetic counselor.  In 2011, Ms. Raraigh joined a research team at Johns Hopkins University, where she is heavily involved in the Clinical and Functional Translation of CFTR (CFTR2) project and database, the CF Genome Project in which 5,000 adults with CF underwent whole genome sequencing, and an initiative to investigate the development of a CF specific genetic counseling service. Her primary interests are genotype-phenotype correlation and the impact of CFTR modulators, as well as communication of genetic information and CF genetics education.  She has participated in the writing of several guidelines regarding CFTR testing and CF care and currently serves as the chair of the Cystic Fibrosis Special Interest Group within the National Society of Genetic Counselors.

person.biography:
Martina Kapatou is a Cystic Fibrosis Specialist Nurse at King’s College Hospital, where she has been part of the multidisciplinary CF team for the past six years. Prior to this role, she worked for three years on a respiratory ward, spending her final year as a Junior Sister, gaining strong clinical and leadership experience in respiratory care.
Martina has chaired the CF Governance Meeting within her team for the last four years, reflecting her commitment to service development, quality improvement, and safe, effective patient care. She has a particular interest in improving patient outcomes and the efficiency of CF services and has actively participated in quality improvement projects focused on service delivery. Most recently, she and her team presented at the Royal Society of Medicine on changes implemented to enhance the annual review process, demonstrating how collaborative team working can lead to more efficient and patient-centred care.
At ECFS, Martina will be speaking on vascular access in cystic fibrosis. She is trained in midline insertion and is passionate about ensuring patients are fully informed about their vascular access options. She strongly advocates for open conversations with patients and improved team understanding to support shared decision-making and optimal care.

person.title: Dr.
person.biography:
Julianna Bailey, PhD, RD is the Senior Cystic Fibrosis & Respiratory Dietitian at Alfred Health in Melbourne, Victoria, Australia. With over 15 years clinical experience across paediatric and adult CF programs in the United States and Australia, she leads clinical respiratory nutrition services, nutrition research, and quality improvement initiatives within the Alfred Health Adult CF Centre.
Dr Bailey’s research explores how CFTR modulators are reshaping nutritional and metabolic phenotypes in cystic fibrosis, as well as the behavioural and systems-level factors that influence these evolving patterns of care. Her broader scholarship includes telehealth integration, Learning Health System and implementation-science approaches, food insecurity and social risk, and patient and clinician experience of care. She has published numerous peer-reviewed abstracts and manuscripts, authored CF nutrition guidelines, written two textbook chapters, and led multiple national and multi-centre quality-improvement initiatives.
Dr. Bailey has held leadership roles with the Cystic Fibrosis Learning Network, the CF Foundation Experience of Care Steering Committee, the CF Foundation Program Planning Committee, and several international working groups focused on nutrition, care design, and guideline development. Her current work integrates metabolic assessment, behavioural nutrition strategies, and implementation science to modernise nutrition care models for adults with CF.

Nicola Hodgson is a musculoskeletal physiotherapist at the Manchester Adults Cystic Fibrosis Unit, UK, specialising in managing musculoskeletal issues and supporting patients with physical activity and exercise. She qualified in 2004 from the University of Manchester and completed an MSc in 2019, focusing on the reliability of the Manchester musculoskeletal screening tool.

She is a past fellow of the North American Primary Care Research Group, the Menopause Society, and the Patrick Nash Cystic Fibrosis Research Institute. She has published three books, numerous articles, and op-eds on disability, and teaches medical and doctoral students about the intersections of health, disability, and disease in society.

person.biography:
Deborah Baines is Professor of Molecular Physiology at the School of Health and Medical Sciences, City St George’s, University of London. She has spent her career working in airway epithelial ion and solute transport and in 2021 she was awarded the Hans Ussing Prize Lecture at Experimental Biology in recognition of her work in the field. Her group were the first to identify that glucose concentration in airway surface liquid (ASL) was increased during hyperglycaemia and with respiratory disease (eg in Cystic Fibrosis Related Diabetes) and that this was associated with increased risk of hospital-acquired respiratory infection. Since then, she has shown that glucose transport and metabolism are important determinants of glucose concentrations in ASL, and that raised glucose affects the innate immune function of the ASL in cystic fibrosis (CF). More recently she has been a PI on two Strategic Research Centre grants funded by the Cystic Fibrosis Trust, developing CRISPR gene editing therapies for cystic fibrosis. She currently leads a CF Foundation project to deliver novel CFTR mRNA gene therapies to the airway using targeted nanoparticles. 
She is a Fellow of The Physiological Society and is an editorial Board Member American Journal of Physiology- Cell and Molecular Physiology.

content.biography: Deborah Baines is a scientist working in the Institute of Infection and Immunity at St George’s, University of London. Her work is predominantly focused on the regulation of ion and solute transport across airway epithelium and how this is altered in diseases such as Cystic Fibrosis.  She developed a new and unexplored area of research, investigating glucose homeostasis in the lungs and how hyperglycaemia promotes respiratory infection. She is currently working on therapeutic gene editing for Cystic Fibrosis (funded by the Cystic Fibrosis Trust).

person.title: Prof.
person.biography: As an assistant professor at KU Leuven's Laboratory of Respiratory Diseases and Thoracic Surgery (BREATHE), the research of my team focuses on precision medicine for chronic lung disease. I am also affiliated to the Center for Molecular Medicine and serve as Co-PI at the Leuven Viral Vector Core. My research centers on advancing genetic therapies for cystic fibrosis. This spans mutation-agnostic gene addition using adeno-associated viral vectors to precise CRISPR/Cas gene editing, particularly targeting drug-refractory CFTR mutations via base and prime editing. We prioritize translational testing of personalized medicine strategies using humanized in vitro models, such as patient-derived organoid models and primary airway cultures. I currently lead projects funded by the Belgian and Italian CF patient association/King Baudouin Foundation and Cystic Fibrosis Foundation. These grants drive the development of genetic therapies and delivery strategies for cystic fibrosis. With our MSCA doctoral training network GET-IN, a GEne Therapy INnovation Training Network, we will leverage expertise and collaboration on gene therapy development, delivery and validation in advanced in vitro model systems (https://www.get-in.org/). With MSCA lifeLUNG (https://www.lifelung.eu/) we leverage CRISPR gene modulation with ex vivo lung perfusion models to unravel the role of extracellular barriers on gene delivery, besides assessing early tolerability to the gene therapy product.

person.biography: I am Assistant Professor at UMinho and Leading Researcher in the Bacterial&Biofilm Group of the Health Biotechnology and Bioengineering Research Line at Centre of Biological Engineering, University of Minho, Portugal.  My research focuses on the control of biofilm- and devices-associated infections; characterization of the antimicrobial resistance phenomena of single- and multispecies consortia and the molecular aspects underlying biofilm-associated infections pathogenesis, deciphering microbial communication and interspecies interactions; the design of bi-functional antibacterial/antifungal coatings and the development of nanocarriers to drug delivery into bacteria and site of infection. person.biography: Migle Gabrielaite has a background in biochemistry and bioinformatics, and during her PhD she investigated chronic infections and their genomic adaptation to the human host. She is currently a senior researcher and Marie Skłodowska-Curie postdoctoral fellow studying the evolution of Achromobacter spp. in the host environment, particularly in people with cystic fibrosis. Her work focuses on how Achromobacter adapts during long-term infection, how resistance mechanisms emerge and change over time, and how clinical isolates relate to those found in environmental reservoirs. She also investigates the origins and spread of epidemic Achromobacter strains: how they emerge, transmit, and persist across patients.

Pierre-Régis Burgel is currently Professor of Respiratory Medicine at Paris Descartes University in Paris, France, where he is also a senior researcher and co-Principal Investigator in the Acute and Chronic Airway Infection Laboratory (Cochin Institute, INSERM, Paris France). Professor Burgel is a senior consultant at the Respiratory Medicine Department of Cochin Hospital in Paris. Professor Burgel completed his medical training at the University of Paris, School of Medicine in 1999. After a post-doctoral fellowship at the University of California in San Francisco (USA) (1999-2001), he obtained a PhD in respiratory cell biology at the University of Paris.

He received the 2022 European Respiratory Society mid-career GOLD medal for Cystic Fibrosis and the ECFS award in 2025.

Mall is Professor and Chair of the Department of Pediatric Respiratory Medicine, Immunology & Critical Care Medicine and the Christiane Herzog Cystic Fibrosis Center at the Charité University Medical Center Berlin, Germany. He received his M.D. from the University of Freiburg, Germany, and completed postdoctoral training at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, USA, and the University of Heidelberg, Germany, where he joined the faculty until his current appointment at Charité - Universitätsmedizin Berlin. He is a pediatric pulmonologist and physician-scientist and one of the founding directors of the German Center for Lung Research (DZL) and the German Center for Child and Adolescent Health (DZKJ). He is a member of the German National Academy of Sciences Leopoldina and a Fellow of the ERS (FERS). Marcus Mall’s research focus is on the pathogenesis and development of novel diagnostic approaches and therapeutic strategies for cystic fibrosis and other muco-obstructive lung diseases. His team uses an interdisciplinary translational approach integrating basic and clinical research to improve our understanding of cystic fibrosis and other muco-obstructive lung disease and accelerate the translation of research results into the clinic.

content.biography: Marcus A. Mall is Professor and Director of the Department of Pediatric Pulmonology, Immunology & Intensive Care Medicine and CF Center at the Charité – University Medical Center Berlin, Germany, and Professor at the Berlin Institute of Health (BIH). He graduated from the University of Freiburg Medical School and trained at the Universities of Freiburg and Heidelberg, Germany, and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, USA. Marcus Mall is board certified in Pediatrics, Pediatric Pulmonology, Allergy and Infectious Diseases. He is a Fellow of ERS (FERS), serves on the Editorial Board of the European Respiratory Journal (ERJ) and Program Planning Committee of the North American Cystic Fibrosis Conference (NACFC). In 2011, Marcus Mall was one of the founding directors of the German Center for Lung Research (DZL), where he continues to serve as coordinator of the CF research program. Marcus Mall’s research focus is on the pathogenesis and development of novel diagnostic approaches and therapeutic strategies for CF lung disease. His research team uses an interdisciplinary translational research strategy, integrating basic research in model systems with cohort studies and early phase clinical trials, to improve our understanding of CF lung disease and the translation of research results and novel therapies into the clinic.

person.title: Dr.
person.biography: Sara Hernando Amado is a microbiologist and a PhD in Biology. She is the Principal Investigator of the "Ecology en evolution of antibiotic resistance: evolution to tackle bacterial infections" group at Centro Nacional de Biotecnología (CNB-CSIC), in Madrid. Her laboratory uses adaptive laboratory evolution experiments to predict and understand the evolution of antibiotic resistance and identify its associated trade-offs. In particular, they study the evolution of mutation-driven antibiotic resistance, with a main interest in the ESKAPE pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Her goal is the design of rational therapeutic strategies using existing antibiotics by the identification of robust trade-offs of evolution.

person.biography: Dr. Eddie (Edwina) Landau, PhD, is a consultant clinical and medical psychologist working at the Graub CF Center, Institute of Pulmonology at the Schneider Children's Medical Center (SCMC), Israel.  Clinical activities involve a wide range of psychotherapeutic and psychodynamic approaches as well as diagnostic work. Research projects include clinical adherence interventions, evaluating coping strategies, as well as assessing the psychological effects and implications of the new CFTR modulators. Dr. Landau is a core committee member of the ECFS Standards of Care projects, and was the co-chair of the ECFS Mental Health Working Group in the modulator era (MHWG) for the past 6 years. Dr Landau has helped to facilitate mental health programming for the ECFS conferences, as well as helping to organize a series of global training webinars for all multidisciplinary CF teams. She has written research papers on psychosocial aspects of CF and participated in multicenter international studies.  Dr. Landau also has a private psychotherapy practice in Tel Aviv, working with adults, children and couples. She works with a wide range of mental health difficulties, including depression, anxiety, trauma, stress‑related problems, and relationship issues. She is also a qualified yoga teacher and is researching the benefits of yoga in breathing techniques in mental well being.
