records.title: Synonymous CFTR variants contribute to functional variability in human nasal epithelial cells
records.authors_text: V. Capurro1, E. Pesce1, V. Tomati1, C. Pastorino1, A. Dighero1, R. Pisani1, A. Quarato1, M. Galli2, L.J.V. Galietta3,4, F. Cresta5, C. Castellani5, N. Pedemonte1
records.affiliations_text: 1IRCCS Istituto Giannina Gaslini, UOC Genetica Medica, Genova, Italy, 2IRCCS Istituto Giannina Gaslini, Laboratory of Molecular Genetics and Biobanks, Genova, Italy, 3Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine (TIGEM), Pozzuoli, Italy, 4University of Naples Federico II, Department of Translational Medical Sciences (DISMET), Napoli, Italy, 5IRCCS Istituto Giannina Gaslini, UOSD Centro Fibrosi Cistica, Genova, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Human nasal epithelial (hNE) cells are a reliable ex-vivo model to study CFTR function. Defining reference CFTR activity in non-CF individuals is crucial to identify subtle functional alterations and to evaluate CFTR rescue strategies. This study aimed to characterize CFTR functional variability in hNE cultures and explore potential genetic determinants of reduced activity.

Methods: hNE cells were collected from ~50 non-CF donors and differentiated in air–liquid interface. CFTR-dependent chloride secretion was measured by short-circuit current under symmetrical chloride (SC) and after imposing a chloride gradient (GC) to enhance CFTR-mediated anion transport. CFTR gene analysis by NGS was performed for most subjects, with sequencing ongoing for a subset.

Results: Under SC, CFTR activity ranged 10–35 µA/cm², with marked inter-individual variability. GC induced ~two-fold increases in most cultures. Among samples <20 µA/cm², one subgroup responded strongly (~three-fold in GC) and another modestly (~1.5-fold), including obligate and unrecognized carriers. NGS revealed synonymous variants potentially affecting protein folding or expression: p.Thr854= (modulating local translation), p.Glu528= (splicing/mRNA structure), p.Glu146= (rare, possible mRNA effects), p.Gly91= (splicing, reduced protein), and a missense p.Arg31Cys (impacting conformation/trafficking). These findings suggest even synonymous changes can contribute to inter-individual variability.

Conclusion: hNE cell coltures robustly detect subclinical CFTR dysfunction. Combined functional and genetic analysis highlights a potential role of synonymous variants in modulating CFTR folding and activity, supporting the use of this ex-vivo model for personalized CFTR assessment.

Supported by Fondazione FFC grants FFC #9/2019 and FFC #10/2021, and Italian MoH grant PNRR-MR1-2023-12378412.

person.biography: I obtained my master's degree in Medical-Pharmaceutical Biotechnology in 2012, at the University of Genoa. In 2016 I obtained my PhD in Genetics at the same University. From 2016 to today I have been involved in projects funded by the Fondazione Ricerca Fibrosi Cistica - ETS and a European Horizon 2020 Project, aimed at identifying new therapeutic strategies for cystic fibrosis. Projects that were carried out at the UOC Medical Genetics of the Giannina Gaslini Institute, where I have been carrying out my scientific activity since 2016 thanks to scientific fellowship, research contracts and since 2023 as a Ricercatore Sanitario. Since 2020 my activity has focused on the management of primary cell cultures obtained from nasal brushing of CF patients within theratyping projects. records.title: Functional characterization of rare variants c.4055A>C and c.3352T>C in the CFTR gene using an intestinal organoids model
records.authors_text: M. Krasnova1, A. Efremova1, N. Kashirskaya2, E. Kondratyeva2, D. Goldshtein1
records.affiliations_text: 1Research Centre for Medical Genetics, Stem Cell Genetics Laboratory, Moscow, Russian Federation, 2Research Centre for Medical Genetics, Moscow, Russian Federation
records.abstract_text:
Objective: To define the functional impact and therapeutic potential of two uncharacterized rare CFTR variants, c.4055A>C (p.Q1352P) and c.3352T>C (p.S1118P), using a patient-derived intestinal organoid model. These specific variants have not been previously described in major cystic fibrosis databases.

Method: We utilized the forskolin-induced swelling assay in intestinal organoids from patients with genotypes c.1392+1G>A/c.4055A>C and c.3528delC/c.3352T>C. Organoids homozygous for F508del were used as a control. Functional response was quantified before and after treatment with CFTR modulators: ivacaftor (IVA), lumacaftor/ivacaftor (LUM/IVA), tezacaftor/ivacaftor (TEZ/IVA), and elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ELX/TEZ/IVA).

Results: Both variants demonstrated high residual CFTR function, with organoid swelling significantly exceeding the F508del/F508del control, classifying them as mild (Class III-VI) mutations. Organoids carrying the c.4055A>C variant responded robustly to all modulators. Similarly, the c.3352T>C variant showed extreme residual function and high efficacy for all tested drugs, including the triple combination. In contrast, F508del/F508del organoids required corrector combinations (LUM/IVA, TEZ/IVA) for rescue, with ELX/TEZ/IVA being most effective.

Conclusion: The rare variants c.4055A>C and c.3352T>C are mild CFTR mutations with significant residual function. Their strong response in organoids to CFTR modulators, particularly the triple-combination ELX/TEZ/IVA, predicts high clinical efficacy of targeted therapy for patients carrying these genotypes.

records.title: In the presence of the D110H mutation: how is the clinical course shaped?

person.title: Dr
person.institution: Hacettepe University İhsan Doğramacı Children Hospital

records.authors_text: E. Altay Tanyer1, E. Yalçın1, T. Kantemir1, B. Çapraz Yavuz1, N. Emiralioğlu1, D. Doğru1, U. Özçelik1
records.affiliations_text: 1Hacettepe University School of Medicine, Department of Pediatric Pulmonology, Ankara, Turkey
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The D110H mutation is a rare variant on exon 4 of the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene. It is more prevalent in Southern Europe, Turkey, Italy, and Iran, and has generally been associated with pseudo-Bartter syndrome (PBS) in the literature. While D110H is defined as "CF-causing" in the CFTR2 database, it is classified as "disease-causing with varying clinical consequence" in CFTR-Fr. This study evaluates the clinical and laboratory findings of cystic fibrosis (CF) patients with the D110H mutation to assess its impact on disease progression.

Methods: We retrospectively analysed 24 years of data from 21 patients carrying the D110H mutation.

Results: Median age at diagnosis was 5 months; 95.2% were diagnosed with CF and 4.8% with Cystic Fibrosis Screen Positive Inconclusive Diagnosis (CFSPID). At presentation, 38.1% of patients exhibited PBS. Other reasons for admission included failure to thrive (28.6%), elevated immunoreactive trypsinogen (IRT) (9.5%), and pancreatitis (9.5%). During a median follow-up of 11 years, 80% maintained their CF diagnosis, while 19% were reclassified as CFTR-related disorder (CFTR-RD). Mean FEV1 was 101.78±12.33% and 47.6% were colonised with methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA). Pancreatic sufficiency was preserved in 8 of 9 patients tested. While 47.6% showed no systemic involvement, 28.6% had PBS, 9.5% pancreatitis, 9.5% recurrent infections, and 4.8% pancreatic insufficiency. In the CFTR-RD group (n=4), second alleles carried residual function or unidentified mutations. In the CF group (n=17), 8 had residual function and 8 had minimal function mutations on the second allele.

Conclusion: D110H is frequently associated with PBS, preserved pancreatic sufficiency, and normal FEV1 values. The clinical phenotype and disease severity are significantly determined by the accompanying mutation. Long-term follow-up and genetic characterisation are critical for optimal patient management.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Large deletions and duplications (copy number variations, CNVs) in the CFTR gene are rare in cystic fibrosis (CF) compared with common mutations. This study aimed to evaluate the frequency of large CFTR CNVs in Türkiye and their clinical impact using data from the National Cystic Fibrosis Registry (NCFR).

Methods: NCFR data from 2024 were retrospectively analyzed. Among 2,150 CF patients followed in 36 centers, those with identified large CFTR CNVs were included. Demographic, clinical, microbiological, and treatment-related characteristics were recorded.

Results: A total of 43 patients (2.00%) had large CNVs, 53.4% of whom were male. Median (min-max) age at diagnosis was 0.33 (min-max: 0.08-9) years. Newborn screening was positive in 44.1%, and 9.30% had a history of meconium ileus. Mean±SD sweat chloride levels were 85.31±25.97 mEq/L and 93.00±22.11 mEq/L. Inhaled antibiotic therapy was used by 34.8% of patients, while advanced respiratory support was required in three patients. CFTR modulator therapy was used by two patients with heterozygous F508del mutations. Median (min-max) BMI Z-score was −0.67 (-2.73-2.72), and the mean±SD FEV₁ value in the spirometry test was 76.81%±26.00. Ten patients (23.2%) experienced a mean±SD of 2.10±1.10 pulmonary exacerbations per year. Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Methicillin-resistance Staphylococcus aureus were detected in 41.8% and 13.9% of patients, respectively. Pancreatic insufficiency and liver disease were present in 23.2% and 20.9% of patients, respectively. ABPA was recorded in 3 patients, diabetes in 2 patients, and Dios in 1 patient.

Conclusions: Children with large CFTR CNVs constitute a small but clinically significant subgroup with increased disease burden, characterized by chronic airway infection, and frequent organ involvement. Systematic evaluation of large CFTR CNVs may improve risk stratification and support genotype-based follow-up strategies in CF.

records.title: Clinical significance of 5T polymorphism genotype in a cohort of cystic fibrosis Portuguese patients

person.institution: Unidade Local de Saúde de São João

records.authors_text: S. Silva1, I. Pais Cunha1, L. Almeida1, A. Amorim1, T. Barbosa2, A.L. Cardoso2, P. Azevedo3, E. Fragoso3, R. Penteado4, T. Reis Silva4, S. Castanhinha5, S. Santos5, I. Azevedo1
records.affiliations_text: 1Unidade Local de Saúde de São João, Porto, Portugal, 2Unidade Local de Saúde de Santo António, Porto, Portugal, 3Unidade Local de Saúde de Santa Maria, Lisboa, Portugal, 4Unidade Local de Saúde de Coimbra, Coimbra, Portugal, 5Unidade Local de Saúde de São José, Lisboa, Portugal
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: A common genetic variant among patients with cystic fibrosis (CF) is 5T. This variant exhibits a highly variable clinical phenotype, particularly when present in combination with other CFTR alleles. The aim of this study was to characterize the clinical and genetic features of Portuguese patients carrying this variant.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective analysis of children and adults followed in 5 CF- Reference Centers in Portugal, who carried at least one 5T variant in trans with another CFTR variant.

Results: Fifteen patients were included (7 males), with a median age 22 years [IQR 13–45], and median age at diagnosis of 13 years [IQR 3–33]; two patients had a positive neonatal screening. Eight patients had 5T in trans with F508del (1 of whom also had another CF-causing (CFc) variant in cis with the F508del mutation), four had 5T in trans with a non-F508del CFc variant, and three had F508del and another CFc variant in cis with 5T. Seven patients had a 5T;12TG genotype, while TG repeat length was unknown in seven. Median sweat chloride was 60 mmol/L [IQR 43–75] at diagnosis. Thirteen patients were diagnosed with CF, one with CF related disorder, and one with CF screen positive inconclusive diagnosis. Chest CT abnormalities were observed in 11 patients. Pancreatic insufficiency was present in two patients, and six reported gastrointestinal symptoms. Respiratory symptoms were present in 11 patients, and five had Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates. Median FEV₁ was 87% [IQR 66-105]. Three patients initiated highly effective modulator therapy, one of whom discontinued treatment due to adverse effects.

Conclusion: This is the first multicentre Portuguese cohort describing patients carrying the CFTR 5T variant. Most patients showed clinically relevant respiratory involvement. These findings reinforce the importance of comprehensive genetic evaluation to understand the impact of the 5T variant in the disease and its genotype-phenotype correlations.

records.abstract_text:
Objective: To conduct an association study of PPARG, PPARD, UCP2, and UCP3 gene variants with nutritional status and body composition in children with cystic fibrosis (CF).

Methods: Patients with CF (F508del/F508del) (n=478) aged 0 to 18 years (11.8 ± 3.8 years). Body composition was analyzed before and after 1 year of targeted therapy. Polymorphisms (SNPs) in the PPARG, PPARD, UCP2, and UCP3 genes were tested using PCR and RFLP analysis.

Results: After 1 year of targeted therapy, body weight in boys significantly increased by 5.3 (±2.5) kg and height by 5.7 (±1.7) cm (p<0.01), while in girls, body weight increased by 4.5 (±1.9) kg and height by 4.8 (±1.3) cm (p<0.01). In boys, %FM increased from -0.23 to 0.13 SD (p=0.04). In girls, %FM increased from -0.15 to 0.08 SD (p=0.02) and %SMM decreased from 0.79 to 0.6 SD (p=0.04).

The TT genotype of the UCP2 gene is associated with excess BMI (+1.1 to +2.0 Z score) and class 2 obesity (+3.0 Z score) (OR=9.583, p=0.044). The CC genotype of the UCP2 polymorphism is associated with normal SMM (-1 to +1 Z score) (OR=6.769; p=0.031). The CC genotype of the UCP3 gene is associated with excess BMI and class 2 obesity (OR=5.926; p=0.050).

The CC genotype of the UCP3 gene is associated with a decrease in ACM (<-1.1 Z score) (OR=12.857; p=0.039). The TT genotype of the UCP3 gene is associated with low body fat (OR=8.000; p=0.016) and high SMM (+1.1 to +2.0 Z score) (OR=7.143 (95% CI: 1.352-37.746; χ2=6.334; p=0.042).

The GG genotype of the PPARG gene is associated with decreased body fat (<-1.1 Z score) (OR=15.500; p=0.015), and the CC genotype of the PPARD gene is associated with decreased body fat (OR=17.500; p=0.016).

Conclusion: Revealed an increase in the proportion of FM after 1 year of targeted drug treatment. Carriage of the TT genotype of the UCP2 gene and the CC genotype of the UCP3 gene is associated with a violation of body composition.

records.title: Genes of phases 1 and 2 of xenobiotic biotransformation and targeted therapy
records.authors_text: E. Zhekaite1,2, A. Voronkova1,2, E. Kondratyeva1,2, Y. Melyanovskaya1,2, M. Tarasov1
records.affiliations_text: 1Research Centre for Medical Genetics, Cystic Fibrosis, Moscow, Russian Federation, 2Research Clinical Institute of Childhood Ministry of Health of the Moscow Region, Moscow, Russian Federation
records.abstract_text:
Polymorphism of xenobiotic biotransformation genes affects the efficacy and safety of therapy.

Objectives: 400 patients (mean age 11.1±3.8 years) receiving ivacaftor/lumacaftor and elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor therapy (ETI) in 2022-2025 were examined.

Methods: study of phase-I: CYP2C9*3, CYP2C9*2, CYP2C19*2, CYP2C19*3, CYP2D6*4, CYP3A4*3, CYP3A4*1B, CYP1A1, CYP1A2 and phase-II drug metabolizing enzymes genes polymorphism: GSTT1 и GSTM1; GSTP1, GCLC, GCLM, NAT2 (c.191G>A; c.282C>T, c.341T>C, c.434A>C, c.481C>T, c.590G>A, c.803A>G, c.845A>C, c.857G>A) was performed by PCR followed by RFLP (restriction fragment length polymorphism) or AFLP (amplified fragment length polymorphism) analysis.

Results: Patients with the AC genotype of the CYP2C9*3 had higher weight (p=0.05), height (p=0.05), and better decrease sweat test (p=0.040) compared to carriers of the CC genotype, indicating a higher efficacy of targeted therapy. Better nutritional status indicators after one year of therapy were observed in patients with the GG genotype of the GSTP1 gene compared to the AA and AG genotypes (p=0.040), as well as in patients with the II genotype of the GSTM1 gene compared to the DD genotype (p=0.002 and p=0.004).

FVC, % pred., FEV1, % pred. after one year of targeted therapy were significantly higher in patients with the TT genotype of the GSLM gene compared to patients with the CC and CT genotypes (p=0.002 and p=0.004). Carriage of the AA genotype of the CYP2C19*2 genetic variant in CF with adverse events (AE) was recorded 4.4 times more often compared to children without AE (p=0.013). Carriage of the CC genotype of the CYP1A2 gene in CF with AE was recorded 2 times more often compared to children without HP (p=0.008). Carriage of the AA genotype of the CYP2D6*4 genetic variant in CF with AE was recorded 2.8 times more often compared to children without AE (p=0.007).

Conclusion: Pharmacogenetic testing allows to identify risk groups for developing AE to targeted therapy for CF.

records.title: Vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor versus elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor in two children homozygous for the complex allele p.Leu467Phe-p.Phe508del
records.authors_text: K. Schütz1,2, A. Linnemannstöns1, R. Dalferth1, F. Stanke1,2, S. Tamm1, N. Alfeis1, J. Berger3,4,5, S.Y Gräber3,4,5, M.A Mall3,4,5, A.-M. Dittrich1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Hannover Medical School, Paediatric Pneumology, Allergy and Neonatology, Hannover, Germany, 2Biomedical Research in Endstage and Obstructive Lung Disease (BREATH), German Center for Lung Research (DZL), Hannover, Germany, 3Charite Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Department of Pediatric Respiratory Medicine, Immunology and Critical Care Medicine and Cystic Fibrosis Center, Berlin, Germany, 4German Center for Lung Research (DZL), Associated Partner Site Berlin, Berlin, Germany, 5German Center for Child and Adolescent Health (DZKJ), Partner Site Berlin, Berlin, Germany
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Homozygosity for the complex allele p.Leu467Phe-p.Phe508del (L467F-F508del) is associated with failure to respond to elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) in vitro and a below average response in vivo. Clinical and functional CFTR response to the newly available vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor (VTD) in vivo in homozygous carriers of these mutations is unknown. We report clinical and functional responses towards ETI and VTD of two L467F-F508del homozygous children.

Methods: An evaluation by clinical symptoms, ppFEV1, sweat chloride concentration (SCC), sweat secretion test (SST), and nasal potential difference (nPD) measurement was assessed in two children prior CFTR modulator, during ETI and during VTD therapy.

Results: The diagnosis of F508del homozygous CF was made in early childhood. Lack of pronounced decrease in sweat chloride after initiation of ETI (- 18mmol/l to 85mmol/l and -15 mmol/l to 93 mmol/l, respectively) led to resequencing of CFTR, which revealed L467F homozygosity in both children. Both children showed low clinical responses to ETI with the girl experiencing continued decline in lung function and the boy demonstrating an above average number of pulmonary exacerbations during ETI therapy. They received nPD measurements prior and with ETI therapy, which showed below average to no responses. After switch to VTD, ppFEV1 increased by 10% in the girl. The boy did not experience any exacerbations anymore and stopped coughing. Results of nPD, SST, and SCC are pending and will be available soon.

Conclusion: Two children with L467F-F508del homozygosity suspect a greater clinical response to VTD compared to ETI. Data on CFTR function will complement clinical results. The investigation of complex alleles on CFTR modulator responsiveness is important.

person.biography: As a paediatric pneumologist, I work in the section of CF, non CF bronchiectasis, lung transplantation,  and infectious pulmonary diseases of our department. As a clinician scientist, I focus on clinical studies on pulmonary infectious diseases such as pneumonia and its complications, cystic fibrosis, and rare lung diseases. I coordinated and published e.g. the multicenter trial pedCAPNETZ and participate as PI on clinical trials in the area of CF, e.g. KaftrioFACTS/Vtx studies. I also focus on antibiotic stewardship. Beside infections and CF/non CF bronchiectasis, I am interested in immunological mechanisms in children with infectious lung diseases which I focus in further projects.

records.title: Ivacaftor versus elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor in CFTR gating mutations in combination with a class I variant: insights from patient-derived intestinal organoids

person.title: MD
person.department: Development & Regeneration, Woman and Child Unit, Cystic Fibrosis Organoid Research Lab

records.authors_text: N. Rodriguez Mier1,2, M. Proesmans1,2, Y. Van Weygaerde3, C. Knoop4, M. Boon1,2, A. Santo Ramalho1, F. Vermeulen1,2, Belgian Organoid Project
records.affiliations_text: 1KU Leuven, Development & Regeneration, Woman and Child Unit, Cystic Fibrosis Organoid Research Lab, Leuven, Belgium, 2Univeristy Hospitals Leuven, Paediatrics, Paediatric Pulomonology, Leuven, Belgium, 3Ghent University Hospital, Respiratory Medicine, Ghent, Belgium, 4Erasmus Hospital, ULB University, Respiratory Medicine, Brussels, Belgium
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To evaluate the potential added benefit of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) and vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (VTI) compared to ivacaftor in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) carrying a class III and class I mutation, and to assess whether patient-derived intestinal organoids (PDIOs) can inform individualised modulator therapy decisions.

Methods: PDIOs were generated from 4 pwCF carrying a CFTR class III mutation in trans with a class I mutation: G178R/Q493X (case 1), S1251N/G542X (case 2), R347H/2183AA>G (case 3) and Q359R/1717-1G>A (case 4). CFTR function was quantified using the forskolin-induced swelling (FIS) assay, following exposure to CFTR modulators (3 μM). Swelling responses (at 0.8 μM forskolin) were quantified as area under the curve (AUC ± SD) and compared between treatment conditions.

Results: Ivacaftor resulted in substantial rescue of CFTR function in all PDIOs. ETI produced the highest swelling responses across all cases, indicating incremental CFTR rescue compared with ivacaftor treatment alone. In cases 2–4, considerable residual CFTR function was observed. FIS responses are summarised in Table 1. Individual case-level comparisons were underpowered, but the multilevel analysis showed a significant overall treatment effect favouring ETI (p = 0.001).

Conclusion: Rectal organoid-based functional testing suggests that ETI could further increase CFTR function compared to ivacaftor treatment alone in pwCF with a combination of a class III and class I mutation. As ETI is now approved for these genotypes, the key question is whether greater in vitro CFTR function translates into meaningful clinical benefit to justify potential risks.

Objectives: To evaluate the potential added benefit of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) and vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (VTI) compared to ivacaftor in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) carrying a class III and class I mutation, and to assess whether patient-derived intestinal organoids (PDIOs) can inform individualised modulator therapy decisions.
Methods: PDIOs were generated from 4 pwCF carrying a CFTR class III mutation in trans with a class I mutation: G178R/Q493X (case 1), S1251N/G542X (case 2), R347H/2183AA>G (case 3) and Q359R/1717-1G>A (case 4). CFTR function was quantified using the forskolin-induced swelling (FIS) assay, following exposure to CFTR modulators (3 μM). Swelling responses (at 0.8 μM forskolin) were quantified as area under the curve (AUC ± SD) and compared between treatment conditions.
Results: Ivacaftor resulted in substantial rescue of CFTR function in all PDIOs. ETI produced the highest swelling responses across all cases, indicating incremental CFTR rescue compared with ivacaftor treatment alone. In cases 2–4, considerable residual CFTR function was observed. FIS responses are summarised in Table 1. Individual case-level comparisons were underpowered, but the multilevel analysis showed a significant overall treatment effect favouring ETI (p = 0.001).
Conclusion: Rectal organoid-based functional testing suggests that ETI could further increase CFTR function compared to ivacaftor treatment alone in pwCF with a combination of a class III and class I mutation. As ETI is now approved for these genotypes, the key question is whether greater in vitro CFTR function translates into meaningful clinical benefit to justify potential risks.

records.title: Differential response to elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor in children and adolescents with cystic fibrosis: a two-year real-world comparison by CFTR genotype
records.authors_text: G. Simonetti1, R. Caporale1, G. Carreras1, M. Lopes-Pacheco2, S. Del Vespa1, V. Terlizzi3
records.affiliations_text: 1Meyer Children Hospital IRCSS, Florence, Italy, 2Emory University School of Medicine, Pediatrics, Center for Cystic Fibrosis & Airways Disease Research, Atlanta, United States, 3Meyer Children's Hospital, IRCCS Department of Paediatric Medicine, Cystic Fibrosis Regional Reference Center, Florence, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Background: Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) has revolutionized cystic fibrosis (CF) care; however, its efficacy in pediatric subjects carrying one ETI-responsive and one non-responsive CFTR variant remains incompletely characterized. This study compared the realworld response to ETI using sweat chloride concentration (SCC) as a key biomarker of CFTR function.

Methods: In this retrospective, single-center study, pediatric subjects aged 6–18 years, carrying at least one p.Phe508del variant and on ETI, were included. Participants were stratified by genotype into those with two responsive variants or one responsive variant. SCC, percent predicted FEV1 (ppFEV1), BMI z-score, and pulmonary exacerbations were assessed at baseline (T0), 3–6 months (T1), 12 months (T2), and 24 months (T3). Longitudinal analyses were performed using mixed-effects models.

Results: Among 80 pediatric participants, those with two responsive variants had significantly lower median SCC at all follow-up time points (T1: 31.0 vs 46.5 mmol/L; T2: 26.0 vs 41.0 mmol/L; T3: 32.0 vs 45.0 mmol/L; all p<0.01) and were more likely to achieve SCC <30 mmol/L. Regression models confirmed that carrying two responsive variants was independently associated with a 30% lower SCC (coefficient −0.36, 95% CI −0.54 to −0.19) and a 97% reduction in odds of elevated SCC (OR 0.03). No significant differences were observed in ppFEV1, BMI z-score, or pulmonary exacerbation rates.

Conclusion: Children and adolescents with CF carrying two ETI-responsive variants exhibit a superior biochemical response to ETI. The absence of differences in clinical outcomes likely reflects preserved baseline status, reinforcing SCC as a sensitive biomarker of CFTR modulation in pediatric individuals.

records.title: Alterations in lung function and lung ventilation after commencement of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor in a paediatric cohort
records.authors_text: M. Bruorton1,2, J. Phillips1,2,3, R. Smith1,2,3, K. Carson-Chahhoud1,4,5, T. Goddard1,2, A. O'Connor2, N. Eikelis6, D. Parsons1,2,3, M. Donnelley1,2,3, A. Tai1,2,3
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Adelaide, Adelaide Medical School, Adelaide, Australia, 2Women’s and Children’s Hospital, Respiratory and Sleep Medicine, North Adelaide, Australia, 3The University of Adelaide, Robinson Research Institute, Adelaide, Australia, 4University of South Australia, Translational Medicine and Technology Group, Australian Centre for Precision Health, Adelaide, Australia, 5South Australian Health and Medical Research Institute, Adelaide, Australia, 64DMedical, Melbourne, Australia
records.abstract_text:
Background: X-ray Velocimetry (XV) is a functional X-ray imaging method that measures local lung ventilation during breathing. XV technology has been validated in animal models and is FDA approved for use in adult humans. In Australia elexacaftor+tezacaftor+ivacaftor (ETI) was approved for children aged 2-6 years in August 2024. The aim of this study was to assess how XV ventilation parameters change in response to ETI.

Methods: This prospective, single-center cohort study aimed to recruit children that were eligible to commence ETI. Children had XV imaging and pulmonary function testing (spirometry and nitrogen multiple breath washout) performed prior to starting ETI, and at 1-3 months post-ETI commencement.

Results: To date eight children have been recruited, with paired lung function and XV scans completed. All were stable and asymptomatic during study visits, although four children (57%) had a mild exacerbation requiring oral antibiotics after commencing ETI. Children were compliant, with 98% of Trikafta doses taken overall. There were no significant differences in the pulmonary function metrics over time, but the Inspiratory Ventilation Defect Percentage (VDP) was significantly higher at follow up compared to baseline. All CF children with matched lung function and XV reports had normal spirometry and LCI. However, XV visualizes regional airflow dynamics at each point in the breath, and showed substantial ventilation abnormalities exist in some of these children.

Conclusions: Our preliminary results indicate that repeated XV analysis can be applied in children and may be of use in evaluating new medications in young children. In this cohort of young children with cystic fibrosis who have normal spirometry and LCI, XV may provide early evidence of altered ventilation following ETI commencement.

Acknowledgements: This study was supported by a seed grant from 4DMedical. MD received funding from MRFF Grant RFRHPSI000013 and AEA Grant IV240100090.

records.title: Assessing lung function in adults and children with cystic fibrosis receiving highly effective modulator therapy using 129Xe MRI and pulmonary function testing

person.department: POLARIS, University MRI, Division of Clinical Medicine

records.authors_text: D. Jakymelen1, Y. Brown1, H. Marshall1, A. Biancardi1, J. Wild1, L. Smith1, Magnify Strategic Research Centre
records.affiliations_text: 1The University of Sheffield, POLARIS, University MRI, Division of Clinical Medicine, Sheffield, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To use 129Xe ventilation MRI and pulmonary function tests to assess lung function in people with cystic fibrosis (CF) receiving highly effective modulator therapy (HEMT).

Methods: Ten children (M=6, F=4) and 18 adults with CF (M=10, F=8) were assessed using Xe-MRI, spirometry and lung clearance index (LCI). Ventilation defect percent (VDP) from Xe-MRI was calculated as the proportion of the lung without ventilation. Adults also had pre-HEMT measurements ~5.5 years earlier using the same methods. Data are presented as mean (SD) or median [IQR].

Results: In children, age, height and weight= 11.4 years [7.7,14.6], 145.6cm [132,156.3] and 35.5kg [28.8,46.1]. In adults, age, height and weight= 29.9 years (11.6), 167.9cm (9.2) and 66.5kg (9.5). All children had an FEV1 within the normal range (FEV1= 105.1% [97.4,113.4]). On average LCI and VDP were normal (LCI=6.3 [6.0,7.1], VDP=1.6% [1.4,1.9]), however 3 children had clear Xe-MRI ventilation defects, 2 of which also had abnormal LCI. In comparison adults had a significantly worse FEV1=78.9% [54.8,102.4] (p=0.002), FEV1/FVC=74.9% (19.3) (p=0.001), LCI=12.7 (5.6) (p=0.0002) and VDP= 25.1% [3.9,35.9] (p<0.001). Age correlated (p<0.001) with FEV1 (r=-0.76), FEV1/FVC (r=-0.79), LCI (r=0.78) and VDP (r=0.82). Compared with pre-HEMT findings, adults on average showed increases in FEV1 and FVC% (mean difference [95% CI] in % =6.9 [3.8–10.0] and 8.2 [4.3–12.0]; p<0.001). LCI deteriorated (median difference [95% CI] =0.9 [0.04–2.8]; p=0.03). VDP showed no significant change, with ventilation abnormalities largely persisting.

Conclusions: Children receiving HEMT had normal lung function and mostly homogeneous ventilation on 129Xe-MRI, contrasting with pre-HEMT studies where ventilation abnormalities on MRI were common. Adults with prior disease had poorer lung function with persistent ventilation abnormalities, despite an FEV1 increase. Xe-MRI provides a powerful and sensitive means of monitoring lung health over time.

records.title: Adherence with baseline and follow-up screening for cataracts in patients on modulators containing ivacaftor.
records.authors_text: O. Moran1, C. Ring1, W. Naqvi1, L. Perrem1, B. Elnazir1
records.affiliations_text: 1Children’s Health Ireland at Tallaght, Respiratory Department, Dublin, Ireland
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Ivacaftor-containing CFTR modulators from infancy are standard care for most children with cystic fibrosis (CF). Lens opacities following ivacaftor exposure have been reported and congenital cataracts described following in utero and breast milk exposure to elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor.

Current guidance recommends pre-treatment (baseline) ophthalmology screening and repeat screening after one year.

We aimed to assess adherence with baseline and follow-up ophthalmology screening in children commenced on ivacaftor-containing modulators in a tertiary paediatric CF centre.

Methods: Between September and October 2025 a retrospective audit was conducted of children with CF commenced on ivacaftor-containing therapies at a tertiary level CF centre. Charts were reviewed for baseline and follow-up ophthalmology screening. Families were contacted for any unavailable data.

Results: A total of 86 children commenced 134 ivacaftor-containing modulators. Baseline screening was performed in 120/134 (89.5%) modulator initiations. 20/134 (14.9%) counted a previous screen, from prior to commencing a different modulator, as their baseline. Patients who had baseline screening were older (mean 5.73 years) than those who did not (mean 2.46 years).

Of the 120 follow-up screenings due (12 were excluded as on modulator for less than 1 year), 2 were excluded as outcomes could not be confirmed. Follow-up screening was completed in 82/118 (69.5%). 28/118 (23.7%) didn’t attend follow-up ophthalmology review until switching to a new modulator.

One patient (0.7%) was found to have cataracts; baseline screening had not been performed and cataracts were detected nine months after initiation.

Conclusion: While baseline ophthalmology screening prior to ivacaftor-containing modulator initiation was high, adherence to recommended follow-up screening after one year was substantially lower. Carers reported cost and access difficulties, particularly for younger children.

Results: A total of 86 children commenced 134 ivacaftor-containing modulators. Baseline screening was performed in 120/134 (89.5%) modulator initiations. 20/134 (14.9%) counted a previous screen, from prior to commencing a different modulator, as their baseline. Patients who had baseline screening were older (mean 5.73 years) than those who did not (mean 2.46 years).
Of the 120 follow-up screenings due (12 were excluded as on modulator for less than 1 year), 2 were excluded as outcomes could not be confirmed. Follow-up screening was completed in 82/118 (69.5%). 28/118 (23.7%) didn’t attend follow-up ophthalmology review until switching to a new modulator.
One patient (0.7%) was found to have cataracts; baseline screening had not been performed and cataracts were detected nine months after initiation.
Conclusion: While baseline ophthalmology screening prior to ivacaftor-containing modulator initiation was high, adherence to recommended follow-up screening after one year was substantially lower. Carers reported cost and access difficulties, particularly for younger children.

records.authors_text: E. Albin1, T. Kahre1,2, K. Õunap1,2, K. Muru1,2, K. Künnapas1, M.-M. Lass1, M. Vasar3, A. Viidebaum3, S. Plado4, S. Pajusalu1,2, K. Reinson1,2

records.abstract_text:
Introduction: Until 2023, Cystic Fibrosis (CF) Newborn Screening (NBS) was not available in Estonia and diagnosis was often delayed. To improve early diagnosis and access to treatment, a national pilot CF NBS programme was initiated on 1 April 2023.

Objective: To evaluate and summarise the outcomes of the Estonian CF NBS pilot programme.

Methods: We retrospectively analysed data from the CF NBS pilot conducted in 2023–2025. Screening followed a three-tier strategy: immunoreactive trypsinogen (IRT), pancreatitis-associated protein (PAP), and CFTR gene sequencing; in cases of extremely high IRT values (≥120 ng/mL), a safety-net was applied.The IRT cut-off was set at the 97th percentile in year 1 and adjusted to the 98th percentile thereafter. PAP cut-offs were 1.8 ng/mL for samples with IRT <100 ng/mL and 0.6 ng/mL for samples with IRT ≥100 ng/mL. The third tier comprised sequencing of all CFTR coding exons. Newborns with ≥1 CF-causing CFTR variant or meeting the safety-net criterion were considered screen positive (SP) and referred for sweat chloride testing and paediatric assessment.

Results: A total of 26,425 newborns were screened. IRT exceeded the cut-off in 876 cases, triggering PAP measurement. CFTR sequencing was performed for 302 newborns. Thirty-one newborns were classified as SP due to ≥1 CF-causing variant and/or safety-net IRT. CF diagnosis was confirmed in three patients. Two infants with a pathogenic variant and a variant of varying clinical consequence were classified as CF Screen Positive, Inconclusive Diagnosis (CFSPID). We identified one false negative patient with a PAP concentration below the cut-off.

Conclusions: Data from the pilot programme indicate that the applied three-tier algorithm can effectively identify newborns with CF. A nationwide screening workflow was successfully implemented, and effective collaboration between the screening centre and CF care centres was established.

records.title: Twelve years of newborn screening for cystic fibrosis in Portugal: impact of algorithm optimization

Joao, Unidade Local de Saude de Sao Joao, Cystic Fibrosis Reference Centre, Department of Paediatrics, Porto, Portugal, 4Hospital Divino Espírito Santo, Department of Paediatrics, Ponta Delgada, Portugal, 5Hospital Santa Maria, Unidade Local de Saude Santa Maria, Cystic Fibrosis Reference Centre, Department of Paediatrics, Lisboa, Portugal, 6Hospital Dona Estefânia, Unidade Local de Saude de Sao Jose, Cystic Fibrosis Reference Centre, Department of Paediatrics, Lisboa, Portugal, 7Centro Materno Infantil do Norte, Unidade Local de Saude Santo Antonio, Cystic Fibrosis Reference Centre, Department of Paediatrics, Porto, Portugal, 8Hospital Pediatrico, Unidade Local de Saude de Coimbra, Coimbra, Portugal
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Newborn screening (NBS) for cystic fibrosis (CF) has been implemented nationwide in Portugal since 2013. Until 2022, the screening algorithm was based on an IRT/PAP/IRT strategy. In order to improve the positive predictive value (PPV), genetic testing was incorporated into the screening algorithm in 2023. In 2024, the currently used algorithm was finally established. This study aims to analyse the results of CF newborn screening since 2024, and to compare the performance of the current algorithm with that of previous screening strategies.

Methods: A total of 172,339 newborns were screened for CF using an IRT/PAP/DNA/IRT strategy. Dried blood spot samples were predominantly collected between the 3rd and 6th days of life. Genetic analysis included the detection of 68 CFTR mutations commonly found in the European population.

Results: Between 2023 and 2024, newborn screening identified 14 patients with CF. One additional patient, presenting meconium ileus, and who had a normal IRT value in the first sample, came to our knowledge. In six cases referred for clinical evaluation at specialized centers, CF was not confirmed. In eight patients (57%) both CF-causing alleles were identified with the genetic study included in the screening algorithm, four of them were homozygous for the F508del mutation. The currently implemented screening algorithm demonstrates superior performance compared with previous algorithms, as indicated by the following estimates (95% confidence intervals): sensitivity 93.3% (68.1–99.8), specificity 99.997% (99.993–99.999), PPV 70,0% (45.7–88.1), and NPV 99.999% (99.996–100).

Conclusion: Since 2013, 1,037,332 newborns have been screened for CF in Portugal, leading to the identification of 100 affected patients and an estimated prevalence of 1:10,478 newborns. Based on the results presented, the current screening algorithm appears to be well adapted to the Portuguese population and will remain in use.

records.title: Thirty years of newborn screening for cystic fibrosis in Buenos Aires Province, Argentina: evolution of incidence in a long-term population-based experience
records.authors_text: V. D'Alessandro1, J. Finocchiaro1, A. Marianelli2, G. Borrajo3
records.affiliations_text: 1Children's Hospital "Sor María Ludovica", Pulmonary, La Plata, Argentina, 2Children's Hospital "Sor María Ludovica", Central Lab, La Plata, Argentina, 3Fundación Bioquímica Argentina, La Plata, Argentina
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: Newborn Screening (NBS) for Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is a cornerstone of public health, enabling early diagnosis, timely treatment, improved quality of life and while facilitating genetic counselling. Although CF NBS has been mandatory in Argentina since 1994, its regulation in Buenos Aires Province (BA) was implemented only in 2008. In July 2010, CF NBS was included in the Programme for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Congenital Diseases (PRODyTEC), Ministry of Health - BA.

Objective: To describe the evolution of CF NBS in BA over a 30-year period, focusing on cumulative incidence trends up to 2024.

Materials and Methods: Immunoreactive trypsinogen (IRT) was measured using AutoDELFIA technology, with a cut-off value of 70 ng/mL. NBS strategy was based on IRT/IRT, with sweat testing as confirmatory diagnosis. Molecular analysis was not part of the NBS strategy, was therefore performed only after sweat test confirmation.

Results: During the initial period (1995–2007), when NBS coverage was limited and 636.134 newborns (NBs) were screened, cumulative incidence was 1:5,437. Following regulatory implementation in 2008, a sustained decrease in cumulative incidence was observed, reaching 1:6,541 up to 2010 in 968.062 NBs tested. After incorporation into PRODyTEC, the cumulative incidence continued to decline steadily, reaching its lowest historical value of 1:9,000 in 2019 out of a population of 2,636,878 screened NBs. In subsequent years (2020-2024), cumulative incidence remained stable, ranging between 1:8,467 and 1:8,862 in more than 3,2 million NBs tested, reflecting long-term consolidation of the NBS programme.

Conclusions: Over 30 years, CF NBS in BA evolved from limited implementation to a consolidated public health programme. Regulatory support and integration into a structured health system were key to achieving sustained coverage and stable cumulative incidence, reinforcing the value of long-term NBS programmes for equitable early CF diagnosis.

records.title: Critical assessment of newborn screening data in a low-income country: insights from a Brazilian reference center

person.institution: Hospital de Clinicas de Porto Alegre

records.authors_text: J. Horn1, E. Procianoy1
records.affiliations_text: 1Hospital de Clinicas de Porto Alegre, Pediatric Pneumology, Porto Alegre, Brazil
records.abstract_text:
Newborn screening (NBS) for cystic fibrosis (CF) is crucial to ensure early diagnosis and timely treatment. However, the multistep process involving IRT1, IRT2, sweat chloride testing may compromise its effectiveness in large and resource-limited countries such as Brazil with centralized screening process.

Objectives: To analyze NBS performance in a public CF center between 2022 and 2025, focusing on diagnostic timelines, nutritional status, early symptoms, and microbiological findings at first assessment.

Methods: A retrospective observational study was conducted with confirmed CF cases identified through NBS. Variables included the age at IRT1, IRT2, sweat test, genotyping, final diagnosis, and first clinical visit. Clinical features such as steatorrhea, cough, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa) colonization were recorded. Data analysis was descriptive and performed using Excel.

Results: Thirty-eight patients were diagnosed via NBS from 2022 to 2025, including 10 with meconium ileus. IRT1 was collected at 3–20 days of life (median 5 days); IRT2 at 7–27 days (median 13). Sweat test was performed at 15–262 days (median 37), and genotyping results were available between 35–441 days (median 117). In 9 cases, diagnosis was based solely on genotyping due to absence of sweat testing. The final diagnosis was confirmed between 16–262 days of life (median 41). The first visit occurred at a median age of 74 days (range 38–275). At first evaluation, 49% of patients were underweight, 59% had steatorrhea, 49% had cough, and 2 had Pa in their first oropharyngeal culture.

Conclusion: Delays in key steps of the IRT1/IRT2/sweat test NBS remain a significant challenge within Brazilian public health system. The high proportion of infants with CF presenting with nutritional deficits and early clinical manifestations at their first CF center visit underscores the urgent need for streamlined diagnostic workflows to ensure earlier intervention.

records.title: Newborn screening for Cystic Fibrosis (CF-NBS) in Wallonia-Brussels Federation (Belgium): evaluation after six years of implementation

person.department: Department of Pediatric Pulmonology and Cystic Fibrosis

records.authors_text: M. Thimmesch1, S. Marie2, J. Dewulf2, L. Marcelis3, G. Luis4, S. Berardis5, L. Hanssens6, C. Quentin6, H. Boboli7, F. Boemer4
records.affiliations_text: 1CHC MontLégia, Department of Pediatric Pulmonology and Cystic Fibrosis, Liège, Belgium, 2Universitary Hospital Saint-Luc, Biochemical Genetics and Newborn Screening Laboratory, Brussels, Belgium, 3Universitary Hospital Erasme, Biochemical Genetics and Newborn Screening Laboratory, Brussels, Belgium, 4University Hospital of Liège, Biochemical Genetics and Newborn Screening Laboratory, Brussels, Belgium, 5Universitary Hospital Saint-Luc, Department of Pediatric Pulmonology and Cystic Fibrosis, Brussels, Belgium, 6Queen Fabiola Children’s University Hospital, Department of Pediatric Pulmonology and Cystic Fibrosis, Brussels, Belgium, 7Universitary Hospital of Liège, Department of Pediatric Pulmonology and Cystic Fibrosis, Liège, Belgium
records.abstract_text:
Objective: To evaluate the performance of the cystic fibrosis newborn screening (CF-NBS) program using an IRT–DNA algorithm, officially implemented in the Wallonia–Brussels Federation (WBF) since January 2020.

Methods: Immunoreactive trypsinogen (IRT1) was measured on dried blood spots collected 48–96 hours after birth. DNA analysis using a 12-mutation CFTR panel was performed when IRT1 was ≥ 99th percentile (P99). Infants with one or two CFTR variants were referred for a sweat test (ST). When IRT1 was ≥P99.9 with negative mutation screening, a failsafe strategy was applied using a repeat IRT at day 21. ST was performed if IRT21 remained > P99. Independently of IRT, meconium ileus (MI) was an indication for ST. Full CFTR gene sequencing was performed when required.

Results: From 2020 to 2025 (results ongoing), 312.623 newborns were screened. CF-NBS was positive and led to ST in 282 infants: 230 due to elevated IRT1 with at least one CFTR mutation, 25 through the failsafe pathway, and 27 with IRT ≥P99.9 and negative mutation screening without repeat IRT at day 21. Nineteen infants were lost to follow-up. CF was diagnosed in 56 newborns: 43 through CF-NBS, 5 with MI, 4 with family history (FH), and 4 missed cases. CF incidence was 1/5.583 live births. Among CF-NBS cases, 40 were identified through IRT ≥P99 with at least one mutation and 3 via the failsafe pathway; one infant died before ST. The program identified 171 healthy CFTR carriers and 17 Cystic Fibrosis Screen Positive Inconclusive Diagnosis (CFSPID) cases. Median age at first CF center visit was 22 days. Sensitivity was 91%, positive predictive value (PPV) 15.3%, and CF/CFSPID ratio 2.5.

Conclusion: This six-year evaluation demonstrates good sensitivity of the CF-NBS program and enables CF diagnosis before one month of age. However, PPV and CF/CFSPID ratio remain suboptimal, highlighting the need for continuous evaluation and optimization of the screening strategy.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Universal Cystic fibrosis (CF) newborn screening (NBS) was introduced in the UK in 2007. However, a small proportion of cases are missed. We aim to characterise a single-centre cohort of children with CF not detected by NBS and identify patterns of missed diagnoses.

Methods: A retrospective cohort study used laboratory NBS and clinical data from 2007 to 2025.

Results: Twenty-two children born between 2009-2025 were identified. Recorded ethnicity was White British/Irish in 15, South Asian in four, and mixed ethnicity in three children.

One case was due to post-analytical delay; the remaining cases were protocol-related false negatives. Data on diagnostic indication were available for 20/22 children: 19/20 were diagnosed following clinical symptoms, three of which were meconium ileus, and one following parental carrier testing. All except four were pancreatic sufficient at diagnosis (see Table 1).

Both CF-causing alleles were identified in 21/22, and 18 of 22 children had at least one CFTR variant included in the initial four-mutation (CF4) panel, including three children homozygous for p.Phe508del.

records.authors_text: J. Roukema1, G.M. Schobers2, M.T. Schepens2, D. Westra2
records.affiliations_text: 1Radboud University Medical Centre, Amalia Children's Hospital, Pediatric Pulmonology, Nijmegen, Netherlands, 2Radboud University Medical Centre, Human Genetics, Nijmegen, Netherlands
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: A patient was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis after positive newborn screening (Immunoreactive trypsinogen 153 ug/L, Pancreatitis associated protein 4.6 ug/L). Sweat-chloride was 86 mmol/L and the patient had exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (faecal elastase <15 ug/g). Only one pathogenic CFTR mutation was found (p.Phe508del). Father had congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens due to CFTR variants p.(Phe508del) and p.(Arg117His). For the mother, the Inno LiPa kit with 37 most common European variants was negative. No residual risk for carriership could be given due to non-Caucasian background. Analysis of the 53 most common European CFTR variants (Elucigene CF-EU2V1 kit), Sanger sequencing and multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplication (MRC Holland kit P091-D1) showed the paternal p.(Phe508del) variant, but no second CFTR mutation. In 2019, exome sequencing with analysis of variants in the coding regio and the splice sites of the CFTR gene again did not show a second pathogenic variant.

Methods: Short read genome sequencing was performed, after which analysis of variants in the complete CFTR gene (exons and introns) was executed.

Results: A heterozygous likely pathogenic mobile element insertion of an alu-element (AluYa5) just upstream of exon 9 on the CFTR gene (NM_000492.4) was detected: c.1117-20_1117-19insAlu r.spl? p.?. This insertion of 281 bp most probably places the branchpoint too far from the splice acceptor site of exon 9, and likely disrupts correct mRNA splicing, potentially leading to the creation of a new cryptic splice acceptor site, the introduction of a premature stop codon, or the loss of functional protein domains. This variant was also found in the mother.

Conclusion: By applying the newest genomic sequencing techniques and expanding the analysis to intronic regions and mobile element insertions, a second hard-to-detect compound heterozygous likely pathogenic variant was found and the genetic etiology was elucidated.

records.abstract_text:
Introduction: The timing of cystic fibrosis (CF) diagnosis is key to disease progression and clinical outcomes. This study aimed to assess the effects of early (≤2 months) and late (>2 months) CF diagnosis on the clinical course and lung function in patients registered in the Turkish National Cystic Fibrosis Registry(CFRT).

Methods: All patients registered in CFRT as of 2024 were included in the study and divided into two groups based on age at CF diagnosis: ≤2 months (Group 1) and >2 months (Group 2). Demographic, clinical, and laboratory data were compared.

Results: A total of 2239 CF patients were recorded; 47.2% were female. Of these, 691 (30.8%) were diagnosed at ≤2 months of age. In Group 1, females were more prevalent (p=0.037).No differences in growth z-scores were observed between the groups (p>0.05).The median current age was lower in Group 1 (p<0.05).The second sweat test was lower in Group 2 (p<0.001). FEV1 and FVC values were higher in Group 1 (p=0.001, p=0.024, respectively).Use of UDCA was higher in Group 1, while use of oxygen and mannitol was higher in Group 2(p < 0.05).CF-related liver disease, pancreatic insufficiency, meconium ileus, and pseudobartter were more common in Group 1, whereas hemoptysis was more frequent in Group 2 (p <0.05).MSSA and Haemophilus influenzae colonization were more common in Group 1(p <0.05).No difference in mortality was detected between the groups(p=0.973).

Conclusion: Diagnosing CF within the first two months of life is linked to better lung function and significant differences in disease features.Improving early detection methods could enhance long-term results.

records.title: Ethnic differences in the frequency of CFTR gene variants in the Russian Federation
records.authors_text: R. Zinchenko1, J. Saidaeva2, A. Bekbotov3, I. Tebieva4,5, O. Golubtsova6, A. Abrukova7, E. Kondratyeva1, S. Kutsev1, N. Kashirskaya1
records.affiliations_text: 1Research Centre for Medical Genetics, Moscow, Russian Federation, 2State Institution "Republican Bureau of Forensic Medical Examination" of the Ministry of Health of the Chechen Republic, Grozny, Russian Federation, 3State Budgetary Institution of the Republic of Ingushetia "Republican Polyclinic", Nazran, Russian Federation, 4Federal State Budgetary Educational Institution of Higher Professional Education "North-Ossetian State Medical Academy" of the Ministry of Health of the RF, Vladikavkaz, Russian Federation, 5Republican Children's Clinical Hospital of the Republic of North Ossetia-Alania, Vladikavkaz, Russian Federation, 6Republican Children's Clinical Hospital of the Chuvash Republic Ministry of Health, Cheboksary, Russian Federation, 7Municipal Clinical Hospital of the Presidential Perinatal Center of the Chuvash Republic Ministry of Health, Cheboksary, Russian Federation
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a genetically inherited disease caused by mutations in the CFTR gene. Marked variation exists in the prevalence of CFTR gene variants among different ethnic groups, leading to a wide range of clinical manifestations and responsiveness to variant-specific therapy (VST). The Russian Federation (RF) is home to more than 190 ethnic groups, including small indigenous and autochthonous nations.

Aim: Genetic testing of people with CF (pwCF) from different ethnic groups was performed to assess the possibility of employing existing VST across the RF.

Methods: Genetic analysis was performed on 1530 blood samples, obtained between 1995 and 2025. The ethnic origin of the corresponding pwCF (up to the third generation) was determined via direct interview.

Results: The five most common CFTR variants among pwCF of Russian nationality (n=1384) were F508del (54.99%), CFTRdele2,3 (7.59%), 2143delT (2.71%), 3849+10kbC-T (2,35%) and 2184insA (2,24%). A high frequency of E92K was found in the Turkic-speaking groups of the Volga region (VR) and North Caucasus (NC): Chuvash (86.36%), Bashkirs (30%), Tatars (16.3%), Chechens (15.28%), Udmurts (6.8%); W1282X - in Turkic-speaking groups: Karachais (90%), Nogais (100%), Abazins (50%) and Ossetians (57.33%); 1677delTA - in autochthonous nations as the Abkhaz-Adygean (Abazins and Circassians over 30%) and Nakh groups: Chechens (81.3%), Terek Kumyks (50%) and Ingush (100%). 1677delTA has also been detected in other ethnic groups from the NC region: Armenians (25%) and Georgians (42,7%). Interestingly, no pwCF have been identified so far in the indigenous Yakuts, Buryats and Kalmyk populations.

Conclusion: Our results demonstrate significant interethnic differences in the spectrum of CFTR gene variants across the RF. Among the variants common to both Russians and other ethnic groups, Сlass I CFTR variants (CFTRdele2,3, 2143delT, 2184insA, 1677delTA, and W1282X) are widespread, limiting the use of available VST.

records.title: c.3310G>T, p. (Glu1104Ter) (E1104X) is a frequent CFTR mutation in Morocco.
records.authors_text: N. Amenzoui1, D. Benchaji2, A.A. Bousfiha2, C. Libioulle3, P. Lebecque4
records.affiliations_text: 1Faculty of Medecine and Pharmacy, Pediatric, Casablanca, Morocco, 2Faculty of Medecine and Pharmacy, Casablanca, Morocco, 3Liège University Hospital, Human Genetics Department, Liège, Belgium, 4Louvain University, Pediatric Pulmonology, Brussels, Belgium
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The prevalence of cystic fibrosis (CF) remains unclear in many resource-limited countries. Morocco has a predominantly Caucasian population and a high consanguinity rate (≈24%). Genetic and clinical data on CF in this country are limited.

Methods: This observational study included all CF patients seen between January 2018 and July 2025 by a single paediatrician at Abderrahim El Harouchi Children’s Hospital, Casablanca.

Results: A diagnosis of CF was confirmed in 39 children (16 males/23 females, median age at first consultation : 1.72 years , 95% CI: 0.71–3.10; range: 0.08–11.47). All patients presented with exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. Two CFTR mutations were identified in each patient, with homozygosity observed in two thirds of the patients (26/39 patients), mainly for F508del (31%), E1104X (13%) and 711+1G>T (8%).

Over the study period, 5 patients (13%) died between 4 and 6.5 years of age, and 5 others were lost to follow-up. At the last visit , the mean age (±SD)of the cohort was 6.3 (±4.3) years, and the mean BMI z- score was −1.15 (±1.72).Pseudomonas aeruginosa was detected in sputum samples in 83% of the patients. Mean FEV1 of 17 patients aged ≥6 years was 81.7 % (±24.1) of predicted value (GLI).

Conclusion: Among 78 alleles, the three most frequently identified mutations were F508del (33/78; 42%), E1104X (11/78; 14%), and 711+1G>T (9/78; 11.5%). These proportions differ significantly from those reported in CFTR2 (65%, 0.02%, and 0.2%, respectively; p<0.0001). Based on their genotype, barely half of the patients in this cohort (49%) would be eligible for modulator therapy at age 6 in Belgium. Clinical outcomes were very poor and highlight the urgent need in Morroco to develop national strategies that include improving access to diagnosis, structuring of specialized reference centers and ensuring equitable access to both symptomatic and innovative treatments.

records.abstract_text:
Cystic fibrosis is a genetic, inherited disorder characterized by a wide range of clinical manifestations and genetic variants.

Methods: The 2024 Registry included data from 3,573 patients and 271 patients who were not followed up that year.

Results: The overall cumulative frequency of identified alleles was 95.7%. 97.1% of alleles were identified in children and 92.5% in adults. A total of 304 variants were identified, 159 of which were detected repeatedly. The most frequent variants were: F508del, CFTRdele2.3, E92K, 1677delTA, 3849+10kbC->T, 2143delT, 2184insA, W1282X, L138ins, N1303K. 33 variants are not included in international databases. Two variants of the CFTR were detected in 94.9% of children and 89.5% of adults, one variant in 4.6% and 6.0%, and none in 0.6% and 4.5% of children and adults, respectively. "Severe" genotypes predominate among both children and adults, but their frequency is 79.5% in those under 18 years of age and 65.9% in those over 18. The "mild" genotype was detected in 20.0% of patients under 12 years of age and in 59.2% of patients over 36 years of age. Of the 3,844 patients, F508del/F508del was found in 28.5%, F508del/not F508del in 46.0%, and not F508del/not F508del in 25.5%.

In the Central (CFD) and Northwestern (NWFD) Federal Districts, genetic testing was conducted more frequently than in other regions – 98.4% and 98.2% of patients, respectively. The first three positions in frequency were occupied by severe genetic variants: F508del - 52.9% (CFD) and 54.4% (NWFD), CFTRdele2.3 - 7.6% (5.0%), 2143delT - 2.7% (2.8%). In the Southern (SFD) and North Caucasian FD genetic testing was conducted in 96.5% and 95.6% of patients. In the SFD, the F508del variant was found in 54.9% of cases, CFTRdele2.3 - 6.9%, and 3849+10kbC->T - 3.3%.

Conclusion: Thus, the RF is characterized by a diversity of genetic variants, and their frequency varies depending on the region of residence and its ethnic composition.

Cystic fibrosis is a genetic, inherited disorder characterized by a wide range of clinical manifestations and genetic variants.
Methods: The 2024 Registry included data from 3,573 patients and 271 patients who were not followed up that year.
Results: The overall cumulative frequency of identified alleles was 95.7%. 97.1% of alleles were identified in children and 92.5% in adults. A total of 304 variants were identified, 159 of which were detected repeatedly. The most frequent variants were: F508del, CFTRdele2.3, E92K, 1677delTA, 3849+10kbC->T, 2143delT, 2184insA, W1282X, L138ins, N1303K. 33 variants are not included in international databases. Two variants of the CFTR were detected in 94.9% of children and 89.5% of adults, one variant in 4.6% and 6.0%, and none in 0.6% and 4.5% of children and adults, respectively. "Severe" genotypes predominate among both children and adults, but their frequency is 79.5% in those under 18 years of age and 65.9% in those over 18. The "mild" genotype was detected in 20.0% of patients under 12 years of age and in 59.2% of patients over 36 years of age. Of the 3,844 patients, F508del/F508del was found in 28.5%, F508del/not F508del in 46.0%, and not F508del/not F508del in 25.5%.
In the Central (CFD) and Northwestern (NWFD) Federal Districts, genetic testing was conducted more frequently than in other regions – 98.4% and 98.2% of patients, respectively. The first three positions in frequency were occupied by severe genetic variants: F508del - 52.9% (CFD) and 54.4% (NWFD), CFTRdele2.3 - 7.6% (5.0%), 2143delT - 2.7% (2.8%). In the Southern (SFD) and North Caucasian FD genetic testing was conducted in 96.5% and 95.6% of patients. In the SFD, the F508del variant was found in 54.9% of cases, CFTRdele2.3 - 6.9%, and 3849+10kbC->T - 3.3%.
Conclusion: Thus, the RF is characterized by a diversity of genetic variants, and their frequency varies depending on the region of residence and its ethnic composition.

records.title: Genetic epidemiology of cystic fibrosis in Lebanon
records.authors_text: K. El Taoum1, H. Sadeghi2, G. Raissi2, M. Macek3, S. Mroueh1
records.affiliations_text: 1American University of Beirut, Pediatrics and Adolescent Medicine, Beirut, Lebanon, 2Columbia University Medical Center, Pediatrics, New York, United States, 3Charles University, Biology and Medical Genetics, Prague, Czech Republic
records.abstract_text:
Background: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive disease caused by pathogenic variants in the CFTR gene. While ΔF508 is the predominant mutation in European populations, the distribution of CFTR mutations exhibits significant geographic and ethnic variability.

Objectives: To characterize the genetic epidemiology of CF in Lebanon and compare it to patterns reported in European and Arab populations.

Methods: In this national cross-sectional study, 94 patients with CF were genetically characterized for common CFTR mutations. Demographic data included age, sex, and adult status (>21 years). Allelic frequencies for the three most common mutations — ΔF508, N1303K, and W1282X — were calculated. Consanguinity prevalence was previously reported at 50%1 in Lebanese CF families which suggests the possibility of undiagnosed patients. Comparative reference data from European and Arab cohorts were synthesized from published mutation frequency studies.

Results: Among 94 Lebanese CF patients (47 males; 24 adults), the allelic distribution was: ΔF508 50%, N1303K 22%, and W1282X 14%. Eight patients have only one identified mutation and three patients are missing their genetic information. The cohort demonstrates a relatively elevated contribution of N1303K and W1282X compared with European registry data where these mutations individually represent ~1–3% of alleles. In some Arab populations, N1303K has been reported at higher frequencies (up to ~27%). This genetic heterogeneity contrasts with the classical European predominance of ΔF508 and highlights a distinct mutation distribution in Lebanon.

Conclusions: The Lebanese CF mutation spectrum reveals substantial genetic heterogeneity with a lower relative ΔF508 frequency and higher representation of N1303K and W1282X compared to European cohorts. This underscores the importance of tailored genetic testing panels and suggests population-specific priorities for screening strategies.

records.title: CFTR gene variants in the group of adult cystic fibrosis patients in Kazakhstan

person.title: MD, PhD
person.institution: Federal Pulmonology Research Institute, Federal Medical and Biological Agency

records.authors_text: E. Amelina1, I. Mukatova1, S. Kim1, A. Serikova1, A. Ramankul1, Y. Kenzhebayeva2
records.affiliations_text: 1Astana Medical University, Department of Internal Medicine N 3, Astana, Kazakhstan, 2Multidisciplinary City Hospital No1, Pulmonology Department, Astana, Kazakhstan
records.abstract_text:
Background: CFTR genotyping has become especially important recently due to the possibility of targeted therapy for CF patients.

The aim: To study the features and frequency of pathogenic CFTR gene variants in adult CF patients in Kazakhstan.

Methods: 29 adult CF patients were tested. Both mutations were identified in all the patients.

Results: 29 pwCF (13 males) were included. The age of the patients in 2025 was 22.5 years (min 18, max 45 yrs.). 9 (31%) of the patients were ethnic Kazakhs, 9 (31%) were Russians, 5(17,2%) were multinational, 3 (10,3%) Ukrainian, 1 (3,4%) Polе, 1 (3,4%) Korean and 1 (3,4%) Turkish.

Severe mutations (class I–III) accounted for approximately 81% of all detected alleles, while mild mutations (class IV–V) represented 19%. The most frequent mutation was F508del (51.7%), it was detected in 20 patients (69%) (10 in homozygous and 10 in heterozygous state) followed by 1677delTA (8.6%) and 2143delT (5.2%). Fourteen other CFTR gene variants were identified, forming 13 different genotypes among adult CF patients.

6 genotypes included at least one “mild” CFTR variant and were therefore classified as “mild” genotypes:1677delTA / 3849+10kb C>T; 1677delTA / V392G; 3849+10kb C>T / R668C; R792X / H1054; F508del / L1335P; R117H / F508del.

7 genotypes represented combinations of two “severe” CFTR variants: F508del / F508del; F508del / N1303K; F508del / 2143delT; F508del / c.1766+2T>C; R1066C / c.4111_4113dupGAA; G542X/F508del; 2184insA/F508del. Most identified genotypes are eligible for targeted therapy. Only 3 patients (≈10%) had genotypes not eligible for approved targeted therapy.

Conclusion: The CFTR variant spectrum in adult pwCF in Kazakhstan is characterized by genetic heterogeneity and a predominance of severe mutations, with F508del remaining the most frequent variant but occurring at a lower rate compared to global data. 90% of adult patients are eligible for CFTR modulators treatment.

person.title: MD, PhD

records.authors_text: T. Marshalkina1, M. Macek jr2, M. Libik2, N. Zhanuzakova1, A. Zaitova1, E. Amelina3
records.affiliations_text: 1Scientific Center of Pediatrics and Pediatric Surgery, Pediatric Pulmonology, Almaty, Kazakhstan, 2Charles University and Motol University Hospital, Department of Biology and Medical Genetics, 2nd Faculty of Medicine, Prague, Czech Republic, 3Astana Medical University, Department of Internal Medicine with a Course of Nephrology, Hematology, Allergology, Immunology, Astana, Kazakhstan
records.abstract_text:
Background: CFTR genotyping is essential for accurate diagnosis of cystic fibrosis (CF) and for identifying patients eligible for mutation-specific therapies.

Aim: To characterize the spectrum and frequency of CFTR gene variants in a pediatric CF cohort in Kazakhstan.

Methods: Children and adolescents under 18 years of age with confirmed CF and available CFTR genetic testing results were included. Variant type, zygosity, and allele frequency were analyzed.

Results: Genetic testing was performed in 180 (85%) of 212 registered CF patients. Two pathogenic CFTR variants were identified in 163 patients (91%), while a single pathogenic variant was detected in 17 patients (9%). In total, 52 pathogenic CFTR variants were identified across 360 alleles, demonstrating marked allelic heterogeneity. The most frequent variant was F508del, with an allele frequency of 47.5%, detected in 111 patients (62%), including 41 homozygous and 70 heterozygous individuals. All other variants occurred at substantially lower frequencies. In eight patients, three CFTR variants were detected, which may indicate the presence of complex alleles; however, family segregation analysis was not performed, and variant phase could not be determined.

Conclusion: The CFTR mutation spectrum in Kazakhstani pediatric CF patients is highly heterogeneous. Standard CFTR screening panels may miss clinically relevant variants, potentially limiting access to CFTR modulator therapy. Population-specific expansion of mutation panels may improve diagnostic yield and personalized treatment strategies.

records.title: Genotypes with two CFTR gene variants and undiagnosed cystic fibrosis in Russian infertile men with CBAVD
records.authors_text: V. Chernykh1,2, E. Marnat2, O. Solovova1, T. Sorokina1, M. Shtaut1, A. Sedova1, T. Adyan1,2, T. Beskorovaynaya1, A. Stepanova1, Y. Melyanovskaya1, T. Kiyan1, S. Krasovskiy1, N. Kashirskaya1, E. Kondratyeva1
records.affiliations_text: 1Research Centre for Medical Genetics, Moscow, Russian Federation, 2Pirogov Medical University, Moscow, Russian Federation
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Cystic Fibrosis, CF is usually diagnosed in children and adolescents, but rarely in adults. Some infertile men with obstructive azoospermia (OA) have undiagnosed mild, atypical CF or CF-related disorders (CF-RD), particularly congenital bilateral aplasia of vas deferens (CBAVD).

The aim of study was to evaluate a prevalence of undiagnosed CF and the CFTR genotypes in infertile men with OA/CBAVD.

Material and methods: 150 Russian patients with CBAVD were examined using by comprehensive clinical, andrological and genetic evaluation. Semen analysis was done in accordance with WHO laboratory manual (2010; 2021). CFTR gene was analyzed using by PCR-AFLP and MLPA, whole exome sequencing (WES) and Sanger sequencing.

Results: In 14 (9.3%) patients, two the CFTR gene variants were found with following CFTR genotypes: F508del/L138ins (n=5), F508del/Met952Ile, F508del/CFTRdele2,3, F508del/Leu159Ser, L138ins/L138ins, 2184insA/E92K, c.2749T>C/Glu993Ala, L138ins/N1303K, 3849+10kbC>T/E92K, Asp1152His/Asp1152His. Eight (F508del, СFTRdele2,3, L138ins, 2184insA, 3849+10kbC>T, E92K, N1303K) of 13 variants were common in Russian populations, five ones (Asp1152His, c.2749T>C, Glu993Ala, Leu159Ser, Met952Ile) were rare, detected by WES. The F508del and L138ins mutations were the most frequent. The Asp1152His variant, when in combination with another one known to cause CF-RD, is associated with an extremely variable phenotype ranging from asymptomatic to CF. Missense variant c.2856G>C(p.(Met952Ile)) has unknown significance, c.2749T>C variant is novel. Positive sweat test and/or bronchiectasis, sinusitis, pancreatitis, were found at least in 10% patients.

Conclusion: About 10% of CBAVD patients can have undiagnosed CF. Rare CFTR mutations are detected by WES/WGS. This should be taken into account during reproductive and genetic examinations. Also, it is very important to evaluate the anamnesis and the phenotype, specially the respiratory, digestive, and reproductive systems.

Results: In 14 (9.3%) patients, two the CFTR gene variants were found with following CFTR genotypes: F508del/L138ins (n=5), F508del/Met952Ile, F508del/CFTRdele2,3, F508del/Leu159Ser, L138ins/L138ins, 2184insA/E92K, c.2749T>C/Glu993Ala, L138ins/N1303K, 3849+10kbC>T/E92K, Asp1152His/Asp1152His. Eight (F508del, СFTRdele2,3, L138ins, 2184insA, 3849+10kbC>T, E92K, N1303K) of 13 variants were common in Russian populations, five ones (Asp1152His, c.2749T>C, Glu993Ala, Leu159Ser, Met952Ile) were rare, detected by WES. The F508del and L138ins mutations were the most frequent. The Asp1152His variant, when in combination with another one known to cause CF-RD, is associated with an extremely variable phenotype ranging from asymptomatic to CF. Missense variant c.2856G>C(p.(Met952Ile)) has unknown significance, c.2749T>C variant is novel. Positive sweat test and/or bronchiectasis, sinusitis, pancreatitis, were found at least in 10% patients.
Conclusion: About 10% of CBAVD patients can have undiagnosed CF. Rare CFTR mutations are detected by WES/WGS. This should be taken into account during reproductive and genetic examinations. Also, it is very important to evaluate the anamnesis and the phenotype, specially the respiratory, digestive, and reproductive systems.

records.title: Characteristics of people with cystic fibrosis in the pediatric clinic in Cuenca, Ecuador
records.authors_text: M.P. Maestre Calderon1, M.V. Lazo Quevedo1, H. Sadeghi2, G. Raissi2, G.E. Vanegas Astudillo1, E.F. Flores Pesantez1
records.affiliations_text: 1Hospital Vicente Corral Moscoso, Pulmonology, Cuenca, Ecuador, 2Columbia University, Fibrosis Center, New York, United States
records.abstract_text:
Background: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive genetic disease caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, with varied clinical expression, which presents a diagnostic challenge. In Ecuador, genetic testing or a standardized protocol remains a limitation for initial diagnosis in pediatric patients. The objective of this study was to determine the mutational profile of the CFTR gene in patients with suspected CF treated at the Vicente Corral Moscoso Hospital in Cuenca, Ecuador.

Methods: A descriptive study was conducted that included 18 patients with clinical suspicion of CF, analyzing a pediatric population.The diagnosis was based on the determination of sweat chloride test values and genetic testing.

Results: In the pediatric patients (N=18), sweat chloride levels above 60 mg/dL predominated in 15 patients, consistent with classic forms of CF. Genetic testing was performed in 14 pediatric patients, in which the H609R variant was the most prevalent (n=2) in non-sibling patients, followed by F508del/N1303K and[HS1] R334W/F508del, observed in siblings. The results showed that the study population presented positive chloride levels above 60 mg/dL (15), positive genetic studies (13), positive and negative chloride studies (2), and negative and positive genetic studies (1).

Conclusions: This study constitutes the first description of the mutational spectrum of the CFTR gene in patients with suspected cystic fibrosis treated at this healthcare facility. The predominance of variants ineligible for modulators highlights the need to expand diagnostic testing and develop strategies to standardize genetic testing, perform accurate newborn screening, and avoid late diagnoses.

[HS1]It looks like H609R is present 8 times, F508del 4x, R334W 2x (this is of30 variants)

records.title: Optimising the diagnosis and management pathway for adults referred into the West Midlands adult cystic fibrosis centre

person.institution: West Midlands Regional Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre
person.department: Birmingham Heartlands Hospital, University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust

records.authors_text: J. Choyce1, C. Brown1, L. Jones1, N. Patel1, C. Morby1, J.L Whitehouse1
records.affiliations_text: 1West Midlands Regional Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Birmingham Heartlands Hospital, University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust, Birmingham, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: Accurate diagnosis of Cystic Fibrosis (CF) versus CFTR-Related Disorder (CFTR-RD) is complex, given the spectrum of CFTR protein dysfunction. CFTR-RD is defined as evidence of CFTR protein dysfunction without meeting the diagnostic criteria for CF. Misdiagnosing those with milder CFTR dysfunction as CF, can cause increased health anxiety and over-medicalisation.

This Quality Improvement (QI) project aimed to standardise diagnostic practice for new referrals by implementing the European Cystic Fibrosis Society (ECFS) standards of care.

Objective: A key goal was to develop and implement a patient-centred diagnosis and management pathway to sensitively and accurately differentiate CF and CFTR-RD, integrating psychological support early in the process.

Methods: A multidisciplinary CFTR-RD working group was established, and using the Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) framework, an evidence-based Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) aligned with ECFS guidelines was developed. The SOP involved a staged assessment, including a history, genetic testing, sweat tests, sputum sampling, and radiology, culminating in a review at a specialist CF/CFTR-RD Multidisciplinary Team (MDT) meeting.

Results: Between October 2019 and December 2025, 36 cases (69% male, mean age 37yrs) were referred to our service. Each case was reviewed and assessed using the new SOP. The most frequent routes to referral were infertility (N=17) and respiratory clinics (N=13).

A diagnosis was given in 29 of the 36 cases:

16 CF diagnoses (44%)

2 CFTR-RD diagnoses (6%)

11 patients found to be ‘Not CF’ and discharged (31%)

Seven remain under investigation via the new pathway.

Conclusion: The QI initiative established a standardised CFTR-RD pathway, promoting patient-centred care while minimising psychological harm. New referrals and those awaiting investigations will continue to be assessed using the SOP to sustain diagnostic consistency, with follow-up care provided in consultant-led clinics as indicated.
