records.affiliations_text: 1Schneider Children's Medical Center of Israel, Pulmonology, Petach Tikva, Israel, 2Gray Faculty of Medicine, Pediatrics, Tel Aviv-YafoIsIs, Israel, 3Hadassah Medical Center and Faculty of Medicine, Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Israel, Pediatric Pulmonary, Jerusalem, Israel, 4Rappaport Children’s Hospital, Rambam Health Care Campus, Pediatric Pulmonary, Haifa, Israel, 5Ruth and Bruce Rappaport Faculty of Medicine, Technion-Israel Institute of Technology, Haifa, Israel, 6Carmel Medical Center, Pediatric Pulmonology, Haifa, Israel, 7Soroka University Medical Center, Unit, Ben Gurion University, Beer Sheva, Pediatric Pulmonary, Beer Sheva, Israel, 8Safra Children’s Hospital, Sheba Medical Center, Pediatric Pulmonary, Ramat Gan, Israel, 9Public Health Services, Ministry of Health, Jerusalem, Israel
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Population genetic carrier screening (PGCS) for cystic fibrosis (CF) has been offered in Israel since 1999 and funded by the Ministry of Health since 2008. We previously demonstrated increased use of preimplantation genetic diagnosis among CF carriers. This study evaluated the impact of PGCS on CF incidence and on the genetic and clinical characteristics of affected children.

Methods: This retrospective national study included children with CF born in Israel between 2000 and 2023. Data were obtained from the national CF registry and medical records, including demographic and genetic characteristics, prenatal parental carrier screening, ethnic origin, and religion.

Results: CF incidence per 100,000 live births declined from 12.17 in 2000 to 2.90 in 2023 (R²=0.760,p<0.0001). Between 2010 and 2023, 118 children were born with CF; median age at diagnosis was 4.2 months (range 0–111). Muslim Arabs (31%) and Orthodox Jews (23%) were overrepresented, whereas secular Jews, comprising ~60% of the population, accounted for 41% of cases.

PGCS was performed by 46 couples; in 27 screen was negative, while 19 were both identified as carriers and continued the pregnancy. 18 couples had an older child with CF. Overall, 37 couples were known carriers prior to birth; 15 (41%) carried at least one residual function variant, mainly D1152H or 5T.

Pancreatic sufficiency was present in 41/118 (35%) patients.

Despite national availability, 70/118 couples did not undergo PGCS. Even if all had been screened, only 45 would have been identified as carrier couples. PGCS uptake was lower among Orthodox Jews (5/27) and Muslims (8/36) than among secular Jews (24/47-51%).

Conclusions: Since implementation of PGCS, CF birth incidence in Israel has markedly decreased, with a higher prevalence of residual function variants and pancreatic sufficiency. Increased screening uptake, particularly in specific populations, and the expanded genetic panel introduced in 2025 may further reduce CF births.

records.title: Whole-exome sequencing–based reassessment of a presumed cystic fibrosis (CF) case reveals primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) disease despite a classical CF phenotype

person.institution: Precision Genomics Research Lab, Centre for Applied Molecular Biology, University of the Punjab

records.authors_text: S. Tahir1, M.U. Ghani1, A.H. Mumtaz1, W.M. Toor2, A. Safdar1, M.F. Sabar3, R.S. Shaikh4
records.affiliations_text: 1Precision Genomics Research Lab, Centre for Applied Molecular Biology, University of the Punjab, Lahore, Pakistan, 2Gulab Devi Teaching Hospital, Lahore, Pakistan, 3School of Biochemistry and Biotechnology, University of the Punjab, Lahore, Pakistan, 4Centre for Applied Molecular Biology, University of the Punjab, Lahore, Pakistan
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Cystic Fibrosis (CF) and Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD) are both recessive genetic disorders with overlapping clinical manifestations including mucociliary dysfunction leading to chronic respiratory infections, sinus disease, and early-onset of bronchiectasis. CF is generally linked to elevated sweat chloride levels and pancreatic insufficiency, whereas PCD is linked with normal sweat chloride levels and intact pancreatic activity although have similar respiratory symptoms. This overlap can create significant diagnostic challenges for clinicians and researchers. We report a diagnostically challenging case with classical CF features, later reclassified as PCD through whole-exome sequencing (WES).

Methods: A 23-year-old female with chronic cough, bronchiectasis, pancreatic insufficiency (fecal elastase:101 µg/g), gastrointestinal complications, and elevated sweat chloride level (95 mmol/L) was enrolled for genetic evaluation. Patient’s DNA was analyzed for targeted Sanger sequencing (exons 11,13,19, and poly-TG/T intron 9–exon10 region) of CFTR gene followed by WES.

Results: The targeted sequencing predicted no pathogenic variants. WES confirmed the absence of CFTR mutations, while identified a homozygous pathogenic frameshift variant in CCDC40 gene [c.1416del (p.I473Ffs*2)], consistent with PCD. The segregation analysis predicted both parents and two female siblings as heterozygous carriers, while one homozygous younger female sibling with similar but less severe symptoms. On clinical follow-up, the patient reported symptomatic improvement after initiation of Trikafta.

Conclusion: This case describes CF-like symptoms in a patient genetically diagnosed with PCD. It underscores the limitations of phenotype-driven and targeted genetic testing and highlights the essential role of comprehensive genomic analysis in resolving CF–PCD diagnostic overlap. The unexpected symptomatic response to CFTR modulator therapy warrants further investigation.

records.title: Cystic Fibrosis Screen Positive Inconclusive Diagnosis (CFSPID)- diagnosis or designation. Impact on emotional well-being and career aspirations

person.title: Dr
person.institution: Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust, Royal Manchester Childrens Hospital (Wythenshawe)

records.authors_text: J. Watkinson1, K. Barker1, D. Poulton1, L. Warburton1, N. Rao1
records.affiliations_text: 1Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust, Royal Manchester Childrens hospital (Wythenshawe), Paediatrics, Manchester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Newborn screening (NBS) in UK for CF was introduced nationally in 2007. The UK CF Trust reports that for 300 babies that have a positive screening result, 225 are diagnosed with CF, 15 have CFSPID, and 60 do not have either (a false positive). Most patients with CFSPID remain well and healthy, but for some Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Regulator-Related Disorder signs may be present or develop as they mature. This uncertainty may lead to emotional turmoil and impact on patient’s ability to follow their desired career choice.

Case report: We discuss a 15-year-old male, identified by NBS who is Heterozygous Delta F508/R117H 9T Allele with normal sweat chloride 21 mmol/L and faecal elastase 254 ug/g.

He was reviewed regularly in clinic from birth and remained well. With the introduction of CFSPID guidelines, monitoring was reduced to biannually. He remains asymptomatic, with no evidence of exercise intolerance or malabsorption. He has a normal chest x-ray and abdominal ultrasound.

Being an air cadet, the patient was keen to pursue a career in the RAF, but he was informed he would be unable to join due to his diagnosis, which left him and parents devastated. Primary care and school records identified him as having CF. Objectives: To examine a case series of patients designated as Cystic Fibrosis Screen Positive Inconclusive Diagnosis (CFSPID) and consider signs, symptoms and test results in determining if diagnosis remains inconclusive or if Cystic Fibrosis Related Disease would be a more appropriate designation.

Methods: The Royal Wolverhampton Hospitals NHS Trust provide shared care to approximately 40 patients with Cystic Fibrosis (CF). The clinical course of these patients has been variable with different phenotypic presentations.

Patients one and two (siblings) had consistent and evolving changes on chest x-rays with a Chrispin-Norman (CN) score of nine; the computed tomography (CT) scans have not demonstrated bronchiectasis. Patient three has isolated Pseudomonas Aeruginosa on respiratory sampling with associated respiratory symptoms. .Patient four presented acutely with seizures due to Pseudo-Bartter Syndrome. Following gastro-intestinal symptoms patient seven has been diagnosed with severe pancreatic insufficiency. Patient 10 has had conductive hearing loss requiring hearing augmentation and significant nutritional concerns. Re-designation has been made in patient 11 after a diagnostic sweat chloride.

records.title: Respiratory manifestations in a Spanish cohort of children with CFSPID
records.authors_text: A. Morales Tirado1, A. Tabares González1, E. Blitz Castro1, C. Gascón Galindo1, S. Vicente Santamaría2, C. Luna Paredes2, E. Salcedo Lobato2, A. Lamas Ferreiro1
records.affiliations_text: 1Hospital Universitario Ramón y Cajal, Madrid, Spain, 2Hospital Universitario 12 de Octubre, Madrid, Spain
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To describe respiratory manifestations and clinical course in a Spanish cohort of children with Cystic Fibrosis Screen Positive, Inconclusive Diagnosis (CFSPID).

Methods: Retrospective observational study including children with CFSPID born between July 2009 and June 2024 and followed at two CF Units in Madrid, Spain. Data collected included respiratory manifestations, hospitalizations, treatments, sweat chloride test (SCT) results, and spirometry from 5 years of age. CFTR variants were verified using CFTR2 and CFTR-France/Montpellier databases. Pulmonary exacerbations (PEx) were defined according to modified Fuchs’ criteria.

Results: Seventy-five children were included (57.3% female; median age at end of follow-up 3.59 years [IQR 1.73–5.43]). Respiratory symptoms occurred in 28 children (37.3%). PEx were the most frequent event (38 episodes in 14 children, 18.7%), followed by pneumonia (8%), bronchiolitis (8%), recurrent bronchospasm (8%), and asthma (2.7%). Six hospitalizations occurred due to pneumonia or hypoxemic bronchospasm; none were related to PEx. All antibiotic courses prescribed for PEx (n=38) were oral. Inhaled corticosteroids were the most frequently used treatment (15.8%); inhaled antibiotics and chronic azithromycin were used in only one girl who progressed to CFTR-related disorder. Airway clearance therapy was infrequently prescribed (11.8%), and dornase alfa was not used. Spirometry (n=11) showed preserved lung function (median FEV₁ z-score −0.06 SD [IQR −1.3 to +0.3]). Three children progressed to CF after a positive SCT and had a higher frequency of PEx and oral antibiotic use than non-converted CFSPID (p=0.0019).

Conclusion: Children with CFSPID show a generally mild respiratory course, with few antibiotic-treated pulmonary exacerbations and infrequent hospital admissions, consistent with reports from international cohorts.

records.title: Metabolomic profiles of newborns with elevated immunoreactive trypsinogen without cystic fibrosis diagnosis
records.authors_text: D. Maksimova1,2, M. Auzenbaha3,1, L. Gailite3, K. Klavins4, A. Kuprjasova5, M. Zolovs6, E. Aleksejeva1,7
records.affiliations_text: 1Children's Clinical University Hospital, Riga, Latvia, 2Riga Stradins University, Department of Residency, Riga, Latvia, 3Riga Stradins University, Scientific laboratory of Molecular genetics, Institute of Oncology and molecular genetics, Riga, Latvia, 4Riga Technical University, Riga, Latvia, 5Riga Stradins University, Riga, Latvia, 6Riga Stradins University, Laboratory of Statistics, Riga, Latvia, 7Riga Stradins University, Department of Paediatrics, Riga, Latvia
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Increased immunoreactive trypsinogen (IRT) concentrations detected through newborn screening (NBS) are commonly associated with cystic fibrosis (CF) but may also occur in infants without CF, resulting in false-positive findings. The metabolic background of elevated IRT in non-CF neonates has not been fully understandable. The objective of this study was to investigate metabolic differences, with a focus on amino acid and acylcarnitine profiles, in newborns with elevated IRT who were confirmed not to have CF, and to examine the potential impact of maternal and perinatal factors on these metabolic changes.

Methods: A retrospective cohort study was conducted with targeted metabolomic profiling. Neonates with elevated IRT levels but without a CF diagnosis were compared with newborns with normal IRT levels. Data were obtained from the CF NBS programme at the Children’s Clinical University Hospital of Latvia between July 2021 and June 2022. Following inclusion and exclusion criteria, 57 infants were included to the elevated IRT group and 53 infants to the control group. Associations between maternal characteristics and neonatal metabolite levels were also analysed.

Results: Newborns with elevated IRT demonstrated increased concentrations of glutamine, acetylcarnitine, propionylcarnitine and asparagine, whereas reduced levels of glutamate, lysine, threonine and serine compared with controls. Evaluation of maternal variables revealed maternal COVID-19 infection as the only factor significantly associated with neonatal metabolic alterations, including higher alanine and lower aspartic acid and hydroxyproline levels.

Conclusions: Non-CF newborns with elevated IRT exhibit alterations in their metabolic profiles, suggesting that transient metabolic responses related to perinatal stress or maternal conditions may contribute to increased IRT levels. These non-CF influences may help refine CF newborn screening strategies and reduce false-positive results.

records.title: Too little to test: a single centre retrospective review of ‘quantity not sufficient’ sweat test samples and associated clinical characteristics in adults

person.institution: Royal Brompton Hospital, part of Guys and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust

records.authors_text: R. Robinson1, L. Weitnauer1, E. Russell-Jones1, A. Downes1, A. Peres1, D. Office1, R. Dunk1, E. Diable1, B. O'Connor1, A. Jones1, I. Felton1,2, N.J. Simmonds1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Royal Brompton Hospital, part of Guys and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust, Department of Cystic Fibrosis, London, United Kingdom, 2National Heart and Lung Institute, Imperial College London, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: Sweat testing (ST) is a key diagnostic test for cystic fibrosis. ECFS guidelines 2022 recommend bilateral arm ST to reduce rates of ‘quantity not sufficient’ (QNS), aiming for <15% samples.

We performed this study to quantify QNS frequency at our adult centre and explore associated clinical characteristics (sex, age, and ethnicity). The study period spanned a switch from the Macroduct® Collection System (MCS) to the Macroduct® Advanced Collection System (MACS). All operators were experienced at ST and samples were collected in line with ECFS guidelines.

Method: All patients (≥16y) who underwent bilateral diagnostic ST over 62 months (MCS 2017-2019; MACS 2023-2025) were included and data collected from medical records. Patients were grouped by QNS sample at first visit: 0 QNS vs ≥1 QNS. Chi2 and Mann Whitney U test were used to assess for statistical difference (p>0.05).

Results: The rate of QNS samples was no different between MCS (9%) and MACS (10%; p=0.73) so results for both devices were combined. 261 patients (median age [IQR]: 39[25-50]yr, 157(60%) female) were included.

There was no significant difference between sexes, 92 (88%) males 0 QNS vs 135 (86%) females, p=0.56). Age difference did not reach statistical significance (0 QNS: median age [IQR]= 38 [26-50] vs ≥1 QNS: 40.5 [29-56], p=0.17).

Comparison between those identified as Asian 36 (14%) vs White 155 (59%), confirmed a higher proportion of QNS in Asian patients (22% vs 8%; p=0.03). Due to small numbers and/or lack of disclosure 47 (18%) further analysis was not possible for other ethnicities (Black 2 (1%), Mixed 6 (2%), Other 15 (6%)).

Conclusion: Bilateral ST at our adult centre ensured QNS rates within recommended standards. Of particular importance is the Asian population as they are more likely to have ≥1 QNS and may require repeat ST. Whilst not statistically significant, older age may also be associated with ≥1 QNS. Further, large-scale prospective studies are required to confirm these findings.

There was no significant difference between sexes, 92 (88%) males 0 QNS vs 135 (86%) females, p=0.56). Age difference did not reach statistical significance (0 QNS: median age [IQR]= 38 [26-50] vs ≥1 QNS: 40.5 [29-56], p=0.17).
Comparison between those identified as Asian 36 (14%) vs White 155 (59%), confirmed a higher proportion of QNS in Asian patients (22% vs 8%; p=0.03). Due to small numbers and/or lack of disclosure 47 (18%) further analysis was not possible for other ethnicities (Black 2 (1%), Mixed 6 (2%), Other 15 (6%)).
Conclusion: Bilateral ST at our adult centre ensured QNS rates within recommended standards. Of particular importance is the Asian population as they are more likely to have ≥1 QNS and may require repeat ST. Whilst not statistically significant, older age may also be associated with ≥1 QNS. Further, large-scale prospective studies are required to confirm these findings.

records.abstract_text:
Background: The sweat test remains the gold standard for confirming cystic fibrosis (CF) diagnosis, requiring experienced personnel (≥80 tests/year), approved equipment, and adherence to (inter)national guidelines. We report our center's experience to identify failure modes and protocol improvements.

Methods: Retrospective analysis of sweat tests performed at the CF Centre for Paediatrics and Adults, Zagreb, using Macroduct™ collection by nurses whose experience exceeds 80 tests/year each. Data spanned March 2024–December 2025 (n=304 tests in children).

Results: Of 304 tests, 14 (4.6%) yielded insufficient sweat (<15 μL) and 2 (0.7%) had analytical errors. Among 16 insufficient samples, CF was diagnosed in 2/16 via repeat testing. Age distribution: 4/16 <1 year, 9/16 aged 1–3 years, 2/16 aged 4–5 years, 1/16 ≥6 years. Primary failure cause was inadequate patient preparation (poor hydration; 9/16). Collector-arm size mismatch affected 2/16 (neonates >2000 g, appropriate gestational age), with performance errors (loose collector/air leak; 1/16) and absent sweat (1/16). Repeat tests used arm (13/16) or leg (3/16). Our quantity non sufficient rates was significantly below Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute C34—A4 limits.

Conclusions: This audit identified hydration as the leading cause of insufficient sweat collection, prompting protocol revisions emphasizing pre-test hydration. Neonatal and infant collector-arm disproportion warrants industry and Society focus to develop appropriately sized devices, enhancing diagnostic reliability in young infants.

records.affiliations_text: 1MSPI Mother and Health Institute, Chisinau, Moldova, Republic of, 2State Medical and Pharmaceutics University «Nicolae Testemițanu», Chisinau, Moldova, Republic of, 3State Medical and Pharmaceutics University «Nicolae Testemițanu»,, Department of Pediatric, Chisinau, Moldova, Republic of
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: Medical genetic counseling (MGC) for families with cystic fibrosis (CF) in the Republic of Moldova is characterized by a number of features, namely, difficulties in molecular diagnosis and lack of neonatal screening. CFTRmutations can be identified only in 61.43% of cases, i. e., F508del with a frequency of 53.21%, G542X–1.79%, 2789+5G>A – 1.07%, 2184insA–1.07%, N1303K–0.71%, 3849+10 kbC->T–0.71%, 1898+G>A–0.71%.

Objectives: To identify the features of MGC in families with a high genetic risk of CF and to evaluate the effectiveness of its implementation.

Methods: The results of a retrospective MGC were analyzed for the period from 2001 to 2024. 72 families in which 81 children (43 boys and 38 girls) suffered with CF. The methods of obtaining fetal material for prenatal DNA diagnostics were chorionic biopsy at 9 – 11 weeks of pregnancy or amniocentesis at 16-18 weeks of pregnancy.

Results: The share of "informative" families in the analysis of the CFTR gene in the studied families was 66.7% (48 families). At the same time, both mutations were identified in 27.8%, and 1 mutation in the CFTR gene was identified in 25.9%. In 33.7% of families, both mutations of the CFTR gene were not detected. 38.8% (28) of the families which are informative decided to continue childbearing, 15 of them used the method of prenatal diagnosis (one family used prenatal diagnosis in three pregnancies). In all these families, the birth of a child with CF was prevented: in 3 cases, 2 mutations in the CFTR gene were detected and the pregnancy was terminated. 46.4% of families (13 out of 28) did not consult a geneticist when planning pregnancy, 8 families(11.1%) out of 72 consulted had children with CF, the total effectiveness of MGC in the surveyed families with CF was 81.9%.

Conclusions: MGC is an essential part of medical care for families with hereditary CF, its effectiveness is 81.9%.

records.title: Discontinuation of cystic fibrosis clinical studies: a cross-sectional analysis
records.authors_text: Y.R. Alnomani1
records.affiliations_text: 1Faculty of Medicine, Benha University, Benha, Egypt
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: Clinical studies in cystic fibrosis are susceptible to early discontinuation and non-publication, contributing to research waste and limiting evidence generation. This study aimed to characterize registered clinical studies in cystic fibrosis and identify factors associated with trial discontinuation and non-dissemination.

Methods: We searched ClinicalTrials.gov for all clinical studies related to cystic fibrosis up to December 2025. Data on enrollment size, study type, study location, and funding source were extracted and analyzed using binomial logistic regression.

Results: Among 1,279 eligible clinical studies, 1,100 (85.5%) were completed and 179 (14.5%) were discontinued. Studies enrolling more than 100 participants had significantly lower odds of discontinuation (OR = 0.35, 95% CI 0.20–0.61; P < 0.001). Observational studies had decreased odds of discontinuation compared with interventional studies (OR = 0.53, 95% CI 0.33–0.88; P = 0.013). Trial discontinuation did not differ significantly between industry-funded and non–industry-funded studies (OR = 1.13, 95% CI 0.74–1.73; P = 0.059), nor between single-center and multicenter studies (OR = 1.08, 95% CI 0.72–1.64; P = 0.70)

Conclusion: A notable proportion of cystic fibrosis clinical studies are discontinued or remain unpublished, indicating persistent non-dissemination bias. These findings highlight ethical concerns regarding participant involvement without corresponding knowledge gain and underscore the need for improved trial feasibility and stronger dissemination practices in cystic fibrosis research.

records.title: A diagnostic role for patient-derived human nasal epithelial cell models in cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: N. Potter1, G. Langeveld6, T. Gunawardena6, B. Quon1, C. Bear6
records.affiliations_text: 1University of British Columbia, Vancouver, Canada, 2The Hospital for Sick Children, Toronto, Canada
records.abstract_text:
Our objective was to assess the likelihood of CFTR dysfunction and potential responsiveness to CFTR modulators for an individual diagnosed clinically with CF in childhood with progression to severe bronchiectasis in adulthood; sweat chloride testing was repeatedly unsuccessful and CFTR sequencing identified just a single P1013L-CFTR variant.

To characterize the P1013L mutation, we transfected HEK293 cells to measure CFTR expression levels by western blotting and CFTR function by monitoring chloride conductance. Next, using primary HNECs collected from the individual with the P1013L variant, we differentiated cells in an air-liquid interface (ALI) model using PneumaCult™-ALI. We examined CFTR activity in HNECs by Ussing chamber studies. Cultures were treated with DMSO vehicle control or Elexacaftor/Tezacaftor/Ivacaftor (ELX/TEZ/IVA).

HEK293 cells transfected with P1013L-CFTR display a class II defect with reduced expression and function, partially rescuable by ELX/TEZ/IVA treatment. In contrast, HNECs from the individual show wild-type levels of CFTR expression and function. HNECs display a high ratio of complex glycosylated CFTR to total CFTR (0.93). CFTR function is in the wild-type range for both activation (ΔIsc = 9.8 μA/cm2) and inhibition (ΔIsc = - 37.8 μA/cm2). Treatment with ELX/TEZ/IVA did not significantly improve CFTR expression (p = 0.75) or function for both activation (p = 0.99) and inhibition (p = 0.84).

These findings demonstrate that P1013L is a class II CF-causing variant. However, the individual in our study exhibits normal CFTR function and expression. This is consistent with the genetic findings revealing a single CF-causing variant (P1013L) on one allele, typical of a carrier. Our HNEC data suggest that CFTR dysfunction is not a major contributor to the individual’s bronchiectasis and demonstrates the diagnostic value of patient-derived HNECs as a potential tool to complement traditional clinical and diagnostic assessments in CF.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) was developed to improve F508del-CFTR function in people with CF. Recently, ETI was approved for people with CF and at least one non-class I mutation. However, the efficacy of many rare variants is unknown. Therefore, we tested the rescue of CFTR activity by ETI in vitro and in vivo in non-F508del people with CF to improve understanding of mutation-specific CFTR modulator responses.

Methods: Highly differentiated primary nasal epithelial cells (pHNEC) were established from 54 people with CF and at least one rare variant and no F508del allele and 29 healthy controls. CFTR activity was assessed by Ussing chamber measurements after ETI/DMSO incubation and expressed as % of healthy CFTR function. In 12 people with CF, who received ETI therapy, we assessed lung function as well as sweat chloride concentration (SCC), intestinal current measurements (ICM) and nasal potential difference (NPD) at baseline and with ETI.

Results: 37 people with CF showed no increased CFTR activity in pHNEC with ETI compared to DMSO. However, 17 people with CF showed ETI response with a mean correction of CFTR activity of 20% of healthy in pHNEC. Of these, 12 people with CF received ETI therapy and showed a mean improvement in ppFEV1 of 12% and reduced SCC of -36mmol/L with ETI. In ICM, the cAMP-dependent chloride secretory response increased from -6µA/cm2 to 98µA/cm2 after ETI initiation and the total chloride secretory response increased from -18µA/cm2 to 130 µA/cm2. In a subgroup of 7 people with CF treated with ETI, total chloride response in NPD increased from 2.8mV to -12mV with ETI.

​Conclusion: We identified non-F508del CFTR variants that show a response to ETI in vitro and result in improvements in ppFEV1%, SCC, ICM and NPD after initiation of ETI. Our data show that in vitro CFTR modulator testing in pHNEC with confirmation of therapeutic effects with in vivo CFTR biomarkers provides a promising approach for personalized medicine.

records.affiliations_text: 12nd Faculty of Medicine, Charles University and Motol University Hospital, Department of Medical Microbiology, Praha 5, Czech Republic, 22nd Faculty of Medicine, Charles University and Motol University Hospital, Department of Pediatrics, Praha 5, Czech Republic
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Infants with positive newborn screening for cystic fibrosis (CF) but low or intermediate sweat chloride levels and/or inconclusive CFTR genotypes are classified as CFSPID (CF screen-positive, inconclusive diagnosis) or CFTR-related metabolic syndrome (CRMS). While most individuals remain healthy, 10–40 % later develop CF or CFTR-related disorders (CFTR-RD). Reliable predictors of disease progression are lacking. We evaluated CFTR function in human nasal epithelial cell (HNEC) cultures from CFSPID/CRMS individuals using Ussing chambers and assessed their response to elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) to explore whether in vitro functional profiling could stratify disease risk.

Methods: HNECs from 30 CFSPID/CRMS individuals (four individuals later reclassified as CF) and 10 healthy controls (WT) were analysed. HNECs were studied untreated or after 48 h pretreatment with 3 μM E and 3 μM T. Short-circuit current (ISC) was measured following sequential stimulation and inhibition, and CFTR function expressed as a percentage of WT activity. Changes after ET pretreatment were compared with those observed in CF-reclassified individuals.

Results: CFTR function in CFSPID/CRMS-derived HNECs was highly heterogeneous, ranging from 22 % to 100 % of WT. Thirteen exhibited residual CFTR function comparable to or lower than that observed in CF-reclassified subjects. When ranked by decreasing in vitro responsiveness to ETI, individuals later reclassified as CF clustered within the upper half (positions 4, 7, 10, 12). The three highest-ranked individuals have been followed for only 2 – 8 years and may not represent true negative cases.

Conclusions: In vitro assessment of ETI responsiveness in HNECs may help stratify CFSPID/CRMS individuals and identify those at higher risk of progression to CF or CFTR-RD. Validation in larger cohorts with longer follow-up is needed.

records.title: Evaluation of HE4 expression associated with epithelial mesenchymal transition in cystic fibrosis epithelial cells

person.department: Department of Laboratory Medicine, Faculty of Medicine

records.authors_text: M. Pócsi1, G.J. Balla1, F. Fenyvesi2, Á. Rusznyák2, Z. Fejes1, I. Balogh3, M. Macek Jr.4, M. D. Amaral5, B. Nagy Jr.1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Debrecen, Department of Laboratory Medicine, Faculty of Medicine, Debrecen, Hungary, 2University of Debrecen, Department of Pharmaceutical Technology, Faculty of Pharmacy, Debrecen, Hungary, 3University of Debrecen, Department of Medical Genetics, Faculty of Medicine, Debrecen, Hungary, 4Charles University, Department of Biology and Medical Genetics, 2nd Faculty of Medicine and Motol University Hospital, Prague, Czech Republic, 5University of Lisboa, BioISI-Biosystems & Integrative Sciences Institute, Faculty of Sciences, Lisboa, Portugal
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Impaired CFTR function results in elevated HE4 expression in cystic fibrosis (CF) and triggered via NF-κB in p.Phe508del-CFTR CFBE 41o− cells in vitro. CFTR dysfunction was associated with epithelial mesenchymal transition (EMT) in CF, but the potential involvement of HE4 in CF-related EMT is still unclear.

Methods: The degree of EMT was compared between CFBE 41o− cells carrying the p.Phe508del-CFTR and wt-CFTR through the level of epithelial and mesenchymal markers by fluorescence microscopy, RT-qPCR and ELISA. EMT was further induced by TGFβ1 in p.Phe508del-CFTR CFBE cells from 24-120h to investigate the relationship between the development of EMT and HE4/MMP9 expression. CFTR dysfunction was restored by VX-445/VX-661/VX-770 to monitor EMT phenotype. The direct effect of HE4 on EMT and MMP9 expression was analyzed after HE4 level was artificially reduced by transfection with HE4 specific siRNA. Cell proliferation was evaluated via Ki67 positivity.

Results: CFBE cells expressing p.Phe508del-CFTR were prone to be more mesenchymal and showed higher basal HE4 and MMP9 expression than wt-CFTR CFBE cells. In response to TGFβ1, even lower E-cadherin with higher N-cadherin and MMP9 levels were observed in p.Phe508del-CFTR CFBE cells vs untreated cells. In contrast, HE4 expression decreased after 48h and further reduced up to 120h. The EMT phenotype could be reversed by the CFTR modulator treatment causing normalized HE4 and MMP9 levels. Finally, downregulated HE4 promoted EMT with induced MMP9 expression and reduced cell proliferation in p.Phe508del-CFTR CFBE cells.

Conclusion: EMT is accompanied with decreasing HE4 expression and upregulated MMP9 expression in the airway epithelial cells of CF.

Grants: This study was supported by FK-135327 grant (BN) and UID/04046/2025 centre grant in MDA lab (to BioISI) from FCT/MCTES Portugal.

records.title: Pregnancy in women with cystic fibrosis: a four-case series in a Portuguese CF centre

person.institution: Maternal Child Centre of the North (CMIN), Santo António Local Health Unit (ULSSA)

records.authors_text: A. Matias1, R. Ribeiro2, A.L. Cardoso3, C. Cruz2, F. Gonçalves2, T. Barbosa3,1
records.affiliations_text: 1Maternal Child Centre of the North (CMIN), Santo António Local Health Unit (ULSSA), Department of Pediatrics, Porto, Portugal, 2Santo António Local Health Unit (ULSSA), Department of Internal Medicine, Porto, Portugal, 3Maternal Child Centre of the North (CMIN), Santo António Local Health Unit (ULSSA), Cystic Fibrosis Reference Centre, Porto, Portugal
records.abstract_text:
Background: As survival improves in cystic fibrosis (CF), pregnancy has emerged as a clinical scenario with heterogeneous maternal and fetal outcomes.

Objectives: To compare maternal and neonatal outcomes in four pregnancies in women with CF.

Methods: Retrospective case series from a CF centre.

Results: Four women (P1–P4) with heterogeneous genotypes and disease severity were included. P1 (F508del/W1282X; FEV₁ ~85–90% predicted) had severe exocrine pancreatic insufficiency requiring long-term gastrostomy feeding and poor nutritional reserve. She remained on elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) during pregnancy with stable respiratory status but inadequate weight gain; intrauterine fetal death occurred at 32+3 weeks despite unremarkable fetal investigations. P2(F508del/F508del; advanced CF lung disease) had frequent pulmonary exacerbations, chronic airway infection and prior lung transplant assessment. Treatment adherence was poor, with uncertain ETI exposure. She developed severe hypoxaemic respiratory infection and sepsis at 33–34 weeks requiring intensive care. Urgent caesarean section at 34 weeks resulted in a preterm neonate with favourable short-term outcome. P3 (F508del/A561E; FEV₁ ~55–60% predicted) continued ETI throughout pregnancy, remained clinically stable and delivered at term by caesarean section; neonatal outcome was favourable, with transient respiratory adaptation. P4 (N1303K/R334W; FEV₁ ~60–65% predicted) wasn't receiving ETI during pregnancy and had a stable maternal course; caesarean delivery resulted in a low-birthweight infant with good neonatal adaptation.

Conclusions: Maternal respiratory complications were associated with advanced lung disease, severe nutritional compromise and poor treatment adherence, while fetal outcomes were variable and not clearly related to CFTR genotype or modulator exposure. Baseline disease severity, nutritional status and treatment adherence are key factors when counselling pregnancy in women with CF.

records.title: Efficacy and stability of a novel microbial enzyme ANG003 measured in gastrointestinal chyme compared to pancrelipase.
records.authors_text: K. Pierzynowska1,2,3, D. Borowitz4, S. Pierzynowski1,5,6, R. Gallotto2
records.affiliations_text: 1Lund University, Department of Biology, Lund, Sweden, 2Anagram Therapeutics Inc., Natick, United States, 3The Kielanowski Institute of Animal Physiology and Nutrition, Polish Academy of Sciences, Department of Animal Physiology, Jabłonna, Poland, 4University at Buffalo, Department of Pediatrics, Jacobs School of Medicine and Biomedical Sciences, Buffalo, United States, 5Anara AB, Trelleborg, Sweden, 6Institute of Rural Health, Department of Medical Biology, Lublin, Poland
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Direct measurement of lipolysis, proteolysis and amylolysis in chyme from different gastrointestinal compartments could ensure a natural environment to measure efficacy and stability of enzymes from pancreatic enzymes replacement therapy (PERT) in the upper small intestine. Stability and efficacy of a novel broad spectrum microbially-derived product (ANG003) and porcine-derived pancrelipase was estimated in chyme from exocrine pancreatic insufficient (EPI) pig model.

Methods: Five EPI pigs were tested. Four weeks after pancreatic duct ligation, cannulas for chyme collection were placed in the stomach, duodenum and ileum. Pigs were fed a high fat meal (1) without enzymes, (2) with two doses of ANG003 (lipase 80-120mg, protease 50-75mg, amylase 120-160mg and (3) with 50,000 pancrelipase units; Kreonâ. Chyme was collected during 360 minutes after feeding and enzyme activity was estimated at pH 6.0 by measuring the release of oleic acid, tyrosine and glucose.

Results: ANG003 showed significantly higher activity of lipase and amylase in stomach and duodenal chyme than Kreon. ANG003 lipase maintained activity from the stomach to the duodenum demonstrating its high stability. Kreon lipase activity in the stomach and duodenum didn’t differ from no enzyme condition likely due to the enteric coating. ANG003 protease was released in the upper small intestine whereas Kreon protease appeared in essential amounts in the ileum.

Conclusions: The ANG003 enzymes had an earlier and more physiological activity profile compared to Kreon. The stabilization of ANG003 lipase makes it immediately active in the stomach and duodenum. The earlier activity of all three ANG003 enzymes stands in contrast to Kreon activity, which revealed minimal lipase and amylase activity in upper small intestine, while excessive protease activity in the ileum. Measuring enzymes activity in chyme from EPI pigs can be a useful tool to assess PERT efficacy in natural prandial conditions.

records.title: The Adult Home Sputum-Induction Trial (CF-Adult_HomeSpIT). Feasibility and acceptability of early morning sputum-induction at home in adults with cystic fibrosis. Preliminary results.
records.authors_text: K. Ronchetti1, Z. Raymond2, H. Carter2, S. Mitchell3, R. Dhillon3, D. Lau2, J.T. Forton1,4
records.affiliations_text: 1The Children's Hospital for Wales, Paediatric Respiratory Medicine, Cardiff, United Kingdom, 2University Hospital of Wales, All Wales Adult CF Centre, Cardiff, United Kingdom, 3Public Health Wales, Microbiology Department, Cardiff, United Kingdom, 4Cardiff University, Cardiff, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The CF-SpIT trials in children show sputum-induction to be an effective approach to pathogen detection both in clinic and at home. CF-Adult_HomeSpIT [ISRCTN86523335] is a prospective internally-controlled interventional trial in 100 adults comparing home-sampling using spontaneous early morning cough-clear (emCC) and home sputum-induction (hSI) with matched same-day clinic sampling using cough swab (CS), spontaneous clinic cough-clear (cCC) and clinic sputum-induction (cSI). Here we present preliminary qualitative data exploring feasibility & acceptability of home sampling in adults with CF.

Methods: Patients at the All Wales Adult CF Centre already using hypertonic saline (HTS) were eligible for recruitment. emCC was obtained on waking, using 3 rounds of standardised expectoration: COUGH, HUFF, COUGH, CLEAR THROAT (hawk), and SPIT. hSI was obtained using HS with normal home physiotherapy routine, using the same standardised expectoration. Same-day clinic samples (cCC and cSI) were taken after routine CS by a physiotherapist using standardised procedures and expectoration.

Results: To date 25 patients have performed sampling events. Median age 29yrs. Median FEV% 81%. 88% were on modulator therapy. Median sweat Cl- 55mmol/L. 4% had a wet cough.

All patients produced emCC and hSI samples (median duration 15 minutes). 16/25 (64%) grew pathogens from all samples combined. 46% of samples were described as mucoid, purulent or mucopurulent on lab processing.

23/25 (92%) and 20/25 (80%) of patients would do emCC and hSI again respectively, with a median chosen frequency of 4/year. Ease of both home procedures on clinic day were rated independantly at median of 0 on a Likert scale of 0-10 (0=easy).

Conclusion: Home-based sputum-sampling on clinic day is feasible and acceptable to adults with cystic fibrosis and could be implemented into routine care. Pathogen detection from home samples compared to clinic samples will be presented at the end of the trial.

records.title: Triple combination therapy modulates airway inflammation and reduces Pseudomonas aeruginosa burden in pediatric cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: F. Kanoun1, Y. Sereme2, I. Jeguirim1, M. Kelly-Aubert1, I. Haï1, F. Zavala1, O. Tabary1, I. Sermet-Gaudelus1,3,4
records.affiliations_text: 1Institut Necker Enfants Malades, Paris, France, 2Institut National de la Santé et de la Recherche Médicale, Paris, France, 3Service de Coprologie Fonctionnelle, Hôpital Universitaire Pitié Salpétrière, Paris, France, 4European Rare Disease Network, Lung, Frankfurt, Germany
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: P. aeruginosa (Pa) lung infections are the leading cause of mortality in Cystic Fibrosis (CF), typically chronic and punctuated by exacerbations. The advent of triple combination therapy (ETI) has reshaped the clinical course of CF, with substantial airway microbiome changes, including a marked reduction in Pa. Here, we aimed to evaluate the effects of ETI on Pa burden and innate immune responses in children with CF.

Methods: Longitudinal sputum cultures were analysed at baseline and at 1 year of ETI therapy allowing classification of patients as chronic, intermittent, or negative. Sputum concentrations of antimicrobial peptides (including Secretory leukocyte protease inhibitor (SLPI)) were measured before and after therapy. To complement these in vivo experiments, primary nasal epithelial cells from healthy donors, Phe508del individuals, and patients carrying a Premature Termination Codon (PTC) were cultured at the air-liquid interface, treated with ETI or vehicle and infected with Pa. Bacterial growth was assessed across genotypes. Experiments were repeated in the presence of a neutralizing anti-SLPI antibody.

Results: After 1 year of ETI therapy, and in the absence of concurrent antibiotic treatment, a subset of patients cleared Pa from their airways. In sputum, concentrations of SLPI increased after treatment (p<0.01). The pattern observed in sputum cultures data was recapitulated ex vivo in Pa-infected primary epithelial cells. Incubation with ETI reduced bacterial growth in cells from CF patients (p<0.05), but not in cells from healthy donors or individuals carrying a PTC. The observed reduction was not due to a direct antibiotic effect, indicating a host-mediated effect. SLPI neutralization reduced the ETI-mediated inhibition of bacterial growth, suggesting a key role for SLPI in controlling Pa under therapy.

Conclusion: ETI enhances host antimicrobial defences, modulating infection burden and airway innate immunity in children with CF.

records.title: Saliva qPCR as a non-invasive approach for detecting Pseudomonas aeruginosa lung infection in people with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: C.C Hanna1, G.G Einarsson1, E. Caamano Gutierrez2, R.W Lord3,4, R.E Maher2, A. Jones3,4, A. Horsley3,4, D.F Gilpin1, M.M Tunney1
records.affiliations_text: 1Queen's University Belfast, School of Pharmacy, Belfast, United Kingdom, 2University of Liverpool, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 3University of Manchester, Manchester, United Kingdom, 4Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust, Manchester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Accurate detection of pathogens in cystic fibrosis (CF) lung infection is essential and traditionally relied on sputum culture. Saliva represents a non-invasive, easily obtainable alternative sample for people with CF (pwCF). This study aimed to determine the limit of detection (LoD) of Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa) in spiked saliva samples using real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR).

Methods: Spiking assays (n=4) were performed using Pa reference isolate (ATCC 27853) and a clinical isolate (0293A) across a dilution range of 1 x 108 – 1 x 101 CFU/mL in pooled saliva from healthy volunteers (n=6). Total viable counts (TVC) were determined by culture on Pseudomonas selective agar. Genomic DNA was extracted using the MagNA Pure 96 system (Roche), and qPCR targeting oprL performed in triplicate. The LoD was defined as the lowest concentration producing Cp values below those of negative controls across replicates.

Results: In spiked saliva, the qPCR LoD was determined as any sample yielding a Cp value below that of the negative control, and corresponded to a mean concentration of 1.18x104 CFU/ml. Above the LoD, no significant differences were observed between total viable counts (CFU/mL) and oprL qPCR copy numbers for corresponding serial dilutions (p > 0.05). qPCR achieved 100% detection of both Pa isolates at concentrations above the LoD.

Conclusion: This work demonstrates the feasibility of detecting Pa in saliva, supporting its potential use as a non-invasive matrix for infection detection in pwCF. Future studies will focus on evaluation in clinical saliva samples.

Funded through PULSE-CF by the CF-Trust and LifeArc.

records.title: How keep identifying chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonisation in the ETI era
records.authors_text: M. Rossitto1, G. Vrenna1, V. Fox1, R. Scutari1, V. Tuccio Guarna Assanti1, S. Raimondi1, M. Cristiano1, N. Essa1, M.S. Lepanto1, F. Majo1, E. Montemitro1, F. Alghisi1, L. Cristiani1, A. Boni1, R. Cutrera1, C.F. Perno1, P. Bernaschi1
records.affiliations_text: 1Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital, IRCCS, Rome, Italy
records.abstract_text:
The introduction of elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor (ETI) therapy significantly reduced sputum production in patients with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). This has made it difficult to recover previous colonising pathogens and to use current chronic infection definitions. In order to monitor chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA) colonisation in patients receiving ETI treatment, we used droplet digital PCR (ddPCR) to detect PA in culture-negative respiratory samples.

We developed an in-house triplex ddPCR assay targeting the oprL, ecfX and gyrB genes, with a detection limit of 3 copies/mL, 100% specificity and 91.7% sensitivity. The assay was applied to 30 culture-negative samples from 18 pwCF on ETI with a history of past PA colonisation. Whenever PA was detected again in respiratory cultures, whole-genome sequencing (WGS) was used to compare strains isolated before and after culture negativity.

ddPCR detected PA in 10 respiratory samples from 7 pwCF on ETI, despite negative conventional cultures. In 4 of these patients, ddPCR positivity preceded the reappearance of PA in culture after a period of apparent microbiological clearance during the study year. WGS comparison of isolates obtained before and after culture negativity demonstrated intra-patient isoclonality, indicating persistence of the same infecting PA strain over time rather than new acquisition.

Although positive ddPCR results may indicate past infections, analysing longitudinal samples can promptly reveal an increase in bacterial burden, suggesting replicating bacteria. In our case, we were able to confirm the ddPCR results in 4 out of 7 pwCF by assessing the isoclonality of PA that reappeared in culture after 'apparent' negativity. These results support the use of ddPCR as a sensitive tool for monitoring pulmonary colonisation in pwCF on ETI, particularly those with reduced sputum production, and suggest a potential benefit for more timely and personalised therapeutic strategies.

records.title: Assessing population-level antibiotic susceptibility in heterogeneous Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections: implications for cystic fibrosis care
records.authors_text: H. Richardson1, M. Shepherd1, R. Wright1, C. Igler1, M. Brockhurst1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Manchester, Manchester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Chronic lung infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a major cause of morbidity in individuals with chronic lung infections like cystic fibrosis (CF). Extensive phenotypic and genotypic adaptation during chronic infection results in highly heterogeneous bacterial populations with varying susceptibility to antibiotics. Traditional antibiotic susceptibility testing (AST) is typically performed on a very limited number of individual isolates and therefore often fails to accurately predict clinical responses in chronic infections, as it does not capture population-level behaviour. The aim of this project was to investigate the extent to which individual isolates reflect the antibiotic susceptibility of heterogeneous P. aeruginosa populations within chronically infected patients.

Methods: A unique global collection of P. aeruginosa isolates obtained from patients with bronchiectasis prior to a phase III clinical trial of inhaled liposomal ciprofloxacin was used to assess resistance behaviour in heterogeneous populations. For each patient, 90 P. aeruginosa isolates were analysed, enabling characterisation of within-host diversity through growth curve analysis and determination of minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) for ciprofloxacin, colistin, levofloxacin, tobramycin, and aztreonam.

Results: The results demonstrate that individual isolate behaviour can predict antibiotic susceptibility of pathogen populations. A mathematical model shows that increasing the number of isolates sampled leads to resistance prediction for populations that approach the maximum observed resistance among isolates of the population, but mean resistance remains a better predictor of population behaviour.

Conclusion: These findings highlight the limitations of using single isolates for AST and emphasise the importance of accounting for population-level heterogeneity when guiding antibiotic therapy in CF care.

records.title: Early detection of cystic fibrosis airway pathogens in paediatric patients: added clinical value of molecular testing beyond culture
records.authors_text: Z. Alfahl1, G.G Einarsson2, M. Herzig3, L. Doherty1, J. Kelly1, L. O’Connor1, P. Cafaro Loureiro1, M. Cormican1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Galway, School of medicine, Galway, Ireland, 2Queens University Belfast, Belfast, United Kingdom, 3Galway University Hospital, Galway, Ireland
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: This longitudinal study aimed to compare conventional culture and targeted quantitative Polymerase Chain Reaction (qPCR) for the early detection of CF-associated pathogens and to characterise airway microbial community composition.

Methods: Fifteen paediatric CF patients attending Galway University Hospital (GUH) provided 4 sputum samples each during clinically stable visits over a one-year period. Samples (n=60) were tested using culture and qPCR to detect and quantify Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA), Haemophilus influenzae (HI) and Staphylococcus aureus (SA). Airway microbial community composition was assessed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Ethical approval was obtained from the GUH Clinical Research Ethics Committee.

Results: Of 15 patients, 60% male, mean (SD) age 11.7 (2.7) years, FEV1 95.3 (17) %. While culture did not detect PA in any sample, targeted qPCR identified PA in 4/15 patients (26.7%) who were culture-negative. Out of the 4 patients, 3 were qPCR-positive on all 4 samples and for 1 patient PA was not detected in the initial sample but was detected in all 3 patient subsequent samples. Bacterial loads were consistently low (10⁰–10¹ copies), indicating low-level molecular detection that may represent early or transient airway presence rather than established colonisation and was not detected by culture. Furthermore, qPCR detected HI in 43.3% (26/60) and SA in 21.7% (13/60) samples, compared with 3.3% (2/60) and 36.7% (22/60) by culture; respectively. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed a diverse and patient-specific airway microbiome dominated by Streptococcus, Veillonella, Haemophilus and Prevotella species, with marked inter-individual variability and temporal stability across visits.

Conclusions: In paediatric CF patients, targeted qPCR detected PA DNA in patients where PA was not detected by culture. The significance of this as a guide to treatment and prognosis is unclear but merits further investigation.

Conclusions: In paediatric CF patients, targeted qPCR detected PA DNA in patients where PA was not detected by culture. The significance of this as a guide to treatment and prognosis is unclear but merits further investigation.

records.title: Paired culture-based analysis reveals heterogeneous airway microbiota restructuring after elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) therapy in adult people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF)

records.authors_text: K.F Deasy1,2, G.G. Einarsson3, S O'Brien3, E. Madden1, Y. McCarthy1, F. Holmes1, C. Fleming1, M. McCarthy1, J. Dorgan1, T. Vagg1, D Gilpin3, H. Ibrahim1,2, D.M Murphy1,2, M. Tunney3, B.J Plant1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Cork Centre for Cystic Fibrosis (3CF), Cork University Hospital, Ireland, Cork, Ireland, 2HRB Clinical Research Facility, University College Cork, Cork University Hospital, Cork, Ireland, 3School of Pharmacy, Queens University Belfast, Belfast, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Chronic airway infection in pwCF is characterised by person-specific microbial communities often dominated by pathogenic taxa. While ETI therapy improves clinical outcomes, its effects on airway microbial ecology remain poorly understood. Using paired culture-based samples, we assessed within-subject changes in airway bacterial community composition pre- and post-ETI therapy.

Paired sputum samples were analysed from 14 pwCF immediately pre- and post-ETI initiation (> 12 months minimum). Viable bacterial communities were characterised using extended aerobic and anaerobic quantitative culture with species identification by MALDI-TOF. Absolute abundances (CFU/g or CFU/mL, log₁₀-transformed) were aggregated at species level. Core pathogen prevalence, alpha diversity (Shannon–Wiener and dominance), and beta diversity (Bray–Curtis dissimilarity) were calculated. Paired statistical analyses and PERMANOVA with subject stratification were used to assess within-patient changes.

ETI therapy was associated with substantial within-patient microbiota restructuring, with a median Bray–Curtis dissimilarity of 0.67 (p<0.001) between pre- and post-therapy samples. Shannon–Wiener diversity increased post-ETI (p<0.001), while community dominance decreased (p=0.001). Pathogen responses were heterogeneous; Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA) abundance decreased significantly (median Δ −4.25 log₁₀ CFU/g, p=0.014), with no detectable (PA) observed in 63% of subjects (n=5/8) where PA was detected on pre-ETI sputum sample. Other core pathogens showed variable or minimal change. Ordination analyses demonstrated patient-specific trajectories rather than uniform directional shifts (R2=0.069; F=1.9262; p=0.018).

ETI therapy was associated with marked within-patient airway microbiota restructuring, characterised by reduced dominance, heterogeneous pathogen response, and patient-specific ecological trajectories, highlighting the individualised microbial responses accompanying ETI therapy.

records.title: Therapeutic drug monitoring–guided beta-lactam dosing in pediatric cystic fibrosis: a case series
records.authors_text: J. Csepiová1, É. Gács1, A. Molnár1, I. Gönczi1, G.B. Karvaly2, K. Bocskai2, A. Párniczky1,3
records.affiliations_text: 1Heim Pál National Pediatric Institute, Budapest, Hungary, 2Semmelweis University, Department of Laboratory Medicine, Budapest, Hungary, 3Institute for Translational Medicine, Medical School, University of Pécs, Pécs, Hungary
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Despite advances with CFTR modulators, children with cystic fibrosis (CF) continue to experience recurrent bacterial pulmonary exacerbations, increasingly complicated by reduced β-lactam susceptibility. Our aim was to evaluated pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) target attainment following implementation of a therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) service, using free trough-to-MIC ratios (fCmin/MIC) ≥1 and ≥4 as targets.

Methods: A center-specific β-lactam TDM protocol was introduced alongside multidisciplinary education. Meropenem and piperacillin–tazobactam were initially administered as 60-minute infusions. When free drug concentrations failed to meet PK/PD targets, infusion duration was prolonged or switched to continuous infusion, accounting for individual tolerability.

Results: Five pediatric patients were included (four received meropenem, one piperacillin–tazobactam). Standard 1-hour infusions failed to achieve PK/PD targets in all cases. Prolonged infusion was not tolerated in one patient. Among three patients receiving prolonged meropenem infusions (3 hours), trough concentrations were unavailable in two cases. In contrast, the patient treated with continuous piperacillin–tazobactam infusion via an elastomeric pump achieved the predefined PK/PD target.

Conclusion: TDM-guided β-lactam dosing is feasible and clinically informative in pediatric CF care but presents practical challenges. Achieving PK/PD targets may require individualized infusion strategies, particularly in the setting of reduced antimicrobial susceptibility.

records.title: ​​​​​​Prevalence of mucoid Staphylococcus aureus from CF airway specimens in the era of modulator therapy

person.title: Phd
person.institution: University Hospital Muenster, Institute of Medical Microbiology

records.authors_text: C.H. Rumpf1, E. Braun1, S. Deiwick1, B.C. Kahl1
records.affiliations_text: 1University Hospital Muenster, Institute of Medical Microbiology, Muenster, Germany
records.abstract_text:
The emergence of a mucoid phenotype is a well‑described adaptive mechanism observed across multiple bacterial pathogens, where increased exopolysaccharide production enhances persistence and biofilm formation. We previously reported the prevalence of mucoid Staphylococcus aureus (Sa) and its association with lung function in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). Since the introduction of highly efficient modulator therapy (HEMT), many studies have investigated shifts in the frequency of classical CF pathogens, demonstrating a clear reduction in the isolation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa) and, to a lesser extent, Sa. As HEMT fundamentally alters the unique environment of the CF lung, an important question arises: whether, and in what ways, Sa adapts to these new conditions, and whether the mucoid Sa phenotype can still be identified in the modulator era.

In a retrospective analysis of our routine CF diagnostic lab, we analysed Sa isolated from airway specimens (sputum/throat swabs) of all pwCF (n=32) from two CF centres in Muenster, Germany between 2023 and 2025. Information on CFTR genotype, coinfection with Pa and modulator therapy are available for all pwCF. So far, 52 mucoid Sa isolates have been identified and are the subject of genomic and phenotypic characterization, including detailed biofilm analyses. A special focus is set on isolates from pwCF who previously participated in the earlier multicentre study.

Our findings indicate that mucoid Sa continues to be isolated from respiratory specimens of pwCF in our routine CF diagnostic lab without intense culture conditions to facilitate the finding of mucoid Sa, even in the era of HEMT. This persistence suggests that, despite substantial improvements, the ecological niche for mucoid Sa is not entirely eliminated. The continued detection of this phenotype raises important questions about its adaptive capacity and underscores the need for ongoing surveillance of Sa phenotypic diversity in pwCF.

records.title: Pulmonary exacerbations and microbiological surveillance in children with cystic fibrosis: lessons from a national newborn screening programme in North Macedonia

person.title: dr
person.institution: University Children's Clinic, Ss.Cyril and Methodius University in Skopje, North Macedonia

records.authors_text: E. Krsteska1, A. Andreevska Stepanovska1, L. Spirevska1, V. Cvejoska Cholakovska1,2, S. Fustikj1
records.affiliations_text: 1University Children's Clinic, Ss.Cyril and Methodius University in Skopje, North Macedonia, Department for Cystic Fibrosis, Skopje, North Macedonia, The Republic of, 2University Children's Clinic, Ss.Cyril and Methodius University in Skopje, North Macedonia, Department of Pulmonology and Allergology, Skopje, North Macedonia, The Republic of
records.abstract_text:
Background: Cystic fibrosis is a multisystem genetic disorder in which progressive pulmonary involvement remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality. Pulmonary exacerbations accelerate lung function decline. Early diagnosis through newborn screening enables timely intervention and systematic follow-up. This study evaluated the frequency of pulmonary exacerbations and associated microbiological findings in children diagnosed through newborn screening.

Methods: A retrospective observational study included 19 children diagnosed via national newborn screening and followed at the paediatric cystic fibrosis centre, University Children’s Clinic, Skopje, North Macedonia. All pulmonary exacerbations recorded between January 2019 and December 2024 were analysed. Exacerbations were defined as clinical deterioration requiring inpatient intravenous antibiotic therapy. Clinical and microbiological data from respiratory samples were extracted from medical records.

Results: Nineteen patients experienced 83 pulmonary exacerbations, with a median of 3 exacerbations per patient per year. Increased cough was the most frequent presenting symptom. One exacerbation occurred in 17.6% of patients, one to 2 in 23.5%, and more than 3 in 58.8%. Staphylococcus aureus was the most frequently isolated pathogen, followed by Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Escherichia coli. Recurrent exacerbations were more often associated with persistent bacterial colonisation.

Conclusion: Despite early diagnosis through newborn screening, children with cystic fibrosis continue to experience a high burden of pulmonary exacerbations, frequently linked to persistent airway infection. Early detection of pathogens such as P. aeruginosa and methicillin-resistant S. aureus allows timely treatment to prevent chronic colonisation and progressive lung damage. Systematic microbiological surveillance and regular follow-up remain essential to optimise long-term respiratory outcomes.

records.title: Impact of adherence to inhaled antibiotics on lung function and pulmonary exacerbations in cystic fibrosis (CF) patients taking elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI).
records.authors_text: N. Macdonald1, R. Birch1, C. Todd2, D. Budden2, T. Mathieson2, R. Tolhurst3, M.D. Waller4,5
records.affiliations_text: 1King's College London, GKT School of Medicine, London, United Kingdom, 2King’s College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, Department of Adult Cystic Fibrosis, Physiotherapy Department, London, United Kingdom, 3King’s College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, Post-Acute Medicine, Pharmacy Department, London, United Kingdom, 4King’s College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, Department of Adult Cystic Fibrosis, London, United Kingdom, 5King's College London, Centre for Human & Applied Physiological Sciences, Faculty of Life Sciences & Medicine, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Improvements in lung function (ppFEV1), airway microbiology and pulmonary exacerbations (PE) are established benefits of ETI. Reducing treatment burden is a key CF care priority, with recent studies reporting non-inferiority from stopping nebulised mucolytics. Long-term value of inhaled antibiotics in people taking ETI is unclear, with some opting to discontinue therapy. This retrospective, single-centre observational study assessed impact of inhaled antibiotic adherence on ppFEV1 and PE frequency during the first 60 months of ETI treatment in CF patients.

Methods: CF patients prescribed ETI and inhaled antibiotics at King’s College Hospital (2020-2025) were classified as adherent or poor/discontinued treatment based on self-reporting and clinical assessment. A subgroup was assessed by electronic nebuliser data and prescription refills for grouping validation. Data were extracted from clinical records and CF Registry database. Baseline characteristics were taken at annual review prior to ETI, with ppFEV1 and PE collected annually up to 60 months. Severity of PE was pre-defined, with severe events requiring IV antibiotics.

Results: This study included 81 patients. Sustained improvements in ppFEV1 across 5-years was greater in patients with good (n=25) compared to poor (n=56) adherence, though this did not reach significance (p=0.052) (table 1). No difference was found in the number of mild/moderate (p=0.38), severe (p=0.45) and total (p=0.30) PE between groups.

records.title: Review of intravenous antibiotic use before and after initiation of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor in people with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: A. Chan1, L. Rossiter1, D. Nazareth1,2, M. Ledson1, F. Frost1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Liverpool Heart and Chest Hospital, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 2University of Liverpool, Liverpool, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: The Antibiotic Spectrum Index (ASI) is a measure of antimicrobial breadth and potential antimicrobial resistance (AMR) burden in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). Following the introduction of elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor (ETI), hospitalisations for pulmonary exacerbations have fallen substantially, but the impact on antibiotic selection and spectrum remains unclear. This study aim to review intravenous (IV) antibiotic use at a large adult CF centre, focusing on ASI before and after ETI initiation.

Methods: All inpatient IV antibiotic courses between 1 June 2013 and 30 September 2025 were reviewed. Data collected included admission and discharge dates, ETI initiation dates, and CF-specific ASI scores based on Cogen et al. (JCF, 2024). Antibiotics not routinely used in the United States (temocillin and teicoplanin) were assigned ASI scores using published spectrum data. Analyses were limited to pwCF receiving ETI, with comparisons made pre- and post-ETI at population and individual levels.

Results: In total, 2,830 IV antibiotic admissions in 322 pwCF were analysed. Annualised admissions decreased significantly after ETI initiation (326 per year pre-ETI vs 94 post-ETI, p = 0.002). Median ASI scores were unchanged (9.0 pre-ETI vs 9.0 post-ETI,median difference= 0, p = 0.13). In a paired analysis of 116 individuals, median ASI was 8.6 [8.1–9.0] pre-ETI and 8.8 [8.0–9.0] post-ETI (p = 0.51). ASI was not associated with time to next hospitalisation, with similar median scores between bottom and top quartiles (9 vs 9, median difference = 0, p = 0.49).

Conclusions: Despite a marked reduction in hospitalisations following ETI, the antimicrobial spectrum of IV antibiotic regimens, as measured by ASI, remained unchanged and was not associated with short-term clinical outcomes. As life expectancy for pwCF increases, antimicrobial stewardship should prioritise reducing cumulative lifetime AMR burden rather than admission-level antibiotic spectrum alone.

records.title: Quantification of antimicrobial resistance in the CFTR modulator era: a retrospective analysis using the relative resistance index
records.authors_text: H. Myat-Noe1, L. William1, L. Rossiter1, D. Nazareth1, G. Hyde1, M. Ledson1, M. Walshaw1, F. Frost1
records.affiliations_text: 1Liverpool Heart and Chest Hospital, Liverpool, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: Little is known about the dynamics of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in P.aeruginosa (Pa) with long-term elexacaftor/ivacaftor/tezacaftor (ETI) treatment. The Relative Resistance Index (RRI) is a validated AMR quantification tool in Pa. This study therefore explored the impact of ETI on RRI.

Study design: A retrospective, microbiological surveillance study was conducted at our large regional adult CF centre including consecutive isolates from people living with CF (pwCF) who started ETI. RRI was calculated from antibiograms of all Pa isolates using scores of 0,0.5,1 for reported S/I/R respectively and scored cumulatively for ciprofloxacin, ceftazidime, meropenem, piperacillin/tazobactam and tobramycin.

Results: We identified 207 pwCF receiving ETI with history of Pa at any time. A total of 8762 Pa isolates were available for analysis for this group. Overall, at the cohort level, median [IQR] RRI for isolates in the pre-ETI era was 0.3 (IQR 0.1-0.7). In the post-ETI era, the median RRI was 0.6 [0.4-0.8]. The median difference between the pre- and post-ETI RRI scores was +0.3, (Mann-Whitney test p < 0.0001). Of 207 pwCF with a Pa isolate pre-ETI, 80/207 did not have a positive post-ETI (38.7%).

At the individual level 97 pwCF were positive for Pa before and after ETI and had available antibiogram, including 5551 isolates. Pre-ETI, median [IQR] RRI was 0.3 [0.2-0.5], post-ETI median RRI was 0.6 [0.4-0.8], median difference +0.26 (p<0.0001).

Conclusions: A significant proportion of individuals are no longer culture positive for Pa, but in those that are, RRI has increased significantly in the post-ETI era. Whether this reflects general temporal increases in AMR, a modulator-specific effect or a subset of sputum-producing patients acting as reservoirs of resistance warrant further evaluation.

records.title: Sustained fluid-associated weight gain following cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator modulator therapy
records.authors_text: E. Tillman1, C. Brown1
records.affiliations_text: 1Indiana University, Medicine, Indianapolis, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) modulators improve lung function and nutritional status in cystic fibrosis (CF). Weight gain is commonly attributed to improved appetite and metabolism, yet sustained hypervolemic edema or fluid-associated weight gain has not been described in clinical trials and remains under-recognized. We report four cases of clinically significant swelling and fluid-associated weight gain following CFTR modulator therapy.

Methods: We retrospectively reviewed four patients with CF or CF-related disorder who developed significant fluid-associated weight gain after CFTR modulator initiation. Data collected included demographics, CFTR genotype, pre- and post-modulator body mass index (BMI), timing and pattern of weight change, clinical evidence of edema, laboratory evaluation, and, when available, cardiac and pharmacokinetic data. CFTR modulator dosing, dose modifications, treatment interruptions and responses were documented. The Naranjo Adverse Drug Reaction Probability Scale was used to assess causality.

Results: All patients developed marked edema and rapid BMI increase temporally associated with CFTR modulator exposure. Mean pre-modulator BMI was 26.3±2.83 kg/m², increasing to 33.45±2.99 kg/m² post-exposure (p=0.05). Three patients required dose reduction and one discontinued therapy to improve swelling. No alternative cardiac, renal or hepatic cause of fluid retention was identified. Naranjo scores ranged from 8–9, indicating probable to definite association with CFTR modulator therapy.

Conclusion: Sustained, fluid-associated weight gain may occur in a minority of patients receiving CFTR modulators and can necessitate dose reduction or discontinuation. Clinicians should consider this adverse effect when evaluating rapid weight gain or unexplained edema following CFTR modulator initiation.

records.title: Safety and outcomes with the discontinuation of inhaled antibiotics in the CFTR modulator era: A Retrospective cohort study at a regional adult Cystic Fibrosis centre
records.authors_text: T. Penrose1, H. Wood1, L. Rossiter1, M. Ledson1, M. Walshaw1, F. Frost1
records.affiliations_text: 1Liverpool Heart and Chest, Liverpool, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Little is known about the consequences of inhaled antibiotic discontinuation for people receiving CFTR modulators. Within our large adult CF Centre, we reviewed the patient outcomes following the discontinuation of their nebulised antibiotic therapy.

Methods: Completing a retrospective analysis at our large regional adult CF centre we reviewed all the cases of nebulised antibiotic discontinuation between 2000 and 2025. We categorised them into 3 groups; Group 1 (Patient choice), Group 2 (Low adherence but clinically stable), Group 3 (Clinician led due to clinical stability). The outcomes between the 3 groups, with a focus on the re-initiation of a nebulised antibiotic.

Results: Of the 420 pwCF at our centre, 70 discontinued nebulised antibiotics between 2020 and 2025 (35 male, median FEV1 87% predicted, 20 Liverpool Epidemic Strain Pseudomonas aeruginosa). Overall, 16/70(22.9%) patients restarted their nebulised antibiotic due to clinical deterioration or new pathogen growth. Restart rates were similar between group 1 (26.7%) and group 3 (25%). Restart rates were significantly higher in those with FEV1 <80% predicted (41% vs. 15%, p=0.03). There was no difference in the restart rates between those with Liverpool epidemic strain P. aeruginosa compared to other P. aeruginosa strains (10% vs. 28%, p=0.12), and restart rates were no similar in those with and without recent P. aeruginosa growths prior to discontinuing their antibiotic nebuliser (31% vs. 20%, p=0.56).

Conclusion: Nebulised antibiotics were discontinued without the need for restarting in over 75% of cases.  Recent P. aeruginosa growth or stain was not associated with differential rates of restarting; however, restart rates were higher in those with lower lung function. These findings can inform discussions and decisions with patients considers inhaled antibiotic discontinuation.

Objectives: Little is known about the consequences of inhaled antibiotic discontinuation for people receiving CFTR modulators. Within our large adult CF Centre, we reviewed the patient outcomes following the discontinuation of their nebulised antibiotic therapy.  
Methods: Completing a retrospective analysis at our large regional adult CF centre we reviewed all the cases of nebulised antibiotic discontinuation between 2000 and 2025. We categorised them into 3 groups; Group 1 (Patient choice), Group 2 (Low adherence but clinically stable), Group 3 (Clinician led due to clinical stability). The outcomes between the 3 groups, with a focus on the re-initiation of a nebulised antibiotic.  
Results: Of the 420 pwCF at our centre, 70 discontinued nebulised antibiotics between 2020 and 2025 (35 male, median FEV1 87% predicted, 20 Liverpool Epidemic Strain Pseudomonas aeruginosa). Overall, 16/70(22.9%) patients restarted their nebulised antibiotic due to clinical deterioration or new pathogen growth. Restart rates were similar between group 1 (26.7%) and group 3 (25%). Restart rates were significantly higher in those with FEV1 <80% predicted (41% vs. 15%, p=0.03). There was no difference in the restart rates between those with Liverpool epidemic strain P. aeruginosa compared to other P. aeruginosa strains (10% vs. 28%, p=0.12), and restart rates were no similar in those with and without recent P. aeruginosa growths prior to discontinuing their antibiotic nebuliser (31% vs. 20%, p=0.56).  
Conclusion: Nebulised antibiotics were discontinued without the need for restarting in over 75% of cases.  Recent P. aeruginosa growth or stain was not associated with differential rates of restarting; however, restart rates were higher in those with lower lung function. These findings can inform discussions and decisions with patients considers inhaled antibiotic discontinuation.

records.title: Temporal impact of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) on oral and IV antibiotic use at a single CF center in the US
records.authors_text: J. Hernandez1, A. Pichler2, O. McElvaney2, S. Kapnadak2, K. Ramos2,3, S. Heltshe4,3, T. Ye1,3, C. Goss2,4,3
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Washington, Biostatistics, Seattle, United States, 2University of Washington, Medicine, Seattle, United States, 3Seattle Children's Research Institute, Pediatrics, Seattle, United States, 4University of Washington, Pediatrics, Seattle, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: ETI has been demonstrated to have a significant impact on lung function, symptoms and exacerbation rates. We aimed to assess prescription trends at the University of Washington adult CF center. We hypothesized that there would be an initial drop in oral antibiotic use with ETI and the Covid pandemic, but that it would slowly rebound in the adult population.

Methods: We performed a longitudinal single center cohort study assessing the temporal impact of ETI on the use of oral antibiotics from December 2014 to December 2024. We included patients who received an ETI prescription during this period. To assess temporal trends, we calculated monthly oral antibiotic prescription rates per patient encounter.

Results: We had a total of 376 CF individuals who fulfilled inclusion criteria. Uptake of ETI was quite rapid with 40% of the cohort receiving ETI by March 2020. During the study period, 82% of individuals received at least one prescription for oral antibiotics. The most common antibiotics used were levofloxacin (34%), trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (31%), ciprofloxacin (16%), amoxicillin-clavulanate (8%) and cephalexin (7%). When assessing prescription trends, we observed an initial decline in monthly prescriptions per encounter following ETI approval and the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. Prescription rates later rebounded in 2023–2024. Average monthly antibiotic rate/100 encounters was 9.84 in 2019, 5.41 from 2020-22, and 7.56 from 2023-2024. Formal time series analysis will be presented for both oral and intravenous antibiotic use.

Conclusions: Oral antibiotic use appears to have decreased with both the approval of ETI and the Covid pandemic only to rebound by the end of 2024 in this population.
