records.title: Multicenter experience with Burkholderia infection in cystic fibrosis: microbiological outcomes and impact of CFTR modulators
records.authors_text: R. Palha Martins1, R. Penteado1, T. Reis Silva1, S. Castanheira2, A.S. Santos2, E. Fragoso3, P. Azevedo3, T. Barbosa4, L. Almeida5, A. Amorim5, F. Gamboa1
records.affiliations_text: 1Unidade Local de Saúde de Coimbra, Coimbra, Portugal, 2Unidade Local de Saúde de São José, Lisbon, Portugal, 3Unidade Local de Saúde de Santa Maria, Lisboa, Portugal, 4Unidade Local de Saúde de Santo António, Porto, Portugal, 5Unidade Local de Saúde de São João, Porto, Portugal
records.abstract_text:
Objetives: To evaluate the clinical, functional and microbiological evolution of cystic fibrosis (CF) patients with chronic Burkholderia cepacia complex (Bcc) infection following initiation of CFTR modulator therapy.

Methods: Multicenter observational study including 16 CF patients with chronic Bcc infection followed at referral centers in Portugal. Patients under follow-up between 2020 and the present who initiated elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) were identified. Clinical data, respiratory cultures and spirometric parameters (FEV1 and FVC, % predicted) were retrospectively reviewed to assess the impact of ETI on microbiological status and lung function.

Results: Mean age at Bcc identification was 24.8 ± 8.7 years, with a male predominance (56.3%). 8 patients were homozygous for F508del, 7 were heterozygous, and 1 carried two non–class I CFTR mutations. Pseudomonas aeruginosa was concurrently isolated in three patients. Intravenous antibiotic eradication therapy and inhaled suppressive antibiotic therapy were each used in 13 cases. After 12 months of ETI, mean FEV1 increased from 51.5 ± 21.0% to 72.1 ± 22.8%, and mean FVC from 69.8 ± 26.7% to 85.5 ± 16.6%. Microbiological eradication of Bcc was observed in 11 patients (69%), occurring at a mean of 29.0 ± 19.7 months (median 25.6 months, IQR 10.9–45.2) after ETI initiation.

Conclusion: In this multicenter cohort, ETI initiation was associated with significant improvement in lung function and with microbiological clearance of chronic Bcc infection in a substantial proportion of patients. These findings suggest a possible link between CFTR modulation and Bcc eradication, although the relative contribution of ETI versus concomitant antimicrobial therapy remains uncertain and warrants further investigation.

records.affiliations_text: 1Fondazione IRCCS CA’ Granda, Ospedale Maggiore Policlinico, Clinical Microbiology and Virology Unit, Milan, Italy, 2Fondazione IRCCS Ca’ Granda Ospedale Maggiore Policlinico, Internal Medicine Department, Respiratory Unit and Cystic Fibrosis Center, Milan, Italy, 3University of Milan, Department of Pathophysiology and Transplantation, Milan, Italy, 4Fondazione IRCCS Ca’ Granda, Ospedale Maggiore Policlinico, Mother and Child Department, Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Milan, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Elexacaftor–tezacaftor–ivacaftor therapy (ETI) significantly improves lung function and reduces pulmonary exacerbations in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). However, its long-term effects on airway colonization are incompletely defined. This study aims to evaluate longitudinal changes in expectorating ability (EA) and respiratory microbiological profiles during the first three years of ETI.

Methods: A prospective study was conducted at the Regional Cystic Fibrosis Center in Milan from 1st September 2020 to 30th September 2025. A cohort of pwCF starting ETI were followed for up to 36 months. EA and the prevalence of key respiratory pathogens (from sputum and nasopharyngeal aspirates) were evaluated at baseline (T0) and after 12 (T12), 24 (T24), and 36 months (T36) of therapy. Statistical analisys was carried out using chi-square and Fisher’s exact tests.

Results: A total of 367 pwCF (205 males; median age 25 years, IQR 14–36.5) were enrolled. Over three years of ETI therapy, EA significantly decreased (81.7% at T12 to 66% at T36; p < 0.001). Significant reductions were observed in Pseudomonas aeruginosa (33.8% → 15.2%, p < 0.001), mucoid P. aeruginosa (30.5% → 21.7%, p < 0.05), Achromobacter xylosoxidans (15.8% → 8.1%, p < 0.05), rapidly growing mycobacteria (RGM) (4.9% → 0.5%, p < 0.01), and Aspergillus spp. (19.1% → 2%, p < 0.001). Non-significant changes were seen for Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Burkholderia cepacia complex. Stenotrophomonas maltophilia decreased significantly until T24 (11.2% → 2.7%, p < 0.001) but not at T36 (7.1%, p > 0.05).

Conclusion: After three years of ETI therapy, reduced expectorating ability likely reflects clinical improvement and lower mucus production. Microbiological trends suggest a shift toward a chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)-like profile, indicating that ETI remodels the respiratory microbiota in pwCF and highlighting the need for ongoing long-term monitoring. In addition, due to the increasing number of non-expectorating pwCF, it will be necessary to identify a new biological sample to serve as gold standard for respiratory sampling.

records.title: Comparison of clinical outcomes in adults with cystic fibrosis with Pseudomonas aeruginosa on and off prophylactic antibiotics: a retrospective cohort study
records.authors_text: J. Cunningham1, W.T. Cheong1, A. Higton1, C. Orchard1, A. Ewence1, A. Lillis1
records.affiliations_text: 1Frimley Park NHS Foundation Trust, Cystic Fibrosis Unit, Frimley, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Inhaled prophylactic antibiotics remain recommended for people with cystic fibrosis (CF) with chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa) infection. In the post-CFTR modulator era, some patients discontinue or do not initiate prophylaxis despite Pa infection, often by patient choice rather than clinical recommendation. This study examined the impact of this on lung function, antibiotic use, and antimicrobial resistance.

This study aimed to compare outcomes in adults with CF and Pa receiving versus not receiving prophylactic antibiotics in a UK adult CF centre.

Methods: Annual review data from 161 adults (2022 and 2024) were analysed using Mann–Whitney U tests for FEV₁% predicted, change in FEV₁% predicted, antibiotic use, and antimicrobial susceptibility, expressed as the percentage of isolates resistant to five antibiotics.

Results: Significant differences were observed between Pa and non-Pa groups for FEV₁% predicted (median 68.4% vs 86.2%; p=0.0001), change in FEV₁% predicted (−1.73% vs +1.12%; p=0.004), annual oral antibiotic use (median 2 vs 1 courses; p=0.007), and IV antibiotic days (p=0.003). Among Pa patients, no significant differences were observed between those receiving prophylaxis versus not for FEV₁% predicted (60.5% vs 74.2%; p=0.139), change in FEV₁% (−2.1% vs −1.4%; p=0.49), oral antibiotic use (median 2 vs 1.5; p=0.219), or IV antibiotic days (p=0.296). Multidrug resistance was higher in patients receiving antibiotics (median 1.5 vs 0.0 resistant agents; p=0.028).

Conclusion: Lung function and antibiotic burden differed between adults with and without Pa. Among Pa patients, outcomes did not differ significantly by prophylaxis status. Higher resistance in patients on prophylaxis may reflect cumulative antibiotic exposure or preferential treatment of established infection. These observational findings do not support withdrawing recommended therapy but highlight the need for ongoing review and shared decision-making in the post-modulator era.

records.title: Reduced sputum pathogen presence but persistent Staphylococcus aureus in throat swabs after three years of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor and its association with lung function
records.authors_text: S.O. Dekker1, B.C.H. de Bont1, H.G.M. Heijerman1, R. van der Meer2, M. Eggermont2, N. Vrisekoop1, L. Koenderman1, I. Bronsveld1
records.affiliations_text: 1University Medical Centre Utrecht, Dept. of Respiratory Medicine, Utrecht, Netherlands, 2Haga Ziekenhuis, Dept. of Pulmonology, The Hague, Netherlands
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) reduces sputum production in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). Therefore, throat swabs are used more frequently to detect pathogens when exacerbations are absent. This study retrospectively examined longitudinal changes in pathogen detection in sputum and throat swab cultures before and up to three years after ETI initiation.

Methods: Microbiological sputum and throat swab cultures of adult pwCF treated at two Dutch CF centres were collected from one year prior to three years after ETI initiation and grouped into six-month intervals. Generalized and linear mixed-effects models were used to assess associations between ETI, time, age, sex, and culture positivity for Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa), Staphylococcus aureus (Sa), and Aspergillus fumigatus (Af), as well as associations with ppFEV1.

Results: ETI initiation was associated with significantly lower odds of positive sputum cultures for Pa (OR = 0.18, 95% CI 0.11-0.18), Sa (OR = 0.45, 95% CI 0.37-0.55) and Af (OR = 0.11, 95% CI 0.08-0.13; all p<0.001). Female sex and higher age were associated with increased odds for Pa positivity in sputum, while higher age was associated with lower odds for Sa positivity in sputum. In contrast, Sa was the only pathogen that showed consistently high predicted probabilities in throat swabs before and after ETI initiation. Moreover, Sa throat swab positivity increased modestly but significantly over time following ETI initiation (OR = 1.15 per six-month interval, 95% CI 1.05-1.27, p = 0.002). Pa positivity was associated with lower ppFEV₁ before and after ETI, whereas Sa positivity in throat swabs was associated with higher ppFEV₁.

Conclusions: ETI is associated with reduced sputum culture positivity for key CF pathogens, while throat swab cultures, particularly for S. aureus, do not reflect these trends. These findings highlight important differences between sputum and throat swab cultures, and its association with ppFEV1.

records.title: Clinical predictors of long-term outcomes following initial Pseudomonas aeruginosa eradication in children with cystic fibrosis: a 10-year retrospective study

records.authors_text: T. Kantemir1, E. Yalçın1, U. Kavgacı1, Ö.F. İpek1, N. Emiralioğlu1, D. Doğru1, U. Özçelik1
records.affiliations_text: 1Hacettepe University İhsan Doğramacı Children Hospital, Pediatric Pulmonology Department, Ankara, Turkey
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To evaluate clinical characteristics,eradication success,and long-term microbiological outcomes in pediatric cystic fibrosis(CF)patients following first-time Pseudomonas aeruginosa(Pa)isolation and tobramycin-based treatment.

Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 10-year data(2015-2025)of 100pediatric CFpatients(51%female).Patients were grouped by response: Group1 (successful eradication,n=43)and Group2 (recurrence,n=57). Group 2was subdivided:Late Eradication(2a,n=18),Chronic Colonization(2b,n=26),and Intermittent Colonization(2c,n=13).Demographics,BMI,FEV₁,Pa phenotype,and co-pathogens at first isolation were analyzed.

Results: Median age at first Pa isolation was89months(IQR: 88.25); median diagnosis age was 2.25months(IQR: 3.00).At isolation,47%were symptomatic. Treatment included inhaled tobramycin alone(57%) or with oral ciprofloxacin(43%). MeanFEV₁ was 91.75%±22.80%and median BMIwas16.13(IQR: 2.91). Microbiologically,19%had a mucoid phenotype and 72%had co-isolations.Group2had significantly lower median BMI compared to Group1 (15.70,IQR:2.40vs.16.6,IQR:4.30;p=0.046).Mucoid phenotype at initial isolation was higher in Group2(26%)thanGroup1(9%)(p=0.032).Co-isolation was higher in Group1(83%) than Group2(63%)(p=0.023),with no significant difference in MRSA(p=0.100)orMSSA(p=0.381).No significant differences were found between Groups1 and2 in age at isolation(p=0.232),diagnosis(p=0.323),FEV₁(p=0.883),or treatment regimen(p=0.543).Subgroup analysis showed mucoid phenotype was most prevalent in group2b(42.3%)vs.2a(16.7%) and2c(7.7%)(p=0.037).Longitudinal analysis showed significant BMI decline during recurrence (t =-4.405, p<0.001). Group1 maintained better BMI than groups2b and 2c (p=0.023).

Conclusion: Pa recurrence is common despite eradication. Lower BMI and mucoid phenotype at first isolation are linked to recurrence, necessitating nutritional optimization and close follow-up.

records.title: To be or not to be? Evaluating the efficacy of nebulised tobramycin regimens for Pseudomonas aeruginosa eradication in children with cystic fibrosis following a reduction of oral ciprofloxacin use
records.authors_text: H. Woodman1, Z. Jennings1, K. Azzopardi1, H. Morgan1, J. Forton1, A. Schmidt1, W. Smith1, D. Rigler1, L.P Thia1
records.affiliations_text: 1Children's Hospital for Wales, Paediatric Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Cardiff, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: Paediatric patients provide respiratory samples for microbiology testing when symptomatic and at routine clinic visits. Eradication is attempted for all first isolates of Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa). First-line treatment is three-months oral ciprofloxacin plus nebulised colistimethate sodium but prescribing of ciprofloxacin has declined following safety warnings. Alternative regimens we use include intravenous (IV) antibiotics, nebulised tobramycin for 28 days or a novel extended regimen of alternate-month nebulised tobramycin for six months in younger children where nebuliser technique may be less effective. Treatment choice is patient-focused following multidisciplinary team review.

Methods: We evaluated Pa eradication regimes for six patients treated between October 2024 and November 2025, assessing re-isolation rates for Pa six months post-treatment.

Results: Two patients received IV antibiotics. One seven-year-old patient received three-months nebulised colistimethate sodium plus oral ciprofloxacin, and one six-year-old patient received 28 days of nebulised tobramycin. All four patients remained Pa free six months post-treatment.

Three younger patients (aged six months, two years and three years) received the extended regimen of nebulised tobramycin cycles for six months; two remained Pa-free while the three-year-old reisolated Pa whilst still on nebulised tobramycin and required escalation to IV therapy.

Conclusion: Effective nebuliser administration is likely to be age-dependant and appears to be a critical determinant for success in Pa eradication. An extended alternate-month regimen of nebulised tobramycin for six months may be more effective than 28 days treatment in younger patients. More data and longer follow-up are needed to assess the success and durability of these regimens.

records.title: Retrospective review of treatment success comparing nebulised colistimethate sodium versus tobramycin for Pseudomonas aeruginosa eradication in paediatric cystic fibrosis in the post modulator era
records.authors_text: C. Chan1, N. Gudka1, R. Brugha1, C. Dawson1
records.affiliations_text: 1Great Ormond Street Hospital, Pharmacy, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Early eradication of Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa) following initial isolation remains central to cystic fibrosis (CF) management, aiming to prevent chronic infection and mitigate long‑term lung damage. In the post‑modulator era, the optimal strategy for Pa eradication remains uncertain. Insufficient evidence exists on the optimal antibiotic regimen for Pa eradication (Hewer et al, 2023). Although modulators have reduced Pa burden, persistent and chronic infections continue to be observed as described by Pescaru et al, 2025.

We compared eradication success between 3-months nebulised colistimethate sodium and 1-month nebulised tobramycin, with 3-weeks oral ciprofloxacin in both regimes, in young people with CF at our centre. We conducted a retrospective review using data from our electronic prescribing system, implemented in 2019. All active patient records as of December 2025, as well as records of patients who transitioned to adult CF services since 2019, were assessed. All individuals with documented Pa growth were included.

Treatment success was defined as absence of Pa regrowth on airway samples (cough swabs, sputum or lavage) during therapy and within three months of completing the nebulised course. Treatment failure was defined as regrowth at any point during treatment or within three months post‑therapy. Patients with no documented Pa growth or those receiving long‑term Pa suppressive nebulised therapy were excluded. Patients who were admitted for intravenous antibiotics for Pa eradication were also excluded. Statistical comparison between groups is by Chi-squared test.

Of 247 patient records reviewed (198 active, 49 transitioned), 73 were excluded for having no Pa growth. Across 381 Pa isolates identified, 116 met inclusion criteria and 265 were excluded. Ninety patients received nebulised colistimethate sodium, and 26 received nebulised tobramycin. Further analysis is ongoing and will be completed ahead of the 2026 ECFS Conference

records.title: Some results of long-term CFTR modulator therapy in adults with cystic fibrosis, chronically infected with Burkholderiales

person.title: Associate Professor
person.institution: N.F. Gamaleya National Research Center for Epidemiology and Microbiology, Ministry of Health of Russia

records.authors_text: O. Voronina1, N. Ryzhova1, M. Kunda1, E. Ermolova1, E. Amelina2, R. Kagazezhev2, A. Gintsburg1
records.affiliations_text: 1N.F. Gamaleya National Research Center for Epidemiology and Microbiology, Ministry of Health of Russia, Moscow, Russian Federation, 2Pulmonology Research Institute under FMBA of Russia, Moscow, Russian Federation
records.abstract_text:
Burkholderiales are the most dangerous of CF pathogens. Over the past decade, the therapeutic landscape for CF has expanded to include CFTR modulators, of which adult pwCFs in Russia use IVA, LUM/IVA, and ELX/TEZ/IVA. Modulator therapy (MT) improves respiratory function, sweat chloride levels, and quality of life in pwCFs. The objective of our study was to investigate the effect of combination therapy, including MT, on the sputum microbiome composition in adult pwCFs infected with Burkholderiales since childhood.

Sputum samples were collected over 7-10 years from pwCFs with B. multivorans ST835 (35 years old, non-F508del/non-F508del), B. cenocepacia ST709 (35 years old, F508del/F508del), and A. ruhlandii ST262 (26 years old, F508del/F508del). CF pathogens were genotyped, 16S rDNA amplicons were sequenced, analyzed using the Microbial Genomics Module of the CLC Genomic Workbench v.21.0.1, and submitted to BioProject PRJNA717158.

IVA and LUM/IVA therapy for 2 and 4 years, respectively, had no effect on the composition of the sputum microbiome. Only the transition to ELX/TEZ/IVA led to a temporary decrease in the proportion of A. ruhlandii and B. cenocepacia in pwCFs with F508del/F508del. In a CF patient with A. ruhlandii, this was accompanied by an increase in the proportion of Prevotella to 23%, followed by an increase in the proportion of Streptococcus to 60%. Subsequently, the proportion of P. aeruginosa and S. aureus increased, and then after 6 years of MT, A. ruhlandii rose to 60%. In a patient with B. cenocepacia the proportion of Streptococcus increased to 60-70%, compared to a normal 13% in the supraglottic space in healthy individuals. The transition to ELX/TEZ/IVA did not affect the proportion of B. multivorans in the microbiome of pwCF with non-F508del/non-F508del. It remained at 91%.

So, normalizing the Burkholderiales-containing microbiome composition in adult CF patients requires long-term treatment and a personalized approach even with targeted therapy.

Objectives: Chronic respiratory infection with methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is associated with worse clinical outcomes in CF (higher mortality). Yet, uncertainty exists about early treatment of asymptomatic MRSA positive patients. Our prior randomized trial (STAR-too) using an intense eradication regimen showed higher rates of MRSA eradication in the treatment compared to no-treatment arm. This follow-up study evaluated the microbiologic outcome of oral antibiotic and topical decontamination in subjects with incident MRSA.

Methods: Open label multi-center treatment study with comparison to control group from the STAR-too trial. Inclusion criteria were incident (first ever or at least 2 year negative and no prior chronic MRSA) MRSA positive culture, being at stable baseline, age 4-45 years. The medication regimen was TMP-SMX (or minocycline if allergic to TMP-SMX and >8 years) and oral gargle with 0.12% chlorhexidine BID for 14 days, and nasal mupirocin 2% nasal ointment for 5 days. This treatment was repeated after Day 28. The primary endpoint was MRSA culture status at Day 28.

Results: Characteristics of the 37 subjects who completed the primary endpoint are in Table 1, 17 were on a CFTR-modulator. As in the prior trial the majority had at least one F508del mutation and were pancreatic insufficient. Oral study medication was TMP-SMX in 33 (89%) of subjects. 56 adverse events (AE) occurred between screening visit through visit 3 (Day 56) of the study, one AE was deemed study related and 3/7 severe AEs were deemed study related (with 2 SAE in the same subject). At Day 28, 11 subjects (30%) had MRSA negative respiratory culture. In comparison, 26% of subjects in the observation arm in STAR-too were MRSA negative at Day 28. At Day 56, 10 of 32 (29%) subjects were MRSA negative.

Conclusion: The current data show limited benefit of a simplified eradication protocol for incident MRSA positive cultures even with a sequential course.

person.title: Professor
person.biography: Marianne Muhlebach, MD has a keen interest in the role of infection, the microbiome and inflammation in the pathogenesis of CF. Using bronchoalveolar lavage samples from infants she showed that anaerobic likely orally derived bacteria are present in early CF lung disease but also in older people with CF who expectorate sputum and that the contribution of these bacteria to inflammation / disease may depend on stage of lung disease. She has conducted several studies related to methicillin resistance Staphylococcus aureus with past and an ongoing studies on treatment of incident infection. Other interests include infection control and use of CF patient registry data to define use and need for inhaled antibiotics for P. aeruginosa. She is Professor of Pediatric Pulmonology/Respirology at the University of North Carolina Chapel Hill where she had moved to for her specialisation and research. Dr. Muhlebach had completed her medical training in Switzerland and her home country Austria.

records.title: Co-treatment with glatiramer acetate enhances the efficacy of tobramycin against other cystic fibrosis pathogens including Staphylococcus aureus
records.authors_text: A. Daly-Gourdialsing1, R.F Rollo1, A.C. Micallef1, M. Zhao1, R.A. Murphy2, T. Vorup-Jensen3, D.A. Hughes1,4, L.P. Allsopp1, J.C. Davies1,4
records.affiliations_text: 1Imperial College London, National Heart and Lung Institute, London, United Kingdom, 2Freie Universität Berlin, Institut Für Biologie, Berlin, Germany, 3Aarhus University, Department of Biomedicine, Aarhus, Denmark, 4Royal Brompton Hospital, Department of Paediatric Respiratory Medicine, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Identifying therapies to reduce the cumulative antibiotic burden in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) is a priority, particularly in chronic lung infections that drive adverse side effects and antimicrobial resistance. Glatiramer acetate (GA) shares similarity to antimicrobial peptides and enhances tobramycin (TOB) activity against the Gram-negative Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa). GA’s proposed mechanism is via interaction with lipopolysaccharides (LPS). Thus, its effect on common co-infecting Gram-positive (G+) organisms like Staphylococcus aureus (Sa), is unclear. Therapeutics for polymicrobial infections should be at least neutral to co-infecting pathogens, not antagonistic.

Method: We assessed the impact of co-treatment with GA on antimicrobial activity of TOB against pathogens found in polymicrobial CF lung environments. This work included 21 Sa, nine Achromobacter xylosoxidans (Ax), nine Stenotrophomonas maltophilia (Sm), and six Burkholderia cenocepacia (Bc) isolates from pwCF. Median minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC50) values for TOB were determined alone and with 200 µg/ml GA.

Results: Addition of GA significantly enhanced TOB activity against Sa; GA reduced the median TOB MIC₅₀ by 40% across all Sa tested (p<0.0001), including a methicillin resistant isolate. Data showed increased TOB activity against other pathogens; co-administration of GA reduced the median TOB MIC50 by 56% against Ax isolates (p<0.01), and by 49% against Sm isolates (p=0.08). Bc isolates demonstrated variable, non-significant MIC50 responses. Screening of a larger panel of pathogens with relevant antibiotics is underway and data will be available at the conference.

Conclusions: GA increases antimicrobial activity of TOB against G+ Sa from pwCF and certain other CF-relevant pathogens, expanding its antibiotic adjuvant role beyond Pa. This potentiation of TOB against Sa, which lacks LPS, raises compelling questions around GA’s mechanism of action.

Funders: LifeArc, CF Trust.

records.title: Agr typing of Staphylococcus aureus isolated from patients with cystic fibrosis

person.institution: N.F. Gamaleya National Research Center for Epidemiology and Microbiology

records.authors_text: L. Avetisyan1, O. Medvedeva1, M. Chernukha1, E. Siyanova1, A. Voronkova2, S. Krasovskiy3, E. Kodratyeva2
records.affiliations_text: 1N.F. Gamaleya National Research Center for Epidemiology and Microbiology, Moscow, Russian Federation, 2Research Centre for Medical Genetics, Moscow, Russian Federation, 3Federal Pulmonology Research Institute, Federal Medical and Biological Agency of Russia, Moscow, Russian Federation
records.abstract_text:
A key role in the pathogenesis of staphylococcal infections belongs to the "quorum-sensing" system, which includes the accessory gene regulator (agr), coordinating the expression of virulence factors. The functional state of agr determines the bacterial strategy — from acute aggression to chronic persistence.

Objective: To define the population structure of S. aureus from cystic fibrosis (CF) patients by agr types and assess links to methicillin resistance.

Materials and methods: 216 S. aureus isolates from CF patients were studied. The agr gene was detected and typed (I–IV) by PCR. Methicillin susceptibility was tested by disс diffusion with cefoxitin. MLST was used for genotyping.

Results: The agr gene was found in 87.5% of isolates (189). Among agr‑positive, type I dominated (67.2%), then types II (23.8%), III (6.9%) and IV (2.1%). This pattern matches the global S. aureus epidemiology, where type I is prevalent. However, a key feature in CF patients is the elevated proportion of agr‑negative isolates (12.5%), suggesting active adaptation in chronic infection. Agr type I showed high genetic diversity (ST8, ST239, ST22, and novel ST6919, ST6972). Importantly, the dominant agr I type was closely linked to methicillin resistance (43.8% MRSA), typical for successful global clones like USA300 (ST8).

Conclusion: Thus, in the population structure of S. aureus from CF patients, the highly virulent agr type I dominates, with 43.8% represented by MRSA, requiring strict epidemiological surveillance. Simultaneously, a substantial proportion (12.5%) of agr‑negative isolates was identified, indicating ongoing pathogen adaptation to chronic infection and highlighting the need for antibiotics effective in chronic settings. The predominance of a functional agr type I makes this virulence‑regulatory system a potential target for the development of novel drugs (e.g. quorum‑sensing inhibitors), and agr typing may serve as a scientific basis for the design of such therapeutic agents.

records.title: Staphyloxanthin provides intra-species protection from oxidative killing of Staphylococcus aureus.
records.authors_text: L. Günther1, J.T.-N. Truong1, B.C. Kahl1, F. Dach1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1University Hospital Münster, Institute of Medical Microbiology, Münster, Germany, 2University Hospital Münster, Department of Pediatrics, Münster, Germany
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Staphylococcus aureus (Sa) is the predominant pathogen in people with Cystic Fibrosis (pwCF). Most isolates produce the carotenoid pigment staphyloxanthin (STX), which confers resistance to oxidative stress and neutrophil mediated killing. Clinically, Sa strains with and without pigmentation frequently coexist, suggesting an advantage of heterogeneity. The aim of this study was to demonstrate the role of STX at the population level and to explore the loss of pigmentation as a potential adaptive process.

Methods: Prevalence of crt deficient Sa strains were analyzed using Whole Genome Sequence (WGS) data from CF samples.

For functional analysis of the crt-operon, a yellow-pigmented JE2 wild type (WT), its non-pigmented transposon mutant, and a clinical CF strain pair carrying the same mutation were used.

STX production was assessed by colony pigmentation and spectrometrically quantified by STX methanol extraction. Intraspecies/ spatial effects on STX synthesis were tested using a proximity assay. To determine whether non-pigmented Sa benefit from coexistence with STX-producing strains, hydrogen peroxide susceptibility assays were performed in mono- and coculture.

Results: WGS showed ~4.7% of clinical isolates with inactivating mutations in the crt-operon. Independent of proximity to non-pigmented strains, pigmented colonies exhibited increased pigmentation over 14 days.

Under oxidative stress, STX expressing Sa strains exhibited greater survival than non-pigmented variants in monoculture. However, when paired in coculture, the white variants showed increased viability, suggesting a protective effect mediated by STX. This effect was observed in both reference- and clinical strains.

Conclusion: STX plays a vital role in heterogeneous Sa populations, providing oxidative stress relief to crt-deficient members. Further analyses are underway to analyze these interactions in a cell culture model and explore the metabolic implications of crt-deficiency.

records.affiliations_text: 1University of Manchester, School of Medical Sciences, Manchester, United Kingdom, 2Royal Manchester Children's Hospital, Department of Paediatric Research, Manchester, United Kingdom, 3Manchester University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, Depart of Biostatistics, Manchester, United Kingdom, 4Royal Manchester Children's Hospital, Department of Paediatric Respiratory Medicine, Manchester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Cystic fibrosis (CF) affects over 10,000 in the UK. S. aureus, a common pathogen in CF, damages lung epithelium and worsens pulmonary decline. This study, conducted at a large tertiary centre, assessed S. aureus isolation and treatment.

Methods: Royal Manchester Children’s Hospital (RMCH), a major tertiary CF centre in northwest England, cares for 330 children with CF, including 200 through direct care and 130 via shared arrangements. A ‘positive swab’ or ‘positive sputum culture’ was defined as lab confirmation of Staphylococcus aureus. Data from an electronic database included cough and sputum samples, positive S. aureus samples, and antibiotic treatments in 2024. For each positive S. aureus, notes from 7 days before and after culture date were reviewed, including clinic, encounter, and nurses’ notes, to confirm if antibiotics were prescribed and taken. Antibiotic treatment was recorded only when there was clear evidence of patient intake.

Results: Complete data were available for 169 patients with CF, aged 1–17 years. On average, each patient submitted 7 swabs or 2 sputum samples in 2024. All patients included in the evaluation submitted at least one sample in 2024. A total of 1,128 cough swabs and 328 sputum samples were collected in 2024, with S. aureus identified in 15.4% and 34.8% of samples, respectively. 40.8% of patients had no positive S. aureus swabs or sputum cultures. Among patients who tested positive, 43% had not received any antibiotic treatment.

Conclusions: This finding highlights strong infection control protocols, but variations in prescribing may cause over- or under-treatment. A decision-support tool could standardise antibiotic prescriptions.

records.title: Evaluating the role of the gut as a reservoir for non-tuberculous mycobacteria in people with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: J. Hudson1, N. Taylor1, M.J Coffey1, B.U. Pushpakumara1, B. Prentice2, A. Jaffe1, S. Visser3, S. Sivam3, A.S Day4, M. Oliver5, S. Ranganathan6, H. Selvadurai7, C. Wainwright8, C.Y Ooi1, J. van Dorst1
records.affiliations_text: 1UNSW, School of Clinical Medicine, Sydney, Australia, 2Department of Respiratory Medicine, Sydney Children’s Hospital, Randwick, Australia, 3Royal Prince Alfred Hospital, Department of Respiratory and Sleep Medicine, Camperdown, Australia, 4University of Otago, Department of Paediatrics and Child Health, Christchurch, New Zealand, 5Royal Children's Hospital, Department of Gastroenterology and Clinical Nutrition, Melbourne, Australia, 6The University of Melbourne, Department of Paediatrics, Melbourne, Australia, 7The Children's Hospital at Westmead, Department of Respiratory Medicine, Sydney, Australia, 8Queensland Children's Hospital, Department of Respiratory and Sleep Medicine, Brisbane, Australia
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) represent a significant disease burden in the cystic fibrosis (CF) population. Whilst the acquisition of NTM to the respiratory tract is predominantly attributed to environmental exposures, the contribution of the gut-lung axis to NTM pulmonary disease remains poorly understood.

Methods: In this study, we retrospectively examined 1285 stool and 223 respiratory microbiomes from 145 children and 52 adults with CF, and 171 healthy control (HC) children, to assess the prevalence, abundance and clinical significance of NTM in gut.

Results: We detected numerous species of low clinical concern in the stool of 2% of people with CF and 1% of HC children sampled, with longitudinal sampling revealing their occurrence to be sporadic and transient. Of the participants studied, only 11 had a history of prior clinical NTM respiratory colonisation or infection, but there was limited evidence to support ongoing persistence in the intestinal tract.

Conclusion: This study suggests that the gut is not a meaningful reservoir for pulmonary NTM infections nor is it likely to serve as a transmission route within the CF population.

Keith Ooi (MBBS, PhD, FRACP, AGAF) is A/Professor of Medicine at the University of New South Wales and Consultant Paediatric Gastroenterologist at Sydney Children’s Hospital Randwick, Australia. He is the Director of the Cystic Fibrosis-Gastroenterology and Pancreas Care Programs at SCH Randwick.

records.title: Management and outcomes of Mycobacterium abscessus complex (MABc) infections in patients with cystic fibrosis: A 10-year Belgian single-centre review

person.department: Laboratory of Respiratory Diseases and Thoracic Surgery (BREATHE)

records.authors_text: N. Jain1,2, E. Pollet3, P.V. Bleyenbergh3, L. Dupont1,3, E. Andre2,4, G.-J. Wijnant2, N. Lorent1,3
records.affiliations_text: 1KU Leuven, Laboratory of Respiratory Diseases and Thoracic Surgery (BREATHE), Leuven, Belgium, 2KU Leuven, Laboratory of Clinical Microbiology, Leuven, Belgium, 3UZ Leuven, Pulmonology Department, Leuven, Belgium, 4UZ Leuven, Department of Microbiology, Leuven, Belgium
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Mycobacterium abscessus complex (MABc) remains a challenging pathogen in cystic fibrosis (CF), given the heterogeneous disease course, lack of biomarkers to guide treatment decisions, and substantial treatment toxicity. We describe management and outcomes of MABc infection in people with CF (pwCF) at a Belgian NTM-CF centre.

Methods: We performed a retrospective chart review of pwCF with ≥1 MABc isolation between 2015-2025. Disease characteristics and microbiological outcomes were evaluated, stratified by receipt of MAB-directed antibiotic therapy.

Results: We included 13 pwCF (median age 31 years; 38% female; median BMI 20.3 kg/m²). All presented with nodular–bronchiectatic MABc pulmonary disease, with one patient having a cavity. Six of 13 pwCF initiated MABc therapy, three in preparation for lung transplantation; two additional patients were offered but refused treatment. Prior to MABc therapy, two patients were on highly effective CFTR modulator therapy (HEMT). Treated patients had lower baseline FEV1 than those not treated (median 51% vs 68% predicted) and more frequent smear positivity (50% vs 14%). ≥ 3 positive sputum cultures in the preceding year occurred in 100% treated vs 57% not treated. All treated patients had M. abscessus, apart from four non-treated patients with M. massiliense. Treatment was initiated at a median 3.2 months after first isolate. Culture conversion occurred in 5/6 (83%; including 3 transplanted) treated at a median 3.7 months (IQR 2.9–29.3) and in 6/7 (86%) not treated at a median 18.2 months (IQR 6.4–35.8), most following HEMT initiation. Recurrent positive cultures after treatment were noted in two (33%) treated patients.

Conclusion: MABc-directed treatment was largely reserved for pwCF with more advanced disease and predated HEMT. Most non-treated cases converted over time following HEMT. Improved tools for stratification based on expected benefit from antimicrobial therapy are needed.

records.title: Mycobacterium abscessus clearance post initiation of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor in patients with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: H. Withers1, N. Bell1, S. Cowman1
records.affiliations_text: 1Bristol Royal Infirmary, Bristol Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Bristol, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Mycobacterium abscessus (MABSC) isolation in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) can have major implications including reduced lung function, high treatment burden, transplant exclusion, and stricter infection control requirements.

Case reports describe clearance of MABSC from sputum following elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) initiation, and observational data suggest decreased nontuberculous mycobacteria prevalence post CFTR modulators. We reviewed MABSC isolation patterns pre- and post-ETI initiation.

Methods: Retrospective analysis of adult pwCF at Bristol Adult CF centre with ≥2 MABSC-positive sputum cultures between 2009 and 2025. Inclusion: regular full dose ETI for >2 year and ≥2 MABSC isolations in the five years pre-ETI initiation. Data were collected using our Centre’s clinical database.

Results: Twenty-five pwCF met the inclusion criteria, sending median 2.8 (range 0.2-5.7) samples per year pre-ETI. Median follow up duration post-ETI was 61 months (range 25-70) with median 0.6 samples (range 0.2-3.3) being sent per year.

Thirteen (52%) had no MABSC isolation post-ETI (median 0.5 [range 0.2-1.1] samples per year over median 60 [range 45-70] months). All patients remained productive post-ETI, with 21 (84%) patients having 2 or more samples sent.

Three pwCF were undergoing MABSC treatment at time of ETI initiation which was subsequently discontinued; all continued to isolate MABSC post-ETI but remained clinically stable with no indication to restart treatment.

Conclusion: ETI initiation was associated with apparent MABSC clearance in half of cases. It is possible that reduced mycobacterial sampling post-ETI could have led to under-detection of MABSC. All three pwCF on MABSC treatment were able to discontinue it having started ETI.

records.title: Signed, Sealed, Sputum: detecting non-tuberculosis Mycobacteria by post in cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: H. Wood1, K.-M. Flaherty1, T. Penrose1, M. Walshaw2,3, L. Rossiter2, M. Ledson2, F. Frost2,3
records.affiliations_text: 1Liverpool Heart and Chest Hospital, Physiotherapy Department, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 2Liverpool Heart and Chest Hospital, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 3University of Liverpool, Liverpool, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: Sputum microbiological surveillance underpins Cystic Fibrosis (CF) care, but the move towards virtual clinics makes this challenging. Whilst postal sputum sampling has been validated for normal culture, its utility for Non-tuberculosis Mycobacteria (NTM) is unclear. To study this further, we prospectively compared NTM positivity in paired postal and fresh samples in our adult CF Centre.

Methods: We looked at 13 pwCF with sputum samples positive for NTM stain or culture (NTM-PD) between 2023 and 2025. We then obtained paired sputum samples from these pwCF at face-to-face clinics or ward visits over a four-month period, and also a control group of five pwCF without NTM. One sample from each pair was sent directly to the laboratory for culture, whilst the other was sent via the existing community postal sputum pathway. We recorded the final growth and NTM stain for each sample.

Results: Of the 13 NTM-PD, for postal samples two were stain positive (one indeterminate) and three culture positive (one Mycobacterium abscessus). For fresh samples, only one was both stain and culture positive. In the control group, all fresh samples were negative but one was stain (indeterminate) and culture positive (Mycobacterium chelonae) in the postal group. Overall, postal samples had 100% negative predictive value and 25% positive predictive value for fresh culture.

Conclusion: We have shown that NTM is recoverable from postal sputum in both patients with known NTM-PD and those without. Our data suggests a negative postal sputum sample is reassuring, but that a positive sample should be followed up with fresh samples given discordant positivity between sampling groups.

records.title: Non-tuberculous mycobacteria in adult cystic fibrosis patients before and after elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor: a real-world cohort analysis
records.authors_text: A.S. Gonçalves1, E. Fragoso2,3, P. Azevedo2,3
records.affiliations_text: 1Funchal Central Hospital, Pulmonology, Funchal, Madeira, Portugal, 2North Lisbon University Hospital Centre, ULS Santa Maria, Pulmonology, Lisbon, Portugal, 3Faculdade de Medicina da Universidade de Lisboa, Lisbon, Portugal
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) are increasingly detected in adults with cystic fibrosis (CF). The relationship between highly effective CFTR modulators and NTM isolation remains uncertain. Our aim is to characterize adult CF patients with NTM infection and to evaluate the timing of NTM isolation in relation to exposure to elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI).

Methods: A cross-sectional study was performed in a single adult CF centre. Among seventy-eight adult CF patients, those with at least one NTM isolation were included (n=8).

Results: Eight patients (10.3%) had NTM isolation. Mean age was 34.6 years and seven patients (87.5%) were female. Five patients (62.5%) carried at least one F508del allele and mean sweat chloride was 78.6 mmol/L. Mean FEV₁ was 63.1% predicted, with lung function classified as severe obstruction in one patient (FEV₁<40%), moderate in five (FEV₁ 40–70%) and mild in two (FEV₁>70%). Five patients had exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and two CF-related diabetes. Six patients (75%) had NTM without ETI exposure, while two patients (25%) experienced their first NTM isolation after initiating ETI. In ETI group, patients maintained mild to moderate lung function and chronic airway infection was limited to Staphylococcus aureus. One patient with long-standing Stenotrophomonas maltophilia isolation no longer had this microorganism detected following NTM identification. In contrast, patients without ETI exposure exhibited lower FEV₁ values, Aspergillus fumigatus colonization, and chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, with two patients requiring long-term inhaled antibiotic therapy. Moreover, one patient developed Burkholderia cepacia infection following completion of NTM treatment.

Conclusion: Adult CF patients with NTM infection present heterogeneous genetic and clinical characteristics. In this cohort, most NTM isolations occurred independently of ETI exposure. Continued microbiological surveillance remains essential in the modulator era.
records.objectives: Non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) are increasingly detected in adults with cystic fibrosis (CF). The relationship between highly effective CFTR modulators and NTM isolation remains uncertain. Our aim is to characterize adult CF patients with NTM infection and to evaluate the timing of NTM isolation in relation to exposure to elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI).
records.methods: A cross-sectional study was performed in a single adult CF centre. Among seventy-eight adult CF patients, those with at least one NTM isolation were included (n=8).
records.results: Eight patients (10.3%) had NTM isolation. Mean age was 34.6 years and seven patients (87.5%) were female. Five patients (62.5%) carried at least one F508del allele and mean sweat chloride was 78.6 mmol/L. Mean FEV₁ was 63.1% predicted, with lung function classified as severe obstruction in one patient (FEV₁<40%), moderate in five (FEV₁ 40–70%) and mild in two (FEV₁>70%). Five patients had exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and two CF-related diabetes. Six patients (75%) had NTM without ETI exposure, while two patients (25%) experienced their first NTM isolation after initiating ETI. In ETI group, patients maintained mild to moderate lung function and chronic airway infection was limited to Staphylococcus aureus. One patient with long-standing Stenotrophomonas maltophilia isolation no longer had this microorganism detected following NTM identification. In contrast, patients without ETI exposure exhibited lower FEV₁ values, Aspergillus fumigatus colonization, and chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, with two patients requiring long-term inhaled antibiotic therapy. Moreover, one patient developed Burkholderia cepacia infection following completion of NTM treatment.
records.conclusion: Adult CF patients with NTM infection present heterogeneous genetic and clinical characteristics. In this cohort, most NTM isolations occurred independently of ETI exposure. Continued microbiological surveillance remains essential in the modulator era.

records.title: Patient-focused Target Product Profiles for the development of phage therapies to treat lung infections in cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: L. Jenkinson1, C. Takawira1, N. Gingles1, P. Sommer2, L. Allen2, L. Jackson3, H. Mok4, J. Fothergill3
records.affiliations_text: 1Medicines Discovery Catapult, Macclesfield, United Kingdom, 2Cystic Fibrosis Trust, London, United Kingdom, 3University of Liverpool, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 4LifeArc, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Despite advances in cystic fibrosis (CF) care, lung infections are a leading cause of morbidity and mortality for people with CF (pwCF). Phage therapy could help address this unmet need by specifically targeting pathogenic bacteria, including antibiotic resistant strains, with reduced toxicity compared to prolonged antibiotic use.

The CF AMR Syndicate joined forces with the TRAILFINDER-CF Innovation Hub to deliver patient-focused Target Product Profiles (TPPs) to catalyse the development of phage therapies for CF lung infections. A TPP describes the characteristics a therapeutic must have to address a specific need

Method: TPP development began with focus groups and one-to-one interviews with pwCF, followed by input from CF clinical care teams and phage therapy innovators, alongside a clinical trial landscape review. These interactions explored phage therapy awareness; integration into current treatment strategies; and barriers to clinical adoption. Clinical trial endpoints and outcome measures, preclinical data, plus regulatory and safety requirements were also explored. Outputs were used to outline an initial set of TPPs, now being refined through stakeholder engagement, consensus survey and a virtual symposium

Results: Three TPPs have been developed for both conventional and modified phage therapy: (1) patient-focused TPP capturing the needs and priorities of pwCF that should be addressed by any phage therapeutic; (2) TPP for the treatment of chronic lung infections using phage therapy; (3) TPP for the eradication of newly acquired lung infections using phage therapy. The TPPs are pathogen-agnostic and applicable to pathogens in CF and other adjacent diseases e.g. bronchiectasis

Conclusion: Stakeholder input is ongoing to refine the TPPs, aiming to deliver consensus-driven documents that define the desired characteristics of a phage therapy for CF lung infections and stimulate activity to address existing technical, regulatory, and clinical challenges

records.title: Disruption of key virulence traits in Stenotrophomonas maltophilia by N-nonyloxypentyl-l-deoxynojirimycin (L-NPDNJ)

person.department: Department of Molecular Medicine and Medical Biotechnology

records.authors_text: M. Stabile1, A. Esposito2, A. Migliaccio3, L. Sepe1, R. Artiano1, V.D. Iula4, R. Zarrilli3, A. Guaragna2, E. De Gregorio1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Naples Federico II, Department of Molecular Medicine and Medical Biotechnology, Naples, Italy, 2University of Naples Federico II, Department of Chemical Sciences, Naples, Italy, 3University of Naples Federico II, Department of Public Health, Naples, Italy, 4Ospedale del Mare - ASL Napoli 1 Centro, Department of Laboratory Medicine, U.O.C Patologia Clinica, Naples, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Stenotrophomonas maltophilia (Sm) is an opportunistic Gram-negative MDR pathogen that causes life-threatening infections in cystic fibrosis patients. Sm has many virulence factors that contribute to host tissue damage and immune evasion. In this study, the synthetic iminosugar L-NPDNJ was tested against Sm strains to evaluate its ability to enhance antibiotic efficacy and reduce pathogenicity.

Methods: Antibacterial activity was assessed through MIC, MBC and checkerboard assays. Biofilm eradication was assessed by crystal violet and tetrazolium salt reduction assay. Transcription of selected virulence-related genes was verified by qRT-PCR. Protease activity, adhesion on abiotic surface and to epithelial cells assays, macrophage infection assay,and an in vivo infection with Galleria mellonella larvae were also performed.

Results: L-NPDNJ showed limited antibacterial activity but showed additive effects with aminoglycosides. It significantly disrupted preformed biofilms (70% reduction in biomass and metabolic activity). qRT-PCR revealed downregulation of genes encoding resistance determinants, biofilm regulators and virulence factors. These transcriptional changes led to reduced protease secretion, resulting in reduced epithelial damage by Sm supernatants, and impaired its adhesion to abiotic surfaces and to epithelial cells. L-NPDNJ treatment stimulates macrophage phagocytosis and enhances the intracellular clearance of Sm by macrophages, as well as enhancing macrophage viability upon bacterial infection. In addition, pretreatment of Sm cells with L-NPDNJ before infection significantly improved larval survival in the in vivo G. mellonella model, confirming its ability to attenuate virulence.

Conclusion: Despite lacking direct bactericidal activity, L-NPDNJ effectively targets multiple virulence mechanisms in Sm, supporting its potential as a non-toxic antivirulence compound that could be used to complement antibiotic therapy and reduce pathogenicity.

records.title: ‘One Bronchiectasis’ in clinical trials of anti-pseudomonal agents: an evidence based approach?
records.authors_text: W.D Smith1,2, F.J Terpstra1,3, A. Cunanan1, O.L Fletcher1, R.A Murphy1, A. Simbo1, C. Hogg1,2, A. Filloux1, A. Bush1,2, J.C Davies1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Imperial College London, London, United Kingdom, 2Royal Brompton Hospital, London, United Kingdom, 3University of Groningen, Groningen, Netherlands
records.abstract_text:
CFTR modulator treated (MT) cystic fibrosis (CF) is considered by some to be clinically similar to other causes of bronchiectasis (Bx); people with CF (pwCF) generally do not eradicate bacterial airway infection. Some recent trials of anti-inflammatory agents are cohorting MT-CF with other causes of Bx under the umbrella concept: ‘One Bx’. A ‘One Bx’ approach may be a worthwhile strategy to increase power in antimicrobial studies, a WHO priority. But are microbes from pwCF and people with Bx (pwBx) similar in phenotype?

Methods: We performed detailed phenotyping of 70 Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa) from pwCF in a pre-MT era and 66 from pwBx, including: antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST; 2019 European Committee on AST (EUCAST) disk diffusion method); ex vivo biofilm forming potential (crystal violet assay); motility and enzymatic activity (agar plate assays).

Each assay had three technical replicates per strain. Inocula were consistent. EUCAST clinical breakpoints were used to identify antimicrobial resistance (R) and R to at least 1 of ≥ 3 different classes of antibiotic was defined multi-drug resistance (MDR).

Results: A greater proportion of Pa strains from pwCF demonstrated MDR in comparison to Bx (86% vs. 55%), p <0.0001, X2. Small, statistically significant differences were seen in biofilm forming potential, twitching motility (greater in CF), and lipase activity (greater in Bx).

Conclusions: These ex vivo assays show small, but statistically significant differences between Pa from pwBx and pwCF in the pre-MT era. Antibiotic exposure likely explains the MDR differences. The clinical significance of these data and how they reflect the in vivo environment is unknown. Assuming the in vivo environment in MT CF more closely resembles that of non-CF Bx, these data may support a One-Bx concept for antimicrobial trials.

Supported by the British Lung Foundation. Affiliated to the UK CF Trust-funded Strategic Research Centre for Pseudomonas infection.

records.title: Utilising loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) to detect Pseudomonas aeruginosa in saliva
records.authors_text: A.M. Kadoom1, G.G Einarsson1, E. Caamano Gutierrez2, R.W Lord3, R.E Maher4, A. Jones3, A. Horsley3, D.F Gilpin1, M.M Tunney1
records.affiliations_text: 1Queens University Belfast, School of Pharmacy, Belfast, United Kingdom, 2University of Liverpool, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 3Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust, Manchester Adult CF Centre, Manchester, United Kingdom, 4University of Liverpool, Centre for Proteome Research, Liverpool, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa) remains a key respiratory pathogen in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). Following the introduction of CFTR modulator therapies, sputum production has decreased in pwCF, highlighting the need to explore alternative sample types such as saliva. This study aimed to develop a loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) assay for the rapid detection of Pa in saliva samples. LAMP utilises four to six primers to amplify DNA at a single temperature, reducing assay time and enabling simpler workflows compared to PCR, whilst maintaining sensitivity.

Methods: LAMP detection targeted the oprL gene in Pa, using an intercalating dye for real-time detection. Optimal assay performance was achieved using a one-step protocol incorporating proteinase K and thermal lysis, totalling 15 minutes. Using spiked saliva samples obtained from healthy volunteers (n=15), eight technical replicates per dilution were tested to determine the limit of detection (LoD; 95% detection rate) of the assay.

Results: The LoD was shown to be approximately 2.4 x 103 cfu/ml (100% detection) when using a 30-minute threshold, with a mean (±SD) detection time of 14 minutes ±2.4 minutes. Pa detection was achieved in 94% of reactions at a concentration of 1.2 x 103 cfu/ml, with a mean (±SD) detection time of 16.5 minutes ±3.9 minutes. At 6.0 x 102 cfu/ml, Pa detection was observed in 80% of reactions, with a mean (±SD) detection time of 17.2 minutes ±3.9 minutes.

Conclusion: At a bacterial load of 2.4 x103 cfu/ml in saliva, Pa was detected in 100% of spiked samples by LAMP, potentially providing rapid and sensitive results from a sample type easier to collect than sputum. This approach could improve surveillance and monitoring of Pa colonisation. Future work will validate the assay on clinical samples, comparing saliva and sputum detection.

Funded through PULSE-CF by the CF-Trust and LifeArc.

records.title: Metabolic adaptation in sulfur-rich cystic fibrosis airways shapes pulmonary pathogen dynamics
records.authors_text: J.T.-N. Truong1, Y.-T. Chen2, G.K. Lohia2, B.C. Kahl1, F. Dach1,3, S.A. Riquelme2
records.affiliations_text: 1University Hospital Münster, Institute of Medical Microbiology, Münster, Germany, 2Columbia University, Department of Pediatrics, New York, United States, 3University Hospital Münster, Department of Pediatrics, Münster, Germany
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Pulmonary infection in people with Cystic Fibrosis (pwCF) shifts from early Staphylococcus aureus (Sa) to later Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa) dominance, exacerbating airway inflammation. Here, we examined how CFTR-driven airway metabolism and pathogen adaptation promote sulfur-dependent progression from Sa to Pa coinfection.

Methods: CFTR-associated airway metabolic alterations were profiled by LC-MS metabolomics of sputum and airway cell supernatants (SN) from CF and non-CF donors. Adaptive mutations were identified by Whole-Genome Sequencing (WGS) of Sa isolates from CF respiratory samples (n=560). Functional studies used the JE2 wildtype (WT) strain and its cysM transposon mutant. Bacterial growth was assessed in LB and Artificial Sputum Medium (ASM)±sulfur-rich metabolites. Infection outcomes - bacterial burden (CFU) and cytokine secretion (ELISA) - were evaluated in non-CF and CF airway epithelial (F508del/W1282X) and differentiated myeloid cells (F508del/F508del), and validated in a mouse respiratory infection model.

Results: CF sputum and airway epithelial cell SN were enriched in sulfur-containing metabolites. WGS revealed inactivating cysM mutations in ~78% of Sa isolates from pwCF. In LB, cysM inactivation confers resilience to the stress imposed by sulfur metabolites like cysteine. ASM provided similar protection to cysM-intact strains, supporting an adaptive convergence between bacterial genetics and the CF metabolic milieu. In CF epithelial cells, cysM inactivation enhanced IL-8 secretion. Although this mutation did not increase Sa persistence in neutrophils, during coinfection with Pa it markedly promoted Pa survival, an effect reproduced in vivo.

Conclusion: CFTR-driven sulfur enrichment of the airway selects for cysM-deficient Sa strains, which are resilient to the CF metabolic milieu, enhance inflammation, and facilitate Pa persistence. Our data identify sulfur metabolism as a key driver of pathogen evolution and community dynamics in CF.

records.methods: CFTR-associated airway metabolic alterations were profiled by LC-MS metabolomics of sputum and airway cell supernatants (SN) from CF and non-CF donors. Adaptive mutations were identified by Whole-Genome Sequencing (WGS) of Sa isolates from CF respiratory samples (n=560). Functional studies used the JE2 wildtype (WT) strain and its cysM transposon mutant. Bacterial growth was assessed in LB and Artificial Sputum Medium (ASM)±sulfur-rich metabolites. Infection outcomes - bacterial burden (CFU) and cytokine secretion (ELISA) - were evaluated in non-CF and CF airway epithelial (F508del/W1282X) and differentiated myeloid cells (F508del/F508del), and validated in a mouse respiratory infection model.
records.results: CF sputum and airway epithelial cell SN were enriched in sulfur-containing metabolites. WGS revealed inactivating cysM mutations in ~78% of Sa isolates from pwCF. In LB, cysM inactivation confers resilience to the stress imposed by sulfur metabolites like cysteine. ASM provided similar protection to cysM-intact strains, supporting an adaptive convergence between bacterial genetics and the CF metabolic milieu. In CF epithelial cells, cysM inactivation enhanced IL-8 secretion. Although this mutation did not increase Sa persistence in neutrophils, during coinfection with Pa it markedly promoted Pa survival, an effect reproduced in vivo.
records.conclusion: CFTR-driven sulfur enrichment of the airway selects for cysM-deficient Sa strains, which are resilient to the CF metabolic milieu, enhance inflammation, and facilitate Pa persistence. Our data identify sulfur metabolism as a key driver of pathogen evolution and community dynamics in CF.

records.title: Modulation of antimicrobial susceptibility in cystic fibrosis pathogens via polymer-based nanohydrogels delivery

person.department: Department of Public Health and Infectious Diseases

records.authors_text: I. Paris1, A. Pietrella1, S. Raimondi2, M. Rossitto3, G. Vrenna3, L. Selan1, M. Artini1, R. Papa1
records.affiliations_text: 1Sapienza University, Department of Public Health and Infectious Diseases, Rome, Italy, 2Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital, IRCCS, Microbiology and Diagnostic Immunology Unit, Rome, Italy, 3Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital, IRCCS, Multimodal Laboratory Medicine, Rome, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Cystic fibrosis (CF) lungs are characterized by a dense mucus layer that promotes chronic colonization by opportunistic pathogens, where Staphylococcus aureus (Sa) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa) are predominant pathogens strongly associated with increased morbidity and mortality. Sa typically establishes colonization early in life, whereas Pa becomes dominant as the disease progresses. However, growing evidence indicates that both pathogens often persist together, forming a polymicrobial environment that accelerates lung function decline. The prolonged residency in CF lung, coupled with recurrent hospitalizations and intensive antibiotic pressure, drives the evolutionary adaptation of these species toward multi-drug resistance (MDR). This has led to the alarming emergence of colistin-resistant Pa and methicillin-resistant Sa (MRSA), neutralizing last-resort therapeutic options. Polymer-based nanohydrogels (NHs) represent a promising platform to bypass the mucosal barrier, the biofilm matrix and potentially restoring antimicrobial potency against MDR pathogens.

Methods: NHs were synthesized and characterized. Their intrinsic antibiofilm activity and synergistic interactions with conventional antibiotics used in therapy were investigated in MDR clinical Pa and Sa isolates from CF patients. Efficacy was evaluated through checkerboard and biofilm eradication assays.

Results: NHs showed high stability and significant intrinsic antibiofilm properties, specifically targeting the initial adhesion phase. In combination with antibiotics, the systems exhibited a marked synergistic effect, significantly reducing MIC values for colistin-resistant Pa and MRSA. Furthermore, the nanocarriers demonstrated higher penetration into the dense biofilm matrix compared to free drugs.

Conclusions: Nanohydrogel systems represent a promising tool to overcome mucosal and biofilm barriers, restoring the potency of last-resort antibiotics against challenging MDR infections in CF.

records.title: Decade-long dynamics in lung sampling and microbiological outcomes at a large adult cystic fibrosis centre
records.authors_text: L. Rossiter1, G. Hyde1, D. Nazareth1, M. Wlshaw1, T. Penrose1, H. Wood1, F. Frost1
records.affiliations_text: 1Liverpool Heart and Chest Hospital, Respiratory Medicine, Liverpool, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: Elexacaftor/Tezacaftor/Ivacaftor (ETI) has transformed microbiological landscape in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). However, the impact of ETI on sampling practices and culture outcomes is not well described. This study evaluated the dynamics of respiratory sampling in CF over the past decade at our large adult CF centre.

Methods: We looked at all 11,697 samples from 384 pwCF currently receiving ETI [9330 sputum (SP), 2367 cough swabs (CS)]. Annualised sampling frequency and positivity for Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa), methicillin‑sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA), methicillin‑resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and Burkholderia (Bcc) were recorded, comparing the pre‑ and post‑ETI eras.

Results: Total respiratory sampling fell, with a marked reduction post-ETI (median samples: pre 1356/yr vs post 783/yr; mean difference 647, p<0.0001), driven by a 7.4% reduction in SP samples. CS sampling remained stable but accounted for a greater proportion post-ETI.

We found a general decrease in Pa positivity rates post ETI (SP: pre 71% vs post 51%; CS: pre 17% vs post 7%; p<0.001). We also observed a reduction in BCC and MRSA for CS and SP (both p<0.02). However, although MSSA had reduced positivity for SP (24% vs 19%, p<0.0001), CS remained similar (5.4% vs 7.2%, p=0.29). Annualised discordance between CS and SP increased post-ETI with lesser agreement between CS and SP seen for Pa and to a lesser degree MSSA.

Conclusions: In the ETI era, marked shifts in respiratory sampling from SP to CS are accompanied by lower culture positivity rates and reduced detection of most CF pathogens. Divergent effects on Pa and MSSA positivity and sampling concordance were seen, reinforcing the need for high-quality respiratory sampling to allow robust microbiological surveillance in pwCF on ETI.

records.title: Changes in faecal antibiotic resistance genes pre and post elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI)
records.authors_text: L.R Caley1, H.M Wood1,2, P. Quirke1,2, D.G Peckham1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Leeds, Leeds Institute of Medical Research, Leeds, United Kingdom, 2University of Leeds, NIHR Leeds Biomedical Research Centre, Leeds, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Antibiotics have been a mainstay treatment for the pulmonary manifestations of cystic fibrosis (CF). Recurrent antibiotic use is associated with increased antibiotic-resistant genes (ARG) in bacteria, conferring a greater risk of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Elexacaftor / Tezacaftor / Ivacaftor (ETI) therapy is associated with reduced intravenous (IV) antibiotic use and early data suggest some gut microbiotal modulation. We investigated whether ARG abundance changes pre and post ETI therapy in stool samples from adults with CF.

Methods: This study was part of an observational cohort study (Igloo-CF). Antibiotic resistant genes were analysed from Whole Metagenome Sequencing data of paired stool samples collected from 57 participants pre and post ETI therapy. Samples were collected a median of 15 months apart (range 4 -21 months), with median duration of ETI being 5 months (IQR 3, 7 months) at follow up.

Results: At baseline, median age and ppFEV1 were 33 years (IQR 29, 39.5) and 47 (IQR 34, 73) respectively, with ppFEV1 increasing to 59 (IQR 44, 85) at follow up (post-ETI). ARG relative abundance significantly decreased post-ETI therapy (p=0.0032). IV antibiotic use also significantly decreased following ETI therapy (p= <0.001).

Conclusions: Following ETI therapy, the relative abundance of ARG in stool samples decreased, which may be owing to the concurrent decrease in IV antibiotics. Analysis is ongoing. Whether the change in AMG alters AMR risk requires further exploration.

Funded by the UK CF Trust (SRC 012).

person.title: Professor of Respiratory Medicine
person.biography: Daniel Peckham is Professor of Respiratory Medicine and Deputy Director of the Leeds Institute of Medical Research at the University of Leeds. He is the clinical lead for the Regional Leeds Adult Cystic Fibrosis, Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia and Bronchiectasis Services. He pioneered the design and implementation of chronic disease electronic patient records and established a strong base for clinical and basic research in Cystic Fibrosis. Active research programs focus on CF-related inflammation, CFTR modulators, gut dysbiosis, cancer, drug allergy, big data, electronic patient records and clinical trials. He is passionate about education and was the founding Director of Education for the European Cystic Fibrosis Society.

records.title: Microbiological changes in cystic fibrosis: the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic and CFTR modulators
records.authors_text: D. Chiariotti1, A. Os2, M. Kolsgaard2, A.S Wathne2, E. Bakkeheim2
records.affiliations_text: 1Padova University Hospital, Woman and Child Health Department (SDB), Padova, Italy, 2Oslo University Hospital, National Centre for Rare Diseaes, Unit for Pulmonology and Cystic Fibrosis, Oslo, Norway
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The lung microbiota in people with Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is shaped by environmental and host factors. The COVID-19 pandemic altered healthcare delivery and social behaviour, while the introduction of Elexacaftor–Tezacaftor–Ivacaftor (ETI), in Norway from July 2022, transformed CF care. We examined changes in chronic lower airway microbiota pre- and post- the pandemic and after >2 years of ETI therapy.

Methods: Data from the Norwegian CF Registry were analysed for 2019 (pre-pandemic), 2021 (post-pandemic, pre-ETI), and 2024 (>2 years post-ETI), excluding lung transplant receivers. Prevalence trends for chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa) and Staphylococcus aureus (Sa) were assessed, and a cross-sectional logistic regression was performed for 2024 in pwCF aged ≥6 years.

Results: Chronic Pa and Sa prevalence was 20% and 53% in 2019 (n=288), 18% and 47% in 2021 (n=309), and 13% and 31% in 2024 (n=353). Reductions from 2021 to 2024 were significant for Pa (p=0.041) and Sa (p<0.01), whereas changes from 2019 to 2021 did not reach statictical significanse. Change in Pa status from 2021 to 2024 was associated with ETI use (p=0.007), and a linear trend indicated greater stability with ≥2 years ETI exposure (p=0.003). A similar non significant trend for Sa was observed. In 2024 regression (n=298), older age increased chronic Pa odds (OR 1.05/year; 95% CI 1.03–1.08; p<0.001), while pancreatic sufficiency (OR 0.39; 95% CI 0.16–0.96; p=0.041) and chronic Sa (OR 0.29; 95% CI 0.11–0.76; p=0.012) were protective. Sex and ETI exposure duration showed no significant association.

Conclusion: The pandemic did not significantly affect chronic infection rates. Prolonged ETI therapy was linked to marked reductions in chronic Pa in longitudinal analyses, suggesting sustained treatment may aid pathogen clearance. In the cross‑sectional 2024 model, host factors such as age and pancreatic status remained key determinants of chronic infection risk in the modulator era.

records.abstract_text:
Objective: Triple CFTR modulator therapy with elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) has substantially changed CF management but its real-world impact on respiratory microbiology remains incompletely characterized. Therefore, the main objective of this study is to evaluate changes in routine respiratory culture positivity for P. aeruginosa, S. aureus, and H. influenzae, as well as P. aeruginosa morphotype diversity, before and after the introduction of ETI.

Methods: A retrospective observational study was conducted including respiratory routine cultures collected from CF patients in our centre between 2017 and 2025. records.title: Real-world outcomes and tolerability of newer antipseudomonal β-lactams (ceftolozane/tazobactam, ceftazidime/avibactam and cefiderocol) in cystic fibrosis pulmonary exacerbations.
records.authors_text: A. Bhatti1, N. Simmonds1, E. Bowman1, I. Felton1, J. Cheong1, A. Jones1, T. Fakeye1
records.affiliations_text: 1Royal Brompton Hospital, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: Pulmonary exacerbations (PEx) in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) are frequently complicated by multidrug-resistant (MDR) Gram-negative infection and advanced lung disease. Newer antipseudomonal β-lactams, including ceftolozane/tazobactam (CZ), ceftazidime/avibactam (CA) and cefiderocol (CD), are increasingly used; however, real-world data on objective clinical response and tolerability in pwCF remain limited.

Aims: To describe inflammatory response, lung function change and tolerability following treatment with CZ, CA and CD for CF PEx.

Methods: Retrospective review of pwCF treated with CZ, CA or CD for PEx at a large adult CF centre (Sept 2023–Jan 2026). Data included chronic airways microbial status, incident PEx sputum microbiology, concomitant intravenous antimicrobials, C-reactive protein (CRP), percent-predicted forced expiratory volume in one second (ppFEV₁), and adverse effects. Pre-treatment CRP and ppFEV₁ were the most recent prior to antibiotic initiation; post-treatment CRP was measured after treatment, and ppFEV₁ was the first available value within 60 days.

Results: Sixteen treatment encounters in 11 patients were included (Table). Median baseline ppFEV₁ was low, reflecting advanced lung disease. In most encounters, the index antibiotic followed exposure to other intravenous regimens during the same hospitalisation. CRP improved in most encounters, with marked reductions in those with high baseline inflammation. Lung function response was heterogeneous. Tolerability was favourable, with few adverse effects and no treatment discontinuations.

Conclusion: In pwCF with advanced lung disease and MDR infection, CZ, CA and CD were well tolerated and associated with improvement in systemic inflammation, with variable lung function response, supporting use in selected patients with severe or refractory CF PEx.

records.authors_text: V. Rojas1, C. Prieto1, M. Algañarás1, M. Bettiol2, C. Vita1, V. D'Alessandro3, F. Rentería3, D.O. Serra4, A. Bosch1, B. León1

records.abstract_text:
Escherichia coli has not traditionally been considered a typical cystic fibrosis (CF) pathogen. However, epidemiological surveillance around the world has revealed its increasing prevalence in respiratory samples from people with CF (pwCF). These observations prompted us to investigate the genomic and phenotypic traits underlying E. coli persistence in the CF lung.

A total of 42 E. coli respiratory isolates from 13 pwCF were analyzed. Special focus was placed on one patient (P1) with chronic infection (CI), from whom eight sequential isolates were recovered over seven years, and on two patients with transient infections (P2, P3). Whole-genome sequencing, sequence typing, pangenome and SNP analyses were performed for all isolates. The resistome, mobilome, and virulome were characterized using ABRicate, along with phenotypic assays for motility, biofilm formation, extracellular matrix composition, and antimicrobial susceptibility.

All isolates from the CI and one transient isolate belonged to the multidrug-resistant ST131 lineage, while the remaining transient isolate corresponded to ST43. Genomic analyses revealed intraclonal evolution during CI and differences in the mobilome and resistome between chronic and transient isolates. CI isolates displayed a broader repertoire of resistance determinants and mobile genetic elements. All isolates carried UPEC-associated virulence genes involved in adhesion, invasion, and toxin production. Phenotypic analyses revealed differences in colony morphology, extracellular matrix composition, and biofilm-related traits between chronic and transient isolates.

Together, these findings indicate that E. coli, particularly ST131, can persist in the CF airway through genomic diversification and phenotypic adaptation. Chronic colonization appears to be shaped by the combined contribution of virulence-associated traits, resistance determinants, and mobile genetic elements, highlighting the clinical relevance of E. coli in CF.

records.title: Investigating linear trends in ABPA markers in cystic fibrosis patients at a large tertiary paediatric CF centre
records.authors_text: M. O'Halloran1, S. Hamrang - Yousefi2, A. Razai3, A. Maitra4,1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Manchester, School of Medical Sciences, Manchester, United Kingdom, 2Royal Manchester Children's Hospital, Department of Paediatric Research, Manchester, United Kingdom, 3Manchester University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, Depart of Biostatistics, Manchester, United Kingdom, 4Royal Manchester Children's Hospital, Department of Paediatric Respiratory Medicine, Manchester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) is a hypersensitivity to Aspergillus fumigatus, mainly affecting those with Asthma or Cystic Fibrosis (CF). Early diagnosis reduces pulmonary complications. This study examined patterns of ABPA biomarkers to evaluate their use for early detection in paediatric CF patients.

Methods: Royal Manchester Children’s Hospital (RMCH), a major tertiary CF centre in northwest England, cares for 330 children with CF, with 200 through direct input and 130 via shared care. A retrospective analysis used data from an electronic record. Patients under 1 year old or with data gaps over 3 years were excluded. Biomarkers, including eosinophil count, total IgE, and A. fumigatus-specific IgE and IgG, were measured and analysed using linear modelling and regression.

Results: Data were available for 173 CF subjects. Among the biomarkers, A. fumigatus IgG showed the strongest correlation (r = 0.321, p < 0.001), identifying all confirmed ABPA cases at the provisional threshold. Total serum IgE and eosinophils showed weaker correlations with confirmed cases (r=0.131, r=0.046). In confirmed ABPA, biomarker levels lacked linear trends after diagnosis, limiting their use for monitoring.

Conclusions: This evaluation supports the use of ABPA biomarkers within a broader diagnostic framework. However, their limitations in early detection and post-diagnosis surveillance highlight the need for further research to refine these tools and improve diagnostic accuracy and clinical outcomes.
