records.title: Vaping is associated with CF-relevant gut-lung microbiome and metabolic remodeling in mice

person.institution: Morsani College of Medicine- University of South Florida

records.authors_text: O. Abou-Assali1, R. Pace2, S.-J. Abi-Aad1, R. Khalaf1, S. Noujaim1
records.affiliations_text: 1Morsani College of Medicine- University of South Florida, Tampa, United States, 2College of Nursing- University of South Florida, Tampa, United States
records.abstract_text:
Background: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is characterized by chronic inflammation, gut-lung axis dysfunction, microbial dysbiosis, and systemic metabolic abnormalities. Human and animal studies suggest that CF-relevant microbiome and metabolomic alterations can arise early and may be influenced by environmental modifiers. Vaping, also known as electronic nicotine delivery system (ENDS) use, is increasingly prevalent, including among individuals with CF, yet its impact on systemic metabolism and gut-lung microbial ecology remains poorly understood.

Methods: Wild-type mice were chronically exposed to flavored ENDS aerosol (N=8) or room air (N=7). Stool and lung microbiomes were analyzed by 16S rRNA sequencing to evaluate diversity, taxonomic composition, and differential abundance. Plasma metabolomics were used to assess systemic metabolic remodeling.

Results: Despite no significant differences in alpha or beta diversity, vaping exposure was associated with alterations of both gut and lung microbiomes. In stool, vaping was associated with increased Firmicutes and Proteobacteria and reduced Bacteroidetes, with depletion of Barnesiella which has been reported in CF. In lung tissue, vaping was associated with taxonomic shifts without significant diversity loss, including reduced Micrococcus, Muribaculum, and Clostridium IV, consistent with microbial remodeling that has been described in CF. Plasma metabolomics revealed vaping-associated systemic metabolic alterations consistent with oxidative stress and altered host-microbial metabolism.

Conclusions: In mice, chronic ENDS aerosol exposure is sufficient to induce CF-relevant microbial and metabolic phenotypes independent of CFTR dysfunction. These findings suggest that vaping-associated oxidative stress may act as an environmental modifier capable of exacerbating gut-lung axis dysfunction and inflammatory vulnerability relevant to CF.

Gamaleya National Research Center for Epidemiology and Microbiology, Moscow, Russian Federation, 2Gamaleya National Research Center for Epidemiology and Microbiology, Moscow, Russian Federation, 3Federal Pulmonology Research Institute, Federal Medical and Biological Agency of Russia, Moscow, Russian Federation, 4Research Centre for Medical Genetics, Moscow, Russian Federation
records.abstract_text:
Pneumocystis jirovecii, a fungal pathogen, is capable of causing infection beyond severely immunocompromised patients, including in those with relatively intact immunity.

Objective: To assess the detection rate of P. jirovecii and evaluate its association with clinical and laboratory parameters in Russian patients with cystic fibrosis (CF).

Materials and Methods: In a pilot study, sputum samples from 31 CF patients (26 adults and 5 children) were analysed for P. jirovecii DNA using real-time PCR. Clinical data were collected from questionnaires completed by attending physicians.

Results: P. jirovecii DNA was detected in 7 patients (22.6%; 95% CI: 10.5–39.6%). The mean threshold cycle (Cq) value was 25.9, indicating a moderate fungal load. No statistically significant differences were observed in microbial co-infections or lung function (FVC, FEV1) between colonised and non-colonised groups. However, exacerbation of chronic pulmonary infection occurred in 42.9% (3 of 7) of colonised patients versus 25.0% in non-colonised individuals. Notably, two of these three patients had high fungal loads (Cq 23.5 and 23.9), possibly implicating P. jirovecii in exacerbation pathogenesis, even in the absence of diagnosed pneumocystosis. Interestingly, 42.9% of colonised patients were receiving co-trimoxazole, which has anti-pneumocystis activity. Persistence of the pathogen despite therapy may suggest reduced susceptibility or suboptimal dosing.

Conclusion: The prevalence of P. jirovecii colonisation (22.6%; median Cq 24.6) in Russian CF patients aligns with global data and shows a trend toward association with pulmonary exacerbations. Although no statistically significant differences emerged in this small cohort, the findings generate important hypotheses warranting validation in larger studies. Even asymptomatic colonisation may be clinically relevant, particularly in assessing risk and determining prophylactic needs in candidates for lung transplantation.

records.abstract_text:
Objective: to assess the dynamics of microbiological parameters in cystic fibrosis patients in the Russian Federation over the period 2011–2024.

Material: data from the Cystic Fibrosis Patient Registry in the Russian Federation for the period 2011–2014.

Results: S. aureus is the dominant microbial species colonizing the respiratory tract of cystic fibrosis patients throughout the entire observation period. The prevalence of MSSA ranges from 53,8% (2013) to 70,0% (2023), with an average of 60,7%. There is a trend towards an increase in these figures in recent years.

The proportion of MRSA ranges from 3,1% (2020) to 6,4% (2015), averaging 4,7%.

The prevalence of P. aeruginosa averaged 47,1%, with the lowest infection rates of 41,7% observed in 2024, which may likely be attributed to the widespread use of targeted therapy among Russian patients. Chronic infection rates ranged from 30,8% to 34,3%, while the incidence of intermittent infection ranged from 9,6% to 16,9%. The lowest values for both indicators were also recorded in 2024.

Over the 14‑year observation period, there has been a trend towards a decrease in the prevalence of Burkholderia cepacia complex‑associated infection, from a maximum of 7,9% in 2013 to 4,3% in 2024. The incidence of S. maltophilia reached its minimum value of 3,1% in 2024, with an average prevalence of 4,0%. The proportion of Achromobacter spp. averaged 5,9%. The average prevalence of non‑tuberculosis mycobacteria over the entire observation period was 1,0%.

Conclusion: According to the Cystic Fibrosis Patient Registry data in the Russian Federation for 2011–2024, there has been an increase in the proportion of MSSA, a decrease in Burkholderia cepacia complex infections, and a trend towards a reduction in P. aeruginosa prevalence.

records.title: Intraspecific variation is key for predicting the outcome of bacterial species interactions in the cystic fibrosis lung
records.authors_text: S. Dodd1, S. O'Brien1, J. Fothergill2
records.affiliations_text: 1Trinity College Dublin, Microbiology, Dublin, Ireland, 2University of Liverpool, Clinical Infection, Microbiology & Immunology, Liverpool, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a common recessively inherited disease characterised by consistent chronic lung infections. Two key pathogens colonizing the CF lung are Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. While S. aureus is the dominant pathogen infecting patients during childhood, P. aeruginosa often appears by early adulthood, displacing or occasionally co-existing with S. aureus. The ability of P. aeruginosa to outcompete S. aureus and dominate the CF lung is a worrying milestone in the life of a patient with CF, as P. aeruginosa infections are associated with worsening disease symptoms and mortality.

Objectives: We aimed to understand the factors that allow P. aeruginosa to outcompete or coexist with S. aureus, with the overall goal of managing disease progression.

Methods: Here, we perform in-depth analysis of a collection of 40 P. aeruginosa isolates from a single CF patient sample. The methods employed include reciprocal supernatant assays, plaque assays, and comprehensive statistical data analysis.

Results: We show that the interactions between S. aureus and P. aeruginosa are lineage-specific – so different within-patient lineages are affected by S. aureus in distinct and opposing ways. We have begun to further uncover these diverse outcomes by investigating phage production, auxotrophy, and within-population cross-feeding of P. aeruginosa.

Conclusion: Our work suggests that the use of a wider range of clinical isolates is necessary to understand the role of interspecies interactions for predicting the evolution of P. aeruginosa in CF.

records.title: Ecological and evolutionary strain-level dynamics of key pathogens in the cystic fibrosis lung microbiome

person.title: PhD student
person.department: Faculty of Biology, Medicine and Health

records.authors_text: R. Wallis Downham1, A. Jones1, M. Brockhurst1, A. Horsley1, F. Whelan1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Manchester, Faculty of Biology, Medicine and Health, Manchester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Recent advancements in therapeutics for cystic fibrosis (CF) have drastically extended the lifespan of people with CF; however, periodic pulmonary exacerbations, in part driven by chronic bacterial infection, remain the leading cause of morbidity and mortality. Management relies on prolonged antibiotic use, which potentiates antimicrobial resistance, a pressing global healthcare concern. Recent studies have highlighted the complexity of the CF lung microbiome, where community composition and microbe–microbe interactions influence disease progression and antimicrobial susceptibility. Notably, the first strain to colonise the CF lung often persists long-term, diversifying into sublineages and suppressing intra-genus competitors except in cases of superinfection. However, how strain composition of key CF pathogens shifts during exacerbation, and how genetic differences between strains contribute to disease severity remains poorly understood.

As part of a multi-centre CF Trust Innovation Hub in the UK (PULSE-CF), this study draws on two longitudinal datasets: a previously collected cohort with up to seven sputum samples collected per individual over the course of pulmonary exacerbation (plus a post-exacerbation stable sample), and an ongoing study sampling up to four timepoints across exacerbation. Samples undergo culture enrichment using optimally selected media under diverse conditions to enrich target microorganisms, followed by metagenomic sequencing, with 209 samples sequenced to date. Additionally, ongoing work utilises high-throughput phenomic screens to quantify evolutionary changes occurring throughout the exacerbation event. We characterise strain-level dynamics across exacerbation and identify genes contributing to intra-genus competition. Thus, exploring the strain-level diversity in the CF lung microbiome is a promising avenue for understanding pathogen evolution, with insights into improved treatment strategies and prevention of exacerbations.

records.title: Validation of an in vitro cystic fibrosis gut microbiome model to investigate drug-microbiome interactions
records.authors_text: J.M Tricker1, R. Marsh1, T.M Monaghan2,3, M. Brodlie4,5, I.J Haq4,5, A.L Jones1, C. van der Gast1
records.affiliations_text: 1Northumbria University, Faculty of Science and Environment, Newcastle, United Kingdom, 2University of Nottingham, Translational Medical Sciences, School of Medicine, Nottingham, United Kingdom, 3NIHR Nottingham Biomedical Research Centre, Nottingham, United Kingdom, 4Newcastle University, Translational and Clinical Research Institute, Faculty of Medical Sciences, Newcastle, United Kingdom, 5Newcastle upon Tyne Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, Paediatric Respiratory Medicine, Great North Children’s Hospital, Newcastle, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Gut symptoms and negative alterations to the gut microbiome in people with cystic fibrosis (CF) persist, despite the use of CFTR modulator therapies. CF polypharmacy and more specifically persistent antibiotic use contribute to this dysbiosis. However, the mechanistic effects of CF drug-microbiome interactions are not understood. Here, we validate high-throughput donor-based in vitro gut microbiome models representative of the CF and healthy gut environments to address this knowledge gap.

Methods: Stool samples from CF (n=7) and healthy (n=7) participants were used to seed respective gut microbiome models. CF and healthy microbiome models were run up to 14 days under anaerobic conditions and subjected to the following analyses: total bacterial cell abundances (cells/ml) using flow cytometry, long read (full 16S rRNA gene) bacterial microbiome sequencing, and targeted metabolomics of short chain fatty acids (SCFA).

Results: Once the gut microbiome models were established, cell abundances remained consistent for the duration. Microbiome characteristics of diversity and composition were consistently stable throughout. Microbiome abundance, diversity, and composition were significantly lower and distinct in the CF model when compared to the healthy model (p<0.05 in all instances using Kruskal-Wallis and PERMANOVA tests). Likewise, SCFA production and levels were also consistent over the 14-day period.

Conclusion: Here, we validated the longitudinal use of CF gut microbiome models contrasted to healthy models. Subsequently, this tractable and representative model combined with multi-omic approaches, will allow for elucidation of drug-microbiome mechanistic interactions in the CF gut.

Objectives: Gut symptoms and negative alterations to the gut microbiome in people with cystic fibrosis (CF) persist, despite the use of CFTR modulator therapies. CF polypharmacy and more specifically persistent antibiotic use contribute to this dysbiosis. However, the mechanistic effects of CF drug-microbiome interactions are not understood. Here, we validate high-throughput donor-based in vitro gut microbiome models representative of the CF and healthy gut environments to address this knowledge gap.
Methods: Stool samples from CF (n=7) and healthy (n=7) participants were used to seed respective gut microbiome models. Microbiome characteristics of diversity and composition were consistently stable throughout. Microbiome abundance, diversity, and composition were significantly lower and distinct in the CF model when compared to the healthy model (p<0.05 in all instances using Kruskal-Wallis and PERMANOVA tests). Likewise, SCFA production and levels were also consistent over the 14-day period.

records.abstract_text:
Background: Viral respiratory infections (VRIs) are a common potential trigger of pulmonary exacerbations in adults with cystic fibrosis (CF) and are associated with significant morbidity. However, prospective data on VRI incidence and clinical impact in people with CF (pwCF) remain limited.

Methods: Adults with CF were recruited as part of CF-Tracker study, an ongoing longitudinal observational study of pulmonary exacerbations using detailed clinical and multi-modal phenotyping. To date, 46 pwCF have been followed prospectively for up to seven months. Nose-and-throat swabs for viral PCR were collected fortnightly via home sampling and at the onset of new pulmonary symptoms. Twenty-two healthy volunteers (HV) provided a single control swab. PCR assays targeted SARS-CoV-2, adenovirus, influenza A/B, human metapneumovirus, parainfluenza (types 1-3), respiratory syncytial virus, and human rhinovirus. Symptom scores and spirometry were recorded at each visit.

Results: To date, 256 viral swabs have been collected, including symptom triggered samples. Twenty-two swabs (8.6%) tested positive (mean cycle threshold (Ct) of 30.57, range 21.19-42). Among symptom-triggered swabs, 6 / 20 (30.0%) were positive (mean Ct 30.66), compared with 16 positive results (6.8%) during scheduled stable visits (mean Ct 30.53). Among asymptomatic HV, 2 / 22 swabs (9.1%) were positive (mean Ct 37.67).

Discussion: Viral positivity was substantially higher during new pulmonary symptoms than during stable visits or in HV, suggesting that VRIs may account for approximately one in four pulmonary exacerbations. Asymptomatic viral carriage in stable adults was similar to healthy controls. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of viral home sampling and reliable detection of viruses in postal samples. This ongoing study will further define the clinical relevance of these infections and their relationship to baseline lung health.

person.biography:
Dr. Sharon Weinberg is a senior registrar in respiratory and general internal medicine based in Manchester, UK, and a clinical research fellow within the Pulse CF Hub at the University of Manchester, supervised by Professor Alex Horsley.
She graduated from New York University with a BA, followed by an MBBS from St George’s, University of London. She has trained internationally, including in Cyprus and Israel, before moving to the UK, where she is completing her specialist training in respiratory and general internal medicine in the North West of England. She has also completed a specialist fellowship at the National Aspergillosis Centre in Manchester.
Her work centres on cystic fibrosis, with a particular emphasis on pulmonary exacerbations and their role in disease progression. Dr. Weinberg is actively involved in the design and coordination of major clinical research studies at the Manchester Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, including the CF-Tracker and Unified-CF projects.
She is currently undertaking a PhD investigating the impact of environmental pollution, viral infections, and treatment adherence on pulmonary exacerbations in cystic fibrosis. Her research aims to identify modifiable risk factors and inform preventative strategies to improve long-term outcomes for people living with the condition.

records.title: Mechanistic and patient-derived insights into virus-bacteria-host interactions during pulmonary exacerbations in children with cystic fibrosis

person.department: Lab of Applied Microbiology and Biotechnology

records.authors_text: J. Bastiaenssen1,2, N. Jouret3, E. Cauwenberghs1, P. Delputte4, S. Verhulst2,3, S. Lebeer1, I. De Boeck1, I. Spacova1, K. Van Hoorenbeeck2,3
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Antwerp, Lab of Applied Microbiology and Biotechnology, Antwerp, Belgium, 2University of Antwerp, Lab of Experimental Medicine and Pediatrics, Antwerp, Belgium, 3University Hospital of Antwerp, Edegem, Belgium, 4University of Antwerp, Laboratory of Microbiology, Parasitology and Hygiene, Antwerp, Belgium
records.abstract_text:
Background: People with cystic fibrosis (CF) face greater clinical morbidity from viral infections, yet the role of these infections in pulmonary exacerbations (PExs) is understudied. Understanding viral involvement may guide targeted treatments and reduce unnecessary antibiotic use.

We investigated how viral infections affect the airway microbiome and immune responses in children with CF (CwCF) during PExs, and explored bacteria-virus-host interactions in vitro.

Methods: Throat swabs from CwCF (<5 years) were collected during routine visits and PExs for microbiome (16S rRNA sequencing), viral RNA (multiplex qPCR), and immune marker (Olink) analyses. In vitro, bacterial binding to RSV A2 was studied using FITC-labeled anti-RSV antibodies and flow cytometry. Indirect immune interactions were examined by measuring IRF and NF-κB immune signaling activation in THP1-Dual monocytes and A549-Dual lung epithelial cells.

Results: 22 children were followed for one year, during which 16 PExs were included. Key respiratory viruses, including rhinovirus, RSV, and coronavirus, were detected in over 70% of PExs. During these events, the airway microbiome showed an increased relative abundance of pathogenic species such as Moraxella, while taxonomic richness declined following antibiotic treatment. Furthermore, PEx samples exhibited elevated cytokine levels (IL-1α, IFN-γ, IL-6), which decreased after antibiotic use.

In vitro, Streptococcus pneumoniae showed strong RSV binding, unlike other isolates such as Staphylococcus aureus. Additionally, most isolates, e.g. S. aureus, induced high NF-κB and IRF activation, suggesting activation of inflammation and/or antiviral immune pathways.

Conclusions: CwCF exhibit diverse airway microbiomes that shift during PExs, coinciding with frequent respiratory virus detection and elevated inflammation. Direct and indirect interactions between CF bacteria and viruses may have implications for improving management of viral and bacterial (co-)infections.

records.title: Socioeconomic status, airway colonization patterns, and disease-related knowledge in children with cystic fibrosis: a preliminary single-center analysis
records.authors_text: U. Kavgacı1, E. Yalçın1, T. Kantemir1, D. Demirel1, N. Emiralioğlu1, D. Doğru1, U. Özçelik1
records.affiliations_text: 1Hacettepe University, Pediatric Pulmonology, Ankara, Turkey
records.abstract_text:
Background: Socioeconomic status(SES) is increasingly recognized as an important determinant of health outcomes in cystic fibrosis(CF);however,data on its relationship with airway colonization remain limited in pediatric cohorts.

Aim: To explore the association between SES,colonization and disease-related knowledge levels in children with CF(cwCF).

Methods: This cross-sectional analysis included 45 cwCF.SES was summarized using a principal component analysis(PCA)–derived score incorporating household income,parental education,maternal employment,smoking exposure,and crowding index.Patients were categorized into two SES groups based on a median split of the PCA-SES score.Knowledge regarding infection control was assessed using a questionnaire(score range:0–15).

Results: The study included 45 cwCF,with a median age of 13 years(IQR 9–15).The median knowledge score was 13(IQR 11.5–14.0).Based on the PCA-SES score, patients were split into lower(n=23)and higher(n=22)SES groups.Knowledge scores were significantly lower in the lower SES group compared with the higher SES group(median 12 vs 14; p< 0.001).Median knowledge scores were similar between patients with and without prior and current MRSA and Pseudomonas aeruginosa(Pa)colonization.Children in the lower SES group had higher prevalence of prior MRSA colonization compared to higher SES group(52.2% vs 27.3%),showing a trend toward significance(p=0.130).No significant differences were observed between SES groups with respect to current MRSA colonization, prior and current Pa colonization.

Conclusion: Lower SES-score was associated with a higher rate of prior MRSA colonization,although statistical significance was not reached.SES was strongly associated with disease-related knowledge levels;however, knowledge scores were not associated with colonization status.These findings suggest that socioeconomic factors may influence infection risk through pathways beyond knowledge levels and underscore the need for larger studies.

person.biography:
Dr. Dilara Demirel is a pediatric pulmonologist and researcher at Hacettepe University Faculty of Medicine in Ankara, Türkiye. Her clinical and academic work focuses on cystic fibrosis, pediatric interstitial lung diseases, and the integration of immunological perspectives into respiratory medicine. She is actively involved in multidisciplinary patient care and translational research aimed at improving outcomes for children with chronic lung diseases.
Dr. Demirel has led and contributed to several clinical studies evaluating the safety and efficacy of CFTR modulator therapies, including their systemic and ophthalmologic effects. She has also participated in research on rare pediatric pulmonary conditions such as pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis, contributing to case series and collaborative publications. Her work emphasizes real-world clinical data and patient-centered approaches to care.
She completed a clinical observership at Hannover Medical School (MHH), Germany, where she gained experience in advanced pediatric pulmonology practices, including bronchoscopy, mechanical ventilation, and lung transplantation. Dr. Demirel is an active member of the European Cystic Fibrosis Society (ECFS) Telehealth Working Group, contributing to initiatives that explore digital health solutions and telemedicine in cystic fibrosis care.
Her accomplishments include presentations at international conferences, collaboration in multidisciplinary research projects, and the development of ethically approved clinical studies. Dr. Demirel remains committed to advancing pediatric respiratory medicine through innovation, collaboration, and academic excellence. She is happily married with a beautiful daughter and four cats. That's her most important achievement.

records.title: Main pathogens of bacterial infections in the lungs of children with cystic fibrosis

person.institution: Federal State Autonomous Institution “National Medical Research Center for Children’s Health” of the Ministry of Health of the Russian Federation

records.authors_text: Z. Sadeeva1, A. Lazareva1, E. Samoilova1, Y. Gorinova2, O. Simonova2
records.affiliations_text: 1National Medical Research Center for Children's Health Federal State Autonomous Institution of the Ministry of Health of the Russian Federation, Laboratory of Microbiology, Moscow, Russian Federation, 2National Medical Research Center for Children's Health Federal State Autonomous Institution of the Ministry of Health of the Russian Federation, Pulmonology, Moscow, Russian Federation
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To determine the spectrum of bacterial pathogens isolated from pediatric patients with cystic fibrosis between 2020 and 2024, determine the antimicrobial susceptibility of the main pathogens, and identify metallo-β-lactamase genes in P. aeruginosa.

Methods: Antimicrobial susceptibility was determined using disk diffusion and broth microdilution methods. β-lactamase genes were identified using immunochromatography and real-time PCR.

Results: We analyzed 4,133 bacterial isolates obtained from patients with cystic fibrosis. The leading positions in the spectrum of microorganisms are occupied by S. aureus - 27% (n = 1108) and P. aeruginosa - 22% (n = 911). When determining the susceptibility of P. aeruginosa, it was determined that resistance to meropenem and imipenem was 19% and 27%, respectively. Resistance to protected cefalosporins reached 25%. 23% of strains were resistant to aztreonam. Up to 40% of isolates were resistant to aminoglycosides. Resistance to protected penicillins and fluoroquinolones reached 30%. Particular attention was attracted by P. aeruginosa strains that showed resistance to colistin - 6%. Isolated cases of the MBL VIM- gene were detected in 9 isolates.

Regarding S. aureus, all isolates studied were susceptible to tigecycline, linezolid, and vancomycin. Resistance to gentamicin, ciprofloxacin, and tetracycline was 7%, 12%, and 19%, respectively. Resistance to erythromycin and clindamycin was 31% and 25%, respectively. Notably, resistance to oxacillin (MRSA) reached 19% of strains during this period.

Conclusion: S. aureus and P. aeruginosa are the main microorganisms isolated from the respiratory tract of patients with cystic fibrosis. P. aeruginosa has a relatively favorable resistance profile to antibiotics, but the emergence of colistin- resistant isolates is alarming. Among S. aureus isolates, increasing resistance to oxacillin and macrolides is noteworthy.

records.title: The link between pulmonary exacerbations and respiratory viruses in young children with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: B. Van Gasse1, M. Somers1, J. Lomelino1, N. Jouret1,2, J. Bastiaenssen2, K. Van Hoorenbeeck1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Antwerp, Antwerp, Belgium, 2Antwerp University Hospital, Pediatric Pulmonology, Edegem, Belgium
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The objective of this study is to assess if viral infections will trigger a Pulmonary Exacerbation (PEx) in children with Cystic Fibrosis (CF) and to identify patient-related risk factors.

Methods: Children with CF, aged zero to five years, were included at the pediatric CF clinic of Antwerp University Hospital (UZA) between January 2024 and 2026. Oropharyngeal swabs for the detection of respiratory viruses by PCR were obtained during routine visits and at the time of PEx. Patients were divided into two groups (with and without PEx) and the following patient-related factors was recorded: age, gender, CFTR gene mutation, bacterial colonization, lung function, BMI and socioeconomic factors.

Results: During the study period, 15 of the 21 included children experienced at least one PEx. Generalized Estimating Equations analysis showed an almost 12 times higher chance of detecting viral presence during PEx compared to routine visits (p=0.010; OR=11.66). The confounders female sex (p=0.046), lower BMI (p=0.013) and seasonal variation (p=0.032) were significantly associated with viral detection. The most prevalent virus detected during PEx was rhinovirus. Only parainfluenzavirus type 3 (PIV3) had a significantly higher presence during PEx compared to routine visits (p=0.027). Multivariate logistic regression showed no significance for patient related factors as a risk factor for the development of a PEx. Univariate analysis did show a significant effect of the patient’s CFTR mutation type (p=0.067). It showed a correlation between the Fdel580 mutation and more frequent exacerbations.

Conclusion: Viral presence is almost 12 times higher during PEx compared to routine visits. Rhinovirus was the most prevalent virus during PEx, and PIV3 showed a significantly higher presence during PEx. There were no patient-related factors found that contribute to the development of PEx.

records.title: Design of a life-course study of cardiovascular risk and preclinical atherosclerosis in children and adults with cystic fibrosis

person.institution: Wilhelmina Children's Hospital, University Medical Center Utrecht

records.authors_text: M. Destoop1, I.A. van der Linden1, J.J.D. Raijmakers1, D.E. Bruil1, M. Spierenburg1, M.A. Kruijswijk2, S. Schotman2, M. Burghard2, S.L. Nijhof3, H.S. Schipper4, D. Muilwijk1, C.K. van der Ent1, I. Bronsveld2
records.affiliations_text: 1Wilhelmina Children's Hospital, University Medical Center Utrecht, Pediatric Pulmonology, Utrecht, Netherlands, 2University Medical Center Utrecht, Pulmonology, Utrecht, Netherlands, 3Wilhelmina Children's Hospital, University Medical Center Utrecht, Social Pediatrics, Utrecht, Netherlands, 4Sophia Children's Hospital, Erasmus Medical Center, Pediatric Cardiology, Rotterdam, Netherlands
records.abstract_text:
Objective: With increasing life expectancy, people with CF may face a growing burden of cardiovascular disease (CVD). Insight into cardiovascular risk and early vascular changes from childhood into adulthood is currently limited. This study aims to assess cardiovascular risk factors and preclinical atherosclerosis across the life course in CF.

Methods: The study consists of two complementary prospective cohort studies: SMART-Youth, including children with CF aged 8–18 years, and SMART-CF, including adults with CF (≥18 years). Both cohorts undergo comparable cardiovascular assessments. Cardiovascular risk profiling includes blood pressure, BMI, anthropometric measurements (chest, waist and hip circumference), abdominal visceral and subcutaneous adipose tissue (assessed by ultrasound), lipid profile, HbA1c and inflammatory markers. Lifestyle and psychosocial factors are collected using validated questionnaires. Physical activity is assessed by a physiotherapist using either a shuttle run test or bicycle ergometry. CF-related factors include CF-related liver disease, pancreatic insufficiency, CF-related diabetes, respiratory colonization, lung function, oxygen saturation, and transplantation history. Preclinical atherosclerosis is assessed using carotid intima-media thickness (cIMT), carotid distensibility, aortic pulse wave velocity (PWV) and endothelial function measurement. All assessments are repeated after two years to evaluate progression.

Results: This abstract describes the study design. Enrolment is ongoing. An update on study progress will be available in June 2026.

Conclusion: By applying a unified and harmonized cardiovascular assessment strategy in both pediatric and adult CF populations, our study enables evaluation of early vascular changes and cardiovascular risk trajectories across the life course. This approach may inform future timing and strategies for cardiovascular monitoring and prevention in CF.

records.title: Gathering strengths to improve digestive health

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Despite the advent of highly effective CFTR modulators, digestive symptoms (DS) remain frequently reported by patients with cystic fibrosis (CF). The French patient organisation Vaincre la Mucoviscidose, in collaboration with healthcare professionals, launched a project to better characterize and manage DS in CF.

Methods: A core committee conducted two surveys. Questionnaire 1 collected patient-reported outcomes from people with CF or parents of children with CF over the previous four weeks, focusing on DS, their impact on quality of life, and current treatments. Questionnaire 2 gathered clinical experience and care management issues related to DS from CF care teams across 47 CF centers. Finally, a multidisciplinary seminar involving patients, healthcare teams, and researchers, including a gastroenterologist specialized in functional gastrointestinal disorders—was held.

Results: DS were reported by 63% of the 458 respondents, 77% receiving modulators. Symptoms were more frequent in adults than in children (60% vs 40%) and in females compared with males (60% vs 40%). The most reported DS were flatulence, bloating, foul-smelling stools, and abdominal pain, affecting 80% of symptomatic patients. Fatigue was the main quality-of-life impact, reported by 65%. Although 80% of respondents were asked about DS during routine visits, only 38% of those with DS consulted a gastroenterologist. This finding is consistent with reports from CF care teams, highlighting limited involvement of gastroenterologists. Only two centers reported no issues. Major challenges included diagnostic complexity (45%) and limited therapeutic options (78%).

Conclusion: The seminar facilitated discussion of survey findings with patients, care and research teams, identified priorities for improving care, including targeted training in CF for gastroenterologists, and enhanced unmet needs, which should be addressed through research.

records.title: Impact of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor on serum lipid profiles in adults with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: S. Van Meerbeeck1, F. Wynants1, N. Duplacie1, L. Moyens1, L. Dupont1,2, N. Lorent1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1UZ Leuven, Leuven, Belgium, 2KU Leuven, Leuven, Belgium
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) has substantially improved outcomes in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) but is increasingly associated with metabolic changes, including alterations in serum lipid profiles. The effects on lipid parameters remain unclear. We evaluated changes in serum lipid levels following initiation of ETI.

Methods: All adults with CF from a single centre who initiated ETI and had serum lipid measurements (total cholesterol (total-c), low-density cholesterol (LDL-c), high-density cholesterol (HDL-c) and triglycerides (TG)) and body mass index (BMI) at baseline and follow-up were included. Measurements were obtained 0-2 months before ETI initiation and 10-18 months after initiation under routine, non-fasting conditions. Additional inclusion criteria were: ≥1 F508del mutation, ≥1 year of ETI treatment, no lung transplantation and documented ETI adherence.

Results: 56 adults with CF were included (31 males; mean age 34.7±12.4 years; 44 with pancreatic insufficiency (EPI); 12 CF diabetes). Mean total-c increased from 140.7 mg/dL (range 59-219) to 153.0 mg/dL (range 81-248) (p<0.01), with significant increases observed in males and individuals with EPI. LDL-c increased from 63.9 mg/dL (range 18-132) to 76.6 mg/dL (range 29-145) (p<0.01), independent of sex and pancreatic status. TG levels decreased from 107.4 mg/dL (range 42-252) to 94.9 mg/dL (range 42-215) (p<0.05), while HDL-c remained unchanged. Mean BMI increased from 23.2 kg/m² to 24.0 kg/m².

Conclusion: ETI initiation was associated with heterogeneous changes in serum lipid profiles. Total-c and LDL-c increased, whereas TG decreased unexpectedly. HDL-c remained unchanged. These changes likely reflect a normalisation of lipid metabolism. However, in an aging CF population, they may signal emerging cardiovascular risk profiles previously less prominent in CF care. Attention to a healthy diet with an appropriate fatty acid composition is advisable.

records.title: An explorative study on the association between hepatic steatosis and glucometabolic profile in children and adults with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: D. Declercq1,2,3, A. Raman1, M. Naessens2, O. Domjan2, S. Van Aken4,1, Y. Vande Weygaerde1,5, X. Verhelst6,2, R. De Bruyne7,2, B. Lapauw1,2,8, E. Van Braeckel1,5,2, S. Van Biervliet2,1,7
records.affiliations_text: 1UZ Gent, Reference Center for Cystic Fibrosis, Gent, Belgium, 2Ghent University, Internal Medicine and Paediatrics, Gent, Belgium, 3UZ Gent, Center for Healthy Nutrition and Dietetics, Gent, Belgium, 4UZ Gent, Department of Paediatrics, Gent, Belgium, 5UZ Gent, Department of Respiratory Medicine, Gent, Belgium, 6UZ Gent, Department of Gastroenterology and Hepatology, Gent, Belgium, 7UZ Gent, Department of Pediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition, Gent, Belgium, 8UZ Gent, Department of Endocrinology, Gent, Belgium
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Cystic Fibrosis Liver Disease (CFLD) comprises a spectrum of hepatobiliary manifestations, including hepatic steatosis, biliary disease and cirrhosis, and is an independent risk factor for CFRD. This exploratory study aims to address the knowledge gaps in the link between early glucose abnormalities and hepatic steatosis.

Methods: All CF patients (n= 252) attending annual review in 2024 at Ghent University Hospital were eligible, excluding CFRD (n=30), CFLD (n=18), and prior liver transplantation (n=2). Assessments included transient elastography (TE), controlled attenuation parameter (CAP), relative fat mass (FM%) and fat mass index (FMI) measured by BIA, HbA1c, and OGTT. Non-parametric statistics and linear regression were used. Results are reported as median [IQR], unless stated otherwise.

Results: Patients’ characteristics are summarized in table 1. In adults, 32/116 (28%) had a CAP >238 dB/m and showed a higher HbA1c% (5.7[5.4; 5.9] vs 5.4[5.2; 5.7]p =.019), FM % (20.6[15; 25.9] vs 26.3[19.9; 32]p=.005) and FMI (kg/m2) 4.5[3.1; 5.5] vs 6.4[4.3; 8.2]p=.002. In children, 17/68 (25%) had a CAP >238 dB/m with higher FM% 26.5[24.2; 29.2] vs 19.5[13.5; 24.3],p=.042 and FMI (kg/m2) 4.3[3.7; 5] vs 3.3[2.2; 4.3],p=.017 and a non-significant higher HbA1c%.

CAP was not a predictor of HbA1c%, whereas FM % and FMI were significantly predicted HbA1c% in adult men. The regression model with FMI explained a significant proportion of the variance in HbA1c% (R2=.357,F(1,44)=23.91,p<.001;(β=.60,t(44)=4.89,p<.001)). Specifically, each one-unit increase in FMI, was associated with 2.68% increase in HbA1c% (B=2.68, 95% CI [1.57,3.78]).

records.title: Oesophageal inflammatory biomarkers correlate with PedsQL gastrointestinal symptom scores in patients with cystic fibrosis on ETI

person.institution: University of South Florida Morsani College of Medicine

records.authors_text: S.-J. Abi-Aad1, R. Pace2, E. Zemanick3, S. Noujaim4, D. Green5, N. Goldenberg6, R. Khalaf1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of South Florida Morsani College of Medicine, Pediatrics, Tampa, United States, 2University of South Florida, College of Nursing and Microbiomes Institute, Tampa, United States, 3University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus and Children’s Hospital Colorado, Pediatrics, Aurora, United States, 4University of South Florida, Molecular Pharmacology & Physiology Department, Tampa, United States, 5Johns Hopkins All Children’s Hospital, Pediatrics, St Petersburg, United States, 6Johns Hopkins University, Departments of Pediatrics and Medicine, St Petersburg, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Gastrointestinal (GI) manifestations remain burdensome for people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) as symptoms and inflammation persist despite elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) use. While stool calprotectin correlates with patient-reported outcomes, data on upper GI symptom burden and esophageal inflammatory markers remain unexplored. We evaluated correlations between proximal (PE) and distal esophagus (DE) inflammation using a novel minimally invasive esophageal string test (EST) and GI-related quality of life (QoL) in pwCF on and off ETI vs. healthy controls (HC).

Methods: This cross-sectional study included pwCF aged 6–25 years on or off ETI and healthy controls. PedsQL™ Gastrointestinal Symptoms Scales (PedsQL GI) were reported (higher scores=better QoL). Biomarker concentrations were measured by multiplex immunoassay using exudates from the EST from the PE and DE (IL-1β, IL-33, IL-6, IL-8, MMP-9, REG3α, TNF-α, and calprotectin). Spearman correlations with mean PedsQL GI items scores were calculated (p<0.05).

Results: A total of 36 individuals completed the study (19 on ETI, 5 off ETI, 12 HC). In the on ETI group, “stomach discomfort when eating” QoL negatively correlated with IL-8 (rho -0.52; p=0.031) and “gas and bloating” QoL negatively correlated with IL-1β (-0.51; p=0.038) in the PE; but positive correlations were observed in the DE. In contrast, those off ETI had no significant correlations. In HC, “trouble swallowing” QoL correlated negatively with IL-1β (-0.67; p=0.024) in the PE.

Conclusion: Increased PE inflammation was associated with worse GI-symptoms in pwCF on ETI and in HC. The lack of similar findings in the DE could indicate that swallowed airway secretions may contribute to inflammation in the PE. No correlations were observed in pwCF off ETI, likely due to small sample size. This suggests that pwCF with upper GI symptoms may have persistent inflammation despite ETI which may be derived in part from airway inflammation.

records.title: Is vitamin D deficiency really the primary reason for raised parathyroid hormone (PTH) in people with cystic fibrosis (PwCF)?
records.authors_text: A. Derry1, H. Gledhill2, D. Waine2, D. Derry2
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Sheffield Medical School, Sheffield, United Kingdom, 2Plymouth Adult CF centre, Plymouth, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: European guidelines recommend routine monitoring of PTH to optimise treatment with vitamin D (vitD). However we observed that PwCF with high PTH were often not vitD deficient. We sought other explanations.

Methods: Blood results from Annual Review of adult PwCF between 2016-2025 were analysed. PTH was compared with paired vitD, calcium, phosphate (PO4) and magnesium (Mg). Oral calcium intake was assessed in a subgroup. PwCF with primary hyperparathyroidism were excluded.

Results: PTH was raised above 7.2 pmol/l (laboratory ULN) in 159/560 (28%) samples from 47/83 PwCF. There was only weak correlation (r=-0.28) between PTH and vitD. Only a minority (27/159) of raised PTHs were paired with deficient VitDs (<25 ng/l; Table). Low serum calcium, Mg and raised PO4 explained a further 1,12 and 5 raised PTHs respectively.

Deficient VitD (<25 ng/l)VitD 25<>74 ng/lOptimal VitD (>=75 ng/l)

Raised PTH >7.2 pmol/l278349Chi square testNormal PTH 1.6<>7.2 pmol/l14173214p<0.0001Table: PTH level by Vitamin D status

20/83 (24%) patients contributed 30% of blood results, but 118/159 (74%) of raised PTHs. All 20 of these patients were pancreatic exocrine insufficient (PEI).

Pancreatic sufficient patients (15/83) contributed 15% of results, but only 4/159 (2.5%) of raised PTHs. No other clinical parameter tested had a stronger association.

Raised PTH did not correlate with low (<1 g/day) oral calcium intake (as assessed in 2025 in 47 patients), but this analysis was confounded as PwCF had previously been prescribed calcium supplements in response to a high PTH.

Conclusions: Although PTH had a weak negative correlation with vitD, PTH was raised in 25% of non-vitD deficient samples, limiting its value as a marker of inadequate vitD replacement. Association was observed between raised PTH and PEI status. Testing the hypothesis that PTH increased in response to reduced calcium absorption (eg after sequestration with excess bile salts) was confounded by analysis not using contemporaneous calcium intake. The possibility of assay interference (ie false positives) is also being considered.

records.title: Prevalance of autoimmun diseases in children with cystic fibrosis: a prospective registry data analysis
records.authors_text: N. Farkas1, R. Molnár2, B. Varga3, M. Imrei2, A. Párniczky2, K. Ocskay2
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Pécs, Medical School, Institute of Bioanalysis, Pécs, Hungary, 2Heim Pál Pediatrics Institute, Budapest, Hungary, 3University of Pécs, Medical School, Institute for Translational Medicine, Pécs, Hungary
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Immune dysregulation in cystic fibrosis (CF) may increase susceptibility to autoimmune diseases (AID). Undiagnosed AID could worsen persistent inflammation, nutritional and endocrine dysfunction, treatment burden, and misinterpretation of CF disease progression.

We assessed the prevalence of celiac disease (CD), hypothyroidism requiring thyroid hormone replacement, and pancreatic islet autoantibodies in a pediatric CF cohort.

Methods: Single-centre prospective registry data (2019-2025) from 150 children were analysed. CD screening followed ESPGHAN guidelines. Thyroid function was monitored annually via TSH, with hypothyroidism requiring levothyroxine defined as persistently elevated TSH plus low free T4. Pancreatic islet autoantibodies (GAD, IAA, IA-2, ZnT8) were measured at least once. Autoantibody positivity was defined as ≥1 positive marker. Descriptive statistics and prevalence rates were calculated.

Results: Median age of the cohort was 10.62 years [IQR 5.25–16.56], 48% male). CD was diagnosed in 7 patients (4.7%; 28.6% male), with age at diagnosis ranging from 1.9 to 9.1 years. Hypothyroidism was identified in 5 cases (3.3%; 80% male), with onset from infancy to adolescence. At least one islet autoantibody (AAB) was present in 21 children (16%; 29% male; median age 11.32 years [IQR 7.64–15.91]), among which, 7 (33%) had CF-related diabetes, 4 (19%) had impaired glucose tolerance, and 10 (48%) had normal glucose tolerance. Co-occurrence of autoimmune conditions was rare: one child had CD plus islet AABs with diabetes, and two had hypothyroidism plus islet AABs with diabetes. No patient presented with all three conditions simultaneously.

Conclusion: In this pediatric CF cohort, the prevalence of celiac disease, hypothyroidism, and pancreatic islet AAB positivity appeared higher than reported rates in the general non-CF pediatric population.

Funding: National Research, Development and Innovation Fund (NKFIH 138929) and PTE ÁOK-KA Grant (KA-2025-19).

records.title: Polyketide synthase island-positive E. coli is strongly associated with ileocolonic neoplasia in adults with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: J. van Dorst1, N. Taylor2,3, B.L.D.U. Pushpakumara1, Z.T. Tan1, D. Buchanan4, P.S. Haber5,6,7, E. Nash5,7, S. Visser2, A. Volovets7, S. Sivam2,5, C.Y. Ooi1,8
records.affiliations_text: 1University of New South Wales, School of Clinical Medicine, Discipline of Paediatrics & Child Health, Randwick, Australia, 2Royal Prince Alfred Hospital, Department of Respiratory and Sleep Medicine, Camperdown, Australia, 3University of New South Wales, School of Clinical Medicine, Medicine & Health, Kensington, Australia, 4University of Melbourne, Department of Clinical Pathology, Melbourne, Australia, 5University of Sydney, Syndey Medical School, Camperdown, Australia, 6Royal Prince Alfred Hospital, Drug Health Services, Camperdown, Australia, 7Royal Prince Alfred Hospital, AW Morrow Gastroenterology and Liver Centre, Camperdown, Australia, 8Sydney Children's Hospital Network, Department of Gastroenterology, Randwick, Australia
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Polyketide synthase island-positive (Pks+) E. coli is a genotoxic gut bacterium linked to colorectal cancer (CRC) tumorigenesis via the genotoxin colibactin. In adults with CF, there is an increased incidence and earlier development of CRC, which includes an accelerated progression of adenomatous polyps. We aimed to determine the prevalence of pks+ E. coli in adults with CF and identify microbial factors that promote a tumorigenesis-permissive niche in the gut.

​Methods: Stool samples and DNA were analyzed from the SCREEN-CF study cohort (X18-0379 & HREC/18/RPAH/536). Intestinal inflammation was assessed via fecal calprotectin. Metagenomic taxonomic libraries were prepared using Illumina protocols and sequenced on the NovaSeq X Plus platform. Detection of the pks island was assessed with polymerase chain reaction (PCR) targeting a 283 base pair sequence in the clbB gene. Individuals were separated into three groups based on their colonoscopy results.

Results: Of the 49 CF patients; 35 (71%) had no pathology (NORMAL), 12 (25%) had adenomatous polyps (AP), and 2 (4%) had malignancy (CRC). pks+ E. coli was detected in 1/35 (3%), 5/12 (42%), and 2/2 (100%) of these groups respectively. Individuals with either AP or CRC (ileocolonic neoplasia) were 34 times more likely to harbor pks+ E. coli than those with NORMAL colonoscopy findings (OR = 34.0, 95% CI 5.00-691, p = 0.002). The presence of pks+ E. coli correlated with higher overall E. coli burden (p = 0.0009), but not with fecal inflammation, bacterial composition, or the presence of other genotoxic bacterial species.

​Conclusion: Pks+ E. coli is not universally abundant among adults with CF, but its presence is strongly associated with ileocolonic neoplasia, indicating a potential role in pathogenesis. If validated in larger cohorts, pks+ E. coli could provide a clinically meaningful biomarker for early detection, risk stratification and a potential target for precision intervention.

records.title: Assessment of abdominal symptoms and intestinal inflammation in children and adolescents with cystic fibrosis before and after initiation of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor therapy
records.authors_text: G.C. dos Santos1, L.C. Montera1, L.M. Genaro2, B.A.G. Rodrigues2, R.F. Leal2, A.F. Ribeiro3, J.D. Ribeiro3, E.A. Lomazi3, UNICAMP Modulators CFTR Study Group (UNIMCS Group)
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Campinas, Campinas, Brazil, 2University of Campinas, Surgery Department, Campinas, Brazil, 3University of Campinas, Department of Pediatrics, Campinas, Brazil
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a rare genetic disease caused by mutations in the CFTR gene that result in dysfunctional protein and affect several body systems, including the gastrointestinal tract. The changes caused by CF in the GI tract include dysmotility, dysbiosis, intestinal inflammation, and abdominal symptoms such as pain, changes in bowel habits, and distension, which are frequent in people with CF. The study aims to establish the prevalence of these complaints in children with CF and investigate associations between symptoms, clinical conditions, and marker of intestinal inflammation before and after the initiation of therapy with CFTR modulator drug (elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor - ETI).

Methods: Twenty-two pediatric patients with genetic diagnosis of CF, treated at a Brazilian reference center, were included. The methods involved systematic assessment of gastrointestinal symptoms using a questionnaire, biochemical analysis of fecal calprotectin (FC) as marker of intestinal inflammation, and collection of clinical and anthropometric data from medical records.

Results: 86.3% of participants (n=19) showed elevated FC levels (>50 mcg/g), indicating high prevalence of intestinal inflammation. The most common abdominal symptoms were pain and flatulence, present in about half of the patients. No significant associations were observed between FC levels and clinical or symptomatic variables. After three months of ETI therapy, there was average reduction of 73% in FC levels, but no statistically significant difference in the frequency of abdominal symptoms.

Conclusion: There is high prevalence of intestinal inflammation and abdominal symptoms in a sample of Brazilian children with CF, and therapy with ETI can reduce the level of intestinal inflammation.

records.title: Assessment of serum liver and kidney function tests 18 months after initiation of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor in patients with cystic fibrosis

records.authors_text: I. Arnaudova Danevska1,2, T. Jakjovska1,2, E. Gjinovska-Tasevska1, L. Proeska Stojanoski1, T. Savin1, M. Atanasova Nadjinska1
records.affiliations_text: 1University Clinic for Respiratory Diseases in Children - Kozle, Skopje, North Macedonia, The Republic of, 2Ss Cyril and Methodius University, Faculty of Medicine, Skopje, North Macedonia, The Republic of
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The novel triple modulatory therapy Elexacaftor/Tezacaftor/Ivacaftor (ETI) has shown clinical efficacy in patients with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). Our aim was to evaluate the impact of ETI on basic serum liver and kidney function tests in pwCF in the University Clinic for Respiratory Diseases in Children - Kozle in Skopje, Republic of North Macedonia 18 months after initiation of the therapy.

Methods: Data of 28 pwCF eligible for ETI was obtained. We have monitored aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), total bilirubin (TB), urea and creatinin on the start and after 18 months of the therapy with ETI. We have used a significant threshold of p<0.05. Sub analysis of age, sex and genotype was performed.

Results: Median age was 29.03 years (range 16-45), 16 male (57%) and 12 female (43%), 11 (39%) homozygous for F508del and 18 (61%) heterozygous for F508del. Mean values at the start were: AST 26.33 U/L (±13.26), ALT 30.11 U/L (±21,27), TB 12.95 μmol/l (±7.77), urea 5.08 mmol/l (±1.13) and creatinin 68.82 μmol/l (±14.81). After 18 month of initiation of the therapy mean values were: AST 27.00 U/L (±13.87), ALT 28.50 U/L (±14.75), TB 20.30 μmol/l (±14.72), urea 5.13 mmol/l (±1.10) and creatinin 75.79 μmol/l (±15.11). At the beginning and after 18 months of treatment, there was no significant change in the serum levels of AST, ALT, urea, creatinin, p=0.396, p=0.944, p=0.278, p=0.108, respectively. There was significant increase in bilirubin levels p<0.05.

Conclusion: Our study has shown that ETI is associated with increased bilirubin levels, but there is no impact on AST, ALT, urea and creatinin plasma levels 18 months after initiation.

records.title: Impact of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor on cholesterol loading and efflux capacity in a cohort of adults with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: G. Putti1,2, A. Gramegna1,2, G. Alicandro1,3, M. Contarini2, S. Misuraca2, M.P. Adorni4, F. Zimetti5, M. Mantero1,2, M. Ruscica6,7, F. Blasi2,1
records.affiliations_text: 1Università degli Studi di Milano, Department of Pathophysiology and Transplantation, Milan, Italy, 2Fondazione IRCCS Cà Granda Ospedale Maggiore Policlinico, Respiratory Unit and Cystic Fibrosis Adult Center, Milan, Italy, 3Fondazione IRCCS Ca' Granda Ospedale Maggiore Policlinico, Mother and Child Department, Cystic Fibrosis Center, Milan, Italy, 4University of Parma, Department of Medicine and Surgery, Parma, Italy, 5University of Parma, Department of Food and Drug, Parma, Italy, 6Università degli Studi di Milano, Department of Pharmacological and Biomolecular Sciences "Rodolfo Paoletti", Milan, Italy, 7Foundation IRCCS Ca' Granda Ospedale Maggiore Policlinico, Department of Cardio-Thoracic-Vascular Diseases, Milan, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The aim of this longitudinal study was to describe changes in HDL Cholesterol Efflux Capacity (CEC) and Cholesterol Loading Capacity (CLC) in adults with CF (awCF) after starting therapy with Elexacaftor/Tezacaftor/Ivacaftor (ETI).

Methods: Serum of awCF was collected before starting ETI therapy and 6 months later, a pool of healthy controls was also enrolled for healthy serum comparison. HDL was isolated and incubated for 6 hours with different cell lines, to evaluate their capacity to promote cholesterol efflux. ABCA1-mediated CEC was studied on J774A.1 cell line, while ABCG1-mediated CEC was studied using CHO-K1 and CHO-L3 cell lines. CLC was instead measured using macrophages derived from THP-1 monocytes. Intracellular cholesterol was determined with fluorimetric method and normalised for protein content.

Results: Fifty eight awCF participated (males 61%; median age 41). Baseline awCF CEC was significantly lower than in health controls (−15% for ABCA1 and −11% for ABCG1). Comparing the two timepoints in awCF, after six months of ETI therapy CEC increased of +13% (ABCA1) and +11% (ABCG1) compared to baseline, reaching values comparable to healthy controls. Regarding CLC, no significant difference between awCF at baseline and controls was found. After 6 months of ETI, CLC decreased of 7%. Higher HDL CEC reduces the risk of foamy macrophages formation, possibly decreasing the risk of atherosclerotic plaques formation at endothelial level. Results also suggest that patients do not have an increased CLC per se, and therapy appears to reduce such phenomenon, reinforcing the hypothesis of a positive clinical net effect.

Conclusion: Our results suggest that the correction of CFTR improves HDL function, possibly exerting a protective cardiovascular effect. Larger population studies with longer follow-up time should certainly be conducted to validate these results and provide a clinical confirmation of atherosclerotic risk reduction induced by ETI in awCF.

Larger population studies with longer follow-up time should certainly be conducted to validate these results and provide a clinical confirmation of atherosclerotic risk reduction induced by ETI in awCF.

records.title: Gastrointestinal manifestations assessed by the CFAbd-Score in patients with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: L.C.M. Wiezel1, J.D. Ribeiro1, A.F. Ribeiro1, E.A. Lomazi1
records.affiliations_text: 1UNICAMP, Campinas, Brazil
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: Gastrointestinal (GI) manifestations are common in patients with Cystic Fibrosis (CF). Their etiology can be attributed to three pathophysiological factors: inflammation, dysbiosis, and GI dysmotility. Better understanding the GI symptom context and developing more specific and early treatments are priorities for managing these patients.

Objective: To evaluate the prevalence and factors associated to gastrointestinal manifestations in patients with Cystic Fibrosis.

Methods: Cross-sectional observational study, conducted between April and September 2024, after approval from the Ethics Committee of the Institution. We included 59 children and adolescents with Cystic Fibrosis treated at the Pediatrics outpatient clinic of the Hospital das Clínicas at Unicamp. Gastrointestinal symptoms were assessed using a validated questionnaire in Portuguese, the CFAbd-Score, to investigate the presence, frequency, and correlation of gastrointestinal manifestations. Data analysis was performed descriptively and inferentially using chi-square tests and Pearson's correlation.

Results: GI manifestations were reported in 53/59 patients. Symptoms of abdominal distension and nausea had a significant positive correlation with abdominal pain. The occurrence of abdominal pain was more frequent in patients experiencing exacerbations, and, although the statistical association was not significant, there was a positive correlation between abdominal pain and respiratory exacerbations.

Conclusion: Gastrointestinal manifestations were reported in approximately 90% of the respondents. The report of abdominal pain was positively correlated to symptoms of abdominal distension, nausea, and respiratory exacerbation. CFAbd-Score worked as a useful tool for assessing GI manifestations in CF patients.

records.title: Effect of metformin on clinical outcomes in adults with cystic fibrosis diabetes (CFD)

person.institution: St Bartholomew's Hospital, Bart's Health NHS Trust, Bart's Adult CF Centre

records.authors_text: L. Alberts1, N. Shafi1, D. Watson1, S. Safavi1
records.affiliations_text: 1St Bartholomew's Hospital, Bart's Health NHS Trust, Bart's Adult CF Centre, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Cystic fibrosis diabetes (CFD) is a common complication of cystic fibrosis (CF), affecting 40-50% of adults with CF (1). Guidelines state: “insulin may not always be the preferred therapy, and consideration should be given to dietary modification and other available anti-diabetic agents” (2). The aim was to assess the impact of metformin on clinical outcomes of adults with CFD, in a single centre.

Method: A retrospective analysis of patients’ data pre- and post-metformin initiation was conducted. Changes in body mass index (BMI), HbA1c, Libre™ time in range (TIR), FEV1 and insulin requirements were evaluated and analysed using paired t-test or Wilcoxon’s signed rank test using SPSS v31.

Results: Twenty-six patients were included (12 male), with average age 33 years (range 18-62). Thirteen were F508del homozygous and 21 on long-term modulator therapy. All were pancreatic insufficient with 19 on insulin at the time of metformin initiation. Metformin dose ranged from 500 mg to 2 g a day, was taken for 9 months on average (range 1.5-31 months) and was well-tolerated.

Parameter (n)Mean/median pre Mean/median postTest significancep-valueBMI kg/m2 (25)24.80 (19.4-34)24.23 (20.1-42.4)Z = -0.970.33HbA1c mmol/mol (24)60 (27-109)56 (26-108)t = 1.210.24Libre™ TIR % (24)64 (15-97)69 (21-99)t = -1.340.20FEV1 % (25)72 (29-100)73 (28-112)t = -0.750.46Basal insulin units/day (16)14.5 (3-60)12 (0-60)Z = -0.590.55

There was a clinically beneficial change in all measured parameters, but these were not statistically significant. Analysis of separate age and BMI categories was not statistically significant either. There was a greater change in HbA1c and TIR when metformin was used as an adjuvant treatment (-9mmol/mol p=0.08, +6% p=0.24) as compared to monotherapy (-2mmol/mol p=0.85, 0% p=0.83).

Conclusion: The main limitation of this study was the small sample size. Nonetheless, it shows a clinical benefit to using metformin in patients with CFD. Future research on longer term effects and clinical outcomes would be useful in larger sample size.

records.title: Changes in fat-soluble vitamin serum concentrations in pediatric patients after introducing cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator modulator therapy – a single center experience

person.department: Cystic Fibrosis Centre Paediatrics and Adult Zagreb

records.authors_text: S. Rupčić1, I.K. Crnogorac2, I. Senečić-Čala2,1, I. Bambir3, L. Omerza3, I. Todorić3, A. Vukić Dugac3,1, D. Tješić - Drinković3
records.affiliations_text: 1School of Medicine, University of Zagreb, Zagreb, Croatia, 2University Hospital Centre Zagreb, Department of Paediatrics, Zagreb, Croatia, 3University Hospital Centre Zagreb, Cystic Fibrosis Centre Paediatrics and Adult Zagreb, Zagreb, Croatia
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a multisystem genetic disorder commonly associated with pancreatic insufficiency and impaired absorption of fat-soluble vitamins. Supplementation is guided by annual measurements. This study evaluated the effect of one year CFTR modulator (CFTRm) therapy on serum levels of vitamins A, D, and E.

Methods: Serum levels of 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D], vitamin A, and vitamin E were measured before initiation of CFTRm therapy (elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor) and after one year. Changes were analyzed using paired-samples t-tests; effect sizes were expressed as Cohen’s d (p<0.05). Statistical analyses were performed using R.

Results: Thirty pediatric patients (7-18 years, median 15) were included. Before initiation of CFTRm therapy, mean serum levels were 81.29 ±28.61 nmol/L for vitamin D (reference value - rv.>75 nmol/L), 1.2±0.43 µmol/L for vitamin A (rv. 1.05-2.80 µmol/L), and 22.91±7.78 µmol/L for vitamin E (rv. 21.8-50.4 µmol/L). After one year of therapy, mean levels for vitamin D were 75.77±24.12 nmol/L, for vitamin A 1.50±0.53 µmol/L and for vitamin E 20.56±6.95 µmol/L. A statistically significant increase in vitamin A levels was observed (t(29)=2.79, p=0.009, Cohen’s d=0.51), while vitamin E concentrations showed a statistically significant decrease (t(29)=-2.42, p=0.022, Cohen’s d=-0.44). No statistically significant change was found for vitamin D (p=0.283). Ultimately, after one year of therapy, the overall number of patients with a deficiency of at least one vitamin remained unchanged, due to a deterioration in vitamin E status, despite an improvement in vitamin A status.

Conclusion: CFTRm therapy was associated with increased serum vitamin A levels, unchanged vitamin D levels, and a redistribution of vitamin E values with a decreased mean after one year. Overall, CFTRm therapy was not associated with a reduced prevalence of fat soluble vitamin deficiencies, potentially due to suboptimal supplementation adherence related to perceived health improvement.

records.title: Appropriateness and acceptability of colonoscopy screening in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF)
records.authors_text: A. Anderson1, J. Catlow1, A. Duffy1, S. Doe1, C. Echevarria1, S.J Bourke1
records.affiliations_text: 1Royal Victoria Infirmary, Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Newcastle upon Tyne, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Because of an increased risk of colonic cancer, colonoscopy screening is recommended for pwCF from the age of 40, and from the age of 30 years post-transplantation. A shared decision approach is advised as pwCF may have other health priorities, complications and co-morbidities. We reviewed the clinical reasons why some pwCF were considered unsuitable for colonoscopy and why some declined the procedure.

Results: Of 366 pwCF at our Centre, 84 fell in the age category for considering screening colonoscopy; 17 (20%) were post lung transplant. Fifteen (18%) pwCF were considered unsuitable for screening colonoscopy for medical reasons (11 had advanced lung disease with mean FEV1 24% predicted; 4 had significant co-morbidities as oesophageal cancer, ischaemic heart or cerebrovascular disease; one was currently pregnant). Four (5%) pwCF were aged over 75 years, above the recommended age in the general population, and 6 (7%) had a CF-related disorder and were not offered colonoscopy. Ten (12%) had already had recent colonoscopy for clinical reasons. Thirty-nine consented to screening colonoscopy although 5 wanted to postpone till next year. Ten declined screening colonoscopy. Reasons for declining colonoscopy included ‘don’t want colonoscopy’, ‘not prepared to take bowel preparation’, ‘not a priority for me’, ‘not key issue at present’, ‘enough medical problems already’, ‘no bowel problems’. To date no patient has been diagnosed with cancer at screening colonoscopy although 2 post-transplant pwCF have previously undergone hemicolectomy for cancer.

Conclusions: Some pwCF are not suitable for screening colonoscopy because of advanced lung disease and co-morbidities. The uptake of screening colonoscopy is good. Other screening methods could be considered to define risk in those who are unsuitable or who decline colonoscopy.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Adequate bowel preparation is critical for effective colorectal polyp and cancer surveillance in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). CF-specific bowel preparation regimens require extended duration and higher cumulative laxative exposure. Real-world preparation quality and protocol standardisation are poorly described. This study aimed to characterise bowel preparation quality across CF centres and evaluate a CF-specific protocol at a single centre.

Methods: A multi-centre retrospective cohort study of pwCF undergoing colonoscopy across three Australian adult CF centres between 2014–2024 was performed. Bowel preparation quality was categorised using the Aronchick scale (excellent, good/satisfactory, fair/adequate, poor/unsatisfactory or unknown) for all procedures. Overall bowel preparation quality was described across centres with pre/post-implementation analysis at a single intervention centre following protocol introduction in 2019, using procedure-level data with patient-level clustering. Pre/post analyses were limited to the intervention centre.

Results: Across all centres, 353 colonoscopies were analysed. Bowel preparation quality was excellent in 15.3%, good/satisfactory in 54.7%, fair/adequate in 13.9%, and poor/unsatisfactory in 13.6%, unknown 2.5%.

At the intervention centre 218 colonoscopies were analysed (48 pre-implementation; 170 post): poor/unsatisfactory preparation decreased from 18.8% (9/48) to 9.0% (15/170) (OR 0.43, 95% CI 0.19–0.99; p = 0.048). Fair/adequate (less than satisfactory) preparation decreased from 29.2% (14/48) to 15.3% (26/170) (OR 0.45, 95% CI 0.22–0.94; p = 0.034).

Conclusion: In adults with CF, bowel preparation quality is variable, with approximately one-quarter of procedures demonstrating less than satisfactory preparation. Implementation of a CF-specific protocol was associated with improved quality, supporting standardised, CF-tailored bowel preparation protocols.

Objectives: Adequate bowel preparation is critical for effective colorectal polyp and cancer surveillance in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). Background: Gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms are common complications of cystic fibrosis (CF), contributing significantly to disease burden and impacting on quality of life. This has led to the development of a CF gastroenterology outpatient clinic within our adult CF service, led by a specialist gastroenterologist and CF dietitian.

Objectives: To describe referral indications, investigations required, and diagnoses made within a specialist CF gastroenterology clinic.

records.title: Dynamics of fibrotic changes in the liver according to transient elastography at the start and after 2 years of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor therapy
records.authors_text: E. Zhekaite1,2, E. Kondratyeva1,2, A. Voronkova1,2, G. Tsurkin1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Research Centre for Medical Genetics, Cystic Fibrosis, Moscow, Russian Federation, 2Research Clinical Institute of Childhood Ministry of Health of the Moscow Region, Moscow, Russian Federation
records.abstract_text:
Hepatic involvement is frequent in patients with cystic fibrosis (CF), with focal biliary cirrhosis being the pathognomonic hepatic manifestation. Transient elastography (TE) (Fibroscan) is a non-invasive, user-friendly and quick technique that provides an objective and reproducible measure of liver stiffness. The aim is to assess the condition of the liver parenchyma according to TE at the start and after 2 years of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) therapy.

Objectives: 24 children with CF (10.0±3.8 years), 8 boys and 16 girls were examined before and after 2 years of ETI therapy.

Methods: In each case, transient elastography measurement was performed immediately after the routine annual ultrasound evaluation of the liver. Sonographic staging of the liver was classified from 1 to 4 by the METAVIR score system. Ten validated TE measurements were performed in each patient with the result expressed in kilopascals (kPa). The median value was considered representative of the elastic modulus of the liver.

Results: Median elasticity in CF patients was significantly higher at the start Me (Q1-Q3) 5.7 (4.7-8.7) kPa than after 2 years of ETI therapy 4.6 (4.0-6.5) (p < 0.001). Among the examined patients, 12 patients had no fibrosis (F0) at the start of therapy, 6 patients had F1, 0 patients had F2, 4 patients had F3, and 2 patients had cirrhosis (F4) by METAVIR. After 2 years of therapy, 19 patients had no fibrosis, 3 patients had F1 fibrosis, 1 child had F2, and 1 patient had cirrhosis (F4).

One 17-year-old female patient, who had been diagnosed with cirrhosis for 6 years and who demonstrated progression of esophageal varices and hypersplenism during 2 years of ETI therapy, significantly reduced TE value from 15 to 7.7 kPa during the third year of therapy.

Conclusion: The obtained results indicate the possibility of a reversible process not only in fibrosis stages 1-2 according to METAVIR, but also in the cirrhosis.

records.title: Analysis of fat-soluble vitamin levels during CFTR modulator therapy
records.authors_text: E. Zhekaite1,2, E. Kondratyeva1,2, A. Voronkova2,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Research Centre for Medical Genetics, Cystic Fibrosis, Moscow , Russian Federation, Russian Federation, 2Research Clinical Institute of Childhood Ministry of Health of the Moscow Region, Moscow, Russian Federation
records.abstract_text:
Patients with cystic fibrosis (CF) have an increased risk of fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, primarily due to malabsorption syndrome and pancreatic insufficiency. Both a deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins and their excess can have a negative impact on health.

The aim of the study was to investigate the effect of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) administration in children with CF on levels of fat-soluble vitamins (FSVs) A, D, E, K.

Objectives: Based on the results of examination of 117 children (9.4±4.6 years).

Methods: Serum vitamin A, E, and K levels were determined before and after 1 year CFTR modulator therapy using HPLC-MS (high-performance liquid chromatography with mass-selective detection), and vitamin D levels were determined using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). All patients were advised to take FSVs from the moment they were diagnosed with CF.

Results: A significant difference was observed in vitamin A and K levels at baseline and after one year of targeted therapy. Vitamin A levels increased from 0.42±0.17 to 0.45±0.18 μg/ml (p=0.010), remaining within the normal range. Vitamin K levels decreased from 0.6±12.4 to 0.59±0.14 ng/ml (p=0.05), also within the normal range. At the start of targeted therapy, 60% of children had normal vitamin D levels, while 40% had deficiency or insufficiency. Low vitamin A levels were established in 20% of patients, normal in 57%. Vitamin E levels were within normal limits in 73% of children, below normal in 2%. An increase in the proportion of children with high levels of vitamins A from 22% to 57% and E from 25% to 42% was observed in those treated with ETI. Normal vitamin D status was established in 52% of patients on targeted therapy.

Conclusion: Treatment with ETI increased the proportion of patients with serum retinol levels above the norm, which can lead to adverse reactions. The study was carried out as part of the research RCIC (122013100175-3).

records.title: Cystic fibrosis and bone mineral density: heterozygous residual function CFTR variant not protective against bone disease
records.authors_text: M. Heching1, A. Lobechov1, L. Slomiansky1, J. Weinberg1, O. Shtraichman1
records.affiliations_text: 1Rabin Medical Center, Pulmonary Department, Petach Tikva, Israel
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Low bone mineral density (BMD) is a common comorbidity in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF), as CFTR dysfunction impairs osteoblastic bone formation. While the "recessive rescue" phenomenon—where a single residual function (RF) variant preserves pancreatic function—is well established, its impact on skeletal health is unclear.

Methods: We retrospectively evaluated adult pwCF at our clinic who completed DEXA scans in the era of highly effective modulator therapy (HEMT). We analyzed BMD at the femoral neck and lumbar spine and stratified pwCF by variant severity: severe/severe (two Class I-III, s/s, n=31), mild/severe (one RF/one Class I-III, m/s, n=37), and mild/mild (two RF, m/m, n=10).

Results: 78 (of 87) adult pwCF completed DEXA scans (mean age 40.2, 45% male, mean FEV1 71%). Mean lumbar Z-score was -0.60; 58% met criteria for osteopenia and 6% for osteoporosis. Age correlated negatively with BMD, with no significant correlation found for gender or vitamin D. m/m pwCF exhibited superior BMD (mean +0.43). In contrast, m/s pwCF had the lowest BMD (mean -1.04, p<0.003 vs m/m) despite having similar age (44 vs 41) and pancreatic function (80% vs 78%) to the m/m group. While HEMT duration trended positively with BMD, it did not normalize outcomes for the m/s group. Notably, despite having preserved pancreatic function and higher BMI (24.8 vs 22.4), the m/s group had lower BMD than the pancreatic-insufficient s/s group (mean -0.84). In particular, pwCF homozygous for Class I (n=10) had greater BMD (mean -0.59) compared to the HEMT-treated m/s group (-1.04).

Conclusion: We observed that the "recessive rescue" phenomenon does not apply to BMD. Carrying a single RF variant fails to protect against bone loss, unlike its protective effect on the pancreas. Clinicians must be vigilant with pwCF carrying a single RF variant, as preserved BMI and pancreatic sufficiency do not imply skeletal protection; these patients represent a vulnerable population for bone disease.

In contrast, m/s pwCF had the lowest BMD (mean -1.04, p<0.003 vs m/m) despite having similar age (44 vs 41) and pancreatic function (80% vs 78%) to the m/m group. While HEMT duration trended positively with BMD, it did not normalize outcomes for the m/s group. Notably, despite having preserved pancreatic function and higher BMI (24.8 vs 22.4), the m/s group had lower BMD than the pancreatic-insufficient s/s group (mean -0.84). In particular, pwCF homozygous for Class I (n=10) had greater BMD (mean -0.59) compared to the HEMT-treated m/s group (-1.04).
Conclusion: We observed that the "recessive rescue" phenomenon does not apply to BMD. Carrying a single RF variant fails to protect against bone loss, unlike its protective effect on the pancreas. Clinicians must be vigilant with pwCF carrying a single RF variant, as preserved BMI and pancreatic sufficiency do not imply skeletal protection; these patients represent a vulnerable population for bone disease.
