records.title: HbA1c-guided use of CGM for CFRD screening: a single-centre service evaluation

person.institution: Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust

records.authors_text: R. Milner1, J. Snowball1, H. Caterson1, M. Matheou2
records.affiliations_text: 1Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, Oxford Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Oxford, United Kingdom, 2Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, Oxford Centre for Diabetes, Endocrinology and Metabolism, Oxford, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Regular screening for cystic fibrosis related diabetes (CFRD) is essential in cystic fibrosis (CF) care. The oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) is the gold standard but is logistically difficult to deliver due to resource constraints. Alternative screening methods include continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) already used locally. The “Cystic Fibrosis–related Diabetes: A First Canadian Clinical Practice Guideline” (2025) recommends an HbA1c-first screening strategy, with OGTT reserved for individuals at higher CFRD risk. This service evaluation assessed CGM-diagnosed CFRD and corresponding HbA1c values to determine whether an HbA1c-first strategy could identify all patients requiring treatment.

Methods: Retrospective data were collected from electronic health records and CGM platforms between January 2024 and December 2025. We included adults without a prior diagnosis of CFRD, who had both a serum HbA1c measurement and a CGM assessment within a six-month interval. Variables collected included HbA1c, % time above target glucose range (3.9–7.8 mmol/L), frequency of glucose excursions >11 mmol/L, CFRD diagnosis based on CGM, and recommended care plans from the diabetes team.

Results: Of 102 patients requiring CFRD screening, 53 had a complete CGM assessment. Based on CGM results, 15 patients were diagnosed with CFRD. Among patients with HbA1c <37 mmol/mol (35/42), five met CGM criteria for CFRD; none required pharmacological treatment and all received dietary advice. Among those with HbA1c ≥37 mmol/mol (18/20), ten met CGM criteria for CFRD; three required medical therapy (insulin or oral agents), while the remainder received dietary advice.

Conclusion: In this cohort, HbA1c would have identified all patients with CFRD requiring medical treatment supporting the feasibility of anHbA1c-first screening strategy for lower-risk patients with targeted CGM use and reducing clinical burden. A patient and multidisciplinary team survey will inform service redesign.

records.title: Intestinal inflammation in pediatric cystic fibrosis - Impact of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor therapy
records.authors_text: C. Sæland1, E. Bakkeheim2, K. Størdal3, K. Solum4, M. Hellan Iversen3, C. Sachs-Strømmen2,4, V. Hovland2,4, A. Wathne2, W. Gjerde4, T. Nyenget5, R.A. Thomassen1, A.C. Brun1, M. Kolsgaard2
records.affiliations_text: 1Oslo University Hospital, Department of Paediatric Medicine, Oslo, Norway, 2Oslo University Hospital, Norwegian Centre for Rare Diseases, unit for pulmonology and cystic fibrosis, Oslo, Norway, 3Oslo University Hospital, Department of Pediatric Research, Oslo, Norway, 4Oslo University Hospital, Children's Department of Allergy and Pulmonary Diseases, Oslo, Norway, 5Oslo University Hospital, Department of Paediatric Medicine, clinical trial unit, Oslo, Norway
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is associated with chronic inflammation affecting both the respiratory and gastrointestinal (GI) tract. CFTR modulators may alter intestinal inflammation, though evidence in young children remains scarce. In this study, we examined changes in three complementary fecal inflammatory markers before and during elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) therapy to explore whether this treatment is associated with reduced intestinal inflammation.

Methods: Fecal samples were collected from 14 children with CF (aged 1.9–6.6 years; all with ≥1 F508del variation; 5 with pancreatic insufficiency) before and ≥6 months after initiation of ETI. The inflammatory markers analyzed were calprotectin (CAL), neopterin (NPT), and myeloperoxidase (MPO), which are markers of neutrophil-driven inflammation, macrophage activation via TNF-γ, and oxidative stress/vasculitis, respectively. Two children were excluded from the calprotectin analyses because of a change in analytical instrument between visit 1 and 2, leaving 12 children for this analysis. We analyzed change from baseline using a paired t-test.

Results: There was a significant reduction in mean (Std. Deviation) NPT from 1355 (777) to 936 (669) nmol/L (p = 0.018). Mean CAL decreased from 240 (429) to 53 (68) mg/kg, and mean MPO from 860 (867) to 408 (605) ng/mL, showing a clear downward trend, even though not statistically significant.

Conclusion: Fecal inflammatory marker levels decreased during ETI therapy, but a statistically significant reduction was only observed for NPT, indicating reduction in macrophage activity. These findings indicate that ETI may reduce intestinal inflammation in young children with CF. Larger studies stratified by pancreatic status are warranted to confirm these results and to further explore the relationship between reduced intestinal inflammation and clinically relevant outcomes, such as GI related quality of life.

records.title: To assess the impact structured Cystic Fibrosis Diabetes (CFD) education sessions have on glycaemic control using HbA1C as a measurement in the adult Cystic Fibrosis (CF) unit in Northern Ireland (NI)

person.title: Dietitian
person.institution: Northern Ireland Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre

records.authors_text: E. Molloy1, O. Holmes1, V. Lynch1, J. Rendall1, A. Nugent1
records.affiliations_text: 1Northern Ireland Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Belfast, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objective: NICE guideline NG17 (2022) recommends that structured education be an integral part of diabetes care. Further research is needed to identify the requirements of structured educational programmes for people with CFD according to CF Trust guidelines (2022). We have created and implemented a structured CFD education programme in the adult CF unit in NI.

Methods: Analysis of electronic care record (ECR) to illustrate most recent HbA1C levels prior to the CFD education sessions. These sessions were presented via Microsoft Teams in a group or on a one-to-one basis as per individual preference, with interaction encouraged. The HbA1C result post education sessions was analysed to help identify changes in glycaemic control.

Results: A total of 50 (53%) adults with CFD participated in the CFD education sessions between December 2020 and December 2025. Twenty-five (50%) people had an improvement in HbA1C post education compared with before education. Three (6%) people maintained their HbA1C level and 17 (34%) showed a deterioration in HbA1C. Post education HbA1C results are pending for 5 (10%) participants. Of those with a deteriorating HbA1C, one (2%) person was non-adherent to treatments, including insulin and 13 (26%) people maintained their HbA1C within target range (NICE NG28 2022).

Conclusion: CFD structured education sessions have identified positive effect on glycaemic control based on HbA1C readings pre and post education. This has supported the roll out of education sessions to the wider adult CFD community in NI. It is important to highlight that Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator (CFTR) modulators were established before pre education HbA1C was recorded.

records.title: Traditional cardiometabolic risk factors trajectories before and after elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor initiation
records.authors_text: H. Girouard1, V. Boudreau1, A. Lavoie2, L. Alexandre-Heymann3, A. Coriati1,4,5
records.affiliations_text: 1Montreal Clinical Research Institute, Montreal, Canada, 2Centre Hospitalier de l'Université de Montréal, Montreal, Canada, 3Université Paris Cité, Paris, France, 4Centre de Recherche CIUSSS Nord-de-l'île-de-Montréal, Montreal, Canada, 5Université de Montréal, Montreal, Canada
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) has demonstrated significant improvements in respiratory function and weight gain among people living with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). Several studies have also shown changes in traditional cardiometabolic risk (CMR) factors. However, these were conducted over short time periods and often without longitudinal pre-ETI clinical measurements. We aimed to compare changes in CMR factors over 3 yrs before and after ETI initiation and identify predictors of post-ETI changes.

Methods: Ongoing systematic bioclinical data collection within the Montreal Cystic Fibrosis Cohort has allowed access to both pre- and post-ETI data in adult pwCF. In our analyses, we included pwCF who initiated ETI prior to 2023 and with pre and post-ETI data available. Mixed effects models were conducted, with both months before and after ETI initiation, sex and age as fixed effects and subject as random effect. Interaction terms were subsequently added.

Results: Sixty participants (median age 36 yrs; 52% female) were included. Glycated haemoglobin (hbA1c) increased pre-ETI (p=0.03) and decreased significantly post-ETI (p<0.001). Inclusion of interaction terms revealed significant interactions between post-ETI hbA1c slope and body mass index <25 kg/m2 (based on first available data during study period) (p=0.04) and between post-ETI slope and hbA1c <5.5% (based on first available data) (p<0.001). Similarly, fructosamine increased pre-ETI (p<0.001) and decreased post-ETI (p<0.001). There was a significant interaction between post-ETI fructosamine slope and pancreatic insufficiency (p=0.03). Systolic blood pressure (BP) and diastolic BP increased pre-ETI (p=0.02 and p<0.01, respectively), but remained stable post-ETI. With interaction terms included, there was a significant interaction between F508del heterozygous and systolic BP slope post-ETI (p=0.04).

Conclusion: Pre-treatment clinical variables likely have an impact on CMR factors post-ETI initiation.

records.title: Dynamics of pancreatic function in CFTR modulator therapy: a single-centre analysis of 132 patients

person.department: Department of Child and Adolescent Health, Paediatrics III

records.authors_text: D. Appelt1, J. Eder2, K. Niedermayr2, H. Ellemunter3, T. Fuchs1
records.affiliations_text: 1Medical University of Innsbruck, Department of Child and Adolescent Health, Paediatrics III, Innsbruck, Austria, 2Tirol Kliniken, Department of Child and Adolescent Health, Paediatrics III, Innsbruck, Austria, 3Cystic Fibrosis Centre Innsbruck, Medical Research Affiliate, Innsbruck, Austria
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Pancreatic insufficiency (PI) is a characteristic of cystic fibrosis (CF) and traditionally considered irreversible once established. Cystic fibrosis transmembrane regulator (CFTR) modulator therapies have prompted reconsideration of this assumption, as emerging reports suggest potential improvement in exocrine pancreatic function. However, natural fluctuation of faecal elastase (FE) concentrations has also been observed in people with CF (pwCF), even without targeted treatment. We present a single-centre analysis evaluating longitudinal FE measurements in patients receiving CFTR modulators.

Methods: We retrospectively analysed 2203 FE values in pwCF 5 years before and during CFTR modulator initiation. FE results were categorised as <100 µg/g, 100–200 µg/g, and >200 µg/g to define pancreatic status. pwCF were classified as sustained pancreatic insufficient (PI), pancreatic sufficient (PS), or undulating if at least one FE value was <200µg/g and one >16µg/g (lower level of detection in local lab).

Results: Among 132 pwCF, 14 (10.6%) had undulating FE values during CFTR modulator therapy, while 8 (6.1%) remained PS and 110 (83.3%) persistently PI. In the undulating group, 8 pwCF (57.1%) became PS, enabling enzyme dose reduction or discontinuation in most cases. Median age in this subgroup was 5.2 years (range 0.2-67.4 years). Two pwCF received ivacaftor and 12 elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI); 5 had prior lumacaftor/ivacaftor exposure before commencing ETI.

Conclusion: Our findings demonstrate that while most pwCF maintain persistent PI under CFTR modulator therapy, a subset of predominantly younger children may exhibit fluctuation or recovery in pancreatic exocrine function, with a trend to becoming PS. These findings suggest that, beyond natural variability of pancreatic status, improvement can occur under modulator therapy. Regular FE monitoring is recommended, particularly in children, or in adults with unstable FE prior to CFTR modulator initiation.

Objectives: Pancreatic insufficiency (PI) is a characteristic of cystic fibrosis (CF) and traditionally considered irreversible once established. Cystic fibrosis transmembrane regulator (CFTR) modulator therapies have prompted reconsideration of this assumption, as emerging reports suggest potential improvement in exocrine pancreatic function. However, natural fluctuation of faecal elastase (FE) concentrations has also been observed in people with CF (pwCF), even without targeted treatment. We present a single-centre analysis evaluating longitudinal FE measurements in patients receiving CFTR modulators.
Methods: We retrospectively analysed 2203 FE values in pwCF 5 years before and during CFTR modulator initiation. FE results were categorised as <100 µg/g, 100–200 µg/g, and >200 µg/g to define pancreatic status. pwCF were classified as sustained pancreatic insufficient (PI), pancreatic sufficient (PS), or undulating if at least one FE value was <200µg/g and one >16µg/g (lower level of detection in local lab).

In the undulating group, 8 pwCF (57.1%) became PS, enabling enzyme dose reduction or discontinuation in most cases. Median age in this subgroup was 5.2 years (range 0.2-67.4 years). Two pwCF received ivacaftor and 12 elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI); 5 had prior lumacaftor/ivacaftor exposure before commencing ETI.
Conclusion: Our findings demonstrate that while most pwCF maintain persistent PI under CFTR modulator therapy, a subset of predominantly younger children may exhibit fluctuation or recovery in pancreatic exocrine function, with a trend to becoming PS. These findings suggest that, beyond natural variability of pancreatic status, improvement can occur under modulator therapy. Regular FE monitoring is recommended, particularly in children, or in adults with unstable FE prior to CFTR modulator initiation.

records.title: Trends in emergency department visits and hospitalizations for gastrointestinal complications in pediatric patients with cystic fibrosis pre and post modulator therapy: a multicenter analysis
records.authors_text: C. Ekezie1, C. Mack1, N. Antos1, K. Yan1, L. Zhang1, J. Morrison2, R. Khalaf3
records.affiliations_text: 1Medical College of Wisconsin, Department of Pediatrics, Milwaukee, United States, 2Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, Department of Pediatrics, St Petersburg, United States, 3University of South Florida Morsani College of Medicine, Tampa, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Highly effective modulator therapy (HEMT) has significantly improved pulmonary outcomes in pediatric patients with cystic fibrosis (PwCF), but its effect on gastrointestinal complications remains unclear. This study aims to evaluate changes in emergency department (ED) visits and hospitalizations for constipation and intestinal obstruction before and after the introduction of HEMT.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the Pediatric Health Information System (PHIS®) database, including PwCF aged 2–18 years during the pre-HEMT (2014–2018) and post-HEMT (2020–2024) eras. ED visits and hospitalizations with primary or secondary diagnoses of constipation or intestinal obstruction were analyzed. Statistical comparisons were performed using Mann–Whitney Wilcoxon, chi-square, and Fisher’s exact tests, with significance defined as p < 0.05.

Results: A total of 483 ED visits and 4,165 hospitalizations were identified. Significant demographic differences were observed between cohorts. ED visits for constipation declined in the post-HEMT era (295 pre vs. 188 post; p = 0.012), as did hospitalizations (2,631 vs. 1,534; p = 0.012). Encounters with constipation as the primary diagnosis also decreased significantly in both ED visits (252 vs. 152; p = 0.012) and hospitalizations (297 vs. 159; p = 0.012). ED visits and hospitalizations for intestinal obstruction declined post-HEMT, with hospitalizations reaching statistical significance (131 vs. 42; p = 0.047).

Conclusion: HEMT is associated with significant reductions in ED visits and hospitalizations for constipation and intestinal obstruction among pediatric PwCF, suggesting beneficial gastrointestinal effects beyond pulmonary outcomes but may also warrant further investigation into evolving management patterns.

records.title: Frequency of liver involvement and its association with genotype in patients with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: F. Gafarova1, C.A. Yıldız1, Ş. Karabulut1, N.M. Çakar1, E.E. Baysal1, F. Özdemircioğlu1, M.M. Akkitap Yiğit1, B. Özgünay1, E. Uğurlu1, G. Alışbeyli1, C. Yılmaz Yeğit1, P. Ergenekon1, D. Kocakaya2, E. Erdem Eralp1, Y. Gökdemir1, F. Karakoç1, B. Karadağ1
records.affiliations_text: 1Marmara University, Division of Pediatric Pulmonology, Istanbul, Turkey, 2Marmara University, Division of Pulmonology, Istanbul, Turkey
records.abstract_text:
Background: Liver disease is a relevant complication of cystic fibrosis (CF); however, the association between CFTR genotype and liver involvement remains unclear. This study evaluated the frequency of liver involvement in CF patients and its relationship with genotype using both classical and functional protein-based classifications.

Methods: A total of 457 patients with genetically confirmed CF were included. Liver involvement was classified as cystic fibrosis-related liver disease (CFLD) or non-cirrhotic hepatobiliary involvement. Genotype–phenotype associations were first analysed according to classical CFTR variant classes. Variants were then reclassified based on functional impact as protein-truncating variants (PTV) or non-PTV, and patients were grouped as PTV/PTV, PTV/non-PTV or non-PTV/non-PTV. Clinical and demographic variables were analysed statistically.

Results: Liver involvement was present in 12.9% (n=59) of patients, most commonly non-cirrhotic disease (10.1%). No association was observed with classical CFTR variant classes (p>0.05). Functional genotype analysis (n=455) showed liver involvement was significantly more frequent in the PTV/PTV group compared with the PTV/non-PTV and non-PTV/non-PTV groups (p=0.0038). Patients with liver involvement were diagnosed at a younger age, were more often male and had lower height Z-scores.

Conclusion: While classical CFTR classification was not associated with liver involvement, functional genotype analysis demonstrated a strong association between the PTV/PTV genotype and hepatobiliary disease. Protein-level classification may better identify CF patients at risk and support closer clinical monitoring.

records.title: Prolonged neonatal jaundice in infants with cystic fibrosis: A retrospective cohort study
records.authors_text: N. Metin Cakar1, C.A. Yıldız1, E.E. Baysal1, F. Özdemircioğlu1, B. Özgünay1, E. Uğurlu1, G. Alışbeyli1, F. Qafarova1, Ş. Bektaş1, G. Taştan2, B. Uzunoğlu2, Ş. Karabulut1, C. Yılmaz Yeğit1, A.P. Ergenekon1, Y. Gökdemir1, E. Erdem Eralp1, B. Karadağ1
records.affiliations_text: 1Marmara University, Division of Paediatric Pulmonology, Istanbul, Turkey, 2Marmara University, Selim Coremen Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Istanbul, Turkey
records.abstract_text:
Background: Neonatal jaundice is common and usually self-limiting; however, persistence may indicate an underlying disorder, including cystic fibrosis, whose role in prolonged jaundice remains unclear.

Objectives: To evaluate the frequency of neonatal and prolonged jaundice in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) and to assess whether prolonged jaundice should be considered a typical early manifestation of the disease.

Methods: We retrospectively compared 298 individuals with cystic fibrosis and 251 healthy children with regard to neonatal jaundice. Prolonged jaundice was defined as lasting more than 14 days in term infants and more than 21 days in preterm infants. CF-related clinical data were obtained from medical records and analysed using appropriate statistical methods.

Results: Infants with cystic fibrosis demonstrated lower rates of neonatal jaundice than healthy controls (Table 1). Neonatal jaundice was significantly less frequent in pwCF compared with controls (30.5% vs 55.0%, p<0.05). Prolonged jaundice occurred in 7.0% of pwCF and 19.1% of controls (p<0.05), while jaundice persisting beyond one month was also less common in pwCF (3.4% vs 14.3%, p<0.05). The median duration of jaundice was shorter in pwCF (0 days [IQR 4]) than in controls (4 days [IQR 10], p<0.05). Phototherapy rates were comparable between groups. No association was observed between CFTR genotype and jaundice-related outcomes, whereas pancreatic insufficiency showed a clear genotype association.

records.title: Changes in pancreatic function and enzyme requirements in children with cystic fibrosis treated with CFTR modulators

person.title: Dr
person.institution: Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust, Royal Manchester Childrens Hospital (Wythenshawe)

records.authors_text: D. Poulton1, J. Watkinson1, K. Barker1, N. Rao1
records.affiliations_text: 1Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust, Royal Manchester Childrens Hospital (Wythenshawe), Paediatrics, Manchester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: CFTR modulator therapy has been associated with improvements in pancreatic function in some children with cystic fibrosis (CF). This study evaluates changes in pancreatic status and pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) requirements following initiation of CFTR modulators.

Methods: A retrospective review was conducted of 15 children with CF aged 0–16 years (10 male, 4 female). Pancreatic status, CFTR modulator use, PERT requirements (lipase units/kg/day), and faecal elastase (FE) were assessed. Twelve patients were receiving CFTR modulators (9 elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor [ETI], 3 lumacaftor/ivacaftor [Orkambi]); three were not on modulators.

Results: At diagnosis, 11/15 patients were pancreatic insufficient (PI) and 4 were pancreatic sufficient (PS). Of the 12 patients on CFTR modulators, 11 were PI at diagnosis. Among those treated with ETI (n=9), one was PS at baseline; six remained PI; and two converted from PI to PS and discontinued PERT. Overall, 2/11 (18%) PI patients became PS, both in the younger age group.

Among six patients assessed for changes in PERT dosing, five demonstrated a 20–48% reduction in lipase requirement per kg body weight per day, while one patient had a 44% increase. Repeat FE measurements in five of six patients continued to show severe pancreatic insufficiency (<5, <28, <15, <15, <8 µg/g), with no significant increase observed.

Conclusion: Pancreatic sufficiency developed in 18% of pancreatic-insufficient children treated with CFTR modulators, consistent with published data (~28%), particularly in younger patients. Although faecal elastase remained low, a clinically significant reduction in PERT requirements was observed in most patients, suggesting improved pancreatic function not fully captured by FE measurements.

records.title: Developing CF-specific diabetes education: insights from a patient involvement group
records.authors_text: H. Winterbottom1, A. Brennan1, L. Kinsey1, F. Lewis1
records.affiliations_text: 1Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust, Manchester Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Manchester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Despite recommendation in national guidance, there is no structured education for people with cystic fibrosis related diabetes (CFRD). A patient discussion group was undertaken to explore what additional education formats and content are valued alongside existing CF-specific one-to-one (1:1) education clinic to inform development of supplementary.

Method: Participants were recruited in CF clinics. Virtual focus group was facilitated by a CF Diabetes Nurse and CF Dietitian exploring five domains: format, content, peer support, family involvement and accessibility. Transcripts were analysed thematically using Copilot-assisted analysis with manual sense-checking.

Results: Seven participants (25–52 years; 57% female), with a mean CFRD duration of 10 years (range 1–23). Six used insulin; one managed diabetes with diet and lifestyle. All were on elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor.

Participants valued continued access to CF-specific one-to-one education, particularly for those with long-standing or complex CFRD. Short (5–10 minute), practical, on-demand videos were favoured to address specific issues or revisit information but were viewed as a supplement rather than a replacement for personalised care. Clear visuals, concise summaries, optional subtitles and practical tools were preferred; quizzes were unpopular. Topics of interest included long-term complications, future treatments, carbohydrate awareness, exercise, technology, stress management. Participants strongly emphasised the need for CF-specific content. Peer support was considered optional. Simple family resources were welcomed. A single platform for accessibility was considered essential.

Conclusion: This small, self-selecting group with experience of personalised CFRD care, valued ongoing CF-specific one-to-one education. Supplementary video-based resources were viewed as useful adjuncts to clinical support, rather than alternatives. These findings will inform co-design of our CFRD education resources.

records.title: Effectiveness of bowel preparation for colonoscopy in people with cystic fibrosis after lung transplantation
records.authors_text: A. Brennan1
records.affiliations_text: 1Manchester University Foundation Trust, Manchester Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Manchester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: People with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) are at increased risk of colorectal cancer (CRC) with risk increasing following lung transplantation (LT). The Cystic Fibrosis Foundation recommends colonoscopy-based CRC screening with intensive bowel preparation. Altered gastrointestinal physiology and treatment-related factors may reduce bowel preparation quality after LT. Data on bowel preparation effectiveness in post-LT pwCF are limited.

Methods: We evaluated bowel preparation quality in our CRC screening protocol for post–LT pwCF using the Boston Bowel Preparation Scale (BBPS) (scores ≥6 adequate) plus subjective assessment by the endoscopist. Extended CF-specific bowel preparation regimen comprised a low-residue diet for 3 days, followed by polyethylene glycol 2 sachets BD for 3 days (6 washes), and senna 15 mg the night before colonoscopy. Preparation adequacy and need for repeat colonoscopy due to poor preparation were assessed.

Results: 18 colonoscopies were performed in 15 post–lung transplant pwCF. A repeat colonoscopy in pwCF with an initial BBPS 1 was excluded from analysis as a further intensified regime was prescribed and results not comparable. BBPS was documented 14 of 17 included studies. Mean BBPS was 6.2 (SD 2.0). In one procedure preparation was described as poor where BBPS was not recorded. Overall, 70.6% achieved adequate preparation. Repeat colonoscopy due to inadequate preparation was required in 2 patients (11%).

Conclusion: In the general population inadequate bowel preparation is reported in approximately 20-25% colonoscopies. In this cohort of post-LT pwCF inadequate preparation occurred in approximately 30% of procedures despite use of an extended CF-specific bowel preparation regime. Nevertheless, acceptable colonoscopy quality was achieved with extended bowel preparation in the majority of cases which highlights the importance of tailored bowel preparation strategies to prevent missed polyps and repeat procedures in this high-risk group.

person.title: Doctor
person.biography:
Dr Amanda Brennan was awarded undergraduate degrees in Medical Science and Medicine&Surgery from the University of Nottingham, UK. She completed her medical training in London specialising in care of patients with Cystic Fibrosis at the Royal Brompton Hospital under the tutelage of Professors Hodson and Geddes. She was awarded the first Cystic Fibrosis Trust Fellowship in the UK which was designed to enhance the training of the future CF consultants. In the early 2000’s, when understanding of the cause for pulmonary decline in people with Cystic Fibrosis Related diabetes was poorly understood, her research provided evidence that airway glucose increases as blood glucose rises and promotes the growth of respiratory pathogens. Dr Brennan is a Consultant at the Manchester Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, UK. She has led the development of the Cystic Fibrosis Related Diabetes service in Manchester since 2009 and established a CF diabetes MDT service  alongside specialist dietitians, nurses and diabetologists, and ensured the rapid introduction of technologies and therapies for evaluating, monitoring and managing glucose dysregulation into the clinic setting. She also developed the first dedicated post-transplant CF and diabetes service in the UK to improve post-transplant outcomes, which has provided useful insights in developing national guidelines with the UK Cystic Fibrosis Medical Association Lung Transplant Working Group.
With Professor Scott Blackman, Dr Brennan co-edited the State of the Art supplement Endocrinology in Cystic Fibrosis in the Journal of Cystic Fibrosis which recruited authors internationally to summarize the optimal evaluation and management of endocrinology issues.

records.title: Colonic polyp burden after lung transplantation in people with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: A. Brennan1
records.affiliations_text: 1Manchester University Foundation Trust, Manchester Adult Cystic Fibrosis Center, Manchester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: In people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) post lung transplant (LT) the risk of colorectal neoplasia is 25-30 times the risk of the general population, likely due to immunosuppression and accelerated adenoma formation. However limited data describe the prevalence, multiplicity, and histological characteristics of colonic polyps in post-LT pwCF.

Methods: We retrospectively reviewed colonoscopy findings in post-LT pwCF managed at a large adult CF center. Indications included CRC surveillance and symptom-driven assessment. Outcomes included polyp detection rate, number of polyps per patient, and histological features. Findings were interpreted in the context of published CF screening cohorts.

Results: Nineteen post-LT pwCF were identified who were eligible for CRC; 15 (79%) underwent colonoscopy, 2 declined investigation, 2 were deemed unsuitable due to co-morbidities. A total of 18 procedures were performed including 2 repeat surveillance examinations. Eleven colonoscopies were performed for CRC screening and 7 for symptomatic indications. Median age at colonoscopy was 37 years (range 27–55).

Twelve polyps were detected in 6/15 patients (40%). Three patients had a single polyp and 3 had multiple polyps. 5 polyps were right-sided, 3 transverse colon and 4 left-sided. Tubular adenoma was the most common histological finding among resected polyps (8/10 cases). Median age of first adenoma detection was 35.5 years (range 30-46 years). No high-grade dysplasia or malignancy was detected.

Conclusion: Forty percent of post-LT pwCF undergoing colonoscopy had colonic polyps detected, often adenomatous and occasionally multiple. The adenoma detection rate was 33%. This is comparable to data from CF Foundation where 41.1% screened post-LT pwCF had adenomatous polyps detected. These results confirm a potential neoplastic burden several years after transplantation and support early, intensive, and ongoing colonoscopic surveillance in lung transplant recipients with CF.

records.title: HbA1c in the diagnosis of CFRD: potential for undetected cases
records.authors_text: F. Lewis1, P. Barry1, S. Punt1, A. Brennan1
records.affiliations_text: 1Manchester NHS Foundation Trust, Manchester Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Manchester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objective: With increasing life-expectancy, prompt diagnosis of CFRD is important to prevent long duration of untreated hyperglycaemia which can lead to microvascular and macrovascular disease. UK guidelines recommend OGTT as gold standard with CGM as a supported screening tool. Canadian guidelines use a two-step approach from age 10 with HbA1c as the initial screen and OGTT reserved for HbA1c 37–48 mmol/mol. We assessed whether this strategy could delay CFRD diagnosis.

Method: We retrospectively reviewed adults diagnosed with CFRD over 4 years using OGTT (0,1,2h) plus CGM analysed with Brompton criteria. HbA1c at diagnosis was recorded to determine eligibility under Canadian guidelines. Outcomes included initiation of glucose-lowering therapy and evidence of microvascular complications.

Results: 36 individuals were diagnosed with CFRD using OGTT plus CGM. 55.6% had HbA1c <37 mmol/mol and 44.4% ≥37 mmol/mol at diagnosis, meaning 55.6% would not have progressed to OGTT under Canadian guidance. None had diagnostic OGTT results at the time of testing. Patients with HbA1c ≥37 mmol/mol were more likely to commence medication (70% vs 15%; OR 13.2, p=0.005). Microvascular complications were uncommon.

Conclusion: Reliance on HbA1c as the initial screening test would have delayed CFRD diagnosis in over half of these individuals. Our findings highlight discordance between HbA1c and CGM metrics in CFRD, where HbA1c frequently underestimates glycaemic exposure. These data support the use of CGM for early detection and clinical decision-making. They also raise concerns about the sensitivity of HbA1c-based screening and highlight the value of broader CGM use to identify dysglycaemia and prevent treatment delays.

Although microvascular complications were uncommon in both groups, reliance on the Canadian approach may delay identification of early microvascular changes. Earlier and tighter glycaemic control substantially lowers microvascular risk.

Conclusion: Reliance on HbA1c as the initial screening test would have delayed CFRD diagnosis in over half of these individuals. records.title: PwCF satisfaction of Hybrid Closed Loop insulin delivery system for CFRD management
records.authors_text: V. Jackson1, R. White1, A. Ochota1, D. Nazareth1
records.affiliations_text: 1Liverpool Heart and Chest Hospital, Liverpool, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: Cystic Fibrosis Related Diabetes (CFRD) is a common complication of CF, with treatment options including oral medication, insulin injections and Continuous Subcutaneous Insulin Infusion (CSII). Hybrid Closed Loop (HCL) CSII has recently become available in the UK, with evidence of improved glycaemic control and quality of life. At our large adult CF centre (n=420), 22 people with CF (pwCF) [13 male, mean age 37 years)] are using HCL; we evaluated their experience of transitioning from standard CSII to HCL.

Method: An online anonymous survey was sent to 22 pwCF using HCL (13 male, mean age 36.7 years), with a 73% (n=16) response rate. The survey assessed treatment burden, glucose control and satisfaction, and included free‑text questions about the transition to HCL.

Results: All respondents agreed or strongly agreed that they were happy with glucose control on HCL. 75% agreed or strongly agreed that they spent less time managing CFRD and were less worried about their control on HCL. 94% would recommend HCL to others. Respondents found the transition easy, largely because they were already experienced with CSII, and valued support from the CFRD multidisciplinary team.

Conclusion: Overall, reported outcomes show a strongly positive experience of transitioning from standard CSII to HCL in this cohort. We are working with our people with CF to increase uptake of HCL therapy.

records.title: Is there a role for C-peptide in the management of cystic fibrosis diabetes?
records.authors_text: A. Ochota1, L. Rossiter2, J. Daniels3, V. Jackson3, R. White1
records.affiliations_text: 1Liverpool Heart and Chest Hospital, Dietitian Department, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 2Liverpool Heart and Chest Hospital, Respiratory Medicine, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 3Liverpool Heart and Chest Hospital, Cystic Fibrosis Nursing, Liverpool, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Measurement of C-peptide can be used to assess endogenous insulin secretion and extent of residual beta-cell secretion in diabetes. It has been used to identify diabetes type and guide suitable treatment options with non-CF populations, reducing unnecessary insulin therapy and episodes of hypoglycaemia. Little is known about its use in cystic fibrosis diabetes (CFD). We investigated C-peptide levels in our adult CF cohort and its association with treatment management of CFD.

Methods: Ninety-six pwCF (mean age 35.2years [SD 11.8], 42% female) had a non-fasting C-peptide test alongside their routine annual screen. Clinical thresholds for serum C-peptide were extrapolated from type-1 diabetes with C peptide <200 pmol/L indicating insulin deficiency, ≥600 pmol/L suggesting preserved endogenous insulin secretion and >900 pmol/L significant insulin resistance. 37 patients had their diabetic treatment reviewed, as part of routine clinical care, and C-peptide levels were subsequently compared for these treatment groups.

Results: 9.3% patients had C-peptide <200 pmol/L, 41.2% ≥200-600 pmol/L, 17.5% ≥600 pmol/L with 32% >900 pmol/L, and insulin treatment was independently used in 100%, 55%, 36% and 25% patients respectively. C-peptide was lowest in insulin-treated patients (median 155.5 pmol/L), while Non-CFRD (851 pmol/L), Sitagliptin (911 pmol/L), and Sitagliptin + Insulin (667 pmol/L) groups had higher levels (H = 25.41, p< 0.0001). Patients with C-peptide <600 pmol/L were three times more likely to require insulin (OR 3.38, 95% CI 1.34–8.62, P=0.004–0.008) and had higher HbA1c than those with C-peptide >600 pmol/L (median 47 vs 41, P=0.042).

Conclusion: C-peptide is a useful marker, alongside other glycaemic parameters, to identify pwCF at risk of CFD, particularly those likely to require insulin. However, further studies are needed to clarify its role in assessing insulin resistance and guiding individualized treatment strategies.

records.title: Long-term trajectories of bone health in the CFTR modulator era
records.authors_text: A. Ochota1, F. Frost2
records.affiliations_text: 1Liverpool Heart and Chest Hospital, Dietitian Department, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 2Liverpool Heart and Chest Hospital, Respiratory Medicine, Liverpool, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: CF related bone disease is a significant comorbidity amongst adult patients with CF. This may prove more problematic with increased life expectancy and additional effects of aging. Pulmonary and nutritional complications have shown substantial improvement with CFTR modulators but the effect on bone health remains unclear. We reviewed the progression of bone density, alongside clinical parameters, in adults with CF following introduction of Elexacaftor/Tezacaftor/Ivacaftor (ETI) therapy.

Methods: Retrospective longitudinal data was collated for consecutive patients undergoing routine dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scans at our large adult CF centre. Participants with DEXA at 3 time points (baseline, pre-ETI and ≥2 years post-ETI initiation) were included. Trajectories over time and multivariable logistic regression for factors associated with increased bone mineral density (BMD) loss were explored.

Results: In total we included 252 scan from 58 pwCF (mean age 28.6 years [SD 9.1], 38% female. Pre-ETI decline in femoral BMD was observed (0.96 to 0.92 p=0.001) and this decline continued post ETI (p<0.05). Consequently, proportion of pwCF with osteoporosis increased post-ETI. Conversely, no significant change in spinal BMD or Z-scores were seen in the pre-ETI or post- ETI periods (p>0.05). Multivariable logistic regression identified chronic steroid use OR [95%CI] 96 [2-1949], p<0.001 and male sex OR 0.11 [0.005 to 0.72] as factors associated with differential BMD loss.

Conclusion: Loss of femoral BMD in CF is not slowed or reversed by ETI use in the short term. Our data suggest classical risk factors for low BMD in CF (steroid use and male sex) persist in the ETI era. Taken together, these results suggest ongoing identification and monitoring of BMD is vital in an ageing CF population.

records.title: Integrating elastography into annual clinical assessments for adults with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: H. Saumtally1,2, I. Clifton1,2, D. Shimmin1, A. Sawant1, G. Spoletini1, A. Smyth3,4, D. Peckham1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Leeds Teaching Hospitals Trust, Leeds Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Leeds, United Kingdom, 2University of Leeds, Leeds Institute of Medical Research, Leeds, United Kingdom, 3Queen’s University Belfast, School of Medicine, Dentistry and Biomedical Sciences,, Belfast, United Kingdom, 4NIHR Nottingham Biomedical Research Centre, Nottingham, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To describe our experience of integrating Vibration Controlled Transient Elastography (VCTE) into the CF annual clinical assessment pathway.

Background: CF-related liver disease (CFLD) remains a major cause of mortality in pwCF. However, progression of CFLD remains poorly understood, with investigations such as ultrasonography and liver function often being the mainstay of monitoring. The advent of non-invasive VCTE provides measures of steatosis (controlled Attenuation Parameter (CAP)), and liver stiffness, both of which have been validated in non-CF liver disease.

Methods: Three respiratory physicians at the Leeds Adult CF Unit were formally trained and certified in undertaking VCTE using Fibroscan®. Patients were fasted prior to annual assessment bloods and scan. A retrospective review of the first eight months of VCTE testing was undertaken. A cut-off of 288 dB/m and 7.0 kPa was used to indicate steatosis and significant fibrosis respectively.

Results: Eighty-nine scans were undertaken (53 male, Median age 36.0 years, range of 18-75) with a median BMI of 24.0 [IQR 5.3] kg/m2. The median CAP score was 204 [IQR 68] dB/m and median liver stiffness was 4.6 [IQR 1.9] kPa. 10/89 (11.2%) and 9/89 (10.1%) were found to have steatosis and significant fibrosis respectively.

Conclusion: VCTE is an operator-dependent, non-invasive scan which has a substantial potential in the monitoring of CFLD during routine CF outpatient appointments. Further analysis is ongoing to correlate the above findings with respect to more conventional biomarkers.

Results: Eighty-nine scans were undertaken (53 male, Median age 36.0 years, range of 18-75) with a median BMI of 24.0 [IQR 5.3] kg/m2. The median CAP score was 204 [IQR 68] dB/m and median liver stiffness was 4.6 [IQR 1.9] kPa. 10/89 (11.2%) and 9/89 (10.1%) were found to have steatosis and significant fibrosis respectively.
Conclusion: VCTE is an operator-dependent, non-invasive scan which has a substantial potential in the monitoring of CFLD during routine CF outpatient appointments. Further analysis is ongoing to correlate the above findings with respect to more conventional biomarkers.

records.title: Assessment of uptake and barriers to bowel cancer screening in patients with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: J. Kane1, B. Hayee1, M. Waller1, K.-L. Watson1
records.affiliations_text: 1King's College Hospital NHS Trust, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: People with cystic fibrosis (CF) have an increased incidence of colorectal cancer (CRC). Screening colonoscopies are currently the gold-standard screening test. Screening is commonly offered from 40yr in the UK, local practice is to offer screening from 30yr. We audited how many eligible patients at our centre had been offered screening, the proportion of patients undergoing screening, and reasons for patients declining screening.

Methods: Audit of clinical notes (2017-2025) of CF patients ≥30yr at a single UK adult CF centre. The number of patients offered screening, completing screening, and declining screening were recorded. A sample of patients who did not consent to referral were asked why.

Results: From 163 eligible patients, 120 (73.6%) were offered screening: 77 (64.2%) consented, 31 (25.8%) deferred a decision to a later date, 9 (7.5%) declined referral, 3 (2.5%) patients declining repeat screening. For those asked about barriers to consenting, common themes were low levels of concern related to CRC screening or concerns about the procedure itself.

Conclusion: CRC screening uptake was comparable to other national screening programmes.

The audit highlighted that 26.4% were not offered screening: most had recently turned 30, others were new to the service or patients with limited engagement. To address this, a section on screening has been added to the review proforma, these patients should be offered colonoscopy at their next review. Additionally, opportunities with less engaged patients must be utilised.

For those who deferred the decision to a later date, documentation on how these patients will be followed up is required as it was lacking.

The barriers to consenting identified that education on the importance of screening and the procedure is vital.

We will repeat this audit to reassess screening uptake following these interventions.

records.title: Central precocious puberty in cystic fibrosis: an uncommon finding raising questions in the CFTR modulator era

person.title: paediatric pulmonologist
person.institution: Hospital del Torax Antonio. A. Cetrangolo

records.authors_text: M.V. Arenal1, M.I. Nabais Robalo1, N. Biancofiore2, M.F. Bernatene1, C. Venialgo1
records.affiliations_text: 1Hospital del Torax Antonio. A. Cetrangolo, Cystic Fibrosis, Vicente Lopez, Argentina, 2Sanatorio Anchorena San Martin, Endocrinology, San Martin, Argentina
records.abstract_text:
Cystic fibrosis (CF) has been associated with delayed puberty, mainly related to malnutrition, respiratory disease severity, and metabolic comorbidities. Over recent decades, improvements in comprehensive care and the introduction of CFTR modulators have allowed pubertal progression in many patients to more closely resemble that of the general population. However, central precocious puberty remains an exceptionally rare finding in this population, with limited available evidence and a lack of studies specifically evaluating its association with CF or CFTR modulator therapy.

Case report: 9 year old female patient with a neonatal diagnosis of CF (homozygous F508del), pancreatic insufficiency, and moderate respiratory disease. She initiated lumacaftor/ivacaftor therapy in 2019 and was transitioned to elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor in 2022. Atelectasis and bronchiectasis in the middle lobe. Chronic infection by Pseudomonas aeruginosa from the first year of life until 2021.FEV1 values at 95%. Body mass index in the 85-90th percentile. At 7 years of age, she developed progressive bilateral thelarche, increased growth velocity, and pubertal gonadotropin levels. Bone age was advanced compared with chronological age, and imaging studies revealed no pathological findings. Treatment with gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) analogues was initiated, resulting in slowing of pubertal progression and preservation of growth potential.

Conclusion: The existing literature primarily describes delayed puberty in patients with CF, and there are no systematic studies or case series addressing precocious puberty in this population or its potential association with CFTR modulator therapy. Although this case does not allow causal inference, it highlights a significant knowledge gap and underscores the need for prospective studies to evaluate the impact of nutritional status, pulmonary function, and emerging therapies on pubertal development in individuals with CF.
records.conclusion: The existing literature primarily describes delayed puberty in patients with CF, and there are no systematic studies or case series addressing precocious puberty in this population or its potential association with CFTR modulator therapy. Although this case does not allow causal inference, it highlights a significant knowledge gap and underscores the need for prospective studies to evaluate the impact of nutritional status, pulmonary function, and emerging therapies on pubertal development in individuals with CF.

records.title: Modified, activated and natural clinoptilolite might influence adsorption capacity and anti-inflammatory effect on the intestinal mucosa in CF
records.authors_text: C. Schwarz1,2, L.M. Bechinger1,2, J.G. Mainz3,4
records.affiliations_text: 1HMU University Potsdam, Internal Medicine, Potsdam, Germany, 2Clinic Ernst von Bergmann, CF Center, Potsdam, Germany, 3Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Brandenburg Medical School (MHB) University, Klinikum Westbrandenburgvel, Germany, Brandenburg and der Havel, Germany, 4Faculty of Health Sciences, Joint Faculty of the Brandenburg University of Technology Cottbus-Senftenberg, The Brandenburg Medical School Theodor Fontane and the University of Potsdam, Brandenburg an der Havel, Germany
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: TOXAPREVENT® MEDI contains the active ingredient MANC® (modified, activated, natural clinoptilolite), which selectively binds harmful substances such as histamine, ammonium, heavy metals and mycotoxins in the gastrointestinal tract and can remove them from the body – without depriving it of nutrients. The combination of adsorption capacity and anti-inflammatory effect on the intestinal mucosa could be particularly beneficial for cystic fibrosis patients. Therefore, we evaluated the use of MANC® in people with CF (pwCF) who received the standard therapy in terms of their gastrointestinal complaints and disease.

Methods: PwCF who received standard of care therapy due to gastrointestinal symptoms, did not respond sufficiently or at all to therapy and took MANC® orally on an individual basis. Patients with an age >18 years, with abdominal symptoms and MANC® therapy over 2 months and more have been included in this observational, retrospective study. Primary outcome parameter was the CFAbd-Score after 2 months of treatment with MANC®.

Results: 20 pwCF could be evaluated between 1 January 2024 and 31 December 2025. The mean age was 41.9 years (Range 26-60 years). 10 pwCF were female. 10 pwCF were homozygous for F508del/F508del, 7 heterozygous for F508del, and 3 other mutations than F508del. 16/20 patients responded with a decrease in the CFAbd-Score and 4 did not show a decrease or even showed an increase in CFAbd-Score.

Conclusion: Interestingly, the observational study showed that people with CF can benefit from modified, activated and natural clinoptilolite therapy after they have already taken the standard therapy for the underlying gastrointestinal complaints. Further prospective studies should be implemented to further understand the benefits of this oral treatment.

person.biography:
I am working as the director of the CF Center in the Clinic Ernst von Bergmann and as the Dean of the HMU University in Potsdam, Dusseldorf and Munich, Germany. The focus of our research group is inflammation and infections in pwCF. We studied the immune response in fungal infections over the last years. We also studied within the ECFS Fungal Pathogens working group the diagnostic approaches as well as therapeutic options in ABPA. Furthermore, we supported with our CF team an educational Programm in the Ukraine to support CF Centers in Lviv and Kiew over several months. Currently we focus on home monitoring of pwCF to enable an easier monitoring for the patients within a study with the German CF Foundation.
I am happy to serve as a board member of the ECFS now for 4 years and support the CF community with my experiences.

records.title: Longitudinal impact of CFTR modulator therapy on hepatobiliary biochemistry and liver stiffness in children with cystic fibrosis: prospectively collected single-centre observational data
records.authors_text: M. Imrei1,2, K. Ocskay1,3, A. F. Kéri1, I. Gönczi1, É. Gács1, M. Polovitzer1, D. Molnár1, A. Párniczky1,2,3
records.affiliations_text: 1Heim Pál National Pediatric Institute, Budapest, Hungary, 2University of Pécs, Institute for Translational Medicine, Medical School, Pécs, Hungary, 3Semmelweis University, Pharmaceutical Sciences and Health Technologies Division, Medical School, Budapest, Hungary
records.abstract_text:
Background: Clinically significant hepatobiliary involvement (HBI) affects 15–30% of children with cystic fibrosis (cwCF). It is unclear whether CFTR modulator therapy alters the natural course of CF-related hepatobiliary disease (CFHBI), and long-term effects on hepatobiliary biomarkers, including liver stiffness, remain largely unknown. We aimed to evaluate the impact of 36-month CFTR modulator therapy on CFHBI in cwCF.

Methods: In this single-centre prospective study, liver biomarkers including aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT), AST to platelet ratio index (APRI), GGT to platelet ratio (GPR), and liver stiffness measurement by 2D-shear-wave elastography (Philips EPIQ 5 ElastQ) were collected prior to and 36 months after initiating modulator therapy.

Results: Forty-five children were included (mean age at modulator initiation 9.4 years [SD 4.7]; 59% male). Thirty-eight received lumacaftor/ivacaftor and six received elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor. At baseline, APRI and GPR were elevated and decreased significantly after 36 months (APRI: 0.29 to 0.18, p<0.001; GPR: 0.20 to 0.11, p<0.001). FIB-4 remained stable (0.21 to 0.22; p=0.973). Significant reductions were observed in transaminase levels: AST decreased from 37.9 to 26.9 U/L (p<0.001), ALT from 36.6 to 23.1 U/L (p<0.001), and GGT from 20.2 to 12.1 U/L (p=0.007). Only two children had elevated transaminases at baseline; none remained elevated at 36 months. LSM data were available for 22 children (mean age 10.4 years [SD 4.2]; 72% male; all on lumacaftor/ivacaftor). Liver stiffness did not change significantly (7.02 kPa to 7.07 kPa; p=0.824).

Conclusions: CFTR modulator therapy over 36 months improved hepatobiliary biochemical indices and transaminases substantially, but did not significantly alter liver stiffness, suggesting potential benefits on CF-related hepatobiliary disease.

(NKFIH 138929, CF Trust NU-00600)

records.title: Effect of CFTR modulators on glucose tolerance in children with cystic fibrosis: an age- and sex-matched cohort study
records.authors_text: S. Kiss1, P. Mátrai2, O. Varannai1, M. Imrei1, A. Kéri1, Z. Vajda1, K. Ocskay1, A. Párniczky1
records.affiliations_text: 1Heim Pál National Pediatric Institute, Budapest, Hungary, 2Institute of Bioanalysis, University of Pécs, Medical School, Pécs, Hungary
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Cystic fibrosis–related abnormal glucose tolerance (CF-AGT) is a progressive, age-dependent complication, with ~50% of patients developing cystic fibrosis–related diabetes (CFRD) by their forties. Despite widespread CFTR modulator use, the impact on glucose tolerance remains uncertain. Most studies use self-controlled pre–post designs that fail to disentangle treatment effects from natural CF-AGT progression. We hypothesised modulators mitigate age-related CF-AGT worsening. We aimed to isolate modulator effects in a prospective pediatric registry-based matched control analysis.

Methods: We analysed prospectively collected registry data comparing CFTR modulator-treated children with untreated controls. Oral glucose tolerance tests (OGTT) were performed per study protocol in every child able to cooperate. 1:1 nearest-neighbour propensity score matching was based on age and sex (age calliper ≤1 year; exact sex match). Pair-stratified linear models compared outcomes. Analyses used the MatchIt R package v4.5.3.

Results: 80 treated children (29 males) were matched, 27 on LUM/IVA and 53 on ETI. OGTT data were available for 60 pairs. BMI z-scores did not differ across groups (Table 1 and Table 2).

NGT vs AGT proportion was 49 (82%)/11 (18%) in controls vs 14 (23%)/46 (77%) in treated (p=0.500), reflecting historical timing and modulator initiation criteria. No statistically significant differences were observed for fasting and 60- or 120-minute glucose, insulin or C-peptide levels. HbA1c values showed no clinically significant difference between groups.

Conclusion: We did not observe any statistically significant effects of CFTR modulator therapy on glucose metabolism. Modulator-specific in-depth analyses are warranted.

Objectives: Cystic fibrosis–related abnormal glucose tolerance (CF-AGT) is a progressive, age-dependent complication, with ~50% of patients developing cystic fibrosis–related diabetes (CFRD) by their forties. Oral glucose tolerance tests (OGTT) were performed per study protocol in every child able to cooperate. 1:1 nearest-neighbour propensity score matching was based on age and sex (age calliper ≤1 year; exact sex match). Pair-stratified linear models compared outcomes. Analyses used the MatchIt R package v4.5.3.

person.biography:
Andrea Párniczky MD, PhD is a pediatric gastroenterologist at Heim Pál National Pediatric Institute and the head of the largest pediatric cystic fibrosis center in Hungary. Her research focuses on pancreatic diseases, glucose metabolism disorders in CF, and CF-gastroenterology. She has extensive experience in registry-based research, utilizing registry data to enhance our understanding of disease progression, treatment outcomes, and epidemiological trends.
Dr. Párniczky is a member of the Conference Scientific Committee of the European Cystic Fibrosis Society and serves as Hungary’s representative in the ECFS Patient Registry Steering Group. She is also an active member of the CF/Pancreas Working Group of the European Society of Pediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology, and Nutrition.
She is committed to maintaining the highest standards of research integrity and data-driven decision-making to improve the lives of individuals with CF.

records.title: Determinants of vitamin D status in children with cystic fibrosis: a GEE-based analysis
records.authors_text: H. Avcı1, Z. Özdemir Uslu2, M. Yıldız Kayaoğlu3, U. Kavgacı3, N.B. Çelik Ertaş2, N. Emiralioğlu3, E. Güneş Yalçın3, U. Özçelik3, D. Doğru3, Z.A. Ozon2
records.affiliations_text: 1Hacettepe University Faculty of Medicine, Biostatistics Department, Ankara, Turkey, 2Hacettepe İhsan Doğramacı Children Hospital, Pediatric Endocrinology Department, Ankara, Turkey, 3Hacettepe İhsan Doğramacı Children Hospital, Pediatric Pulmonology Department, Ankara, Turkey
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Vitamin D insufficiency is common in children with cystic fibrosis (CF). Despite routine supplementation, maintaining adequate serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D) levels remains challenging. The aim of this study was to evaluate determinents of vitamin D status, and examine the relationship between vitamin D supplementation dose and vitamin D status.

Methods: Repeated measurements from 275 children with CF are used to classify vitamin D status as sufficient (>30), insufficient (20–30), and deficient (<20). For determinants of this outcome we applied a Generalized estimating equations (GEE)-based ordinal (cumulative logit) model with an exchangeable working correlation structure in order to account for within-subject correlation in repeated measurements. The associations of sex, pancreatic enzyme replacement (PERT), ursodeoxycholic acid use, and body mass index (BMI) SDS with vitamin D status were also assessed in the model.

Results: Female sex was associated with a lower risk of insufficient/deficient vitamin D levels (B = −0.474, p<0.001; OR = 0.62, 95% CI: 0.47–0.82). Interestingly, patients who were not prescribed PERT was associated with a higher risk of insufficient/deficient vitamin D status (B=0.660, p<0.001; OR = 1.93, 95% CI: 1.32–2.83). Ursodeoxycholic acid prescription and BMI SDS were not associated with the risk of insufficient/deficient vitamin D status (B=0.134, p=0.455 and B=−0.020, p=0.237). An approximate daily vitamin D dose of 4500 IU/day would be required to increase the probability of achieving 25(OH)D >30 ng/mL above 50% in children with CF.

Conclusion: Patients deemed clear of pancreatic insufficiency based on clinical and laboratory criteria, and who didn't use PERT, had a higher risk of insufficient or deficient vitamin D status, suggesting a mild subclinical impairment in fat absorption. A daily intake of 4,500 IU of vitamin D or more may be necessary for adequate vitamin D levels.

records.title: Empowering people with cystic fibrosis (CF) related diabetes: preliminary findings from the rollout of CF specific structured diabetes education sessions
records.authors_text: C. Bradshaw1, C. Merrells1, A. Higton1, C. Orchard1, A. Ewence1, A. Lillis1
records.affiliations_text: 1Frimley Health NHS Foundation Trust, Cystic Fibrosis Unit, Frimley, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Structured diabetes education is recommended by the UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, as it supports effective self-management and improves outcomes such as HbA1c. A third of people with CF aged ≥16 years receive treatment for CF-related diabetes (CFRD) in the UK. To promote equitable access to structured education for people with CFRD (pwCFRD), we developed a session modelled on existing courses for Type 2 Diabetes.

Method: CF dietitians designed a structured, interactive session covering CFRD aetiology, monitoring, complications, treatments, carbohydrate awareness, glycaemic index (GI) and food labels. Since late 2023, sessions have been delivered online in small groups or individually in person. Anonymous feedback was collected and HbA1c levels pre- and post-education were compared using the paired t-test.

Results: Eighteen pwCFRD completed the session; 14 provided feedback. All attendees found the session helpful and reported a ‘good understanding’ of what causes high blood glucose levels afterwards, representing a 50% shift from limited prior knowledge. Post-education, all participants also reported a ‘good understanding’ of what to eat with CFRD, with 71% improving from ‘no idea’ or ‘some idea’. Regarding managing their diabetes going forwards, 57% were ‘extremely confident’ and 43% ‘somewhat confident’. Learning about carbohydrate types, GI and food-related glucose responses were the most frequently cited benefits. Participants valued the interactive format, and 50% expressed interest in sessions exploring the emotional and psychological impact of CFRD. The median HbA1c change pre- and post-education was −2 mmol/mol (mean change −2.21 mmol/mol; range −7 to 2 mmol/mol; p=0.013).

Conclusion: Bespoke structured education for pwCFRD enhances self-management and is associated with improvements in HbA1c. These findings support the development of a national structured education programme to ensure equitable access for all pwCFRD.

records.title: Prevalence of hypercalciuria in the era of highly effective CFTR modulators

person.title: Dr
person.institution: Fondazione IRCCS Ca' Granda Ospedale Maggiore Policlinico
person.department: Mother and Child Department, Cystic Fibrosis Regional Center

records.authors_text: V. Daccò1, A.M.C. Bulfamante1, C. Rizza1, N. Faelli1, L. Claut1, F.A. Blasi2,3, G. Alicandro1,3
records.affiliations_text: 1Fondazione IRCCS Ca' Granda Ospedale Maggiore Policlinico, Mother and Child Department, Cystic Fibrosis Regional Center, Milan, Italy, 2Fondazione IRCCS Ca' Granda Ospedale Maggiore Policlinico, Respiratory Unit and Cystic Fibrosis Adult Center, Milan, Italy, 3University of Milan, Department of Pathophysiology and Transplantation, Milan, Italy
records.abstract_text:
The introduction of Elexacaftor/Tezacaftor/Ivacaftor (ETI) has significantly improved the prognosis for People with Cystic Fibrosis (pwCF). However, increased survival has shifted clinical attention toward long-term complications, including metabolic and renal disorders. Among these, hypercalciuria, defined as elevated urinary calcium excretion in the absence of hypercalcemia, may predispose to nephrocalcinosis, kidney stones, and potential impairment of renal function. In pwCF not treated with ETI, the reported prevalence of hypercalciuria ranges from 30% to 60%. In the era of highly effective CFTR modulators, its prevalence and clinical relevance remain largely unknown.

Aim: To evaluate the prevalence of hypercalciuria in pwCF receiving ETI therapy.

Methods: In this cross-sectional study, we included pwCF who had been receiving ETI therapy for at least 6 months. The presence of hypercalciuria was defined based on sex and age-specific normative values of the urinary calcium-to-creatinine (UCa/Cr) ratio.

Results: The study included 118 subjects with a median age of 16 years (range: 2–32). Nine patients exhibited Uca/Cr ratios indicative of hypercalciuria with an estimated prevalence of 7.6% (95% confidence interval: 3.5–14.0). Among these, four patients (44%) had radiographic evidence of urinary calculi; all of them were asymptomatic.

Conclusions: The prevalence of hypercalciuria in pwCF treated with ETI is comparable to that of the general population. Nevertheless, given the aging CF population and its association with silent urinary calculi, routine monitoring of urinary calcium excretion should be considered to prevent long-term renal complications.

records.title: The syndrome of electrolyte disturbances (Pseudo-Bartter's syndrome, PBS) in children with cystic fibrosis from various subjects of the North Caucasus

person.institution: Federal State Autonomous Institution “National Medical Research Center for Children’s Health” of the Ministry of Health of the Russian Federation

records.authors_text: M. Simonov1, Y. Gorinova1
records.affiliations_text: 1Federal State Autonomous Institution “National Medical Research Center for Children’s Health” of the Ministry of Health of the Russian Federation, Moscow, Russian Federation
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: In some previous articles, it was shown that the main feature of cystic fibrosis in patients from the Chechen Republic is the predominance of PBS. Currently, there are no studies aimed at analyzing the prevalence of PBS in other regions of the North Caucasus and its association with CFTR gene mutations has not been established.

Aim: To investigate the prevalence of PBS among patients in the North Caucasus and establish its association with CFTR gene mutations.

Methods: This study included 160 patients from various republics of the North Caucasus: Chechen – 83 patients, Karachay-Cherkess – 28, Dagestan – 22, Ingushetia – 13, North Ossetia-Alania – 9, Kabardino-Balkaria – 5. In Chechen, correlation analysis was used with patients who had at least one allele of variant 1677delTA(1), E92K(2) and patients with other mutations of the CFTR gene(3), in Karachay-Cherkessia: patients with variant W1282X on at least one allele and patients with other mutations of the CFTR gene. In Dagestan: at least one allele has variant 1677delTA(1), R1066C(2), and patients with other CFTR gene mutations.

Results: Electrolyte disorders were detected in 94 (58.7%) patients. A high frequency of PBS was found in three republics, significantly more often in Chechen – 66.7% (p<0.01), less often in Karachay-Cherkessia (57,1%) and Dagestan (55%). The occurrence of PBS is not associated with CFTR gene mutations in both the Chechen (p1,2= 0.96; p1,3 = 0.1), Karachay-Cherkessia (p= 0.56) and the Republic of Dagestan (p1,2 = 0.52; p1,3 = 0.31). It was found that in three regions with a high frequency of PBS, excessive wrapping of infants is observed.

Conclusion: Children with cystic fibrosis from various regions of the North Caucasus have a high incidence of PBS (from 50 to 66.7%), mainly in the Chechen Republic. The occurrence of PBS does not depend on mutations of the CFTR gene and is probably related to the continental climate of the district and intraethnic characteristics.

A high frequency of PBS was found in three republics, significantly more often in Chechen – 66.7% (p<0.01), less often in Karachay-Cherkessia (57,1%) and Dagestan (55%). The occurrence of PBS is not associated with CFTR gene mutations in both the Chechen (p1,2= 0.96; p1,3 = 0.1), Karachay-Cherkessia (p= 0.56) and the Republic of Dagestan (p1,2 = 0.52; p1,3 = 0.31). It was found that in three regions with a high frequency of PBS, excessive wrapping of infants is observed.
Conclusion: Children with cystic fibrosis from various regions of the North Caucasus have a high incidence of PBS (from 50 to 66.7%), mainly in the Chechen Republic. records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Elexacaftor/Tezacaftor/Ivacaftor (ETI) is approved for people with CF (pwCF) ≥2 years with at least one F508del variant. This retrospective single-center study aimed to evaluate liver involvement in pwCF treated with ETI.

Methods: PwCF treated with ETI at the CF Center of the Basilicata Region were included. Demographic data and laboratory parameters (gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), total bilirubin (TB), and platelet count) were collected at baseline and after 6, 12, and 24 months. Non-invasive biomarkers of CF–related liver disease (CFLD) were calculated, including the AST-to-platelet ratio index (APRI), the GGT-to-platelet ratio (GPR), and the Fibrosis-4 index (FIB-4). Steatosis (controlled attenuation parameter [CAP] ≥288 dB/m) and fibrosis (liver stiffness measurement [LSM] ≥7 kPa) were assessed in 26 of 73 patients at the last visit using FibroScan® (Echosens).

Results: 73 patients (37 M; median age 25 yrs [IQR 15–36]) were included. Median AST, GGT, and TB showed slight, non-significant (NS) increases at 12 and 24 months. Median (IQR) ALT increased from 22 (17–27) U/L at baseline to 23 (18–24) U/L at 12 months and 24 (19–30) U/L at 24 months (p<0.05). The median (IQR) APRI score increased from 0.18 (0.139–0.24) to 0.219 (0.171–0.273) at 12 months (p<0.05); however, 98.63% of patients had an APRI <0.5 both at baseline and at 12 months, indicating absence of significant fibrosis. The median (IQR) GPR score decreased from 0.168 (0.123–0.227) at baseline to 0.152 (0.12–0.211) at 12 months (p<0.05). A NS increase in median FIB-4 was observed. Median (IQR) CAP and LSM values were 164 dB/m (164–223) and 3.83 kPa (2.93–3.98), respectively. One patient showed steatosis (CAP 335 dB/m) and fibrosis (LSM 11.8 kPa), consistent with clinical and laboratory findings.

Conclusions: ETI demonstrated a favorable hepatic safety profile, with no meaningful changes in non-invasive biomarkers of CFLD.

records.title: The impact of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor on bone mineral density in children and adults with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: D. O'Keeffe1, E. Byrne2, R. Cregan3, L. Kirwan4, J.C Davies5, P. McNally6, D.W Cox1
records.affiliations_text: 1Children's Health Ireland at Crumlin, Department of Paediatric Respiratory Medicine, Dublin, Ireland, 2St. Vincent’s University Hospital, Department of Respiratory Medicine, Dublin, Ireland, 3RCSI University of Medicine and Health Sciences, 3. Department of Paediatrics, Dublin, Ireland, 4Royal Brompton & Harefield Hospitals, Department of Paediatric Respiratory Medicine, London, United Kingdom, 5National Heart and Lung Institute, Imperial College London, London, United Kingdom, 6Children’s Health Ireland at Crumlin, Department of Paediatric Respiratory Medicine, Dublin, Ireland
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The highly effective cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) therapy elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) has transformed the management of people with Cystic Fibrosis (PwCF). However, its effects on bone mineral density (BMD) remain uncertain.

Methods: We conducted a longitudinal cohort study assessing changes in BMD before and after ETI initiation in children and adults with CF across five Irish hospitals. Participants were identified from RECOVER, a multicentre observational study of real-world ETI outcomes. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) scans were analysed both pre- and post-ETI initiation. Paired t-tests assessed BMD changes, with effect sizes calculated using Cohen’s dz. Secondary outcomes included biochemical markers of bone metabolism.

Results: Paired DXA data were available for 22 adults (age range 18-49 years) and 12 children (age range 6-17 years). The median interval between pre- and post-ETI DXA scans was 58.4 months (range 15.7-111.4) in adults, and 77.3 months (range 21.3-137.7) in children. In adults, lumbar spine BMD showed a small increase after ETI initiation (mean change +0.13 Z-score; p=0.24; dz=0.27), while hip BMD showed a non-significant decrease (−0.32 Z-score; p=0.09; dz=0.84). In children, no significant changes were observed at the lumbar spine (−0.05 Z-score; p=0.84; dz=0.08) or total body less hip (TBLH) (−0.15 Z-score; p=0.74; dz=0.05). Baseline lumbar z-scores were predominantly within normal range with no patients demonstrating values ≤ -2.0 at ETI initiation. No significant biochemical changes were identified.

Conclusion: No statistically significant changes were observed over a median follow-up of approximately 3 years after ETI and BMD. The absence of severe baseline bone deficit may partly explain the lack of significant BMD change observed following ETI initiation in children. Longer-term studies are needed to determine whether sustained ETI exposure influences bone health in PwCF.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Chronic intestinal inflammation is a hallmark of CF and is associated with a markedly elevated burden of abdominal symptoms (AS) in people with CF (pwCF). Consequently, comparing AS in pwCF, people with inflammatory bowel disease (pwIBD) and healthy controls (HC) may provide new insights and contribute to a better understanding of GI involvement in pwCF.

COMET-CF-IBD (Comprehensive Omic and SyMptom Evaluation, a Translational study) aims to improve understanding of chronic gastrointestinal inflammation and its clinical impact in pwCF.

Methods: Using the CFAbd-Score, the first CF-specific GI-PROM developed and validated following FDA-guidelines, we assessed and compared AS in children and adults with CF, IBD and HC. Higher scores in CFAbd-Score represent an increased burden of symptoms. The analysis included retrospective data of a subgroup of pwCF before commencing a new therapy with elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI).

Results: 37 pwCF receiving ETI, 41 pwIBD and 63 HC were prospectively included. Retrospective data of 19 pwCF before ETI yielded a median total CFAbd-Score of 10.6pts which during ETI decreased to 5.8pts (p=0.07).

Altogether, of the three subgroups, pwIBD were observed to have the highest total scores (median: 13.2pts), significantly higher than pwCF (7.7pts/p<0.05) and HC (5.9pts/p<0.0001). Analogously, scores related to disorders of appetite (DA) and quality of life (QoL) domains were significantly higher in pwIBD (DA:4pts/QoL:12.5pts) compared to pwCF (DA:0pts/QoL:0pts) and HC (DA:0pts/QoL:0pts). Furthermore, scores related to bowel movement were highest in pwIBD (16.7pts), compared to pwCF (10pts/p>0.05) and HC (7.5pts/p<0.01).

On the other hand, total CFAbd-Scores and the disorders of appetite domain resulted significantly elevated in pwCF, compared to HC (p<0.05).

Conclusions: The burden of AS is lower in pwCF compared to pwIBD. However, compared to HC, the CF-related mulltiorgan abdominal involvement causes a relevantly enhanced burden of symptoms, above all, in pwCF not receiving highly potent CFTR-modulating therapies.

person.biography:
Jochen G Mainz currently works at the Clinic of Pediatric and Adolescent Medicine, Brandenburg Medical School (MHB) Klinikum Westbrandenburg, Brandenburg an der Havel, Germany. He is Professor for Pediatric Pulmonology and Allergology as well as head of the Universities´ Cystic Fibrosis Center. Jochen does research in CF-related gastrointestinal involvement, Pulmonology, Pediatrics, and Respiratory as well as regarding sinonasal involvement in CF. Their current projects are `Abdominal involvement in CF´ , as well as 'Upper airway (sinonasal) involvement in Cystic fibrosis'.
With his team he developed a new CF specific multimodal questionnaire for identification and quantification of GI, hepatic and pancreatic involvement in the inherited disease (CFAbd-Score). This Patient Related Outcome Measure (PROM) has been translated in 15 languages worldwide, and it has been found to be highly sensitive to detect effects of therapies on CF-related GI-symptoms.

records.affiliations_text: 1Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, CF Unit, 3rd Paediatric Dept, Hippokration Hospital, Thessaloniki, Greece, 2University of Thessaly, Department of Nutrition and Dietetics, School of Physical Education, Sport Science and Dietetics, Trikala, Greece
records.abstract_text:
Aim: To assess the bone health of adolescents and young adults with CF, and explore the correlation between bone mineral density, physical activity, and markers of nutritional status.

Methods: Our study included 30 patients with CF. Bone mineral density was assessed by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA). Measurements were performed at the right and left femoral bones and the lumbar spine; results were expressed as Z-scores. Physical activity levels were assessed using the Godin Leisure-Time Activity Questionnaire. With respect to nutritional markers, we examined body mass index (BMI), 25-hydroxyvitamin D, calcium, phosphorus, and handgrip strength (HGS). person.biography:
Elpis Hatziagorou is a Professor in Respiratory Pediatrics of the Paediatric Pulmonology and CF Unit at Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, Greece. Dr. Hatziagorou received her degree in Medicine from the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki and earned her Ph.D. in studies of exhaled NO in patients with chronic lung disease. She worked as a Clinical Fellow in Respiratory Pediatrics at Sheffield Children’s Hospital, University of Sheffield, UK (2010), and got the European Diploma in Paediatric Respiratory Medicine (2012).
She is a clinical researcher; her main interests are Cystic Fibrosis, non-CF bronchiectasis, Multiple Breath Washout, and Exercise testing. She has been a Steering Group Member of the European Cystic Fibrosis Registry (since 2007) and a Member of the Scientific Committee of the European Cystic Fibrosis Registry since 2018. She has also been a member of the ECFS Exercise Working Group since 2015. Elpis Hatziagorou has been a member of the European Cystic Fibrosis Society Diagnostic Network Group since 2009. In the past decade, her interest has remained focused on outcome parameters (lung clearance index, quality of life, exercise testing indices), clinical trials, and diagnostic/epidemiologic issues in CF.
