records.title: Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor effects on pancreatic involution in cystic fibrosis: a longitudinal CT study
records.authors_text: G. Paiola1, M.C. Ambrosetti1, F. Omboni1, E. Pintani1, G. Puppini1, M. Cipolli1
records.affiliations_text: 1AOUI Verona, Verona, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Objective: To evaluate the potential influence of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) therapy on the progression of pancreatic imaging abnormalities in patients with Cystic Fibrosis.

Methods: A total of 196 patients with Cystic Fibrosis treated with ETI and who underwent High-Resolution Computed Tomography (HRCT) were included (93 males, 103 females; mean age at first CT 15 years; mean age at start of therapy 24 years). A longitudinal evaluation of the pancreatic parenchyma included in the caudal portions of chest HRCT scans was performed using available pre- and post-therapy examinations (mean follow-up 88 months; 774 CT scans analyzed). Pancreatic parenchyma was independently segmented by two readers, and Hounsfield Unit (HU) density histograms were computed using dedicated research image analysis software (Mango, Research Imaging Institute, UTHSCSA). A multivariate analysis using a generalized linear mixed model was conducted to assess the effect of ETI therapy on changes in the distribution of acinar (18–70 HU) and adipose (–34 to –190 HU) pancreatic components before and after treatment.

Results: A statistically significant time-related increase in the adipose component (β = 9.04; p = 0.0036) and a reduction in the acinar component (β = –12.85; p = 0.0031) were observed. Although pancreatic involution continued over time, a significant difference in the temporal response slope (β) was found post-treatment compared to pre-treatment for both the adipose (β = –0.40; p = 0.0022) and acinar components (β = 0.63; p = 0.0011) (p < 0.001). These findings indicate that ETI therapy induces significant changes in both intercept and slope for pancreatic adipose and acinar components.

Conclusion: Despite the ongoing loss of acinar tissue and increase in adipose tissue, ETI therapy appears to significantly influence the progression of pancreatic structural changes in patients with Cystic Fibrosis.

records.title: Changing pancreatic status of patients in a UK paediatric cystic fibrosis network from diagnosis to present
records.authors_text: C.A. Berry1, C.J. Woodland1
records.affiliations_text: 1Alder Hey Children's NHS Trust, Nutrition and Dietetics, Liverpool, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Pancreatic insufficiency (PI) is a common complication in cystic fibrosis (CF), historically considered irreversible in most patients. However, with earlier diagnosis and improved therapies, pancreatic status may change over time, particularly in patients who are able to start highly effective modulator therapy (HEMT) at a younger age. Our aim was to evaluate changes in pancreatic status among paediatric CF patients within our regional network, from diagnosis to present.

Methods: We undertook a retrospective audit of all faecal elastase (FE-1) levels measured in all CF patients in a paediatric network, from their diagnostic test, up to present. Exclusion criteria were patients with a Cystic Fibrosis Screen Positive Inconclusive Diagnosis (CFSPID) designation. Patients both on and off HEMT were included in the data. We defined PI as those who had a FE-1 level <200µg/g.

Results: Of 282 patients included, 260 (92%) patient’s pancreatic status remained unchanged from diagnosis, 224 (86%) of which were PI. Of the 22 patients who had a change in pancreatic status, 6 patients changed from pancreatic sufficiency (PS) to PI. 13 patients changed from PI to PS. Three patients changed from PS to PI back to PS. The mean age of the 16 patients who changed from PI to PS was 5 years, compared to a mean age of 10 years of the whole patient cohort. The median age of starting HEMT was 23 months and the median time from starting HEMT to PS was 10 months in these patients.

Conclusion: Our results show that the patients who recovered pancreatic function are preschool age children and started HEMT at a young age. CF patients are able to start HEMT at a younger age and our results reinforces the importance of regular nutritional assessment and routine monitoring of FE-1 for all CF patients both PI and PS. Getting faecal samples from patients can be challenging but there is increasing clinical justification for requesting this as part of routine CF care.

records.title: Reviewing the necessity for annual liver ultrasounds in children with cystic fibrosis - A comparison to the Cystic Fibrosis Standards of Care
records.authors_text: J. Coulson1, K. Lock1, R. Poole2, W. Kozlowska1
records.affiliations_text: 1Addenbrooke's Hospital, Paediatric Respiratory, Cambridge, United Kingdom, 2Addenbrooke's Hospital, Paediatric Gastroenterology, Cambridge, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: National CF standards recommend liver ultrasound (USS) from age three, with further imaging as clinically indicated. At CUH, a paediatric CF centre, local guidance mandates annual liver USS from age one, creating a more intensive surveillance programme. This audit assessed adherence to both national and local standards and explored whether surveillance frequency could be reduced whilst still enabling earliest possible detection of liver complications.

Methods: Electronic records for all children with CF at CUH (2014-2025) were reviewed. Exclusions: aged <12 months, >16 years, or CF-SPID. Data collection included USS frequency per patient, positive USS liver findings, age at detection, and if subsequent management was initiated. Data from 2020-2021 were excluded due to Covid‑19 disruption.

Results: All 123 included patients met the national minimum standard for USS screening. Adherence to the local annual USS standard was 79.7%. A total of 34 patients (27.6%) had positive USS findings, with 23 commencing ursodeoxycholic acid. Only two positive USS findings were detected in children under age three. 25 patients missed ≥1 scan (33 total missed scans), with 66.7% of missed scans from 2022 onwards. Results were discussed with consultants across hepatology, gastroenterology and respiratory, with recommendations that annual USS is most appropriate for patients with GI surgical history, who are at higher risk of portal hypertension and biliary complications whereas lower risk patients could follow official national surveillance guidelines.

Conclusion: Current local surveillance exceeds national guidance and may not be necessary for all patients. A risk‑stratified approach - annual USS for patients with GI surgical history from age one and USS as indicated from age three for lower risk groups - could reduce unnecessary imaging while maintaining safety. Updating local policy, refining USS indications, and ongoing monitoring of outcomes will support safe implementation.

records.title: Comparison of carbohydrate metabolism in children with cystic fibrosis with and without variant-specific therapy

person.institution: National Medical Research Center for Children’s Health» of Ministry of Health of Russian Federation

records.authors_text: N. Lyabina1, D. Dzhurtubaeva1, O. Simonova1,2,3, N. Kashirskaya4
records.affiliations_text: 1«National Medical Research Center for Children’s Health» of Ministry of Health of Russian Federation, Moscow, Russian Federation, 2I.M.Sechenov First Moscow State Medical University, Moscow, Russian Federation, Moscowrs, Russian Federation, 3Morozovskaya Children's City Clinical Hospital, Moscow, Russian Federation, Moscow, Russian Federation, 4Research Centre for Medical Genetics, Moscow, Russian Federation
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: carbohydrate metabolism disorders (CMD) in people with cystic fibrosis (CF) remain clinically relevant even in the era of variant-specific therapy (VST). Despite the pronounced clinical effect of VST in CF, published data on its impact on glucose metabolism are contradictory, and the prevalence and patterns of glucose abnormalities in children are still insufficiently studied. Therefore, assessment of glucose metabolism in children with CF (cwCF) receiving VST is of interest.

Methods: twenty cwCF and elevated HbA1c were included in the study. Group I — 10 children receiving VST (median age (Me) = 14.27 years [11.64–14.73]; 2 children on two-component and 8 on three-component regimens); Group II — 10 children not receiving VST (Me = 12.58 years [11.24–14.83]). All cwCF underwent an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) with measurements at three time points (0, 60, 120 minutes).

Results: HbA1c was elevated in both groups (Group I: Me = 6.4% [6.17–6.59]; Group II: Me = 6.41% [6.28–6.54]). After OGTT, CMD were identified in 6/10 (60%) children in Group II (median age of affected children Me = 12.58 years [11.49–13.67]): indeterminate glycemia (INDET) n = 4 (40%), impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) n = 1, and cystic fibrosis-related diabetes (CFRD) n = 1. Group I had lower numbers of cwCF with CMD (two children with INDET and two with IGT); the median age of affected children in Group I was Me = 12.81 years [11.54–14.33]. Correlation analysis of blood glucose levels at the three OGTT time points between groups showed no statistically significant differences (p0 = 0.481; p60 = 0.165; p120 = 0.393).

Conclusion: our observations suggest that VST may have a potentially favorable effect on glucose metabolism in children with CF. These findings underscore the need for regular metabolic monitoring, including OGTT, in all children with CF regardless of whether they receive targeted therapy or not. Follow-up of the cohort will continue.

Results: HbA1c was elevated in both groups (Group I: Me = 6.4% [6.17–6.59]; Group II: Me = 6.41% [6.28–6.54]). person.title: Dietitian
person.institution: Verona Cystic Fibrosis Center - AOUI VERONA

records.authors_text: C. Brignole1, V. Spina1, R. Guarise1, S. Volpi1, G. Tridello1, M. Signorini1, M. Cipolli1
records.affiliations_text: 1Verona Cystic Fibrosis Center - AOUI VERONA, Verona, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Cystic fibrosis (CF) can lead to nutritional challenges in pediatric patients, including malnutrition and growth failure. The advent of CF modulators, such as elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI), has brought significant improvements in lung function and nutritional status. The aim of our study is to explore the impact of ETI treatment on growth parameters in children aged 6-12 years (yrs) with CF.

Methods: Patients with CF (pwCF) were evaluated before the start (T0), after 1 year (T1), and after 2 yrs (T2) of ETI treatment. At each time point, weight (kg), weight Z-score, height (cm), height Z-score, Body Mass Index (BMI, kg/m²), BMI Z-score, Fat Mass (FM, kg), Fat Free Mass (FFM, kg), Mid-Upper-Arm Circumference (MUAC, cm), MUAC Z-score, Triceps Skin Fold (TSF, mm), and Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 second (FEV1,%) were measured. Data were compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. The correlation between variables was assessed using the Pearson correlation coefficient. A p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Results: A total of 28 pwCF (8 male, 20 female) with a median age of 9 years (range 6-12) were included. Significant increases were observed after 1 year of ETI in weight (3.3 kg, p<0.001), weight Z-score (0.1, p=0.01), height (6 cm, p<0.001), BMI (0.4 kg/m², p<0.001), FM (0.3 kg, p<0.01), FFM (3 kg, p<0.001), TSF (1.5 mm, p<0.01), MUAC (1 cm, p=0.001), MUAC Z-score (0.1, p=0.04), and FEV1 (8.5%, p=0.001). After 2 years, 18 out of 28 had available data, and similar results were found for most variables. The increase in BMI after 1 year was strongly correlated with the increase in FM (r = 0.8, p<0.001).

Conclusion: We found encouraging improvements in growth parameters in children with CF, with benefits continuing beyond the first year of ETI treatment. These findings should be monitored prospectively to provide valuable insights into the evolving nutritional needs of children with CF starting ETI early.

records.title: EASE-CF: a randomised controlled feasibility trial of intentional weight loss in adults with cystic fibrosis

person.title: Mrs.
person.department: Nuffield Department of Primary Care Health Sciences

records.authors_text: J. Snowball1,2, A. Adler3, P. Lally4, N. Talbot2, D. Koutoukidis1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Oxford, Nuffield Department of Primary Care Health Sciences, Oxford, United Kingdom, 2Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, Oxford Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Oxford, United Kingdom, 3University of Oxford, Radcliffe Department of Medicine, Oxford, United Kingdom, 4University of Surrey, Guildford, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background and objectives: Approximately 40% of adults with cystic fibrosis (CF) now live with overweight or obesity due to advances in CF care and improved survival. Despite this emerging clinical issue, no trials of intentional weight loss strategies have been conducted in this population, and the feasibility , acceptability and safety of weight loss programmes remain unknown. The primary objective of this study is to determine the feasibility of progression to a definitive randomised controlled trial (RCT).

Methods: This abstract describes the protocol for a 24-week, multicentre, unblinded, parallel-group randomised controlled feasibility trial with an embedded qualitative study. A sample of 30 adults with CF and body mass index (BMI) ≥27 kg/m² will be randomised in a 2:1 ratio to either a structured weight loss intervention or usual care. Randomisation will be stratified by age (<40 years vs ≥40 years) and presence of CF-related diabetes. The trial is delivered remotely, with study assessments and intervention support provided via video consultation. The intervention provided free of charge includes weekly behavioural support from a specialist CF dietitian, a meal replacement product, and a portion-controlled fresh ready meal. Semi-structured interviews will be conducted with participants and healthcare professionals. Feasibility will be assessed through recruitment, engagement, adherence and retention, with exploratory analyses of between-group differences in body weight, body composition, health-related quality of life, lung function, blood pressure, glycaemic control and blood lipids measured at baseline and 24 weeks. Adverse events will be monitored to assess intervention safety.

Conclusion: EASE-CF will generate feasibility, acceptability and safety data to inform the design of a future definitive RCT of intentional weight loss in adults with CF. Ethical and regulatory approvals have been obtained, and recruitment is due to commence in January 2026.

person.biography:
Joanna is a specialist dietitian at the Oxford Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre in the UK, with 20 years of clinical experience supporting both adults and children living with CF. She is also an active researcher at the University of Oxford, where her work focuses on understanding and addressing the evolving nutritional needs of adults with CF.
She has published qualitative research in the Journal of Cystic Fibrosis examining clinician perspectives on managing excess weight in people with CF. In 2024, she was awarded an NIHR Doctoral Clinical Academic Fellowship and is now undertaking her PhD, leading the EASE-CF study, which explores the feasibility of a dietitian-supported weight-loss intervention for individuals with CF who have excess weight.
Joanna co-chairs the European Cystic Fibrosis Nutrition Group and serves as the allied health professional representative on the UK CF Registry Steering Committee.

records.title: A cystic fibrosis-specific nutritional screening questionnaire for early identification of patients at nutritional risk

person.department: Department of Hospital Nutrition and Dietotherapy

records.authors_text: A. Tomažič1, I. Ćatić2, D. Cigulajkić2
records.affiliations_text: 1University Medical Centre Ljubljana, Department of Hospital Nutrition and Dietotherapy, Ljubljana, Slovenia, 2University Medical Centre Ljubljana, Department of Pulmonology and Allergy, Ljubljana, Slovenia
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To develop and evaluate a cystic fibrosis (CF) specific nutritional screening questionnaire for early identification of adult patients at nutritional risk in routine outpatient care.​

​Methods: A CF-specific nutritional screening questionnaire was developed by a clinical dietitian and implemented in routine outpatient care over an 8-month period. The questionnaire assesses recent weight loss, appetite changes, gastrointestinal symptoms, stool consistency, and self-reported functional capacity. Items were weighted and scored, classifying patients as low (0–4 points), moderate (5–8 points), or high (≥9 points) nutritional risk. Four questionnaires were excluded due to incomplete completion. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics.​

​Results: Twenty-four adult CF patients were included (13 males, 11 females), with a mean age of 30.2±8.5 years and a mean BMI of 21.8±3.1 kg/m². Overall, 75.0% of patients were classified as low nutritional risk, 20.8% as moderate risk, and 4.2% as high risk. Female patients more frequently reported gastrointestinal and appetite-related symptoms, whereas male patients more commonly reported reduced physical endurance. The patient classified as high nutritional risk (11 points) had a normal BMI (21.5 kg/m²) but presented with reduced appetite, early satiety, nausea during meals, decreased physical strength, and bloating. Among patients with moderate nutritional risk, BMI ranged from 16 to 26 kg/m², demonstrating that clinically relevant nutritional risk would not have been identified by BMI alone.​

​Conclusion: This CF-specific nutritional screening questionnaire is a practical and time-efficient tool for early identification of clinically relevant nutritional risk, including in patients with normal BMI. By capturing symptom burden and functional decline beyond anthropometry, it supports timely dietetic intervention in routine CF care. Further validation against established nutritional assessment tools is needed.

records.title: Longitudinal trends in nutritional status and associations with lung function in adults with cystic fibrosis: data from the UK CF Registry

person.institution: University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust
person.department: West Midlands Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre

records.authors_text: J. Barrett1, S. Collins2, E. Granger3, J. Lowdon4, V. Lynch5, S. Maguire3, K. Powell6, C. Smith7, J. Snowball8, R. Keogh3
records.affiliations_text: 1University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust, West Midlands Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Birmingham, United Kingdom, 2Royal Brompton & Harefield Hospitals, Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, London, United Kingdom, 3London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, London, United Kingdom, 4Leeds Children's hospital, Leeds, United Kingdom, 5Belfast Health and Social Care Trust, Northern Ireland Regional Respiratory Centre, Belfast City Hospital, Belfast, United Kingdom, 6York and Hull Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, York Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, York, United Kingdom, 7Royal Alexandra Children's Hospital,, Brighton, United Kingdom, 8Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, Oxford, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: Optimising nutritional status (NS) remains a key priority for adults with CF (awCF). Reports on NS trends in the UK are limited and the relationship between BMI and lung function in the CFTR modulator era remains unclear.

Aim: To describe longitudinal trends in NS in UK awCF and associations of BMI and BMI change with clinical outcomes by modulator use.

Method: Data on all awCF aged ≥ 18 years recorded in the UK CF Registry between 2007-2023 were analysed. AwCF were categorised by BMI according to ESPEN-ESPGHAN 2024 definitions: underweight, target range, overweight, and obese. Linear models were used to study the associations of BMI and BMI change with lung function, by modulator use.

Results: Data on 8,869 awCF from 82,604 annual reviews were available. Between 2007 and 2023, awCF within the target BMI range decreased from 71.5% to 57.0%, overweight rose from 15% to 28.8%, obesity rose from 2.7% to 9.7%, and underweight decreased from 10.7% to 4.5%. Higher BMI was associated with better lung function. Increasing BMI in underweight awCF saw the largest increase in lung function. BMI increases in overweight/obese awCF was not associated with better lung function. Modulator therapy did not influence the association between BMI and lung function (p=0.99).

Conclusion: This large, registry-based study is the first to examine trends in nutritional status in awCF in the UK and associations with clinical outcomes. Our findings align with other national registry data and highlight the need to prioritise the management and understanding of excess weight and its clinical implications. These trends highlight the need for proactive nutritional management strategies to optimise health outcomes, to minimise the risk of overweight/obesity and associated co-morbidities in awCF.

records.title: Impact of early elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor treatment on growth and pancreatic function in children with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: M. Mala1,2, Z. Kocurova1,2, B. Korenkova1,2, A. Holcikova1,2, L. Homola1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1University Hospital Brno, Department of Paediatric Infectious Diseases, Brno, Czech Republic, 2Masaryk University, Faculty of Medicine, Brno, Czech Republic
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To evaluate real-world effects of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) on nutritional status and pancreatic exocrine function in children with cystic fibrosis (CF) following its introduction into clinical practice in the Czech Republic.

Methods: A retrospective analysis was performed 12 months after ETI became available for children aged 2–6 years. Patients younger than 12 years at ETI initiation were included. Changes in body mass index (BMI, percentile) and faecal pancreatic elastase were analysed. Subgroup analyses were conducted according to prior treatment with lumacaftor/ivacaftor (LUM/IVA). Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used for paired comparisons.

Results: The cohort comprised 38 children with CF (18 females, 20 males) with a mean age of 7.3 ± 2.7 years (median 6.6). ETI was initiated at a mean age of 5.7 ± 2.0 years (median 5.8). Twenty-four patients had received prior (lumacafotr/ivacaftor) LUM/IVA therapy. In this subgroup, no statistically significant change in BMI percentile was observed after ETI initiation (p = 0.19), although a positive trend was noted (median change +6.5). In contrast, children without prior LUM/IVA therapy demonstrated a significant increase in BMI percentile following ETI initiation (p = 0.0023; 95% CI 3.97–14.56). In this group, faecal pancreatic elastase levels increased significantly after ETI compared with baseline (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 24, p < 0.000001), with a median increase of 252 µg/g (95% CI 170–360).

Conclusion: In routine clinical practice, ETI therapy was associated with significant improvements in nutritional status and pancreatic exocrine function in children with CF, particularly in those without prior LUM/IVA treatment. These findings support early initiation of ETI in paediatric CF patients.

records.abstract_text:
Background: Nutritional impairment remains a major challenge in patients with cystic fibrosis and is strongly associated with poorer pulmonary outcomes and reduced survival. The introduction of highly effective CFTR modulator therapy, particularly the triple combination elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) has been associated with significant improvements in nutritional status, including weight gain and body mass index (BMI).

Aim: To evaluate changes in BMI and nutritional status after 1 year of ETI in patients with cystic fibrosis.

Methods: This retrospective observational cohort included 54 patients with cystic fibrosis (mean age 19.5±6.8 years; range 7–40 years). Anthropometric data were collected at baseline and after 3, 6, 9, and 12 months of therapy. Changes in BMI were analysed using repeated-measures analysis of variance with Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons. Changes in nutritional categories (underweight, normal weight, overweight/obesity) were assessed using McNemar’s test. Statistical significance was set at p<0.05.

Results: Mean BMI increased significantly from 20.2±4.1 kg/m² at baseline to 21.6±4.2 kg/m² after 12 months (mean change +1.45 kg/m²; p<0.001). The largest increase occurred within the first 3 months (+0.82 kg/m²; p<0.001), followed by smaller but statistically significant increments thereafter. The proportion of underweight patients decreased from 40.7% to 20.8%, while the prevalence of normal weight increased from 44.4% to 58.5% (p=0.001). In the paediatric subgroup (n=23), BMI percentiles improved significantly (+11.5 percentile points; p=0.001)

Conclusion: One year of ETI therapy resulted in statistically and clinically significant improvements in BMI, characterised by rapid early gains and sustained improvement over time, leading to a marked reduction in undernutrition.

records.authors_text: C. Pascon1, E.A. Lomazi1, M.A. Bellomo-Brandão1, J. Dirceu Ribeiro1
records.affiliations_text: 1UNICAMP, Campinas, Brazil
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To describe the quality of the diet and its relationship with lung function and nutritional status in adolescents with cystic fibrosis (CF).

Methods: A questionnaire was applied to 47 adolescents (12–19 years old) followed at a university reference center. Lung function impairment was classified as mild (FEV1pp≥60%), moderate (FEV1pp 41–59%) or severe (FEV1pp<40%) using spirometry. Food consumption frequency was classified as rarely, 1-2 times/week, 3-4 times/week, or ≥ 5 times/week. Linear regression analysis was used to model the relationship between lung function, BMI/age Z-score and food frequency. Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed to identify patterns of diet quality.

Results: The mean BMI/age Z-score was -0.62. Approximately 60% of adolescents had FEV1≥60%, and 21% had severe impairment (FEV1<40%). Better BMI/age Z-score were observed in groups with higher consumption frequencies of vegetables and fruit (≥5/week), white meat (>3-4/week), and oil (>3-4/week). Linear regression models identified significant relationships: BMI/age Z-Score=-3.25+ 0.8182*meat_b+0.5082*vegetables_fruit (p<0.001): Increased white meat, fruit, and vegetable consumption positively influenced the BMI/age Z-Score; lung function = 0.6927 + 0.3356*vegetables-0.2406*fruit_vegetables-0.4550*fast_food (p<0.001): Lower consumption of fruit and vegetables and higher fast-food intake were associated with more severe lung function; and lung function = 0.39376 -0.32345 *ZSCORE (p<0.0001): The BMI/age Z-Score positively influenced lung function. PCA confirmed the positive relationship between fruit, vegetables and white meat consumption and BMI/age Z-score.

Conclusion: Higher consumption of fruit, vegetables and meat has a positive influence on the BMI/age Z-score and lung function among adolescents with CF.

records.title: Nutritional status and bone strength in children and adolescents with cystic fibrosis: an observational study
records.authors_text: E. Dionisio1, S. Castanheira2, R. Bragança3, S. Castanhinha3, A.C. Moreira4
records.affiliations_text: 1ULS São José, Nutrição, Lisboa, Portugal, 2Escola Superior de Saude de Lisboa, Nutrição, Lisboa, Portugal, 3ULS São José, Pneumologia, Lisboa, Portugal, 4Escola Superior de Saude de Lisboa; H&TRC-Health Technology Research Center, Nutrição, Lisboa, Portugal
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive hereditary disease. Malnutrition is a common clinical manifestation, mainly due to malabsorption, decreased energy intake, and increased nutritional needs. Additionally, bone metabolism in these patients may also be compromised, resulting in low bone density and a consequent increased risk of fracture. This study aims to characterize the nutritional status and the bone strength (BS) of children and adolescents with CF.

Materials and Methods: This is an observational, analytical, cross-sectional study. Clinical history (type of mutation, pharmacotherapy, FEV1, and serum parameters) was collected in 25 patients. Nutritional status was characterized by weight, height, and BMI. Bone Strength was evaluated by the speed of sound in the radius and tibia using bone ultrasound. A 95% confidence level was established.

Results: Median age was 8.4 ± 5.03 years, with the majority (56%) aged between 2 and 12 years. According to the BMI-age-z-score, 88% of patients had adequate nutritional status, but 2 children had weight impairment, and 1 child had height impairment, when assessed by weight-for-age and height-for-age z-scores, respectively. Although most patients had adequate BS for age and sex, there were 35.3% and 16.7% cases of osteopenia, when assessed in the radius and tibia, respectively. There were no significant correlations between BS and nutritional status, but when compared by groups, we found were significantly lower FEV1 values in the group with compromised BS, both in the radius (p=0.045) and in the tibia (p=0.048).

Conclusion: Although the data reflect a population mostly with adequate nutritional status, some cases of osteopenia have already been verified. It is therefore essential to have follow-up appointments with specialized CF specialists that provide preventive care not only on nutritional status but also in promoting bone health, thus increasing the quality of life of these patients.

records.title: Assessment of Fat Mass Index and Fat-Free Mass Index in adult patients with cystic fibrosis after initiation of triple modulator therapy
records.authors_text: S. Pereira1, J. Laureano1, M. Pitta Grós Dias1, G. Pipa2, A.C. Moreira3, P. Almeida Nunes4, E. Fragoso5, P. Azevedo5
records.affiliations_text: 1ULS Santa Maria, Departmant of Dietetics and Nutrition, Lisboa, Portugal, 2Lisbon School of Health Technology Polytechnic Institute of Lisbon, Lisboa, Portugal, 3Lisbon School of Health Technology Reserch Center, Lisboa, Portugal, 4Department of Dietetics and Nutrition, Lisboa, Portugal, 5ULS Santa Maria, Cystic Fibrosis Reference Centre, Lisboa, Portugal
records.abstract_text:
Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is a hereditary disease characterized by a mutation in the Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator (CFTR) gene. Progressive pulmonary disease, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, and increased concentrations of chloride and sodium ions in sweat are the most evident manifestations of CF. Therapeutic approaches aim to delay pulmonary deterioration and maintain an adequate nutritional status. Advances in multidisciplinary CF care have been reflected in improved disease prognosis. Triple modulator therapy (TMT) is an effective therapeutic option, contributing to improvements in nutritional status.

Objectives: Analyze the impact of TMT on Fat Mass Index (FMI) and Fat-Free Mass Index (FFMI) in a group of adult patients with CF, before and after the initiation of this therapy.

Methods: Observational, cross-sectional study including 30 adult patient under TMT, followed in a Nutrition outpatient clinic. Nutritional assessment was done prior to the start of TMT, at least 3 months after TMT initiation, and during the 2 subsequent follow-up visits. FMI and FFMI, with respective classifications according to reference percentile values. Data were analyzed using SPSS statistical software and were considered statistically significant at (p<0,05).

Results: Statistical analysis demonstrated the presence of significant changes over time, confirming the beneficial effect of TMT on the nutritional status. However, some patients transitioned to elevated body composition states, such as increased FMI, or in some cases consistently remained at low FFMI levels. Certain factos, such as physical activity level and dietary patterns, were not included in this analysis, which may represent a limitation of this study.

Conclusion: This study demonstrates the significant impact of TMT on FMI and FFMI variables; but the implementation of a highly personalized intervention is essential. This study provides valuable insights into body composition in adults with CF.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: ETI has significantly altered the nutritional trajectory of cwCF, with clinical rollout outpacing the development of nutritional guidance. This study aimed to 1. systematically review the literature on ETI and nutrition 2. develop expert consensus-based guidance 3. highlight research gaps.

Methods: This project was registered on PROSPERO (ID: 587618) and guided by a multidisciplinary panel of 22 clinicians and a parent representative. Research questions were developed using the PICO framework across domains including anthropometry, body composition, vitamins, minerals, cholesterol, diet, endocrine and exocrine pancreatic status and ETI administration. A literature search was conducted across Medline, Embase, CINAHL, and Cochrane (up to and including April 2025). Studies were screened, assessed using SIGN criteria, and summarised in evidence tables. Draft statements were refined through iterative discussion, with final consensus achieved (≥80% agreement) using real-time Delphi. Research priorities were determined based on the highest proportion of “Strongly Agree” responses.

records.title: A retrospective analysis of the relationship between body composition, muscle strength and function in cystic fibrosis

person.title: Ms.
person.department: National Referral Centre for Adult Cystic Fibrosis

records.authors_text: C. Reilly1, C. Landers1, C. O'Connor1, S. Carter1, T. Nicholson1, E. McKone1
records.affiliations_text: 1St Vincent's University Hospital, National Referral Centre for Adult Cystic Fibrosis, Dublin, Ireland
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Reduced muscle mass, strength and function are associated with poor exercise tolerance, and survival in people with CF. This study aimed to characterise and explore the relationship between body composition, muscle strength and function in people with CF (pwCF).

Methods: Retrospective data was collected from clinically stable adults who attended annual review assessments in 2024 and 2025. Data on age, genotype, CFTR modulator use, FEV1, exocrine pancreatic status, diabetes status and P. Aeruginosa colonisation was recorded. Body composition was measured using bioelectrical impedance analysis (Seca M515). Muscle strength was assessed using Peak Torque at 60°/s (Biodex® PRO 3), and muscle function using peak workload (Wpeak - watts) during cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET). Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS v29, with significance set at p<0.05.

Results: The study included 123 pwCF (54% male); mean age was 33 years (SD 10.8). 108(88%) were pancreatic insufficient, 33(27%) had CF related diabetes and 82 (67%) were colonised with P.aeruginosa. Mean BMI was 24kg/m2 (SD3.46), and mean FEV1 was 81%.

Clinical Data CategorySub-CategoryNumber Percentage %Wpeak n=63Low1931%Normal 1829%High2540%Peak torque % of predicted value n=60

Low3050%Normal 2237%High813%Skeletal Muscle Mass (SMM) n=123Low2925%Normal 9275%High0 Fat Mass Index (FMI) n=123Low22%Normal 7661%Increased 3529%High108%

Independently, as age and BMI increased, muscle strength decreased (p<0.05). FEV1 positively correlated with muscle function but negatively with age (p<0.05). Muscle mass was positively associated with BMI, muscle function and strength (p<0.05).

Conclusion: Impaired muscle mass, strength and function were common despite normal FEV1 and BMI in pwCF. Results reinforce the clinical need for body composition measurement rather than BMI as a determinant of muscle strength and function. Targeted interventions including resistance exercise and nutritional strategies are important to preserve muscle health and functional outcomes in pwCF.

records.title: Dietetic prescribing for the nutritional management of cystic fibrosis

person.institution: St Bartholomew's Hospital, Bart's Health NHS Trust

records.authors_text: M. Dunnage1
records.affiliations_text: 1St Bartholomew's Hospital, Bart's Health NHS Trust, Bart's Adult CF Centre, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Non-medical prescribing (NMP) can improve service efficiency, innovation and is cost saving (Babashahi et al, 2025). In the UK, legislation changed in 2016 and dietitians can now train to become supplementary prescribers (SP). Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a multisystem disease involving pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, diabetes and gastrointestinal symptoms such as reflux and constipation. The CF Dietitian has the specialist knowledge to prescribe medications related to the nutritional management of patients with CF (NHS England, 2015). SP prescribe medications from a clinical management plan (CMP) agreed between a doctor and the SP. There are no specific formulary restrictions, though the SP must prescribe for conditions within their scope of practice. (BDA, 2016; RPS, 2021) This service evaluation sought to review the prescribing activity of a dietetic SP in one adult CF centre.

Methods: All medications prescribed between September 2024 and December 2025 were recorded, including the dose and any adverse events. The location of the prescribing activity was also reviewed.

Results:

MedicationFrequencyPancreatic Enzyme Replacement Therapy27Laxatives (Macrogol, sodium docusate, Gastrografin®, Picolax®)14Insulin (Degludec, Lispro, Glargine, Aspart)4Flash glucose sensors1Proton pump inhibitors1Vitamin supplements (colecalciferol, CF specific multivitamin)3Table 1: Frequency of medications prescribed by a dietetic supplementary prescriber in one cystic fibrosis centre in the UK

Fifty medications were prescribed in 40 episodes, for 18 patients. Three were inpatients. All patients had a CMP signed prior to SP. All patients consented to dietetic prescribing. There were no medication errors or adverse events noted. Pancreatic Enzyme Replacement Therapy was the most common medication prescribed due to the recent shortage in UK community pharmacies, requiring this to be dispensed from the hospital pharmacy. The signing of the CMP was a barrier to prescribing more frequently on an ad hoc basis and during inpatient admissions.

Conclusion: Dietetic SP in CF brings dietetic and medical management strategies together. It is safe, efficient and can reduce the number of referrals to other prescribers which is likely to result in cost savings. Further research is needed to review the efficacy of dietetic prescribing in CF in comparison to other medical or NMPs.

records.title: The impact of modulator therapies on pancreatic function in children with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: E. Sheppard1, G. Buckley1, A. Maitra2, A. Shawcross2, K. Rose2
records.affiliations_text: 1Royal Manchester Children's Hospital, Therapies and Dietetics, Manchester, United Kingdom, 2Royal Manchester Children's Hospital, Paediatric Respiratory Medicine, Manchester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: Recent studies show that CFTR modulator use in children with Cystic Fibrosis (CF) improves gastrointestinal symptoms, reduces pancreatic enzyme use, improves vitamin status and may lead to recovery of pancreatic function (Rosenfeld Lancet Resp Med 2018). A 2022 review at our centre found 3/9 children with CF on modulators, who had a faecal elastase (FE) sample collected had become pancreatic sufficient (PS; FE >200μg/g). Since 2022, modulator therapy has been extended to children aged over 1 or 2 years, depending on genotype.

Aim: To assess the sustained effects of modulator therapy on pancreatic function in children who became PS and to determine whether earlier modulator initiation increases PS rates.

Methods: Children aged 1–14 years prescribed a CFTR modulator at our large paediatric centre were identified. Patient records were reviewed for FE and fat-soluble vitamin levels.

Results: Of 105 children on a modulator with baseline pancreatic insufficiency (PI), 59 underwent FE testing after reported gastrointestinal changes or >6 months of modulator use. Nine patients (8.5%) became PS. Twenty-three (22%) showed a rise in FE to 15–200μg/g, while 27 remained <15μg/g. No repeat FE was available for 46 patients due to presence of gastrointestinal symptoms or reluctance to provide samples. Of those who became PS, median age at modulator initiation was 2 years (range 1–9 years). Time to PS ranged from 3 months to 5 years across different modulator therapies. Repeat testing (n=3) showed sustained FE >200μg/g for up to 3 years. In patients with rising FE who remained PI, 19/23 required reduction of fat-soluble vitamin doses due to elevated levels.

Conclusion: This real-world data demonstrates that children with CF can become PS up to 5 years after starting modulator therapy, with sustained improvement in those retested. Partial recovery of pancreatic function is often associated with elevated vitamin levels. Monitoring of fat-soluble vitamins post modulator initiation and consideration of annual FE testing may be beneficial.

records.title: Lumacaftor/ivacaftor at 1 year of age and improved pancreatic function
records.authors_text: E. Sheppard1, G. Buckley1, A. Maitra2, A. Shawcross2, K. Rose2
records.affiliations_text: 1Royal Manchester Children's Hospital, Therapies and Dietetics, Manchester, United Kingdom, 2Royal Manchester Children's Hospital, Paediatric Respiratory Medicine, Manchester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: In the UK the licence for prescribing lumacaftor/Ivacaftor (Orkambi®) was extended to children over 1 year with a diagnosis of cystic fibrosis homozygous for F508del in early 2023 (Rayment AM J Respir Crit Care Med 2022). Our large tertiary paediatric centre and shared care network routinely offer initiation of Orkambi® to eligible patients age one year, prior to initiation of ETI at two years.

Aim: We aimed to look at trends in pancreatic function in children with pancreatic insufficiency in the first year of life who were commenced on Orkambi® prior to age two years.

Methods: Patients born between January 2021 and June 2024 were identified from our patient cohort and information on age at initiation of modulator therapy and any faecal elastase (FE) results were obtained from our electronic patient record.

Results: We identified 20 patients who were F508del homozygous and commenced on Orkambi® prior to two years of age. Faecal elastase was checked in 13/20 patients (clinical decision – usually if any changes in stool / gastrointestinal symptoms were noted during clinical reviews). 7/20 (35%) patients have become pancreatic sufficient (PS, with FE level >200ug/g), with six of these becoming PS within a year of commencing Orkambi® and prior to moving to ETI. The 7th patient became PS after moving onto ETI. All 7 have discontinued pancreatic enzyme therapy. A further six patients had some increase in pancreatic function (with a FE 15-200ug/g). FE hadn’t been tested in 7 patients.

Conclusion: Our real-world data has demonstrated that early therapy with CFTR modulators including lumacaftor/ivacaftor which is licenced from 12 months of age may lead to greater numbers of pwCF becoming pancreatic sufficient.

records.title: Service evaluation of a virtual ‘vitamin club’ for optimising fat-soluble vitamin management in children with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: M. Healy1, L. Schembri2, S. Kenny2, C. Walker2, I. Balfour-Lynn3, S. Bentley1
records.affiliations_text: 1Royal Brompton Hospital, Pharmacy, London, United Kingdom, 2Royal Brompton Hospital, Dietetics, London, United Kingdom, 3Royal Brompton Hospital, Paediatric Respiratory, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: Annual assessments at our paediatric cystic fibrosis (CF) centre include serum vitamins A, D and E to guide supplementation. With widespread CFTR modulator use (such as elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor [ETI]), studies report elevated fat-soluble vitamin levels, especially vitamin A [1], reinforcing the need for monitoring.

A fortnightly virtual ‘vitamin club’ was introduced to streamline result follow-up, comprising of a specialist paediatric respiratory dietitian and prescribing pharmacist. This multidisciplinary approach aimed to improve efficiency, reduce delays in decision making, and ensure consistent specialist-led care.

Aim: To evaluate the ‘vitamin club’ by quantifying reviewed results, abnormal findings and prescription changes.

Methods: Retrospective review of children with CF managed within ‘vitamin club’ between August ’24 and July ’25. Data were collected from annual review records and electronic patient records.

Results: 246 children were reviewed; complete results were initially available for 228 (93%), while 17 (7%) required repeat sampling. Interventions were needed in 68 (28%) children, 87% on CFTR modulators. Adjustments included:

• Vitamin A: nine dose increases, six decreases (five on ETI), no discontinued prescriptions. Zinc added for two children.

• Vitamin E: 14 reductions (all on ETI), seven increases, two discontinued.

• Vitamin D: 20 high one-off doses for deficiency (<50 ng/mL), six maintenance dose increases.

Adherence was addressed in five children without changing the prescription.

Conclusion: ‘Vitamin club’ enabled specialist-led interventions in over a quarter of children, ensuring optimal supplementation. Continued monitoring remains essential in the modulator era. A key strength is the effective use of the multidisciplinary team for streamlined care.

References: Schembri L, et al. Impact of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor on fat-soluble vitamin levels in children with cystic fibrosis. J Cyst Fibros.2023;22(5):843-846.

Objective: To evaluate changes in pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT), dietary intake and body composition in preschool children aged 2–5 years with cystic fibrosis (CF) who initiated modulator therapy with elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor® (ETI), evaluated after 12 months of treatment.

Materials and Methods: This was a prospective, single-centre pilot study. Variables analysed before (pre) and after (post) 12 months of ETI included body mass index (BMI) z-score, fat mass percentage, fat-free mass percentage, energy intake, van de Kamer test, fat intake, lipase units (LU) per kg per day and LU per gram of fat consumed. A 3-day dietary record including PERT was collected (nutritional analysis performed using DietSource® 4.0 software). Body composition was assessed by electrical bioimpedance analysis (Maltron®). Statistical analysis was performed using STATA 18.0.

Results: A total of 17 children with CF (69% female) initiated ETI treatment. Median age was 3.4 years (interquartile range 2.9–4.8), and 100% were diagnosed through newborn screening. All patients had pancreatic insufficiency. All carried at least one F508del mutation (31% homozygous). Table 1 summarises the values of the variables of interest and the associated p values for differences between time points.

However, the significant adjustment in lipase units per gram of fat consumed indicates a more appropriate matching of pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy to dietary fat intake following ETI, which may enhance nutritional management in this age group.

records.title: Nutritional status of cystic fibrosis patients in a country without neonatal screening: data from the Republic of Moldova

person.institution: Nicolae Testemitanu State University of Medicine and Pharmacy

records.authors_text: C. Tomacinschii1,2, C. Conica1,2, D. Efros1, N. Buga1, R. Selvestru1, N. Barbova1,2, S. Sciuca1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Nicolae Testemitanu State University of Medicine and Pharmacy, Pediatrics, Chișinău, Moldova, Republic of, 2Institute of Mother and Child, Chișinău, Moldova, Republic of
records.abstract_text:
Optimal nutritional status is a key determinant of pulmonary function and survival in cystic fibrosis (CF).

Aim: To assess the nutritional status of CF patients followed at the national CF center in the Republic of Moldova (RM).

Methods: We performed a retrospective cross-sectional analysis of CF patients registered at the Center for Cystic Fibrosis during the follow-up year 2024. Demographic data, age at diagnosis, anthropometric parameters and pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy use were analyzed descriptively.

Results: A total of 60 patients were included, of whom 52 were actively followed. The mean age at follow-up was 14.6 years (range 0.6–38.7), and 29.8% of patients were adults. The mean age at diagnosis was 3.23 years, reflecting delayed diagnosis in the absence of neonatal screening. Mean height Z-scores were below international reference values across all age groups, with the most pronounced deficit observed in adolescents aged 12-17 years (mean −1.4). Weight impairment was more severe, particularly in adolescents (mean weight Z-score -2.0) and young adults aged 18-29 years (mean -2.2), with extreme values as low as -6.8.

In children, the mean BMI Z-score was -1.2; 50-57.1% of adolescents aged 12-17 years had BMI Z-scores <−2, with similar prevalence in males and females. Among adults, mean BMI was 18.5 kg/m², with lower values observed in males compared with females; the majority of adult patients had BMI ≤20 kg/m².

Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy was prescribed in 92.3% of patients, consistent with a high prevalence of pancreatic insufficiency.

Conclusions: CF patients in the RM exhibit marked nutritional compromise, likely related to delayed diagnosis and lack of disease-modifying therapies. These findings emphasize the critical need for early diagnosis strategies, optimized nutritional interventions and improved access to comprehensive CF care in resource-limited settings.

records.title: Exploring hand grip strength to promote a healthy weight and lifestyle in adults with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: A. Marshall1, A. Smith1, H. Sheddon2, S. Hunt3
records.affiliations_text: 1NHS Tayside, Adult CF Service, Dundee, United Kingdom, 2Queen Margaret University, Physiotherapy (MSc Student), Edinburgh, United Kingdom, 3Robert Gordon University, Physiotherapy (MPhys Student), Aberdeen, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Hand grip strength (HGS) is an emerging biomarker associated with overall health status, mortality risk, disability, and nutritional assessment in the general population. Lower HGS has been linked to poorer clinical outcomes in individuals with cystic fibrosis (CF), including increased exacerbations, reduced lung function, lower BMI, and poorer bone health. This project aimed to explore associations between HGS, BMI and lung function, and assess patient acceptability. Secondary aims were to evaluate whether monitoring HGS has a place at annual review assessment, as a tool to motivate adults with cystic fibrosis (CF) to improve physical activity and nutritional status.

Methods: 9 adults with CF attending outpatient clinics and due for annual review, were recruited for assessment. Baseline measures included hand grip strength (dynamometer), BMI, dietary intake, physical activity and lung function (FEV₁). Participants received feedback on grip strength and tailored advice to encourage activity and improve energy balance. Qualitative feedback captured patient perspectives on the approach.

Results: Across the cohort, mean grip strength corresponded to the 28th percentile relative to normative data. No clear correlations were observed between HGS and physical activity, BMI, or lung function; notably, the patient with the highest grip strength reported no regular exercise. Most participants demonstrated normal BMI ranges, limiting the ability to detect nutrition-related trends. Nonetheless, patients expressed high engagement with the HGS testing process and viewed grip strength feedback as motivating and informative.

Conclusion: Grip strength monitoring appears feasible and acceptable in CF care, with potential to open conversations on physical activity and nutritional health. Incorporating this approach into dietetic practice could enhance patient motivation, support weight management, and contribute to long-term outcomes.

records.title: Impact of nutritional quality improvement project: the first 1000 days of life
records.authors_text: D. Kocaman1,2, M. Selçuk3, Ş. Karabulut3, A.C. Yıldız3, N.M. Çakar3, F. Özdemircioğlu3, E.E. Baysal3, M. Akkitap3, B. Demirel Özgünay3, E. Uğurlu3, B. Uzunoğlu1, G. Taştan1, A.P. Ergenekon3, E. Erdem Eralp3, Y. Gökdemir3, F. Karakoç3, B. Karadağ3
records.affiliations_text: 1Marmara University, Cystic Fibrosis Center, Istanbul, Turkey, 2Acıbadem Mehmet Ali Aydınlar University, Faculty of Health Sciences, Department of Nutrition and Dietetics, Istanbul, Turkey, 3Marmara University, Pediatric Pulmonology, Istanbul, Turkey
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: Newborn screening for cystic fibrosis (CF) offers an opportunity for early medical and nutritional interventions, potentially leading to improved clinical outcomes. Higher body mass index (BMI) percentiles at two years of age have been strongly associated with improved pulmonary function in later childhood. Epidemiological evidence indicates that enhancing the nutritional status of young children is linked to more favorable pulmonary outcomes. The aim of this study is to investigate the effects of the quality improvement project implemented at our center on children under the age of two who are closely monitored by dietitian.

Methods: This is a single center QI project initiated in 2019. CF patients diagnosed via newborn screening or symptoms within the first year of life were included. These patients were evaluated monthly by the CF dieatitian in the center or reported their measurements to the dietitian via phone, email, or other communication methods. Based on their anthropometric data and clinical symptoms, nutritional recommendations were provided and enzyme replacement therapy dosages were adjusted accordingly.

Results: Over a period of six years, 66 patients were included. Six patients were diagnosed after the six month years old. The median age (min-max) at initiation of follow-up is 92.5 ( 3.0–365.0) days. Diagnosis was made via newborn screening program in 53 (75.7%) of the patients. The median age (min-max) at diagnosis was 0.1 (0.0-1.0) years. An increase in weight, height, and BMI percentiles was observed during follow-up. Over a two-year follow-up period, the weight percentile increased from 23.3 to 56.3, the height percentile from 20 to 30.3, and the BMI percentile from 20.7 to 46.6.

Conclusion: Close monitoring in patients with cystic fibrosis has been found to have a positive impact on growth. This study is also important in demonstrating the positive impact of quality improvement projects implemented at the cystic fibrosis center.

records.title: Leeds experience of PERT usage in the CFTRm era
records.authors_text: J. Lowdon1, T. Lee1
records.affiliations_text: 1Leeds Children's Hospital, Cystic Fibrosis Unit, Leeds, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Pancreatic Insufficiency (PI) was previously thought to be irreversible in Cystic Fibrosis (CF), but in the era of Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator modulators (CFTRm), this is now being refuted (1). Our aim was to identify and review the clinical status of children with CF (cwCF) who are PI, on a CFTRm, who have been able to stop Pancreatic Enzyme Replacement Therapy (PERT), in our clinical cohort.

Methods: A total of 160 cwCF were reviewed in our clinical cohort. PI was determined with a faecal pancreatic elastase-1 (FE-1) level of <100ug/g stool for moderate PI and <200ug/g stool for severe PI at diagnosis. Medical notes were reviewed for those who had stopped PERT, including genetics, pancreatic elastase 1 level (FE-1 level), date when PERT was stopped, clinical symptoms, vitamin supplementation and growth parameters post stopping PERT.

Results: Eleven PI cwCF have stopped PERT after commencing a CFTRm. Three presented with meconium ileus at diagnosis. Ten are homozygous for Phe508del. Eight were on elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (Kaftrio®) at the time of stopping PERT, one on lumacaftor/ivacaftor (Orkambi®). Age at time of stopping PERT ranged from one year six months - 11 years five months. Only four were able to provide a FE-1 level within the accepted range for a pancreatic sufficient (PS) level (>200ug/g stool). Five remain low, one has refused to provide a sample and one is awaiting the result. The main reason cited for stopping PERT, despite a low FE-1 level, is constipation. Weaning off PERT varied individually. Since stopping PERT, no worsening gastro-intestinal (GI) symptoms or growth parameters have been identified. No one has managed to stop vitamin supplementation.

Conclusions: It is important to continue to monitor pancreatic function in cwCF on any CFTRm. Whilst some cwCF demonstrated an improvement in FE-1 levels consistent with PS, others were still able to stop PERT based on clinical symptoms. Consideration therefore needs to be given to GI symptoms, as well as FE-1 levels.

1. Stephenson et al. Changes in fecal elastase-1 following initiation of CFTR modulator therapy in pediatric patients with cystic fibrosis. Journal of Cystic Fibrosis 22 (2023) 996–1001.

records.title: The effect of targeted therapy with CFTR modulators on the relationship between nutritional status, carbohydrate and lipid metabolism in children with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: A. Pushkareva1, O. Simonova2,1, T. Borovik2,1, I. Sokolov2, N. Liabina2, N. Kashirskaya3
records.affiliations_text: 1I.M. Sechenov First Moscow State Medical University (Sechenov University), Moscow, Russian Federation, 2National Medical Research Center for Children's Health, Moscow, Russian Federation, Moscow, Russian Federation, 3Research Centre for Medical Genetics, Moscow, Russian Federation, Moscow, Russian Federation
records.abstract_text:
Relevance: Targeted therapy (TT) has become integral to cystic fibrosis (CF) management by addressing the underlying defect. Alongside its pulmonary benefits, TT may systemically affect metabolic parameters such as glycemic control and lipid profiles, which are common complications impacting prognosis and quality of life in CF. Understanding this metabolic influence is essential for holistic patient care.

Materials and methods: A total of 76 children with CF (cwCF) aged 6 to 17 years and 11 months were included in the comparative study. Among them, 39 cwCF (Group 1) received only basic therapy, and 37 were on TT (Group 2). The groups were comparable in terms of age and sex. CwCF in Group 2 had been receiving TT for at least 3 months. We assessed the impact of therapy on nutritional status as body mass index for age Z-scores (BAZ), glycemic control (fasting glucose, HbA1c), and lipid profile (total cholesterol, HDL, LDL). Statistical comparisons used Student's t-test or the Mann-Whitney U-test, as appropriate. Effect size was calculated using Cohen's d. Correlations between BAZ and biochemical parameters were analyzed with Pearson's coefficient.

Results: cwCF receiving TT (Group 2) showed a significant 75.7% increase in BAZ (p=0.0087, d=0.65) and a 5.7% reduction in HbA1c (p=0.0003, d=0.47) compared to those on basic therapy (Group 1). The lipid changes presented a dual effect: while beneficial HDL cholesterol increased significantly (16.1%; p=0.0101), there were also concerning rises in both total cholesterol (14.6%; p=0.0024) and LDL cholesterol (16.4%; p=0.0390), respectively. No significant difference was found in fasting glucose (p=0.377), and no strong correlations (|r|<0.26, p>0.1) were detected between BAZ and other metabolic markers.

Conclusions: TT in CF has a dual metabolic effect: improving glycemic control but inducing dyslipidemia. This warrants personalized monitoring of both respiratory and metabolic parameters for timely intervention.

records.title: Essential fatty acid imbalance in a paediatric cystic fibrosis population: a single-centre study
records.authors_text: C. Arriaga1, B. Alves Costa1, I. Melo2,1, C. Maia1, S. Almeida1, R. Ferreira1, J. Roda1, R. Penteado1
records.affiliations_text: 1Hospital Pediátrico, ULS Coimbra, Paediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition Unit, Coimbra, Portugal, 2Serviço de Pediatria, USF Dão Lafões, Viseu, Portugal
records.abstract_text:
Introduction/Objectives: Essential fatty acids (EFA) imbalance, characterized by increased levels of arachidonic acid (AA) and decreased levels of docosahexaenoic acids (DHA), has been documented in cystic fibrosis (CF). EFA intestinal absorption is particularly compromised in CF due to pancreatic insuficiency. Despite this detrimental pro-inflammatory profile, DHA suplementation is not widely recommended. This study aimed to evaluate EFA levels in a paediatric CF population and look for associations with clinical features.

Materials and Methods: Observational, prospective, single-centre study evaluating paediatric patients with CF. Data collected included serum levels of AA, EPA and DHA, inflammatory markers, pulmonary function, chronic respiratory infections, nutritional status, exocrine pancreatic function and cystic fibrosis hepatobiliary involvement (CFHBI).

Results: The cohort included 27 CF patients, 16 were males, with a mean age of 8.27 years (0.4–16.7). Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency was present in 88.9% of patients and CFHBI in 14.8%. CFTR modulator therapy was used by 66.7% of patients. Mean BMI z-score was −0.23 (−2.22–1.87). Median CRP was 0.05 mg/dL (IQR 0.04–0.14). Most patients presented EFA levels within reference ranges. However, 3 (11%) patients had DHA deficiency; 2 had AA deficiency and 1 had high AA levels. Mean AA/DHA ratio was 4.29 (1.69-9.12). Patients with DHA deficiency had significantly higher AA/DHA ratio (p=0.028). An association between DHA deficiency and CFHBI (p=0.049) was found. No other significant associations between low EFA and clinical or laboratory parameters were found.

Conclusion: Most patients exhibited serum EFA levels within reference ranges, however 3 patients had DHA deficiency. Larger prospective studies may help to determine clinical significance of EFA imbalance and to clarify the benefit of targeted EFA supplementation strategies, particularly in patients with CFHBI.

records.title: Early development profile in children with cystic fibrosis: findings of the ages and stages questionnaires inventory and affecting factors
records.authors_text: E. Altay Tanyer1, N. Ünsal2, E. Yalçın1, E.N. Özmert2, B. Çapraz Yavuz1, N. Emiralioğlu1, D. Doğru1, U. Özçelik1
records.affiliations_text: 1Hacettepe University School of Medicine, Department of Pediatric Pulmonology, Ankara, Turkey, 2Hacettepe University School of Medicine, Department of Developmental Pediatrics, Ankara, Turkey
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a multisystemic disease where malnutrition, recurrent infections, and frequent hospitalizations may negatively impact child development. The Ages and Stages Questionnaires (ASQ) are a reliable screening tool designed to evaluate communication, gross motor, fine motor, problem-solving, and personal-social domains. This study aims to examines developmental characteristics of children with CF using the ASQ inventory and investigates relationship with developmental scores and demographic, anthropometric, and clinical data.

Method: Files of 20 CF patients evaluated at Developmental Pediatrics outpatient clinic between January 2019 and July 2025 were reviewed. ASQ domain scores, demographic, anthropometric, clinical, and laboratory data were recorded. Relationships were analyzed using Spearman correlation; simple and multiple linear regression analyses were performed to identify independent predictors.

Results: In 20 patients (n=11, 55% female), median age was 4.59 years; median BMI was 15.6 kg/m². Developmental delays occurred in fine motor (n=5), problem-solving (n=3), personal-social (n=2), and communication (n=1). Maternal education (rs=0.632, p=0.003) and Vitamin D levels (rs=0.494, p=0.027) positively correlated with problem-solving scores. Daycare attendance linked to higher fine motor scores (p=0.045). records.title: Do pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy doses reduce in young children with cystic fibrosis post-elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor? A single-centre experience

person.institution: Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children NHS Trust

records.authors_text: E. Owen1, P. Roper1, R. Brugha2, C. Edmondson2
records.affiliations_text: 1Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children NHS Trust, Dietetics, London, United Kingdom, 2Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children NHS Trust, Respiratory Unit, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: CFTR modulators may improve or restore pancreatic function in young children with CF (cwCF)(1). There is limited evidence on pancreatic recovery and weaning pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT). Following our previous work on changes in PERT and faecal elastase-1 (FE-1) in cwCF aged 2-5 years post-elexacaftor/ivacaftor/tezacaftor (ETI) at 3 months, we sought to review changes in PERT through to 1 year.

Methods: We retrospectively collected the following data: genotype, FE-1(µg/g), average daily PERT dose, anthropometry and prior modulator (PM) use in cwCF aged 2-5 years at baseline and 3 monthly intervals post-ETI. Pancreatic insufficiency (PI) was classified as (µg/g stool): <100 severe, 100-200 borderline, >200 pancreatic sufficient. High PERT dose >10,000 as per ECFS guideline(2), moderate PERT dose 3,000-9,999 and <3,000 low dose (units/lipase/kg). Data were analysed using PRISM, comparisons by Wilcoxon signed rank test.

Results: 29 cwCF were included: 17 homozygous dF508, 11 heterozygous dF508 and one other. 17 were PM. All had severe PI and were taking PERT at baseline. Median (IQR) age 4.4 (3.3-5.15) years at ETI initiation.

There was a statistically significant reduction in PERT doses at all time points compared to baseline. At 6 and 12 months improvements in FE-1 were seen in some children, however only one was able to stop PERT at 12 months. BMI z-score remained optimal.

Conclusion: We showed a reduction in average daily PERT doses of 1,433 units/lipase/kg in this cohort of young children at 1 year post-ETI, without compromising growth. While this reduction was statistically significant, it remains unclear if it is clinically significant as only one patient was able to stop PERT. Attempts are being made to standardise FE-1 monitoring and PERT adjustments with ETI, however our data suggests further work is needed and an individualised approach may be required.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: CFTR modulators may improve Fat Soluble Vitamin (FSV) absorption with risk of high levels (1). We investigated change in serum FSV levels A, D and E, and CF specific supplementation in a real world population of young children with Cystic Fibrosis (cwCF) after initiation of Elexacaftor/Tezacaftor/Ivacaftor (ETI).

Methods: Retrospective data review was performed in pancreatic insufficient patients aged 2-5 years at baseline, 3, 6 and 12-months post ETI initiation. Routine non-fasting serum FSV levels taken when clinically stable were analysed against local reference ranges. Data collected also included genotype, prior modulator (PM) use and CF specific FSV supplementation dosing at baseline and 12-months. Data was analysed using PRISM.

Results: Twenty nine children were included 17 homozygous dF508, 11 heterozygous dF508, 1 other. Median (IQR) age 4.4 (3.3-5.2) y at ETI initiation. 17 were PM.

While not statistically significant vitamin A peaked 6-months post ETI with 34% having high levels. Vitamin E peaked at 12-months. Vitamin D levels fluctuated with statistical significance between baseline to 6-months. records.title: Changes in vitamin levels in cystic fibrosis patients receiving CFTR modulator therapy
records.authors_text: F.G. Ersan1, A.T. Aslan1, A.B. Cetinkaya1, T. Sismanlar Eyuboglu1
records.affiliations_text: 1Gazi University Faculty of Medicine, Pediatric Pulmonology, Ankara, Turkey
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: CFTR modulators improve pancreatic function and may increase fat-soluble vitamin levels in cystic fibrosis (CF). This study aimed to evaluate changes in vitamin levels in patients receiving CFTR modulator therapy.

Methods: CF patients receiving modulator therapy for ≥3 months were retrospectively analyzed. Vitamin levels, BMI Z-score, sweat chloride, pulmonary function, fecal elastase, and bone mineral density (BMD) were assessed at baseline, 3 and 12 months.

Results: Twenty-seven patients (66% male, mean age 12.2±5.2 years) were included. Nineteen patients (70%) received elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor + ivacaftor and the remaining patients received ivacaftor. BMI Z-score improved from −1.19±0.19 to −0.72±0.97 and −0.52±1.10 at 3rd and 12th months (p<0.001, p=0.03). Sweat chloride decreased from 83.6±17.3 to 67.5±16.2 and 53.7±13.7 mmol/L (both p<0.001). FEV₁ Z-score increased from −1.18±1.76 to −0.06±1.32 and −0.06±1.45(p=0.02, p=0.04). Median fecal elastase increased from 41.6 to 176.6 µg/g (p=0.286). Median vitamin A levels increased significantly from 0.32 to 0.47 and 0.40 mg/L (p=0.05, p=0.014). Vitamin E showed a non-significant increase, while vitamin D and INR remained unchanged. Vitamin levels changes were not associated with modulator type. Vitamin supplementation was reduced in 15% of patients. BMD Z-scores did not change significantly.

Conclusion: CFTR modulator therapy was associated with a significant increase in vitamin A levels in patients with CF. Although vitamin E levels showed a numerical increase, this was not statistically significant. Close monitoring of vitamin levels in CF patients receiving modulator therapy is essential to prevent unnecessary supplementation and to reduce the risk of hypervitaminosis.

records.title: Body composition in adult cystic fibrosis patients, dynamics under targeted therapy.

person.title: MD, PhD
person.institution: Federal Pulmonology Research Institute, Federal Medical and Biological Agency

records.authors_text: N. Krylova1, E. Amelina1, S. Krasovsky1, R. Kagazezhev1, M. Afanasyeva1
records.affiliations_text: 1Federal Pulmonology Research Institute, Federal Medical and Biological Agency, Cystic Fibrosis, Moscow, Russian Federation
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To compare body composition in CF patients receiving standard and pathogenetic therapy.

Methods: The study included 64 CF patients over 18 years of age; 40 of them received targeted therapy.

Results: In the targeted therapy group (TTG), men had a BMI of 21.4 kg/m2 (15-32.8 kg/m2), with BMI below 22 kg/m2 = 68%; women had a BMI of 19 kg/m2 (16.6-24.8 kg/m2), with BMI below 22 kg/m2 = 81%. 52% of men had low FFM (fat-free mass) values; 24% of women had a FFM deficiency. %FM (the ratio of body fat to body weight) was normal in 58% of men, exceeded normal range in 32%, and was low in 10%. Among women, normal %FM values were observed in 62% of female patients, exceeded the norm in 33%, and low values were observed in 5% of patients.

In the non-target group (NTTG): BMI in men = 18 kg/m2 (14.6 - 22 kg/m2), less than 22 kg/m2 in 92%; BMI in women 19.5 kg/m2 (16.4 - 31.2 kg/m2), less than 21 kg/m2 in 75%. 37% of men have low FFM values; in women, 16% have a FFM deficiency. The average %FM value in men was 11.8% (4.7 - 17.4%). 77% of men had normal %FM values, while 23% had low values. The average %FM value in women was 26.9% (17 - 46%). Among women, 56% had normal %FM values, 32% had excess values, and 12% had low values.

In TTG Waist-to-Hip Ratio (WHR) ratio in men = 0.9 (0.79-1.08), WHR ratio in women = 0.82 (0.72-0.96). In NTTG WHR ratio in men was 0.88 (0.8 - 1.07). The average WHR ratio in women was 0.78 (0.66 - 1.08), indicating an increase in visceral fat compared to non-targeted patients.

Conclusion: These data indicate an increasing risk of metabolic disorders during targeted therapy, necessitating adjustments of dietary recommendations.

records.abstract_text:
The ECFS twinning project gives an opportunity for mentee centers to gain experience and to have methodical support from the mentor CF centers. The CF centers of Rotterdam and Sofia were twinned, and visited each other in Oct 2024 and May 2025. Since November 2024 there have been regular multidisciplinary case discussions. There is a marked difference between the BMI’s of both centers (0.23 vs. -0.7 for children and 24 vs. 20.49 for adults). Since 2021 CFTR modulators (CFTRm) was introduced in Bulgaria for pwCF aged > 6 years of age.

Aim: One of the goals of our twinning project was to improve the nutritional status in the people with CF (pwCF) in Sofia.

Methods: For this purpose valuable recommendations and suggestions as well as regular multidisciplinary case discussions were held thought out the 1,5 year of the project. Diet recommendations especially regarding salt intake as well as a different approach for pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) were made. BMI data of 107 children and 92 adults (total 199) of Sofia CF center were compared prior to CFTRm initiation (2021-2023), prior to the beginning of the twinning project (2024, and at least one year on CFTRm) and their last known result now (end of 2025).

records.title: NutriActe: evaluation of the self-management of fat-soluble vitamin levels by a nutritionist at a paediatric cystic fibrosis clinic in Quebec, Canada.
records.authors_text: C. Beaudry1, P. Daigneault2, L. Gregori3, C. Héroux3
records.affiliations_text: 1CHU de Québec-Université Laval, Department of Nutrition, Québec, Canada, 2CHU de Québec-Université Laval, Department of Pediatrics, Québec, Canada, 3CHU de Québec-Université Laval, Department of Pharmacy, Québec, Canada
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Cystic fibrosis (CF) often causes pancreatic insufficiency and malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins. Monitoring levels is vital for growth and bone health, yet results may take as much as 15 days, requiring later follow-up. This study evaluates the impact of systematic review by a nutritionist to adjust vitamin supplements at a pediatric CF clinic. Since 2019, the newly updated activities for nutritionists in Québec in 2019 includes the ability to prescribe vitamins and minerals.

Methods: We reviewed pediatric CF charts for vitamins A, D, and E levels during pre- (PRE) (June 2018–May 2019) and post-implementation period (POST) (June 2024–May 2025), excluding the pandemic period. The primary objective was to compare the time interval between the release of vitamin panel results and management by the care team, defined as the point when a team member reviewed the complete vitamin panel. Secondary outcomes comprised the global rate of follow-up and the rate of follow-up following abnormal findings.

Results: A total of 140 patients with CF were included: 107 in PRE and 98 in POST. These patients accounted for 175 and 142 samples for each study periods respectively. The average time for result management decreased from 28.2 days in PRE to 7.0 days in POST (P<0.0001). Rate of follow-up within 4 months of sampling increased from 42% in PRE compared to 91% in POST (P<0.0001). In PRE, 138 samples contained at least one abnormal value compared to 89 in POST; of these, 46% versus 89% were managed. During PRE, management was performed in 25.7% of cases by a physician, 5.1% by a nutritionist, and 10.9% by a pharmacist, compared to 1.4%, 88.7%, and 4.2%, respectively, during POST.

Conclusions: Analysis of both study periods indicates a marked improvement in the management of vitamin panel results for patients in our CF clinic. This improvement coincides with the 2019 expansion of nutritionists’ scope of practice in Québec, which introduced new allowable activities.

records.title: Is sweat test a reliable marker for adjusting sodium supplementation in CF patients treated with modulators?
records.authors_text: H. Attew1, A. Coudrat1, R. Theiler1, M. Argenson1, D. Trioleyre1, J. Genuardi1, J. Tenenbaum2, S. Ramirez1, E. Lamour1, F. Socchi1, R. Chiron1,3
records.affiliations_text: 1CHU de Montpellier, CRCM/Hopital Arnaud de Villeneuve, Montpellier, France, 2CHU de Montpellier, Pédiatrie Spécialisée / Hopital Arnaud de Villeneuve, Montpellier, France, 3Université de Montpellier, HydroSciences Montpellier, CNRS, IRD, Montpellier, France
records.abstract_text:
In the era of CFTR modulators, optimizing sodium intake in patients with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) remains a major clinical challenge. Excessive supplementation may cause long-term complications, while discontinuation increases the risk of dehydration. Sweat test (ST), historically used for diagnosis, varies across individuals and genotypes and could potentially guide salt intake. This study aimed to assess whether ST correlates with tools used to estimate sodium requirements in these patients.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective analysis of sodium intake, urinary ionograms, and ST measurements in adult and pediatric patients followed at the Montpellier CF Reference Center. Correlation analyses, as well as sensitivity and specificity tests, were performed to explore the relationship between ST (including its change before and after ETI therapy) and parameters used to estimate sodium needs based on French HAS recommendations for healthy populations.

Results: No significant correlation was observed between post-ETI sweat tests (or its pre/post-ETI delta), salt intake, percentage of sodium needs covered, or urinary Na/K ratio (P > 0.05) in our cohort. However, we also confirm that ST variation differed by mutation class, with a smaller decrease observed in heterozygous class III mutations.

Conclusion: In CF patients treated with CFTR modulators, ST does not appear to be a reliable marker for evaluating or adjusting sodium needs. Recommendations should continue to rely on a comprehensive clinical and biological assessment rather than on sweat chloride alone.

records.title: Effects of CFTR modulator therapy on pancreatic, and nutritional outcomes in adults with cystic fibrosis: a single-center study
records.authors_text: F. Vandamme1, C. Audousset2,3, H. Bernard3, T. Perez2,3, D. Seguy1
records.affiliations_text: 1CHU de Lille, Service de Diabétologie/Nutrition, Lille, France, 2CHU de Lille, Service de Pneumologie, Lille, France, 3CHU de Lille, CRCM, Lille, France
records.abstract_text:
Elexacaftor/Tezacaftor/Ivacaftor (ETI) is a highly effective CFTR modulator for patients with cystic fibrosis (CF) carrying the F508del variant. However, data on extra-pulmonary outcomes in patients without this variant remain limited. This study aimed to confirm the beneficial effects of ETI in our cohort, which included 30% of patients without the F508del variant.

Methods: We conducted a single-center observational study in adult CF patients (≥18 years) treated with ETI for at least 12 months at Lille University Hospital, France. All patients carried at least one ETI-responsive mutation. Data of annual report on respiratory function, nutritional status, body composition (assessed by bioimpedance analysis), pancreatic function, and diabetes were collected at baseline and 12 months later.

Results: A total of 49 patients (mean age ± SD, 32.5±10.5 years; 26.5% without the F508del variant) were included.
