records.title: Triangulation of findings from patients and healthcare professionals on challenges in eating behaviours and evaluation of potential utility of mindful eating practices in supporting healthy eating.
records.authors_text: H. Egan1, M. Miley1, R. Massey-Chase2, K.-L. Watson2, R. Keyte1
records.affiliations_text: 1Birmingham City University, Psychology and Counselling, Birmingham, United Kingdom, 2Kings College Hosptial, Adult Cystic Fibrosis Service, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To explore how patients and Health care professionals (HCP) understand and experience challenges in providing and receiving eating behaviours support. To explore barriers and facilitators to using mindful eating (ME) practices to support healthy eating behaviours.

Methods: Triangulation was conducted across four data sources: patient evaluation of ME practices after a 5-day intervention (n=10), patient interviews (n=5), HCP ME workshops/focus groups (n=37), HCP ME practices evaluation (n=13). Each dataset was analysed independently and then compared using a triangulation matrix to identify convergence, complementarity, dissonance and silence. These comparisons were used to develop integrated meta-themes.

Results: Findings from patients and HCP converged on the understanding that changing legacy eating behaviours is challenging due to perceptions of higher weight as being safer, lack of experience and knowledge around weight management, unpreparedness for weight changes and medicalisation of eating behaviours. There was some dissonance around perceived reasons for weight gain and the extent to which these were attributable to changed eating behaviours. Both HCP and patients reported that further training was needed to understand and utilise ME practices effectively. Evaluations of ME practices were mixed, patients found considering levels of hunger and satiety before eating helpful, but focusing on the taste and texture of food unhelpful as it reduced social aspects and pleasure in eating.

Conclusion: Synthesising HCP and patient perceptions of eating behaviours informs more effective practice to support weight regulation, behaviour change and understanding of the sustained emotional impact of legacy eating behaviours. Constructs of ME such as non-judgement and acceptance aid healthier eating and wellbeing. HCP report needing practical training, resources and case-study examples to increase confidence and skills in delivering psychosocial support to patients.

person.biography: Dr Rachel Massey-Chase has been the lead Clinical Psychologist in the Adult Cystic Fibrosis Service at King’s College Hospital in the UK since she joined the team in 2012. The King’s College Hospital adult CF service currently cares for over 280 patients across the South East of England. As an embedded member of the multi-disciplinary team Rachel provides individual psychological support to patients as well as working jointly with other members of the team to both directly support patients and work on service improvement projects. Rachel is an active member of the CF community, she is co-chair of the UK Psychosocial Professionals in CF (UKPPCF) Group and has previously presented at both the European and North American CF conferences as well as collaborating on a number of projects with the CF Trust.

records.title: Audit of magnesium levels in UK paediatric cystic fibrosis patients: assessing the clinical value of routine testing
records.authors_text: C.J. Woodland1, C.A. Berry1
records.affiliations_text: 1Alder Hey Children's NHS Trust, Nutrition and Dietetics, Liverpool, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: The prevalence and clinical significance of hypomagnesemia in paediatric cystic fibrosis (CF) patients remains unclear. There is variation in CF guidelines regarding recommendation for routine Magnesium (Mg) monitoring, raising questions about its value in clinical practice. Furthermore, the impact of the introduction of Highly Effective Modulator Therapy (HEMT) on Mg monitoring requires consideration. This audit aims to evaluate Mg levels in paediatric CF patients and determine if there is clinical justification for routine testing of patient’s Mg levels.

Method: We conducted a retrospective audit of all Mg measurements taken from paediatric CF patients at Alder Hey Children’s Hospital over a 10-year period. The audit assessed the frequency of abnormal results, both elevated and reduced Mg levels. Data from neonates who were receiving parental nutrition (PN) was not included. Ninety eight patients had data audited with eighty nine included in study results. Nine patients were excluded: those with a Cystic Fibrosis Screen Positive Inconclusive Diagnosis (CFSPID) (n=5). ; patients receiving PN for prolonged periods (n-1) and patients that had missing Mg data (n=3).

Results: Across the 10-years, 775 Mg levels were collated from the included patients. Of these, 42 (5%) were below the reference range and 4 (0.5%) were above. Notably, only 7 of the 42 low results (16%) occurred after initiation of HEMT.

Conclusion: Mg abnormalities were infrequent in the paediatric CF cohort, with only 5% of measurements below and 0.5% above the reference range. No treatment for these abnormal levels was commenced. The low prevalence, suggests that routine Mg monitoring may offer limited clinical benefit especially in an increasingly healthy CF population on HEMT. Targeted testing based on individual risk factors may be a more appropriate approach.

records.title: Eye-movement desensitisation and reprocessing as a treatment for medical trauma in cystic fibrosis

person.department: East of Scotland Adult Cystic Fibrosis Service

records.authors_text: R. Jamieson1
records.affiliations_text: 1NHS Lothian, East of Scotland Adult Cystic Fibrosis Service, Edinburgh, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Medical traumatic stress refers to the psychological and physiological responses to pain, injury, serious illness, medical procedures and invasive or frightening treatment experiences. It is associated with decreased medication adherence and impaired relationships with the clinical team. People living with cystic fibrosis face a lifetime of illness related experiences that have the potential to be traumatic. Eye-Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing (EMDR) is a widely used evidenced based therapy in the treatment of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder and other anxiety based conditions. This presentation aims to explore the utility of EMDR as a treatment for symptoms of medical trauma in adults living with cystic fibrosis.

Methods: Adults living with cystic fibrosis who presented to the psychology service with symptoms of medical traumatic stress were offered EMDR as a treatment option. EMDR was carried out either in person or online via video call, according to patient preference. Symptoms of generalised anxiety, post-traumatic stress and mood were assessed by standardised self report measures before commencing treatment, and again on completion of therapy. Qualitative feedback on the acceptability of the therapy was also gathered on completion.

Results: EMDR treatment led to a reduction in anxiety and trauma related symptoms for most patients. It also led to an improvement in mood for some patients. Patients often reported increased engagement with healthcare, and they described an improved ability to advocate for themselves in the healthcare setting and in their personal lives.

Conclusion: Results suggest that EMDR is a viable treatment option for symptoms of medical traumatic stress, leading to a reduction in symptoms of trauma and anxiety for most. Patients found EMDR to be an acceptable treatment option, and overall reported that the therapy was a challenging and worthwhile process.

records.title: Mental health and neurocognitive effects in children with cystic fibrosis taking elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor: A 12-month follow-up

person.title: Dr.
person.department: Psychology Unit, Child & Adolescent Psychiatry Unit

records.authors_text: S. Graziano1, C. Di Savino1, A.L Quittner2, F. Alghisi3, A. Boni3, E. Montemitro3, S. Vicari1, R. Cutrera3, D. Menghini1
records.affiliations_text: 1Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital, IRCCS, Psychology Unit, Child & Adolescent Psychiatry Unit, Rome, Italy, 2Joe DiMaggio Hospital, Cystic Fibrosis, Pulmonary & Sleep Center, Hollywood, United States, 3Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital, IRCCS, Cystic Fibrosis and Pulmonology Unit, Rome, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Elexacaftor/Tezacaftor/Ivacaftor (ETI) therapy was extended to children with CF aged 6–11 years in October 2022. ETI is associated with clinical improvements and enhanced health-related quality of life. While potential mental health side effects have been reported in adults, data in pediatric populations remain limited.

Methods: Children eligible for ETI and their parents completed longitudinal assessments during routine visits at baseline (T0), 3-mos (T1), 6-mos (T2), 12-mos (T3) after ETI. Measures: a) physical parameters (FEV₁, BMI); b) HRQoL (CFQ-R); c) mental health (PSC-17); d) parental depression (PHQ-9) and anxiety (GAD-7); and e) ad hoc neurocognitive side-effects questionnaire.

Results: This study included 45 children (F/M=23/22; M age=8.1 years; M FEV₁=100, SD=15.4; M=BMI 16.9, SD=3.8). FEV₁ remained stable across all time points, while BMI showed a significant increase at 12-mos (T0<T3; p<.001). Parents reported improvements in CFQ-R: Body Image (T1<T3; p<.05), Health Perceptions (T0<T3; p<.05), and Respiratory Symptoms Functioning (T0>T1–T3; p<.001) in their children. Treatment Burden remained low, indicating substantial burden (range 59–66). On the PSC, attention problems were reported most frequently (9–19%). The percentage of patients with internalizing problems and attention difficulties increased from T0 to T1 (4 to 10 and 16 to 19, respectively). Neurocognitive side-effects were reported at all assessment points, including irritability (48–59%), agitation/hyperactivity (41–59%), concentration difficulties (50–59%), insomnia (16–25%), and headache (34–50%). No significant improvements over time were found.

Conclusions: Overall, ETI was associated with significant improvements across physical domains. Attention difficulties, agitation/hyperactivity, and irritability were common in children receiving ETI. These findings confirm the need for systematic monitoring of ETI effects over time.

person.biography: Dr. Graziano is a clinical psychologist and psychotherapist and she works at the Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital in Rome in the Child & Adolescent Psychiatry Unit and in the Pneumology and Cystic Fibrosis Unit. She is a co-chair of the European Cystic Fibrosis Society (ECFS) Mental Health Working Group and a member of the CF Foundation Mental Health Advisory Committee in the US. Her primary research and clinical interests focus on trauma and stressors related to managing a chronic illness. Her research focuses on depression, anxiety and HRQoL in individuals with CF and caregivers. In 2019, she attended the CF-CBT training in Boston (Massachusetts General Hospital) and is applying this intervention at the children’s hospital in Rome. She is a co-founder of the Italian National Trauma Center (INTC), and attended several training sessions to prepare for this role. For example, she completed the \"Mastery in Global Mental Health: Trauma and Recovery Certificate Program\" - Harvard Medical School in 2009, and from 2011 to 2013, she attended the Harvard/MGH Trauma Program as a research fellow. records.abstract_text:
Objectives: People with cystic fibrosis (PWCF) face a lifetime of potentially traumatic, illness-related experiences including medical visits, lab tests and invasive procedures (PICC lines, surgeries). These can cause symptoms of trauma and medical traumatic stress (MTS), such as negative mood, anxiety, and hyperarousal which may lead to decreased adherence, avoidance of procedures, and worse mental health (MH). This study assessed knowledge, training, clinical practices and barriers to addressing MTS in a national US sample of CF providers.

Methods: A REDCap survey was developed by the CFF Mental Health Advisory Committee (Research) and emailed to CF providers by the CF Foundation May 1, 2025.

Results: Surveys were completed by 285 providers. Respondents were from pediatric (40%), adult (32%) and combined (28%) centers s (20%), and included multidisciplinary providers: mental health (36%) respiratory/physical therapists (16%) and others (8%). Over 90% agreed that nearly all PWCF experience MTS, that providers should routinely assess for symptoms and teach coping skills. Most recognized MTS signs and symptoms (69%), but fewer knew about prevention strategies (48%) or screening tools (25%). Knowledge gaps were identified in scientific basis of MTS, trauma reactions, basic interventions and trauma-informed care (TIC). Among MH providers, the main barriers were limited resources and time (%). For other providers, barriers included insufficient training (>93%), limited time (physicians 98%, nurses 76%), perceptions that TIC was outside their scope (physicians 75%, nurses 73%, RT/PTs 54%). Personal distress was a barrier for 37% of non-MH providers. Half of respondents had evidence-based training in TIC, however, nearly all (99%) wanted additional training.

Conclusion: Providers widely recognized the importance of MTS in CF care but lacked effective training and resources. Robust TIC education and systematic support are essential to improve care.

records.title: Correlation of substance use among adolescent cystic fibrosis patients with mental health screenings using CRAFFT, PHQ-9, and GAD-7 screening tools
records.authors_text: S. Hill, B.S.1, C. Fowler, M.D.2, H. Searcy, Pharm.D.2
records.affiliations_text: 1UAB Heersink School of Medicine, Birmingham, United States, 2UAB Medicine, Pediatric Pulmonology, Birmingham, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To assess correlations between PHQ-9 and GAD-7 mental health screening scores with CRAFFT scores indicating problematic substance use behaviours.

Methods: Participants diagnosed with Cystic Fibrosis ages 15-20 (n=40) were recruited over a 4-month period. Substance use was characterised using the CRAFFT survey, with scores categorised as negative (0-1) or positive (>2). The GAD-7 and PHQ-9 are validated screening tools for generalised anxiety disorder and depression in adolescents, with scores characterised as minimal (0-4), mild (5-9), moderate (10-14) and severe (>15). Associations between CRAFFT, PHQ-9, and GAD-7 were analysed using Spearman’s rank correlation test. Statistical analyses were performed with significance defined as p<0.05.

Results: Of 40 patients surveyed, with a mean age of 17.7±1.66, 42.5% screened positive for any substance use in the past year. The most common substances used were alcohol (30%) and marijuana (28%). Of those who reported substance use in the past year, 47% reported polysubstance use. 20% of patients surveyed recorded CRAFFT scores of >2. A moderate positive monotonic relationship between increasing GAD-7 scores and increasing CRAFFT scores was found with a Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient of 0.455 and p<0.05. No other statistically significant correlations between mental health screening tools and the CRAFFT screening tools were found.

Conclusion: There is notable substance use among adolescent CF patients and implementing screening tools could help those at-risk for problematic substance use. There was a moderate positive monotonic relationship between increasing GAD-7 scores and increasing CRAFFT scores. More research is needed to determine the full scope of the correlation between mental health disorders and substance use among adolescent CF patients. CF adolescents need to be screened for substance use and mental health separately to determine risk level for anxiety, depression, and substance misuse.

records.title: Procedural anxiety in children with cystic fibrosis: child and parent-reported assessment using CFPAS and Spence anxiety scales
records.authors_text: F. Ozdemircioglu1, H.N. Kekec2, A. Gumus2, S. Karabulut1, N.M. Cakar1, C.A. Yildiz1, M.M. Yigit1, E.E. Baysal1, B. Ozgunay1, E. Ugurlu1, G. Alishbayli1, A.P. Ergenekon1, Y. Gokdemir1, E. Erdem Eralp1, F. Karakoc1, B.T. Karadag1
records.affiliations_text: 1Marmara University, Division of Paediatric Pulmonology, Istanbul, Turkey, 2Marmara University, Selim Coremen Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Istanbul, Turkey
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To evaluate procedural and general anxiety levels in children with cystic fibrosis and to explore age-related patterns of anxiety in routine clinical care.

Methods: Children aged 0–18 years with cystic fibrosis followed at the Paediatric Pulmonology Cystic Fibrosis Centre, were included. Procedural anxiety was assessed using the Children’s Fear of Medical Procedures Scale (CFPAS). General anxiety was evaluated using the Spence Children’s Anxiety Scale (SCAS): preschool parent-report (0–6 years), child and parent-report (7–13 years), and self-report (≥14 years). Anxiety scores were analysed across three age groups. CFPAS scores were categorised as low (0–1) or moderate–high (2–3) anxiety.

Results: A total of 147 children with cystic fibrosis were included (76 males, 71 females). Anxiety related to venepuncture, intravenous cannulation and throat swab collection decreased with increasing age, whereas anxiety related to spirometry, procedures under general anaesthesia and bronchoscopy showed an increasing age-related trend. Bronchoscopy was associated with the highest anxiety levels. SCAS assessments demonstrated clinically relevant anxiety across all age groups. In children aged 0–6 years, parent-reported anxiety was identified in approximately 29%. In the 7–13-year age group, anxiety was reported by children in 9.2% of cases, whereas parent-reported anxiety was observed in 49.2%. Among adolescents aged ≥14 years, clinically relevant anxiety was identified in approximately 25% based on self-report. Across age groups, obsessive–compulsive symptoms and fear of physical injury were the most frequently reported anxiety subdomains.

Conclusion: Procedural and general anxiety are common in children with cystic fibrosis and demonstrate age-related patterns. Routine anxiety screening and age-tailored procedural preparation strategies should be integrated into multidisciplinary cystic fibrosis care to improve patient experience and clinical engagement.

records.title: The effect of cognitive behavioural therapy in cystic fibrosis: a systematic review
records.authors_text: N. Akyazı1, A. Demirel2, S. Bilgin2
records.affiliations_text: 1Tarsus University, Physiotherapy and Rehabilitation, Mersin, Turkey, 2Hacettepe University, Physiotherapy and Rehabilitation, Ankara, Turkey
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Cystic fibrosis (CF), in addition to its multisystem involvement and increased life expectancy, is associated with psychological problems such as depression, anxiety, and difficulties coping with chronic illness. Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is a goal-oriented psychotherapeutic approach that aims to improve emotional and psychological functioning by modifying maladaptive thought patterns and behaviours. However, its effects in this population remain underexplored. This review aimed to synthesise current evidence on CBT-based interventions for managing psychosocial problems associated with cystic fibrosis.

Methods: PubMed, PEDro, MEDLINE, Scopus, EMBASE, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to 2025 using MeSH terms. Study selection, data extraction, risk of bias assessment, and methodological quality assessment were conducted independently by two reviewers. The study protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251016152).

Results: A total of 6,499 records were identified in the initial search. Following screening and duplicate removal, three randomised controlled trials were included. Despite the limited number of studies, strong evidence supported the effectiveness of CBT-based interventions in reducing depressive symptoms in patients with CF. Evidence regarding the effects on anxiety and coping skills was limited. Furthermore, strong evidence indicated that CBT-based interventions had no significant effect on quality of life or pulmonary function.

Conclusion: CBT-based interventions appear effective in reducing depressive symptoms in children and adolescents with CF. However, further studies are required to clarify their effects on coping skills, anxiety, quality of life, and pulmonary function.

Keywords: cystic fibrosis; cognitive behavioural therapy; depression; anxiety; coping; quality of life; pulmonary function.

records.title: When the mind matters: psychological burden, medical adherence and sweat chloride variability during long-term treatment with elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor

person.department: Department of Pediatrics, Cystic Fibrosis Centre for Children and Adults

records.authors_text: A. Moeser1,2, M. Pavlova1, N. Beiersdorf1, K. Erler1, A. Nader1, M. Lorenz1
records.affiliations_text: 1Jena University Hospital, Department of Pediatrics, Cystic Fibrosis Centre for Children and Adults, Jena, Germany, 2Jena University Hospital, Institute for Infectious Diseases and Infection Control, Jena, Germany
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) sustainably improves lung function (FEV₁), quality of life and sweat chloride (SC) levels in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). Psychological comorbidities may impair treatment adherence. This study assessed ETI adherence using SC and medication possession rate (MPR) and evaluated the impact of psychological distress.

Methods: In this retrospective observational study, 34 pwCF aged 12–21 years (median 17.3) initiating ETI between 2020 and 2022 were included. SC and FEV₁ were measured at baseline and annually over four years (VK1-4). Psychological distress was screened annually using the PHQ-9 (score ≥7). Adherence was assessed by MPR (1.0 = full medication supply). Patients with prior CFTR modulator therapy, insulin-dependent diabetes or organ transplantation were excluded.

Results: Fourteen pwCF (44.1%) showed psychological distress (mean PHQ-9 scores 11.1 vs. 2.8). Median SC decreased significantly from 101.9 mmol/L (SD 9.1) at baseline to 46.8 mmol/L (SD 17.6) in year 1 (p<0.001) and remained stable thereafter. pwCF with psychological distress demonstrated greater SC variability during follow-up, with significantly higher SC levels in VK 4 (p<0.05). In this group, MPR declined significantly from 95.4% to 75.5% (p<0.01). FEV₁ improved significantly in year 1 compared to baseline (+14.1%, p<0.001) and remained stable in both groups.

Conclusion: ETI leads to sustained improvements in lung function and sweat chloride in pwCF. A substantial proportion of patients exhibited psychological distress, which was associated with increased long-term variability in sweat chloride and declining MPR but not lung function. Structured psychological monitoring and targeted interventions may be essential to support adherence and long-term treatment success.

Objectives: Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) sustainably improves lung function (FEV₁), quality of life and sweat chloride (SC) levels in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). Psychological comorbidities may impair treatment adherence. This study assessed ETI adherence using SC and medication possession rate (MPR) and evaluated the impact of psychological distress.
Methods: In this retrospective observational study, 34 pwCF aged 12–21 years (median 17.3) initiating ETI between 2020 and 2022 were included. SC and FEV₁ were measured at baseline and annually over four years (VK1-4). Psychological distress was screened annually using the PHQ-9 (score ≥7). Adherence was assessed by MPR (1.0 = full medication supply). Patients with prior CFTR modulator therapy, insulin-dependent diabetes or organ transplantation were excluded.
Results: Fourteen pwCF (44.1%) showed psychological distress (mean PHQ-9 scores 11.1 vs. 2.8). Median SC decreased significantly from 101.9 mmol/L (SD 9.1) at baseline to 46.8 mmol/L (SD 17.6) in year 1 (p<0.001) and remained stable thereafter. pwCF with psychological distress demonstrated greater SC variability during follow-up, with significantly higher SC levels in VK 4 (p<0.05). In this group, MPR declined significantly from 95.4% to 75.5% (p<0.01). FEV₁ improved significantly in year 1 compared to baseline (+14.1%, p<0.001) and remained stable in both groups.
Conclusion: ETI leads to sustained improvements in lung function and sweat chloride in pwCF. A substantial proportion of patients exhibited psychological distress, which was associated with increased long-term variability in sweat chloride and declining MPR but not lung function. Structured psychological monitoring and targeted interventions may be essential to support adherence and long-term treatment success.

Objectives: A growing literature indicates adults with CF (AWCF) struggle with mental health (MH) challenges in addition to depression and generalized anxiety; however, limited prevalence data exists on these other conditions (e.g., medical traumatic stress {MTS}). Our primary aim is to conduct a national psychometric validation of two newly developed measures: General Mental Health Screener (GEMS-CF) to assess MH comorbidities and CF transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) modulators (GEMS-ModSE) to assess side-effects.

Methods: Three novel recruitment and design features characterize this protocol: 1) purposive sampling in development phase to enhance representativeness of AWCF (yielding 35% minoritized, 27% LGBTQ+, 30% low income) and 2) “planned missing data design” to reduce respondent burden, and 3) testing resilience as a moderator of MH conditions on quality of life. Five CF Centers will enroll 250 AWCF to complete: a Core Battery of measures (e.g., MTS, resilience), with 125 AWCF completing Battery A (e.g., substance misuse, disordered eating), 125 Battery B (e.g., cognition, trauma), and a random sample (n=100) completing test-retest of GEMS-CF and GEMS-ModSE, test of memory and processing speed (SDMT) and the MINI diagnostic interview.

Proposed Analyses:1) reliability (Cronbach’s alpha >0.70, test-retest reliability >0.80, convergent validity r’s>0.50, criterion validity Spearman Rho >0.50; 2) higher prevalence of MH comorbidities in AWCF vs community; 3) >75% rating screeners as “very acceptable” and “very helpful;”4) resilience will moderate the negative impacts of mental health symptoms on quality of life.

Results: Recruitment at 5 CF Centers begins in Q1 2026.

Conclusion: GEMS-CF will assess mental health comorbidities not currently addressed by annual MH screening. GEMS-ModSE will identify side-effects for AWCF taking CFTR modulators. These instruments will be disseminated to ECFS CF Centers to enhance mental health screening and treatment.

records.title: ACT with CF Self-Help Toolkit: a standalone targeted mental health intervention for adults with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: M. Genecov1, M. Renner2, P.J Smith3, C.F. Drescher4, K. Ingle5, H. Bruschwein6, C.V. O'Hayer1, M. Marden7
records.affiliations_text: 1Thomas Jefferson University Hospital, Psychiatry & Human Behaviour, Philadelphia, United States, 2Thomas Jefferson University Hospital, Psychiatry & Human Behavior, Philadelphia, United States, 3University of North Carolina - Chapel Hill, Psychiatry, Chapel Hill, United States, 4Augusta University, Augusta, United States, 5Duke University Medical Center, Durham, United States, 6University of Virginia, Charlottesville, United States, 7Boomer Esiason Foundation
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Given the effectiveness of ACT with CF (O’Hayer et al., 2024), to further our aim of making this protocol accessible to all adults with CF, we have designed and implementing and testing an ACT with CF Self-Help Toolkit.

Methods: The Toolkit delivered via electronic platform is offered to 60 adults (18+) with CF, with elevated PHQ-9 and/or GAD-7 score (<4). Participants are randomly assigned to receive the Toolkit immediately or after a six-week delay. Participants complete self-report measures of anxiety, depression, psychological flexibility, cognitive fusion, and quality of life at baseline, after the Toolkit, and three months later. Electronic health record data inform spirometry (FEV1, FVC). Measures of satisfaction and time spent on each component are obtained. The Toolkit comprises 6 sequential modules and associated kernels, one per week including brief (1-3 minute) videos delivered by young adults living with CF, and infographics demonstrating key ACT with CF interventions.

Results: Data collection is ongoing, complete by ECFS. We will examine changes in outcome variables over time, as well as differences between the immediate-access and six-week delay groups. Power calculations were based on a pre-to-post R² of 0.60 between covariates and post-treatment psychological functioning, an attrition rate of 20%, and regression modelling controlling for baseline psychological functioning and FEV1, with treatment group as the variable of interest. We anticipate 80% power to detect a Cohen’s d = 0.85 effect size difference using a sample of 60 participants.

Conclusion: If effective, the ACT with CF Self-Help Toolkit could be a workable alternative to individual psychotherapy for adults with CF who are not ready for, or are unable to access, traditional psychotherapy, due to barriers such as work, childcare, geographical constraints, financial limitations, and a lack of providers trained in empirically supported psychotherapies for living with CF.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Elevated rates of depression and anxiety in The International Depression and Anxiety Epidemiological Study (TIDES) led to international guidelines which integrated mental health (MH) screening into CF care. However, TIDES did not include children <12 years. Increased awareness of MH in young children and side-effects of CFTR modulators have increased the urgency for addressing MH concerns in young children. This study (named MindKids-CF in Italy) aims to: 1) evaluate Italian prevalence of depression, anxiety and behavior problems in children 2-11; 2) compare performance of two widely used measures, Pediatric Symptom Checklist (PSC) and PROMIS modules and 3) characterize the neuropsychological side-effects of modulator therapy.

Methods: As adapted from the US TIDES 2.0 protocol, we will enroll 500 children with CF <12 years at 11 Italian CF Centers, generating national prevalence estimates. Parents and children will complete a MH assessment twice at routine visits, separated by 6-9 months: PSC, PROMIS (sleep, cognition, emotional functioning), SDQ for convergent validity, CFQ-R (QOL), CF-PAS (procedural anxiety), modulator side-effects; and parental PHQ-8, GAD-7.

Results (expected): A higher prevalence of MH problems will be found in children with CF compared to published norms; PSC and PROMIS will demonstrate adequate reliability (α >.70), sensitivity and specificity (>.80). Prevalence estimates will be generated and the best screener will be identified to update MH guidelines for children < 12 years in the EU.

Conclusions: Use of these screening measures will facilitate development of prevention and intervention efforts for young children to improve daily functioning and quality of life. TIDES 2.0 will provide critical evidence to extend MH screening and care to younger children with CF in the EU and US.

Funding: Supported by a grant from the Fondazione per la Ricerca sulla Fibrosi Cistica (FFC# Strategic Project 2025-2028).

person.biography: Dr. Graziano is a clinical psychologist and psychotherapist and she works at the Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital in Rome in the Child & Adolescent Psychiatry Unit and in the Pneumology and Cystic Fibrosis Unit. She is a co-chair of the European Cystic Fibrosis Society (ECFS) Mental Health Working Group and a member of the CF Foundation Mental Health Advisory Committee in the US. Her primary research and clinical interests focus on trauma and stressors related to managing a chronic illness. Her research focuses on depression, anxiety and HRQoL in individuals with CF and caregivers. In 2019, she attended the CF-CBT training in Boston (Massachusetts General Hospital) and is applying this intervention at the children’s hospital in Rome. She is a co-founder of the Italian National Trauma Center (INTC), and attended several training sessions to prepare for this role. For example, she completed the \"Mastery in Global Mental Health: Trauma and Recovery Certificate Program\" - Harvard Medical School in 2009, and from 2011 to 2013, she attended the Harvard/MGH Trauma Program as a research fellow. Her specialization in trauma treatment led to her role in training primary care practitioners after the Earthquakes in Italy in 2010 and 2016.

records.title: Objective assessment of behavioural adverse effects of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor in children
records.authors_text: H. Marsden1, K. Knox1, A. Murad1, A. Hegab1, P. Singleton1
records.affiliations_text: 1South Tees NHS Trust, Paediatrics, Middlesbrough, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Behavioural and sleep disturbances are increasingly recognised adverse effects of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI). With ETI licensed from 2 years of age in the UK, distinguishing drug-related effects from developmental or pre-existing behavioural symptoms is challenging.

Methods: We report two paediatric cases where the Paediatric Pre-School/School Symptom Checker (PPSC/PSC) supported objective assessment and decision-making.

Results: Case 1: A girl with cystic fibrosis (CF), homozygous for F508del, commenced ETI at 2 years of age. She had normal growth, neurodevelopment, sleep, and a non-clinical baseline PPSC score. Within weeks she developed irritability, emotional lability, hyperactivity, and sleep disturbance, with a clinically elevated PPSC score (25/36). There were no intercurrent illnesses or psychosocial stressors, and behavioural strategies were ineffective. Symptoms caused family disruption and parental distress, requiring psychological support. ETI cessation led to symptom resolution within two weeks and PPSC normalisation (3/36). Re-challenge at reduced dose caused rapid recurrence, prompting discontinuation.

Case 2: A boy with CF, homozygous for F508del, commenced ETI at 6 years of age, having previously tolerated lumacaftor/ivacaftor. He had mild baseline behavioural symptoms (PSC 10/70). Following ETI initiation, behavioural and sleep symptoms worsened (PSC 20/70), unresponsive to behavioural strategies or melatonin. After 4-week ETI withdrawal, symptoms improved (PSC 5/70). ETI was recommenced at half dose with stable behaviour and acceptable sweat chloride (45 mmol/L).

Conclusion: Objective symptom monitoring demonstrated reproducible ETI-associated behavioural adverse effects. These symptoms impact family wellbeing and create difficult decisions around dose reduction or cessation of a life-prolonging therapy. Routine screening, multidisciplinary review, and shared decision-making are essential when initiating ETI in children.

Objectives: Behavioural and sleep disturbances are increasingly recognised adverse effects of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI). With ETI licensed from 2 years of age in the UK, distinguishing drug-related effects from developmental or pre-existing behavioural symptoms is challenging.
Methods: We report two paediatric cases where the Paediatric Pre-School/School Symptom Checker (PPSC/PSC) supported objective assessment and decision-making.
Results: Case 1: A girl with cystic fibrosis (CF), homozygous for F508del, commenced ETI at 2 years of age. She had normal growth, neurodevelopment, sleep, and a non-clinical baseline PPSC score. Within weeks she developed irritability, emotional lability, hyperactivity, and sleep disturbance, with a clinically elevated PPSC score (25/36). There were no intercurrent illnesses or psychosocial stressors, and behavioural strategies were ineffective. Symptoms caused family disruption and parental distress, requiring psychological support. ETI cessation led to symptom resolution within two weeks and PPSC normalisation (3/36). Re-challenge at reduced dose caused rapid recurrence, prompting discontinuation.
Case 2: A boy with CF, homozygous for F508del, commenced ETI at 6 years of age, having previously tolerated lumacaftor/ivacaftor. He had mild baseline behavioural symptoms (PSC 10/70). Following ETI initiation, behavioural and sleep symptoms worsened (PSC 20/70), unresponsive to behavioural strategies or melatonin. After 4-week ETI withdrawal, symptoms improved (PSC 5/70). ETI was recommenced at half dose with stable behaviour and acceptable sweat chloride (45 mmol/L).
Conclusion: Objective symptom monitoring demonstrated reproducible ETI-associated behavioural adverse effects. These symptoms impact family wellbeing and create difficult decisions around dose reduction or cessation of a life-prolonging therapy. Routine screening, multidisciplinary review, and shared decision-making are essential when initiating ETI in children.

records.affiliations_text: 1Royal Brompton Hospital, Part of Guys and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust, Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, London, United Kingdom, 2Harefield Hospital, Part of Guys and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust, Familial Hypercholesterolaemia and Lipid Management Clinic, Harefield, United Kingdom, 3National Heart and Lung Institute, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: People with CF (pwCF) are living longer. A rising number are overweight, and 20–30% have CF diabetes (CFD). Prior work shows higher cardiovascular (CV) events than in non-CF population (Frost 2023). QRisk3 guides 10-year CV prevention in the general population (Hippisley-Cox 2017). We created a nurse-led pathway using a locally adapted CF-QRisk3 tool.

Methods: We developed a CF-CV multidisciplinary pathway with a Preventative Cardiology Team. CF Nurse Specialists screened pwCF aged 40–84 years (Sept 2025–Jan 2026). QRisk3 tool was modified: rheumatoid arthritis served as a surrogate for CF-chronic inflammation; scores further adjusted for CFD. Eligible pwCF attending in-person CF clinics had non-fasting lipids, HbA1c, thyroid, BP, smoking status, and family history checked. Subsequent interventions advised and high-risk cases (>20% risk CV event in 10 years) were reviewed in the CF-CV MDT.

Results: Overall, 48 pwCF were screened. Nineteen (39.6%) warranted interventions, some multiple, due to high CV risk (Table). Five (10.4%) declined advised management, one stopped statin therapy due to side effects.

Conclusion: A high proportion of pwCF had elevated CF-CV risk warranting investigative and therapeutic intervention. We achieved full assessment uptake, and minimal refusal of interventions. This pathway is feasible for proactive CF specific CV-risk management in liaison with primary care. Screening is ongoing with the CF-CV protocol being part of clinical practice.

records.authors_text: C. Whitton1, K. Vincent1, A. Owen1
records.affiliations_text: 1University Hospitals Plymouth NHS Trust, Cystic Fibrosis Team, Plymouth, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: The National Institute of Clinical Excellence recommended the discontinuation of heparinised saline in all central venous catheters in the UK in 2012, however, this recommendation has not yet been fully embraced in cystic fibrosis (CF) care. Heparinised saline use is associated with risks such as infection, thrombocytopenia, bleeding and interactions with other drugs. Research indicates that 0.9% sodium chloride presents a safer, equally effective, and more cost-efficient option,1 therefore we ceased use of heparinised saline in TIVAD maintenance at University Hospitals Plymouth in February 2024.

Method: We conducted a retrospective review of TIVAD maintenance and complications.

There were no incidents of line occlusion in any of the 12 patients. One patient (p11) reported resistance in their TIVAD following admission at their transplant centre. Linogram was normal and subsequent flushes had no resistance. There was one incident of line infection following home intravenous antibiotic administration (p9).

Conclusion: We found no TIVAD occlusion after 18 months of using 0.9% sodium chloride for TIVAD maintenance, even when patients have had flushes less frequently than advised. Longer studies with larger numbers may be beneficial.

During the COVID-19 pandemic flush frequency was reduced in line with shielding, patients have demonstrated a reluctance to return to prior frequency.

TIVAD insertion is declining due to modulator therapy significantly reducing the frequency of intravenous antibiotic use. Concurrently, improved vascular access methods, such as ultrasound-guided longline, offer less invasive alternative.

records.title: A new era in cystic fibrosis: how is care changing in adult and paediatric settings?
records.authors_text: J. Witt1, S. Lewis1, J. Lowdon2, L. Blaikie3, S. Bell4, T. Daniels5, A. Maitra6, D. Nazareth7, K. Brownlee8, S.L Clarke1
records.affiliations_text: 1Cystic Fibrosis Trust, Research and Healthcare Data, London, United Kingdom, 2Leeds Children's Hospital, Cystic Fibrosis Unit, Leeds, United Kingdom, 3NHS Highland, Raigmore Hospital, Inverness, United Kingdom, 4Cystic Fibrosis Trust, Involvement Group, London, United Kingdom, 5York and Scarborough Teaching Hospitals, York Hull Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, York, United Kingdom, 6Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust, Cystic Fibrosis Unit, Manchester, United Kingdom, 7Liverpool Heart and Chest NHS Foundation Trust, Adult Cystic Fibrosis Unit, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 8Cystic Fibrosis Trust, Medical Affairs, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: At a time of significant transformation in cystic fibrosis (CF) care in the United Kingdom, we explored how workload for CF professionals is evolving in paediatric and adult care settings.

Methods: A bespoke questionnaire was developed with advice from CF professionals and people with CF. Questions were tested and refined in early 2025 with CF professionals not previously involved in development. It was then disseminated via professional networks and Cystic Fibrosis Trust. Responses were collected online March-April 2025 and analysed descriptively by setting, with a complementary thematic analysis of free text comments.

Results: Sixty-nine respondents worked in adult care; 49 worked in paediatrics. The sample included doctors, nurses, physiotherapists, dietitians, and other staff from more than 40 different CF centres and clinics.

Table 1: Proportion of respondents who perceived a change in workload since early 2020 in three of 19 areas covered in the questionnaire.

Area of work:Inpatient CareVirtual / Remote careInterventionsPerceived changeAdult (n=66)Paediatric (n=47)Adult (n=66)Paediatric (n=38)Adult (n=64)Paediatric (n=47) Increased7.6%2.1%81.8%57.9%59.4%51.1% No change7.6%8.5%9.1%13.2%32.8%34.0% Decreased84.8%89.4%9.1%28.9%7.8%14.9%

Qualitative comments confirmed that workload is moving from inpatient settings to more outpatient, virtual and community care. Simultaneously, the focus of care is shifting from lung health to a wider range of issues, such as CF diabetes, gastrointestinal symptoms, mental health, and social wellbeing. In paediatric care, there is a new focus on prevention and healthy living, while adult services are dealing with increasing demand for fertility, pregnancy, and menopause support, and emerging complexities of older age.

Conclusion: In adult and paediatric settings, CF workload is evolving, rather than reducing. Monitoring this evolution will be vital in future to ensure clinical standards and guidelines are updated in line with new needs, innovations, and emerging best practices.

1Cystic Fibrosis Trust, Research and Healthcare Data, London, United Kingdom, 2Leeds Children's Hospital, Cystic Fibrosis Unit, Leeds, United Kingdom, 3NHS Highland, Raigmore Hospital, Inverness, United Kingdom, 4Cystic Fibrosis Trust, Involvement Group, London, United Kingdom, 5York and Scarborough Teaching Hospitals, York Hull Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, York, United Kingdom, 6Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust, Cystic Fibrosis Unit, Manchester, United Kingdom, 7Liverpool Heart and Chest NHS Foundation Trust, Adult Cystic Fibrosis Unit, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 8Cystic Fibrosis Trust, Medical Affairs, London, United Kingdom

Objectives: At a time of significant transformation in cystic fibrosis (CF) care in the United Kingdom, we explored how workload for CF professionals is evolving in paediatric and adult care settings.
Methods: A bespoke questionnaire was developed with advice from CF professionals and people with CF. Questions were tested and refined in early 2025 with CF professionals not previously involved in development. It was then disseminated via professional networks and Cystic Fibrosis Trust. Responses were collected online March-April 2025 and analysed descriptively by setting, with a complementary thematic analysis of free text comments.
Results: Sixty-nine respondents worked in adult care; 49 worked in paediatrics. The sample included doctors, nurses, physiotherapists, dietitians, and other staff from more than 40 different CF centres and clinics.

Qualitative comments confirmed that workload is moving from inpatient settings to more outpatient, virtual and community care. Simultaneously, the focus of care is shifting from lung health to a wider range of issues, such as CF diabetes, gastrointestinal symptoms, mental health, and social wellbeing. In paediatric care, there is a new focus on prevention and healthy living, while adult services are dealing with increasing demand for fertility, pregnancy, and menopause support, and emerging complexities of older age.
Conclusion: In adult and paediatric settings, CF workload is evolving, rather than reducing. Monitoring this evolution will be vital in future to ensure clinical standards and guidelines are updated in line with new needs, innovations, and emerging best practices.

presentation.title: A new era in cystic fibrosis: how is care changing in adult and paediatric settings?

records.abstract_text:
Background: Recent publications from the European Cystic Fibrosis Society [1] highlight major progress in Cystic Fibrosis (CF) management and quality of life, while recognising that people with CF (pwCF) continue to face evolving challenges. Previous studies [2] emphasise that adults with CF wish to discuss issues such as fatigue, work or study, reproductive health, and disease progression with their multidisciplinary teams (MDTs).

Aims & Objectives: The Cork Adult CF Centre (3CF) designed a digital mixed-methods survey to identify key areas where pwCF may require additional information/support, and their preferred formats for receiving it.

Method: The survey, developed and validated collaboratively with the CF MDT, was distributed via SMS to 180 adult pwCF (pre- and post-transplant) attending 3CF. Responses were anonymised.

Results: 80 pwCF responded to the survey. Table 1 demonstrates topic breakdown, response number, mean ages, positive and negative topic ratings. All 14 topics presented identified in the survey were considered important by respondents. One-to-one sessions were the preferred format for receiving support and information.

In specific subgroups certain topics were identified as particularly relevant, e.g. perimenopause and menopause in 16 perimenopausal women (mean age 39).

Discussion & Conclusions: These findings underscore the continued importance of the MDT in reviewing and addressing the evolving holistic needs of pwCF. One-to-one support is preferred.

Southern KW, et al. Standards for the care of people with cystic fibrosis; establishing and maintaining health. J Cyst Fibros. 2024 Jan;23(1):12-28.

Dury et al. Identifying specific needs in adult cystic fibrosis patients: a pilot study using a custom questionnaire. BMC Pulm Med. 2021;21:270.

records.title: Healthcare professionals’ ideas and priorities for the future of cystic fibrosis care
records.authors_text: J. Witt1, S. Lewis1, J. Lowdon2, L. Blaikie3, S. Bell4, T. Daniels5, A. Maitra6, D. Nazareth7, K. Brownlee8, S.L Clarke1
records.affiliations_text: 1Cystic Fibrosis Trust, Research and Healthcare Data, London, United Kingdom, 2Leeds Children's Hospital, Cystic Fibrosis Unit, Leeds, United Kingdom, 3NHS Highland, Raigmore Hospital, Inverness, United Kingdom, 4Cystic Fibrosis Trust, Involvement Group, London, United Kingdom, 5York and Scarborough Teaching Hospitals, York Hull Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, York, United Kingdom, 6Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust, Cystic Fibrosis Unit, Manchester, United Kingdom, 7Liverpool Heart and Chest NHS Foundation Trust, Adult Cystic Fibrosis Unit, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 8Cystic Fibrosis Trust, Medical Affairs, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To explore cystic fibrosis (CF) professionals’ ideas and priorities for the future at a time of significant transformation due to new treatments and technologies.

Methods: We worked with CF professional and community representatives to co-produce a questionnaire to understand the changing care landscape in CF in the United Kingdom (UK), and to capture ideas for the future. We specifically asked for up to three ideas as well as respondents’ top priority.

Responses were gathered online March-April 2025. Free text comments were analysed thematically to identify common themes and sub-themes.

Results: Over 135 top priorities and 350 ideas were shared by 142 CF professionals. Ideas and priorities often aligned, with the latter describing high level ambitions while ideas provided actionable suggestions to achieve said ambitions.

Two key themes emerged. Priorities in Theme 1 focused on ensuring equitable access to treatments and care that adapts around individual patients’ needs and seeks to reduce burden. Ideas under this theme included widened access to modulators, enhanced psychosocial support offers, and patient empowerment. To reduce burden, professionals suggested patient-initiated contact, rationalising appointments and tests, moving care to the community, as well as leveraging technology.

Theme 2 focused on staff and team development, as well as ways of working, to maintain ability to deliver high quality CF care. Ideas in this theme highlighted opportunities to upskill existing staff in new and emerging areas, and to increase collaboration with primary care and other disciplines. Professionals also felt continued multidisciplinary working was vital.

Conclusion: CF professionals in the UK saw equitable access and person-centred approaches as a top priority to maintain quality of care. Staff development and exploring new ways of working within and beyond the CF team were identified as critical facilitators to enable this.

records.title: Introducing a digital platform for patient goal setting to support the delivery of high value care
records.authors_text: R. Massey-Chase1, K. Channon1, S. Floyd1, R. Heise1, H. Parkinson1, E. Walton1, K.-L. Watson1, C. Elston1
records.affiliations_text: 1King's College Hospital, Adult Cystic Fibrosis Team, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Values-Based Health Care emphasises the measurement of what matters to patients alongside clinical parameters to deliver meaningful outcomes whilst reducing unnecessary burden. Standardised patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) are often used, assuming uniform priorities, which may not reflect the diverse needs of adults with cystic fibrosis (CF) in the post-modulator era. Our adult centre is trialling a digital platform (PerEmpo) designed to facilitate person-centred value and goal setting.

Methods: At annual review, patients are supported to identify values and goals which matter to them and to rate how much CF is currently getting in the way of these on a 0-5 Likert scale (lower scores represent less negative impact). They also set health management specific goals and rate their attainment of these on a 0-5 Likert scale (higher scores represent greater attainment). Information is stored on a central system (with patient access) and re-rated during their next appropriate clinical contact (approximately 3-monthly intervals).

Results: To date, 18 people have completed the initial stage with the pilot ongoing. Thematic analysis of qualitative information within the goals and values showed three main themes: 1. Personal Wellbeing, including health management and maintaining independence; 2. Social and Leisure, highlighting the importance of relationships, hobbies and travel; 3. Career growth and development, reflecting aspirations for progression. However, within these themes the values and goals were specific to each individual. The median rating of the impact of CF was 2 (range 1-5) and median rating of attainment of CF specific goals was 2 (range 1-5).

Conclusion: This project aims to better understand what matters most to patients to support collaborative decision making about their health and care. Systematic ways of individualising care to ensure high value is particularly important with the growing CF population.

person.title: Dr
person.biography: Dr Rachel Massey-Chase has been the lead Clinical Psychologist in the Adult Cystic Fibrosis Service at King’s College Hospital in the UK since she joined the team in 2012. The King’s College Hospital adult CF service currently cares for over 280 patients across the South East of England. As an embedded member of the multi-disciplinary team Rachel provides individual psychological support to patients as well as working jointly with other members of the team to both directly support patients and work on service improvement projects. Rachel is an active member of the CF community, she is co-chair of the UK Psychosocial Professionals in CF (UKPPCF) Group and has previously presented at both the European and North American CF conferences as well as collaborating on a number of projects with the CF Trust.

records.title: The introduction of a new annual review process for the modern era of cystic fibrosis: a single centre’s experience

person.institution: King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust

records.authors_text: K. Channon1, M. Kapatou1, H. Parkinson1, S. Floyd1, R. Heise1, M.D Waller1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, Adult Cystic Fibrosis, London, United Kingdom, 2King's College London, Centre for Human & Applied Physiological Sciences, Faculty of Life Sciences & Medicine, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The annual review (AR) process for adults with CF at King’s College Hospital comprised a one-day assessment with patients reviewed by each MDT speciality. Imaging scans were requested but not timetabled. Patients found this AR lengthy, repetitive and stressful. Improved health on modulators and a drive to optimise the value delivered led to reviewing of the AR process.

Methods: Changes were iterative over 2 years. These included: single point of contact review by CF practitioner, formal MDT AR meeting to discuss each patient (with individual specialty review then arranged as required), scans scheduled, and formalised assessment template sent to GP with feedback summary. Additionally, feedback is discussed with patients during telephone consultation 6 weeks post-AR. Anonymised patient and staff feedback were collected to evaluate the new process.

Results: In 4-months, 62 AR were completed. From these, 27/62 patients completed a questionnaire. 25/27 rated their AR as extremely useful/useful. 21/27 patients rated the new process as better, citing reasons as “quicker”, “less repetitive”, “more convenient”, “less stressful” and “more joined up”. 5/27 patients rated it as the same. Patients reported the most important aspects at AR were discussing overall health and reviewing their test results. 11/18 members of the MDT completed a feedback questionnaire. They reported the new AR process was notably less repetitive for patients, had clear ownership of plans and feedback, shorter time for patient but less rushed, and MDT AR meeting was useful/very useful.

Conclusion: Overall, patients and staff feel that the new system has less repetition and increased efficiency. Some staff were initially resistant to change but with open conversations and MDT AR meetings this had led to more efficient use of clinical time. We next plan to integrate linking patients’ values and goals from a digital platform (PerEmpo) into their annual review as part of ongoing AR development.

Objectives: The annual review (AR) process for adults with CF at King’s College Hospital comprised a one-day assessment with patients reviewed by each MDT speciality. records.title: Meeting the need when it matters most: Creating a unique, specialist out-of-hours cystic fibrosis (CF) multidisciplinary team (MDT) on-call service at the York Hull CF Centre
records.authors_text: K. France1, K. Hasney2, J. Ackerley1, M. Robinson2, R. Thomas1, D. Shiferaw2, T. Daniels1
records.affiliations_text: 1York Hull Cystic Fibrosis Centre, York, United Kingdom, 2York Hull Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Hull, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: In the UK, CF Centres need to provide 24-hour access to specialist advice as part of NHSE service requirements (NHSE, 2018), CF Trust (CF Trust, 2024) and NICE guidelines (NICE, 2017). Prior to 2020, the CF Centre lacked a dedicated out-of-hours service, relying upon a generic respiratory ward for urgent CF queries. We developed a responsive and safe way of delivering an on-call service, staffed by the specialist CF MDT.

A nationwide survey of UK CF centres, highlighting practices and challenges in delivering 24-hour specialist advice, demonstrate that this is a unique and bespoke on-call model.

Methods: The CF team developed a specialist emergency on-call service. The model incorporates all clinical members of the CF MDT. The model provided a direct telephone advice line, enabling clinicians to deliver out-of-hours support. As the service evolved, monthly supervision and review were introduced to refine pathways and optimise procedures. On-call clinicians documented patient interactions. Support included updated standard operating procedures, clinical and patient resources, information cards, and website content.

Results: In 2025, there were 136 calls. 64% of these calls were at the weekends and 36% during the week. Out of these calls, 41% were emergencies, 30% were planned with the remaining 29% were patient or clinician initiated and non-urgent.

No adverse events or clinical incidents were reported, highlighting maintenance of safe and effective practice.

Conclusion: This adaptive, multidisciplinary on-call model enables safe and timely access to expert specialist CF care which is scalable and adaptive for emergency service delivery.

records.title: Uniting the Cystic Fibrosis Nursing Association (CFNA) through digital and social media platforms
records.authors_text: C. Whitton1, S. Basford2, A. McGrath3, C. Fagan4, S. Geoghegan5, R. Hodgson4, L. Wooldridge6, K. Mulholland7, E. Ellen8, D. O'Neill9, R. Rogers10, J. Daniels11, A. Walls12
records.affiliations_text: 1University Hospitals Plymouth NHS Trust, Plymouth, United Kingdom, 2Royal United Hospitals Bath NHS Foundation Trust, Bath, United Kingdom, 3NHS Lothian Royal Hospital for Children and Young People, Edinburgh, United Kingdom, 4The Newcastle Upon Tyne Hospital Foundation Trust, Newcastle, United Kingdom, 5Barts Health NHS Trust, London, United Kingdom, 6Birmingham Women's and Children's NHS Foundation Trust, Birmingham, United Kingdom, 7NHS Tayside, Ninewells Hospital, Tayside, United Kingdom, 8NHS Grampian, Aberdeen Royal Infirmary, Aberdeen, United Kingdom, 9Belfast Health and Social Care Trust, Belfast, United Kingdom, 10Royal Devon University Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust, Exeter, United Kingdom, 11Liverpool Heart and Chest Hospital NHS Trust, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 12Cambridgeshire and Peterborough NHS Foundation Trust, Peterborough, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: The CFNA is dedicated to empowering cystic fibrosis nurses through education, resources, and peer support, helping them deliver exceptional care to patients and families. A survey of CFNA members conducted in 2023 highlighted a lack of use of the CFNA website with members stating it was ‘outdated’ and ‘not user friendly’.1

66% of members reported they would like content on social media platforms.

Method: In response the CFNA committee worked with Amperative® to develop an updated website (www.cfna.org.uk). The new website featured a public area to showcase CFNA’s work and a private members-only forum for discussions, educational resources and regional/national networking.

The CFNA also welcomed a ‘social media and content representative’ to the committee.

CFNA members were resurveyed in January 2026.

Results: Since July 2024, the forum has grown to 184 members generating 153 posts and generated 354 comments, with acitivty rising monthly. In the last quarter, 16 users contributed 24 posts and 58 comments across diverse topics.

Social media accounts were created, Instagram has 91 members, Facebook 74 and X 53. A LinkedIn account has recently been added.

The 2026 survey received 47 responses. 96% were aware of the new website, 77% had used the website, comments included ‘User friendly and very interactive’ ‘Much improved’

Usefulness of the forum was rated 4.42 out of 5.

CFNA Member forum use20232026Never20%9%Yearly48%15%4-6 times yearly25%47%1-2 times monthly5%23%Weekly2%6%

20232026Aware of Fiona Lomas award58%94%Aware of education grants76%89%

Members are happy with the level of presence on social media and enjoy updates via these channels.

Conclusion: Increased visibility and ease of use has positively impacted members. There is an increased awareness of educational grants and awards.

Forum use has increased and continues to grow, fostering communication and an increased sense of community among CFNA members.

records.title: Managing cystic fibrosis newborn screening results: implications of transferring notification responsibility to CF nurses

person.institution: Birmingham Women's and Children's NHS Foundation Trust

records.authors_text: L. Wooldridge1, A.-M. Martin1, S. Evans1, L. Churchill1, S. Stone1
records.affiliations_text: 1Birmingham Women's and Children's NHS Foundation Trust, Cystic Fibrosis, Birmingham, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To assess the impact of transferring responsibility for Cystic Fibrosis (CF) suspected and CF carrier Newborn Screening (NBS) notifications to the CF nursing team, focusing on workload, timeliness of follow-up, and the ethical challenges.

Methods: A retrospective review was conducted of all CF suspected and CF carrier NBS notifications managed by the CF nursing team between August and December 2025. Data included number and type of notifications, time to family contact, diagnostic outcomes, and contextual factors affecting communication and care delivery.

Results: Eight infants were identified through NBS: five with suspected CF and three as CF carriers. Follow-up telephone contact occurred within 0–5 days, with a mean response time of two days. One family had not been contacted due to a consultant-led decision in the context of planned withdrawal of neonatal care. Most infants notified as suspected CF were subsequently confirmed to have CF; one was designated as CF Screen Positive, Inconclusive Diagnosis (CFSPID). Families of infants identified as CF carriers received appropriate counselling regarding future implications. One additional CF case was identified outside the NBS programme. Despite a substantial increase in workload and the ethical discomfort associated with describing results as “CF suspected” in line with national pathways, as well as the psychological burden of conveying complex and life-changing information by telephone, follow-up remained timely and compliant with NBS standards.

Conclusion: The transfer of NBS notification responsibilities to the CF nursing team has increased workload and highlighted significant ethical and emotional challenges. Compliance with national standards has been maintained, these findings underscore the need for greater recognition of the psychological impact, ethical complexity, and service capacity implications inherent in delivering CF NBS notifications.

records.title: Digital transformation of paediatric cystic fibrosis care: a cost-benefit evaluation
records.authors_text: F. Lundqvist1, M. Svedberg1, V. Mellqvist1
records.affiliations_text: 1Queen Silvia’s Children’s Hospital, Gothenburg, Sweden
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Specialized care for children and adolescents with cystic fibrosis (CF) involves complex and resource-intensive care pathways. To optimize workflows, support multidisciplinary teams, and enable structured evaluation, the CF centre in Gothenburg, Sweden implemented the digital care platform Hope. This study assessed the economic impact and cost–benefit of digital tools in CF care.

Methods: A before–after evaluation was performed using routinely collected operational data from the CF care team, including healthcare professionals and patients/caregivers, collected in 2023–2024. Benefits were identified using semi-structured national benefit calculation templates linked to defined tasks, volumes, and stakeholders. For key activities, quantitative time-and-motion studies were conducted before and after implementation, recording minimum, most likely, and maximum time spent. Results are presented as verified benefits observed in clinical practice and as an extended scenario including planned workflow improvements to be implemented from July 2026, with full effect expected in 2027. All costs were converted using an average exchange rate of 1 EUR = 10.75 SEK.

Results: Verified clinical implementation yielded a likely net economic benefit of approximately €746,000 over 2025–2030 (uncertainty interval €740,000–€772,000), with a positive net benefit already in 2025. This corresponds to a return on investment of approximately 2:1 over six years. Including planned workflow improvements from July 2026 increased the estimated net benefit to approximately €1.21 million. The main contributors were reduced staffing needs enabled by digital workflows and substitution of in-person monthly visits with digital video visits, followed by automated national CF registry transfers and more efficient planning and booking.

Conclusion: Implementation of a digital care platform in paediatric CF care was associated with early economic benefits and a positive return on investment.

records.title: Preliminary validity of the Flemish lung transplant quality of life survey for lung transplanted people with Cystic Fibrosis.
records.authors_text: T. Havermans1, M. Nicasy2, L. Moyens3, L. Dupont3, F. Wynants3, N. Duplacie3, C. Ruelens3, S. Bos3
records.affiliations_text: 1Trudy Havermans, Leuven, Belgium, 2Katholieke Universiteit Leuven, Leuven, Belgium, 3University Hospitals Leuven, Leuven, Belgium
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: This study reports on the preliminary validation of the Flemish Lung Transplant Health Related QOL survey (FLT-QOL). The aim is to construct a valid Quality of Life (QOL) scale to use during annual outpatient LT clinic to guide and improve multidisciplinary care for lung transplanted people with CF (LTpwCF).

Method: The Lung Transplant Health-Related Quality of Life (LT-QOL) Survey (Singer et al, 2015) includes 60 items (10 scales measuring: symptoms, health perceptions, functioning, and well-being) and was translated into Flemish using standard translation guidelines. Patients completed the FLT-QOL survey during outpatient clinics as well as the GAD-7, PHQ-9, WHO5 and a Visual Analogue scale (VAS-QOL). Demographic and medical variables were obtained from medical records.

Results: The LT clinic cares for 119 LTpwCF of whom 85 (71%) were stable at the time of the study. 69/85 (81%) participated: mean age 43 (range 23-65); 38 females. Time since LT was 11,9 years (SD=3.5; range 3-26). Mean lung function FEV1%pred. was 79% (SD=19%; range 39-129%); mean was BMI 21 (SD=3.5; range 16-32); and 54 (78%) were diagnosed with CFRD.

Cronbach alpha’s for the FLT-QOL scales ranged from 0.76 to 0.96 indicating good internal consistency. High correlations (possible redundancy) were found for FLT-health distress and FLT-worry about future health (r=.82). Correlations between FLT-QOL scales were moderate to good (r=.23 to r=.82).

Hypothesized associations between medical variables and FLT scales were weak. Hypotheses regarding concurrent validity were confirmed with significant correlations found between FLT-QOL scales and scores on the GAD7, PHQ9, WHO5 and VAS (r= 0.28-0.84; p<0.05-0.01) (table 1).

Conclusion: This study shows preliminary construct and concurrent validity of the FLT-QOL. Association with medical parameters was weak. Inclusion of the FLT-QOL survey in an annual screening program can provide important additional information of wellbeing in LTpwCF.

person.title: PhD
person.biography:
Trudy Havermans is a CF clinical health psychologist at the Cystic Fibrosis Centre of the University Hospital Leuven, Belgium. She has obtained her PhD at the University of Exeter, UK. For the past 25 years she has been responsible for the psychological care of a large cohort of paediatric, adult and transplanted people with CF. She has written several reviews and research papers on psychosocial aspects of CF and participated in multicentre international studies. She was speaker at the ERS courses on Cystic Fibrosis in 2013 and 2015.
Trudy Havermans is an active member of the European Cystic Fibrosis Society. For example, she participated in the ECFS Standard of Care projects, Scientific and Steering committees and contributed to three ECFS books. She was a member and treasurer of the ECFS board from 2019-2022. Trudy has set up and jointly led the ECFS Mental Health Working group for three years. At present she is a member of the ECFS Education committee, the ECFS Mental Health working group, the ECFS Telehealth for CF (THCF) working group and resides in the organising committee of the Special CF lunchtime webinars.

records.title: Work Forwards: employment programme evaluation
records.authors_text: G. Silverman1, J. Gregory1, B. Kilgariff1
records.affiliations_text: 1Cystic Fibrosis Trust, Information, Services and Programmes, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Work Forwards (WF) is an innovative programme, run by the Cystic Fibrosis Trust, supporting people affected by CF into secure and fulfilling employment. A three-year pilot was funded by the National Lottery Community Fund. In 2025, we evaluated the programme to understand its impact, reach and success.

Methods: We employed an independent researcher to assess the WF programme by reviewing existing service data and internal resources. The evaluator spoke directly with people involved with the programme. This included 12 in-depth interviews with staff, referrers and beneficiaries. Survey responses and feedback were analysed to build a clear picture of the effectiveness and successes of the programme.

Results:

​

2022-2025TargetAchievedOne-to-one advice135265Workshops3030Digital Case studies100110Target Reach70050,035 - 453 direct and 49,582 indirect via resources/communications

Video resources on employment rights and workplace support for people affected by CF were co-produced with the community. Beneficiaries valued the support on discussing CF, rights, discrimination, and reasonable adjustments. They all reported increased confidence to have these conversations at work.

Feedback showed:

89% feel more confident about steps to find or stay in work that is right for them and move their employment situation forward

93% feel more hopeful about career opportunities.

95% feel satisfied with the support

97% would likely recommend WF to others

Conclusion: WF has delivered a highly successful, pioneering pilot. Across the three-year funded period the programme exceeded targets for one-to-one advice and digital case studies. It produced valued resources including podcasts, employer videos and achieved measurable positive outcomes. Clients reported increased confidence, hope, practical progress in work and improved ability to balance CF and employment. This work has evidenced that there is an ongoing need for specialist, CF-focused, employment support.

records.title: A ‘life-line’ – delivering enhanced winter support to low income households affected by cystic fibrosis through the Cystic Fibrosis Trust’s welfare grant programme
records.authors_text: B. Kilgariff1, M. Delooze1, W. Coates1, L. Horne1
records.affiliations_text: 1Cystic Fibrosis Trust, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Cystic Fibrosis Trust has offered an enhanced package of winter support since 2021, aiming to protect CF health by targeting financial support at low income households. Between Oct 21 and Mar 25, 1927 grants were provided, to 1222 households. Grant recipients were also offered support and signposting from our welfare team. In 21-22, grants were £500. In subsequent years, grants were £225, usually split over 3 months.

Methods: Each year, we have conducted detailed surveys to understand the impact of the grants and the challenges faced by low income households. In early 2026, we combined all available survey data since 2021, to evaluate the support provided over the past 5 years.

Results: People affected by CF reported positive impacts on their physical and mental health:

% strongly agree/agree

Average (2021-2025)I have felt less stressed and anxious93%I have felt happier87%I have been less worried about basic costs83%I feel that the grant is helping to keep me / the person with CF well this winter99%

Over 89% agreed that without the grant, they would have struggled with essential costs of heating/eating.

“It's prevented me from going back into hospital during a period that I was going downhill sat in the cold house.”

All CF professionals surveyed felt that the support improved their patients’ physical and mental health. Some commented that this was “a life-line”. 60% reported that they felt the support ‘helped reduce the risk of my patient(s) being admitted to hospital this winter’.

Survey data showed the reality of life with CF on a low income:

In the past 12 months…% strongly agree/agree

Average (2021-2025)Have you found yourself having to choose between buying the food you need or heating your home?59%Have you struggled to buy the basics needed to stay well with CF? (e.g. buying enough food, keeping your home warm)78%Have you gone without basic toiletries or hygiene products because you couldn't afford to buy what you needed?40%Have you missed a hospital or CF clinic appointment because you didn't have enough money to go?24%

Conclusion: These surveys show the precarious nature of life with CF on a low income, with people forced to choose between essentials, go without hygiene products, and miss hospital appointments due to cost.

Evidence shows the value of a relatively small financial intervention, supported by information and further support. Professionals and households affected by CF feel this support has improved physical and mental health. This is important for policymakers, charities, and CF teams to consider.

records.title: Quality of life and stress levels in people with cystic fibrosis in Kazakhstan
records.authors_text: A. Ramankul1, I. Mukatova1, E. Amelina1, S. Kim1, A. Serikova1, Y. Kenzhebaeva2
records.affiliations_text: 1Astana Medical University, Department of Internal Diseases N3, Astana, Kazakhstan, 2Multidisciplinary City Hospital No1, Pulmonology Department, Astana, Kazakhstan
records.abstract_text:
Objective: To assess anxiety levels and quality of life in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF).

Methods: The study included 31 (15 male) pwCF, aged 23,3 (17 to 45) yrs. Psychoemotional state was assessed using the GAD-7 and quality of life (QoL) - the SF-36 questionnaires,

Results: The lowest QoL scores were observed for role functioning due to emotional state (43,7) and general health (41,1). The highest average scores were observed for the domains of physical functioning (69,1), pain intensity (61,1) and social functioning (56). The life activity domain and physical role functioning domain had similar mean scores of 49,8 and 50 points, respectively. When analyzing the overall data, the physical health component total score was 55,3 (female 55.9; male 51,9) and the psychological health component 50,7 points, respectively (female 52,6; male 53,5).

The overall GAD-7 score averaged 7,83 for the patient cohort, female - 9,1 and male 6,5. The highest scores were observed for "excessive worry about various things" – 1,35; "inability to relax" – 1,22. Fewer responses were found for "inability to cope with anxiety" (0,9), "extreme anxiety: "I can't find a place for myself" (0,9) and "fear of something scary" (0,9). Older age was associated with more frequent anxiety symptoms, including irritability (p=0,031), difficulty relaxing (p=0,026), increased susceptibility to anxiety (p=0,009). The GAD-7 total score did not show a statistically significant correlation with age (ρ=0,268; p=0,145).

Conclusion: Adult pwCF demonstrate a heterogeneous, generally reduced QoL, the presence of anxiety symptoms of varying severity. Older age is associated with increased anxiety manifestations. These findings suggest the need of a comprehensive approach to managing pwCF, including psychosocial support along with basic therapeutic options.

records.title: Self-Identity for adolescents and adults with cystic fibrosis: a qualitative synthesis
records.authors_text: S. MacFarlane1, C. Murray1, R. Faulkner2
records.affiliations_text: 1Lancaster University, Division of Health Research, Lancaster, United Kingdom, 2Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust, Manchester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: People with cystic fibrosis, a typically childhood-onset condition, develop their identity alongside their illness. While identity coherence supports wellbeing and adjustment, cystic fibrosis, demands may disrupt this process. Research on identity in cystic fibrosis, is fragmented, with findings often embedded in broader topics. This review aimed to synthesised qualitative studies to provide a coherent understanding of identity in adolescents and adults with cystic fibrosis.

Methods: A systematic search of seven databases identified 34 eligible studies, which were analysed using thematic synthesis.

Results: Four themes were generated: (1) Making sense of identity: Normality versus difference; (2) Made to feel different: Social perceptions emphasising CF; (3) Maintaining identity and reducing difference; and (4) Shifting identities: Health status changes disrupting identity.

Conclusion: Identity in CF is dynamic, shaped by negotiations of normalcy, social perceptions, and health changes, with strategies employed by people with cystic fibrosis to reduce difference.
