records.title: ‘Mum Culture’ in hospital care: an interpretative phenomenological analysis of identity, scrutiny, and coping among mothers of children with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: R. Day1,1
records.affiliations_text: 1Arden University, Psychology, Coventry, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Parents of children with cystic fibrosis (CF) frequently remain in hospital during repeated admissions, yet their psychological experiences are often overlooked. This study explored how parents experience identity, scrutiny, and coping within the hospital environment, and how everyday communication practices shape emotional safety and resilience.

Methods: A qualitative study using Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA) was conducted. Five parents of children with CF who had experienced repeated or prolonged hospital admissions participated in semi-structured interviews. Interviews explored emotional impact, parental identity, interactions with healthcare professionals, coping strategies, and unmet support needs. Data were analysed idiographically and across cases. Internal Family Systems (IFS) and Polyvagal Theory informed interpretation.

Results: Three superordinate themes were identified:

(1) “Mum culture” and loss of identity, where parents described being addressed by generic labels rather than by name, contributing to feelings of invisibility and reduced confidence;

(2) Scrutiny and the institutional gaze, characterised by vigilance, fear of judgement, and safeguarding-related anxiety, which limited expression of vulnerability;

(3) Protective coping through emotional control, where parents relied on suppressive strategies to appear competent. Outward resilience was maintained at significant emotional cost.

Conclusion: Hospital culture strongly shapes parental identity, emotional safety, and coping during CF admissions. Routine communication practices and perceived scrutiny can promote emotionally suppressive coping rather than supported resilience. Simple relational changes such as addressing parents by name, acknowledging expertise, and brief emotional check-ins may reduce burden and improve parent–professional collaboration.

records.title: Exploring processes and experiences of comfort among adults living with cystic fibrosis: a qualitative study

person.title: Master
person.institution: Universidade Católica Portuguesa - Faculdade de Ciências da Saúde e Enfermagem

records.authors_text: A. Nabais1,2, H. Laranjeira3, A. Góis3, M.C. Roquette Viana4, P. Pontífice-Sousa4
records.affiliations_text: 1Universidade Católica Portuguesa - Faculdade de Ciências da Saúde e Enfermagem, PhD Student, Lisboa, Portugal, 2Escola Superior de Enfermagem da Universidade de Coimbra, Enfermagem de Reabilitação, Coimbra, Portugal, 3Unidade Local de Saúde de Coimbra, Serviço de Pneumologia, Coimbra, Portugal, 4Universidade Católica Portuguesa - Faculdade de Ciências da Saúde e Enfermagem, Enfermagem, Lisboa, Portugal
records.abstract_text:
Background:

Advances in cystic fibrosis (CF) care, particularly CFTR modulator therapies, have increased life expectancy and transformed CF into a long-term adult condition. However, not all people with CF are eligible for these therapies, resulting in different therapeutic contexts. While outcomes have improved, little is known about how comfort is experienced within these changing realities. Understanding comfort as a dynamic and multidimensional process is essential to inform nursing care beyond symptom control.

Aim:

To explore experiences and processes of comfort among adults living with cystic fibrosis under different therapeutic conditions and identify implications for nursing practice.

Methods:

This ongoing qualitative study adopts an interpretive, constructivist approach. Ten semi-structured interviews were conducted with adults living with CF, including participants receiving CFTR modulators and others not eligible. Interviews explored experiences of adulthood with CF, meanings of comfort and strategies used to manage comfort in daily life and healthcare. Data analysis is iterative and inductive.

Preliminary findings:

Comfort was described as a dynamic process shaped by physical, emotional and relational dimensions. It was linked to adaptation to adult life and maintaining daily activities and life projects. Among participants receiving modulators, comfort was associated with symptom relief, bodily normalisation and emotional changes, including relief, hope, uncertainty and identity renegotiation. Those not eligible relied more on relational support, routines and continuity of care. Nurses were central in sustaining comfort across contexts.

Conclusions:

Comfort emerges as an evolving, context-dependent process. Nursing care that recognises these differences while supporting adaptation may better address long-term needs in adult CF.

records.title: ​Understanding the evolving needs of the cystic fibrosis (CF) community in Australia: challenges, priorities and opportunities
records.authors_text: G. Handley1, S. Quattromani1, K. Johnson1
records.affiliations_text: 1CF Together, Carnegie, Australia
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The CF landscape has changed significantly in recent years with widespread access to CFTR modulators (CFTRm), leading to more people living longer and shifting social, health and economic needs. This study aimed to explore the current lived experience of people with CF (pwCF) and their families in Australia, to inform responsive and future-focused care and support systems.

Methods: An online anonymous survey was distributed nationally via social media and emails lists, focussing on demographics, diagnosis experiences, physical and mental health, treatment history and access, and social and economic impacts of CF. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively to summarise outcomes across domains. Free-text responses were analysed using thematic coding.

Results: 231 responses were received, including 50% pwCF, 47% parents of pwCF and 3% partners of pwCF, from all Australian states and territories.

Nearly half of respondents reported a diagnosis or experience of anxiety (48%) and over one-third reported depression (36%). The burden of managing CF was rated as moderate to very high by 84% of respondents. While majority (75%) reported currently taking a CFTRm, 68% experienced at least one CFTRm side effect, most commonly brain fog (24%), and 18% reported modifying CFTRm use due to side effects. Gaps in primary care integration were identified, with 22% lacking regular general practitioner (GP) access and 41% reporting no coordination between their GP and CF team. Financial strain was common: 63% reported a major to moderate impact of CF on household finances, and 35% reported not purchasing a medicine due to cost.

Conclusion: While CFTRm have transformed clinical outcomes for many, pwCF and their families continue to face significant mental health challenges, treatment burden, care coordination gaps and financial strain. These findings highlight the need for evolving care and support models to address the broader and changing needs of the CF community.

records.title: Helen Barrett Bright Ideas (HBBI): Supporting the CF community into sustainable self-employment
records.authors_text: J. Gregory1, G. Silverman2, B. Kilgariff2
records.affiliations_text: 1Cystic Fibrosis Trust, Information, Services and Programmes, London, United Kingdom, 2Cystic Fibrosis Trust, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Self-employment, and the flexibility to schedule workloads around CF, is an enticing option for adults with CF who want to work. However, it comes with its own set of challenges. HBBI was set up in memory of Helen Barrett, a business woman with CF, following her death in 2013. The award has been supporting adults with CF in the UK to build confidence and pursue their business ideas.

Methods: HBBI aims to provide a platform for adults with CF to pursue their business ambitions through grant funding, whilst also providing business planning support and a range of online sessions dedicated to business development and sustainability.

Results: To date, HBBI has provided grant funding to 87 CF owned businesses, including winners who are post-transplant and/or who are currently unable to benefit from modulators.

Winners told us the award built their confidence, improved their mental health, and enabled them to take positive steps towards achieving their career goals

“The award gave me a huge sense of confidence in my own ability which further down the line has helped me immensely in my career.” HBBI is now developing its offer to ensure that supported businesses are able to launch sustainably through our business plan, one-to-one business planning support, online networking; and webinar sessions on a range of business topics.

Conclusion: The demand after over a decade of delivery of HBBI, highlight the ongoing need for access to support for business owners with CF. Funding has helped to establish businesses across a wide range of sectors. Winners have opened physical premises, and a winner secured further funding through BBC’s Dragon’s Den. Others have been able to use their business to build confidence and improve their employability. However, there is a need for further support, and the Trust is looking to expand HBBI to build an effective support framework to help ensure that CF owned businesses can find long-term success.

records.title: Developing the use of qualitative research methods in cystic fibrosis: establishing the Cystic Fibrosis Qualitative Research Network (CFQRN)
records.authors_text: D. Beever1, R. Dobra2,3, J. Snowball4,5, Cystic Fibrosis Qualitative Research Network
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Nottingham, School of Medicine, Nottingham, United Kingdom, 2Imperial College London, National Heart and Lung Institute, London, United Kingdom, 3Royal Brompton Hospital, Department of Respiratory Paediatrics, London, United Kingdom, 4University of Oxford, Nuffield Department of Primary Care Health Sciences, Oxford, United Kingdom, 5Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, Oxford Adult CF Centre, Oxford, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Incorporating stakeholders’ views into care delivery is rightly gaining traction across healthcare. Qualitative research is a robust way to gain systematic and valuable insights into the experiences and perspectives of those with lived and professional experience of cystic fibrosis (CF). It can provide important contextual information either independently or alongside quantitative methods.

In the post-modulator era, with significant changes to the physical, emotional and social wellbeing of many people with CF (pwCF), as well as changes to care delivery, understanding the experiences and perspectives of those living with, and working in, CF is arguably more important than ever.

The Cystic Fibrosis Qualitative Research Network (CFQRN) was established to provide a space for peer support, shared learning & collaboration amongst those interested in qualitative research in CF.

Methods: Social media and personal networks were used to promote the CFQRN. As an initial collective formed, a website (https://cfqrn.carrd.co/) was established as a landing page for interested individuals.

Results: The network currently has 46 members (with 30 new members in the last 6 months) across 36 organisations and includes healthcare professionals, researchers and pwCF. The research interests of group members are diverse, including ageing, exercise and diet. Since December 2024, we have held quarterly virtual meetings, including research presentations, methodological discussion, training opportunities and promotion of group members’ research.

Conclusion: The growth of the CFQRN indicates significant interest in the use of qualitative methods in CF. The network aims to support individuals to develop their understanding of qualitative research, enhance their skills and increase the quality when using such methods. We plan to expand the network to collaborate on grant applications and obtain funding to undertake qualitative research at this important juncture in CF care.

person.biography:
Dan is a PhD student at the University of Nottingham, England, and part of the MAGNIFY Strategic Research Centre, which is exploring the use of lung magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in CF. His work is specifically focused on the development of a toolkit of resources to support the communication and understanding of lung MRI results.
Dan has a particular interest in the use of qualitative research methods and public involvement in health research. He has experience of using both in the development of the MRI toolkit, as well as interventions in type 1 diabetes and motor neuron disease.
In 2024, he established the CF Qualitative Research Network, an international group of researchers with an interest in the use of qualitative methods in CF research. The network provides a space for peer support, shared learning & collaboration.

records.title: Developing an early career writers’ forum for healthcare professionals and scientists working in cystic fibrosis research
records.authors_text: R. Dobra1,2, C. Short1,2, J.C Davies1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Imperial College London, National Heart and Lung Institute, London, United Kingdom, 2Royal Brompton Hospital, Department of Respiratory Paediatrics, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Many training pathways, especially in healthcare, place little emphasis on teaching academic writing skills. These become increasingly important as healthcare professionals’ (HCPs) and scientists’ careers progress. In line with The ECFS’s commitment to develop the next generation of CF researchers, we set up an Early Career Writers’ Forum (ECWF), a programme for early career (EC) researchers to expand their writing and presenting skills with the support of each other and the guidance of established researchers.

Methods: We shared a survey within the integrated CF care and research teams at The Royal Brompton Hospital and Imperial College London to gauge the value of an ECWF and collate session suggestions. 29/30 respondents said they would find an ECWF 'really useful' or ‘would have found it really useful’ earlier in their career. Specific sessions were requested.

Results: Since Jan 2025, we have organised eight hybrid sessions by internal and external speakers using a variety of formats. Sessions are recorded. Topics include guidance on Imperial’s PhD assessments and “How to Write a Lay Summary”. Core sessions will be repeated two-yearly for new staff. The forum is iterative; for example, learners requested a ‘trouble shooting’ workshop which was popular and will be repeated within the programme. Further sessions will be added if requested.

Sessions have been attended by >55 EC writers (~25 AHPs, 15 medics, 15 scientists) who consider themselves EC, 28 recordings have been shared. Although aimed at our local team, the ECWF has been advertised by word of mouth; staff from seven external UK-based institutions have joined sessions.

Conclusion: The ECWF is an evolving, responsive forum that has been well attended by our CF team and beyond. Learners have shaped the forum to meet their needs. Those outside our team have sought to join sessions. Given the apparent need and interest, we would encourage others to establish a similar programme.

In line with The ECFS’s commitment to develop the next generation of CF researchers, we set up an Early Career Writers’ Forum (ECWF), a programme for early career (EC) researchers to expand their writing and presenting skills with the support of each other and the guidance of established researchers.
records.methods: We shared a survey within the integrated CF care and research teams at The Royal Brompton Hospital and Imperial College London to gauge the value of an ECWF and collate session suggestions. 29/30 respondents said they would find an ECWF 'really useful' or ‘would have found it really useful’ earlier in their career. Specific sessions were requested.
records.results:
Since Jan 2025, we have organised eight hybrid sessions by internal and external speakers using a variety of formats. Sessions are recorded. Topics include guidance on Imperial’s PhD assessments and “How to Write a Lay Summary”. Core sessions will be repeated two-yearly for new staff. The forum is iterative; for example, learners requested a ‘trouble shooting’ workshop which was popular and will be repeated within the programme. Further sessions will be added if requested.

Sessions have been attended by >55 EC writers (~25 AHPs, 15 medics, 15 scientists) who consider themselves EC, 28 recordings have been shared. Although aimed at our local team, the ECWF has been advertised by word of mouth; staff from seven external UK-based institutions have joined sessions.
records.conclusion: The ECWF is an evolving, responsive forum that has been well attended by our CF team and beyond. Learners have shaped the forum to meet their needs. Those outside our team have sought to join sessions. Given the apparent need and interest, we would encourage others to establish a similar programme.

records.title: Rebuilding a patient led cystic fibrosis community through a patient led focus group
records.authors_text: J. Swarbrooke1, L. Haigh1, D. Ross1, N. Shaw1, I.J Clifton1, A. Sawant1, G. Spoletini1, D.G Peckham1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1St James University Hospital, Adult Cystic Fibrosis, Leeds, United Kingdom, 2Leeds Institute of Medical Research at St James's, University of Leeds, Leeds, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Our primary objective was to rebuild a Cystic Fibrosis (CF) community in a safe and sustainable way, giving people with CF (PwCF) the chance to lead conversations and shape their own care. We wanted to create a group where patients felt heard, valued, and connected and improve the experience of care and patient outcomes for PwCF.

Methods: Patients were approached to be part of the CF patient focus group through face-to-face interaction and multiple social media and patient network platforms, to establish a patient representative group for PwCF. Patients set the agenda and crucially, staff from across the multidisciplinary team attend not to lead, but to listen and learn. Group guidelines were set to encourage and positive safe space, and to protect patient confidentiality.

Results: The patient focus group has led to tangible, co-produced improvements in the inpatient environment, communication, and service delivery for PwCF. Patient feedback has directly informed changes to the ward environment, ensuring it is safer, more comfortable, and better aligned with patient needs. The group has also improved communication by keeping patients informed of changes within the multidisciplinary team, and the services. The group influences the future of PwCF by discussing what matters most to them, ensuring that our research portfolio reflects their priorities. This approach helps improve patient recruitment and retention.

Conclusion: The group continues to generate ideas, communicate openly and build on the momentum we’ve created. Together, we have developed a flexible platform that can adapt to the evolving health and social needs of PwCFs, while keeping them safe and minimising the impact on their daily lives.

records.title: A tale of two cities: evaluating the twinning visit between the Royal Brompton Hospital, London, UK and the adult and paediatric cystic fibrosis centres in Lviv, Ukraine
records.authors_text: R. Dobra1,2, M. Sheremet3, B. Belkarty4, J. King2,1
records.affiliations_text: 1Imperial College London, National Heart and Lung Institute, London, United Kingdom, 2Royal Brompton Hospital, Department of Respiratory Paediatrics, London, United Kingdom, 3Clinical Center of Children’s Healthcare, Lviv, Ukraine, 4Royal Brompton Hospital, Department of Adult Cystic Fibrosis, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objective: The ECFS Twinning Programme partners experienced & emerging sites to optimise CF care at the emerging site. Royal Brompton Hospital, London, & adult/paediatric CF centres in Lviv, Ukraine are twinned. Due to the war in Ukraine, the London team could not visit Lviv, so Lviv teams visited London. Here we evaluate the visit, sharing our findings for those interested in the programme.

Methods: Surveys shared via Qualtrics, interviews conducted/transcribed in Teams. Interview transcripts & survey free-text coded in NVivo. Content analysis used to interpret themes.

Results: Dec25-Jan26; 29 surveys(7 Lviv,22 London) & 4 interviews(1 Lviv,3 London); 4 themes.

Benefits to both teams The Lviv team praised the visit, feeling it would improve patient care. The London team highlighted multiple benefits including prestige of participating.

Comparing cultures Lviv noted London’s clinicians were more guideline driven; both teams noted a greater emphasis on the multidisciplinary team in London. However, teams discovered many challenges e.g. poor adherence are cross-cultural.

Logistical challenges Covering service delivery/personal commitments in their absence required significant planning for the Lviv team. Setting up the visit was time consuming for the London team. Securing funding e.g. for interpreters & accommodation was difficult, compounded by London’s high costs.

Strengths & weaknesses Both teams felt the programme was well balanced & enjoyed the case exchange & social programme. The Lviv team commented that being in London meant they could engage in the visit away from clinical/personal demands. Both teams emphasised the need for more interpreters.

Conclusions: The twinning visit was useful, enjoyable & rewarding for both teams. Adequate funding, especially for interpreter services, is essential to ensure a successful visit. Although deviating from the expected visit structure, both teams highlighted benefits to the emerging team visiting the established centre.

records.title: Treatment adherence and mental health in people with cystic fibrosis and advanced lung disease treated with elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor

person.title: Dr.
person.department: Psychology Unit, Child & Adolescent Psychiatry Unit

records.authors_text: V. Terlizzi1, S. Graziano2, S. Presti3, M.A. Malanima4, C. Fevola1, A. Castaldo5,6, C. Teodori1, S. Bresci7, A. Avarello7, A.L. Quittner8, E. Lucenteforte9
records.affiliations_text: 1Meyer Children's Hospital IRCCS, Cystic Fibrosis Regional Reference Center, Firenze, Italy, 2Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital, IRCCS, Psychology Unit, Child & Adolescent Psychiatry Unit, Roma, Italy, 3San Marco Hospital, Pediatric Respiratory Unit, Catania, Italy, 4University of Pisa, Department of Surgical, Medical and Molecular Pathology and Critical Care Medicine, Pisa, Italy, 5Santobono-Pausillipon Hospital, Pediatric Pneumology and Sub Intensive Care and Rehabilitation Unit, Napoli, Italy, 6University of Naples Federico II, Department of Public Health, Napoli, Italy, 7Careggi University Hospital, Cystic Fibrosis Unit, Firenze, Italy, 8Pulmonary and Sleep Center, Joe DiMaggio Cystic Fibrosis, Hollywood, United States, 9University of Florence, Department of Statistics, Computer Science and Applications "G. Parenti", Firenze, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Advanced lung disease (ALD) is a leading cause of mortality in CF. While Elexacaftor/Tezacaftor/Ivacaftor (ETI) has shown significant clinical benefits, little is known about treatment adherence neuropsychological side-effects in the ALD population following ETI. This study evaluated self-reported adherence, health-related quality of life (HRQoL), mental health, and ETI-related side-effects in patients with ALD.

Methods: A prospective, cross-sectional study was conducted at the CF Center of Florence, Italy. Participants (N=31, age>12y) with ALD (ppFEV1<40% or transplant referral at baseline) were enrolled from an ETI compassionate use program. After 36m of therapy, patients completed the Treatment Adherence Questionnaire-CF (TAQ-CF), CF Questionnaire-Revised (CFQ-R), PHQ-9 (depression), GAD-7 (anxiety), and an ad-hoc neuropsychological side-effect survey. Clinical data (ppFEV1, BMI, sweat chloride SC) were tracked from baseline to 36m.

Results: Clinical parameters improved significantly from baseline to 36m: SC decreased, while ppFEV1 and BMI increased (p<0.05). HRQoL scores significantly improved across most CFQ-R domains. The mean overall adherence rate was 75.6%; 45.2% reported high and 51.6% moderate adherence. No significant association was found between adherence levels and clinical or mental health outcomes. However, neuropsychological side-effects were prevalent: 29% reported concentration difficulties and 19% reported insomnia. Significant correlations were found between GAD-7 scores and the number of reported side-effects (p<0.05).

Conclusion: Patients with ALD maintain high-to-moderate treatment adherence 36m after initiating ETI, likely due to high disease burden. While ETI provides pulmonary and HRQoL improvements, a subset of patients experiences persistent neuropsychological side-effects correlated with anxiety. These findings highlight the need for a holistic approach to ALD management that monitors both physical and mental well-being.

person.biography: Dr. Graziano is a clinical psychologist and psychotherapist and she works at the Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital in Rome in the Child & Adolescent Psychiatry Unit and in the Pneumology and Cystic Fibrosis Unit. She is a co-chair of the European Cystic Fibrosis Society (ECFS) Mental Health Working Group and a member of the CF Foundation Mental Health Advisory Committee in the US. Her primary research and clinical interests focus on trauma and stressors related to managing a chronic illness. Her research focuses on depression, anxiety and HRQoL in individuals with CF and caregivers. In 2019, she attended the CF-CBT training in Boston (Massachusetts General Hospital) and is applying this intervention at the children’s hospital in Rome. She is a co-founder of the Italian National Trauma Center (INTC), and attended several training sessions to prepare for this role. For example, she completed the \"Mastery in Global Mental Health: Trauma and Recovery Certificate Program\" - Harvard Medical School in 2009, and from 2011 to 2013, she attended the Harvard/MGH Trauma Program as a research fellow. Her specialization in trauma treatment led to her role in training primary care practitioners after the Earthquakes in Italy in 2010 and 2016.

records.title: Patient-provider communication and shared decision-making in CF pain management
records.authors_text: D. Friedman1, T.M. Mullen1, M. Behrman2, J. Robichaud2, R. Wei1, N. Chaudhary1, J. He2, A. Chadwick2, J. Greenberg1, L. Yonker1, A.M. Georgiopoulos1, A.S. Bruce2
records.affiliations_text: 1Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, United States, 2University of Kansas Medical Center, Kansas City, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Sixty to 90% of adults with cystic fibrosis (AWCF) experience pain, often chronic in nature. Effective communication between patients and CF care teams is crucial for optimal pain management. Our goal was to learn from AWCF about their pain management experiences through in-depth interviews.

Methods: We recruited 14 AWCF experiencing chronic pain via CF Foundation’s Community Voice and conducted semi-structured qualitative interviews about living with CF and pain, including questions about pain management and experiences of shared decision-making. We developed a codebook and conducted thematic analysis.

Results: Participants were 23-64 years old; 10 identified as female, 3 male, 1 gender non-binary; 2 as Hispanic/Latinx; 12 White; 7 were taking elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI). Most (92.9%) reported trying multiple pain treatments (medication and non-medication). Participants reported largely positive pain management experiences with CF teams, and more negative experiences with non-CF providers, especially when inpatient. Themes highlighted key elements of pain management communication (e.g., validation of pain, empathetic care, effective care coordination, responsiveness and consistency). Table 1 presents exemplar quotes of these elements and components of shared decision-making.

Conclusion: Interviews with AWCF highlight experiences with effective patient-provider communication in CF pain management, as well as experienced barriers to optimal care. Increased understanding and validation of CF pain as well as coordinated and co-developed pain management plans are needed.

Table 1. Key themes of pain management communication

Key themes of pain management

communicationPositive experiencesNegative experiencesValidation of pain experiences“I am so grateful for the team I have now, because they have never made me feel like it's all in my head...[my CF doctor] will say ‘absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, if you tell me that’s how you feel I believe it.’”“As far as like pleurisy, I've had doctors say, ‘Well, that's not a real pain’ or...’You're calling it pain, but it's not pain. It's...inflammation’ or something like that.”Empathetic care“Some will still sit down and talk to you at eye level. One...she'll come in and talk to you...at the end, she's like,‘OK, now it's time for you to ask me questions.’ She specifically stops early enough to be sure that she's covering anything else that you might be concerned about. So that really helps with at least feeling heard.”“I had a GI physician who I actually had to go to counseling for medical trauma because...she would tell me things like ‘no one wants you for a patient, because you're so complicated’.Effective Care Coordination“The pulmonology team…will have my records to say, ‘Okay, this is how we have to treat and take care of him, because he has cystic fibrosis’ and the...GI team, and Endo, and everyone else …will be able to take that over...because they have all of my …chart notes.”“I had one [J tube] surgically that was excruciatingly painful...The surgeon had never done one on a CF patient and it was a different type of surgery for him, so I guess he and the GI doctor didn't really communicate about what to put in, so I had this big inflexible tube sticking out of me for seven months. It was awful.”Care team is responsive and accessible“With Epic and MyChart, I can just shoot a message to my doctor and the whole CF team and get a response or a phone call within probably 30 minutes. And you're like, “okay, this is what's happening. Do I need to make an appointment? Should I go to the ER?”“It's difficult at times getting into contact with them, because the doctors are not always in the clinics every day. Once I'm finally in contact, it's a whole other difficulty, because …over the phone, they can't understand what your pain is like and where it's coming from and … how it's affecting you, which sometimes it can also be difficult for them to take it serious enough to understand that we need to do something about it. Sometimes…they just tell me to wait …for the pain to slowly improve on its own.”Consistency/Feeling well known by the provider“My pain management doctor and I have been able to discuss things, and...we know each other very well, we see each other every other month, and we understand each other.”“But I have had…the hospital pain team see me. They're not, obviously, the same pain physician that I see outpatient every few months. So they just look at my file and walk in, and say, “hey, how's your pain? Is the pump covering everything while you're here?”, that kind of stuff.”Shared decision-makingShared understanding of cause of pain

“My doctors now know that I am in a science-based field... and so they've done a good job of explaining it in terms that I will understand. So that I can better understand my body.”“I think mostly frustrating. Because like I said, they don't really have an answer and, sometimes they brush it off like it's, something you just have to learn to accept sometimes. So it gets very frustrating and sometimes it gets to a point where…I wonder whether or not to bring it up in the first place.”Experiences with providers eliciting patient treatment preferences“It's been better since...I switched from pediatric to adult, and I think that really made a difference ...I started going to those doctor’s appointments by myself and I kind of led that conversation as opposed to my mom or dad leading that conversation when I was a pediatric patient. And I think the adult doctor does a better job of talking to me on my skill level than they used to just explain everything to my parents while I was sitting there.”“You want to know what's wrong...it cannot be in your head. records.title: The socioeconomic determinants of lung function in children with cystic fibrosis
records.authors_text: I. Jordan1, S. Hamrang - Yousefi2, R. Harwood3, A. Maitra4,1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Manchester, School of Medical Sciences, Manchester, United Kingdom, 2Royal Manchester Children's Hospital, Department of Paediatric Research, Manchester, United Kingdom, 3Manchester University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, Depart of Biostatistics, Manchester, United Kingdom, 4Royal Manchester Children's Hospital, Department of Paediatric Respiratory Medicine, Manchester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Children with cystic fibrosis (CF) from socioeconomically deprived backgrounds have poorer health outcomes, including reduced lung function. This study assessed the relationship between socioeconomic status and lung function among children with CF at a large paediatric CF centre.

Methods: Royal Manchester Children’s Hospital (RMCH), a leading tertiary CF centre in northwestern England, cares for 330 paediatric CF patients, including 200 receiving direct treatment and 130 through shared care. A retrospective study was conducted using anonymised data, including the Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD decile) as a socioeconomic indicator, percentage predicted FEV₁ (ppFEV₁), BMI z-score, sweat chloride levels, CF genotype, the number of antibiotic courses in the past year, and reports of adherence issues. Relationships between FEV₁ and these variables were assessed via Pearson correlation coefficients. Scatter plots with trend lines were created to illustrate the link between IMD decile and FEV₁. P values were calculated to determine statistical significance.

Results: Data were complete for 129 children with CF aged 5 to 17 years. The IMD decile distribution was predominantly low, suggesting most participants lived in deprived areas. A weak positive correlation was observed between IMD decile and ppFEV1 (R² = 0.06), suggesting that children from less deprived areas had slightly better lung function. Nonetheless, the IMD decile explained only a small part of the variation. Additionally, ppFEV1 showed a weak correlation with younger age and male sex.

Conclusions: Findings indicate that socioeconomic disparities in lung function persist, but to a lesser extent than at the national level, where deprivation accounts for more variability.

records.title: Knowledge level of home healthcare personnel on cystic fibrosis: evaluation before and after training
records.authors_text: G. Alışbeyli1, Ş. Karabulut1, E. Değermenci2, R. Açıncan3, B. Hoş4, C.A. Yıldız1, N.M. Çakar1, E.E. Baysal1, M.M. Akkitap Yiğit1, F. Özdemircioğlu1, B. Özgünay1, E. Uğurlu1, C. Yılmaz Yeğit1, A.P. Ergenekon1, E. Erdem Eralp1, Y. Gökdemir1, F. Karakoç1, B. Karadağ1, F. Gafarova1
records.affiliations_text: 1Marmara University, Pediatric Pulmonology, İstanbul, Turkey, 2Marmara University, Selim Çöremen Cystic Fibrosis Center, İstanbul, Turkey, 3Tuzla State Hospital, Family Medicine, İstanbul, Turkey, 4Marmara University Pendik Research and Training Hospital, Medical Directorate, İstanbul, Turkey
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Advances in diagnosis and treatment have prolonged the life expectancy of patients with cystic fibrosis (CF). The increasing number of diagnosed cases underscores the importance of primary healthcare providers, including home healthcare personnel, in patient management. To evaluate the knowledge level of home healthcare staff regarding CF and to assess knowledge gain following a structured training session.

Methods: A total of 35 healthcare professionals participated in the study. A 22-item questionnaire covering CF characteristics, treatment options, and clinical management was administered before and after a three-hour visual training program. Pre- and post-training results were compared, and subgroup analysis was performed according to profession.

Results: Participants’ mean age was 32.7±8.5 years, and 54% were female. 34% of the participants were physicians, 40% nurses, 17% emergency medical technicians. Only 32.4% had received formal CF training during their education. Correct response rates significantly improved in general knowledge (66.6% → 91%), nutrition (33.3% → 100%), medication knowledge (0 → 75%), airway clearance (25% → 50%), and exacerbation management sections (50% → 75%) (p<0.05). No significant change was observed in the nebulizer hygiene section. Pre-training correct response rates were 63.6% for physicians, 45.5% for nurses, and 40.9% for technicians, increasing post-training to 93.1%, 72.7%, and 68.2%, respectively. Physicians, as expected, demonstrated significantly higher knowledge levels than nurses and technicians (p<0.05).

Conclusion: Targeted training programs for primary healthcare personnel significantly improve knowledge regarding CF and contribute to more effective patient care. Expanding such educational initiatives may enhance the quality and efficiency of home healthcare services.

records.title: Demographic and clinical factors associated with depression and anxiety symptoms among adults with cystic fibrosis in Ireland

person.department: National Referral Centre for Adult Cystic Fibrosis

records.authors_text: D. McMahon1, D. Goldstone1, S. Carter1, L. Kirwan2,3
records.affiliations_text: 1St Vincent's University Hospital, National Referral Centre for Adult Cystic Fibrosis, Dublin, Ireland, 2Cystic Fibrosis Registry of Ireland, Dublin, Ireland, 3University College Dublin, School of Public Health, Physiotherapy and Sport Science, Dublin, Ireland
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: While research has established that people with CF (PWCF) show elevated rates of anxiety and depression, gaps remain in understanding factors influencing mental wellbeing in the current era. This study aims to (1) explore associations between mental health and demographic and clinical factors in PWCF in Ireland and (2) develop a predictive model showing factors associated with anxiety and depression in PWCF in Ireland.

Methods: Retrospective medical chart reviews were conducted from January 2023 to the present date, with data collection ongoing until April 2026. Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) and Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD-7) scores were extracted, alongside relevant demographic (age, gender, relationship status, education level, employment status) and clinical data (current FEV1, baseline FEV1, genotype, diabetes status, insulin requirement, liver disease status, whether prescribed highly effective modulator therapy, number and length of hospital admissions in the prior 12 months). Descriptive statistics will show prevalence and symptom severity, with regression analyses examining associations between mental health and demographic and clinical factors.

Results: Of data analysed to date, most of the sample was female; in a relationship; educated at college level; and working full time, respectively. Preliminary results show anxiety and depression scores above clinical thresholds in 13% and 11% of study participants, respectively. We hypothesise that those with lower lung function, diabetes, requiring insulin, not taking highly effective modulator therapy, and with more hospital stays to be the sub-group(s) at greater risk of elevated depression and anxiety scores based on regression analyses.

Conclusions: Anxiety and depression remain prevalent among PWCF. By identifying risk factors for mental health symptoms, we can refine mental health screening and access to psychosocial support to further develop comprehensive models of CF care.

records.title: Cystic Fibrosis education: what do families want?
records.authors_text: N. Murray1, J. Witt2, E. Dixon1, M. Puckey1, S. Bentley1, K.J Henney1, T. Nickels1, M. Ovens1, I. Balfour-Lynn1
records.affiliations_text: 1Royal Brompton Hospital, Dept of Paediatric Cystic Fibrosis, London, United Kingdom, 2Cystic Fibrosis Trust, Research and Healthcare Data, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: From the time of cystic fibrosis (CF) diagnosis, good quality information and education about CF are vital to support families. We sought to explore how we could improve our approach to information and education provision at the Royal Brompton Hospital paediatric CF centre.

Methods: We used a semi-structured interview approach to explore parents’ experiences of information and educational materials about CF, and their ideas for improvements. Families were invited to complete an interview with a member of the CF team in clinic, by phone, or at a home visit. Responses to interview questions were transcribed and coded thematically to identify opportunities for improvement.

Results: Seven families were interviewed. Verbal information given by the CF team was rated highly, as it was felt to be more useful and relevant to the individual family. Opinions on written resources, such as leaflets, varied and these were rated less highly.

Some parents recalled feeling overwhelmed during the period after diagnosis, noting it is important to have the right amount of information provided at the right time. Parents felt the best times for information provision were routine touchpoints (newborn screening visit, home visits, clinics) and important milestones (e.g. diagnosis, starting nursery/school).

Key recommendations:

Provide clear and up to date contact details from the outset

Stagger information provision and focus on what is most relevant to the family at the time

Share structured, practical information and advice, such as action plans and tips from peers

Offer information in different formats so parents can use what works best for them

Conclusion: Interviews with families have provided valuable insights into how information offers around CF could be strengthened. The recommendations generated identify key considerations to help CF teams enhance their education provision. We now plan to update our current approach and resources in light of these findings.

records.title: Medication burden in children and young people with cystic fibrosis following initiation of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor
records.authors_text: V. Pankhania1, S. Popple1, C. Shentall1, E. Wilson1, C. Mulcahy1, I. Ahmed1
records.affiliations_text: 1University Hospitals of Leicester, Leicester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor(ETI) has transformed outcomes in cystic fibrosis (CF), but its impact on long-term medication burden in children and young people(CYP) is incompletely described. We evaluated the extent and safety of deprescribing following ETI initiation in a paediatric CF cohort.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective, single-centre observational study of CYP with CF aged 2–18 years who commenced ETI between 2020 and 2024 and received therapy for ≥1 year. The number and type of long-term medications stopped after ETI initiation were recorded. Outcomes were assessed using clinical stability and drug-specific objective monitoring, including microbiology surveillance, spirometry, sweat chloride(SwCl), serum vitamin levels, faecal elastase (FE), and antibiotic use.

Results: 58 CYP initiated ETI; 39 (67%) stopped ≥1 long-term medication.In total, 78 medications were deprescribed, with 4 (5%) restarted. Of those stopping treatment, 14 (36%) stopped 1 medication, 10 (26%) stopped 2, and 15 (38%) stopped 3.Nebulised anti-pseudomonal therapies accounted for 14 (18%) withdrawals, with no re-isolation during follow-up.Dornase alfa was stopped in 11 cases(14%),with 1 restart. Sodium chloride supplements accounted for 26 (33%) withdrawals; 3 were restarted. Prophylactic antibiotics were stopped in 4 patients, antibiotic use was reduced in 3 and unchanged in 1 the next year. Fat-soluble vitamins comprised 16 (20%) withdrawals, with 4 patients requiring vitamin D supplementation. Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy was withdrawn in 7 patients (8%), all remaining off treatment with sustained FE. Overall, 38 (65%) CYP remained off ≥1 medication.

Conclusion: ETI enabled rationalisation of long-term CF therapies, with only 5% requiring reintroduction, supporting reduced treatment burden. Available clinical and biochemical data supported safe deprescribing. Standardised monitoring and structured follow-up are recommended to maintain clinical stability.

records.title: Evolving patient preferences in cystic fibrosis following introduction of highly effective CFTR modulators
records.authors_text: RA Cameron1,2, AP Wagner1,2, A Jones3, M Rowley4, NJ Simmonds5, KW Southern6, J Whitty7, G Davies8, SB Carr5
records.affiliations_text: 1University of East Anglia, Norwich Medical School, Norwich, United Kingdom, 2NIHR ARC East of England, Cambridge, United Kingdom, 3University of Manchester, Division of Infection, Immunity & Respiratory Medicine, Manchester, United Kingdom, 4Patient Representative, London, United Kingdom, 5Imperial College London, London, United Kingdom, 6University of Liverpool, Women's and Children's Health, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 7Evidera, London, United Kingdom, 8University College London, Great Ormond Street Institute of Child Health, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: In 2020, we ran a discrete choice experiment (DCE) that showed people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) valued reductions in treatment burden, including inhaled therapies and physiotherapy, alongside clinical outcomes. Since then, introduction of highly effective CFTR modulators has changed clinical trajectories and daily treatment experience. This study aimed to reassess patient preferences for clinical and non-clinical treatment outcomes in a UK CF population following introduction of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI).

Methods: An open-invitation online survey incorporating a patient co-designed DCE was administered to adults with CF across the UK. Participants completed 12 choice tasks comparing hypothetical CF treatment profiles defined by effects on lung function, abdominal symptoms, life expectancy, mental wellbeing, inhaled medication use, and physiotherapy requirements. Preferences analysed using a multinomial logit model.

Results: The DCE analysis included 117 pwCF (median age 40 years [range 19–79]; 47% men; mean self-reported ppFEV1 69.5% [standard deviation 22.9]). Maintaining lung function and life expectancy remained most valued outcomes. Respondents showed a marked aversion to deteriorations in lung function, worsening abdominal symptoms, and declines in mental wellbeing. Compared with the 2020 survey, a reduction in treatment burden from inhaled medications or physiotherapy was now less prominent in mean preferences, although individual priorities varied.

Conclusions: Following ETI introduction, pwCF continue to prioritise preserving lung function and avoiding deterioration in health and wellbeing. Treatment burden remains important for some, but appears less central to average preference than previously observed. These findings suggest that maintaining current health states may be more salient to pwCF than treatment simplification alone, with implications for treatment evaluation and shared decision-making.

records.title: Does socio-economic status impact the efficacy of modulator therapy amongst adults with cystic fibrosis?
records.authors_text: B. Miller1, V. Holland1, T. Sharp1
records.affiliations_text: 1Nottingham University Hospital, Wolfson Cystic Fibrosis Unit, Nottingham, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: A literature review by McGarry et al. in 2019 concluded that low socio-economic status was associated with increased mortality and worse lung function amongst people with Cystic Fibrosis (CF). The objective of this study is to consider how socio-economic status may impact the efficacy of modulators amongst adults with CF.

Method: Delta F508 homozygous patients on a full dose of Elexacaftor/Tezacaftor/Ivacaftor (ETI) were selected from our center. Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD) scores were obtained, then allocated into two groups. Group 1 had IMD scores between 8 and 10 (least deprived), Group 2 had IMD scores between 1 and 3 (most deprived). 10 patients were randomly sampled from each.

Each person’s FEV₁% from their 2019 and 2024 annual assessment was collected. The Medicines Possession Ratio (MPR) for two years (2024/2025) was also collected. We analysed the relationship between membership of each cohort and change in FEV₁% after commencing ETI and MPR rate.

Results: Each cohort was separated into two groups. For group 1 (age=18-25), cohort 1 had a higher FEV₁% in both 2019 and 2024. The rate of improvement in FEV₁% predicted between the two cohorts on ETI is very similar. For group 2 (age≥26), both cohorts began with a mean FEV₁% of approximately 50%. However, those in the cohort 1 had a greater rate of improvement on ETI. The MPR suggests that people over 25 in cohort 1 have the best adherence. However, there may be other factors impacting the rate of FEV₁% improvement.

Mean FEV₁%20192024Cohort 1 (Age=18-25)83.496.5Cohort 1 (Age≥26)49.370.4Cohort 2 (Age=18-25)69.282Cohort 2 (Age≥26)47.162.5Conclusion: This study suggests that people living in the most deprived areas experience less improvement in FEV₁% after starting ETI, when compared with those living in the least deprived. Research should be conducted with a larger sample size to establish the statistical significance of this relationship and the reasons why.

person.biography:
Bryony is a Specialist Pharmacist and Co-lead of the Wolfson Cystic Fibrosis unit in Nottingham, UK. She has worked in Cystic Fibrosis since 2017, and prior to that worked in critical care, cardiology and education and training.
She was a member of the of the EMBRACE team, and has presented work at past conferences. Her MSc was in the patient experience of the medication journey and she is currently credentialling as an RPS Consultant Pharmacist.
Recently she has hosted a national online pharmacist meeting, and has recently submitted abstracts about pneumococcal vaccination in CF, a series of case studies about international supply of medication for patients whose travel has been made possible by CFTR modulators, and first reports of UK side effect data for Alyftrek.

records.title: Adherence, tolerability and clinical response to elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor in adults with cystic fibrosis: real-world findings from Stockholm CF Centre
records.authors_text: U. Skogeland1,2, I. de Monestrol1,2, K. Lindblom2, T. Godskesen3,4, T. Pincikova1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Karolinska Institutet, Department of Paediatrics, CLINTEC, Huddinge, Sweden, 2Karolinska University Hospital, Stockholm CF Centre, Huddinge, Sweden, 3Nord University, Faculty of Nursing and Health Sciences, Bodø, Norway, 4Centre for Research Ethics & Bioethics, Department of Public Health and Caring Sciences, Uppsala, Sweden
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To examine real-world adherence, tolerability, and clinical responses to ETI in adult pwCF.

Methods: In total, 115 participants aged ≥18 years treated with ETI at Stockholm CF Centre were included from 1 December 2023 to 30 November 2025. Adherence was defined as taking the prescribed ETI dose within two hours of the scheduled time; participants with an adherence score ≥ 0.80 were considered adherent. A study-specific questionnaire was completed during clinical visits (1–6 per participant). Associations between adherence and changes in forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV₁) and weight were analysed using Spearman’s and Pearson’s correlation tests.

Results: Sixty-eight participants (60%) were non-adherent (<0.80). Median adherence was 0.50 (IQR 0.00–1.00); mean 0.54 (SD = 0.43). Seventeen participants improved their adherence during the study; however, despite fewer missed doses, adherence remained below the predefined threshold (≥0.80). Lung function improved following ETI initiation, with median FEV₁ changes varying by age groups. Adherence was not associated with FEV₁ change (Spearman’s ρ = –0.014, p = 0.885). However, FEV₁ change showed a significant positive correlation with weight gain (Spearman’s ρ = 0.189, p = 0.044). Median relative weight gain was 3.8%. Thirty-four participants (29.5%) were prescribed reduced ETI doses due to adverse effects; their adherence was comparable to that of participants taking the full dose.

Conclusion: Self-reported adherence to ETI was suboptimal. Despite limited adherence, participants showed improvements in lung function and weight. Changes in FEV₁ correlated with weight gain but not with adherence. ETI was generally well tolerated, although over one-quarter of participants required a dose reduction. Further studies are needed to evaluate adherence to ETI and its effects over a longer time period.

Conclusion: Self-reported adherence to ETI was suboptimal. Despite limited adherence, participants showed improvements in lung function and weight. Changes in FEV₁ correlated with weight gain but not with adherence. ETI was generally well tolerated, although over one-quarter of participants required a dose reduction. records.abstract_text:
Background: CFTR modulators (CFTRm) have transformed CF care. Real-world patient-reported outcomes (PROs) are essential to understand improvements and unmet needs. This study evaluated PROs in adults receiving CFTRm and explored patient perception of effectiveness and drivers of dissatisfaction.

Methods: Over a 3-month period, adults attending CF clinics completed a bespoke, non-validated questionnaire capturing PROs. Additional items assessed perceived effectiveness, side effects, adherence, and overall satisfaction. Demographic data and clinical history were recorded. Responses were analysed descriptively.

Results: Of the cohort of 88 patients, 94% were currently on CFTRm and 67% on ETI; 54% were male, and 80% were under 45 years. Values represent change in PROs compared with pre-CFTRm status. Improvements were most pronounced for respiratory symptoms (90%), exercise tolerance (77%), energy (70%), and quality of life (91%). Nutrition and gastrointestinal outcomes showed more modest gains (41–70%). Mental health and sleep demonstrated substantial heterogeneity, with worsening reported by 27%.

Overall, 90% believed CFTRm effectively managed symptoms. Side effects were acceptable to 69% whereas 6% reported unacceptable side effects, most related to sleep disturbance or anxiety. Adherence was high and 40% reported no missed doses. Forgetting and travel were the main reasons for missed doses. Dissatisfaction (14%) was primarily linked to mental health and sleep disturbances.

Conclusions: In this real-world adult cohort, CFTRm were associated with patient-reported improvements in respiratory outcomes, energy, and quality of life, alongside high adherence and overall satisfaction. Mental health and sleep disturbances were key drivers of dissatisfaction and non-adherence. Use of a non-validated questionnaire represents a limitation. Future studies incorporating validated PRO instruments are needed to fully understand patient experiences and long-term outcomes.

records.title: Impact of modulator therapy on unscheduled patient contact in a paediatric cystic fibrosis (CF) shared care service

person.title: Dr
person.institution: Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust, Royal Manchester Childrens Hospital (Wythenshawe)

records.authors_text: N. Rao1, K. Barker1, D. Poulton1, L. Warburton1, J. Watkinson1
records.affiliations_text: 1Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust, Royal Manchester Childrens Hospital (Wythenshawe), Paediatrics, Manchester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
CF patients rely on the multidisciplinary team (MDT) for clinical support, advice, and care coordination though both scheduled and unscheduled contacts.. We previously reviewed and presented data on nature of unscheduled contacts in our service at ECFS 2019 (ref P084). This was prior to CF modulator era.

Objective: To analyse and compare unscheduled patient/carer contacts at our paediatric CF service following the commencement of modulator therapy and to identify themes and outcomes for patient management.

Methods: A retrospective evaluation of the patient electronic system was conducted from 01/10/2024 to 01/10/2025. 16 patients aged 0–15 years were included. Patient satisfaction surveys were also performed. Results were compared with the 2019 audit.

Results: A total of 1761 contacts were recorded, of which 1609 (91%) were unscheduled, an increase from 61% in 2019. Scheduled contacts decreased to 152 (8.6%) from 39%. Unscheduled contact by method shifted significantly with text/WhatsApp 89.8% (42% in 2019) being the preferred method followed by telephone 6.7% (39%), email 1.7% (10%), PAU 1.1% (6%), ward 0.37% (2%), A&E 0.19% (0%). Reasons for unscheduled contact were for treatment (38%), advice/support (13.9%), home visits (6.2%), results (6%), and other queries (6.7%). Reductions were noted in contact for symptom management (12%), equipment (1.8%), and IV therapy (0.3%). Patient satisfaction remained high, with a mean score of 5/5 for MDT communication, knowledge, and service provision.

Conclusion: Unscheduled patient contact remains significant, with a strong preference for rapid digital communication. Our findings highlight there is a need for ongoing role of the MDT in supporting patients in the modulator era and emphasises the importance of flexible communication methods and proactive care planning to. The introduction of modulator therapy correlates with reduced IV antibiotic use and fewer hospital-based reviews, allowing greater community-based management.

records.title: Service evaluation on initiation of CFTR modulators in an adult cystic fibrosis population

person.institution: Northern Ireland Regional Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre

records.authors_text: J. Hanna1, S. Armstrong1, S. Bansal2, J. Faughey1, V. Mills1, E. Wright1, S. Caskey1, D. Downey1,3
records.affiliations_text: 1Northern Ireland Regional Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, BHSCT, Belfast, United Kingdom, 2Queen’s University Belfast, School of Medicine, Belfast, United Kingdom, 3Centre for Experimental Medicine, Queen's University Belfast, Belfast, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: Introduction of CFTR modulators has changed the care of people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). As treatment options continue to expand, understanding pwCF perspectives on the initiation of these therapies through real-world patient-reported outcomes is key. Therefore, we aimed to evaluate the initiation of CFTR modulators in an adult CF population attending a regional CF centre.

Method: A structured questionnaire was developed by CF multidisciplinary (MDT) team and over a three-month period was completed by eligible pwCF during clinic appointments. Anonymised patient experiences on starting CFTR modulators were transcribed into Microsoft Excel and coded for descriptive analysis.

Results: Eighty-eight pwCF completed the survey and were predominantly male (55%), with 67% receiving ETI. Most common ages groups were 18-24, 25-34 and 35-44 years, representing 23%, 32% and 26% of respondents. Respondents agreed that before commencement, they received clear information and felt involved in the decision-making process, with over 95% selecting agree or strongly agree. Over 90% agreed that their questions and concerns had been addressed, and over 97% reported that they felt supported when commencing by selecting agree or strongly agree. Free-text responses to two open ended questions corroborated quantitative findings, with respondents most often describing initiation as well explained with clear information. Suggestions for improvement included local LFTs and information on patient experiences to date, particularly side effects.

Conclusion: Initiation of CFTR modulators was associated with high levels of patient-reported understanding, involvement in decision-making, and perceived support, with findings consistent across quantitative and free-text responses. Use of a non-validated questionnaire represents a limitation. Future studies with validated questionnaires, qualitative interviews and more diverse populations are needed to further understand patient experiences.

records.title: Democratizing cystic fibrosis care: effects of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor on quality of life, depression, and anxiety in patients with cystic fibrosis in a low-income population
records.authors_text: M.P.R. de Oliveira1, F.R. Silva1, V.H.V. Bomfim1, G.T.d.O. Piñeiro1, J.C.B. Costa2, F.M. Fontenelle2, R. Terse-Ramos2,1, E.L.D. Souza2,1
records.affiliations_text: 1Faculdade de Medicina da Bahia da Universidade Federal da Bahia, Medicine, Salvador, Brazil, 2Hospital Universitário Professor Edgard Santos, Salvador, Brazil
records.abstract_text:
Objective: To evaluate the impact of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) therapy on quality of life, depression, and anxiety in individuals with cystic fibrosis (CF).

Methods: This was a prospective, longitudinal, observational study. Participants were recruited and assessed at baseline (T0) and after 3 (T1), 6 (T2), and 9 (T3) months of ETI use. Outcomes included quality of life (CF Questionnaire–Revised, CFQ-R), depression (Patient Health Questionnaire-9, PHQ-9), and anxiety (Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7, GAD-7). Paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used to compare baseline and follow-up outcomes, depending on the data distribution. A p<0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results: Twenty-three participants were included, with a mean age of 14.3 (SD: 5.9) years, median age at diagnosis 7.0 months. Most were male (56.5%), non-White (73.9%), and 56.5% were F508del heterozygous. Quality-of-life assessment demonstrated significant improvement after initiation of ETI in multiple domains, particularly physical functioning, vitality, health perceptions, social functioning, weight, and respiratory symptoms, all of which showed consistent increases at T1, T2, and T3 compared with baseline (p<0.05). In contrast, the treatment burden, body image, role functioning, and digestion domains did not show significant differences across the evaluated periods. A reduction in depression scores was also observed, with lower values at T1 and T2 compared with baseline. Conversely, anxiety scores showed only a downward trend, without statistical significance.

Conclusion: ETI therapy was associated with improvements in quality of life and depressive symptoms in individuals with cystic fibrosis, suggesting psychosocial benefits beyond its well-established clinical effects. However, no difference was found in anxiety.

records.title: Perspectives and experiences of people with cystic fibrosis regarding long-acting reversible contraceptives
records.authors_text: O. Stransky1, L. Kirkpatrick1, E. Friel1, C. March1, M. Poranski2, M. Teribery3, T. Kazmerski1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Pittsburgh, Pediatrics, Pittsburgh, United States, 2Adult with Cystic Fibrosis, St. Paul, United States, 3Adult with Cystic Fibrosis, Pittsburgh, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Improvements in life expectancy and quality of life among people with CF (PwCF) have led many to consider their reproductive needs and goals. Additionally, CF modulators have improved female fertility and pregnancy rates in the United States (US) have doubled in the modern era. We explored the experiences and decision-making of PwCF related to long-acting reversible contraception (LARC).

Methods: We recruited PwCF aged 18-35 years from across the US who had ever used an intrauterine device (IUD) or implant to participate in semi-structured interviews related to LARC initiation, use, and removal. We conducted thematic analysis on the transcripts.

Results: We interviewed 21 PwCF. Key themes included: 1) PwCF have misconceptions about the impact and safety of hormonal contraception on CF and their interactions with CF modulators; 2) Reasons for obtaining LARC included desires to simplify their daily health routine, desire for high efficacy methods, and improving menstrual symptoms; 3) The 2022 decision by the US Supreme Court to overturn protections for abortion is very concerning to PwCF and, in many cases, influenced participants’ LARC decisions; 4) Many participants who had used an IUD desire improved pain management during the insertion and removal process; 5) Most participants report no coercion from healthcare providers to choose LARC with the majority making the decision to receive a LARC independent of their CF team.

Conclusions: Use and selection of contraception is increasingly relevant for PwCF. Future work should be done to address misinformation and uncertainty related to the impact and safety of contraception in CF.

records.title: Improving inclusivity in cystic fibrosis care- medical considerations when treating transgender people with CF
records.authors_text: N. Robinson1,2, L. Johnston2, G. MacGregor2, R. Gray1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Glasgow, School of Infection and Immunity, Glasgow, United Kingdom, 2West of Scotland Adult CF service, Respiratory Medicine, Glasgow, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: In the UK, there are rising numbers of people with gender dysphoria and 0.5% of the population identify as transgender. Transgender people with CF (TpwCF) are becoming more common in paediatric and adult services with little research or guidance available into specific care for them. Many people with gender dysphoria seek help from online or private gender services, rather than their GP or CF medical teams- creating a vacuum of knowledge surrounding key parts of their care. Many health services operate binary sex based coding for all patients, and as such, physiological outcomes and automatic sex-based cancer screening services may become challenging for TpwCF.

Aims: To understand the prevalence of gender dysphoria within our local CF service and highlight several key discussion points for CF teams looking after TpwCF

Results: The West of Scotland Adult CF service has a prevalence of 1.3% of TpwCF (n=5 of 372). 4 are transgender men and 1 is a transgender woman. 20% have socially transitioned (living in preferred gender without medical intervention), 80% have medically transitioned gender (are taking exogenous hormones and/or surgery). 2 additional pwCF have de-transitioned back to their gender assigned at birth.

Individual discussion regarding TpwCF’s preferred pronouns and agreed documentation of transgender status as a medical diagnosis is necessary for clarity for the MDT. Several physiological outcomes also need to be considered- such as utilising biological sex for haemoglobin levels, pulmonary function testing and cancer screening services to ensure that appropriate care is not missed or recorded inadequately.

Open discussion with patients regarding planning for additional private healthcare needs such as exogenous hormone prescriptions and gender related surgeries should be approached openly and documented.

Conclusions: Further research into this field with TpwCF is crucial to provide guidance for those with gender dysphoria and their CF teams.

person.biography:
Nicola Robinson is an Adult Respiratory and general medical specialty trainee with a special interest in Cystic Fibrosis, based in Edinburgh, Scotland. She has been involved with multiple clinical trials during her training. She completes her medical training to become a consultant in August 2024.
She is also a pre doctoral MRC funded Clinical research fellow with the University of Edinburgh, looking specifically at lung repair in the CF lung as well as changes in pulmonary and systemic inflammation following highly effective CFTR modulator therapies. She has also undertaken real world clinical studies with CFTR modulator therapies, looking at the clinical outcomes and side effects of these drugs.

records.title: Romantic relationships in adults with cystic fibrosis: an interpretative phenomenological study
records.authors_text: S. MacFarlane1, C. Murray1, R. Faulkner2
records.affiliations_text: 1Lancaster University, Division of Health Research, Lancaster, United Kingdom, 2Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust, Manchester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Romantic partners are a key source of support for adults with cystic fibrosis, therefore building and sustaining good quality romantic relationships is important. However, the physical and

psychological demands of this life-limiting condition can complicate navigation of romantic relationships.

Methods: This qualitative study aimed to explore the experience of romantic relationships for adults with cystic fibrosis. Semi-structured interviews were conducted and interpretative phenomenological analysis (IPA) was utilised to analyse the data from seven participants with cystic fibrosis.

Results: Four themes emerged: To share or not to share: fear and visibility influencing cystic fibrosis communication; For better or for worse: cystic fibrosis informing partner choice; “There are three people in the relationship: Me, cystic fibrosis, and my partner”: integrating cystic fibrosis in romantic relationships; and Coping alignment: relationship success versus health.

Conclusion: The findings offer novel insights into how cystic fibrosis influences romantic relationships, with implications for clinical practice and directions for future research.

records.title: Perceptions of women with cystic fibrosis regarding their obstetrical care and healthcare providers' perspectives during the journey to parenthood
records.authors_text: F. Delacollette1, L. Ardana2, J. Pirson3, M. Denef4, M. Timmesh5, H. Boboli1
records.affiliations_text: 1CHR Citadelle, Cystic Fibrosis Center, Liège, Belgium, 2Independent Mindwife, Billere, France, 3CHR Citadelle, Director of CF Center, Liège, Belgium, 4CHR Citadelle, Gynecology, Liège, Belgium, 5CHC Mont Legia, Cystic Fibrosis Reference Center, Liège, Belgium
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Improved life expectancy and the arrival of CFTR modulators have made motherhood a realistic goal for many women with cystic fibrosis (CF). However, the transition to obstetrical care remains complex. This study explores the gap between the perceptions of women with CF regarding their maternity care and the perspectives of the healthcare professionals(HCPs) supporting them.

Methods: A dual-methodological approach was employed : 1) A descriptive qualitative literature review of PubMed-indexed articles(IMRaD format) from the last five years.

2) Semi-structured interviews conducted with women living with CF and HCPs involved in their care to compare lived experiences with clinical approaches.

Results: The study identifies significant barriers to optimal care. Women with CF report a lack of clear information regading fertility, contraception and the specific impact of pregnancy on respiratory function. They often perceive their pregnancy as being managed through the lens of "high risk" rather than a physiological process. Conversely, HCPs express a sense of helplessness for want of standardized guidelines, insufficient interprofessional coordination and limited data on the long-term safety of CFTR modulators during pregnancy. Psychological support was found to be consistently undervalued in both the literature and fields interviews.

Conclusion: Obstetrical care for women with CF is often perceived as inadequate, largely due to uncertainty and limited knowledge rather than individualized understanding. Enhancing nursing education, strengthening interdisciplinary collaboration, developing clear care pathways and recognising women with CF as active partners in care are essential to improving support for motherhood in CF.

records.title: Clinical and psychological factors influencing transition readiness in adolescents and young adults with cystic fibrosis

person.institution: University Children's Hospital, University Medical Centre Ljubljana

records.authors_text: A. Veronese1, M. Praprotnik1, S. Lužar1, M. Oštir1, D. Potočnik Kodrun1, J. Rodman Berlot1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1University Children's Hospital, University Medical Centre Ljubljana, Department of Paediatric Pulmonology, Ljubljana, Slovenia, 2University of Ljubljana, Faculty of Medicine, Ljubljana, Slovenia
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Advances in cystic fibrosis (CF) care have improved survival rates, leading to an increase in adolescents and young adults (AYAs) needing to transition from paediatric to adult healthcare. Transition readiness is crucial for maintaining continuity of care and optimising long-term health outcomes, yet its psychological and clinical factors in CF remain understudied.

Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional observational study of AYAs with CF aged ≥12 years at a single CF centre. Transition readiness was evaluated using the Transition Readiness Assessment Questionnaire (TRAQ 6.0). Depressive and anxiety symptoms were measured with PHQ-9 and GAD-7. Demographic variables included age and gender, while clinical variables included BMI, ppFEV₁, use of CFTR modulator therapy, pulmonary exacerbations in the previous year, and CF-related diabetes. Determinants of transition readiness were analysed through multivariable linear regression.

Results: Thirty-three patients were included (36.4% female; mean age 16.1±2.8 years); 84.8% received CFTR modulators, and 21.2% had CF-related diabetes. Age was an independent predictor of overall transition readiness (β=0.728, p<0.001), while higher depressive symptom burden was associated with lower readiness (β=−0.800, p=0.006). The model explained substantial variance (R² = 0.60, p = 0.006). Age and depressive symptom burden influenced all four TRAQ domain subscales as well. CF-related diabetes showed a positive association with the domains Keeping appointment (β=0.474, p=0.031) and Tracking health issues (β=0.492, p=0.034) on TRAQ. Other clinical variables were not significantly associated with TRAQ scores.

Conclusion: The results of our study indicate that age and depressive symptoms are key determinants of transition readiness in AYAs with CF, while CF-related diabetes may enhance engagement in self-management. These findings support integrating mental health screening and targeted transition support into routine CF care.

records.title: Strong beginnings: peer support for parents of babies and toddlers with CF
records.authors_text: E. Lee Mindel1
records.affiliations_text: 1Cystic Fibrosis Trust, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: We developed Strong Beginnings so that families have a community of peer support from the start of their journey with CF. We aim to create connections between parents of children aged under 24 months, thereby improving wellbeing and reducing anxiety for parents in the early days of coping with the condition.

Methods: We run one online event per month, for parents of children with CF aged up to 24 months. We run informal peer-support sessions, led by parent volunteers. These sessions are unstructured and are a relaxed place to talk, share experiences and connect. We also pilot various events, including baby massage, a presentation and conversation around anxiety and infection risk facilitated by a CF Psychologist, and a Q+A with our youth group (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tBF33g3XwCs).

Results: Parents say how beneficial our events are for their wellbeing and mental health. They tell us that meeting other parents is immensely valuable. Parents often identify attending our events as a turning point on their journey with CF:

“Our experience with CF was incredibly isolating… it was a very lonely place to be. Then we joined the call and everything changed. It was the first time we had found true comfort in sharing with people who genuinely understood”.

Parents say that our events contribute to them feeling able to live their lives and support their child to experience the world, when previously, anxiety had limited them.

“We went to the farm which we hadn’t been brave enough to do before and this was directly linked to the confidence that came from the session. We’re really grateful (as I’m sure my son was whilst riding a tractor around and seeing the animals!!)”

Conclusions: Facilitating peer-support for parents of new babies with CF is vitally important. The impact of sharing experiences with others in the community is huge. These connections improve wellbeing and help parents to think positively about their child’s life and future.
