1Cystic Fibrosis Trust, London, United Kingdom

Objectives: We developed Strong Beginnings so that families have a community of peer support from the start of their journey with CF. We aim to create connections between parents of children aged under 24 months, thereby improving wellbeing and reducing anxiety for parents in the early days of coping with the condition.
Methods: We run one online event per month, for parents of children with CF aged up to 24 months. We run informal peer-support sessions, led by parent volunteers. These sessions are unstructured and are a relaxed place to talk, share experiences and connect. We also pilot various events, including baby massage, a presentation and conversation around anxiety and infection risk facilitated by a CF Psychologist, and a Q+A with our youth group (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tBF33g3XwCs).
Results: Parents say how beneficial our events are for their wellbeing and mental health. They tell us that meeting other parents is immensely valuable. Parents often identify attending our events as a turning point on their journey with CF:
“Our experience with CF was incredibly isolating… it was a very lonely place to be. Then we joined the call and everything changed. It was the first time we had found true comfort in sharing with people who genuinely understood”.
Parents say that our events contribute to them feeling able to live their lives and support their child to experience the world, when previously, anxiety had limited them.
“We went to the farm which we hadn’t been brave enough to do before and this was directly linked to the confidence that came from the session. We’re really grateful (as I’m sure my son was whilst riding a tractor around and seeing the animals!!)”
Conclusions: Facilitating peer-support for parents of new babies with CF is vitally important. The impact of sharing experiences with others in the community is huge. These connections improve wellbeing and help parents to think positively about their child’s life and future.

presentation.title: Strong beginnings: peer support for parents of babies and toddlers with CF

records.title: Children and parents’ experiences of being diagnosed and living with cystic fibrosis diabetes: a qualitative service evaluation in a UK paediatric cystic fibrosis service
records.authors_text: H. Fogg1, A. Warner2, C. Berry3
records.affiliations_text: 1Alder Hey Children's NHS Trust, Clinical Health Psychology, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 2University of Liverpool, Department of Primary Care and Mental Health, Liverpool, United Kingdom, 3Alder Hey Children's NHS Trust, Nutrition and Dietetics, Liverpool, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Few qualitative studies explore paediatric Cystic Fibrosis Diabetes (CFD). This service evaluation explored experiences of CFD diagnosis and Cystic Fibrosis (CF) multidisciplinary team (MDT) support.

Method: Two patients and parents were interviewed by a Trainee Clinical Psychologist who was not part of the normal patient care team. Interviews were recorded by Microsoft Teams, transcribed and anonymised. The interviewer, CF Dietitian and Psychologist used Thematic Analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006).

Results: Themes identified:

Making sense of CFD

Diagnosis can feel unexpected despite prior awareness of the potential.

Diagnosis as a process

Adjustment was influenced by whether diagnosis felt gradual/logical or sudden. Clear, relational communication supported coping.

Impact and burden

CFD increased treatment complexity and burden; parents experienced more emotional and future-focused burden while patients experienced more practical, bodily and social challenges.

Normalisation with time

Routines established and became less emotionally charged in time. Patients described challenges with injections and device visibility, while parents considered skill acquisition/adherence. Routines reduced anxiety; adjustment required support beyond instruction.

Quality communication

MDT communication was valued by all, including relational continuity, clear explanation, honesty about uncertainty, accessibility and feeling heard. Patients prefer negotiation, not instruction.

Visibility, identity and social context

CFD affects body image, peer relationships and identity. Visible treatments heighten feelings of difference/social discomfort.

Conclusion: Despite a small sample, findings give insight for best practice delivering CFD diagnosis from the understanding that CFD awareness did not equate to psychological readiness. MDT support was valued for providing individualised support, with repeated developmentally appropriate discussion and reassurance identified as helpful.

records.title: An exploration of the experiences of childhood cystic fibrosis in family systems
records.authors_text: R.E.M. Hatton1, T. Lee2, G. Latchford1, S. Pini1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Leeds, Leeds, United Kingdom, 2Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust, Leeds, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Whilst treatment for Cystic Fibrosis (CF) has been recently transformed with developments in modulator drugs (De Boeck, 2020), it remains a serious genetic condition (Bowen & Hull, 2015). Due to the changes in the CF landscape, it is important to develop an up-to-date understanding of CF experiences. Moreover, previous research has mainly focused on individuals or dyads, but working together with whole families is key to improving clinical care (Hisert et al., 2023). Thus, an understanding of experiences at a family-level was sought.

Methods: Four families with a child with CF were recruited and asked to provide creative items to depict their experiences of CF. Family-level interviews were conducted and the creative items provided by the family were used as the stimuli for discussions. Interviews were analysed with Interpersonal Phenomenological Analysis (IPA).

Results: Results showed that the diagnosis and subsequent adjustments required can feel overwhelming. Families learn to navigate this through negotiations both within and outside of the family. This can look different for each unique family. As the child develops or health needs change, renegotiations are needed. Children and families with CF stand out from peers and this can be difficult. Fear exists around the child becoming unwell and things becoming overwhelming again.

Conclusions: This study shows a journey that families engage in when CF is diagnosed. CF clinical teams should consider how they communicate the initial diagnosis and pacing the information they provide. Consideration is also needed when exacerbations or complications occur.

Peer support from families with more experience of CF may help newly diagnosed families. Changes in treatment can require changes to family roles and families may benefit from support in thinking through these changes.

person.title: Dr
person.biography: Dr Tim Lee is Lead Clinician and Consultant at the Leeds Regional Paediatric Cystic Fibrosis Centre, UK. He has been involved in the clinical care of children and young people with cystic fibrosis since 1995. He has a PhD focussed on improving the effectiveness of gene therapy, and is Principal Investigator on a number of current clinical trials. Leeds is part of the UK CF Clinical Trial Accelerator Platform and the European Cystic Fibrosis Society Clinical Trial Network, which comprises 57 large and experienced CF Centres across 17 European countries, caring for a total of 21,500 people with CF. The aim of the ECFS-CTN is to increase the quality and quantity of CF clinical research by having a co-ordinated approach to realising efficient and high quality clinical trials addressing the most important priorities for people with CF.

records.title: Safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics of novel NBD1 stabilizers SION-719 and SION-451 from two Phase 1 first-in-human studies

session.title: ePoster Session 07 - Old and new – exploring the portfolio for cystic fibrosis treatment

records.authors_text: J. Maley1, H. Wolff2, J. Hauben2, S. Altmann3, G. Hurlbut3, K. Huttner1, M. Cotreau4, S. Raines4, C. McKee1
records.affiliations_text: 1Sionna Therapeutics, Clinical Development, Waltham, United States, 2Sionna Therapeutics, Clinical Operations, Waltham, United States, 3Sionna Therapeutics, Discovery Research, Waltham, United States, 4Sionna Therapeutics, Waltham, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: At least two-thirds of people with CF (pwCF) on standard-of-care (SOC) modulators do not achieve normal CFTR function, defined by sweat chloride levels <30 mmol/L. Further, some do not tolerate these modulators. Therefore, a significant unmet need exists for novel modulators.

The F508del mutation directly destabilizes the nucleotide-binding domain 1 (NBD1) of CFTR. Stabilization of NBD1 may be critical to achieving complete correction of the F508del-CFTR defect. None of the approved modulators directly stabilize NBD1.

Methods: We assessed the safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics of two novel oral NBD1 stabilizers, SION-719 and SION-451, in two randomized, placebo-controlled single-agent phase 1 single ascending dose and multiple ascending dose clinical trials in healthy adult participants.

Results: SION-719 and SION-451 were generally safe and well tolerated at all dose levels administered. No serious adverse events were reported. Most treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) were mild to moderate. No TEAEs led to participant discontinuation of study drug, and none met dose-limiting criteria. There were no trends of significance in clinical safety data.

Based on in vitro CF human bronchial epithelial cell assay data, the concentration targets for clinically meaningful benefit compared with SOC for SION-719 and SION-451, as either an add-on to SOC or in dual combination with one of Sionna’s complementary modulators, were achieved with single and multiple doses.

Conclusion: Novel NBD1 stabilizers SION-719 and SION-451 were generally safe and well tolerated in healthy participants, and both compounds achieved concentrations that are predicted to deliver clinically meaningful benefit in pwCF and the F508del genotype. SION-719 is advancing in a Phase 2 proof of concept study and SION-451 is in a Phase 1 dual combination study.

records.title: Outcomes of lung transplantation in older adults with cystic fibrosis

session.title: ePoster Session 08 - Life course outcomes in modern cystic fibrosis: transplantation, ageing and pregnancy across registries

person.institution: The Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine

records.authors_text: S.N. Feng1, A. Oak1, A. Bermudez1, A. Casillan1, S. Agbor-Enoh1, C. Merlo1, E. Bush1
records.affiliations_text: 1The Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Baltimore, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To examine whether older cystic fibrosis (CF) patients experience inferior outcomes following lung transplant (LT).

Methods: Adult (≥18 years) CF patients undergoing LT from 01/2005-09/2024 were identified in the United Network for Organ Sharing database and stratified by age at transplant: 18-29, 30-39 (reference), 40-49, and ≥50 years. Postoperative outcomes were acute rejection, hospital length of stay, and post-transplant dialysis, ventilator support, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), reintubation, airway dehiscence, tracheostomy, and stroke. Survival was assessed using Kaplan-Meier curves and multivariable Cox proportional hazards models. Sensitivity analyses examined whether effects differed pre- vs. post-2020 with introduction of CF modulator therapy.

Results: Of 3,195 CF patients undergoing LT (median age 30 years), 1,528 (47.8%) were 18–29, 959 (30.0%) 30–39, 471 (14.7%) 40–49, and 237 (7.4%) ≥50. Compared to recipients aged 30–39, older patients were more likely male and to have a smoking history (p<0.001), but less likely to receive pre-transplant ECMO (p=0.014) and had shorter waitlist times (p=0.006). Older recipients also received organs from progressively older donors (p<0.001). Post-transplant, reintubation rates (p<0.001) and hospital length of stay (p=0.007) increased with age. After adjustment, older age was not independently associated with postoperative complications. Despite similar morbidity, 1-year survival was significantly lower for recipients ≥50 years versus the reference group (aHR=3.95, 95% CI=1.61–9.73, p=0.003). Compared to patients 30–39, those 40–49 (aHR=1.68, 95% CI=1.32–2.14, p<0.001) and ≥50 (aHR=3.25, 95% CI=2.13–4.94, p<0.001) had progressively higher overall mortality. These associations remained consistent pre- vs. post-2020.

Conclusions: Advanced age predicts worse post-LT survival among CF patients, with recipients ≥50 years showing nearly fourfold higher 1-year mortality despite similar complications.

records.title: A proposed Canadian airway clearance therapy risk assessment tool

session.title: ePoster Session 09 - Rethinking airway clearance and physical activity in the CFTR modulator era: adherence, burden and innovation

records.authors_text: M. Richmond1, K. Wu2,3, C. Smith4, N. Carr5, J. Fairbairn1, N. Lee Son1, N. Nunes6, B. Owen7, V. Pinto8, A. Sweetland9, M. Chilvers1, Canadian Cystic Fibrosis Physiotherapy Advisory Group
records.affiliations_text: 1BC Children's Hospital, Vancouver, Canada, 2Toronto Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, St. Michael's Hospital, Respirology, Toronto, Canada, 3University of Toronto, Temerty Faculty of Medicine, Toronto, Canada, 4University of Calgary Foothills Medical Centre, Calgary, Canada, 5Saint John NB Clinic Adult and Kids, Saint John, Canada, 6Children's Hospital, London Health Sciences Centre, London, Canada, 7Sick Kids The Hospital for Sick Children, Division of Respiratory Medicine, Toronto, Canada, 8Children's Hospital of Eastern Ontario (CHEO), Ottawa, Canada, 9NL Health Services, Cystic Fibrosis Program, St. John's, Canada
records.abstract_text:
Objective: To describe the development of a proposed risk assessment tool by the Canadian Cystic Fibrosis Physiotherapy Advisory Group (CCFPAG) to guide clinicians in decision-making around decreasing or stopping daily airway clearance therapies (ACT).

Methods: In recent years, despite a lack of clinical trial data to support the de-escalation of ACT, people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) are decreasing or stopping ACT independently. The CCFPAG is a trans-Canadian group of physiotherapists with varying years of clinical experience. For some, without the historical context of CF lung disease, it can be challenging to continue recommending traditional ACT and for others, it is equally challenging to recommend decreasing daily ACT without strong scientific evidence. In 2025, the CCFPAG met in a series of working groups to develop a preliminary tool to support clinicians in evaluating which pwCF may be able to decrease/stop daily ACT.

Results: A list of clinical factors and their associated values was produced and then stratified in lower, moderate or higher risk zones. Thresholds of risk were set for each factor that aligned with Canadian consensus guidelines. Table 1 outlines the three risk categories and current considerations that need to be evaluated when determining whether ACT routines can be changed for pwCF. For all risk zones, ACT should be increased during pulmonary exacerbations, with a drop in percent predicted FEV1 (ppFEV1) from baseline, changes in baseline health status and/or with clinical discretion.

session.title: ePoster Session 10 - Precision monitoring and management of cystic fibrosis related diabetes

records.authors_text: L. Lewis1, D. Shimmin1, H. Saumtally2,1, S. Pearson1, I. Clifton2,1, G. Spoletini1, A. Sawant1, D.G Peckham2,1
records.affiliations_text: 1St James's University Hospital, Leeds Adult Cystic Fibrosis Unit, Leeds, United Kingdom, 2University of Leeds, Leeds Institute of Medical Research, Leeds, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: While insulin remains the mainstay of CF diabetes (CFD) management, increasing use of non-insulin glucose lowering therapies is emerging in clinical practice. This evolution may be partly attributable to the adoption of CFTR modulators (CFTRm), which improved nutritional status, reduce pulmonary infections and decreases inflammation, factors that contribute to altered insulin sensitivity. This study describes contemporary diabetes management practices within a large adult CF centre.

Methods: Clinical and prescribing data was extracted in 2025 from the electronic patient records (EMIS Web). Individuals with transient gestational diabetes were excluded.

Results: 439 adults were included (245 m; median age 35 yrs, range 17–79). 160 subjects (36.5%) (90 m; median age 40 yrs, range 18–75) had CFD. Non-insulin therapies included, metformin, DPP-4 inhibitor, GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist and SGLT2 inhibitors.

111/160 (69.4%) were on insulin (57 m; median age 40 years, range 18–75).Sixteen patients received adjunctive glucose-lowering therapy alongside insulin, including metformin (n=6), tirzepatide (n=6), sitagliptin (n=11), tirzepatide/metformin (n=1), and dapagliflozin/tirzepatide (n=1).

Forty-nine patients with CFRD (30.6%) were not on insulin (33 m; median age 40 years, range 21–65). Management included diet (n=12), sitagliptin (n=24), linagliptin (n=4), tirzepatide/metformin (n=4), tirzepatide (n=1), dapagliflozin/metformin (n=1), and empagliflozin/metformin/tirzepatide (n=1). Analysis of longer-term clinical outcomes is ongoing.

Conclusion: Diabetes management in CF is evolving in response to changing disease phenotypes and an expanding range of glucose lowering therapies. Targeting insulin resistance, particularly in the context of CFTRm associated weight gain, may be of increasing clinical relevance. As therapeutic options broaden, a more individualised approach to CFD is likely to play a central role in optimising metabolic and clinical outcomes.

records.affiliations_text: 1Cork University Hospital, University College Cork, Cork Centre for Cystic Fibrosis (3CF), Cork, Ireland, 2University College Cork, The HRB funded Clinical Research Facility, Cork, Ireland, 3University College Cork, Department of Medicine, Cork, Ireland, 4Cork University Hospital, University College Cork, Digital Health Literacy (DHL) Public Patient Involvement (PPI) Team, 3CF,, Cork, Ireland
records.abstract_text:
Background: DHL is the combination of health literacy and digital competency skills needed to allow patients/care teams to engage with care through digital health tools and online environments. Within CF Telehealth, there is no clear framework for what skills and proficiencies are needed for both care teams and patients to engage properly with telehealth. The EU DigComp 2.2 (EU-DC) Framework outlines the digital competencies needed for EU citizens.

Objective: Using the EU-DC, this research sought to identify what proficiency levels are needed for each competency for both CF teams and PwCF.

Methods: The EU-DC competency and proficiency tables were converted into an online survey. This survey was then distributed to the ECFS Telehealth Working Group to determine the required proficiency level for PwCF and CF teams using telehealth (54 members with expertise in CF telehealth).

Results: 27 experts completed the survey [Table1 summarises the average proficiency level score for each competency]. All 5 EU-DC competencies were seen as necessary for CF telehealth. Generally, CF care teams should have advanced proficiency levels (so that they could also support PwCF & carers), while PwCF/Carers were expected to have a foundational knowledge in most competency areas.

Conclusion: The EU-DC framework provides a useful foundation for what DHL competencies and proficiencies are needed to support CF telehealth. Overall, all competencies were seen as necessary, with greater emphasis on CF care teams having a higher proficiency level in these areas.

Funding: Supported by a Vertex CF-RIA award.

person.biography:
Tamara is a multidisciplinary Research Fellow with the Cork Centre for Cystic Fibrosis (3CF) at the Cork University Hospital and University College Cork. As of 2022, she co-ordinates data collection at the Cork adult service for the Cystic Fibrosis Registry of Ireland. Tamara is currently in receipt of a Vertex Research Innovation Award that is exploring Digital Health Literacy for telehealth to support PwCF and the MDT.
Tamara is the current co-ordinator of the ECFS Telehealth for CF Working Group (THCF), starting in 2023. She is a member of the ECFS education committee, ECFS social media working group, ERS CONNECT CRC Network, IEEE Consumer Technology Society for Healthcare and Wellbeing, and the EU Digital Competency (DigComp) Community of Practice.

Tamara’s previous research (PhD & Postdocs) has focused on Virtual Reality, Gamification/Serious Games, Interactive 3D, Educational Animations, Mobile Multimedia, mHealth, and eHealth for Cystic Fibrosis and other areas in medicine and healthcare.

records.title: Finding the right route to the lung: precision gene editing therapy for cystic fibrosis

session.title: ePoster Session 07 - Old and new – exploring the portfolio for cystic fibrosis treatment

person.institution: iBET - Instituto de Biologia Experimental e   Tecnológica
person.department: Cell   Line Development & Molecular Virology Lab - Animal Cell Technology Unit

records.authors_text: L. Santos1, M. Branco1, D. Schenkwein2, A.S. Coroadinha1
records.affiliations_text: 1iBET - Instituto de Biologia Experimental e Tecnológica , Cell Line Development & Molecular Virology Lab - Animal Cell Technology Unit, Oeiras, Portugal, 2A.I. Virtanen Institute for Molecular Sciences, Kuopio, Finland
records.abstract_text:
Effective treatments for all individuals with cystic fibrosis (CF) continue to present significant challenges. CRISPR-based technologies, especially base editing, offer a promising avenue towards finding a cure. However, to minimize off-target effects, the components required for base editing must be expressed transiently in the target cells. Delivering these components as ribonucleoprotein (RNPs) complexes via engineered virus-like particles (eVLPs) presents a potentially safer alternative, given their limited lifespan within cells. By utilizing envelope glycoprotein pseudotyping, eVLPs can be customized to specifically target lung epithelial cells, addressing a crucial gap in CF treatment.

Objectives: Our goal is to evaluate the effectiveness of eVLPs pseudotyped with three different viral envelope glycoproteins in delivering base editing components to target lung cells.

Methods: As proof of concept, we developed a lung epithelial cell line that stably expresses a mutant version of the Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP) that lacks fluorescence. This will allow us to assess how effectively the eVLPs can deliver the editing components to cells.

Results: Our findings show that eVLPs can effectively deliver base-editing components into cells, allowing precise correction of the GFP mutation and restoring its fluorescence. Of the three tested envelopes, one exhibits a high affinity for lung cells, resulting in four times more editing efficiency.

records.title: Trends in lung transplantation for cystic fibrosis following introduction of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor: a United States Registry analysis

session.title: ePoster Session 08 - Life course outcomes in modern cystic fibrosis: transplantation, ageing and pregnancy across registries

person.institution: The Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine

records.authors_text: S.N. Feng1, A. Oak1, A. Bermudez1, A. Casillan1, S. Agbor-Enoh1, C. Merlo1, E. Bush1
records.affiliations_text: 1The Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Baltimore, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To characterize trends in cystic fibrosis (CF) lung transplantation (LT) following approval of elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor (Trikafta).

Methods: We identified CF patients ≥18 years undergoing LT from 01/2016-09/2024 in the United Network for Organ Sharing database. Patients were stratified into pre- and post-Trikafta eras (2016-2019 vs. 2020-2024). We compared transplant volumes, transplant centers, recipient characteristics, and post-transplant survival between eras. Temporal trends in transplant volume were evaluated using the Mann-Kendall test. Survival was assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis and multivariable Cox regression.

Results: In total, 1,135 CF patients underwent LT during the study period (pre-Trikafta: 922; post-Trikafta: 213). Annual CF LT volume decreased by 81%, from 231 transplants/year pre-Trikafta to 45 transplants/year post-Trikafta, representing a significant downward trend (p=0.001). The number of centers performing CF LT decreased from 63 to 52, with median transplants per center declining from 10 (IQR: 7-19) to 3 (IQR: 2-6.5) (p<0.001). High-volume centers (>10 transplants) declined from 31 (49%) to 3 (6%). Post-Trikafta recipients had similar age at LT compared with pre-Trikafta (median 32 vs. 31 years, p=0.15), as well as comparable rates of pre-LT extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) and mechanical ventilation. Post-Trikafta recipients spent less time on the waitlist (median 40 vs. 53 days, p=0.34). Racial distribution also shifted significantly, with proportionally more Black (6.1% vs 3.7%) and Hispanic (13.6% vs 5.6%) recipients post-Trikafta (p<0.001). One-year post-LT survival was similar between eras (91.5% vs 91.7%, p=0.84).

Conclusions: The introduction of Trikafta was associated with an 81% reduction in CF LT volume and marked consolidation of center participation, with near elimination of high-volume CF LT programs. This shift has profound implications for transplant program planning, resource allocation, and organ distribution policy.

records.title: Airway clearance and chronic inhaled mucoactive therapy use decreases substantially after the start of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor

session.title: ePoster Session 09 - Rethinking airway clearance and physical activity in the CFTR modulator era: adherence, burden and innovation

records.authors_text: N. Lee Son1, E. Wen2, J.N Bone2, M.A Chilvers1,2,3, J.H Rayment1,2,3
records.affiliations_text: 1British Columbia Children's Hospital, Vancouver, Canada, 2British Columbia Child and Research Institute, Vancouver, Canada, 3University of British Columbia (Pediatrics), Vancouver, Canada
records.abstract_text:
Background: In the context of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) treatment, the anecdotally reported frequency of airway clearance (AC) and chronic inhaled mucoactive therapy (CIMT) has declined with many people with CF (pwCF) stopping altogether, some on their own accord. This study aims to quantify AC and CIMT de-escalation after ETI initiation.

Methods: This quality improvement project included all pwCF at our pediatric CF centre who started ETI between December 2019 and September 2025. AC and CIMT practice were collected from the electronic medical record.

Results: Between December 2019 and September 2025, 92 pwCF started ETI (51% female, mean age 8.3 years, 47% F508del homozygous, mean ppFEV1 92.0%). Prior to ETI, 76/92 (83%) individuals performed daily AC. Of these, 24/76 (32%) stopped and 18/76 (24%) reduced AC after starting ETI. 17/24 (71%) stopped AC within two years of starting ETI; 10 (42%) within the first year. 11/18 (61%) reduced AC within two years of starting ETI; 3 (17%) within the first year. The median (interquartile range) time to stopping AC was 14.2 (7.6, 24.9) months and for reducing AC 21.6 (16.8,42.4) months.

Prior to starting ETI, 45/92 (49%) pwCF were taking hypertonic saline (HTS) and 26/92 (28%) were taking dornase alfa (DA). After starting ETI, 24/45 (53%) stopped HTS and 22/26 (85%) stopped DA. 17/24 (71%) stopped HTS within two years of starting ETI; 5 (21%) within the first year. 16/22 (73%) patients stopped DA within two years of starting ETI; 9 (41%) within the first year. The median time to stopping HTS was 17.2 (13.4, 26.7) months and for DA 13.6 (9.14, 24.76) months.

Analysis of AC and CIMT de-escalation kinetics using logistic mixed-effects models is ongoing.

Conclusion: The reduction of AC and CIMT use after ETI initiation is substantial, but variable in extent and timing. Understanding the impact of this treatment de-escalation on long term lung health is critical to appropriate treatment of pwCF in the modern era.

records.title: Continuous glucose monitoring to track metabolic changes in children and adolescents with cystic fibrosis before and after ETI initiation

session.title: ePoster Session 10 - Precision monitoring and management of cystic fibrosis related diabetes

records.authors_text: A. Galderisi1, L. Weiss2, H. Marchiori3, A. Besancon4, D. Sakhi5, A.S. Bonnel6, I. Sermet-Gaudelus5
records.affiliations_text: 1Assistance Publique Hopitaux Paris, Pediatric Endocrinology, Paris, France, 2CHU Strasbourg, Pediatrics, Strasbourg, France, 3University of Padova, Bioengineering, Padova, Italy, 4Hopital Necker Enfants Malades, Pediatric Endocrinology, Paris, France, 5Hopital Necker Enfants Malades, Paediatric Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Paris, France, 6Hopital Necker Enfants Malades, Paris, France
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: The oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) remains the recommended screening and monitoring test starting the age of 10 years for abnormal glucose tolerance in people with cystic fibrosis (CF). However, there is evidence for earlier onset of glucose tolerance abnormalities in those with CF and need for minimally invasive tool to track their trajectory and quantify the impact of CFTR modulator Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI). We tested changes in continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) metrics before and after ETI initiation across different pediatric age groups.

Methods: We included participants to the French MODUL-CF registry aged 3-18 years with at least 24 hours of CGM data preceding the initiation of ETI and a 2nd CGM 12±3 months following drug initiation. The cohort was stratified in 3 groups based on the age at ETI initiation: <6 (n=), 6-12 (n=) and >12 years (n=). Percentage time in hypo- (<70mg/dL) and hyper-(>140mg/dL)glycemia and in target range (TIR, 70-140mg/dL) were compared before and after ETI.

Results: We included 98 patients with CF who were started on ETI. Those aged >12 y displayed a marked increase of TIR (p=0.029) with a reduction of percentage time in hypoglycemia at 12 months ETI(<70mg/dL) (p <0.001). The 6-12 years group displayed a lower time spent in hyperglycemia (p < 0.001), while CGM metrics did not differ before and after starting ETI in participants younger than 6 years.

Conclusion: CGM metrics describe an improvement of glucose control in those older than 6 years receiving ETI , with relatively stable profile in the youngest ones.

records.title: Expanded use of remote objective monitoring during telehealth visits for people with CF experiencing acute symptoms: the EUROPA study project

session.title: ePoster Session 11 - Telehealth and digital tools in care and education

records.authors_text: N. Lechtzin1, W. Hunt2, C. Forseen3, G. Hong4, P. Mogayzel5, K. McKie6, D. Peeler5, M. Phillips1, M. Rey4, O. Reis2, V. Taskar3, N. Wimmer6
records.affiliations_text: 1Johns Hopkins University, Pulmonary and Critical Care, Baltimore, United States, 2Emory University School of Medicine, Medicine, Atlanta, United States, 3Medical College of Georgia at Augusta University, Medicine, Augusta, United States, 4University of Pennsylvania Perelman School of Medicine, Medicine, Philadelphia, United States, 5Johns Hopkins University, Pediatrics, Baltimore, United States, 6Medical College of Georgia at Augusta University, Pediatrics, Augusta, United States
records.abstract_text:
Background: Acute pulmonary exacerbations (APEs) are often managed by phone without spirometry. This QI project studies a protocolized evaluation and treatment of pwCF with acute respiratory symptoms thru telehealth and remote objective monitoring.

Methods: This multi-site QI initiative expands urgent telehealth evaluation. Inclusion criteria were pwCF age 6 years and up. Subjects enrolled received spirometers, scales, and pulse oximeters. A protocol for APE treatment was based on FEV1 and CRISS score at the time of exacerbation. Key process measures included number of acute telehealth visits scheduled within 48 hours, number of visits with objective data collected and adherence to treatment algorithm.

Results: 153 subjects have been enrolled. Mean age is 29.8±14.7 and 65% are female. 89% are Caucasian, 4.8% African American, 4.1% Hispanic. Baseline FEV1 is 72.6±27.0 % predicted. 84% of subjects reported current use of a CFTR modulator. There have been 144 acute calls, which have resulted in 107 telehealth visits for urgent evaluation. At the telehealth visit, mean FEV1 was 63.6±19.6. In 62% of cases an oral antibiotic was prescribed, in 10.5% IV antibiotics were prescribed. Hospitalization was recommended for 16%. 80% of participants had follow up visits scheduled. At follow up FEV1 was 69.7±25.7. 6.9% of patients had further escalation of antibiotic therapy and 12.6% were hospitalized. Data collection is ongoing.

Conclusion: pwCF and CF providers have been willing to utilize telehealth with expanded remote monitoring for APEs. By using process maps and PDSA cycles we have been successful in scheduling telehealth visits within 2 business days of a sick call and have utilized home spirometry in 75% of telehealth calls and had follow up visits in 80% of cases. The initiative is ongoing with a remaining goal being to assess patient satisfaction with the use of telehealth for APEs.

records.affiliations_text: 1Royal Brompton Hospital, Guys and St Thomas's NHS Foundation Trust, Adult Cystic Fibrosis, London, United Kingdom, 2Imperial College, National Heart and Lung Institute, London, United Kingdom, 3University of East Anglia, Norwich Medical School, Norwich, United Kingdom, 4NIHR Applied Research Collaboration East of England, Cambridge, United Kingdom, 5Cystic Fibrosis Trust, London, United Kingdom, 6No institution, Sydney, Australia
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Health benefits of yoga are widely recognised for the general population and some medical conditions, but evidence of clinical efficacy is limited for CF. We conducted ‘Yoga Outcomes Get Assessed in CF (YOGA-CF)’ – a UK multicentre RCT, to investigate effectiveness of a bespoke CF-specific online 12-week yoga intervention for adults with CF.

Methods: Participants were randomised to usual care or yoga. Spirometry, one-minute sit-to-stand, the Cystic Fibrosis Questionnaire-Revised (CFQ-R) and other questionnaires were collected via video-call pre- and post-intervention (0 and 12 weeks), and after 12-weeks of follow-up (week 24). The primary outcome measure was difference in respiratory-related quality of life as measured by CFQ-R at 12-weeks. Sample size was calculated to detect a minimally clinically important difference of 4 on the CFQ-R respiratory domain, with power of 80%, 5% significance level, assuming a standard deviation (SD) of 12 (total n=314 including 10% allowance for drop-out). An economic evaluation will estimate cost-effectiveness.

Results: 27 sites opened from April 2024; 1,265 patients screened with 340 (27%) recruited (108% of target). Main reasons for ineligibility (n=568; 45%) included: unstable CF (n=116) and other trial involvement (n=93). 357 (28%) declined participation [main reason: lack of time (n=142)]. Recruited demographics: 66% female; mean age 36y (SD=11); mean percent predicted FEV1 78% (SD=21) (table). To date, 31 serious adverse events, all unrelated, or unlikely related, to intervention. 30 withdrawals, main reason: lack of time (n=13). Final follow-up January 2026. Primary outcome data to be presented.

Conclusion: YOGA-CF completed to time and target, highlighting the CF community’s appetite and desire to identify non-pharmacological strategies to improve outcomes. Main results will be available for ECFC 2026, contributing significantly to the evidence base for yoga as an exercise option for people with CF.

person.institution: Royal Brompton Hospital, Guys and St Thomas's NHS Foundation Trust
person.biography: Dr Gemma Stanford is a Clinical Specialist Physiotherapist in Adult Cystic Fibrosis (CF) at the Royal Brompton Hospital, London where she has worked since 2005. Her PhD investigated outcome measures for airway clearance in adults with CF and she is the current Lead Co-Ordinating Investigator of the UK multisite YOGA-CF RCT. Gemma has published and presented internationally on several aspects of physiotherapy and CF care including non-invasive ventilation, airway clearance and the challenges of ageing. Gemma is the chair of the European Cystic Fibrosis Society’s Physiotherapy Specialist International Interest Group (PhySIIG), a member of the UK’s Association of Chartered Physiotherapists in Cystic Fibrosis (ACPCF) and UK lead of the REACH for CF collaboration.

content.biography: Gemma Stanford is a Highly Specialist Physiotherapist in Adult Cystic Fibrosis (CF) at the Royal Brompton Hospital, London where she has worked since 2005. She recently completed a HEE/NIHR Clinical Doctoral Research Fellowship. Her PhD investigated outcome measures for airway clearance in adults with CF. Gemma has published and presented internationally on several aspects of physiotherapy and CF care including non-invasive ventilation, airway clearance and the challenges of ageing. Gemma is the chair of the European Cystic Fibrosis Society’s Physiotherapy Specialist Interest Group (PhySIG), a research representative on the committee of the UK’s Association of Chartered Physiotherapists in Cystic Fibrosis (ACPCF) and part of the REACH for CF collaboration.

records.title: Waitlist and lung transplant outcomes by sex for adults with cystic fibrosis: the United States experience

session.title: ePoster Session 08 - Life course outcomes in modern cystic fibrosis: transplantation, ageing and pregnancy across registries

records.authors_text: A. Oak1, L. Fan1, A. Feng1, A. Bermudez1, A. Casillan1, S. Agbor-Enoh1, E. Bush1, C. Merlo1
records.affiliations_text: 1Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, Baltimore, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a key indication for lung transplantation (LT). Despite medical advances, many adults develop end-stage lung disease and require LT; women with CF experience earlier infections and worse life outcomes. The impact of sex on access to LT and post-LT outcomes is unclear. We aimed to quantify differences in waitlist and post-LT outcomes by sex.

Methods: We utilized the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) database, including adults listed for single-organ LT from January 2005 to November 2023. We analyzed baseline and post-LT outcomes with Chi-square and Kruskal-Wallis tests. Waitlist and transplant outcomes were modeled with Fine-Gray and Cox proportional hazards respectively. We adjusted for age, BMI, lung allocation score (LAS), waitlist time and post-LT length of stay (LOS). Medians were reported as median [IQR] and hazard ratios (HR) as 95% confidence interval.

Results: Women were younger (28[23-37] vs 30[25-39]; p<0.001), had lower BMI (19.2[17.9-20.9] vs 19.8[18.2-22.0]; p<0.001) and more diabetes (52.9% vs 45.9%; p<0.001) with similar LAS to men. Women waited longer (79[20-216] vs 57[17-166] days; p<0.001), had lower 1-year transplant rates (68.9% vs 77.0%; p<0.001) and higher 1-year waitlist death/deterioration (12.1% vs 8.6%; p<0.001). Fine-Gray subdistribution HR for female sex for waitlist deterioration was 1.329[1.07-1.65], p=0.009. Among recipients (male 1490, female 1417), ventilation was prolonged in women (>5d vent 19.4% vs 13.1%; p<0.001) and LOS was longer (18[13-28] vs 17[13-25]; p=0.01). Post-LT survival was similar by sex (1-year 90.3% vs 91.4%; 5-year 61.7% vs 62.6%). Adjusted HR for female sex in post-LT mortality was 0.928[0.831-1.036], p=0.18.

Conclusion: Among US adults with CF evaluated for LT, female sex is associated with longer wait time, worse waitlist outcomes and greater postoperative resource use; long-term post-LT survival is comparable. Expedited LT workup and listing for women must be considered.

records.title: Patient reported experience trialling a intrapulmonary ventilation device

session.title: ePoster Session 09 - Rethinking airway clearance and physical activity in the CFTR modulator era: adherence, burden and innovation

person.institution: All Wales Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre

records.authors_text: S. Maroo1, R. McFerran1, J. Duckers1, S. Caunter1, H. Carter1
records.affiliations_text: 1All Wales Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Cardiff, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objective: To trial Intrapulmonary Ventilation (IPV); a new airway clearance technique (ACT) device at the All Wales Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre (AWACF) and gain insight into patient subjective experience using Sentec’s IPV1® device. The IPV1® delivers fast air bursts during inspiration and expiration to loosen secretions, reduce atelectasis, and splint the airways for gas exchange.

Purpose: i) To identify patient perceived benefits/difficulties of IPV1® system during respiratory exacerbations at the AWACF ii) To compare patient experience of the IPV1® to their prior experience using the discontinued MetaNeb device.

Method: The IPV1® was trialled on people admitted from 15/10/25-18/11/25. Average stay was 12 days. 6 patients used the IPV1®, 4 completed the questionnaire (2 male and 2 female) on discharge to note comparisons to the MetaNeb, duration of treatments, changes in symptoms and overall opinion.

Results: All patients reported improved mucus clearance and preferred IPV1® over MetaNeb. 75% found the IPV1® easier to use and more comfortable, with improved breathing. 75% of patients found exercise tolerance improved since using IPV1® and noted they would feel confident using the device independently. In fact, one patient was able to at the end of their stay. Participants noted their overall impression. Positive thoughts included that the device was ‘easy to set up’, ‘easy to use’ and ‘not complicated’. They felt the adjustable amplitude allowed vibrations to ‘shake all parts of the body’ and aid ‘deeper breaths’. One said it is ‘an awesome device’. Some challenges highlighted that, ‘it took a while to get used to', caused ‘cheeks and jaw to hurt’ and the ‘display screen is too small’.

Conclusion: The IPV1® was reported as a preferable ACT by all when compared to the MetaNeb. Overall, it seems benefits outweighed the challenges. As the MetaNeb is being discontinued, the questionnaire shows the IPV1® to be a positive alternative therapy for inpatient treatment.

records.title: Early metabolic predictors of cystic fibrosis-related diabetes: the predictive value of beta-cell glucose sensitivity and 30-minute C-peptide

session.title: ePoster Session 10 - Precision monitoring and management of cystic fibrosis related diabetes

records.authors_text: A. Foppiani1, F. Sileo1, B. Marelli1, C. Premuda2, A. Gramegna2, F. Ciciriello3, F. Alghisi3, S. Costa4, M.C. Lucanto4, C. Colombo2, A. Battezzati1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Milan, ICANS-DIS, DeFENS, Milan, Italy, 2Policlinico of Milan, Milan, Italy, 3Bambino Gesù Children's Hospital, Rome, Italy, 4Hospital University Hospital "G. Martino ", Messina, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: This study aimed to identify early predictors of cystic fibrosis-related diabetes (CFRD) in children by comparing standard oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) categories against physiological markers of beta-cell function.

Methods: Data from 161 pediatric patients with cystic fibrosis (CF) were analyzed. Researchers reviewed historical metabolic data, including OGTT glucose categories, insulin sensitivity (OGIS), and beta-cell glucose sensitivity (B-GS)—calculated via modeling glucose, insulin, and C-peptide levels over 180 minutes. Simple plasma C-peptide levels at 30 minutes (CP30) were also evaluated. The primary outcome was a CFRD diagnosis. Logistic regression assessed predictors, including the impact of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) modulator therapy.

Results: Over a median seven-year follow-up, 27% of patients developed CFRD. While 60% of the cohort initiated ETI therapy, it was not a statistically significant protective factor in the models. Traditional OGTT categories and insulin sensitivity (OGIS) showed poor predictive power.

Conversely, beta-cell markers were highly discriminatory:

B-GS: Higher sensitivity was a significant protective factor (OR 0.96, 95% CI 0.93-0.99; p=0.004).

CP30: Higher levels were a strong independent protective factor (OR 0.51, 95% CI 0.27-0.81; p<0.01), identifying patients with preserved function unlikely to progress.

person.title: Prof. Dr.
person.department: CF Unit, 3rd Paediatric Dept, Hippokration Hospital

records.authors_text: S.-S. Kyrvasili1, E.-A. Chrysochoou1, M. Galogavrou1, A. Sopiadou1, E. Hatziagorou1
records.affiliations_text: 1Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, CF Unit, 3rd Paediatric Dept, Hippokration Hospital, Thessaloniki, Greece
records.abstract_text:
Aim: To assess an intervention of lung function telemonitoring in patients with Cystic Fibrosis (pwCF) and the level of adherence to this program, and examine if this supports effective management of pulmonary exacerbations.

Methods: This was a randomized, two-arm trial in pwCF, children, and adults, conducted over 52 weeks in a paediatric CF Unit. The study population consisted of two groups: a Usual Care (UC) group, in which pwCF received routine follow-up at cystic fibrosis outpatient clinics, and a Home Spirometry (HS) group, in which telemonitoring with weekly home spirometry was implemented in addition to usual care. Lung function was assessed using electronic devices connected to a centralized platform accessible via the CF Unit.

Results: Overall, 104 pwCF were included in the analysis, comprising 52 patients in the HS group and 52 in the UC group, with median age 16 years (SD: 7). The adherence of patients in the telemonitoring program in the period of 52 weeks was 21.2% with 11 of 52 patients performing a spirometry once per week in more than 80% of their chances of spirometry follow-up, while twenty five patients performed a spirometry in more than 50% of their chances (48.1% adherence). A statistically significant difference was observed between the two groups in the time to initiation of antibiotic therapy following the first exacerbation (p= 0.026). The HS group was associated with a higher hazard of earlier antibiotic initiation than the UC group (hazard ratio [HR]: 1.67; 95% CI: 1.06-2.64). Moreover, time to antibiotic initiation after the second exacerbation differed significantly between groups (p = 0.026), with a higher hazard of earlier treatment in the HS group (HR: 1.92; 95% CI: 1.08-3.39).

Conclusion: PwCF participated in a telemonitoring program for 52 weeks and demonstrated adequate adherence. The implementation of the program improves the management of pulmonary exacerbations by facilitating earlier initiation of antibiotic therapy.

person.biography:
Elpis Hatziagorou is a Professor in Respiratory Pediatrics of the Paediatric Pulmonology and CF Unit at Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, Greece. Dr. Hatziagorou received her degree in Medicine from the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki and earned her Ph.D. in studies of exhaled NO in patients with chronic lung disease. She worked as a Clinical Fellow in Respiratory Pediatrics at Sheffield Children’s Hospital, University of Sheffield, UK (2010), and got the European Diploma in Paediatric Respiratory Medicine (2012).
She is a clinical researcher; her main interests are Cystic Fibrosis, non-CF bronchiectasis, Multiple Breath Washout, and Exercise testing. She has been a Steering Group Member of the European Cystic Fibrosis Registry (since 2007) and a Member of the Scientific Committee of the European Cystic Fibrosis Registry since 2018. She has also been a member of the ECFS Exercise Working Group since 2015. Elpis Hatziagorou has been a member of the European Cystic Fibrosis Society Diagnostic Network Group since 2009. In the past decade, her interest has remained focused on outcome parameters (lung clearance index, quality of life, exercise testing indices), clinical trials, and diagnostic/epidemiologic issues in CF.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The emergence of Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Receptor modulators (CFTRm) and digital health technologies create opportunities to reorganise cystic fibrosis (CF) care. MuCopilot is a software as a medical device designed for remote patient monitoring, integrating smartphone-based tests assessing lung function (Mobile Sustained Phonation Test), exercise capacity (Mobile Endurance Walking Test), nocturnal cough (Mobile Sleep Cough Monitoring Test) and a CF-specific symptom and quality-of-life questionnaire (CF-scan). The validation study MuControl (NCT06147778) evaluates the clinical performance of MuCopilot.

Methods: French people with CF (pwCF), aged ≥18 in a stable condition, were recruited from eight French CF centers (Bordeaux, Lyon, Marseille, Nice, Reims, Roscoff, Rouen, Toulouse). Over 3 months, participants completed 9 times the MuCopilot modules: at Day 0 (inclusion), D3, D5, D7, M1, M2 and one day before the exit visit (M3) with supervised evaluations at D0 and M3. The association between at-home digital tests and in-clinic standard tests will be assessed using Pearson correlation.

Results: Seventy pwCF were enrolled (52.9% female, mean age 33.5 ± 11.3 years, 92.9% using CFTRm). 1869 digital evaluations were collected: 540 phonation tests, 538 walking tests, 363 cough tests and 428 questionnaires. Two participants discontinued due to serious adverse events unrelated to MuCopilot. The completion rates of the modules varied from 69.1% for CF-scan questionnaire to 55.9% for the sleep cough monitoring test. Correlations between digital and standard clinical tests will be available for congress.

Conclusions: This analysis demonstrates the feasibility of implementing MuCopilot across multiple French CF centers. MuControl allowed the collection of a high volume of digital evaluations with strong engagement from pwCF. These early results support the potential use and clinical integration of a clinically validated MuCopilot for remote monitoring of CF.

records.title: Cystic fibrosis is associated with the greatest long-term survival after lung transplantation: 30 years of the Zurich experience​

session.title: ePoster Session 08 - Life course outcomes in modern cystic fibrosis: transplantation, ageing and pregnancy across registries

records.authors_text: A. Alonso1, R. Hage1, J. Mueller1, C. Steinack1, G. Lang2, S. Ulrich1, I. Opitz2, M. Schuurmans1
records.affiliations_text: 1University Hospital Zurich, Department of Pulmonology, Zurich, Switzerland, 2University Hospital Zurich, Department of Thoracic Surgery, Zurich, Switzerland
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Lung transplantation (LTx) is an established therapy for patients with advanced cystic fibrosis (CF), yet robust long-term, single-centre outcome data remain limited. We analysed three decades of LTx in Zurich, focusing on survival by transplant indication and the relative long-term advantage in CF.

Methods: This retrospective single-centre cohort included all lung transplantations performed at the University Hospital Zurich between 1992 and 2024 (n=688). Survival status was systematically verified using hospital follow-up and official registries. Overall survival was estimated using Kaplan–Meier methods and compared by log-rank tests. Cox proportional hazards models assessed the association between indication and mortality, with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) as reference.

Results: Median overall survival was 8.04 years, with survival of 86%, 60%, 40%, 29% and 16% at 1, 5, 10, 15 and 20 years, respectively, and survival extending beyond 30 years. Survival did not differ across transplant decades (p=0.50). Indication was a strong determinant of outcome. CF recipients showed the most favourable long-term survival (mean 9.50±6.88 years; median 9.25 years). Compared with COPD, CF was associated with substantially lower mortality (HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.41–0.68; p<0.001), while idiopathic interstitial pneumonia, idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension and other indications did not differ significantly. Increasing recipient age was associated with higher mortality (per-year HR 1.02, 95% CI 1.02–1.03; p<0.001), as was older donor age (>60 vs <30 years: HR 1.98; p<0.001). Survival was comparable between donation after circulatory death and donation after brain death (HR 0.88; p=0.56). Bilateral transplantation was associated with improved survival compared with single LTx (p=0.005).

Conclusions: Over 30 years, long-term survival after LTx in Zurich remained stable, with CF showing a sustained survival advantage over other indications. These findings reinforce CF as an indication with particularly favourable long-term post-transplant outcomes and highlight age and procedure type as key determinants of survival.

session.title: ePoster Session 09 - Rethinking airway clearance and physical activity in the CFTR modulator era: adherence, burden and innovation

person.title: Dr.
person.institution: Cystic Fibrosis Center of Verona, Azienda Ospedaliera Universitaria Integrata

records.authors_text: E. Salonini1, R. Guarise1, E. Salamon1, A. Malvezzi1, S. Tomezzoli1, M. Cipolli1
records.affiliations_text: 1Cystic Fibrosis Center of Verona, Azienda Ospedaliera Universitaria Integrata, Verona, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Exercise and airway clearance techniques (ACTs) are both routinely recommended for people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). In the era of Elexacaftor/Tezacaftor/Ivacaftor (ETI) therapy, some people using physical activity as a substitute for traditional ACTs.

To investigate how adults CF on ETI self-changed home ACTs routines with physical activity.

Methods: An observational analysis was conducted on 230 patients undergoing ETI therapy aged ≥18 years referred to Verona Cystic Fibrosis Center. A self-administered questionnaire was provided to pwCF to assess the participants’ and practice regarding the use of exercise as a substitute for traditional airway clearance techniques.

records.title: Higher BMI, higher hyperglycaemia? Continuous glucose monitoring-detected hyperglycaemia is associated with increased BMI and reduced lung function in young people with cystic fibrosis

session.title: ePoster Session 10 - Precision monitoring and management of cystic fibrosis related diabetes

person.institution: Faculty of Medicine, University of Ljubljana

records.authors_text: J. Rodman Berlot1,2, L. Klemenčič Hansen2, D. Šmigoc Schweiger3,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Department of Paediatric Pulmonology, University Children’s Hospital, University Medical Center Ljubljana, Ljubljana, Slovenia, 2Faculty of Medicine, University of Ljubljana, Ljubljana, Slovenia, 3Department of Paediatric Endocrinology, Diabetes, and Metabolic Diseases, University Children’s Hospital, University Medical Center Ljubljana, Ljubljana, Slovenia
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) can detect glycaemic abnormalities before the onset of cystic fibrosis-related diabetes (CFRD), yet whether these early changes have clinical importance remains uncertain. This study investigated the associations between CGM-derived metrics and key clinical parameters in young people with cystic fibrosis (CF).

Methods: This retrospective analysis included young people with CF aged 10–21 years who had at least one CGM assessment within a three-year period from 2021 to 2024. Patients on insulin therapy or with confounding health conditions were excluded from the study. CGM metrics included estimated HbA1c, average glucose levels, time below range (TBR; glucose<3.9 mmol/L), time in range (TIR; glucose 3.9–10.0 mmol/L), and time above range (TAR; glucose>10 mmol/L). Clinical variables included ppFEV₁, BMI z-score, frequency of pulmonary exacerbations, bacterial colonisation status, and CFTR modulator therapy. Associations were analysed using linear mixed models.

Results: Twenty-six patients (58% male; 77% homozygous for the ΔF508 mutation; all pancreatic insufficient) contributed a total of 48 CGM measurements. None of the participants received systemic corticosteroids during the assessment periods. TAR emerged as the main CGM parameter linked to clinical status: higher BMI z-score predicted increased TAR (β=1.20, 95% CI 0.09–2.31; p=0.035), while higher ppFEV₁ was associated with decreased TAR (β =-0.12, 95% CI -0.20 to -0.05; p=0.002). No significant associations were observed between clinical parameters and other CGM metrics.

Conclusions: In our study, higher TAR was associated with higher BMI and lower lung function, suggesting that improved nutritional status in the era of CFTR modulators might be accompanied by underlying metabolic vulnerabilities. These findings support including CGM in routine surveillance, particularly among patients with higher BMI or declining lung function, to enable earlier intervention before overt CFRD develops.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Cough has been associated with disease severity and identified as a sign of inadequate disease control and early symptom of pulmonary exacerbation in different chronic lung diseases. In the presented study, continuous nocturnal cough monitoring is evaluated in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) to describe the natural history of nocturnal cough in CF patients receiving standard of care CF treatment.

Methods: International, multi-centre prospective observational study on nocturnal continuous, objective cough monitoring by a therapy monitoring app (PARI Connect App) over a 24 weeks period in pwCF >12years aiming to enroll 250 pwCF. Subjective cough severity is reported daily by a visual analogue scale also integrated in the therapy management app. Clinical and sociodemographic parameters, CF specific and cough related quality of life are assessed initially and at 3 and 6 months.

Results: 89/250 pwCF have been enrolled so far, 58% female, median age 28y (IQR 19.0-37.5y), median FEV1 79%pred (IQR 60-95%pred), 78/89 (87.6%) receiving CFTR modulator therapy (74/78 (94.9%) elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor). 55/87 (63.2%) had no pulmonary exacerbation in the previous 12months before inclusion in the study. So far, over a median observation duration of 129 days/patient 4,939 cough monitorings with a median duration of 7.7 hours (IQR 6.9-8.6 hours) and a median number of 1 cough (IQR 0-5 coughs) per monitoring have been recorded. The individual statistical analysis of cough frequency per patient is still pending but will be available by the time of the ECFS.

Conclusion: This study will provide evidence on the suitability of non-invasive, nocturnal cough monitoring as a measure of disease control. Additionally, our study will provide a critical assessment of the utility of digital cough monitoring as a remote endpoint in future therapy studies.

The study is funded by an independent innovation grant from Vertex pharmaceuticals.

records.title: Resurrecting ancestral actin-resistant DNase for cystic fibrosis lung disease therapy

session.title: ePoster Session 07 - Old and new – exploring the portfolio for cystic fibrosis treatment

person.department: Department of Chemistry, Life Sciences and Environmental Sustainability

records.authors_text: G. Mori1, D. Delfino2, L. Capelli1, G. Merici1, G. Cappelloni1, A. Bertucci1, R. Percudani1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Parma, Department of Chemistry, Life Sciences and Environmental Sustainability, Parma, Italy, 2University of Parma, Department of Food and Drug, Parma, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Pulmonary symptoms in cystic fibrosis (CF) dramatically impair patient health and quality of life. The FDA-approved mucolytic recombinant human DNase1 (dornase alfa) shows reduced efficacy in many patients due to actin-rich mucus. Next-generation DNase-based therapeutics must combine resistance to actin inhibition, robust catalytic activity, and scalable manufacturing. Simple cells such as E. coli offer ideal production platforms but have so far failed to express soluble, active human DNase1L2, a DNase1 paralog naturally resistant to actin inhibition. To overcome this bottleneck, we exploited ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR), an evolutionary protein engineering technique that resurrects ancient enzymes with potentially superior properties, aiming to identify actin-resistant, catalytically active DNase variants optimized for efficient microbial production.

Methods: ASR was used to infer ancient DNase sequences predating the divergence of DNase1 and DNase1L2. Reconstructed variants were expressed in E. coli and evaluated for solubility, enzymatic activity, and resistance to actin inhibition. DNase activity was characterized with agarose gel assays and fluorescence-based assays using fluorophore-labeled DNA. AlphaFold structural predictions were used to analyze active-site conservation and potential determinants of actin resistance.

Results: An ancestral DNase variant inferred from deep evolutionary nodes of the DNase1/DNase1L2 clade showed improved solubility compared to DNase1L2 while retaining catalytic activity and strong resistance to actin inhibition under conditions that markedly inhibit recombinant human DNase1.

Conclusions: This study identifies a robust, actin-resistant ancestral DNase with potential to overcome key limitations of current CF mucolytic therapy. Leveraging ASR enables access to DNase functionalities not readily achievable with extant human enzymes, supporting the development of more effective and accessible CF treatments.

records.title: The fastest growing demographic in CF: the life and times of older adults age ≥40 with CF in Canada.

session.title: ePoster Session 08 - Life course outcomes in modern cystic fibrosis: transplantation, ageing and pregnancy across registries

records.authors_text: S.Y. Cheng1, N. Abdulrahem1, P.D.W. Eckford1, A.L. Stephenson2
records.affiliations_text: 1Cystic Fibrosis Canada, Toronto, Canada, 2St. Michael's Hospital, Adult CF Program, Toronto, Canada
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Once thought of as a pediatric disease, the proportion of adults living with cystic fibrosis (CF) in Canada soared from <10% in the 1970’s to over 65% today. As care improves, people with CF are living longer and healthier lives, but little is known about these older adults. The objectives of this study were to: 1) quantify the population of older adults over time, and 2) describe the cohort of older adults.

Methods: This study included all individuals age ≥40 years reported in the Canadian CF Registry between 2015-2024. Objective 2 was restricted to 2024. Continuous variables were summarized using median and interquartile range (IQR), and categorical variables using frequency and proportion.

Results: The number of people age ≥40 increased by nearly 70% from 2015 to 2024, with the largest increase among those age ≥60. The proportion of individuals age ≥40 among the whole CF population increased from 15.1% in 2015 to 23.4% in 2024.

Table 1 describes characteristics of older adults in 2024. The proportion of individuals who were homozygous F508del decreased with age, and among those age ≥60 only 68.0% had an F508del (compared to >85% of the younger age groups). 27.8% of those age ≥60 had two non-F508del variants, and most were considered mild variants (class III-V). The majority of those aged <60 years were diagnosed with CF before age 5, while most of those age ≥60 were diagnosed in adulthood, and 32.2% were diagnosed after age 50. There were no differences in clinical outcomes between the age groups, however the oldest age group had the lowest prevalence of common CF-related comorbidities (CF-related diabetes and pancreatic insufficiency) but highest prevalence of osteoporosis. The oldest age group also had the lowest proportion of history of CFTR modulator use.

Conclusion: In 2024, nearly a quarter of all Canadians with CF were age ≥40, with the cohort age ≥60 being the fastest growing. This oldest age group appeared to be the healthiest, with lower prevalence of typical CF comorbidities. Prevalence of traditional age-related comorbidities (e.g., cardiovascular disease) were unknown due to data limitations, so it is critical that CF registries evolve to capture this information, for a more fulsome understanding of the health of older adults with CF.

records.abstract_text:
Background: Elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor (ETI) therapy improves respiratory function and prognosis in CF patients (pwCF). Given the benefits, physical activity (PA) must be incorporating into pwCF's lifestyle, for their health and quality of life (QoL).

Objectives: We evaluate PA and sedentary behavior (SB) of adults pwCF and assess correlation between PA/SB, with clinical and socio-demographic parameters, QoL and motivation towards health-oriented PA.

Methods: Participants were enrolled in the ‘Lyon Adult CF Center‘, in a cross-sectional observational single-center study (clinicaltrials.gov identifier NCT06507956). All subjects answered self-administered questionnaires: Global Physical Activity Questionnaire-ONAPS-PAQ for PA and SB; CF Questionnaire-Revised (CFQ-R) for QoL; EPICES score for social deprivation and motivation scale towards health-oriented physical activity (EMAPS). Clinical data were also collected.

Results: Two hundred and ninety participants were included: 162 males; 18 lung transplanted patients; 231 taking ETI; median (m) age 32 years; m FEV1 79 of predicted; m BMI 22.5kg/m2; m EPICES score 17. Activity profiles were characterized by the combination of PA level and SB:

Conclusion: We identified pwCF whose lifestyle habits reflect a greater health risk. By successfully identifying this patient profile, physiotherapists and adapted physical activity instructors could offer them specific and tailored MVPA interventions for the benefit of their global health. A subgroup of high sedentary or inactive pwCF taking ETI will be studied more specifically using accelerometers follow-up and a qualitative semi-structured interview identifying motivational barriers and levers for action.

Keywords: CFTR; Cystic Fibrosis; Adult; Chronic disease; Physical Activity; Sedentary behavior; Lifestyle; Aging; Quality of Life.

records.abstract_text:
Aim: To evaluate the effect of CFTRm on glucose tolerance and insulin secretion in children with CF.

Methods: Prospectively collected registry data from children with CF undergoing a 3-hour frequently sampled OGTT were analyzed before and after 24 months of CFTR modulator therapy. Glucose and insulin were measured every 30 minutes; fasting HbA1c, C-peptide, HOMA-IR, Matsuda index and glucose tolerance categories were assessed and compared with baseline.

Results: 41 children (median age at start of therapy: 9.6 years (IQR: 5.8-13.9); 49% boys). 29 received LUM/IVA and 12 ETI. Fasting glucose levels did not differ significantly (p=0.083), while the 120-minute value decreased from 6.2 (IQR: 5.6-7.4) to 5.9 (IQR: 4.6-7.2) (p=0.012). By the second year of therapy, three more children were in the "normal glucose tolerance" fsOGTT category. HOMA index, and Matsuda index did not change substantially.

Conclusion: CFTR modulator therapy was associated with improved glucose tolerance in children with CF.

Funding: National Research, Development and Innovation Fund (NKFIH 138929), CF Trust SRC grant (NU-00600)

records.title: Clinical state transitions identified by unsupervised machine learning are associated with improved lung transplant-free survival in cystic fibrosis

session.title: ePoster Session 11 - Telehealth and digital tools in care and education

person.institution: Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine

records.authors_text: T. Cybulski1, R. Nelson1, M. Ross1, M. Jain1
records.affiliations_text: 1Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine, Chicago, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: There is significant heterogeneity in outcomes of people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). Understanding when and why clinical trajectories diverge will be critical in identifying at-risk pwCF. Here, we apply unsupervised machine learning to Cystic Fibrosis Foundation Patient Registry (CFFPR) data to identify clusters of clinically-similar encounters, then examine whether transitions between these clusters are associated with changes in outcomes.

Methods: We examined encounter-level data (therapeutics, microbiology, and laboratory data) from 1.9M clinical encounters in the CFFPR from 2011 to 2023, from 41K pwCF without lung transplant. We utilized a mean imputation and forward-fill strategy for missing data, used k-means clustering to identify encounters with similar characteristics, then identified encounters that directly precede cluster transitions (“transition-associated encounters”). Differences in characteristics were examined using t-tests for continuous variables and chi-squared tests for categorical variables.

Results: Optimizing for differences in lung transplant-free survival, we identified 8 distinct clusters of encounters. 505K encounters were transition-associated out of 1.8M non-terminal encounters; 38K of 41K pwCF experienced at least one cluster transition. Transition-associated encounters were associated with a higher rate of 1-year lung transplant-free survival than those that were not (98.5% vs. 97.4%, p<0.001). Transition-associated encounters were associated with lower average age and higher average percent-predicted FEV1.

Conclusions: Unsupervised clustering identifies clinical states associated with lung transplant-free survival. Our findings suggest that transitions between clinical states are common and are associated with improved morbidity and mortality. These transitions are more frequent in younger patients with higher FEV1, suggesting that clinical "flux" may be a hallmark of earlier disease stages.

Methods: We examined encounter-level data (therapeutics, microbiology, and laboratory data) from 1.9M clinical encounters in the CFFPR from 2011 to 2023, from 41K pwCF without lung transplant. We utilized a mean imputation and forward-fill strategy for missing data, used k-means clustering to identify encounters with similar characteristics, then identified encounters that directly precede cluster transitions (“transition-associated encounters”). Differences in characteristics were examined using t-tests for continuous variables and chi-squared tests for categorical variables.
Results: Optimizing for differences in lung transplant-free survival, we identified 8 distinct clusters of encounters. 505K encounters were transition-associated out of 1.8M non-terminal encounters; 38K of 41K pwCF experienced at least one cluster transition. Transition-associated encounters were associated with a higher rate of 1-year lung transplant-free survival than those that were not (98.5% vs. 97.4%, p<0.001). Transition-associated encounters were associated with lower average age and higher average percent-predicted FEV1.
Conclusions: Unsupervised clustering identifies clinical states associated with lung transplant-free survival. Our findings suggest that transitions between clinical states are common and are associated with improved morbidity and mortality. These transitions are more frequent in younger patients with higher FEV1, suggesting that clinical "flux" may be a hallmark of earlier disease stages.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Forskolin-induced swelling (FIS) in patient-derived intestinal organoids (PDIOs) is a promising biomarker to predict individual drug response in pwCF. Previous communication with EMA underlined biomarker validation needs, including evaluation of rare CFTR variants and identification of low or non-responders. We aimed to characterise preclinical FIS responses of rare CFTR variants to a novel triple CFTR modulator, diponecaftor. Based on FIS responses, patients were stratified as presumable responders or non-responders for inclusion in a phase IIb double-blind diponecaftor clinical trial, supporting validation by EMA.

Methods: The predictive value of FIS was evaluated using diponecaftor, across three cohorts. Cohort A (n=26) included randomly selected pwCF with rare variants. Cohort B (n=15) included pwCF with rare variants preselected for high FIS response. Both cohorts participated in an 8-week double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial with outcomes including ppFEV₁ and SCC. FIS assays were done for A and B. Cohort C (n=11) consisted of F508del homozygotes from a 4-week diponecaftor trial and served as reference. FIS was measured in matched CF-PDIOs enabling validation of FIS as biomarker of therapeutic response.

Results: Mean FIS responses were higher in cohort B than in cohort A and comparable to cohort C. Improvements in ppFEV₁ and SCC were greater in cohorts B and C than in cohort A. FIS correlated more strongly with clinical outcomes than clinical outcomes with each other. Placebo responses showed substantial intra-patient variability.

Conclusion: FIS in PDIOs may predict individual clinical responses to CFTR modulators more reliably than clinical outcomes alone. Placebo variability highlights limitations of relying only on clinical measures. Combining FIS with clinical data may facilitate identification of non-responders and enable personalized therapy development for pwCF with rare CFTR variants in future trials. H2020-SC1-2017-755021

session.title: ePoster Session 08 - Life course outcomes in modern cystic fibrosis: transplantation, ageing and pregnancy across registries

person.title: MD
person.department: National Centre for Rare Diseases, Unit for Pulmonology and Cystic Fibrosis

records.authors_text: A.C.S. Wathne1,2, M. Kolsgaard1, C. Sachs-Strømmen1, K. Størdal3,4, K.C.L. Carlsen2, E. Bakkeheim1
records.affiliations_text: 1Oslo University Hospital, National Centre for Rare Diseases, Unit for Pulmonology and Cystic Fibrosis, Oslo, Norway, 2University of Oslo, Institute of Clinical Medicine, Division of Paediatric and Adolescent Medicine, Oslo, Norway, 3University of Oslo, Department of Paediatric Research, Institute of Clinical Medicine, Faculty of Medicine, Oslo, Norway, 4Oslo University Hospital, Division of Paediatric and Adolescent Medicine, Oslo, Norway
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a genetic, multiorgan disorder associated with meconium ileus, reduced birth weight and shorter gestational age. However, evidence on gestational characteristics in pregnancies affected by foetal CF remains limited. We aimed to investigate potential intrauterine effects of foetal CF on pregnancy and at birth outcomes.

Methods: Data from the Medical Birth Registry of Norway (1967–2021) were linked to the Norwegian CF Registry. Foetal CF was defined as offspring with a confirmed diagnosis according to the CF registry criteria. A total of 308 CF births were compared with 3.1 million non-CF births. Data were prospectively recorded during pregnancy and at birth. Multiple pregnancies and cases with combined maternal and foetal CF were excluded. We compared live births with and without foetal CF using independent samples T-test or Mann-Whitney U test for continuous variables, and chi-square test for categorical variables.

Results: CF newborns had mean birth weight 157 g lower than non-CF newborns (95% CI 96–219). The z-score for birth weight specific for sex and gestational length was modestly but significantly reduced (-0.2; 95% CI -0.3– -0.1). The birth weight to placenta weight ratio was significantly lower (median 5.1; IQR 4.5–5.8) in CF than in non-CF newborns (median 5.4; IQR 4.8–6.0; p<0.01), while placenta weight did not differ. CF pregnancies were associated with a significantly increased risk of polyhydramnios, with an odds ratio of 7.1 (95% CI 4.3–11.8) compared to non-CF pregnancies. Pre-eclampsia and gestational hypertension were not associated with CF in the offspring.

Conclusion: Lower birth weight in CF newborns is consistent with previous reports; however, the increased prevalence of polyhydramnios and altered birth weight to placenta weight ratio suggest distinct gestational adaptations associated with foetal CF. These findings may have clinical implications as intrauterine precision therapies for CF evolve.

records.title: Moving and grooving: exercise levels and barriers to exercise within a paediatric cystic fibrosis centre

session.title: ePoster Session 09 - Rethinking airway clearance and physical activity in the CFTR modulator era: adherence, burden and innovation

records.authors_text: O. Mc Ginley1, C. Pao1
records.affiliations_text: 1Barts Health NHS Trust, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: People with cystic fibrosis (CF) are often less active than their healthy peers. Previous research has demonstrated that increased exercise levels correlate with an improvement in FEV1 while aerobic capacity is an important survival predictor within CF. This study aimed to explore current exercise levels within a paediatric CF centre and identify barriers to increasing these levels.

Methods: A 31 question anonymous electronic survey was sent to children with CF aged 5 - 17 years old (n=63) and their parents in December 2025. The survey consisted of a mixture of multiple choice and open ended questions looking at; demographics, current exercise levels, perceptions of the benefits of exercise and barriers to exercise.

Results: A 30% response rate (n=19) was achieved (58% female, n=11; 42% male, n=8) of which 73.6% (n=14) were taking modulators. 100% (n=19) of respondents engaged in moderate-vigorous weekly exercise with 36.8% (n=7) completing over 300mins per week.

Respondents identified the following themes with regards to the benefit of exercise – positive impact on lung health, keeping physically fit and healthy, keeping strong and enjoying it.

Barriers to exercise identified by paediatric respondents included time, weather, cost, motivation and being unwell. Parents were in agreement, citing lack of space as an additional barrier.

Both children and parents highlighted ideas for and access to local gyms/clubs as the most useful strategies to encourage increased exercise levels.

Conclusion: Although all respondents engage in weekly exercise the majority are not meeting the World Health Organisation guidelines. In the era of highly effective modulator therapy, improved treatments and life expectancy for people with CF, focus on preventable secondary diseases is important. It is imperative that we empower this population to build a positive, healthy and consistent relationship with exercise throughout their life.
