records.title: Hybrid closed loop insulin pump therapy improves glycaemic control for adults with Cystic Fibrosis Related Diabetes

session.title: ePoster Session 10 - Precision monitoring and management of cystic fibrosis related diabetes

records.authors_text: F. Lewis1, P. Barry1, S. Punt1, A. Brennan1
records.affiliations_text: 1Manchester NHS Foundation Trust, Manchester Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Manchester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Cystic fibrosis–related diabetes (CFRD) is the most common complication of cystic fibrosis (CF) and is associated with poorer long-term outcomes and reduced quality of life. Its management places a substantial treatment burden on affected individuals. Hybrid closed-loop (HCL) insulin pump therapy is well established in type 1 diabetes, but evidence for its effectiveness in CFRD remains limited.

Methods: We conducted a single-centre retrospective study of adults with CFRD who had transitioned to HCL therapy for more than six months. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) metrics were collected prior to HCL initiation and after six months of therapy. In individuals previously using open-loop insulin pump therapy, additional data on insulin dosing requirements were analysed.

Results: Data were available for 11 individuals (8 previously using open-loop insulin pump therapy and 3 using insulin injections). Significant improvements were observed across multiple glycaemic parameters, including increases in median time in range 4–10 mmol/L from 43% [34-50] to 76% [ 59-79] (p=0.003) and mean time in range 4–8 mmol/L from 24.4%±8.6 to 47.2%±13.2 (p<0.001), alongside significant reductions in mean time above range (p<0.001) and average glucose 11.2 [10.5-12.5] to 8.2 [8-10.4] mmol/L (p=0.003). At baseline, no individual achieved a time in range >70%, compared with 64% at six months. Mean HbA1c decreased significantly (60.1±6.1 vs 50.2±9.4 mmol/mol, p=0.004). There were no significant changes in glycaemic variability or time below range. Among individuals previously using insulin pumps, the proportion of total daily insulin delivered as basal insulin increased from 38% to 51%.

Conclusions: In routine clinical practice, initiation of HCL therapy was associated with significant improvements in glycaemic control in adults with CFRD, without increased hypoglycaemia, and with potential to reduce treatment burden, supporting the emerging role of advanced diabetes technologies in CFRD management.

records.title: Expanding global reach through virtual education: a four-year review of the ECFS Education webinar programme

session.title: ePoster Session 11 - Telehealth and digital tools in care and education

person.title: Dr.
person.department: Leeds Regional Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre

records.authors_text: H.K Chadwick1,2, C. Smith3,4, D.G Peckham1,2, and the European Cystic Fibrosis Society (ECFS) Education Committee
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Leeds, Respiratory Medicine, Leeds Institute of Medical Research at St James's, Leeds, United Kingdom, 2Leeds Teaching Hospital NHS Trust, Leeds Regional Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Leeds, United Kingdom, 3Royal Alexandra Children's Hospital, Brighton, United Kingdom, 4Brighton and Sussex Medical School, Brighton, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: In response to evolving global educational needs and increasing digital access, the ECFS Education Committee launched a structured webinar programme. Building on its earlier success and informed by international feedback from a previously published survey, the committee prioritised this initiative. The aim was to enhance international knowledge exchange, promote inclusivity, and support continuous professional development across diverse healthcare systems.

Methods: Between 2022 and 2025, the committee coordinated, supported and delivered speciality group open access webinars covering core clinical topics, key publications, and interdisciplinary themes. Annual registration, attendance and geographic data were collected and analysed.

Results: Webinar frequency increased from six in 2022 to 20 in 2025 with attendance growing from 565 to 1664. Across the four year period, the programme has supported 48 live webinars attended by 4,412 individuals. These webinars have been viewed in 37 countries across four continents: 26 in Europe, 5 in Asia, 3 in North America, and 3 in South America. Education content was accessed in 10 low- and middle- income countries. Growing engagement from ECFS Special Interest and Working Groups has been pivotal in broadening the diversity of topics and strengthening overall interest.

Table 1. Number of webinars held, registrations, attendance, and Special Interest/ Working Groups contributing, between 2022 and 2025

2022202320242025Webinars held681420Registrations972154226443395Attendance56585213311664Special Interest / Working Groups contributing2358

Conclusion: The expansion of the Society’s online webinar programme has significantly improved global engagement, educational reach, and diversity of topics. Continued investment in digital learning supports equitable access to international medical education and fosters cross-border collaboration. Future directions include the potential for real-time translation and further development of novel webinar packages.

session.title: ePoster Session 07 - Old and new – exploring the portfolio for cystic fibrosis treatment

records.authors_text: E. Pesce1,2, V. Capurro1, V. Tomati1, A. Quarato1, C. Pastorino1, A. Dighero1, R. Pisani1, A. Mantero1, F. Cresta3, C. Castellani3, N. Pedemonte1

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The most effective treatment for people with CF (pwCF) carrying F508del mutation has been, until now, the triple combination of Elexacaftor-Tezacaftor-Ivacaftor (ETI). Although initially developed for F508del, CFTR modulators can correct the underlying defect(s) in other CFTR mutants, such as missense variants located in the ICL4 domain. However, several CFTR variants showed minimal or no functional improvement following ETI exposure. We evaluated the responsiveness of selected CFTR variants unresponsive to ETI to the novel combination of CFTR modulators Vanzacaftor-Tezacaftor-Deutivacaftor (VTD).

Methods: CFTR variants previously classified as non-responsive to ETI were analyzed using functional assays in Ussing chambers on primary nasal epithelia cells collected from pwCF. CFTR activity was assessed after treatment with ETI and VTD, and results were compared to untreated controls to determine changes in channel function.

Results: For this analysis, we recruited patients carrying ETI non-responsive variants, particularly missense variants not reported to belong to class I. As an example, we analyzed two patients heterozygous for the rare missense variant H147P and a minimal function, non-rescuable class I variant. Short-circuit current analysis of CFTR-mediated chloride transport in DMSO-treated epithelia showed severely reduced CFTR activity (2.7 ± 0.44 µA). Total CFTR current increased to 4.4 ± 0.36 µA after ETI treatment and reached 9.4 ± 0.91 µA following VTD treatment. These findings indicate a differential response of certain CFTR variants to VTD compared with ETI.

Conclusion: VTD demonstrates potential efficacy in some CFTR variants unresponsive to ETI, supporting its role as a promising therapeutic option for expanding personalized treatment strategies in Cystic Fibrosis. Further studies are warranted to confirm these findings and assess their clinical relevance.

records.title: Pregnancy-related outcome reporting across countries contributing to the European Cystic Fibrosis Society Patient Registry

session.title: ePoster Session 08 - Life course outcomes in modern cystic fibrosis: transplantation, ageing and pregnancy across registries

records.authors_text: G. Hennessy1,2, A. Downes3,4, I. Bokobza5,6, J.C Davies5,6, I. Felton3,6
records.affiliations_text: 1Imperial College London, Faculty of Medicine, London, United Kingdom, 2Imperial College London, School of Public Health, London, United Kingdom, 3Royal Brompton Hospital, Part of Guys and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust, Department of Adult Cystic Fibrosis, London, United Kingdom, 4Imperial College London, Department of Metabolism, Digestion and Reproduction, London, United Kingdom, 5Royal Brompton Hospital, Part of Guys and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust, Department of Paediatrics, London, United Kingdom, 6National Heart & Lung Institute, Imperial College London; NIHR Biomedical Research Centre, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Pregnant females with cystic fibrosis (FwCF) are at increased risk of obstetric and perinatal complications. As pregnancy among FwCF becomes increasingly common, robust surveillance of pregnancy-related outcomes is essential to inform safe clinical practice and promote maternal health equity. While selected pregnancy outcomes are included in the 2023 European Cystic Fibrosis Society Patient Registry (ECFSPR) report, country-level and demographic data are unavailable. We aimed to assess the availability, scope and harmonisation of pregnancy-related data reporting in national CF registry reports from countries contributing to the ECFSPR.

Methods: Publicly available national CF registry reports from ECFSPR-contributing countries were reviewed to assess inclusion of pregnancy data. Pregnancy-related outcomes and maternal characteristics were extracted to permit cross-country comparison and appraisal of data harmonisation.

Results: National CF registry reports were available for 14 of the 43 ECFSPR-contributing countries, of which 8 included pregnancy data. Marked variation was observed in the scope of reported outcomes, ranging from basic documentation of births to detailed pregnancy outcomes, maternal characteristics and antenatal CFTR modulator (CFTRm) exposure. Heterogeneous terminology was used to define common outcomes, and the inclusion criteria for minimum age and lung transplant status of pregnant FwCF differed between countries.

Conclusion: The reporting of pregnancy-related outcomes in national registry data is limited across ECFSPR-contributing countries, and substantial variation in scope, terminology and population characteristics hinders cross-country comparison. In the CFTRm era, efforts are needed to standardise national reporting of salient pregnancy outcomes to support effective surveillance, particularly for offspring exposed to CFTRms in utero, and to promote equity in CF maternal health. Granular, country-level data analysis is ongoing.

records.title: Impact of cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator modulator therapy on symptom and treatment burden, physical activity and participation: A South African mixed-methods study

session.title: ePoster Session 09 - Rethinking airway clearance and physical activity in the CFTR modulator era: adherence, burden and innovation

records.authors_text: B. Morrow1, J. Verstraete1, S. Thistlewhite2, C. Abrahams2, N. Nkosi2, T. Donnelly2, D. Kennedy2, M. Zampoli1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Cape Town, Paediatrics & Child Health, Cape Town, South Africa, 2University of Cape Town, Health & Rehabilitation Sciences, Cape Town, South Africa
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Patient-reported outcomes regarding daily functioning and participation are under-explored relative to clinical outcomes of Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator modulator (CFTRm) therapy, particularly in resource-limited settings. This study describes the lived experiences of people living with CF (PLwCF) following CFTRm initiation in South Africa.

Methods: Convergent mixed-methods study incorporating an online survey (n=37, 48% response rate) and semi-structured interviews (n=6) with South African PLwCF aged 6-60 years receiving CFTRm. Survey data compared pre- and post-CFTRm experiences using chi-square tests. Qualitative data from interviews and open-ended survey responses reached data saturation and underwent inductive thematic analysis.

Results: Participants reported dramatic improvements in the frequency, nature and severity of distressing respiratory symptoms (p<0.0001) after implementing CFTRm. Duration of airway clearance and inhalation treatment duration reduced from majority 1-3+ hours to <1 hour (p<0.0001); regular exercise and social/recreational participation increased from 62% to 92% (p=0.04); and 21.6% to 48.6% (p = 0.006) respectively, with reduced school/work absenteeism (p<0.0001). The proportion with perceived 'excellent health' increased from 5% to 64% (p<0.0001) after CFTRm. Thematic analysis revealed ten major themes including respiratory health transformation, dramatic treatment burden reduction, liberation and normalization of daily life, enhanced physical capacity, profound psychosocial impact, improved growth, reduced hospitalizations, positive family impact, increased energy, and altruistic hope for universal CFTRm access.

Conclusions: CFTRm profoundly transforms the lived experiences of South African PLwCF, with meaningful improvements in daily functioning, participation, and wellbeing. Findings provide compelling evidence supporting advocacy for equitable CFTRm access in resource-limited settings.

Prof. Brenda Morrow
PhD 2005; PG Diploma (Paediatric Palliative Medicine) 2019; Postgraduate Diploma (Health Research Ethics) 2014; BSc Physiotherapy 1995
Brenda Morrow is a Physiotherapist and Full Professor in the Department of Paediatrics, University of Cape Town (UCT), South Africa. Brenda is an active clinician-scientist with a special interests in interdisciplinary paediatric cystic fibrosis and critical care practice and research; acute and chronic cardiopulmonary rehabilitation; palliative care; and medical ethics. Brenda has over 160 peer reviewed publications; 13 book chapters; numerous national and international congress presentations and holds a National Research Foundation (NRF) B rating. She is immediate past- President of the World Federation of Pediatric Intensive and Critical Care Societies (WFPICCS); current President of the Critical Care Society of Southern Africa (CCSSA);  past-Chair of the Cardiopulmonary Rehabilitation Special Interest Group of the South African Society of Physiotherapy and current secretary of the South African Medical and Scientific Advisory Council for Cystic Fibrosis. Within the University of Cape Town, she chairs the Faculty of Health Sciences Doctoral and research Masters Committee; is a scientific member of the Health Research Ethics Committee, a member of the Doctoral Degrees Board and serves on the Department of Paediatrics’ Research and Postgraduate Education committees. Brenda is also Editor-in-Chief of the Southern African Journal of Critical Care; Senior Associate Editor of Pediatric Critical Care Medicine and Associate Academic Editor of PlosOne and Frontiers in Pediatrics (Critical Care). She is a regular reviewer for over 40 international journals and grant funding agencies.

records.affiliations_text: 1Fondazione IRCCS Ca' Granda Ospedale Maggiore Policlinico, Mother and Child Department, Cystic Fibrosis Regional Center, Milan, Italy, 2University of Milan, Department of Pathophysiology and Transplantation, Milan, Italy, 3Fondazione IRCCS Ca' Granda Ospedale Maggiore Policlinico, Endocrinology Unit, Milan, Italy, 4Fondazione IRCCS Ca' Granda Ospedale Maggiore Policlinico, Mother and Child Department, Cystic Fibrosis regional center, Milan, Italy, 5Fondazione IRCCS Ca' Granda Ospedale Maggiore Policlinico, Respiratory Unit and Cystic Fibrosis Adult Center, Milan, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Background: Abnormal glucose tolerance (AGT) can develop early in children with cystic fibrosis (CF). The Insulinogenic Index (IGI), derived from the Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT), is a surrogate marker of pancreatic β-cell function and has been proposed as a risk stratification tool for CF-Related Diabetes (CFRD) in adults. However, its utility has not yet been evaluated in children.

Objectives: To investigate the association between AGT and IGT over the course of Elexacaftor/Tezacaftor/Ivacaftor (ETI) therapy in children with CF aged 6-11 years.

Methods: Twenty-two children (median age 7 years, range 6–11) underwent OGTT before starting ETI and after 12 months. AGT was defined as Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG), Indeterminate Glycemia (INDET), Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT), or CFRD. IGI was calculated as Δinsulin (µUI/mL) over Δglucose (mmol/L) during the first 30 minutes of the OGTT. Mixed models were used to estimate marginal means for IGI by AGT status and ETI therapy, adjusting for age.

Results: Before ETI, seven children had AGT (4 INDET, 2 INDET+IGT, 1 IGT), increasing to 10 after 12 months of ETI (4 INDET, 1 CFRD, 1 INDET+IFG, 1 INDET+IFG+IGT, 1 INDET+IGT, 1 IFG+IGT, 1 IGT). AGT was associated with lower IGI (p=0.04), while IGI did not change significantly over the course of ETI therapy (p=0.60).

Conclusion: AGT is common in children with CF before routine CFRD screening age. ETI therapy does not appear to modify this condition. Larger studies are needed to determine whether IGI can be a useful early risk stratification tool.

records.title: Optimising health: digital programmes driving health and connection in cystic fibrosis

session.title: ePoster Session 11 - Telehealth and digital tools in care and education

records.authors_text: J. Stoker1, C. McDonald1, A. Usher1, K. Burbidge1, M. McRoberts1, N. De Leon1, J. Hepworth1, N. Hincks1
records.affiliations_text: 1Intermountain Health Primary Children's Hospital, Salt Lake City, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Optimising Health (OH) is a quality improvement, multidisciplinary team comprising social workers, dietitians, a physiotherapist, and parent partners at a paediatric CF centre (n=325) serving a multistate area in the western USA. OH aims to identify perceived barriers to CF care, resource gaps, and underserved age groups. Four digital health programmes were developed by the OH team to foster community, improve health literacy, and promote the well-being of children with cystic fibrosis (CwCF) and their families.

Methods: Surveys of CwCF (ages 8–15) and parents identified priority topics for virtual education. The pilot programme, Great Outcomes Achieved Together (GOAT), enrolled 30 CwCF (ages 8–12) in two online cohorts, focusing on healthy lifestyles, health literacy, and peer connection. Youth Engaged in Treatment Independently (YETI) targeted 13 teens (ages 13–15) with independence, self-care, and connection topics. Two additional programmes—Salty Seminars (webinars for parents of CwCF) and CF Strong Challenges (family-based health activities)—aimed to engage families across all age groups. Pre- and post-programme digital surveys assessed impact.

Results: Mean improvements in healthy behaviours were 11.8% (GOAT Cohort 1), 15.5% (GOAT Cohort 2), and 12.2% (YETI). Confidence in managing CF care rose 28% among YETI participants. Feedback emphasised empowerment and peer support: “I liked knowing I’m not the only CF kid in the world.” Parents reported improved confidence and adherence to CF care. Since 2024, 88 participants have joined OH programmes; 100% of survey respondents supported continuation.

Conclusion: These innovative, multidisciplinary digital programmes demonstrated measurable gains in health behaviours, confidence, and engagement among CwCF and families. Future priorities include scaling to broader age ranges, enhancing carer involvement, integrating gamified learning, and developing longitudinal tracking to assess sustained impact.

records.title: Additive effect of combinational treatment with Splisense ASO SPL84 and elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor

session.title: ePoster Session 07 - Old and new – exploring the portfolio for cystic fibrosis treatment

records.authors_text: E. Ozeri-Galai1, Y. Cheng2, Y.S Oren1, J. Harrington2, A. Hatton3, G. Hart1, K. Coote2, H. Bihler2, I. Sermet-Gaudelus3, M. Mense2, B. Kerem1,4
records.affiliations_text: 1Splisense, Haddasah Ein Kerem, Jerusalem, Israel, 2CFFT Lab, Cystic Fibrosis Foundation, Lexington, United States, 3Institut Necker Enfants Malades, INSERM U1151 Université de Paris, Paris, France, 4Hebrew University, Genetics, Jerusalem, Israel
records.abstract_text:
Background: SPL84 is an inhaled antisense oligonucleotide (ASO), currently being evaluated in an ongoing global Phase 2 study in pwCF with the 3849+10kb C->T (3849) mutation. Interim results indicate that SPL84 is safe, well tolerated, and shows positive preliminary efficacy. SPL84 directly and specifically corrects the underlying splicing defect, restoring wild-type CFTR mRNA and translation of a fully functional CFTR channel. In studies with 3849 patient-derived

HBE and HNE cells, SPL84 treatment restored CFTR function to normal levels. In 3849/modulator-responsive mutation heterozygous patients, combined treatment with SPL84 and CFTR modulators may provide an additional benefit beyond either therapy alone.

Methods: The effect of SPL84, ETI (VX-661, VX-445, VX-770) and the combinational treatment of SPL84+ETI were assessed in HBE cells derived from heterozygous patients carrying the 3849 and F508del mutations. The effect was determined by analysis of CFTR-mediated Cl- current measured in Ussing chamber or TECC Ieq assays.

Results: SPL84 treatment from the basal or apical side of fully differentiated 3849/F508del HBE cells leads to substantial restoration of functional CFTR expression from the 3849 allele. Combinational treatment with SPL84+ETI led to significantly higher levels of CFTR function compared to each drug alone, indicating the potential for additive benefit of both drugs in heterozygote patients.

Conclusions: Studies in HBE cells support the potential benefit of combinational treatment with SPL84 and modulator drugs over each drug alone in heterozygote people with CF carrying the 3849 mutation and a modulator responsive mutation. The combinational additive benefit will be evaluated in the 2nd part of the phase 2 study.

records.title: Description of pregnancies to women with cystic fibrosis before and after elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor therapy at the Stockholm CF centre

session.title: ePoster Session 08 - Life course outcomes in modern cystic fibrosis: transplantation, ageing and pregnancy across registries

records.authors_text: E. Roberts1, J. Jägerstedt1, S. Salomonsson1, C. Rodriguez Hortal1, A. Hedborg Harris1
records.affiliations_text: 1Karolinska University Hospital, Stockholm CF Centre, Huddinge, Sweden
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The prevalence of pregnancies in women with cystic fibrosis (CF) has increased since introduction to elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) but there is still a lack of knowledge about the impact of pregnancy. The aim was to describe the pregnancies to women with CF at the Stockholm CF centre.

Methods: Data from all female patients at the Stockholm CF centre was collected from the Swedish CF Registry during the period 2010 to 2025. Outcome variables included: pregnancy, lung function as forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) and ETI therapy.

Results: Of a total of 104 women with CF, 37 (36%) have had at least one live birth with a total of 63 live births (range 1-4 births). Of the 37 women, 17 were homozygous for F508del and 32 were pancreas insufficient. Baseline data prior to first pregnancy: age 31 (±4.7) years, body mass index 22.5 (±3), FEV1 2.4 L (±0.68). Prior to ETI, 49 births were reported (1.2 births/year) and 14 births were reported since ETI (3.5 births/year). Eight continued ETI therapy throughout pregnancy and the remaining six paused during the first trimester but then resumed. The number of births resulting from in vitro fertilization (IVF) decreased from 51% before ETI to 7% after ETI.

Lung function data was analysed for 23 women, as women with a CF diagnosis after pregnancy and shared care patients were excluded due to no data. From a baseline FEV1 of 2.27 L (range 1.05-3.72), there was a decrease of 3% during pregnancy but no clear difference related to ETI. There was an overall decrease in FEV1 of 5% one year postpartum. Despite a small sample, it was interesting that those on ETI improved 2% whilst those without decreased 8%.

Conclusion: The data showed a marked increase in the number of spontaneous conceptions since introduction to ETI. No data is available about unsuccessful pregnancies. ETI may have a positive impact on postpartum lung function. We will continue careful follow up and support of peri- and postpartum women.

records.title: Physical activity, adherence to physiotherapy, exercise capacity, and quality of life among patients with cystic fibrosis in the era of CFTR modulators

session.title: ePoster Session 09 - Rethinking airway clearance and physical activity in the CFTR modulator era: adherence, burden and innovation

person.title: Prof. Dr.
person.department: CF Unit, 3rd Paediatric Dept, Hippokration Hospital

records.authors_text: P. Peftoulidou1, E. Kirvasili1, E.-A. Chrysochoou1, M. Galogavrou1, A. Sopiadou1, A. Chalkia2, E. Hatziagorou1
records.affiliations_text: 1Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, CF Unit, 3rd Paediatric Dept, Hippokration Hospital, Thessaloniki, Greece, 2International University of Thessaloniki, Dept of Physiotherapy, Thessaloniki, Greece
records.abstract_text:
Background: CFTR modulators have improved QOL and lung function among pwCF and seem to affect the face of CF.

Objectives: The study aimed to evaluate physical activity, exercise capacity, adherence to physiotherapy, and QoL among children with CF 2 years after initiation of CFTR modulators.

Methods: Forty-five children and adolescents with CF were evaluated before and 2 years after the initiation of CFTR modulators. They completed three self-administered, validated questionnaires: the Godin Leisure-Time Exercise Questionnaire, the Manchester Q, and the DISABKIDS for QoL. The Godin Leisure-Time Exercise Questionnaire was used to evaluate physical activity; QOL was assessed using the DISABKIDS Questionnaire; the Manchester Questionnaire was used to assess adherence to CF treatment. Moreover, pwCF performed spirometry and the six-minute walking test (6MWT).

Results: Mean age of the CF population was 14.5 (±7.6) years, mean BMI 19.58 (±4.1) kg/m2, and mean FEV1% 91.15 ± 20.46%. Before the initiation of ETI, the majority of children (48%) reported performing physiotherapy once or twice a day, 36% reported performing it daily, and 16% reported performing it occasionally. According to the GODIN Questionnaire, 68% of the CF group were active, 27% were moderately active, and 5% were sedentary before initiation of CFTR modulators. Two years later, adherence to physiotherapy and inhaled medication decreased significantly (p<0.05), while QOL, physical activity, FEV1pp, and exercise capacity assessed with the 6MWT improved significantly (p<0.05).

Conclusions: CFTR modulators showed significant benefits among pwCF in lung function, physical activity levels, exercise capacity, and QOL, despite decreased adherence to physiotherapy and inhaled medication. More research is needed on changes in the everyday lives of pwCF.

person.biography:
Elpis Hatziagorou is a Professor in Respiratory Pediatrics of the Paediatric Pulmonology and CF Unit at Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, Greece. Dr. Hatziagorou received her degree in Medicine from the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki and earned her Ph.D. in studies of exhaled NO in patients with chronic lung disease. She worked as a Clinical Fellow in Respiratory Pediatrics at Sheffield Children’s Hospital, University of Sheffield, UK (2010), and got the European Diploma in Paediatric Respiratory Medicine (2012).
She is a clinical researcher; her main interests are Cystic Fibrosis, non-CF bronchiectasis, Multiple Breath Washout, and Exercise testing. She has been a Steering Group Member of the European Cystic Fibrosis Registry (since 2007) and a Member of the Scientific Committee of the European Cystic Fibrosis Registry since 2018. records.authors_text: S. Diemer1,2,3, K. Kozjek4, L. Påhlman2,3,5

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a genetic disorder characterised by progressive lung function decline and chronic airway inflammation. Cystic fibrosis-related diabetes (CFRD) is the most common extrapulmonary complication of CF and is associated with increased morbidity and mortality. Although a strong association between CFRD and impaired lung function has been established, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study aimed to compare airway microbiome composition between individuals with CF with and without CFRD.

Methods: Sputum samples from pwCF with and without CFRD were analysed for inflammatory cytokines using MesoScale assays and total bacterial load via quantitative PCR targeting the 16S rRNA gene. Microbiome profiling was performed using high-resolution 16S rRNA sequencing, with diversity assessed through richness and evenness metrics. Bray–Curtis dissimilarity was applied to evaluate differences in microbial community composition between groups.

Results: Forty-four pwCF were included, of whom 59% had CFRD. The CFRD group exhibited significantly lower lung function and elevated sputum IL-1β levels compared to pwCF without CFRD. Microbiome analysis revealed reduced bacterial diversity in the CFRD group, although overall community composition did not differ significantly between groups. Genera such as Abiotrophia, Anaeroglobus, and Escherichia-Shigella were enriched in CFRD, whereas Neisseria, Prevotella, and Streptococcus were more abundant in pwCF without CFRD.

Conclusion: CFRD is associated with impaired lung function and increased airway inflammation. This study provides the first evidence of reduced bacterial diversity in the sputum microbiome of individuals with CFRD. While CFRD status alone did not markedly alter overall microbial composition, findings indicate a trend towards a more dysbiotic microbial profile in pwCF with CFRD.

records.title: Real-world perspectives on home spirometry in the telehealth era: insights from people with cystic fibrosis and clinicians

session.title: ePoster Session 11 - Telehealth and digital tools in care and education

records.authors_text: A. Azam1,2, R.J. Bright-Thomas1,2, A. Horsley1,2, P.J. Barry1,2, A.M. Jones1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Manchester Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Manchester, United Kingdom, 2The University of Manchester, Manchester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: Home spirometry has become an integral component of CF care following the widespread adoption of telehealth and hybrid care models. While its feasibility and clinical utility have been well described, less is known about longer-term real-world perceptions among pwCF and CF healthcare professionals (HCPs).

Methods: A cross-sectional, paper-based survey was conducted at an adult CF centre using the NuvoAir home spirometry system. Eligible participants included pwCF with ≥1 year of home spirometry experience and HCPs actively involved in CF care. Surveys comprised Likert-scale and open-ended questions exploring engagement with spirometry around clinic visits, knowledge and understanding of spirometry, perceived clinical value, and psychological impact. Open-ended responses were analysed using inductive thematic analysis (Table 1).

Results: Surveys were completed by 101 pwCF and 30 HCPs. Most pwCF reported frequent completion of spirometry before and after both face-to-face (F2F) and virtual clinics. In contrast, HCPs generally perceived lower levels of engagement. There were no difference in reported spirometry engagement between F2F and virtual clinics, suggesting similar attitudes to home spirometry between the two clinics. Over half of pwCF reported high confidence in interpreting their spirometry results. Both pwCF and HCPs viewed home spirometry as clinically valuable for routine monitoring and during exacerbations. 30% of pwCF reported to be “never anxious” when completing spirometry. 74% pwCF were “very comfortable” completing spirometry in front of HCPs, 10.1% were "uncomfortable". HCPs, especially physiotherapists, expressed that there is an existing role for in-clinic supervised spirometry for selected patients.

Conclusion: Home spirometry is well accepted by both pwCF and HCPs. Flexible, individualised implementation is required to maximise clinical benefit while minimising psychological burden.

Main themes from open-ended responses:Example quotesPositive attitudes towards home spirometry among HCPs

“Remote appointments would not be possible without it.”

“Extremely valuable resource for some patients.”

“Overall, I think it is a positive addition… can be helpful when unwell and patients perform at home.”

Positive attitudes towards home spirometry among pwCF

“Happy and content. Allows me to check my lungs’ condition.”

“Very positive. I wouldn’t want to not have it now.”

“I prefer it at home for easy access when needed.”

“It’s good to be able to keep track of your blows, rather than every few months during visits.”

“Very useful in situations such as prolonged bouts of illness.”

Clinical utility of supervised in-clinic spirometry compared with unsupervised home spirometry (responses from HCPs)

“Still important to complete supervised spirometry from time to time, as you can assess more about technique than can be shown by the flow volume loop.”

“Useful to observe the patient doing their blow during clinic as part of assessment.”

“Whilst it is useful to have some spirometry results before a clinic visit, it is often useful to observe the patient doing their blow during clinic as part of the assessment.”

“As a physio, I like doing spirometry with patients as it is a way of assessing their chest. Can often hear sputum – and can open up conversations – even if they say they are non-productive.”

Anxiety related to home spirometry (responses from pwCF)

“Don’t mind, just anxiety around results.”

“Have anxiety regarding results, so avoid”

“Sometimes does not connect, stressful, sometimes does not work”

Home spirometry monitoring frequency and patient anxiety (responses from HCPs)

“[Should do spirometry] before routine appointments and when unwell, [although] too frequent spirometry can lead them to become fixated on numbers alone”

“Ideally 3 to 4 [spirometry sessions] a year minimum. Sometimes doing it more frequently increases anxiety, and there is no opportunity to discuss or alleviate this unless at clinic.”

Table 1: Sample quotes from respondents

records.title: Electrophysiological and morphological comparison of modulator and mRNA-based therapies on the function of CFTR

session.title: ePoster Session 07 - Old and new – exploring the portfolio for cystic fibrosis treatment

records.authors_text: R.N. Singh1, M. Juko1, A. Kampshoff1, W.-M. Weber1, H. Omran1, J. Grosse-Onnebrink1
records.affiliations_text: 1University Hospital Muenster, Department of General Paediatrics, Münster, Germany
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is caused by pathogenic CFTR variants, leading to defective epithelial chloride transport, increased mucus viscosity, and impaired airway function. Although CFTR modulators including Trikafta® have improved outcomes for many people with CF (pwCF), those carrying rare or class I CFTR variants still lack effective therapy.

Methods: We evaluated CFTR modulators and chitosan-mediated wild-type CFTR (wtCFTR) mRNA therapies in patient-derived nasal air–liquid interface (ALI) cultures using integrated functional and morphological approaches. Primary ALI cultures from pwCF (N = 21) and healthy controls (N = 20) were assessed using electrophysiology with a modified Multi Transepithelial Current Clamp (MTECC) Ussing chamber, immunofluorescence imaging, and analyses of mucus viscosity and epithelial barrier integrity.

Results: CFTR modulators restored chloride channel function in 10 of 13 pwCF cultures, as measured using the MTECC Ussing chamber and validated by apical CFTR localization via immunofluorescence. However, cultures from pwCF with rare or class I CFTR variants showed no functional improvement. These non-responsive cultures were treated with wtCFTR-mRNA delivered via chitosan-based nanoparticles, resulting in restoration of CFTR function across the treated cohort, with transepithelial conductance ΔGt increasing from -0.01135 ± 0.04027 mS/cm2 before treatment to 0.2566 ± 0.04621 mS/cm2 (N = 11, n = 34) after treatment. CF cultures exhibited elevated MUC5AC and claudin-1 expression, increased mucus viscosity, and compromised epithelial barrier integrity, all markedly improved following successful CFTR rescue by both modulators and mRNA therapy.

Conclusion: This study highlights the therapeutic potential of chitosan-mediated CFTR mRNA delivery as a personalised therapeutic strategy for CF patients, particularly those with rare CFTR variants that are non-responsive to current modulator therapies.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is characterized by marked heterogeneity in disease severity and progression. While genetic determinants play a central role, growing evidence suggests that environmental exposures may significantly modulate clinical outcomes. The objective of this study was to identify distinct clinical trajectories of CF in children and to assess the contribution of environmental factors—particularly air pollution and passive exposure to tobacco smoke—to disease severity and progression using data from the French Cystic Fibrosis Registry.

Methods: We analyzed data from the French CF Registry, which covers ~90% of CF patients in France. For this study, we selected children aged 6–12 years (n=909). Unsupervised clustering, including latent class analysis of longitudinal lung function, identified patient subgroups. Clinical, environmental, and sociodemographic data—including passive smoke exposure and air pollution (NO2, PM2.5, PM10), were integrated to characterize subgroup profiles.

Results: Four distinct CF subgroups emerged. Patients with accelerated lung function decline and lower baseline lung function were disproportionately exposed to air pollution (p<0.001 worse lung function group vs others) and second-hand smoke (p<0.001). These exposures were associated with increased rates of infections, bacterial colonization, digestive comorbidities, and hospitalizations.

Conclusion: Environmental exposures, particularly air pollution and second-hand smoke, are linked to more severe CF trajectories. Integrating exposome data into clinical phenotyping can improve risk stratification and inform targeted interventions to optimize patient outcomes.

Acknowledgements: We thank Vaincre la Mucoviscidose and the CF centres of the French CF Registry for data access, as well as all participating patients. This work is part of the REMEDIA project, funded by the EU Horizon 2020 Program (Grant No. 874753).

records.title: ImpACT4CF: real-time breath sensing and visual feedback to improve quality of airway clearance treatments

session.title: ePoster Session 09 - Rethinking airway clearance and physical activity in the CFTR modulator era: adherence, burden and innovation

person.title: Professor
person.department: Great Ormond Street Institute of Child Health

records.authors_text: P. Chawan1, H. Douglas2,1, G. Saul1, S. Stanojevic3, E. Main1
records.affiliations_text: 1University College London, Great Ormond Street Institute of Child Health, London, United Kingdom, 2Brunel University of London, Health Sciences, London, United Kingdom, 3Dalhousie University, Community Health and Epidemiology, Halifax, Canada
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Airway clearance treatments (ACT) are essential for maintaining lung health in many people with cystic fibrosis. Project Fizzyo suggested that correctly performed ACTs are associated with improved lung function, but many children and young people (CYP) with CF often use ineffective techniques (Filipow, 2023). ImpACT4CF integrates a real-time breath sensor with visual feedback to optimise ACT technique, guiding breath quality, monitoring adherence, and logging treatment data. This preliminary study evaluates the effect of real-time feedback on ACT quality in healthy adults.

Methods: Adults (>18 years) without respiratory disease and naïve to ACT, were recruited. In a randomised crossover design, each participant acted as their own control across two devices (Acapella, PEP mask), two sessions (7-14 days apart) and three feedback modes Record: no feedback, Graph: breath waveforms, and Coach: real-time coaching with target cues. Breath pressure and length were recorded using the sensor. Breaths were classified as conformant if mean expiratory pressure was between 5-25cmH₂O and length 2.3-4.5s.

Results: 16 healthy adults completed 2,844 breaths. Conformity increased stepwise with feedback intensity. Record: 66% (Acapella) vs 62% (PEP); Graph: 83% vs 73%; Coach: 96.5% vs 100%. This within-device increase was statistically significant (p<0.001) with a large effect size. ACT technique errors related to breath length being too short (51%) or long (28%) were almost entirely eliminated in Coach mode. Breath‑to‑breath variability was greatest in Record, reduced in Graph, and lowest in Coach, for both devices. There was a learning effect with higher conformity in Record mode on second visit (p<0.004), but no device-specific order effect.

Conclusion: Real-time visual feedback produced much improved breath conformity, and may support more effective ACTs. The ImpACT4CF pilot trial is now evaluating the impact of real‑time feedback on ACT quality in CYP with CF.

session.title: ePoster Session 11 - Telehealth and digital tools in care and education

records.authors_text: L. Botermann1, A. Wagner1, C. Fuchs2, L. Schlick1, S. Thee3,4,5, M. Stahl3,4,5, S. Sutharsan6, R. Fischer7, M. Ballmann8, M.A. Mall3,4,5
records.affiliations_text: 1PARI GmbH, Starnberg, Germany, 2PARI Medical Holding GmbH, Starnberg, Germany, 3Department of Pediatric Respiratory Medicine, Immunology and Critical Care Medicine, Division of Cystic Fibrosis, Charité - Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Berlin, Germany, 4Berlin Institute of Health (BIH), Berlin, Germany, 5German Center for Child and Adolescent Health (DZKJ), Partner Site Berlin, Berlin, Germany, 6Department of Pulmonary Medicine, Division of Cystic Fibrosis, University Medicine Essen - Ruhrlandklinik, University of Duisburg-Essen, Essen, Germany, 7Cystic Fibrosis Centre Munich-West, Munich, Germany, 8Department of Pediatrics, University Medicine Rostock, Rostock, Germany
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Digital interventions are often postulated to be most relevant for adolescents, but little is known on differential effects across life stages in cystic fibrosis (CF). This analysis investigated age-specific effects of a telemonitoring-supported intervention on inhalation adherence in people with CF (pwCF).

Methods: We conducted a post-hoc subgroup analysis of the conneCT CF study, a randomized controlled trial comparing standard of care (control group, CG) with a digital intervention (intervention group, IG) (Thee S. BMC Pulm Med. 2021). The intervention combined among others objective adherence monitoring via the eFlow® rapid Nebuliser System, a self-management app (PARI Connect App), and coaching. In this post-hoc analysis, median adherence was compared between CG (n=109) and IG (n=95) across 5 age groups (12–16, 17–21, 22–30, 31–40, >40 years).

Results: In the overall cohort, previously published analysis showed no difference between IG and CG for the primary endpoint time to first pulmonary exacerbation (PEx). However, higher adherence was significantly associated with lower risk of PEx. Also, adherence was significantly higher in the IG compared to the CG (52% vs. 38%) (Thee S. ECFS 2025). Age-stratified analysis showed nearly the same high adherence in the IG and CG in pwCF aged 12–16 and >40 years (53-60%). In the 17–21 and 22–30 year age groups, median adherence dropped overall but the IG demonstrated 20% higher adherence compared to the CG (IG 30%, 29%; CG 10%, 12%, respectively). The main effect was observed in pwCF 31–40 years, with a median adherence of 75% (IG) compared to 39% (CG).

Conclusion: This post-hoc analysis indicates the impact of digital-supported self-management on inhalation adherence in CF may be age-dependent. While parental supervision in adolescents and established routines in older adults seem to result in high adherence levels, pwCF aged 17–40 years appear to derive the greatest benefit of using digital support tools.

records.title: From therapeutic breakthrough to professional reconfigurations: The impact of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor on CF care teams in France

session.title: ePoster Session 07 - Old and new – exploring the portfolio for cystic fibrosis treatment

records.authors_text: C. Boubal1, C. Fevres1, S. Saetta1, Q. Raynaud2, I. Durieu2, T. Nouvel3, F. Giraud3, S. Poupon-Bourdy2, J. Haesbaert2, P. Reix2
records.affiliations_text: 1Enseis, Villeurbanne, France, 2Hospices Civils de Lyon, Lyon, France, 3Vaincre la Mucoviscidose, Paris, France
records.abstract_text:
Since the introduction of Kaftrio® in France in 2020, the clinical condition of the majority of patients with cystic fibrosis who are eligible for this treatment has improved substantially. This improvement has led to a drastic reduction, or even the discontinuation, of certain forms of care, such as respiratory physiotherapy and courses of antibiotics. How has hospital-based care evolved following the arrival of this new therapy? To address this question, we conducted a sociological study involving healthcare professionals and patients. Using a qualitative methodology, we carried out 80 semi-structured interviews and conducted observations within care centers. This research is part of the Horizon CRCM project, whose objective is to define a new model for the organization of care in France.

First, we demonstrate how this therapeutic promise has generated a loss of meaning for some healthcare professionals and, in some cases, a redefinition of their professional roles. Physiotherapists, in particular, may withdraw from the care of certain patients, while others engage in collaboration with adapted physical activity instructors. We then examine how care centers have implemented organizational changes in response to patients’ requests for reduced follow-up, while also anticipating a potential loss of institutional resources. Physicians, in particular, advocate for extending care provision to other rare diseases. However, the delegation of care to community-based providers remains a largely unmet objective. Finally, we show that other professional groups have been more adversely affected by these developments. This is notably the case for nurse coordinators, who perform largely invisible work to facilitate access to treatment and to organize patient monitoring. Contrary to expectations, their workload has increased.

These findings should enable us to propose a new model of care that meets the needs of both healthcare professionals and patients.

records.title: Target trial emulation to evaluate the long-term effect of insulin in people with Cystic Fibrosis-Related Diabetes using European Cystic Fibrosis Society Patient Registry

session.title: ePoster Session 08 - Life course outcomes in modern cystic fibrosis: transplantation, ageing and pregnancy across registries

records.authors_text: A. Adamoli1, A. Orenti1, S. Gambazza1, F. Ambrogi1, A. Zolin1, R. Keogh2
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Milan, Milan, Italy, 2London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Cystic Fibrosis-Related Diabetes (CFRD) is the most common comorbidity in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) and insulin is the standard treatment. However, the association between insulin-treated CFRD and lung function is unclear: observational studies suggest clinical benefits but are limited by small samples and confounding. We assessed the long-term effects of insulin therapy in pwCF and CFRD using data from the European Cystic Fibrosis Society Patient Registry (ECFSPR).

Methods: Using a Target Trial Emulation (TTE) approach, we compared pwCF aged ≥12 newly diagnosed with CFRD between 2018 and 2023 who initiated and sustained insulin therapy versus those who did not initiate insulin, over 5 years of follow-up. The endpoint was longitudinal changes in percent predicted FEV₁ (ppFEV₁). Treatment effects were estimated using Marginal Structural Models (MSMs) with inverse probability weighting to handle measured confounders and censoring. Effect modification by CFTR modulator use was assessed using an extended MSM with a treatment-modulator interaction.

Results: The study included 1,371 pwCF (median age 22 years, 49.2% male); 61.8% initiated insulin within the first year after CFRD diagnosis. We found no evidence that insulin use affects long-term ppFEV₁ trajectories compared with no insulin (difference -3.62; 95% CI: -9.33 to 2.10). Among pwCF not receiving CFTR modulators, sustained insulin use over 5 years was associated with lower ppFEV₁ compared with no insulin use (-7.64; 95% CI: -13.78 to -1.50). In contrast, among modulator users, this long-term difference was attenuated (-0.36; 95% CI: -8.48 to 7.75).

Conclusions: Using ECFPSR data, we found no evidence that insulin therapy was associated with long-term improvement in lung function overall. However, the association between insulin use and ppFEV₁ varied by CFTR modulator use: differences were smaller among modulator than among non-users, suggesting heterogeneous treatment effects.

In contrast, among modulator users, this long-term difference was attenuated (-0.36; 95% CI: -8.48 to 7.75).
Conclusions: Using ECFPSR data, we found no evidence that insulin therapy was associated with long-term improvement in lung function overall. However, the association between insulin use and ppFEV₁ varied by CFTR modulator use: differences were smaller among modulator than among non-users, suggesting heterogeneous treatment effects.

session.title: ePoster Session 09 - Rethinking airway clearance and physical activity in the CFTR modulator era: adherence, burden and innovation

records.authors_text: H. Day1, A. Gates1, L. Warnock1, N. Hough1, H. Caterson1
records.affiliations_text: 1Oxford University Hospital, Cystic Fibrosis John Radcliffe Hospital, Oxford, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Cystic fibrosis (CF) pregnancy rates have risen following initiation of highly effective modulator therapy. Current physiotherapy standards of care (SOC) have not been updated to reflect this. We aim to describe current UK practice in maternal CF physiotherapy and identify priorities for standardised care and future research.

Methods: Lead physiotherapists at all 23 UK CF centres were invited to complete a bespoke online questionnaire.

Results: Twelve (52%) centres responded. Mean centre size was 298 (SD 128), with a mean annual pregnancy of 6.5 (SD 3.7). Three centres (25%) had a CF and Obstetrics pathway. Time to initial MDT review following confirmed pregnancy varied: 2 weeks (n=4), 4 weeks (n=3), 8 weeks (n=2), or dependent on pre-maternal health (n=3). Review frequency ranged from 2-12 weeks, most commonly every 4 weeks (41%) increasing with gestation: 41% in the first, 50% in the second, and 58% in the third trimester. All physiotherapists review at MDT clinics and ad hoc, reviewing lung function (n=12), inhaled therapies (n=12), respiratory status (n=11), airway clearance techniques (ACT) (n=11), exercise (n=11). ACT was commonly altered in second (42%) and third trimesters (67%), with addition of inspiratory pressure (n=4) or PEP (n=4); 50% added or increased inhaled mucolytics. Exercise prescription varied. 70% of centres review within 24 hours post-partum, the remainder limited by off-site obstetric care. Post-partum management were mixed.

Conclusion: Despite common management themes in CF pregnancy, variation exists reflecting a lack of evidence-based guidance. Clinically, this may result in inconsistent care and inequitable patient experience. The update of the CF physiotherapy SOC alongside development of integrated CF–obstetric MDT pathways, may improve consistency and quality of care. Future research should focus on defining optimal physiotherapy interventions, timing of reviews, exercise and ACT strategies to inform evidence-based guidelines.

session.title: ePoster Session 11 - Telehealth and digital tools in care and education

person.institution: University Hospitals Bristol & Weston NHS Foundation Trust

records.authors_text: C. Evison1, I. Smith1, I. Biggin2, G. King2
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Bath, Department of Psychology, Bath, United Kingdom, 2University Hospitals Bristol & Weston NHS Foundation Trust, Psychological Health Services, Bristol, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: UK National guidance indicates that all patients in paediatric and adult cystic fibrosis (CF) services should be offered psychology annual reviews (PAR). The Bristol Lifespan CF Psychology service trialled implementing an automated online PAR questionnaire. A service evaluation of this initiative aimed to audit uptake of PAR and gather patient feedback on the experience.

Methods: An audit of the online PAR was conducted over a 3-month period. Within this time frame, adult patients (n = 86) received a service specific questionnaire and paediatric patients (n = 20) an adapted version of a paediatric wellbeing measure. Psychologist attendance at paediatric annual review appointments supported data collection. The number of patients who received an invite to PAR during this period was compared to the previous year. Patient feedback questionnaires were sent to patients who received the online offer of PAR.

Results: More patients were offered PAR during the audit period (paediatrics = 100%, adults = 91%) than the previous year (paediatric = 29%, adults = 40%). 70% of paediatric patients and 22% of adult patients completed the PAR questionnaires. There was an increase of patient contact with CF psychology following the introduction of online PAR. Whilst response rates were low; overall PAR feedback generally indicated positive support for this process.

Conclusions: Overall, the online PAR system appeared successful in supporting the services to adhere to national guidance, patients were satisfied with the process and there was an increase of patient contact with the psychology service. This did however increase workload for psychologists in terms of active monitoring and increased uptake of support.

records.authors_text: Y. Liu1,2, R. Gorissen1, G. Karanikas1, A. de Bruijn1, B. Manaï2, F. Gama Franceschi3, L. Slimmen1,2, D. Mager2, S. Estevão1, L. Mezzanotte3, H. Janssens2, W. Unger1
records.affiliations_text: 1Erasmus University Medical Centre - Sophia Children's Hospital, Department of Paediatrics, Laboratory of Paediatrics, Infection and Immunity group, Rotterdam, Netherlands, 2Erasmus University Medical Centre - Sophia Children's Hospital, Department of Paediatrics, division of Respiratory Medicine and Allergology, Rotterdam, Netherlands, 3Erasmus University Medical Centre, Department of Radiology and Nuclear Medicine, Erasmus MC Cancer Institute, Rotterdam, Netherlands
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: Cystic fibrosis (CF) lung disease is hallmarked by chronic infection and inflammation. We previously showed that airway macrophages, crucial for defence against infections and resolution of inflammation, are dysfunctional in CF. However, the relative influence of cell-intrinsic (CFTR) and extrinsic (lung environment) factors in driving these processes is unclear.

Aim: To assess the role of intrinsic and extrinsic factors in dysfunction of airway macrophages in CF.

Methods: Monocyte–derived macrophages (MDMs) from people with CF and healthy donors (HD) were incubated with either control medium only or exposed to bronchoalveolar-lavage fluid (BALF) from highly inflamed CF lungs (BALFInfl-HI; n=4) or low-inflamed CF lungs (BALFInfl-LO; n=3) to mimic CF lung environment. Cytokine production, surface marker expression, and phagocytic capacity were analysed.

Results: Exposure to BALFInfl-HI induced a stronger inflammatory phenotype in CF MDMs than in HD MDMs, characterized by 2-fold higher levels of secreted TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β. In contrast, BALFInfl-LO elicited less strong activation of CF and HD MDMs. CF MDMs exposed to BALFInfl-HI expressed consistently lower levels of scavenger receptors CD163, CD206 and CD91 than HD MDMs. Consequently, phagocytosis of Pseudomonas aeruginosa was reduced in CF MDMs compared to HD MDMs. In both CF and HD MDMs, BALFInfl-HI increased the expression of PD-1 and PD-L1, which was linked to impaired efferocytosis. MDMs exposed to BALFInfl-LO showed similar levels of phagocytosis and efferocytosis as control medium exposed MDMs.

Conclusion: These data show that both intrinsic and extrinsic factors impact on macrophage phenotype and their bacterial uptake capacity. However, only extrinsic factors affect their tissue-cleaning and pro-resolving functions. Our data may explain why inflammation is not completely resolved after initiation of CFTR modulator therapy.

records.title: Assessment of the burden of treatment and illness on quality of life in lung transplanted people with cystic fibrosis

session.title: Workshop 11 - The changing face of cystic fibrosis wellbeing, risk and reproductive realities

records.authors_text: T. Havermans1, M. Nicasy2, L. Moyens1, N. Duplacie1, C. Ruelens1, F. Wynants1, F. Hoebrechts1, L. Dupont1, S. Bos1
records.affiliations_text: 1University Hospitals Leuven, Leuven, Belgium, 2Katholieke Universiteit Leuven, Leuven, Belgium
records.abstract_text:
Background: Data of lung transplanted (LT) people with Cystic Fibrosis (pwCF) are often embedded in larger studies on LT. This study aims to specifically review the burden of treatment and illness (Burden) on stable LTpwCF.

Method: Demographic and medical variables and indicators of Burden were obtained from medical records over the past year. Quality of life (QOL) was assessed using the Flemish LT Quality Of Life survey (FLT-QOL).

Results: The Leuven (Belgium) LT clinic cares for 119 LTpwCF of whom 85 (71%) were stable at the time of the study. 69/85 consented to the study: mean age 43 (range 23-65), 38 females. Time since LT was 11,9 years (SD=3.5; range 3-26). Mean lung function FEV1%pred. was 79% (SD=19; range 39%-129%); mean BMI was 21 (SD=3.5; range 16-32) and 54 (78%) were diagnosed with CFRD. Common complications related to LT were CLAD (25%), cancer (15%) and PTLD (7%).

Patients were prescribed with 9-28 different drugs, mostly for LT and CF. Other common prescriptions were pain medication (34%) and psychotropic medicines (23%). Patients attended the multidisciplinary LT clinic at least 3 times a year.

Over the past year, patients consulted a mean total of 24 specialist (range 3-21). Patients attended a mean sum of 32 outpatient clinics (range 7-81); 33% had been hospitalized and 24% had undergone surgery.

Table 1 shows associations between Burden parameters and scales of the FLT-QOL. Regression analyses showed that sum of outpatient visit and number of treatments were strong predictors of variance in FLT-QOL scales (p<.001-<0.05). BMI predicted variance on the FLT general QOL (p<.001).

Conclusion: The data indicate to high burden in terms of treatments, prescriptions and hospital visits. Patients consulted many specialists over and above LT and CF care. Sum of outpatient clinics was a strong predictor of variance in several areas of QOL. LTpwCF pay a high price to stay well and are in need of well-coordinated inter- and multidisciplinary care.

person.biography:
Trudy Havermans is a CF clinical health psychologist at the Cystic Fibrosis Centre of the University Hospital Leuven, Belgium. She has obtained her PhD at the University of Exeter, UK. For the past 25 years she has been responsible for the psychological care of a large cohort of paediatric, adult and transplanted people with CF. She has written several reviews and research papers on psychosocial aspects of CF and participated in multicentre international studies. She was speaker at the ERS courses on Cystic Fibrosis in 2013 and 2015.
Trudy Havermans is an active member of the European Cystic Fibrosis Society. For example, she participated in the ECFS Standard of Care projects, Scientific and Steering committees and contributed to three ECFS books. She was a member and treasurer of the ECFS board from 2019-2022. Trudy has set up and jointly led the ECFS Mental Health Working group for three years. At present she is a member of the ECFS Education committee, the ECFS Mental Health working group, the ECFS Telehealth for CF (THCF) working group and resides in the organising committee of the Special CF lunchtime webinars.

records.title: The CF Home Sputum-Induction Trial (CF-HomeSpIT): primary outcome data for early morning sputum-induction at home compared to same-day sputum-induction in clinic in children with cystic fibrosis

session.title: Workshop 12 - Finding airway pathogens after ETI: where, when and how should we sample?

records.authors_text: K. Ronchetti1, J.-D. Tame2, H. Morgan1, S. Mitchell3, R. Dhillon3, E. Mahenthiralingam4, A. Aseeri4, L. Thia1, J.T. Forton1, CF-SpIT Research Group
records.affiliations_text: 1The Children's Hospital for Wales, Paediatric Respiratory Medicine, Cardiff, United Kingdom, 2Cardiff University, Cardiff, United Kingdom, 3Public Health Wales, Microbiology Department, Cardiff, United Kingdom, 4Cardiff University, Biosciences, Cardiff, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: CF-HomeSpIT [ISRCTN86523335] is a prospective internally-controlled interventional trial in children comparing home-sampling using spontaneous early morning cough-clear (emCC) and home sputum-induction (hSI) with matched same-day clinic sampling using cough swab (CS), spontaneous clinic cough-clear (cCC) and clinic sputum-induction (cSI). https://www.uhwchildren.com/respiratory/cf-homespit/

Methods: Children age>6 yrs with CF at the Children’s Hospital for Wales already using Hypertonic saline (HS) were eligible for recruitment. emCC was obtained on waking, using 3 rounds of standardised expectoration: COUGH, HUFF, COUGH, CLEAR THROAT (hawk), and SPIT. hSI was obtained using HS with normal home physiotherapy routine, using the same standardised expectoration. Same-day clinic samples (cCC and cSI) were taken after routine CS by a physiotherapist using standardised procedures and expectoration.

Results: 64 patients performed 96 sampling events. Median age was 11 yrs. Median FEV1% was 94%. 93% were on modulator therapy. 20% had a wet cough.

92/96 (93%) home sampling attempts were successful (median duration 13 minutes (range 15-40)). 40 CF pathogens were identified in 34 (35%) individuals from all sampling combined. emCC, hSI, CS, cCC and cSI isolated 22, 22, 10, 23 & 23 pathogens respectively. 28/40 (sensitivity 0.7) were isolated on home samples combined. 31/40 (sensitivity 0.77) were isolated from clinic samples combined.

Conclusions: Home sputum-induction using a standardised approach to expectoration is possible, well tolerated, and has comparable pathogen yield to supervised clinic sputum-induction.

Pre-saline spontaneous cough-clear sampling gives additional gains in pathogen detection, may contain higher pathogen titre and should be incorporated into all sputum-induction protocols.

Clinic spontaneous cough-clear samples in isolation identify twice as many pathogens as CS and present a novel, quick addition to pathogen surveillance in clinic.

records.title: No country for bystanders: a split and inducible precise adenine base editor for the correction of W1282X

session.title: Workshop 13 - From allele to human: the complexity of CFTR

person.institution: Department of Physiology, BioSciences Institute, University College Cork

records.authors_text: J. Alves1,2, L. Santos3,4, I. Zollo2, C. M Farinha2, P. T Harrison5,1
records.affiliations_text: 1Department of Physiology, BioSciences Institute, University College Cork, Cork, Ireland, 2BioISI-Biosystems and Integrative Sciences Institute, Faculty of Sciences, University of Lisbon, Lisbon, Portugal, 3iBET - Instituto de Biologia Experimental e Tecnológica, Oeiras, Portugal, 4ITQB, Universidade Nova de Lisboa, Oeiras, Portugal, 5Cincinnati Children’s Hospital, Division of Pulmonary Medicine, Cincinnati, United States
records.abstract_text:
W1282X, the 5th most common Cystic Fibrosis causing variant, generates a premature terminating codon (PTC), causing lack of full-length functional CFTR protein production and nonsense-mediated mRNA decay. Adenine base editing (ABE) can in theory correct any PTC mutation with minimal levels of unwanted indels. ABE uses a fusion of a Cas9 nickase and a synthetic TadA enzyme modified to convert Adenine (A) to Guanine (G) in a varying editing window in the spacer region. The Harrison lab has previously reported efficient ABE of W1282X, but high levels of bystander editing leading to the unwanted generation of the R1283G type II variant, led us to search for new strategies.Based on reports of reduced off-target/bystander editing and duration of nuclease activity upon splitting the TadA domain protein of a base editor, we designed two fusion proteins that split the Cas9 nickase: NLS-FKBP12-Cas9(C)-NLS and TadA-Cas9(N)-FRB; dimerising in the presence of rapamycin to form a functional ABE (splitABE).

The editing window of parental ABE (Addgene #140003) and splitABE was characterized in two genomic loci with four gRNAs in HEK293T cells to assess on-target and bystander editing. Editing was detected at positions 4 to 7 of the spacer region, peaking at position 5. In the presence of rapamycin (72h), splitABE showed 53% A5-to-G5 editing levels, only slightly lower than the parental ABE (67%). In the absence of rapamycin, splitABE editing at A5 was only 10%, indicating low level of spontaneous dimerization. Thus, a 5.1-fold increase in editing confirms that splitABE can be used for temporal control of editing in a drug-dependent manner.

Details of the optimal rapamycin dose and exposure time for precise correction with minimal bystander-edits in the 16HBE14o and BCi-NS1.1 W1282X cell lines will be reported. This will lead to an understanding of the potential of splitABE reduced bystander-edits, and impact of temporal control of editing as a safer gene editing approach.

records.title: Beyond genotype: alterations in the ion transport environment as a potential source of variable CFTR function

session.title: Workshop 14 - New actors in epithelial pathophysiology

records.authors_text: V. Capurro1, E. Pesce1, V. Tomati1, C. Pastorino1, F. Cresta2, A. Dighero1, A. Mantero1, R. Bocciardi1,3, C. Castellani2, N. Pedemonte1
records.affiliations_text: 1IRCCS Istituto Giannina Gaslini, UOC Genetica Medica, Genova, Italy, 2IRCCS Istituto Giannina Gaslini, UOSD Centro Fibrosi Cistica, Genova, Italy, 3University of Genoa, Department of Neurosciences, Rehabilitation, Ophthalmology, Genetics, Maternal and Child Health (DINOGMI), Genova, Italy
records.abstract_text:
CFTR-mediated ion transport displays significant variability across the population. This heterogeneity is observed not only in people with Cystic Fibrosis (pwCF) where individuals with identical genotypes may showvariable CFTR activity and responses to modulators, but also in non-CF subjects, who exhibit a wide range of baseline CFTR activity. This suggests that factors extrinsic to the CFTR gene itself modulate its functional output. We hypothesized that intrinsic differences in the broader epithelial ion transport network, such as the balance between sodium absorption and auxiliary chloride secretion, may constitute a common mechanism driving this functional variability in both healthy and disease states.

Methods: To characterize this "background" ion transport environment, we performed differential gene expression analysis on airway epithelial cells. We specifically screened for dysregulation in non-CFTR ion channels, focusing on the soluble carrier (SLC) and epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) families, to identify factors limiting airway hydration independently of CFTR expression.

Results: Transcriptomic profiling indicated that CFTR mRNA levels were stable and not the primary driver of functional divergence. However, the supporting ion transport network was significantly altered. We observed upregulation of the amiloride-sensitive ENaC subunits SCNN1B and SCNN1G, favoring sodium hyperabsorption. Simultaneously, the alternative chloride transporter SLC26A9 was strongly downregulated, as was SLC26A4.

Conclusion: These data suggest that an unfavorable transporters ratio may act as a "functional brake," decoupling CFTR expression from physiological airway hydration. This mechanism may provide a molecular rationale for the unexplained variability in CFTR activity. It implies that in subjects with this specific transcriptomic signature, CFTR correction alone may be insufficient, highlighting the existence of alternative critical targets to promote chloride secretion.

Nicoletta Pedemonte – Biosketch
 
Nicoletta Pedemonte obtained her PhD in Human Genetics at the University of Turin, Italy in 2007 and a postgraduate specialization in Clinical Pathology at the University of Genoa, Italy in 2011. She is Senior Scientist at the UOC Genetica Medica of the IRCCS Istituto Giannina Gaslini in Genoa, Italy, where she leads a group of seven researchers.
She has a strong expertise in drug discovery strategies and functional genomics.  Her research activity is focused on transepithelial ion transport mechanisms in airway epithelial cells, mechanisms associated to mutant protein maturation and degradation, and identification of novel small molecules to rescue mutant CFTR protein in cystic fibrosis. 
She has authored >100 international peer-reviewed publications with >4,500 citations, H-factor 29 (Scopus). Scopus Author Identifier: 8095389700

records.title: IL-17A and IL-17F differentially modify ion transport and apical surface properties in human bronchial epithelia

session.title: Workshop 10 - Immune and inflammatory processes in the cystic fibrosis airway: novel insights

person.title: Dr
person.institution: Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine

records.authors_text: D. Guidone1, M. De Santis1, C. Ferrari2, F. Nicola2, N.I. Lorè2, L.J. Galietta1,3
records.affiliations_text: 1Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine, Pozzuoli (Naples), Italy, 2Infections and Cystic Fibrosis Unit, Division of Immunology, Transplantation and Infectious Diseases, IRCCS San Raffaele Scientific Institute, Milan, Italy, 3Department of Molecular Medicine and Medical Biotechnology, University of Naples “Federico II", Naples, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: In cystic fibrosis (CF), defective CFTR-mediated chloride secretion leads to airway surface dehydration, impaired mucociliary clearance (MCC), bacterial infection, inflammation, and lung damage. Although Trikafta improve CFTR function in patients carrying the F508del mutation, airway inflammation often persists. IL-17A and IL-17F play a key role in CF lung inflammation. This study aimed to compare their impact on ion transport and airway surface properties in bronchial epithelia.

Methods: Human bronchial epithelia were treated with IL-17A, IL-17F, or their combination. Transepithelial ion transport was assessed using short-circuit current recordings. The IL-17RA-neutralizing antibody brodalumab was used to dissect receptor-specific signaling. Airway surface viscosity was measured by fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP).

Results: Both IL-17A and IL-17F enhanced CFTR function; however, only IL-17A significantly increased ENaC activity. Brodalumab inhibited the IL-17A-induced upregulation of both CFTR and ENaC but did not block CFTR stimulation mediated by IL-17F. FRAP analysis revealed that IL-17A promoted a hyperviscous airway surface, whereas IL-17F favored a more fluid airway environment. In F508del epithelia treated with Trikafta, CFTR function was markedly amplified by IL-17A, IL-17F, or their combination. Notably, IL-17F-mediated enhancement of F508del-CFTR rescue persisted even in the presence of brodalumab.

Conclusions: IL-17A and IL-17F exert distinct effects on airway epithelial ion transport and surface properties. While IL-17A promotes airway surface hyperviscosity, IL-17F supports a more fluid surface and enhances CFTR rescue independently of IL-17RA signaling. These findings suggest that selective inhibition of IL-17A signaling, while preserving IL-17F activity, may represent a promising therapeutic strategy in CF, although possible side effects associated with IL-17RA inhibition should be carefully considered.

person.biography: I am a post-doc researcher in Luis J.V. Galietta ‘s lab at Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine (TIGEM) in Pozzuoli, Italy. I graduated in 2017 at Federico II University in Naples, then I joined TIGEM, first as fellow and then as PhD student. I obtained my PhD at the European School of Molecular Medicine (SEMM) in 2023. During my PhD, I attended many conferences in Italy and abroad. I was selected for oral presentation at: ECFS Summer School on Epithelial System, Lisboa 2019; ECFS Basic Science Conference, Albufeira 2022 (Travel grant by Italian Cystic Fibrosis Foundation); European Young Investigator Meeting, Paris 2023; Resolute Conference Unlocking transporters for drug discovery, Vienna 2023. I received ECFS Young Fellows Travel Award at ECFS Basic Science Conference, Valletta 2024. I was the author of 14 peer-reviewed articles and, in November 2022, I published my first-author paper entitled “Airway surface hyperviscosity and defective mucociliary transport by IL-17/TNF-α are corrected by β-adrenergic stimulus” on JCI insight. My main project regards how human bronchial epithelia respond to inflammatory stimuli to fight bacterial infections and how these processes are impaired in cystic fibrosis.

session.title: Workshop 11 - The changing face of cystic fibrosis wellbeing, risk and reproductive realities

records.authors_text: A. Ward1, G. Davidson2, (.C.Y Ooi3, N. Rosic1
records.affiliations_text: 1Southern Cross University, Faculty of Health, Gold Coast, Australia, 2Sydney Children's Hospital, Sydney, Australia, 3University of New South Wales, Discipline of Paediatrics & Child Health, Randwick Clinical Campus, School of Clinical Medicine, Sydney, Australia
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Pain can be a significant burden in people with CF (pwCF). The objective of this study was to evaluate pain in adults and its characteristics across multiple countries, and to develop pain profiles for pwCF.

Method: Adults from the United States of America (USA), Canada and the United Kingdom (UK) were invited to complete an online questionnaire from April 2024 to June 2025, consisting of four validated tools: Brief Pain Inventory (BPI), Pain Catastrophising Scale (PCS), PAGI-SYM and PAC-SYM and open-ended questions surrounding their experiences with pain and pain management. The data were then collated to identify the characteristics of individuals who experience different levels of pain severity and to explore the clinical characteristics or risk factors associated with pain.

Results: There were 75 international respondents, including 43 from the USA, 17 from Canada, 15 from the UK, and 117 Australian respondents. The pain severity cohorts (i.e., “mild”, “moderate” and “severe”) showed significant differences in age, specifically in the mild and severe cohorts, BMI, pain interference, catastrophising, PAGI-SYM and PAC-SYM scores. Conclusion: This international study highlights that the under-management and under-recognition of pain in pwCF is a global issue. It is the first study to identify pain profiles based on severity, grouping pain locations, and nutritional status. Further investigations are needed to improve the evaluation of pain patterns, identify causality factors, and increase awareness within CF clinics, in order to personalise pain management in CF and improve health outcomes.

records.title: Are postal cough swabs accurate surrogates for those sent from clinic in children with cystic fibrosis?

session.title: Workshop 12 - Finding airway pathogens after ETI: where, when and how should we sample?

records.authors_text: G. Wilson1,2, N. Collins1, S. Angus1, F. Eyles1, C. MacAllister1, C. O'Keeffe1, T. Price1, N. Ramadan1, A. Taylor1, B. Tin1, C. Worger1, S. Carr1,2, J. Davies1,2, D. Hughes1,2, R. Pabary1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Royal Brompton Hospital, London, United Kingdom, 2Imperial College London, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Remote microbiological surveillance has become commonplace in Cystic Fibrosis (CF), however, there is minimal evidence with variable results on the potential effect of postage.

Objective: To determine whether postage impacts microbiological growth of paired paediatric cough swabs sent from clinic and via post.

Methods: Two simultaneous cough swabs were taken by physiotherapists from children attending in person CF clinics between Dec 2024–Aug 2025. At random, one was sent via usual protocols to the microbiology lab whilst the other was packaged into biological specimen postal kits. Microbiological growths between paired samples were compared. Time and date of postal sample arrival were used to calculate time delay to the closest 0.5hr. Actions taken on positive postal samples were documented.

Results: Ninety-three paired samples were received; 19/93 postal samples were positive, the majority being Gram negative bacteria and most commonly Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa) (4/19). Only 2/93 non-postal samples were positive (1 Pa, 1 Staphylococcus aureus (Sa); both also detected on their paired postal samples). In the prior 18months, 22% of the patients had isolated Sa and 12% isolated Pa.

Median time delay for positive postal samples was 93.5hrs (IQR 70.5-130.3hrs) compared with 72hrs (IQR 65.3-96.3hrs) for negative postal samples (p>0.05).

A positive postal sample prompted a change in management in 7/19 cases (6 commenced antibiotics, 1 had an induced sputum).

Conclusion: Postal samples were more likely to be positive than non-postal samples, with Pa being a prominent pathogen isolated from postal samples. Clinical decisions around treatment of positive postal results varied, influenced by patient symptoms and uncertainty about the validity of the results.

This project is ongoing with the intention to include adults and other chronic suppurative lung diseases to further understand the validity of discrepant postal samples and add to the required body of evidence in this field.
