person.title: Dr.
person.biography:
I am a London-based Paediatric Respiratory GRID Trainee currently taking time out of training as a Clinical Research Fellow to undertake a PhD at Imperial College London. My PhD is investigating novel infection detection and sampling techniques in Cystic Fibrosis (CF). This has involved setting up the 'Precision Partners Platform Study' (P3), part of the CF Trust and LifeArc funded Precision-CF Innovation Hub. P3 is a multi-centre, multi-sample type approach to establish alternatives to sputum culture for detecting lung infections, and to better understand host/microbe interactions. We aim to recruit up to 850 people with CF, chronic suppurative lung disease and healthy volunteers over 5 years.
Alongside my research, I continue clinical work as a Paediatric Respiratory Registrar at the Royal Brompton Hospital, undertaking a General Respiratory clinic and CF clinic each week.
I have previously worked as a Cystic Fibrosis Clinical Trials Fellow at the Royal Brompton Hospital between 2021-2022 which involved working on multiple commercial and academic clinical trials, recruiting both adults and children with CF.

records.title: Patient-derived human pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived epithelia for the high-throughput screening (HTS) and ciliary beat frequency-based assessment of chemically optimised CFTR modulators

session.title: Workshop 13 - From allele to human: the complexity of CFTR

person.title: PhD
person.department: Leibniz Research Laboratories for Biotechnology and Artificial Organs (LEBAO)

records.authors_text: U. Martin1, S. Merkert2, N. Natrup2, M.C. Klassen2, L. Czichon2, L. von Schledorn2, O. Plettenburg3, R. Olmer2
records.affiliations_text: 1Hannover Medical School, Leibniz Research Laboratories for Biotechnology and Artificial Organs (LEBAO), Hannover, Germany, 2Hannover Medical School, LEBAO, Hannover, Germany, 3Leibniz University Hannover, Center of Biomolecular Drug Research, Hannover, Germany
records.abstract_text:
We have recently exploited the advantages of CF patient-specific hiPSCs over immortalised cell lines and primary airway cells in a HTS approach (1), and have identified novel CFTR modulator candidates. We have also demonstrated that patient-specific hiPSC-derived Air-Liquid Interface (iALI) cultures represent an excellent in vitro model of CF lung disease (2). Unlike intestinal organoids, iALI cultures recapitulate the central pathophysiology of CF lung disease –defective mucociliary clearance (MCC) arising from impaired epithelial ion transport and airway surface liquid dehydration. iALI cultures show characteristic (ultra)structural features of highly polarised airway epithelial cells, including ciliated cells, goblet cells, club cells and underlying basal cells, covered with mucus the height and density of which depend on CFTR function.

We have now developed an automated in vitro assay on iALI cultures to determine ciliary beat frequency (CBF), which closely reflect impaired MCC – the predominant pathomechanism of CF lung disease. Standardizing the workflow enabled unattended operation and reduced the hands-on analysis time. Preliminary results suggest that small scale, iterative testing of novel HTS-derived, medicinal chemistry-optimized CFTR active compounds can be conducted within the same iPSC/CBF framework.

In summary, the CBF assay provides consistent results on hiPSC-derived airway epithelia and could serve as a scalable, patient-specific, automated platform for evaluating CFTR-modulators and supporting theratyping across CFTR genotypes. While full high-throughput deployment will require adaptation to 96 - 384well plates and further automation, the current data support using the CBF assay to evaluate CFTR modulators on patient-specific iPSC-derived cells, as well as for the secondary testing of HTS-derived, chemistry-refined drug candidates.

1. Merkert et al. Stem Cell Rep, 2019

2. Klassen et al., Stem Cell Res Ther, 2025

person.biography:
Since 2007 Prof. Ulrich Martin, PhD, has been head of the Leibniz Research Laboratories for Biotechnology and Artificial Organs (LEBAO). In 2008 he became a full professor for ‘Cardiorespiratory Tissue Engineering’ and director of research of the Clinic for Cardiothoracic-, Transplantation and Vascular Surgery, both at Hannover Medical School (MHH). Ulrich Martin is vice coordinator of the Research Center for Translational Regenerative Medicine ‘REBIRTH - From Regenerative Biology to Reconstructive Therapy’ and dean of the PhD program ‘Regenerative Sciences’. Besides, he is principle investigator, member of various scientific boards and coordinator of numerous national and international research projects.
 
Research of Prof. Martin basically focuses on induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), the differentiation of pluripotent stem cells into cardiovascular and respiratory lineages, genetic engineering, and cardiovascular tissue engineering. U. Martin has a strong translational focus aiming at the development and conduction of hiPSC-based in vitro assays, drug screens and cellular therapies, including development of GMP-compliant cell production technologies and risk assessment.

records.title: TRPV4-driven ATP release activates CFTR through ADORA2B and P2RY2 receptors in the airway epithelium

session.title: Workshop 14 - New actors in epithelial pathophysiology

person.institution: Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine (Tigem)

records.authors_text: M. De Santis1, M. Genovese1, L.J.V. Galietta1
records.affiliations_text: 1Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine (Tigem), Pozzuoli, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The CFTR chloride channel is essential for airway surface hydration and mucociliary clearance, and its activity is regulated by cAMP-dependent phosphorylation. We previously observed that pharmacological activation of the TRPV4 calcium channel stimulates CFTR function, but the mechanism underlying this interaction was unclear. In this study we show that TRPV4 and CFTR are expressed in distinct epithelial cell types, indicating that TRPV4-induced CFTR activation occurs through a paracrine mechanism.

Methods: Expression patterns of TRPV4 and CFTR were analyzed in airway epithelial cells to determine their cellular localization. A luciferase-based assay was used to measure ATP release following TRPV4 activation at the apical surface. Pharmacological inhibitors and receptor antagonists were employed to dissect the contribution of purinergic and adenosine signaling pathways to CFTR activation.

Results: TRPV4 and CFTR were found to be expressed in distinct epithelial cell types, indicating that CFTR activation occurs via a paracrine mechanism. Activation of TRPV4 induced significant ATP release at the apical surface. Extracellular ATP stimulated CFTR activity through activation of both P2Y2 purinergic receptors and A2B adenosine receptors. Combined inhibition of these receptors nearly abolished TRPV4-dependent CFTR activation.

Conclusion: These findings identify a TRPV4–ATP/adenosine–CFTR signaling axis that links mechanical and chemical stimuli to the regulation of airway surface hydration. This paracrine pathway provides new insight into the control of mucociliary clearance and may have important implications for airway diseases.

session.title: Workshop 10 - Immune and inflammatory processes in the cystic fibrosis airway: novel insights

person.institution: Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland
person.department: School of Pharmacy and Biomolecular Sciences

records.authors_text: J. Hynes1,2, E. Almenar Perez1,2, F. Ringolz1,2, R. Cregan1,2, K. Wynne3, P. McNally1,2, J. Coppinger1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland, School of Pharmacy and Biomolecular Sciences, Dublin 2, Ireland, 2Children’s Health Ireland at Crumlin, Children’s Health Ireland Translational Research Centre, Dublin 12, Ireland, 3University College Dublin, Systems Biology Ireland, Dublin 4, Ireland
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Highly Effective Triple Modulator Therapy (HEMT), such as Kaftrio, that targets the Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Regulator (CFTR), channel has revolutionised treatment in People with CF (PwCF). However, some individuals receiving modulator therapy continue to exhibit residual airway inflammation and bronchiectasis. Extracellular Vesicles (EVs) are nanoparticles involved in intracellular communication and regulating inflammation. We aim to characterise the effect of Kaftrio on EVs and their associated protein targets in clinical samples from PwCF, to identify potential EV proteins regulating inflammation.

Methods: Sputum (n=40) and Nasal Lavage (NL) (n=60) samples from PwCF were obtained (at base point (0M), six months (6M) and 12 months (12M) post-Kaftrio initiation). EVs were isolated by precipitation/ultracentrifugation and characterised using Nanoparticle Tracking Analysis (NTA), immunoblotting, Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) and Mass Spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics.

Results: NTA revealed significant reductions in EV numbers at 12M post-Kaftrio initiation, in the 50-1000nm size range (p>0.05). Particles were confirmed to be EVs using immunoblotting and TEM. MS-based proteomics revealed 189 significantly changing proteins post-Kaftrio, with 92 proteins changing from 0M to 6M and 89 changing from 0M to 12M. These proteins represented pathways and processes dysregulated in CF relating to CFTR misfolding (e.g. proteasome), CF immune biology (neutrophil activation) and extracellular matrix remodelling.

Discussion: We observed a decrease in the number of EVs in NL and sputum from PwCF undergoing modulator therapy. Post-treatment protein profiles demonstrated that Kaftrio has a restorative effect on dysfunctional CF signalling modulated by EVs. However several regulators of inflammation, including neutrophil regulators from the S100 family, were not corrected by Kaftrio, indicating their potential as therapeutic targets.

records.title: Cancer screening information, promotion and care for people with cystic fibrosis: patient and clinician perspectives from qualitative interview studies

session.title: Workshop 11 - The changing face of cystic fibrosis wellbeing, risk and reproductive realities

records.authors_text: L. Ashley1, R. Morrow1, N. Parkin1, R. Spencer1, H. Gales2, L. Parkinson-Baxter2, S. Mills2, M. Shore2, D. Jayne3, M. Thoufeeq4, K. Lippiett5, S. Bourke6, N. Simmonds7, D. Peckham3
records.affiliations_text: 1Leeds Beckett University, Leeds, United Kingdom, 2Patient Representative, -, United Kingdom, 3University of Leeds, Leeds, United Kingdom, 4Sheffield Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, Sheffield, United Kingdom, 5University of Southampton, Southampton, United Kingdom, 6The Newcastle Upon Tyne Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, Newcastle, United Kingdom, 7Imperial College London, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: As people with cystic fibrosis (CF) live longer, it has become apparent they have an increased risk of developing cancer, at a younger age, especially bowel cancer. In the UK, CF care teams have begun to offer cancer screening and surveillance information, promotion and care. We aimed to conduct, to our knowledge, the first qualitative studies to examine patients’ and clinicians’ experiences, challenges and needs in this growing area of CF care.

Methods: Semi-structured interviews with, to date, 29 people with CF and 34 multidisciplinary clinicians (e.g., consultants, nurses, dietitians, endoscopists) (N=63), recruited from six UK adult CF centres. Data are analysed concurrently using the framework method of thematic analysis. A patient representative group is involved in all research stages including data analysis and dissemination.

Results: Key emerging findings, from ongoing data collection, show generally low awareness of CF-increased cancer risk among patients, and desire for more and earlier information from CF teams, and increasing provision of CF-tailored colonoscopy screening by CF teams, with high patient receptivity to this. Data suggest lower focus by CF teams on the national cancer screenings (e.g. cervical, breast), with potential for patients to therefore view these as not crucially important if not promoted within CF care. Interviews elucidate patients’ questions, concerns, and misunderstandings around cancer risk and care, and highlight patients’ evolving use of internet-based information and support (e.g. peer social media, AI chatbots).

Conclusion: Data are providing rich insight into potential ways to enhance experiences and effectiveness of cancer preventive and early detection care for people with CF. Findings will help inform and develop patient information and support, practice recommendations and service provision.

Funded by: UK National Institute for Health and Care Research, Bowel Research UK & UK CF Trust.

records.abstract_text:
Background: Regular screening for bronchopulmonary colonisation is standard of care for people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). Induced sputum (IS) is considered the gold standard for microbiological surveillance. Since the initiation of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI), sputum production has declined, potentially affecting surveillance strategies. This study investigated changes in bronchopulmonary colonisation before and after ETI initiation using IS samples.

Methods: Microbiological data from IS samples were retrospectively analysed over 3 years. Analyses assessed dynamics of chronic colonisation and the emergence of intermittent pathogen detection (≥2 but <4 positive detections/year). Findings were correlated with structural lung disease assessed by CT using the Bhalla score.

Results: A total of 1,535 IS samples (576 pre; 959 post-ETI) from 101 pwCF (61.4% adults; 51% female; mean age 22 years [6–48]) were analysed. Chronic colonisation in adults declined significantly 2 years after ETI initiation (68% vs. 42%, p=<.001), with marked reductions in Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus (p=.008 and <.001). Although paediatric numbers were limited for statistical analysis, chronic colonisation halved. Pathogens were detected intermittently in 27% of adults and 36% of children, most commonly S. aureus. Structural lung abnormalities persisted in 89% of patients. No association was found between intermittent colonisation and bronchiectasis, whereas chronic colonisation was associated with bronchiectasis in the paediatric cohort (p=.004).

Conclusion: IS sampling reveals a significant reduction in chronic bronchopulmonary colonisation in adults, despite persistent structural lung disease. Intermittent pathogens remain prevalent across age groups; long-term studies are required to clarify the clinical relevance of these microbiological findings. Regular IS-based surveillance should remain an integral component of CF care.

records.title: F508del-CFTR complex alleles sensitivity to clinically approved modulators

session.title: Workshop 13 - From allele to human: the complexity of CFTR

records.authors_text: V. Tomati1, V. Capurro1, E. Pesce1, C. Pastorino1, F. Cresta2, A. Mantero1, A. Dighero1, A. Quarato1, M. Ambroni3, L. Claut4, V. Daccò4, C. Castellani2, N. Pedemonte1
records.affiliations_text: 1IRCCS Istituto Giannina Gaslini, UOC Genetica Medica, Genova, Italy, 2IRCCS Istituto Giannina Gaslini, UOSD Centro Fibrosi Cistica, Genova, Italy, 3Ospedale Maurizio Bufalini, Cystic Fibrosis Center, Cesena, Italy, 4Fondazione IRCCS Ca' Granda, Ospedale Maggiore Policlinico, Department of Pediatrics, Cystic Fibrosis Center, Milano, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Complex alleles (CA) of F508del-CFTR, i.e. the presence of more than one variant in cis with F508del variant, are reported to modify both clinical manifestations and the response to modulators. In a large cohort of Italian people with Cystic Fibrosis (pwCF), we recruited unrelated CF patients, heterozygous for the F508del and a minimal function variant, who were referred as having limited or negligible beneficial effects following treatment with Elexacaftor, Tezacaftor, Ivacaftor (ETI). CFTR NGS analysis revealed that the majority of these subjects were carriers of F508del CA, not responsive to ETI. We asked whether these patients benefit from the treatment with the newly approved combination Vanzacaftor, Tezacatfor (VT).

Methods: We performed functional and biochemical studies ex vivo on primary cultures of nasal epithelial cells (HNEC) derived from patients with CF and in vitro on heterologous expression systems.

Results: Functional studies on differentiated nasal epithelia confirmed a lack or negligible rescue of CFTR activity by ET treatment for all patients. By contrast, pharmacological modulation with VT increased by two-fold the CFTR-dependent current only on one of the CA under study.

In vitro functional and biochemical studies on heterologous expression systems regarding the rescue of CA-derived protein by both ET and VT, showed, in some cases, differences in the pattern of rescue as compared to data collected on primary HNECs, possibly due to the different cell background.

Conclusions: Our study provides information regarding the sensitivity of ultra-rare F508del-CFTR CA to treatment with the novel Vanzacaftor combination. Data collected suggest that pwCF carrying F508del-CFTR CA and not responding to ET, could benefit from the treatment with VT, extending precision medicine–based therapeutic approaches.

Supported by The Italian Ministry of Health (PNRR-MR1-2023-12378412), FFC Ricerca (FFC#10/2021, Kaftrio nella vita reale substudy 1).

2004: doctoral degree in Biological Sciences (University of Genoa)
2008: PhD in Internal Medicine (University of Genoa)
2008 – 2023 Post-doctoral Fellow at IRCCS Giannina Gaslini Institute (UOC Molecular Genetics)
2023 – to date Researcher at IRCCS Giannina Gaslini Institute (UOC Molecular Genetics)
I am a member of the Cystic Fibrosis and Innovative Therapies group directed by Dr. Nicoletta Pedemonte. I investigate the basic defect of rare and orphan CFTR variants that cause the loss of function of the channel, through functional and biochemical characterization. I evaluate ex vivo the efficacy of CFTR modulators on primary nasal cells of patients to define their \"teratype\" (personalized medicine approach). I contributed to drug discovery projects aimed at identifying modulators of the CFTR channel like the strategic project Task Force for Cystic Fibrosis (TFCF), funded by Fondazione Ricerca FC. The project led to the identification of a novel type 1 CFTR corrector endowed with very high potency (ARN23765). Through transcriptomic and proteomic studies I contributed to the identification of alternative molecular targets belonging to the F508del-CFTR interactome.

Co-investigator of “PTSuppress – Novel lead compounds as potential suppressor drugs for CFTR PTC mutations” – PI Dr. Mike Gray – Cystic Fibrosis Trust (UK).

records.title: Transcriptomic analysis of G542X-CFTR bronchial epithelial cells indicates inhibition of nonsense mediated decay by IL-4 treatment

session.title: Workshop 14 - New actors in epithelial pathophysiology

records.authors_text: A. Borrelli1, A. Venturini2, M. De Santis2, D. Guidone2, R. De Cegli2, E. Montemitro3, F. Alghisi3, F. Ciciriello3, L.J. Galietta2,4
records.affiliations_text: 1TIGEM- Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine, Cell Biology, Pozzuoli, Italy, 2TIGEM- Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine, Pozzuoli, Italy, 3Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital IRCCS, Pneumology and Cystic Fibrosis Unit, Rome, Italy, 4University of Naples Federico II, Department of Translational Medicine, Naples, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Background: Nonsense mutations in the CFTR gene hamper protein synthesis, generating severely truncated CFTR forms unresponsive to present therapies. Recently we reported that in vitro cultured human bronchial epithelial cells (HBECs) showed an enhanced response to a triple compound combination including VX-809 as CFTR corrector, ELX-02 as a RT agent and the eRF3a degrader CC-90009 when treated for 72 hours with IL-4 or TNFα plus IL-17. We are currently investigating at the molecular level the mechanism by which cytokine stimulation together with drug treatment enhance CFTR function.

Methods: In vitro differentiated HBECs from a patient with the G542X mutation were cultured ± IL-4 or TNFα/IL-17A for 72 h. In the last 24 h, cells received ELX-02 + VX-809 and CC-90009 (combo). Bulk RNA-seq assessed gene expression changes under treatments.

Results: We focused on IL-4 given its strong effect on full-length CFTR expression. Gene-set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of RNA-seq data showed significant downregulation of the reactome terms “nonsense mediated decay (NMD) pathway”, “rRNA processing”, “response of EIF2AK4-GCN2 to amino acid deficiency” in epithelia treated with IL-4 alone compared to control condition. The same datasets appear downregulated also in epithelia treated with the combo alone and in epithelia where IL-4 was added to the combo. IL-4 appears to contribute to the downregulation of the NMD pathway decreasing UPF3A and PABPC1 transcripts.

Conclusions: Transcriptomic analysis of G542X-CFTR bronchial epithelial cells suggests inhibition of NMD by IL-4 treatment. A deeper investigation is needed to reveal novel molecular targets belonging to translation fidelity and/or other post-translational modifications pathways that can be modulated with other pharmacological strategies.

Funding: Cystic Fibrosis Foundation (GALIET22I0), Italian Cystic Fibrosis Foundation (FFC#9/2022, GMRF#1/2024), and Italian Ministry of Health (GR-2018-12367126).

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Progressive lung damage in cystic fibrosis (CF) is tightly linked to chronic infection and inflammation, yet the immune mechanisms connecting early Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonization to sustained immunopathology remain incompletely defined. We aimed to characterize pathogenic Th17 responses in CF lungs and their microbial drivers.

Methods: We combined immune profiling of CF lung and blood samples with transcriptomics, TCR repertoire analysis, epithelial injury assays, and dendritic cell–T cell polarization models using early and chronically adapted clinical P. aeruginosa isolates.

Results: We identify two IFNγ-producing pathogenic Th17 subsets—Th1/17⁺ and pTh17 cells—selectively enriched in CF lungs colonized by P. aeruginosa. These populations derive from protective conventional Th17 precursors through in situ reprogramming and clonal expansion, acquiring the capacity to impair epithelial barrier integrity and amplify pro-inflammatory signaling. P. aeruginosa persists within dendritic cells and promotes an IL-1β/IL-23–dominated polarizing milieu that favors IFNγ⁺ Th17 differentiation over classical Th1 responses. Strikingly, early clinical isolates, prior to chronic adaptation, already display a strong ability to rewire Th17 fate, inducing a transcriptional reprogramming that mirrors pathogenic Th1/17⁺ and pTh17 cells resident in CF lungs

Conclusion: Our data identify a clinically relevant immune–microbial circuit linking P. aeruginosa infection to pathogenic Th17 plasticity and epithelial damage in CF, highlighting novel targets for precision immunomodulatory interventions.

records.title: A qualitative exploration of the assisted reproductive technology experiences and needs of men with cystic fibrosis and their partners

session.title: Workshop 11 - The changing face of cystic fibrosis wellbeing, risk and reproductive realities

records.authors_text: O. Stransky1, A. Prangley1, S. Ladores-Barret2, A. Georgiopoulos3, A. Trimble4, D. Velez5, T. Kazmerski1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Pittsburgh, Pediatrics, Pittsburgh, United States, 2University of Nevada, Las Vegas, School of Nursing, Las Vegas, United States, 3Massachusetts General Hospital, Psychiatry, Boston, United States, 4Oregon Health and Science University, Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine, Portland, United States, 5Rutgers University, Surgery, New Brunswick, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Nearly 98% of males with cystic fibrosis (MwCF) are born with congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens. With recent advancements in treatment and quality of life, more adults with CF are pursuing family building, yet infertility remains unchanged among MwCF, requiring them to utilize assisted reproductive technology (ART) or other family-building methods..

Methods: We recruited MwCF and their partners from across the United States who have considered or pursued biologic parenthood via ART to participate in semi-structured dyadic interviews. We explored experiences with fertility referral and evaluation, sperm extraction, in vitro fertilization (IVF), and other family-building methods. Thematic analysis is ongoing.

Results: To date, we have interviewed 21 MwCF (age range 28-48 years) and their partners (age range 25-45 years). Preliminary themes include: 1) Most couples cited cost as their primary concern about pursuing ART, even among those who had insurance coverage or received charitable subsidies; 2) Couples desired more information about the impact of cystic fibrosis (CF) on sperm quality, ART success rates in CF, and expected timelines of the ART process; 3) Many MwCF feel guilt or helplessness about the physical toll of IVF on their partners; 4) For MwCF, the greater medicalization of the female partner in ART was a role reversal; 5) Couples highlighted the importance of teamwork and communication while undergoing ART.

Conclusions: Preliminary results show that pursuing ART involves financial, logistical, physical, and emotional challenges. Given the near universality of infertility among MwCF, future work should focus on reducing barriers and providing multi-factorial support, and investing in research to optimize sperm quality for MwCF, all of which could have implications for patient populations beyond CF.

records.title: Detection of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in cystic fibrosis: a national survey of practices in French Cystic Fibrosis Resource and Expert Centres (CRCM) in the era of CFTR modulators

session.title: Workshop 12 - Finding airway pathogens after ETI: where, when and how should we sample?

records.authors_text: K. Phan1, S. Ramel2,3, A. Barzic2
records.affiliations_text: 1CHU BREST, Pediatrie, Brest, France, 2Fondation Ildys, CRCM, Roscoff, France, 3Univ Brest, INSERM, UMR 1078, GGB, Brest, France
records.abstract_text:
Background: ​​​​Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa) is a major pathogen associated with progressive lung function decline in cystic fibrosis (CF), making early detection crucial. Sputum culture remains the reference method but has limited sensitivity in cases of low bacterial load or viable but non-culturable bacteria. Pa-specific quantitative PCR (qPCR), due to its higher sensitivity, is particularly relevant for patients producing little or no sputum, a situation increasingly frequent with CFTR modulators.

Objectives: To describe respiratory sampling practices and the use of Pa-specific qPCR across French CRCMs, and to assess practice, result interpretation, and clinicians’ interest.

Methods: A national questionnaire developed by the Roscoff CRCM was distributed via the MUCO-CFTR network to physicians working in adult, paediatric, or mixed CRCM. It focused on respiratory sample collection, sputum induction, and Pa-specific qPCR use.

Results: Forty-one of 47 CRCMs (87%) responded. In sputum-producing patients, sputum culture remained the standard diagnostic method. In non–sputum-producing patients, practices varied: 62.5% performed induced sputum, 16.5% used pharyngeal swabs, and 12.5% used both. Induced sputum was performed systematically in 37.5% of centres and annually or based on clinical criteria in 31.3%. Only 20.8% of centres had access to Pa-specific qPCR, although 86.1% expressed interest. qPCR was mainly used in Pa-never/free or intermittently infected patients and rarely in chronic infection. A positive qPCR with negative culture usually led to closer monitoring or eradication therapy, most commonly inhaled tobramycin. In asymptomatic patients, 1 positive target prompted follow-up, whereas 2 or 3 led to treatment.

Conclusion: This survey highlights marked heterogeneity in respiratory sampling practices and limited access to Pa-specific qPCR across French CRCMs, despite strong professional interest. Harmonisation of Pa surveillance strategies is needed in the era of CFTR modulators.

session.title: Workshop 13 - From allele to human: the complexity of CFTR

person.title: Assistant Professor
person.institution: Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine
person.department: Gynecology & Obstetrics, Division of Maternal-Fetal Medicine

records.authors_text: K.A. Miller1, A. Pion2, A. Topasna2, A.J. Ostmann3, J.D. Meeker3, H. Morgan3, G. Kelly3, J. Brewington3, N. Sharma2, G.R. Cutting2, K.S Raraigh2
records.affiliations_text: 1Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Gynecology & Obstetrics, Division of Maternal-Fetal Medicine, Baltimore, United States, 2Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, McKusick-Nathans Department of Genetic Medicine, Baltimore, United States, 3University of Cincinnati College of Medicine and Cincinnati Children’s Hospital Medical Center, Department of Pediatrics, Division of Pulmonary Medicine, Cincitnatti, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The relationship between CFTR function and phenotype remains incompletely understood. Prior work has yielded heterogeneous findings, suggesting linear and non-linear associations. We sought to characterize the CFTR genotype-function-phenotype relationship using data from the Clinical and Functional TRanslation of CFTR (CFTR2) database and human nasal epithelial (HNE) theratyping assays.

Methods: Mean sweat [Cl-] from 85,737 individuals in the CFTR2 database harboring 478 CFTR genotypes were linked to variant functional measures obtained in heterologous cell lines. Total CFTR genotype function was calculated as the average percent wild-type chloride conductance of both alleles. Linear regression models weighted by sample size were applied to evaluate the function- sweat [Cl-] relationship. A similar framework was applied to a cohort with available HNE data, linking sweat [Cl⁻] to CFTR function for 85 individuals with 42 genotypes.

Results: The association between CFTR function and sweat [Cl-] varied across the functional spectrum. While a global linear model demonstrated an overall significant association in CFTR2 data, this approach obscured substantial heterogeneity across the functional range. Piecewise linear regression models fit within specified functional ranges revealed marked attenuation of slope magnitude with increasing function, with the steepest associations observed at low function and progressively reduced slope magnitude at higher function. Despite markedly smaller sample size, directionally similar attenuation was observed in HNE data.

Conclusion: Large-scale registry data suggest that the function-sweat [Cl-] relationship is not sufficiently described by a single linear effect but may be more accurately represented by a logarithmic relationship in which incremental changes in CFTR activity have differential phenotypic impact across the functional spectrum. Further modeling incorporating complementary data may provide additional insights.

records.title: Improving airway epithelial repair in cystic fibrosis through CFTR-dependent and -independent pathways

session.title: Workshop 14 - New actors in epithelial pathophysiology

person.title: Prof.
person.institution: Centre hospitalier de l’Université de Montréal (CRCHUM)
person.department: Département de Médecine, Université de Montréal (UdeM)

records.authors_text: E. Brochiero1, S. Moustadraf1, N. Labonté1, G. McKay2, D. Nguyen2, C. Inkel3, F. Malouin3, D. Adam1
records.affiliations_text: 1Centre hospitalier de l’Université de Montréal (CRCHUM), Département de Médecine, Université de Montréal (UdeM), Montréal, Canada, 2Department of Medicine, McGill University Health Centre (MHUC), Montréal, Canada, 3Département de Biologie, Université de Sherbrooke, Montréal, Canada
records.abstract_text:
Background: Pulmonary disease is the main cause of morbidity and mortality in cystic fibrosis (CF), and recovery of lung function relies on efficient repair of airway damage, particularly in advanced disease. Beyond its role in mucociliary clearance, CFTR directly regulates epithelial repair. Therefore, both the CFTR defect and chronic infection impair this process in CF airways, highlighting the need for pro-repair therapeutic strategies.

Objectives and methods: Our aim was to dissect how CFTR contributes to epithelial repair and how CFTR modulators (CFTRm), alone or combined with complementary CFTR-independent approaches, enhance repair. Primary airway epithelial cultures from people with CF (pwCF) carrying diverse CFTR mutations were used to assess early and late repair processes, including directed cell migration, progenitor cell proliferation and regeneration of a differentiated ciliated epithelium.

Results: Our data confirm CF airway epithelia displayed defective repair. CFTR rescue using CFTRm (Lumacaftor/Ivacaftor or Elexacaftor/Tezacaftor/Ivacaftor) enhanced coordinated cell migration with activation of integrins at the wound edge, accelerated wound closure and promoted restoration of a tight, ciliated epithelium. Strategies reducing P. aeruginosa and S. aureus virulence preserved epithelial repair under infectious conditions. In parallel, activation of K+ channels induced significant pro-repair effects, including in cultures from pwCF carrying CFTRm non-responsive mutations.

Conclusion: These findings identify CFTR as a central regulator of airway epithelial repair and support combined targeting of CFTR, K+ channels and/or bacterial virulence to restore epithelial integrity, with potential benefits in patients with advanced pulmonary disease or limited responsiveness to current CFTR modulators.

Funding: CIHR, AIRS Network

person.biography:
Emmanuelle Brochiero is a Professor in the department of Medicine of the Université de Montréal and researcher at the Centre de Recherche du CHUM (CRCHUM).
Her research focuses on the pathophysiology of lung diseases, especially cystic fibrosis, acute respiratory distress syndrome and primary graft dysfunction after lung transplantation. Her lab has pioneered ion channel-based therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring functional epithelial integrity in damaged lungs, using complementary state-of-the-art approaches, rare human samples, animal models and innovative preclinical models. The main goal of her projects in cystic fibrosis is to develop innovative therapeutic strategies for improvement of CFTR-targeted treatments and restoration of airway epithelial integrity in infected lungs from patients carrying various types of mutations.
Over the past years, Dr. Brochiero has been supported by research grants including from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR), the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC), the Respiratory Health Network of Québec, the Canadian National Transplant Research Program, and the Association Vaincre le Mucoviscidose.
She is the Director of the Respiratory Tissue and Cell Biobank of CRCHUM. Based on her expertise, she has also been invited to chair the Advisory and Scientific Committee of the Respiratory Health Research Network (RHN) of Québec as well as the CF Strategic Group, and then the research axis on pulmonary infections and pathogens of RHN. She also led the Immunopathology research theme of the CRCHUM over the past five years.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Despite the transformative impact of Highly Effective CFTR Modulator Therapy (HEMT) on people with Cystic Fibrosis (pwCF), persistent pulmonary inflammation remains a critical driver of progressive lung damage. Current anti-inflammatory options are limited by significant side effects, highlighting an urgent need for safe, HEMT-compatible therapies that specifically target the excessive influx of polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs) into the airways. We characterized GY971, a novel anti-inflammatory candidate designed to reduce PMN recruitment by downregulating chemokine expression in respiratory epithelial cells, without the cyclooxygenase (COX) inhibition associated with traditional NSAIDs.

Methods: GY971 was evaluated across several in vitro, ex vivo, and in vivo models, including primary CF bronchial/nasal cells (ALI culture), zebrafish, and murine lung infection models.

Results: Our findings demonstrate that GY971:

-Inhibits the release of PMN-recruiting chemokines at nanomolar concentrations in primary CF epithelial cells.

-Decreases in vivo PMN infiltration in infected models without compromising bacterial clearance.

-Maintains full compatibility with HEMT, showing no interference with F508del-CFTR functional rescue.

-Exhibits a favorable safety profile, with no detectable toxicity in zebrafish or murine organs, no genotoxicity, and no significant off-target activity on the SafetyScreen44™ panel.

Conclusion: The activity of GY971 is mediated by interference with the interaction between activated NF-kB and its consensus DNA sequences within the promoters of key pro-inflammatory cytokines. This mechanism parallels the beneficial effects of high-dose ibuprofen on PMN reduction but avoids the gastrointestinal toxicity linked to COX-1 inhibition. Recognized as an Orphan Drug by the EMA in 2024, GY971 represents a promising, highly specific approach to managing CF airway inflammation.

records.title: Exploring the impact of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor on conception and pregnancy outcomes in Dutch people with cystic fibrosis

session.title: Workshop 11 - The changing face of cystic fibrosis wellbeing, risk and reproductive realities

records.authors_text: S. Schotman1, E.C. Van der Hout1, R.W. Hofland1, M.A. Kruijswijk1, C. Verbeek1, D. Muilwijk1, I. Bronsveld1
records.affiliations_text: 1UMC Utrecht, Pulmonology, Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Utrecht, Netherlands
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: CFTR modulators such as elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) have improved life expectancy and health outcomes for people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF), leading to an increasing number choosing the path of parenthood. This study evaluates maternal, paternal, and neonatal outcomes in pwCF using ETI during conception and/or pregnancy in a large adult CF center with over 300 pwCF in the Netherlands.

Methods: A retrospective medical record study included at least 35 pwCF (25 women, 10 men). Data from before conception until one year postpartum were collected. The main focus was maternal health; these outcomes included FEV₁, pulmonary exacerbations, antibiotic use, BMI, and pregnancy-related complications. Secondly, we wanted to evaluate obstetric and neonatal outcomes and breastfeeding practices. Thirdly, the health and outcomes of fathers using ETI during TESE/PESA procedures were evaluated.

Results: Maternal FEV₁ and body weight of mothers remained stable before, during, and after pregnancy. Pulmonary exacerbations increased during pregnancy and were significantly more frequent postpartum (P=0.03). Gestational diabetes occurred in 30% of pregnancies. Rates of labor induction and caesarean section were relatively high. Except for two cases of ileus in neonates, all pregnancies resulted in healthy infants; 85% were full-term without obstetric complications. Despite recommendations against breastfeeding during ETI therapy, 20% of mothers breastfed. All six men using ETI during TESE/PESA became fathers of healthy infants. Additional data are currently collected and will be available at the conference meeting.

Conclusion: In this cohort ETI use during the perinatal period was associated with stable maternal lung function and weight and favorable neonatal outcomes. Although pulmonary exacerbations increased in mothers, particularly postpartum, nearly all pregnancies resulted in healthy infants, supporting the safety of ETI during pregnancy and parenthood in pwCF.

records.title: Evaluating alternative respiratory sampling methods as surrogates for sputum in adult people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) on elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI)

session.title: Workshop 12 - Finding airway pathogens after ETI: where, when and how should we sample?

records.authors_text: G.G. Einarsson1, K.F. Deasy2,3, S. O'Brien1, E Madden2, Y. McCarthy2,3, F Holmes2, C Fleming2, M McCarthy2, J Dorgan2, T. Vagg2, D.F. Gilpin1, D Murphy2,3, H Ibrahim2,3, B.J. Plant2,3, M.M. Tunney1
records.affiliations_text: 1Queen's University Belfast, School of Pharmacy, Belfast, United Kingdom, 23CF, Department of Respiratory Medicine, Cork University Hospital, Cork, Ireland, 3HRB Clinical Research Facility Cork, University College Cork, Cork, Ireland
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Sputum is the gold standard for routine respiratory microbiology in cystic fibrosis (CF); however, in pwCF on ETI it has become more difficult to obtain in clinical practice. This study compared bacterial burden and pathogen detection using a series of different sampling methods to determine how closely they approximate sputum, in a cohort of pwCF who were Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA) negative on standard hospital culture post-ETI.

Methods: Total bacterial density was calculated by summing colony-forming units across all cultured species per subject (n=32) and sample type, and reported using method-specific units (CFU/g for sputum [SPU], CFU/mL for bronchoalveolar lavage [BAL], bilateral panlobar wash [BLW] and saliva [SAL] and cough swab [SWA] as CFU/mL QSRS diluent). Results are shown as median and IQR range. Core pathogens were defined according to the literature.

Results: Total bacterial burden differed substantially by sampling method. SAL samples showed highest bacterial counts (median 3.7 × 10⁸ CFU/mL; IQR 9.6 × 10⁷-9.5 × 10⁸; n=23). SPU samples also showed high bacterial burden, with a median of 2.9 × 10⁷ CFU/g (IQR 1.3 × 10⁷-5.9 × 10⁷; n=26). BAL and BLW samples yielded substantially lower bacterial counts, with median values of 1.0 × 10⁴ CFU/mL (IQR 3.7 × 10³-3.4 × 10⁴; n=27) and 6.9 × 10³ CFU/mL (IQR 2.0 × 10³-2.4 × 10⁴; n = 27) respectively. SWA samples demonstrated median values of 2.6 x 105 CFU/mL diluent (IQR 2.3 × 10³-1.9 × 106; n=23). For detection of core pathogens, relative to SPU, BAL and BLW detected 33% of core pathogens, compared with 22% for SAL and SWA samples. PA was detected in SPU only from one subject and SPU, BAL and BLW samples from two subjects, but was not detected in either SAL or SWA specimens.

Conclusions: BAL and BLW most closely approximated SPU for lower-airway microbial detection of core pathogens, while SAL provided broader but less specific microbial recovery. No alternative sampling method fully recapitulated SPU.

person.biography: Dr Einarsson (PhD) is a senior research fellow at Queens University Belfast in Northern Ireland with 14 years post-PhD research experience focusing on microbiology, molecular biology and bioinformatics with a key emphasis on large-scale genomic data from bacteria observed in chronic respiratory diseases such as cystic fibrosis, non-CF bronchiectasis and COPD. The main research interests are focused around the resident microbiota of complex communities (microbiological culture and microbiome studies based on marker-gene sequencing), comprehensive community analysis using shotgun-metagenome sequencing (metagenomics), whole-genome sequencing (WGS) of bacterial strains found in chronic infections, resistome analysis (phenotypic traits from extended-culture and genotypic traits from WGS data).

records.title: Development of an unbiased and sensitive AI-based morphological pipeline for challenging cystic fibrosis diagnoses

session.title: Workshop 13 - From allele to human: the complexity of CFTR

person.department: School of Cardiovascular and Metabolic Medicine & Sciences

records.authors_text: M.K. Afzal Mirza1, E. Russell-Jones2, Y. Lei1, S. Spelier3, B. Hayee4, D. Hughes5,6, J. Beekman3, N.J Simmonds2,5, G. Bewick1

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Diagnosing CF can be challenging in individuals carrying rare or poorly characterised CFTR variants, where conventional tests (genetics and sweat chloride test) are inconclusive. Forskolin-induced swelling (FIS) of patient-derived intestinal organoids (PDIOs) is used to determine CFTR function but does not capture steady-state organoid morphology. Previous morphology-based approaches, such as rectal organoid morphology analysis (ROMA), rely on predefined thresholds or manual bias, limiting diagnostic utility . To address this, our consortia (ADVANCE-CFTR), have developed an unbiased AI-based morphological analysis pipeline to sensitively analyse steady state morphology for diagnostic use.

Methods: Calcein green fluorescence images of PDIOs were analysed using this pipeline to extract quantitative morphological features, including lumen/organoid intensity ratios (IR) and size. Morphological profiles were assessed at steady state and following FIS assays. Proof-of-concept analysis was performed using one wild-type (WT) and one CF organoid line (F508del/F508del), with additional assessment following CFTR modulator exposure (ETI).

Results: Compared with ROMA, AI-derived analysis classified a significantly higher fraction of organoids as WT-like across matched images (paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n=10 images, p <0.01). Using this approach, WT and CF organoids were clearly distinguished, with WT organoids characterised by an IR <1 profile. Following CFTR treatment with ETI under FIS, the proportion of CF organoids classified as WT-like increased from 2% to 69%, consistent with functional rescue observed in FIS assays.

Conclusion: AI-based analysis of organoid morphology can distinguish WT from CF organoids in an unbiased way and detect modulator-associated recovery, providing a complementary diagnostic readout to FIS. This proof-of-concept study supports further validation of AI-driven morphology for challenging CF diagnostics.

Objectives: Diagnosing CF can be challenging in individuals carrying rare or poorly characterised CFTR variants, where conventional tests (genetics and sweat chloride test) are inconclusive. Conclusion: AI-based analysis of organoid morphology can distinguish WT from CF organoids in an unbiased way and detect modulator-associated recovery, providing a complementary diagnostic readout to FIS. This proof-of-concept study supports further validation of AI-driven morphology for challenging CF diagnostics.

records.authors_text: P. Bigot1, M. Badaoui1, R. Vivès2, M. Chanson1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Geneva, Department of Cell Physiology and Metabolism, Geneva, Switzerland, 2University of Grenoble, Structural Biology Institut, Grenoble, France
records.abstract_text: Structural changes in the CF lungs result from a protease/anti-protease imbalance favouring recurrent respiratory infections by opportunistic bacteria such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa). We have recently shown that the CF airway epithelium exhibits a defect in apicobasal polarization, characterized by luminal deposition of fibronectin that promotes the adhesion of Pa. Interestingly, it is not fibronectin in its integral form that is responsible for Pa adhesion, but the fragments generated by proteolysis. To target efficiently Pa adhesion, it is crucial to uncover the proteases involved in fibronectin remodelling. We did not observe quantitative changes in proteases secretion by CFTR knockdown (CFTR-KD) airway epithelial Calu-3 cells as compared to control (CFTR-CTL) cells. Using a fluorogenic substrate, however, a tremendous increase in matrix metalloproteases (MMPs) activity was measured in the CF cell secretome. MMPs are secreted as inactive pro-forms and further activated in the extracellular matrix. Using chemicals that activate pro-MMPs into active MMPs, we found that the increased MMPs activity in the CFTR-KD secretome was due to an over-activation of MMPs. Among MMPs, MMP-7, which is critical during the wound repair process, is known to degrade fibronectin. We confirmed that MMP-7 is over-activated in the CFTR-KD secretome whereas its expression was not different from control secretome. Moreover, specific pharmacological inhibition of MMP-7 prevented both fibronectin remodelling as well as PAO1 adhesion. Mechanistically, glycosaminoglycans such as chondroitin sulfate (CS) have been shown to modulate MMP-7 activity in vitro. In this context addition of chondroitinases to the CFTR-KD secretome reduced MMP-7 activity, fibronectin remodeling and PAO1 adhesion. These results indicate that suppression of the MMP-7 overactivity by targeting CS may represent a potential mean to prevent Pa adhesion to the CF airway epithelium.

records.title: Unlocking inflammation in CF: spatially resolved transcriptomics reveals expression of major CF biomarker calprotectin by multiple epithelial cell types in addition to neutrophils

session.title: Workshop 10 - Immune and inflammatory processes in the cystic fibrosis airway: novel insights

records.authors_text: R. Carvajal Quisilema1, N. Robinson1, A. Montes Gomez1, M Brodlie2, I Haq2, C Kennedy Dietrich3, N. Jamieson3, R. Gray1
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Glasgow, School of Infection and Immunity, Glasgow, United Kingdom, 2Newcastle University, Translational and Clinical Research Institute, Faculty of Medical Sciences, Newcastle upon Tyne, United Kingdom, 3University of Glasgow, School of Cancer Sciences, Glasgow, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: Calprotectin (S100A8/A9) is a major biomarker of CF lung disease, being associated with increased inflammation during exacerbation, predicting future exacerbation in people with CF and improvements with CFTR modulators. Although calprotectin is thought to be expressed primarily by neutrophils, advanced spatial and single cell RNA sequencing techniques allow us to refine the expression pattern of calprotectin across multiple cell types in primary lung tissue. This study will define the cellular populations in CF and non-CF expressing calprotectin in the lung and how this relates to inflammation.

Aims: To determine lung cell expression of S100A8/A9 and visualise the spatial expression of S100A8/A9 in the inflamed lung.

Methods: Using publicly available data (Schupp et al and Carrero et al) and our own source data (lung explants) we mapped calprotectin expression across major cell types in the lung. For spatial assessment we employed Naonstring CosMx SMI platform with 6000plex gene panel. A bespoke analysis pipeline was developed for cell margin identification, transcriptional profiling and data visualisation.

Results: Re-analysis of publicly available data demonstrates the expression of S100A8 and S100A9 in granulocytes, monocytes and epithelial cells. S100A9 expression is generally higher than S100A8 expression in epithelial populations. Spatial analysis demonstrates multiple significant differentially expressed genes between healthy and CF samples across multiple cell types including immune cells, epithelial cells and stromal cells. S100A9 is expressed by ciliated, secretory and basal cells as well as transcriptionally active neutrophils. Expression of S100A9 in control epithelial cells was lower with fewer inflammatory cells present.

Conclusions: This data supports the hypothesis that calprotectin may have a multi-faceted role across several cell types and demonstrates the power of spatial technologies in visualising inflammation in the lung.

records.title: A nurse-led initiative to reduce unplanned pregnancies in women with cystic fibrosis

session.title: Workshop 11 - The changing face of cystic fibrosis wellbeing, risk and reproductive realities

records.authors_text: S. Parker1, A. Duffy1, N. Malloy1
records.affiliations_text: 1Royal Victoria Infirmary, Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Newcastle upon Tyne, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Women with CF have suboptimal use of contraception and a significant rate of unplanned pregnancy. We developed a nurse-led initiative to provide advice and initial prescription of contraception to women attending the CF clinic.

Results: Of 50 pregnancies in wwCF attending our Centre, 17 (34%) were not planned, 15 (30%) did not have partner CF gene testing pre-conception and 5 pregnancies were terminated. Of 67 wwCF who were in a heterosexual relationship, 9 (13%) stated that they did not want to become pregnant but were not using contraception and 11(16%) were relying on condom contraception. As part of a service improvement project a CF nurse-prescriber, supported by a gynaecologist, undertook further training in contraception to provide advice to wwCF on their contraceptive options and to offer initial bridging contraception prescription of a progestogen only pill directly from the CF clinic. Discussions during these consultations indicate that some wwCF demonstrate reluctance to engage with family-planning services. Some have misunderstandings about fertility in CF and concerns around contraception and aspects of CF such as absorption of medication, bone health and potential interactions with other CF medications. Areas of ongoing development include staff training, written patient information, and links with women’s health and specialist family planning services.

Conclusions: Currently pregnancy planning and pregnancy prevention are suboptimal, and some wwCF do not access family planning services. A consultation with a CF nurse prescriber, focused on contraception advice and prescription aims to reduce the rate of unplanned pregnancy.

session.title: Workshop 12 - Finding airway pathogens after ETI: where, when and how should we sample?

records.authors_text: T. Bryrup1,2, K. Aanæs3,4, M.V. Kragh1,2, I.H.M. Mathiesen1,2, T. Pressler1,2, M. Kolpen5,6, T. Bjarnsholt5,6, H.K. Johansen4,5, M. Perch4,7, D. Faurholt-Jepsen1,2,4, T. Qvist1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Danish Cystic Fibrosis Cohort, København Ø, Denmark, 2Rigshospitalet, Dept. of Infectious Diseases, København Ø, Denmark, 3Rigshospitalet, Dept. of Otorhinolaryngology, Head & Neck Surgery, and Audiology, København Ø, Denmark, 4University of Copenhagen, Dept. of Clinical Medicine, København Ø, Denmark, 5Rigshospitalet, Dept. of Clinical Microbiology, København Ø, Denmark, 6University of Copenhagen, Costerton Biofilm Center, København Ø, Denmark, 7Rigshospitalet, Dept. of Cardiology, Heart and Lung Transplant Unit, København Ø, Denmark
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa pulmonary infection has long been considered irreversible in People With Cystic Fibrosis (pwCF). After the initiation of the highly effective modulator treatment elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI), pathogen detection rates have declined with some patients even becoming culture negative. This study tests the hypothesis that P. aeruginosa persists in the airways of pwCF previously classified as chronically infected, even when routine cultures have remained negative for at least one year following initiation ETI.

Methods: Prospective, single-centre cohort study (May 2024–June 2025). Including pwCF aged >18 years with prior chronic P. aeruginosa infection, who had become culture-negative for ≥12 months after ETI initiation. Participants underwent a Complete Broncho-Sinus Sampling (CBSS) protocol, including systematic bronchoalveolar lavage of all lung lobes and sinonasal endoscopy, with culture and 16S nanopore sequencing. Daily suppressive antibiotic therapy was paused ≥14 days prior to sampling.

Results: Ten participants (median age 31 years; median duration of prior chronic infection 24 years) were enrolled. No P. aeruginosa was detected by culture in any CBSS sample. 16S sequencing identified a single occurrence of P. aeruginosa (relative abundance 1.9%) from one participant, who subsequently experienced microbiological relapse during follow-up. Across 2,539 cumulative, antibiotic-free, follow-up days and 71 sputum cultures, only this single relapse occurred.

Conclusion: These findings demonstrate that long-standing chronic P. aeruginosa infection can be cleared following ETI. This study adds evidence that chronic infections might not be irreversible and highlights the need to re-evaluate antibiotic treatment guidelines in the era of CFTR modulators.

records.title: The CFTR & chloride conundrum: comparing sweat chloride and clinical phenotype between the D1152H and R117H-7T variants

session.title: Workshop 13 - From allele to human: the complexity of CFTR

person.institution: Royal Brompton Hospital, Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust

records.authors_text: R. Jackson1, L. Carty1, A. Dewar2, L. Weitnauer1, D.A Hughes1,3, N.J Simmonds1,3, J.C Davies1,3
records.affiliations_text: 1Royal Brompton Hospital, Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust, Cystic Fibrosis, London, United Kingdom, 2Poole Hospital, University Hospitals Dorset NHS Foundation Trust, Poole, United Kingdom, 3National Heart and Lung Institute, Imperial College London, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: D1152H and R117H-7T are variants of variable clinical consequence (VVCC) that differ in clinical presentation. Sweat chloride concentration (SCC) is a key diagnostic and prognostic measure for CF. SCC can be variable with VVCCs and more likely to fall in the normal or borderline diagnostic range. We hypothesised that people with D1152H have a lower SCC, yet paradoxically higher rates of bronchiectasis compared to R117H-7T.

Aim: A between-group comparison of SCC and clinical phenotype for the 2 VVCCs.

Methods: A retrospective review of adults and children compound heterozygous for D1152H or R117H-7T and a CF-causing variant attending CF, CFTR-related disorder or CF screen-positive inconclusive diagnosis clinics before January 2024. Data included sex, age at diagnosis, referral route, SCC, FEV1, bronchiectasis and other CFTR-related complications. For some analyses, adults (typically presenting clinically) and children (primarily detected via newborn screening) were considered separately. Data are presented as median [IQR]. Applicable non-parametric tests were used for analysis.

Results: Sixty-nine people were included; 21 with D1152H and 48 with R117H-7T. Of these, 38 were adults (12 D1152H and 26 R117H-7T) and 31 were children (9 D1152H and 22 R117H-7T). There was no association between variant and adult vs children.

Median SCC was lower in those with D1152H (21.2 mmol/L [17.5-27.0]) than R117H-7T (33.0 mmol/L [28.1-53.4]; p<0.001). There was no statistically significant different between SCC in adults and children with D1152H (26.8 vs 19.0 mmol/L, p>0.05). Adults with R117H-7T had significantly higher SCC than children (49.2 mmol/L [32.5–56.8] vs 30.5 mmol/L [23.9–33.0]; p<0.001). CT-confirmed bronchiectasis was present in 6/11 adults with D1152H vs 2/26 with R117H-7T (54.5% vs 7.7%; p=0.0016).

Conclusion: Adults with a D1152H variant have markedly higher rates of bronchiectasis than the R117H-7T group, despite normal median SCC. A normal SCC in D1152H should not be assumed to indicate mild disease and close attention should be paid to those with this variant.

We hypothesised that people with D1152H have a lower SCC, yet paradoxically higher rates of bronchiectasis compared to R117H-7T.
Aim: A between-group comparison of SCC and clinical phenotype for the 2 VVCCs.
Methods: A retrospective review of adults and children compound heterozygous for D1152H or R117H-7T and a CF-causing variant attending CF, CFTR-related disorder or CF screen-positive inconclusive diagnosis clinics before January 2024. Data included sex, age at diagnosis, referral route, SCC, FEV1, bronchiectasis and other CFTR-related complications. For some analyses, adults (typically presenting clinically) and children (primarily detected via newborn screening) were considered separately. Data are presented as median [IQR]. Applicable non-parametric tests were used for analysis.
Results: Sixty-nine people were included; 21 with D1152H and 48 with R117H-7T. Of these, 38 were adults (12 D1152H and 26 R117H-7T) and 31 were children (9 D1152H and 22 R117H-7T). There was no association between variant and adult vs children.
Median SCC was lower in those with D1152H (21.2 mmol/L [17.5-27.0]) than R117H-7T (33.0 mmol/L [28.1-53.4]; p<0.001). There was no statistically significant different between SCC in adults and children with D1152H (26.8 vs 19.0 mmol/L, p>0.05). Adults with R117H-7T had significantly higher SCC than children (49.2 mmol/L [32.5–56.8] vs 30.5 mmol/L [23.9–33.0]; p<0.001). CT-confirmed bronchiectasis was present in 6/11 adults with D1152H vs 2/26 with R117H-7T (54.5% vs 7.7%; p=0.0016).
Conclusion: Adults with a D1152H variant have markedly higher rates of bronchiectasis than the R117H-7T group, despite normal median SCC. A normal SCC in D1152H should not be assumed to indicate mild disease and close attention should be paid to those with this variant.

records.affiliations_text: 1University of Geneva, Department of Cell Physiology and Metabolism, Geneva, Switzerland, 2University of Geneva, Department of Microbiology and Molecular Medicine, Geneva, Switzerland, 3Neuroscience Institute of Castilla y León, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Salamanca, Spain
records.abstract_text: Epithelial polarity is essential for airway epithelial maturation, regeneration, and defense against microbes. In cystic fibrosis (CF), apicobasal polarity is disrupted. The mechanisms and temporal progression of these defects remain poorly defined, particularly in the context of persistent bacterial infections in people with CF (pwCF) even under highly effective CFTR modulator therapy. Using transcriptomic and post-transcriptional analyses of CF human airway epithelial cells, we identified dynamic stabilization of the gap junction protein Connexin 43 (Cx43) during epithelial maturation. Aberrantly sustained Cx43 expression resulted in disorganized collective cell alignment and impaired epithelial barrier integrity. Mechanistically, we uncover a bidirectional crosstalk between Cx43 hemichannel activity and adenosine signaling. This perturbs microtubule organization and disrupts the ER-Golgi secretory pathway leading to ectopic apical fibronectin deposition, a key substrate facilitating Pseudomonas aeruginosa adherence and trapping. Both CRISPR-Cas9 and mimetic peptide–based targeting of Cx43 restored epithelial polarity, normalized fibronectin distribution, and prevented enhanced P. aeruginosa adhesion to the CF epithelium. Together, these findings identify temporally controlled Cx43-mediated intercellular communication as a critical regulator of epithelial polarity and highlight Cx43 as a potential therapeutic target to mitigate persistent infection risk in pwCF.

records.abstract_text:
Background: SPL84 is an inhaled antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) for the treatment of people with pwCF carrying the 3849 +10kb C->T (3849) mutation. SPL84 was shown to fully restore CFTR function in patient-derived human nasal epithelial cells (HNEs) and human bronchial epithelial cells (HBEs). A Phase 1 study was successfully completed in healthy volunteers. SPL84-002 is a global Phase 2a multiple ascending dose study in 3849 pwCF to evaluate the safety and preliminary efficacy of SPL84.

Methods: Participants had diagnosis of CF and two CF causing mutations, with the 3849 mutation on at least one allele, were above age 18, with FEV1 40-90 % predicted, and were not taking CFTR modulators. Two dose cohorts were completed; 25 mg and 50 mg; n=8 in each group, randomized at a ratio of 3:1 active:placebo (6 active, 2 placebo), for a total of 12 participants receiving 9 weekly active doses of SPL84.

Results: There were no drug-related Serious Adverse Event (SAEs) in the study, and there were no significant drug-related AEs.

A meaningful clinical improvement in lung function was observed in ~70% of 25 mg participants and 50% of 50 mg participants, as reflected by change from baseline in ppFEV1 ≥ 5. In both cohorts, an average upward improvement trend in ppFEV1 over time was observed, with an average change from baseline in ppFEV1 of 5 for both cohorts. A positive response in change from baseline in ppFEF25-75 was also observed, which was in general in correlation to the response in ppFEV1. Additionally, ~70% of 25 mg participants and 50% of 50 mg participants had a positive response in the CF Questionnaire-Revised Respiratory Symptom Score (CFQ-R RSS) quality of life measurement.

Conclusions: This is the first evidence of potential clinical benefit of inhaled ASO therapy in a pulmonary disease, supporting advancement of the program to the expanded 3849 patient population. An additional cohort is planned to examine the combined effect of SPL84 and CFTR modulators.

person.title: Prof. Dr.
person.biography: Prof. Kerem, born in Jerusalem, graduated from the Hebrew University-Hadassah Medical School and completed his pediatric residency in Jerusalem, followed by a fellowship at the HSC, Toronto, Canada. He acted as the Chairman of Pediatrics at the Hadassah University Hospital in Jerusalem. He founded the Center for Children with Chronic Diseases integrating all the services needed for the treatment of chronically ill children based on a holistic approach for both the child and his family. The center has grown to be a well-known role-model for training colleague health providers and staff members. Prof. Kerem has published many papers in this field and is known for his advocacy for children in need. He served as a principal investigator in many multi-center clinical trials and is an author of key publications in the field. Recently he is focusing on the clinical aspects of drug development to cure CF. Kerem served as a Board member of ECFS, being in charge of the development of the Patient Registry. Prof. Kerem has a record of building bridges between Israelis and Palestinians. This includes training programs for Palestinian residents and fellows, and organizing collaborative seminars and workshops including a CF team from Gaza. Prof. Kerem is the recipient of the prestigious Ordine Della Stella Della Solidarieta Italiana Award, the “Shalem” award for the development of services for individuals with intellectual disabilities, the ECFS Award acknowledging his remarkable contribution to CF research and received Honorary Fellowship from the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, UK.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) has been shown to be safe and effective in people with cystic fibrosis (CF) aged >6 years with at least one F508del-CFTR allele but there are very few studies in pre-school children (PSC-CF) regarding CF lung structural damage.

The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the impact of ETI on lung structure in children with CF aged 2–5 years.

Methods: Clinical data, pulmonary function tests and sputum induction were performed at baseline (M0) and at 1 year (M12) in 211 children enrolled within the French real-life study, MODUl-CF (NCT04301856). Neutrophil elastase, calprotectin, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8 and TNF-α concentrations were measured at M0 and M12 in sputum secretions.

Results: 63 children experienced transient sleep and or behavior disorders, which were resolved for most of them at M12. Decreases in sweat chloride concentration (-55.2mmol/L; 95% confidence interval [CI],-59.2 to -51.1; n=120 at M12), weight z-score (+ 0.15; 95% CI,+0.07 to +0.22; n = 208) and ppFEV1 (+ 17.8; 95% CI,+6.9 to +28.7; n = 71) were observed at M12.

There was a significant reduction in mucus plugs (p=0.003) and airway wall thickening (p=0.006). at M12 (paired analysis of 55 chest CT). This was correlated with improvements in sputum pro-inflammatory markers. The median ratio of Bronchial outer diameter relative to that of its adjacent Artery (Bout/A) was within normal range at baseline (1.14 (0.94 ; 1.28, n=71) and did not change significantly at M12. Baseline Bout/A was predictive of the decrease of the proportion of severely dilated Bronchial/artery pairs (Bout/A ≥ 1.5) (OR=0.02(95% CI 0.001, 0.23); p=0.006).

Conclusion: Inflammatory airway remodeling improves significantly at 12 months ETI in children 2 to 5 years old. Bronchial dilatation at baseline is predictive of lung structure change at 1 year. Early intervention with ETI may reverse the progression of structural lung disease in young children with CF.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Elexacaftor/Tezacaftor/Ivacaftor (ETI) therapy has greatly changed the course of CF for most people living with this disease. While the impact of ETI on bacterial lung pathogens and the wider microbiota is now being increasingly studied, fungal pathogens and the respiratory mycobiota are poorly understood. Here we investigated changes to the respiratory mycobiome before and through 3 years of ETI therapy in adults with CF (awCF).

Methods: Targeted ITS1 sequencing of the respiratory mycobiome was performed on pre- and on-ETI respiratory samples from 276 awCF attending clinics in the UK (Cardiff, Manchester, Southampton), USA (Vermont, Pittsburgh) and Canada (Calgary). Pre-samples were taken within 6-months prior to starting therapy. On-ETI samples were stratified by duration (6 months, 1 year, 2 years, and 3 years).

Results: Only 169 awCF had a detectable fungal signature, with 32.0% of pre-ETI and 66.3% of on-ETI samples fungal positive. Mycobiota diversity increased with duration on therapy, and composition became significantly more similar over time from 1 year on-ETI (Mann-Whitney p<0.0001, all timepoints from 1 year). Aspergillus fumigatus prevalence reduced on treatment (from 11.6% pre-ETI to 3.3% at 3 years on-ETI). records.title: The challenging case of a child with cystic fibrosis whose mother has come to believe she is a sovereign citizen. How did we get here and what do we do now?

session.title: Workshop 18 - Complex psychosocial issues/nursing case studies

records.authors_text: A. Gravelle1, M. Chilvers1, J. Louie1, T. Theriault1,1
records.affiliations_text: 1British Columbia Children's Hospital, Cystic Fibrosis Clinic, Vancouver, Canada
records.abstract_text:
Background: AG is a 15-year-old child with pancreatic insufficient cystic fibrosis (CF) whose parents are ‘May’ and ‘Ed’. Growing up, AG appeared to be happy and well-cared for in an insular and home-schooled environment. While May believed strongly in naturopathy and AG was unvaccinated, most CF therapies were still accepted. From diagnosis, May voiced strong opinions on perceived lapses in governmental responsibilities. Her first child had been removed from the home by child protection services (CPS). Despite these challenges, the CF team developed a relationship with the family that could be described as built on fragile trust.

May and Ed’s marriage ended during the covid-19 pandemic; Ed became estranged from the family and May experienced significant emotional distress. Over the next three years May and AG moved multiple times and there was great effort to support the family with housing, food security, and legal aid. After several years of no contact Ed called the clinic asking about AG’s health, triggering May and AG to flee. A series of events ensued and CPS became involved. Thereafter, May sent increasingly strange and threatening emails and derogatory phone messages to CF staff indicating she felt betrayed by those on the team she had trusted.

After May stopped bringing AG for CF health visits, a court ordered AG to be examined. May tried to stop this which culminated in AG's removal from May’s care and placement into a group home. Staff reported that AG appeared very traumatized by the forced separation from May. While AG initially continued daily CF care, over time AG stopped all CF therapies (including pancreatic enzymes and elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor). AG refused health assessments and referred to themself as a “stolen child” who would only listen to their mother. When AG’s health was thought to have deteriorated (reported daily coughing and thin appearance), CPS and the CF team met for a complex case consult but before any strategies could be implemented, AG fled the foster home and was reported missing for one week. AG was located at May’s home where she informed police that the no-contact order did not apply as she was a “sovereign citizen” [one who believes they are not subject to government laws]. AG is now back in foster care and refusing all CF therapies; this case is ongoing.

Discussion: The main issues arising from this case study include:

Legal: under the Infants Act, AG could be considered a “mature minor” who can legally refuse healthcare but requires a medical assessment in order to determine competency.

Ethical: all four principles of medical ethics (beneficence; non-maleficence; autonomy; and justice) apply to this complex case.

Mental Health: an assessment is required after which AG could be admitted as an involuntary patient but this could further erode trust and needs to be carefully considered.

Roles of Nursing and Social Work: these have been crucial throughout AG’s life while building a therapeutic relationship with May and AG, and after AG was placed into foster care.

Distress of CF healthcare team who are witnessing in effect AG’s ‘slow suicide’.

Questions:

Did the CF team stray from core components of a therapeutic relationship by not acting sooner on May’s growing ideology?

How could the CF team have intervened differently?

What is the most difficult part of this case?

If AG becomes an ‘involuntary patient’ how can the CF team begin to build trust again?

How can the CF team begin to heal?

person.biography:
Dr. Taylor-Cousar is a tenured professor of adult and pediatric pulmonary medicine at National Jewish Health (NJH), where she serves as the Medical Director of Clinical Research Services, President of the Medical Staff, and is co-director of the Adult Cystic Fibrosis (CF) Program and Director of the CF Therapeutics Development Network (TDN) center. She received her undergraduate degree in human biology from Stanford University, and completed her doctorate in medicine, combined residency in internal medicine and pediatrics, and her combined fellowship in adult and pediatric pulmonary medicine at Duke University. She obtained her Master of Clinical Science from the University of Colorado.
 
Dr. Taylor-Cousar’s expertise is clinical trial design and conduct; she has been national/global primary investigator on multiple CF TDN pharmaceutical trials. Her investigator-initiated research focuses on the development and evaluation of novel therapies for the treatment of CF, and the long-term impacts of these therapeutics on health outcomes in people with CF; she is currently co-leading the 41-site prospective Maternal and Fetal Outcomes in the Era of Modulators (MAYFLOWERS) study. She has published more than 140 manuscripts as well as a book and multiple book chapters. Additionally, she serves on a number of national scientific advisory committees for Emily’s Entourage, the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation, American Thoracic Society and the National Institutes of Health. She is an Associate Editor for the Journal of Cystic Fibrosis and a member of the International Advisory Board for the Lancet Respiratory Medicine.

content.biography:
Dr. Taylor-Cousar is a tenured professor of adult and pediatric pulmonary medicine at National Jewish Health (NJH), where she serves as the Medical Director of Clinical Research Services, President-elect of the medical staff, and is co-director of the Adult CF Program and Director of the CF Therapeutics Development Network (TDN) center.  She received her undergraduate degree in human biology from Stanford University in 1993, and completed her doctorate in medicine in 1998, combined residency in internal medicine and pediatrics in 2002, and her combined fellowship in adult and pediatric pulmonary medicine in 2006 at Duke University Medical Center. She obtained her Master of Clinical Science from the University of Colorado in 2015.
She has been site primary investigator on more than 60 clinical studies, and national/global primary investigator on 5 clinical trials. She is an elected member of the American Society for Clinical Investigation (2020). Her investigator initiated research focuses on the development and evaluation of novel therapies for the treatment of CF, and on the unique health needs of women with CF. She is also investigating the etiology and treatment of bronchiectasis in non-human primates.
 
She serves on numerous local and national committees including as the adult care representative to the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation’s (CFF) Board of Trustees, on the CFF’s Clinical Research Advisory Board, the CFF Racial Justice Working Group, the CF TDN’s Clinical Research Executive Committee and as Immediate Past Chair of the CF TDN’s Women’s Health Research Working Group. She is an Associate Editor for the Journal of Cystic Fibrosis. She serves on the American Thoracic Society (ATS) Scientific Grant Review and Clinical Problems Programming Committees (Chair 2020-2021). She has co-chaired numerous sessions and given invited lectures at the ATS International Conference, the British Thoracic Society conference, and the North American, European, Israeli, Mexican, Spanish, Swiss and Australian CF Conferences, as well as at regional CF and pulmonary conferences and national and international veterinary conferences. She is an active member of the Colorado Chapter CF Board.

records.title: Temporospatial regulation of adenine base editing to identify therapeutic target cells in the airway epithelium

person.title: Mrs.
