person.department: Faculty of Sciences, University of Lisboa

records.authors_text: I. Zollo1, L. Santos1,2,3, J. Alves1,4, P.T Harrison4,5, C.M Farinha1
records.affiliations_text: 1BioISI - Biosystems and Integrative Sciences Institute, Faculty of Sciences, University of Lisboa, Lisbon, Portugal, 2iBET, Instituto de Biologia Experimental e Tecnológica, Oeiras, Portugal, 3Instituto de Tecnologia Química e Biológica António Xavier, Universidade Nova de Lisboa, Oeiras, Portugal, 4Physiology Department, University College Cork, Cork, Ireland, 5Cincinnati Children’s Hospital, Cincinnati, OH, United States
records.abstract_text:
For people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) who lack a causal treatment, gene-based therapies offer the greatest potential for a cure. However, it remains unclear which airway epithelial cell types must be corrected to achieve clinically meaningful CFTR restoration. To address this, we developed a gene editing tool that combines temporal and spatial control of editing in the airway epithelium. We focused on Adenine Base Editing (ABE) to target the W1282X nonsense variant, which is not responsive to current CFTR modulators.

Temporal regulation was achieved using a SplitABE system in which the Cas9 C-term is fused to FKBP and a Nuclear Localization Signal (NLS), while the Cas9 N-term is fused to the ABE domain, FRB and a Nuclear Export Signal (NES). The FKBP/FRB domains enable rapamycin-inducible heterodimerization. For spatial control, the SplitABE/sgRNA cassette was cloned into lentiviral vectors downstream of cell-type–specific promoters1.

The KRT5-driven SplitABE construct, targeting basal cells, was validated in non-differentiated W1282X-BCi cells, confirming correct expression and rapamycin-dependent nuclear dimerization.

To generate stable models, lentiviral particles were produced in 293T cells and used to transduce W1282X-BCi cells. To improve cell selection, hygromycin resistance was replace with TurboGFP, enabling direct monitoring of transduction efficiency and enrichment of positive cells by Fluorescence-Activated Cell Sorting (FACS). Cells electroporated with the TurboGFP-based construct showed higher Cas9 levels, particularly upon rapamycin induction, suggesting improved editing potential.

In conclusion, this temporospatial editing platform provides a powerful tool to define therapeutic target cells for CFTR correction and guide future clinical translation.

1. Zollo I et al (2024) J Cyst Fibr 23 (S2), S162.

Work supported by grant FARINH24G0 from CFF and UID/04046/2025 - Biosystems and Integrative Sciences Institute Centre grant from FCT, Portugal.

person.biography:
My research is centered on advancing personalized therapeutic strategies for cystic fibrosis (CF) through innovative molecular and translational approaches. I have developed strong expertise in CRISPR-based gene editing technologies, including CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) and adenine base editing, contributing to the design of novel strategies to correct disease-causing CFTR mutations, including clinically relevant variants.
In parallel, I have extensive experience with ex vivo human models, particularly human nasal epithelial cell cultures, to investigate CFTR function and evaluate patient-specific responses to existing and emerging therapies. This work has contributed to expanding treatment opportunities for individuals carrying rare and ultra-rare CFTR variants.
Additionally, I have been involved in the identification and functional characterization of uncommon CFTR variants, highlighting limitations in standard diagnostic approaches and supporting improved genetic diagnosis.
Overall, my work integrates gene editing, functional genomics, and patient-derived models to address unmet clinical needs in CF, with the aim of advancing precision medicine and developing more effective, individualized therapeutic strategies.

records.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted chest HRCT analysis in cystic fibrosis patients

session.title: Workshop 16 - Further optimising measures of cystic fibrosis pulmonary disease

records.authors_text: E. Aydınlı Çınaroğlu1, A. Eryılmaz2, Ö. Yapıcı3, R. Yerebasmaz3, C. Vural2, B. Karadağ4
records.affiliations_text: 1Marmara University, Pediatrics, Istanbul, Turkey, 2Marmara University, Faculty of Engineering, Electrical and Electronics Engineering, Istanbul, Turkey, 3Marmara University, Radiology, Istanbul, Turkey, 4Marmara University, Pediatric Pulmonology, Istanbul, Turkey
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is an inherited multisystem disorder primarily affecting the respiratory system. Pulmonary involvement remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in CF patients. High-Resolution Computed Tomography (HRCT) is considered the gold standard for evaluating structural lung abnormalities. However, manual interpretation of HRCT images is time-consuming, observer-dependent, and may result in variable outcomes. Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based automated analysis methods hold the potential to overcome these limitations.

Methods: In this retrospective study, chest HRCT images from 48 patients with CF aged 10 to 18 years, were analyzed. Five distinct pulmonary findings bronchiectasis, bronchial dilatation, bronchial wall thickening, mucus plugging, and attenuation increase in the HRCT images were annotated by two experienced radiologists. A deep learning-based diagnostic model was developed, and its performance was evaluated using sensitivity, specificity, F1 score (a balanced measure of sensitivity and precision), and Jaccard index (overlap between predicted and actual findings) metrics.

Results: The developed deep learning-based model achieved an average accuracy of 97%, sensitivity of 97%, specificity of 97%, and F1 score of 97% across the five evaluated pathological findings in chest HRCT images of CF patients.

Conclusion: This study demonstrates that deep learning-based models can accurately detect multiple pulmonary abnormalities in chest HRCT images of patients with CF. AI-assisted systems have the potential to support clinicians in clinical decision-making, facilitate early identification of complications, and contribute to individualized patient monitoring. Nevertheless, ensuring the safe and responsible use of AI requires careful attention to data security, algorithmic transparency, and rigorous validation processes.

Results: The developed deep learning-based model achieved an average accuracy of 97%, sensitivity of 97%, specificity of 97%, and F1 score of 97% across the five evaluated pathological findings in chest HRCT images of CF patients.
Conclusion: This study demonstrates that deep learning-based models can accurately detect multiple pulmonary abnormalities in chest HRCT images of patients with CF. AI-assisted systems have the potential to support clinicians in clinical decision-making, facilitate early identification of complications, and contribute to individualized patient monitoring. Nevertheless, ensuring the safe and responsible use of AI requires careful attention to data security, algorithmic transparency, and rigorous validation processes.

records.authors_text: L. Rossiter1, D. Nazareth1, M. Ledson1, G. Hyde1, M. Walshaw1, F. Frost1
records.affiliations_text: 1Liverpool Heart and Chest Hospital, Respiratory Medicine, Liverpool, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: Although the initiation of highly effective modulator therapy (ETI) results in the eradication of Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa), a major cause of morbidity and mortality, in some people with Cystic Fibrosis (pwCF), factors which predict successful eradication are not well defined. We evaluated such in our large cohort of adult pwCF commencing ETI.

Methods: Annual review data from 2019 (pre ETI) for 388 pwCF at our centre were compared with the 2025 cohort of 384 receiving ETI and to all respiratory microbiology samples obtained over a 10‑year period (n=11697). Analyses included pwCF chronically infected with Pa pre-ETI, with eradication defined as no positive sputum samples (>=3) post-ETI. Clinical characteristics were compared between those who had/had not eradicated Pa using multivariable logistic regression to determine independent associations.

Results: There were 103 pwCF with chronic infection with sufficient sampling pre/post-ETI. Eradication occurred in 30/103 (29.1%). Those who eradicated were younger (age 30 vs 35, P = 0.0147), had better lung function (ppFEV1 79 vs. 53.0, p<0.0001). 22 had Liverpool epidemic strain Pa of which 27% had eradicated.

Multivariable logistic regression identified Liverpool Epidemic Strain [OR (95%CI) 0.23 (0.05-0.91) p=0.03], ppFEV1 [OR (5%CI) 1.05 (1.01-1.11) p=0.02], baseline Northern Score [OR (95%) 0.73 (0.92-1.1) p=0.049] and CFLD [OR (95%) 5.7 (1.2- 26.6) p=0.02] as independent predictors of sustained infection despite ETI. Age commencing ETI, BMI, pancreatic insufficiency, CFRD and use of nebulised antibiotics were not related to Pa eradication.

Conclusion: A combination of host and microbial factors appear to be relevant for predicting post-ETI eradication of Pa where, in general, markers of milder disease severity increased chances of eradication. The association between CFLD and eradication warrants further investigation and the long-term clinical outcomes of post-ETI eradication require evaluation.

records.title: Reproductive decision-making in advanced cystic fibrosis: an ethical dilemma in a woman seeking pregnancy through in-vitro fertilization

session.title: Workshop 18 - Complex psychosocial issues/nursing case studies

person.title: Professor Pediatric Pulmonologist
person.department: Pediatric Pulmonology and Cystic Fibrosis Center

records.authors_text: M. Cohen-Cymberknoh1, A. Hershko Klement2
records.affiliations_text: 1Hadassah Hebrew University Medical Center, Pediatric Pulmonology and Cystic Fibrosis Center, Jerusalem, Israel, 2Hadassah Hebrew University Medical Center, IVF Unit, Mount Scopus, Jerusalem, Israel
records.abstract_text:
Background: Advances in cystic fibrosis (CF) care have improved survival and quality of life, and more women with CF (wwCF) now pursue pregnancy. Although outcomes have improved overall, wwCF with advanced lung disease and nutritional compromise remain at high risk for maternal morbidity and adverse fetal outcomes. Assisted reproductive technologies (ART), including in vitro fertilization (IVF), are increasingly needed due to higher rates of infertility in wwCF, creating dilemmas where reproductive autonomy intersects with substantial medical risk. We report a 31-year-old wwCF (two class I CFTR mutations, non-responsive to CFTR modulators) with severe lung disease and comorbidities who requested IVF, highlighting the clinical and ethical tension between patient-centered goals and uncertainty in advanced CF.

Discussion: A 31-year-old wwCF (pancreatic insufficiency, CF-related diabetes, BMI ~20 kg/m²) and long-standing severe lung disease (FEV₁ ~25% predicted) sought pregnancy after >1 year of unsuccessful attempts to conceive. Despite multiple pulmonary exacerbations (PEx) requiring intravenous antibiotics over the previous 4 years, she was clinically stable. Her reproductive evaluation was normal, but her partner had severe oligo-terato-asthenospermia (CFTR-mutations negative), making IVF with intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) the only viable option. A multidisciplinary team (CF, fertility, maternal–fetal medicine, ethics) counselled extensively on risks of ovarian stimulation and pregnancy, including respiratory decline, anesthesia/procedural risk, increased PEx, and fetal complications. The team expressed high concern and uncertainty rather than an absolute recommendation against pregnancy. The patient, an orthodox Muslim, declined surrogacy for cultural reasons, and remained committed to biological motherhood. After counselling, she showed sustained behavioral change with improved adherence, modest weight gain, and clinical stabilization with slight lung function improvement over the next year, prompting reassessment of physiologic reserve while acknowledging persistent high risk. This case illustrates a recurring dilemma in contemporary CF care: how to balance respect for autonomy with non-maleficence when pregnancy is desired in the context of severe disease. It also highlights the importance of structured shared decision-making, transparent communication of uncertainty, and institutional ethical support. As increasing numbers of wwCF, some with significant comorbidity, pursue pregnancy and ART, multidisciplinary pathways that integrate CF, fertility, maternal-fetal medicine and ethics are essential, alongside clearer guidance for counselling and risk stratification in advanced CF.

Conclusion: As reproductive aspirations rise among wwCF, high-risk scenarios requiring IVF/ICSI are increasingly encountered. This case underscores the complex interface between patient autonomy, clinician responsibility, and medical uncertainty in severe CF, and suggests that strong patient motivation may meaningfully improve adherence and short-term clinical status, factors that can influence risk assessment. Early fertility counselling, coordinated multidisciplinary care, and clearer frameworks for shared decision-making in advanced disease are urgently needed to support equitable, consistent and ethically grounded care for wwCF pursuing pregnancy.

person.biography:
Prof. Malena Cohen-Cymberknoh, M.D.
Prof. Malena Cohen-Cymberknoh, M.D. is Associate Professor in Pediatrics at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. She is the Head of the Pediatric Pulmonology Unit and the Cystic Fibrosis (CF) Center at Hadassah Ein-Kerem and Mount Scopus Medical Center. Her special research interest fields include Cystic fibrosis, Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia, asthma, and other chronic lung diseases. Prof. Cohen-Cymberknoh is involved in CF research as principal investigator of many national and international multi-center clinical trials, and since 2024, she has been a member of the Executive Committee of the European Cystic Fibrosis Society Clinical Trials Network (ECFS-CTN). She is also involved in international collaborations and teaching CF teams all over the world. Since 2008, Prof. Cohen-Cymberknoh is invited to give lectures and to serve as a moderator in national and international scientific conferences. She received numerous national and international prizes, awards, and research grants. Her scientific publications, more than 100, include several papers published in some of the highest accredited journals e.g., American Journal of Respiratory Critical Care Medicine, Lancet Respiratory Medicine, European Respiratory Journal, Thorax, Chest, Journal of Cystic Fibrosis, Respiratory Medicine, PlosOne, and Pediatric Pulmonology.

records.title: Clinical-stage NBD1 stabilizers can increase F508del-CFTR protein half-life to wild-type levels when used alone or in combination with other CFTR modulators

person.title: SVP Research and Co-founder Sionna Therapeutics

records.authors_text: S. Bercury1, A. Madanjian1, S. Altmann1, J. Foley1, A. Hunnicutt1, J. Liao1, Z. Gao1, G. Topalov1, M. Munson1, G. Hurlbut1
records.affiliations_text: 1Sionna Therapeutics, Waltham, United States
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: F508del, the most prevalent CF-causing mutation, leads to a loss of F508 within CFTR’s first nucleotide-binding domain (NBD1). This destabilizes NBD1, impairing CFTR folding and weakening NBD1’s interface with CFTR transmembrane domains. In preclinical studies, combining suppressor mutations that stabilize NBD1 with others that improve CFTR assembly has been shown to correct F508del to wild-type (WT) levels. Without NBD1 stabilization, correction of F508del was significantly reduced. Approved modulators have significantly improved outcomes for people with CF (pwCF), but do not restore normal CFTR function in two-thirds of patients. No approved modulator directly stabilizes NBD1. With the goal of further improving CFTR function to deliver meaningful clinical benefit to pwCF, Sionna has advanced two potent first-in-class small molecule NBD1 stabilizers, SION-451 and SION-719, into clinical trials. Here we assess their impact on F508del-CFTR protein half-life in the presence and absence of CFTR domain assembly correctors.

Methods: Using metabolic pulse-chase labeling, we assessed the impact of SION-451 and SION-719 on the half-life of mature F508del-CFTR in the presence and absence of TMD1-directed corrector SION-2222, ICL4-directed corrector SION-109, or ETI.

Results: We demonstrate that NBD1 stabilizers can increase the half-life of the F508del-CFTR to levels seen with WT CFTR. This effect was apparent even when NBD1 stabilizers were used as single agents, an effect not observed with ETI.

Conclusions: We have previously shown that SION-451 or SION-719, in combination with complementary modulators, enable full correction of F508del-CFTR maturation, trafficking and function in preclinical CF models. Here we show robust increases in CFTR half-life in vitro in response to treatment with NBD1 stabilizers that was not seen in response to ETI treatment alone, suggesting NBD1 instability is a central driver of F508del-CFTR’s greatly increased degradation rate.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) has transformed cystic fibrosis (CF) care, with significant improvements observed across multiple clinical outcomes. However, reports of its potential effect on structural lung disease, including bronchiectasis (Bx) and bronchial wall thickening (BWT), remain sparse. We assess ETI’s impact on Bx and BWT among people with CF (pwCF) in Denmark, hypothesising that ETI reduces Bx and BWT severity as evaluated by high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT).

Methods: One baseline and one follow-up HRCT scan were included for each pwCF. All scans were performed during clinician-assessed clinical stability and evaluated for structural lung abnormalities using automatic bronchus-artery ratio (BA) scoring. Outcomes included %Bx1.1 and %Bx1.5, defined as the percentage of bronchi with an outer diameter widening of ≥1.1 and ≥1.5 times that of the adjacent artery, respectively, and %BWT, defined as the percentage of bronchi with wall thickening.

Preliminary Results: By now, 312 HRCT scans from 156 pwCF (54 children, 102 adults; 53% females) have been evaluated, nearly half of our cohort. Median (IQR) time between HRCT and ETI initiation was -0.17 (-0.5; -0.07) years for baseline and 1.02 (0.97; 1.16) years for follow-up. Mean (95%CI) %Bx1.1 decreased from 61.6% (58.3; 64.9) pre-ETI to 56.2%(49.5; 62.9)% post-ETI, a reduction of -5.43 (-8.81; -2.05), p=0.0018. Mean %Bx1.5 changed from 24.2% (21.6; 26.8) to 23.2% (18.3; 28.0) post-ETI, with non-significant difference of -0.98 (-3.21; 1.24), p=0.3842. In contrast, mean %BWT decreased markedly from 74.6% (71.5; 77.7) pre-ETI to 57.2% (51.1; 63.3) post-ETI, yielding a substantial reduction of -17.5 (-20.4; -14.5), p<0.0001.

Conclusion: ETI reduces bronchial widening and wall thickening after the first year of ETI treatment, though larger bronchiectasis persists. Further analyses and longer follow-up will increase our understanding of ETI’s effect on structural lung disease in pwCF.

Objectives: Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) has transformed cystic fibrosis (CF) care, with significant improvements observed across multiple clinical outcomes. However, reports of its potential effect on structural lung disease, including bronchiectasis (Bx) and bronchial wall thickening (BWT), remain sparse. We assess ETI’s impact on Bx and BWT among people with CF (pwCF) in Denmark, hypothesising that ETI reduces Bx and BWT severity as evaluated by high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT).
Methods: One baseline and one follow-up HRCT scan were included for each pwCF. All scans were performed during clinician-assessed clinical stability and evaluated for structural lung abnormalities using automatic bronchus-artery ratio (BA) scoring. Outcomes included %Bx1.1 and %Bx1.5, defined as the percentage of bronchi with an outer diameter widening of ≥1.1 and ≥1.5 times that of the adjacent artery, respectively, and %BWT, defined as the percentage of bronchi with wall thickening.
Preliminary Results: By now, 312 HRCT scans from 156 pwCF (54 children, 102 adults; 53% females) have been evaluated, nearly half of our cohort. Median (IQR) time between HRCT and ETI initiation was -0.17 (-0.5; -0.07) years for baseline and 1.02 (0.97; 1.16) years for follow-up. Mean (95%CI) %Bx1.1 decreased from 61.6% (58.3; 64.9) pre-ETI to 56.2%(49.5; 62.9)% post-ETI, a reduction of -5.43 (-8.81; -2.05), p=0.0018. Mean %Bx1.5 changed from 24.2% (21.6; 26.8) to 23.2% (18.3; 28.0) post-ETI, with non-significant difference of -0.98 (-3.21; 1.24), p=0.3842. In contrast, mean %BWT decreased markedly from 74.6% (71.5; 77.7) pre-ETI to 57.2% (51.1; 63.3) post-ETI, yielding a substantial reduction of -17.5 (-20.4; -14.5), p<0.0001.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Elexacaftor/Tezacaftor/Ivacaftor (ETI) provides clinical benefits for people with Cystic Fibrosis (pwCF), although treatment response varies, possibly due to lung microbiological features. We investigated Pa adaptation to ETI by integrating genomic, transcriptomic, phenotypic, and clinical data to identify adaptive traits and explain outcome variability.

Methods: Fifty-four clonal Pa isolates were collected from 11 pwCF before and up to 28 months after ETI initiation. Phenotypic traits associated with acute and chronic infection were analyzed. Whole-genome and RNA sequencing of 35 isolates tracked within-host evolution. Six isolates were exposed in vitro to ETI to assess possible direct impacts. Clinical outcomes were evaluated and associations with bacterial features were explored using Factorial Analysis of Mixed Data.

Results: Pa adaptation to ETI was strain-dependent, with limited overlap across clonal lineages. However, conserved pathways related to metabolism, virulence, and antibiotic resistance were consistently affected at genomic and transcriptomic levels. Phenotypic changes included biofilm modulation, variable pyocyanin production, and altered antibiotic susceptibility. In vitro ETI exposure induced transcriptional and genetic changes partially overlapping with in vivo findings, supporting a direct ETI effect. Clinically, pwCF showed significant improvement, with a median 15.5% increase in FEV₁ and reduced exacerbations, hospitalizations, and intravenous antibiotic use. Greater benefit was associated with isolates lacking mucoidy and LasR-associated phenotypes, hypermutability, and reduced pyocyanin production.

Conclusion: While ETI markedly improves clinical outcomes, Pa persists through flexible, strain-specific adaptive mechanisms. Monitoring pathogen evolution during ETI therapy may support precision management of chronic infection in CF. Study supported by the Italian CF Foundation (FFC#16/2021) and the ECFS/CF Europe Research Fellowship.

records.affiliations_text: 1New Cross Hospital, Respiratory, Wolverhampton, United Kingdom, 2Royal Stoke University Hospital, Respiratory, Stoke-on-Trent, United Kingdom, 3Chelsea and Westminster Hospital, London, United Kingdom, 4Royal Brompton Hospital, Respiratory, London, United Kingdom, 5National Heart and Lung Institute, Imperial College London & NIHR Biomedical Research Centre, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Introduction: Burkholderia cenocepacia (Bcc) in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF), can increase mortality. CFTR modulators have changed the course of CF, with women living in better health increasingly pursuing pregnancy. Literature on pregnancy in pwCF and Bcc is limited. A case series, published by Tanser et al. (2000), reported 4 deaths in pregnancy; 3 colonised with Bcc. A case report by Ciaverell et al. (2025), describes a successful pregnancy in pwCF with Bcc on CFTR modulators complicated by pre-term labour.

Case: A 34-year-old pwCF first colonised with Bcc in 2017 elected to have a child by IVF and surrogacy in 2020, prior to CFTR modulators, due to uncertain pregnancy outcomes in pwCF and Bcc. In November 2020 she started Elexacaftor/Tezacaftor/Ivacaftor (ETI) and whilst sputum volume was reduced, bronchoscopy in June 2023 confirmed persistent Bcc colonisation. This impacted shared-decision making regarding her wish to try for biological pregnancy. Advice was sought via a dedicated CF Maternal Health service in the UK who shared experience of successful CF-maternal pregnancies in the context of Bcc infection.

She subsequently underwent updated preconception counselling, and the decision was made to plan for natural conception and to continue ETI during pregnancy.

Spirometry was well preserved pre-conception (FEV1 92% predicted (2.84L)) and remained stable antenatally with average FEV1 90% predicted (2.78L) in third trimester. Weight during third trimester was 80kg. Pregnancy was not complicated by gestational diabetes mellitus and she had no exacerbations during pregnancy requiring hospital admission. CFQ-R score in vitality and emotion domains during pregnancy were 83% and 87% respectively.

In February 2025 at 42 weeks’ gestation, she gave birth via spontaneous vaginal delivery. Baby did not require NICU but was observed for 12 hours due to meconium-stained amniotic fluid. Post-partum progress was encouraging with no decline in spirometry pulmonary exacerbation requiring hospital admission within the first year.

Discussion: This pwCF and Bcc colonisation taking ETI, was able to conceive and have a full-term pregnancy. This pwCF and Bcc colonisation taking ETI, was able to conceive and have a full-term pregnancy. During pregnancy, her FEV1 remained stable and there were no exacerbations requiring hospital admission and first year post-partum.

The collaborative approach offered by a UK dedicated CF Maternal Health service, sharing their experience of Bcc CF-pregnancies in ETI-era, was fundamental to contextualise and individualise shared decision making regarding our patients' reproductive goals and maternity choices. The development of a formalised framework for a National Specialist Maternal CF MDT could provide further support in decision making for pwCF and their care teams in relation to notable pathogens in the future.

records.title: A randomised 28-day, double-blind cross-over study to evaluate the safety, efficacy & pharmacokinetics of ETD001, an inhaled ENaC blocker, in people with cystic fibrosis

person.title: Prof. Dr.
person.institution: Imperial College London & Royal Brompton Hospital

records.authors_text: R. Gupta1, S. Sutharsan2, M. Cipolli3, K. Woodward1, P. Russell1, H. Danahay1, M. Gosling1, M.A Mall4, J.C Davies5
records.affiliations_text: 1Enterprise Therapeutics, Falmer, United Kingdom, 2Division of Cystic Fibrosis, Department of Pulmonary Medicine, University Medicine Essen -Ruhrlandklinik, Essen, Germany, 3Cystic Fibrosis Center, Azienda Ospedaliera Universitaria Integrata, Verona, Italy, 4Charite-Universitatsmedizin, Berlin, Germany, 5Imperial College London & Royal Brompton Hospital, National Heart and Lung Institute, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: ETD001 is a blocker of the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) that is predicted to show a long duration of activity in the airways following inhalation (1). This study is the first to administer ETD001 to people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF), and was designed to be run in two parts: Parts A and B. In both parts only pwCF ≥18 years with ppFEV1 ≥ 40% and ≤ 90% of normal and who were not taking CFTR modulator therapy were included.

Methods and results: Part A enabled a first evaluation of the safety, tolerability and PK of repeat doses of ETD001 over 7 days in pwCF. ETD001 (4.5 mg) was delivered as an inhaled aerosol generated by a Pari eFlow nebuliser, over 2-3 minutes, twice daily (BiD). Part A enrolled 10 pwCF (3 placebo, 7 treated) with a mean (±SD) age of 37.1 (11.9) years and mean BMI (±SD) of 21.5 (2.4) kg/m². ETD001 was well tolerated, with no safety signals to prevent progression into Part B. A single serious adverse event (pulmonary exacerbation) was reported during the post-treatment phase that was considered unlikely related to treatment. There was no incidence of hyperkalaemia.

Part B used a double-blind, placebo-controlled, cross-over design to examine the effect of repeat BID dosing of ETD001 (4.5 mg) over 28 days on absolute change in ppFEV1 in addition to safety and PK. Participants were randomised to receive either placebo or ETD001 for 28 days in a 2 group, 2 sequence cross-over design, with a 28-day washout period. The primary objective was to understand whether ETD001 delivers a clinically meaningful, and statistically significant change in ppFEV1 from baseline to day 28 compared to placebo. Part B enrolled a total of 47 pwCF with a mean (±SD) age of 35.0 (10.4) years, mean BMI (±SD) of 21.4 (3.0) kg/m² and mean (±SD) ppFEV1 of 61.2 (14.8)%.

Conclusions: Data are being analysed as of the time of abstract submission and will be presented in full at the meeting.

person.biography:
Prof Davies works between the National Heart & Lung Institute, Imperial College London and the Royal Brompton Hospital, London, UK. Jane trained in paediatric respiratory medicine, with additional posts in infectious diseases and immunology, before settling on cystic fibrosis as a speciality. The Brompton clinic is one of the largest in Europe, caring for almost 900 people from infancy to late stage disease.
Her main areas of research interest are chronic lung infection and clinical trial design. She leads a UK CF Trust funded Strategic Research Centre for Pseudomonas, a multidisciplinary group seeking to improve detection, understanding and therapy of this prevalent organism. records.title: ​Respiratory abnormalities in subjects referred for congenital absence of the vas deferens and carrying two CFTR mutations

session.title: Workshop 16 - Further optimising measures of cystic fibrosis pulmonary disease

records.authors_text: E. Krantschenko1, A. Pagin1, T. Perez1, C. Leroy1, F. Marcelli1, O. Le Rouzic1, C. Audousset1
records.affiliations_text: 1CHU de Lille, Lille, France
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: The majority of patients with congenital absence of the vas deferens (CAVD) have two mutations in the CFTR gene and are diagnosed with a CFTR-RD. CAVD has been associated with mild respiratory disease assessed by spirometry and physical evaluation.

The objective of this study is to characterize respiratory abnormalities on CT scans in subjects with CAVD carrying two CFTR mutations.

Method: We conducted a single-center retrospective study of 122 subjects referred to CAVD assessment for which two CFTR mutations were identified from 2002 to 2025 (next-generation sequencing). They underwent a systematic evaluation of CFTR-related organ dysfunction (medical history, sweat test, chest CT scans, spirometry). CT scan abnormalities were classified as presence of bronchiectasis, mucus plugging or airway wall thickening based on radiology reports. Airflow obstruction was defined by FEV1/FVC<0.70.

Results: Among the 122 subjects, 119 was classified as CFTR-RD. The median age was 32 years [29;35], mean FEV1 was 4.23 L (±0.58) and 101% predicted (±12.3). The median value for sweat test was 65.5 mEq/L [47.2;91]. The most common mutations were F508del (53%, n=64) associated in trans with a TG12T5 mutation (34%, n=38), R117H (21%, n=19), and D443Y, G576A, R668C (15%, n=11). The prevalent CT scan abnormalities were airways wall thickening, bronchiectasis, and bronchiolectasis in 13% (n=15), 4% (n=5) and 4% (n=5) of cases, respectively. Twenty percent (n=23) had CT scan abnormalities, including 3 subjects with airflow obstruction and 5 with respiratory symptoms.

Conclusion: Among subjects with CAVD and carrying two CFTR mutations, 20% had abnormal CT scan among them, 5% had an airflow obstruction. The initial assessment of airway involvement in patients with CAVD carrying two CFTR gene mutations should include a chest CT scan and pulmonary function tests that are more sensitive than spirometry.

records.title: Microbial and host functional signatures in three distinct pulmotypes revealed by metaproteomics during elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor therapy in patients with cystic fibrosis

session.title: Workshop 17 - Airway microbiology in the CFTR modulator era: pathogen dynamics, adaptation and the changing microbiome

person.department: Département Médicaments et Technologies pour la Santé (DMTS)

records.authors_text: L. Grenga1, H. Hachemi1, H. Marchandin2, O. Ardizzoni1, J. Armengaud1, R. Chiron3
records.affiliations_text: 1Université Paris-Saclay, CEA, INRAE, Département Médicaments et Technologies pour la Santé (DMTS), Bagnols sur Cèze, France, 2HydroSciences Montpellier, Université de Montpellier, CNRS, IRD, Service de Microbiologie et Hygiène hospitalière, CHU de Nîmes, Montpellier, France, 3HydroSciences Montpellier, Université de Montpellier, CNRS, IRD, Centre de Ressources et de Compétences de la Mucoviscidose, CHU Montpellier, Montpellier, France
records.abstract_text:
Background: Elexacaftor/Tezacaftor/Ivacaftor (ETI) therapy has shown clinical benefit for numerous patients with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). While its impact on the airway microbiome is increasingly investigated, the influence of the microbiome on the therapy effectiveness and its potential prognostic value for clinical outcome, remain poorly understood.

Methods: Sputum samples from 54 pwCF were collected at different time points. Samples underwent metaproteomic analysis to characterize the dynamic of the microbiome profile. Metaproteomic data were integrated with clinical parameters, including lung function (ppFEV1) microbiology and antibiotic use.

Results: ETI therapy was associated with significant increase in microbiome alpha diversity and anaerobes abundance. Longitudinal analysis identified three distinct pulmotypes based on microbiome trajectories, one associated with lower lung function (ppFEV1 <70%) and two associated with higher initial ppFEV1 values. In addition, patients showing ppFEV1 improvements after ETI initiation displayed distinct functional dynamics compared to those who did not. Machine-learning models leveraging these longitudinal profiles accurately predicted ppFEV1 values at the individual level.

Conclusions: Under ETI therapy, the airway microbiome undergoes heterogeneous, patient-dependent changes that can be captured by distinct pulmotypes. Importantly, microbial functional activity emerged as a strong predictor of clinical outcomes, supporting the potential of microbiome-based stratification and prognostic tools in CF.

records.title: Addressing disengagement and health decline: what are we missing?!

session.title: Workshop 18 - Complex psychosocial issues/nursing case studies

records.authors_text: H. Green1, M. CLegg1, H. Oxley1, F. Dowdall1, W. Foo1, F. Lewis1, A. Orr1, H. Winterbottom1, A. Jones1
records.affiliations_text: 1Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust, Manchester Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Manchester, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Background: In our large adult cystic fibrosis (CF) centre, we adhere to national guidelines on the management of CF. However, "standard CF care" does not suit all patients. We have a cohort of patients that deteriorate rapidly despite receiving standard CF MDT care. Typical patient characteristics include poor adherence, unstable lung function, low or falling BMI, frequent exacerbations and reliance on frequent rescue intravenous (IV) antibiotics, frequent non attendance at appointments, psychological and/or social difficulties and difficulty communicating honestly with the MDT. We have created a bespoke outpatient service to engage such patients and support adherence called BOOST (Better Outpatient Outcome Support Team). BOOST consists of a consultant, specialist nurses, physiotherapist, occupational therapist, dietitian and the psychosocial team. Any MDT member can refer a patient to BOOST. Each enrolled patient receives intensive home support using a combination of weekly texts or calls, regular face to face reviews in a day case setting or home visits. Patients have open access to contact all MDT members in working hours. Biweekly MDT meetings are held to discuss progress, problems, patient feedback and priorities. Mel, who is ineligible for CFTR modulators, was one of the first patients enrolled on this programme in 2020 and had poor adherence, high IV antibiotic requirements, accelerated FEV1 decline and frequent non attendance in clinic. With intensive support Mel had periods of stability but these were short lived and although her engagement with the CF team hugely improved she was unable to sustain adherence. With growing experience of managing similar patients within this service, and the extremely high proportion of disengaged and non adherent patients we have found to be neurodiverse, we screened Mel for ADHD despite her displaying no significant physical hyperactivity. In the 12 months prior to her ADHD assessment Mel had 6 courses of rescue IV antibiotics, achieving a maximum end of IV antibiotic treatment FEV1 of 50% predicted. Mel was diagnosed with ADHD at her assessment and commenced on Methylphenidate and was then able to put into practice all the things she had worked on with the BOOST MDT. Her lung function increased to 61% predicted and in the 12 months post treatment initiation for ADHD successfully maintained an FEV1 >50% predicted with no courses of intravenous antibiotics.

Discussion: We have had very successful outcomes with providing intensive MDT support to a selected group of disengaged and rapidly deteriorating patients with CF. In our experience “completely disengaged” patients often have a very in depth knowledge of their disease, objective measurements and prognosis. With individualized intensive support, habits of a lifetime and prognosis can be changed. We have found that patients communicate very well by text message (often better than verbally). A combination of positivity, praise, frequent communication (between MDT members and to the patient), joint problem solving and visual feedback are key factors in improving these patients’ outcomes. Recognising and treating ADHD in non adherent, disengaged patients can have a significant positive impact on their physical and mental health.

Conclusion: Using an alternative approach with rapidly deteriorating, non-adherent, disengaged patients and screening for and treating ADHD can result in significant improvements in patient outcomes and satisfaction.

records.title: SPL5AC, MUC5AC lowering ASO for cystic fibrosis and other muco-obstructive diseases
records.authors_text: E. Ozeri Galai1, Y.S. Oren1, N. Liu2, C.D Stampfer1, R.M. Elgrabli1, T. Blinder1, S.A. Jubeh1, T. Mordechai1, C.M. Evans2, B. Kerem1,3, G. Hart1
records.affiliations_text: 1Splisense, Haddasah Ein Kerem, Jerusalem, Israel, 2University of Colorado, Division of Pulmonary Science and Critical Care Medicine, Colorado, United States, 3Hebrew University, Genetics, Jerusalem, Israel
records.abstract_text:
Background: Airway mucus is a key defense barrier and is primarily composed of the mucins MUC5AC and MUC5B. In cystic fibrosis (CF), impaired CFTR function causes airway dehydration and increased mucin concentration. In addition, goblet cells and glandular hyperplasia in CF and other muco-obstructive diseases (asthma, COPD, NCFB) drives mucin overproduction. An elevated MUC5AC-to-MUC5B ratio in patients leads to thick, obstructive mucus and chronic infection and inflammation, with higher MUC5AC levels and mucus plugging correlating with increased disease severity. Splisense is developing an antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) to specifically reduce MUC5AC, aiming to improve mucus clearance and relieve airway obstruction and inflammation.

Methods: The efficacy and durability of SPL5AC was tested in IL-13 induced HBE cells and in muco-obstructive disease mouse models (IL-13, ovalbumin, Aspergillus and House dust mite) by analyzing MUC5AC RNA and protein (Western Blot or immunohistochemical staining). The effect on airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR) was analyzed using a FlexiVent.

Results: SPL5AC, the clinical lead candidate, demonstrated robust efficacy and durability in multiple in vitro and in vivo disease models. In IL-13–induced HBE cells, SPL5AC penetrated the thick apical mucus layer and reduced MUC5AC RNA and protein. In vivo, SPL5AC lowered Muc5ac expression, reduced mucus plugging and inflammation, and inhibited methacholine-induced airway hyperresponsiveness. Pharmacodynamic analyses showed high potency and stability, with durable effects lasting at least 28 days, supporting dose selection and regimen for Phase 1/2 studies.

Conclusions: Restoring proper mucus viscoelasticity and clearance in the lungs of patients with muco-obstructive diseases like CF, remains a major goal. Our results demonstrate that SPL5AC ASO has a potential therapeutic benefit for CF and other muco-obstructive patients with the objective to advance to first in Human in 2026.

records.title: Using free-breathing 3D magnetic resonance imaging to assess proximal airway dynamics in health and cystic fibrosis

session.title: Workshop 16 - Further optimising measures of cystic fibrosis pulmonary disease

person.department: POLARIS, University MRI, Division of Clinical Medicine

records.authors_text: Y. Brown1, N. Stewart1, D.J. Jakymelen1, L. Smith1, J. Wild1, MAGNIFY Strategic Research Centre
records.affiliations_text: 1University of Sheffield, POLARIS, University MRI, Division of Clinical Medicine, Sheffield, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: To quantify static and dynamic airway morphology using 1H-MRI in healthy volunteers (HV) and people with Cystic Fibrosis (CF).

Method: 3D Ultrashort Echo-Time (UTE) MRI of the lungs was acquired during tidal breathing and reconstructed at both end-inspiration (EIVT) and end-expiration (FRC). Synopsys’ Simpleware™ and a custom python script were used to segment and quantify the size and shape of visible airways. The ellipse axis ratio (EAR) quantified airway shape (EAR=1 represents a circle and 0 a line). The lumen cross-sectional area (CSA) quantified size. To account for differences in patient size, the CSA of each airway was normalised by the CSA of the trachea and the dynamic change in CSA was found using EIVT - FRC/EIVT(trachea).

Results: The median (IQR) of HV/CF subjects are: M:F=3:2/4:6, age=34 (34-39)/24 (23-38) years, BMI=24.2 (22.9-24.7)/23.5 (20.4-25.9) kg/m2, FEV1pp=74 (55-89) %. At both EIVT and FRC, 100% of airways were segmentable to the 3rd generation and 37.5% (HV) and 62.5% (CF) to the 4th generation. Greater variance in lumen size and shape was observed across the CF cohort when compared to the HV cohort. Median (IQR) EAR at FRC and normalised change in CSA in the trachea respectively were 0.83 (0.12), 0.04 (0.07) in CF and 0.88 (0.04), 0.04 (0.01) in HV. At generation 4, normalised CF airways were larger and had a greater dynamic change in CSA when compared to HV. Those with lower FEV1pp had the largest CSA and the largest dynamic change. At generation 4, EAR at FRC was lower in CF compared to HV: 0.06 (0.01), CF: 0.07 (0.04), suggesting these airways are more elliptical compared to HV.

Conclusion: Using 1H UTE-MRI, airway morphology can be segmented to the 4th generation and often beyond enabling dynamic airway analysis. session.title: Workshop 17 - Airway microbiology in the CFTR modulator era: pathogen dynamics, adaptation and the changing microbiome

records.authors_text: A. Mundell1, D. Fenn2, J. Ish-Horowicz2, M. Mossop2, N. Ramadan1, M. Rosenthal1, T. Semple3, C. Short2, J. Davies1,2, J. King1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1Royal Brompton Hospital, Paediatric Respiratory, London, United Kingdom, 2National Heart and Lung Institute, Imperial College London, London, United Kingdom, 3Royal Brompton Hospital, London, United Kingdom
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Investigate the association of baseline structural lung disease with changes to Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa) isolation frequency following elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) in people with chronic Pa infection.

Methods: Retrospective cohort analysis of 136 people with CF at Royal Brompton Hospital with Leeds defined chronic Pa infection in ≥1 of 2 years pre- individualised ETI start date. Using computerised tomography (CT) reports pre-ETI initiation, subjects were classified as diffuse or focal bronchiectasis (Bx) and the proportion of total cough swab/sputum samples provided in years -2 pre- and +2 post-ETI start date that were Pa positive (+) was calculated as median[IQR}% per person per year, pppy). Data normality was checked (Shapiro-Wilk) and groups based on Bx distribution were compared using Mann Whitney (for proportions pppy) and Chi square tests (for apparent clearance).

Results: Of 136 people (67:69 M:F, mean age 41.3 years, range 16-83 years), 131 had pre-ETI CT imaging within 6.5 years; reports described 85 diffuse Bx, 41 focal Bx, 2 none and 1 not specified. Fewer samples pppy were collected post-ETI (year -2, 8.0[4.5], +2, 3.1[2.2]), with no difference in provision by Bx distribution. Pre-ETI (year -2) 100[23.8]% samples pppy were Pa+; no difference by Bx distribution. Post-ETI (year +2) people with focal Bx had fewer Pa+ samples pppy (33.3[100]%) than those with diffuse Bx (100[73.9]%; p<0.05). 22 people had no Pa+ samples in year +2. This apparent clearance was more likely with focal (n=14, 34.1%) than diffuse (n=8, 9.4%) Bx (OR 5.0 [95% CI 1.9-13.3], p<0.001).

Conclusion: Focal Bx appears associated with greater reduction in Pa isolation frequency and greater apparent clearance following ETI treatment in people with chronic Pa infection. Formal CT scoring (PRAGMA-CF) is now underway to examine effect of Bx distribution as well as severity, wall thickening, and mucus plugging on Pa isolation frequency (results available for conference).

records.title: Challenging adult cystic fibrosis cases with chronic kidney disease

session.title: Workshop 18 - Complex psychosocial issues/nursing case studies

records.authors_text: B. Akyol1, Y. Yalçın1, A. Alkan1, O. Karcıoğlu1
records.affiliations_text: 1Hacettepe University, Chest Diseases, Ankara, Turkey
records.abstract_text:
Background: Although hepatic side effects of modulator drugs used in cystic fibrosis (CF) treatment are known, renal side effects have not been clearly described. Dosage adjustment of modulator drugs based on glomerular filtration rate(GFR) has not been defined. Here we share the clinical outcomes of our patients with low GFRs who are on modulators.

Discussion: Patient 1: A 35-year-old male, diagnosed CF at 6 months. His mutations were F508del and 2789+5G>A that are eligible for Trikafta that he is on since May 2024. In 2007 during follow-ups, proteinuria was detected and a kidney biopsy revealed focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. Until 2023, he was not a on dialysis routinely, but occasionally presented with flank pain and later told he needed a kidney transplant. In April 2025, he started undergoing hemodialysis 3/7 routinely. His renal function tests remained at baseline levels. Neither a decrease in FEV1, nor any exacerbations were observed during the hemodialysis periods.

Patient 2: A 31-year-old male, born in Saudi Arabia, with a homozygous F508del mutation, was diagnosed CF after birth. In 2022, his creatinine levels was increased, prompting a kidney biopsy, then revealed a diagnosis of IgA nephropathy. He was started Trikafta in August 2024, but treatment was interrupted due to a court order requiring the drug to be obtained at that time. During follow-ups, an indication for kidney transplantation emerged, and he was started on peritoneal dialysis until the transplant. With the inclusion of Trikafta in Türkiye’s reimbursement coverage, Trikafta resumed almost simultaneously with peritoneal dialysis. Since there is no defined protocol on the dosage adjustment of Trikafta in patients with low GFRs, Trikafta was administered once in two days for a month with close monitoring. Then the dosage was raised to full regimen after not seeing any drop in GFRs. With Trikafta, FEV1 levels increased, exacerbations ceased, and cough and sputum production resolved. Our patient is still on treatment.

Patient 3: A 34-year-old female with G85E and 1811+1.6kbA>G mutations was diagnosed at 11 months old. In 2018, when she was 27 years old, she was put on the waiting list for lung transplantation. She has received Trikafta in August 2021. She was able to use Trikafta for 3 weeks prior to the lung transplant. After the transplant, she was started on Tacrolimus and her GFRs began to drop. It was thought that the patient had persistent renal impairment resulting from immunosuppressive therapy, so the treatment was switched to Everolimus. Due to the patient's recurrent sinusitis, she was decided to reinstate Trikafta. Again, since there is no defined protocol on the dosage adjustment of Trikafta in patients with low GFRs and also with lung transplant, we started to administer Trikafta twice in every 3 days with close monitoring. There was no decrease in the GFRs so far, and we will be sharing the follow-up results.

Conclusion: While the renal dosage of modulator drugs remains unspecified, we have endeavored to monitor adverse effects in our patients through the implementation of adaptive regimens. The lack of renal adverse effects observed with Trikafta in three patients with chronic kidney disease indicates that such side effects are infrequent. Nevertheless, additional data is required to ascertain if modulator medications can be administered safely to patients with renal impairment.

records.title: Gamma secretase inhibition restores histologic and functional parameters of primary airway cultures of cystic fibrosis donors
records.authors_text: M. Milla1, I. Rebbapragada1, J. Edwards1, R. Rao1, C. Milla2
records.affiliations_text: 1Alentar Bioscience, Research and Development, Palo Alto, United States, 2Stanford University, Department of Pediatrics, Center of Excellence in Pulmonary Biology, Stanford, United States
records.abstract_text:
Cystic fibrosis (CF) airway pathology is marked by the presence of hypertrophic goblet cells as faithfully modeled in air-liquid interface (ALI) primary cultures from CF donors, exhibiting functional deficits in mucociliary clearance (reduced air surface liquid and particle transport velocity). The Notch pathway has been implicated in goblet cell hyperplasia and can be targeted with gamma-secretase inhibitors (GSIs), which abrogate its activation. We evaluated the activity of multiple GSIs for correction of those phenotypic defects.

Recombinant HEK293 cell cultures expressing reporter constructs for amyloid precursor protein (APP) or Notch were treated with 5 GSIs: DAPT, avagacestat, semagacestat, MK-0572, and RO4929097, followed by detection of APP/Notch cleavage. CF donor (ΔF508 homozygous) ALI cultures were treated for 2 weeks with those GSIs. Hypertrophic goblet cells and multiciliate cells were quantified, and functional readouts were also monitored: air surface liquid reabsorption, and mucociliary clearance (particle transport velocity). We performed single cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) of avagacestat or RO4929097-treated ALI cultures.

GSIs dramatically decreased hypertrophic goblet cell counts in CF ALI cultures and did not appear to be toxic even at the highest compound levels tested. The molecules promoted fluid retention at the apical surface and for avagacestat and RO4929097, increased the velocity of transport of microbeads through the apical surface. In general, GSIs exhibited balanced inhibitory potency against APP and Notch processing in recombinant cell-based assays. scRNAseq of GSI-treated ALI cultures derived from multiple CF donors with different CFTR mutations not only confirmed reductions in goblet cells but also indicated that this effect was independent of donor's CFTR mutation.

Our results suggest that GSIs may reprogram the CF airway epithelium to restore fluid homeostasis and mucociliary clearance regardless of the CFTR genetic lesion.

records.affiliations_text: 1Centre de Ressources et de Compétences de la Mucoviscidose Pédiatrique, Hôpital Femme Mère Enfant, Hospice Civils de Lyon, Bron, France, 2Laboratoire de Biologie Médicale Multi-Sites (LBMMS), Service de Biochimie et Biologie Moléculaire Grand Est, Hospices Civils de Lyon, Bron, France, 3Université de Lyon, Université Lyon 1, CNRS, Laboratoire de Biométrie et Biologie Evolutive UMR 5558, Equipe EMET, Villeurbanne, France
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Clinical and functional response to elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) is heterogeneous in children with cystic fibrosis (CF). We analyzed if the number of ETI-responsive CFTR variant could predict sweat chloride concentration (SCC) and lung clearance index (LCI) evolution in children treated with ETI, using real-world data.

Methods: SCC and LCI evolution were collected in children with CF in our local pediatric center before and during their first year of treatment by ETI. Data included children without F508del treated by ETI off-label thanks to the French compassionate program. CFTR variant responsiveness to ETI was determined using the program’s classification.

Results: Among 201 children included, 131 carried two ETI-responsive CFTR variants and 70 carried only one. 26% started ETI before 6 years of age and 34% between 6 and 12 years. 49% received CFTR modulators prior to ETI. Median SCC under ETI was 25 mmol/L (IQR 16-38) in children with two ETI-responsive CFTR variants and 36 mmol/L (27-51) in those with only one (p<0.0001). Multivariable analyses showed that number of ETI-responsive CFTR variant and age at ETI initiation were predictive factors of SCC in children treated by ETI (p=0.01 and p=0.0006 respectively). records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) has significantly improved quality of life for people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). As shown in culture- and sequencing-based studies of pwCF 12 years and older, ETI decreases the abundance of typical CF pathogens in the airways. For three years, ETI has also been available for children with CF aged 6-11 years. To investigate the impact of early ETI treatment on the airway microbiome our study employs shotgun metagenomics for high resolution identification of bacteria, fungi and DNA viruses.

Methods: In this prospective post-approval study, cough swabs from n=15 cwCF aged 6-11 years at baseline, 3 months and 24 months after initiation of ETI therapy were collected. DNA was extracted under ultra-clean wet-lab conditions, followed by metagenome sequencing. Fragment libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq. Processing of the sequencing reads was performed by our in-house developed sequencing pipeline Wochenende prior to statistical analyses.

Results: In this prospective post-approval study, treatment with ETI improved CFTR function and clinical parameters in cwCF aged 6-11 years, similar to published studies. With respect to airway microbiology, microbial α-diversity remained unchanged throughout ETI therapy. However, the high resolution of metagenomics permitted us to identify age as a central factor influencing the abundance of several commensal taxa. During the course of our study, we did not detect colonization with Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Staphylococcus aureus occurred only at low abundance in six of 15 baseline samples and in two of 13 samples at month 3 but was absent from the two-year follow-up time point.

Conclusion: Metagenomic profiles appeared to be more strongly influenced by age than by ETI treatment status, suggesting that, in this age group, inter-individual variability and developmental factors may play a more dominant role in shaping the respiratory microbiome than therapeutic intervention(s).

records.title: Pancreatic pain resolved by elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor, psychologic complications resolved by vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor - 12year-old patient genotype N1303K/3849+10kbC>T - A case report

session.title: Workshop 18 - Complex psychosocial issues/nursing case studies

records.authors_text: V. Greiner1,2, G. Dunay1,2,3, S. Lindstedt-Wolter2,3, C. Zagoya1,2, P. Sadrieh1,2, J.G. Mainz1,2
records.affiliations_text: 1CF-Center Klinikum Westbrandenburg, Brandenburg an der Havel, Germany, 2Medizinische Hochschule Brandenburg , Universitätsklinikum, Brandenburg an der Havel, Germany, 3Pediatric Gastroenterology, Universitätsklinikum, Brandenburg an der Havel, Germany
records.abstract_text:
Background: Psychologic side effects in people with CF (pwCF) receiving elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) are rare, albeit they have been reported. Recently, the new triple therapy with vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor (VTD) was approved for pwCF with at least one non-class-1-mutation. It is highly relevant to see whether similar VTD-related neuropsychological effects may emerge.

Discussion: We report on a 12-year-old male pwCF with primary exocrine pancreatic sufficiency carrying both class-2 and class-5 CFTR mutations. Thriving regularly without pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy, since 2024 he reported periods of increasingly severe acute abdominal pain associated with moderate increases in serum lipase and a decline of fecal pancreatic elastase. The recurrent pain combined with pain-induced panic attacks, required repeated inpatient treatment and pain control with opioids.

Nevertheless, MRI and ultrasound imaging only revealed non-severe pathologies, including minimal liver abnormalities. Upper GI endoscopy revealed a small ulcus, and colonoscopy showed an abnormal sigma-rotation, which did not explain the severity of his symptoms.

In November 2024, he started treatment with ETI, which substantially improved his abdominal symptoms. However, severe psychological distress resulted, including suicidal thoughts, necessitating a pause of ETI therapy. Under continuous psychological therapy, ETI then was reintroduced but administered only once a week in order to control abdominal symptoms while avoiding psychological decompensation.

In October 2025, the patient transitioned to therapy with VTD, and a relief of abdominal symptoms, normalization of serum-lipase and fecal elastase have been achieved. Notably, he has since remained free of psychological symptoms, even while receiving full-dose VTD.

Conclusion: In the reported case, the switch from ETI to VTD resulted in the relief of pancreatic pain, without the psychological side effects related to previous ETI therapy.

person.biography:
Dr. Sharon Weinberg is a senior registrar in respiratory and general internal medicine based in Manchester, UK, and a clinical research fellow within the Pulse CF Hub at the University of Manchester, supervised by Professor Alex Horsley.
She graduated from New York University with a BA, followed by an MBBS from St George’s, University of London. She has trained internationally, including in Cyprus and Israel, before moving to the UK, where she is completing her specialist training in respiratory and general internal medicine in the North West of England. She has also completed a specialist fellowship at the National Aspergillosis Centre in Manchester.
Her work centres on cystic fibrosis, with a particular emphasis on pulmonary exacerbations and their role in disease progression. Dr. Weinberg is actively involved in the design and coordination of major clinical research studies at the Manchester Adult Cystic Fibrosis Centre, including the CF-Tracker and Unified-CF projects.
She is currently undertaking a PhD investigating the impact of environmental pollution, viral infections, and treatment adherence on pulmonary exacerbations in cystic fibrosis. Her research aims to identify modifiable risk factors and inform preventative strategies to improve long-term outcomes for people living with the condition.

person.biography:
I am working as the director of the CF Center in the Clinic Ernst von Bergmann and as the Dean of the HMU University in Potsdam, Dusseldorf and Munich, Germany. The focus of our research group is inflammation and infections in pwCF. We studied the immune response in fungal infections over the last years. We also studied within the ECFS Fungal Pathogens working group the diagnostic approaches as well as therapeutic options in ABPA. Furthermore, we supported with our CF team an educational Programm in the Ukraine to support CF Centers in Lviv and Kiew over several months. Currently we focus on home monitoring of pwCF to enable an easier monitoring for the patients within a study with the German CF Foundation.
I am happy to serve as a board member of the ECFS now for 4 years and support the CF community with my experiences.

person.biography:
Frank Bodewes (born February 14, 1966, Eelde, The Netherlands) is Head of the Department of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Hepatology at the University Medical Center Groningen (UMCG).
Research focus
Effects of CFTR modulators on cystic fibrosis–related hepatobiliary disease (CFHBI)
Impact of CFTR modulators on gastrointestinal function in cystic fibrosis
Career
Dr. Bodewes obtained his MD from the University of Groningen in 1994 and completed his medical training in several hospitals across the Netherlands. Since 2005, he has served as a pediatric gastroenterologist and hepatologist at UMCG, with a focus on pediatric hepatology, liver transplantation, and complex cystic fibrosis cases.
He received his PhD in 2014, with a thesis on the pathophysiology of cystic fibrosis–related liver disease.
Leadership and collaborations
Contributor to the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation guideline on CF-related liver disease
Participant in the ESPGHAN–NASPGHAN initiative on CFHBI classification
Academic impact
His research focuses on bile acid metabolism and hepatopancreatobiliary manifestations of cystic fibrosis, resulting in numerous peer-reviewed publications.

content.biography:
Frank Bodewes, born on February 14th, 1966, in Eelde, The Netherlands, is an experienced medical senior consultant specializing in pediatric gastroenterology, hepatology, and cystic fibrosis. After graduating with an M.D. from the Medical School of Groningen in 1994, Bodewes began an extensive residency, shaping his expertise in various Dutch hospitals. In 2005, he assumed the Senior Consultant Pediatric Gastroenterologist and Hepatologist role at the University Medical Center Groningen, focusing on pediatric hepatology and managing complex cystic fibrosis cases.
Earning his Ph.D. in 2014, Bodewes delved into the pathophysiology of cystic fibrosis-related liver disease, a topic on which he has since become a leading authority. His leadership extends beyond clinical practice as he chairs the Cystic Fibrosis and Pancreas Working Group of the European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology Hepatology and Nutrition (ESPGHAN). Notably, he has played a pivotal role in developing the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation guideline on CF-related liver disease and the ESPGHAN-NASPGHAN collaboration for a new CF Hepatic Biliary Involvement (CFHBI) classification.
Bodewes's commitment to his field is evident through his extensive research on bile acid metabolism and cystic fibrosis liver-pancreas gastrointestinal disease, culminating in numerous influential peer-reviewed publications. Awarded an ESPGHAN Network grant in 2020, his work is internationally recognized and respected. Frank Bodewes's career is dedicated to advancing medical knowledge and improving patient outcomes in pediatric gastroenterology and cystic fibrosis.

Margarida D. Amaral is Full Professor of Biochemistry/ Molecular Biology at the Faculty of Sciences, University of Lisboa (Portugal) and Group Leader at the BioISI - Biosystems & Integrative Sciences Institute (FCUL, Portugal). MDA is alumna of EMBL-European Molecular Biology Laboratory (2008-10; 2016) and of IGC - Gulbenkian Institute of Science (1983-1993). Member of EMBO – European Molecular Biology Organization and of the Portuguese Academy of Sciences and received multiple awards, among which the Pfizer-SCML Award for Basic Biomedical Research and the Annual Award of ECFS – European Cystic Fibrosis Society. She was a Visiting Researcher (2012-15) at UniCamp-University of Campinas (SP, Brazil) and since 2023 she has been teaching at the University of Shanghai (China).
Research: The Amaral lab has its major focus on the molecular mechanisms of the genetic disease Cystic Fibrosis (CF) and on translating this knowledge into the benefit of people with CF. To understand CF mechanisms globally we use transcriptomics, proteomics, and functional genomics, namely functional high-content siRNA screens. Recently, we are focussing on the CF pathways leading to cancer. Our results translate into the clinic for better CF diagnosis, prognosis, and personalized therapies. Mall is Professor and Chair of the Department of Pediatric Respiratory Medicine, Immunology & Critical Care Medicine and the Christiane Herzog Cystic Fibrosis Center at the Charité University Medical Center Berlin, Germany. Mall is Professor and Director of the Department of Pediatric Pulmonology, Immunology & Intensive Care Medicine and CF Center at the Charité – University Medical Center Berlin, Germany, and Professor at the Berlin Institute of Health (BIH). He graduated from the University of Freiburg Medical School and trained at the Universities of Freiburg and Heidelberg, Germany, and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, USA. Marcus Mall is board certified in Pediatrics, Pediatric Pulmonology, Allergy and Infectious Diseases. He is a Fellow of ERS (FERS), serves on the Editorial Board of the European Respiratory Journal (ERJ) and Program Planning Committee of the North American Cystic Fibrosis Conference (NACFC). In 2011, Marcus Mall was one of the founding directors of the German Center for Lung Research (DZL), where he continues to serve as coordinator of the CF research program. Marcus Mall’s research focus is on the pathogenesis and development of novel diagnostic approaches and therapeutic strategies for CF lung disease. His research team uses an interdisciplinary translational research strategy, integrating basic research in model systems with cohort studies and early phase clinical trials, to improve our understanding of CF lung disease and the translation of research results and novel therapies into the clinic.

Dr. Dilara Demirel is a pediatric pulmonologist and researcher at Hacettepe University Faculty of Medicine in Ankara, Türkiye. Her clinical and academic work focuses on cystic fibrosis, pediatric interstitial lung diseases, and the integration of immunological perspectives into respiratory medicine. She is actively involved in multidisciplinary patient care and translational research aimed at improving outcomes for children with chronic lung diseases.
Dr. Demirel has led and contributed to several clinical studies evaluating the safety and efficacy of CFTR modulator therapies, including their systemic and ophthalmologic effects. She has also participated in research on rare pediatric pulmonary conditions such as pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis, contributing to case series and collaborative publications. Her work emphasizes real-world clinical data and patient-centered approaches to care.
She completed a clinical observership at Hannover Medical School (MHH), Germany, where she gained experience in advanced pediatric pulmonology practices, including bronchoscopy, mechanical ventilation, and lung transplantation. Dr. Demirel is an active member of the European Cystic Fibrosis Society (ECFS) Telehealth Working Group, contributing to initiatives that explore digital health solutions and telemedicine in cystic fibrosis care.
Her accomplishments include presentations at international conferences, collaboration in multidisciplinary research projects, and the development of ethically approved clinical studies. Dr. Demirel remains committed to advancing pediatric respiratory medicine through innovation, collaboration, and academic excellence. She is happily married with a beautiful daughter and four cats. That's her most important achievement.

person.biography:
Emmanuelle Brochiero is a Professor in the department of Medicine of the Université de Montréal and researcher at the Centre de Recherche du CHUM (CRCHUM).
Her research focuses on the pathophysiology of lung diseases, especially cystic fibrosis, acute respiratory distress syndrome and primary graft dysfunction after lung transplantation. Her lab has pioneered ion channel-based therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring functional epithelial integrity in damaged lungs, using complementary state-of-the-art approaches, rare human samples, animal models and innovative preclinical models. The main goal of her projects in cystic fibrosis is to develop innovative therapeutic strategies for improvement of CFTR-targeted treatments and restoration of airway epithelial integrity in infected lungs from patients carrying various types of mutations.
Over the past years, Dr. Brochiero has been supported by research grants including from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR), the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC), the Respiratory Health Network of Québec, the Canadian National Transplant Research Program, and the Association Vaincre le Mucoviscidose.
She is the Director of the Respiratory Tissue and Cell Biobank of CRCHUM. Based on her expertise, she has also been invited to chair the Advisory and Scientific Committee of the Respiratory Health Research Network (RHN) of Québec as well as the CF Strategic Group, and then the research axis on pulmonary infections and pathogens of RHN. She also led the Immunopathology research theme of the CRCHUM over the past five years.

She is a recipient of the CF Foundation Program for Adult Care Excellence award. Dr. Albon published multiple manuscripts related to telehealth (TH) delivery in the Cystic Fibrosis clinic. She co-led the Cystic Fibrosis Learning Network Telehealth iLab with Dr. Powers and researched the impact of the TH implementation on patient outcomes.

person.biography:
I am a London-based Paediatric Respiratory GRID Trainee currently taking time out of training as a Clinical Research Fellow to undertake a PhD at Imperial College London. My PhD is investigating novel infection detection and sampling techniques in Cystic Fibrosis (CF). This has involved setting up the 'Precision Partners Platform Study' (P3), part of the CF Trust and LifeArc funded Precision-CF Innovation Hub. P3 is a multi-centre, multi-sample type approach to establish alternatives to sputum culture for detecting lung infections, and to better understand host/microbe interactions. We aim to recruit up to 850 people with CF, chronic suppurative lung disease and healthy volunteers over 5 years.
Alongside my research, I continue clinical work as a Paediatric Respiratory Registrar at the Royal Brompton Hospital, undertaking a General Respiratory clinic and CF clinic each week.
I have previously worked as a Cystic Fibrosis Clinical Trials Fellow at the Royal Brompton Hospital between 2021-2022 which involved working on multiple commercial and academic clinical trials, recruiting both adults and children with CF.

person.biography: Dr. Hettie Janssens works as a pediatric pulmonologist in the Erasmus Medical Center- Sophia Children's hospital, where she is leading the CF-center since 2009. Her research is focused on monitoring early CF-lung disease in children. She aims to develop minimally invasive techniques to monitor infants with CF and is collaborating with partners nationally and internationally. Furthermore, she is an expert in inhalation therapy and wrote many guidelines and chapters on this subject. She is a member of the ECFS-CTN Executive committee, a member of the steering committee of the ECFS congress and chair of the Dutch pediatric CF working group.

person.biography:
Patrick Flume is a Distinguished Professor of Medicine and Pediatrics at the Medical University of South Carolina.  He serves as the Powers-Huggins Endowed Chair for Cystic Fibrosis and oversees the largest adult CF program in South Carolina.  He also leads large clinical programs dedicated to patients with bronchiectasis and non-tuberculous mycobacterial (NTM) infections.
 
He is recognized by the national and international CF community having served on the CF Foundation Center Committee, the Adult Care Consensus Committee, and the Advisory Task Force on Adult Issues, the Professional Education Committee, the European CF Society’s Best Practices committee, and as founding co-chair of the CF Foundation’s Pulmonary Practice Guidelines Committee.  He co-led the International Working Group on Antimicrobial Resistance in Cystic Fibrosis.  He is the Editor-in-Chief for the Journal of Cystic Fibrosis.

person.biography:
Prof Davies works between the National Heart & Lung Institute, Imperial College London and the Royal Brompton Hospital, London, UK. Jane trained in paediatric respiratory medicine, with additional posts in infectious diseases and immunology, before settling on cystic fibrosis as a speciality. The Brompton clinic is one of the largest in Europe, caring for almost 900 people from infancy to late stage disease.
Her main areas of research interest are chronic lung infection and clinical trial design. She leads a UK CF Trust funded Strategic Research Centre for Pseudomonas, a multidisciplinary group seeking to improve detection, understanding and therapy of this prevalent organism. She advises many of the pharma companies developing CF drugs on trial design, co-leads the site’s trials team and established a pan-London network of CF trial sites under the umbrella of the UK’s Clinical Trials Accelerator Platform. The team has participated in many CF drug trials ranging from gene therapy, CFTR modulators to mucolytics and antimicrobials. She directs the ECFS Core Facility for Lung Clearance Index, which is supporting standardised procedures across sites, providing trials in younger, healthier children with a sensitive outcome measure, and is also closely involved in the ECFS Strategic Planning Task Force to speed up access to new therapies.
She is current President of the ECFS.
